response:
Henry Tolliver came home from the colored graded school at a quarter past five, which was his invariable hour. He was a man who believed that a regular life was the outward sign of a well-ordered mind, and he had preached that doctrine so long to the boys and girls under his charge that he had come in time to practise it himself. He was perhaps thirty-five years of age, of a complexion which the census-taker, after a moment's hesitation, had set down as "black," and which his friends more charitably described as a rich brown. He was tall, a little stooped from much bending over slates and copy-books, and his face, which was not handsome, had that look of patient intelligence which is sometimes found in men who have been compelled to win by merit what others receive by favor.

His house stood on the upper side of Front Street, in that quarter of the town of Clarendon where the better class of colored people had built their homes since the war. It was a neat cottage of five rooms, painted white, with green blinds and a little porch overgrown with a climbing rose, and it represented eight years of saving and self-denial. Henry was justly proud of it, and he never opened the gate without a certain quiet satisfaction, as a man might feel who has made a fortress of his own against a world not over-friendly.

On this particular afternoon, however, the satisfaction was absent. He had been aware for three days that something was amiss in his household, and he had borne the knowledge with the forbearance of a man who knows that women, like the weather, are not to be hurried. But forbearance has its limits, even in a schoolmaster; and as he hung his hat upon the rack in the narrow hall and heard no light step coming to meet him, he resolved that the matter should be brought to an issue before he slept.

He found his wife in the little parlor, seated by the window with a piece of needlework in her lap, at which she was not working. Marian Tolliver was some six years younger than her husband, and so fair that strangers in the town, seeing her upon the street, were frequently at a loss to account for her presence in that neighborhood. Her hair was brown and soft, her eyes gray, and her features of that regular cast which the novelists are fond of calling patrician, and which, in the South of that day, was more often the token of an irregular descent. It was known in Clarendon, though it was not much spoken of, that she was the daughter of Colonel Edmund Revel of Revel Hall, in the adjoining county, by a woman who had been his housekeeper; that the colonel had educated the girl at a Northern seminary, and had afterward, upon his marriage with a lady of his own station, settled a small sum upon the mother and dismissed both from his life with the decent completeness of a gentleman closing an account. The mother had died some years since. The colonel, as the newspapers had announced with suitable expressions of regret, had died a fortnight ago.

"You are home early, Henry," said Marian, looking up.

"I am home at my usual hour," he replied, seating himself opposite her. "It is you, I think, who have lost count of the time."

She made no answer, but bent over her work, and drew a thread through with unnecessary care. Henry watched her for a moment in silence. He was not a man of quick speech, and he was accustomed to arrange his thoughts before he uttered them, as he would have arranged a lesson in arithmetic.

"Marian," he said at length, "you received a letter on Monday. I saw it on the hall table before you took it up. It bore a Richmond postmark, and it was addressed in a lawyer's hand. You have not mentioned it to me, and you have not been yourself since it came. I do not ask to read your letters. But I think I have a right to know what it is that has come between us."

"Nothing has come between us," she said quickly.

"Then something is standing very near," he returned, "for I can feel the shadow of it."

She laid down her needlework, rose, and went to the little writing-desk in the corner, which had been his wedding gift to her. From one of the pigeon-holes she took a long envelope, and, after a moment's hesitation, placed it in his hands. Then she returned to the window and stood looking out into the street, where the long shadows of the elms were stretching across the dust.

Henry unfolded the letter and read it slowly, as he read everything. It was written upon heavy paper, and it was couched in that elaborate and careful phraseology by which the legal profession contrives to say disagreeable things without seeming to say anything at all. It informed Mrs. Marian Tolliver that the writer, Mr. Archibald Pettigrew, attorney-at-law, had the honor to act for the estate of the late Colonel Edmund Revel; that the said colonel, by a codicil executed some months before his death, had bequeathed to his natural daughter, Marian, the sum of eight thousand dollars, the same to be paid to her in four annual instalments; that the bequest was, however, subject to certain conditions, which the writer was instructed to communicate. These conditions were, in brief, that the legatee should remove, within six months, to some place north of the Ohio River, at a distance of not less than five hundred miles from the county of her birth; that she should there assume such name as she might choose, other than that of Revel; and that she should "sever, completely and permanently, every tie of association connecting her with the colored race, to which the testator, in his affection for her, did not wish her to be held to belong." In the event of her compliance, the writer would be happy to assist her in every way consistent with his duty. In the event of her refusal, the bequest would lapse, and the sum would be applied to the endowment of a chapel in the parish church at Revelton, in the testator's memory.

Henry read the letter through twice. Then he folded it and laid it on the table beside him, and sat for some time without speaking. When he looked up, his wife had turned from the window and was watching him.

"Well?" she said.

"It is a handsome sum," he answered quietly. "Your father was a generous man, after his fashion."

"His fashion!" she cried, with a little catch in her voice. "Is that all you have to say?"

"What would you have me say, Marian? The letter is addressed to you, not to me. I observe that I am not mentioned in it, except by implication. I am one of the ties of association."

She flushed scarlet, and then grew pale.

"You need not put it so," she said.

"How else should I put it? The colonel was a man of exact mind, and his lawyer is a man of exact words. 'Every tie of association connecting her with the colored race.' I am the closest of those ties, I take it, unless the law of the State of North Carolina has been changed without my knowledge."

There was a silence. Outside, a wagon rattled past, and the voice of old Aunt Peggy Lane, who did washing for half the street, was heard calling to her grandson.

"Jim! You Jim! Come 'long heah wid dat basket 'fo' I wears you out! Ain' got no mo' sense dan a June-bug, dat boy ain'!"

The interruption seemed to break the tension, and Marian came and sat down again in her chair, her hands clasped in her lap.

"Henry," she said, "I have not answered the letter. I have not decided anything. I only wished to think before I spoke to you, for I knew how you would take it."

"And how is that?"

"As you are taking it now—coldly, as if it were a question of right and wrong, and nothing else. You do not consider what it means."

"I consider that it means eight thousand dollars," he said, "and a new name, and a new life, among people who will never know that you were once the wife of a colored schoolmaster in a little Southern town. I consider that it means you would be free of all that you have borne since you married me—the slights in the shops, the Jim Crow car, the women who stare at you on the street and whisper behind their hands, wondering what such a lady can be doing among such people. I have considered all these things, Marian, for three days, while you were considering them in silence. I am not so cold as you suppose."

His voice had grown unsteady toward the end, and she looked at him with a sudden softening.

"You know that I have never complained," she said.

"No, you have never complained. That is what has made it the harder to bear."

She was silent for a moment, and when she spoke again it was in a lower tone.

"You do not know what it is, Henry. You cannot know. You were born to it; you have never been anything else. But I—I was brought up in a white school, among white girls, who thought I was one of themselves. I learned their ways and their thoughts; I read their books and dreamed their dreams. And then I came home, and found that the world had a place for me already marked out, and that it was not the place I had been taught to expect. Do you suppose I have forgotten what that was? When I married you, I chose my side, and I have never regretted it. But sometimes, when I see a white woman go into a door that is shut to me, and know that there is no difference between us but a word in a book that nobody can read—"

She stopped, and pressed her handkerchief to her lips.

Henry rose and walked twice across the little room. It was a habit he had when a pupil gave an answer that was both right and wrong, and he wished to find the point of error without wounding the scholar.

"Marian," he said, stopping before her, "I have never asked you to pretend that you are other than you are. I knew when I married you that you might have married otherwise, and I have always counted it the greatest honor of my life that you chose me. But I will not stand in your way now. If you wish to go, you shall go. I will not hold you by any claim of law or of sentiment. The law, indeed, would scarcely trouble itself on my behalf; and as for sentiment—" he smiled a little bitterly—"I have heard it said that sentiment is a luxury of the well-to-do."

"Do you mean," she said slowly, "that you would let me go—that you would consent?"

"I mean that I would not prevent you. Consent is another matter."

"And you would remain here?"

"Where else should I go? My work is here. My people are here. The colonel's lawyer has not offered me a new name, nor would it be of much service to me if he did. A man may change his name, Marian, but he cannot change his face, and mine has been very clearly labelled by Providence."

There was a touch of his old dry humor in the words, and she looked up at him with something between a smile and a sob.

"You are making it very hard for me," she said.

"I am trying to make it easy," he answered. "That is perhaps why it is hard."

She sat for a long time without answering, looking down at her clasped hands. Henry resumed his seat and waited. He had learned, in his profession, that the most important part of a lesson is often the silence which follows it, when the mind of the learner is left to work upon what it has received.

"I will tell you what I have been thinking," she said at last. "I have thought that it would be easy. I have pictured myself in some city of the North—in Cleveland, perhaps, or Philadelphia—with a little house of my own, and friends who would never ask me any questions, and nothing to remind me of all this. I have thought how pleasant it would be to go where I liked, and sit where I liked, and never feel that cold look upon me. I have even thought," she went on, with an effort, "that you would be better without me—that I have been a burden to you, and that people have said you married above yourself, and that it has hurt you among your own people."

"It has not hurt me," he said.

"It has, Henry. I have heard them. Mrs. Barrow said at the church supper that you were 'too high-toned to marry in your own color,' and I saw your face when it was repeated to you. Do not deny it."

He did not deny it.

"And then," she continued, "I thought of what it would really be. I thought of living always in fear—fear that someone from the South would come and know me, fear that some letter would be opened, some old acquaintance met in the street. I thought of making friends and never daring to tell them the truth; of hearing them talk about 'darkies' and 'niggers' at the dinner-table, and laughing with them, as I should have to laugh. I thought of my mother, who is buried in the colored cemetery out on the Wilmington road, and that I could never go to her grave again. And I thought of you, Henry—here, in this house, alone—going to school at eight o'clock and coming home at a quarter past five, and no one to meet you at the door."

Her voice broke, and she covered her face with her hands.

Henry sat very still. A man of more impulsive temper would have gone to her at once; but he had a certain fine reticence which made him unwilling to claim a victory until it had been freely yielded.

"And what conclusion have you reached?" he asked, gently.

She lowered her hands and looked at him with wet eyes.

"I have reached the conclusion that my father was a cruel man," she said. "He gave me his blood and his features, and he took away my birthright. He educated me to be a lady, and then he left me to be a servant's child. And now that he is dead, he would buy from me the only things I have that are truly my own—my husband, and my mother's memory, and my self-respect. He thought he was being kind. I suppose he even thought he was being generous. Eight thousand dollars! It is a great deal of money, Henry, and we have so little. But I think I should feel, every time I spent a dollar of it, that I was spending a piece of my own soul."

She rose, and taking the letter from the table, held it for a moment in her hand.

"Will you get me a match?" she said.

Henry went to the mantel and took one from the little china box that stood there. But instead of handing it to her, he paused, and drew from the inner pocket of his coat a folded sheet of paper.

"Before you burn that," he said, "you had better burn this also. I wrote it last night, when you were asleep."

She took it from him wonderingly and unfolded it. It was written in his own careful, schoolmaster's hand, and it was addressed to Mr. Archibald Pettigrew, attorney-at-law, of Richmond, Virginia. It stated, in language as formal as the lawyer's own, that the undersigned, Henry Clay Tolliver, being informed of the conditions attached to the bequest of the late Colonel Revel to his wife, desired to remove any obstacle which his existence might present to her compliance therewith; that he would interpose no objection to any proceedings she might institute for the dissolution of their marriage, upon whatever ground the law might allow; and that he would hold himself at Mr. Pettigrew's disposal for the execution of any papers that might be required.

Marian read it to the end, and then looked up at her husband with an expression which he never afterward forgot.

"You would have sent this?" she whispered.

"If you had wished it."

"Without a word to me?"

"I would have given it to you, and let you send it, or not, as you chose. I did not wish you to feel that you must stay for my sake. A woman who stays from pity is a heavier burden than a woman who goes from choice."

She stood for a moment looking at him; and then she struck the match herself, upon the rough edge of the mantel, and held the two papers together in the flame. They curled and blackened, and the lawyer's heavy paper burned more slowly than the schoolmaster's thin sheet, so that for a little while the words "every tie of association" stood out in brown letters upon the charred surface before they too crumbled into ash. She dropped the last fragment into the empty grate and watched it until it was quite consumed.

"There," she said, turning to him. "Now there is nothing standing near."

Henry took her hands in his, and for once in his life he did not stop to arrange his thoughts before he spoke; which was perhaps the reason that what he said has not been recorded.

It may be added, for the benefit of those who like to follow the fortunes of property, that the chapel at Revelton was duly built, of good red brick with a slate roof, and that a handsome tablet was placed in it to the memory of Colonel Edmund Revel, "a just man, a kind master, and a lover of his kind." The rector, in his dedicatory sermon, dwelt with much feeling upon the colonel's well-known benevolence toward the colored people of the county; and it is said that several of them, who sat in the gallery reserved for their use, were visibly affected. Among these, however, was not Mrs. Henry Tolliver, who had not been invited, and who was, in any case, engaged that afternoon in hearing a class of small boys recite the multiplication table, in the absence of her husband, who was ill with a cold.

response:
The town of Dunmore, in the county of Cumberland, had not changed greatly in the twenty years since Hamilton Merrill had last set foot upon its sandy streets, though it had changed enough to trouble the heart of a man who had carried away with him, through two decades of absence, a picture of it which he had no wish to see disturbed. The railroad had come, to be sure, and with it a brick depot of somewhat pretentious design, which stood at the foot of the main street like a stranger who has arrived too early for a party and does not know quite what to do with himself. The market-house, with its clock that had never in the memory of man told the correct time, still occupied the square, and beneath its arches the same idle figures, or others so like them as to make no difference, lounged and whittled and discussed the price of cotton and the iniquities of the revenue officers. But the old tavern was gone, and a cotton-mill had been erected by the river, and a row of cottages for the operatives straggled along the bluff where once the boys of the town had gathered chinquapins and fought their mimic battles of the late war.

Mr. Merrill was a man of perhaps forty years, of good figure and erect carriage, with a complexion which the casual observer would have described as somewhat sallow, and which a more curious one might have attributed to a residence in the tropics, or to an inheritance from some remote Latin ancestor. His hair, which was dark and slightly inclined to wave, was cut close in the fashion of the day; his mustache was carefully trimmed; and his clothing, of a quiet gray, bore the unmistakable stamp of a good tailor in a Northern city. He carried a leather bag in one hand and a light cane in the other, and he stepped down from the train with the air of one who is accustomed to being waited upon, and who does not expect to be disappointed.

He had not, however, sent word of his coming to any one in Dunmore, and he was therefore surprised, and not altogether pleasantly, when a voice addressed him from the end of the platform.

"Ham! Ham Merrill! Is it you, or am I dreamin'?"

The speaker was a man of about Mr. Merrill's own age, though he looked somewhat older, being a little bent in the shoulders, as men become who have labored much with their hands. He was of a brown complexion, several shades darker than the traveler's, and his features, though regular and pleasing, bore more plainly the impress of that race which, in the Southern States at least, is held to be determined not by what a man looks like, but by what his grandmother was. He wore a suit of black broadcloth, much worn but scrupulously brushed, and he held in his hand a hat which he had evidently snatched from his head in the first excitement of recognition.

Mr. Merrill's first impulse, it must be confessed, was to glance about him. There were upon the platform at that moment two or three white men, a baggage-master, and a young woman with a parasol, and none of them, so far as he could perceive, was paying the slightest attention to him. He felt the blood come into his face, and was ashamed of it, and was ashamed of being ashamed; and in the confusion of these several emotions he put out his hand with rather more warmth than he had intended.

"Tom," he said. "Tom Dabney. Upon my word."

"It's me, sho' enough," said the other, wringing the extended hand with a grip that made its owner wince. "I was down here to see about a box of goods that was to come on this train, an' I seen you step off, an' I says to myself, 'That's Ham, or else it's his ghost.' An' then I says, 'Ham ain't dead, 'cause I'd 'a' heard of it.' An' so I knowed it must be you."

It may be remarked, for the benefit of those who are unfamiliar with the social customs of that region, that the relations between Thomas Dabney and Hamilton Merrill were those of first cousins, their mothers having been sisters, and both of them the daughters of one Nancy Merrill, a free woman of color, who had kept a cake-shop in Dunmore in the days before the war, and had acquired by her industry a small house and lot on Pigeon Street, together with a reputation for piety and plain speaking that had survived her by many years. The two boys had been reared almost as brothers, had attended together the little school which a Northern lady had opened in the basement of the African church after the surrender, had fished together in the mill-pond, and had stolen watermelons together from the patch of old Judge Halsey, who knew perfectly well who took them, and was wise enough to say nothing. When Hamilton, at the age of nineteen, had gone North to seek his fortune, it was Thomas who had walked with him to the stage-coach, for there was no railroad then, and had pressed into his hand a five-dollar gold piece which represented the savings of a twelvemonth.

That gold piece had never been repaid. Mr. Merrill remembered it now with a pang, and resolved that it should be repaid, with interest, before he left the town.

"You'll come home with me," said Thomas, when the box of goods had been located and consigned to a dray. "Mary'll never forgive me if I let you go to the hotel. Besides," he added, with a certain hesitation, and a glance at his cousin's clothing, "I reckon the hotel wouldn't—that is to say—"

He did not finish the sentence, and Mr. Merrill did not ask him to. Both men understood perfectly well what was meant, and both understood, moreover, that the matter was not quite so simple as it would have been twenty years before. For it was entirely within the power of Hamilton Merrill to walk into the Dunmore Hotel, write his name upon the register, and be shown to the best room in the house, provided only that no one recognized him; and it was entirely certain that, if he did so in the company of his cousin, he would be shown nowhere at all.

"I shall be very glad to come," he said.

They walked up the main street together, past the market-house, where one of the loungers looked up and stared for a moment, and then returned to his whittling; past the court-house, where Mr. Merrill had once seen a man sold for debt, and where he now observed a notice of the next term of the Superior Court; past the Presbyterian church, whose spire had been struck by lightning in his boyhood and had never been quite straight since; and so on into the quarter of the town where the colored people chiefly lived. And as they walked, Thomas talked, with the volubility of a man who has a great deal to say and has been saving it for a long time.

"You'd hardly know the old place, Ham. They've got a colored school now, with two teachers an' a principal, an' the town pays for it, or pays for part of it, anyhow. My oldest boy goes there. An' we've built a new church—brick, Ham, with a bell that come all the way from Baltimo'. I'm a deacon in it. You remember old Elder Pugh? He's gone to his reward, these ten years. An' Sis Patsy Lowery—you remember her, that used to give us ginger-cakes?—she's still livin', a hundred if she's a day, an' sharp as a tack. She'll know you, sho'. She knows everybody."

"And Aunt Viney?" asked Mr. Merrill. "Is she living?"

Thomas's face, which had been all animation, grew suddenly grave.

"Aunt Viney's livin'," he said. "She lives with us. She's mighty feeble, Ham, an' her mind wanders sometimes. But she talks about you. She talks about you a heap. Seem like the older she gets, the mo' she goes back to the old times."

Aunt Viney was the elder sister of their mothers, and the last surviving daughter of old Nancy Merrill. She had never married, having devoted her life, as she was fond of saying, to raising other folks' children; and in the hard years after the war, when the mothers of both boys had died within a twelvemonth of each other, it was Aunt Viney who had taken them in, fed them, clothed them, and switched them, impartially and with a liberal hand, whenever she thought they needed it. Mr. Merrill had written to her, at intervals growing longer as the years went on, and had sent her money at Christmas; but he had not written at all during the last five years, for reasons which seemed to him sufficient, and which he did not care to examine too closely.

The house of Thomas Dabney stood upon Pigeon Street, upon the very lot which old Nancy Merrill had purchased with the profits of her cake-shop. The original cabin had been enlarged by the addition of two rooms and a porch, and the whole had been painted white, with green blinds, and surrounded by a picket fence, within which grew a profusion of roses, hollyhocks, and four-o'clocks. A chinaberry-tree shaded the porch, and beneath it, in a split-bottomed rocking-chair, sat a very old woman, wrapped in a shawl despite the warmth of the afternoon, with her hands folded in her lap and her eyes fixed upon the street.

"Aunt Viney," said Thomas, opening the gate, "look who I done brung you."

The old woman turned her head slowly. Her face was wrinkled like a winter apple, and her eyes, though dim with age, had in them a certain piercing quality which Mr. Merrill remembered well, and which had been, in his boyhood, more effective in detecting falsehood than any process known to the law.

"Who dat?" she said. "Who dat wid you, Tom?"

"It's Ham, Aunt Viney. Ham Merrill. Come all the way f'om the No'th to see you."

The old woman looked at the visitor for a long moment, while he stood before her with his hat in his hand, feeling, for the first time in many years, like a small boy who has been caught in some misdemeanor and awaits sentence.

"Ham," she repeated. "Ham Merrill. Naw, suh. Dat ain' Ham. Ham's a little boy. Ham's down to de mill-pon' wid Tom, a-fishin', when dey oughter be in school. Dis heah's a w'ite gent'man."

Mr. Merrill knelt beside her chair and took one of her withered hands in his.

"It's Ham, Aunt Viney," he said. "I've grown up, that's all. I've been away a long time."

She peered into his face, and something in it seemed to reach her through the mists that clouded her mind; for her eyes filled with tears, and she laid her other hand upon his head, as she had done a thousand times when he was a child.

"Ham," she said. "Lawd, chile, is dat you? Is dat sho' 'nuff you? I knowed you'd come back. I tol' 'em you'd come back. Dey said you done forgot us, but I knowed better. Blood's thicker'n water, I tol' 'em. Ham ain' gwine fergit his own folks."

Mr. Merrill made no reply, for the very good reason that he could not trust his voice; and Thomas, with a delicacy for which his cousin was grateful, went into the house to summon his wife.

Mrs. Dabney proved to be a comely woman of thirty-five or thereabouts, with a pleasant voice and a bustling manner, who welcomed the visitor with a cordiality that was only slightly tempered by curiosity, and who immediately set about the preparation of a supper which, when it appeared upon the table an hour later, would have done credit to a much more pretentious establishment. There were fried chicken and hot biscuits, and sweet potatoes baked in the ashes, and collards cooked with a piece of side-meat, and a blackberry cobbler, and coffee such as Mr. Merrill had not tasted since he left the South. There were also four children, ranging in age from fourteen to six, who stared at the visitor with round eyes, and answered his questions in monosyllables, and were sent from the table in disgrace when the youngest inquired, in an audible whisper, whether Cousin Ham was a white man or a colored man.

"Children will be children," said Mr. Merrill, laughing; but he did not laugh very heartily, and Mrs. Dabney, who was a woman of perception, changed the subject.

It was not until the supper was over, and the children had been put to bed, and Aunt Viney had been helped to her room, and Mrs. Dabney had retired to the kitchen with the dishes, that the two cousins found themselves alone together upon the porch, with the moon rising over the chinaberry-tree, and the frogs singing in the branch at the foot of the street, and the scent of the four-o'clocks heavy upon the evening air.

For a while they smoked in silence, for Mr. Merrill had brought cigars, of a quality which Thomas had never before enjoyed, and which he puffed with a slow and reverent appreciation. Then Thomas spoke.

"You've done well, Ham," he said. "Anybody can see that."

"I have been fortunate," replied Mr. Merrill. "I went into the lumber business in Lakeport, as you know, and it has prospered. I have a share in a mill and some timber lands in Michigan. I am not a rich man, as riches are counted there, but I am comfortable."

"An' you're married, I reckon?"

There was a pause, of a length sufficient to be noticed.

"Yes," said Mr. Merrill. "I am married. I have two daughters."

"I'm glad to hear it," said Thomas heartily. "You must bring 'em down some time, so's Aunt Viney can see 'em befo' she dies. She'd set a heap of sto' by that."

Mr. Merrill flicked the ash from his cigar, and watched it fall upon the floor of the porch, where it glowed for a moment and went out.

"Tom," he said, "I don't think I can do that."

Thomas said nothing, but waited, as a man waits who already knows what he is about to hear, and would spare the speaker the pain of saying it, if he could.

"When I went to Lakeport," continued Mr. Merrill, speaking slowly, and with his eyes fixed upon the moon, "I meant no harm. I took a room at a boarding-house, and nobody asked me what I was, and I did not tell them. I got a place in a lumber-yard, and nobody asked me there, either. It did not seem necessary to tell. It did not seem to be anybody's business but my own. And then, after a while, it was too late to tell. I had friends who would have dropped me, and an employer who would have discharged me, and a position that I should have lost. And then I met—my wife. Her people are good people, Tom, plain people from New England, with no particular prejudices that they know of; but I could not tell her. I tried to, more than once. I could not. And so I did not. And now there are the girls. They do not know. They do not know that they have a cousin named Tom, or an aunt named Viney, or that their great-grandmother sold ginger-cakes in a little shop on Pigeon Street. They think my people were from Virginia, and that they are all dead."

He stopped, and there was a long silence, broken only by the frogs and by the clatter of dishes in the kitchen.

"I stopped writing to Aunt Viney," he said at length, in a lower tone, "because my wife found one of her letters, and asked me who she was. I told her she was an old servant of the family. God forgive me, Tom, I told her that."

Thomas Dabney did not answer at once. He was a man of no great learning, though he read his Bible diligently and could figure interest more accurately than the cashier of the Dunmore bank; but he possessed that native wisdom which is sometimes found in those who have been compelled to study human nature in order to survive it, and he knew that there are moments when silence is more eloquent than speech.

"Well, Ham," he said finally, "it ain't for me to judge you. I've thought about it myse'f, mo' times than one. When I was young, an' folks would push me off the sidewalk, or cuss me fur nothin', or cheat me out o' my wages an' laugh in my face when I complained, I used to think, 'If I was jes' a few shades lighter, I'd go off somewhar an' be white, an' never look back.' But I wasn't, an' so I couldn't, an' I reckon the Lawd knowed what He was doin'. I've got my house, an' my sto', an' my church, an' my wife an' chillen, an' I don't have to tell nobody no lies about who I am. That's somethin', Ham. It ain't much, maybe, to a man that's got a sawmill an' timber lands in Michigan; but it's somethin'."

"It is a great deal," said Mr. Merrill. "It is more than I have."

"I didn't mean it that way," said Thomas quickly.

"I know you didn't. But it is true, nevertheless."

They sat for some time longer, and talked of other things: of the old schoolmistress, Miss Haskell, who had gone back to Vermont and died there, and whose memory was still kept green by an annual exercise in the colored school; of the night the cotton-gin had burned, and the two boys had carried water until their arms ached, and had been rewarded by the owner with a silver quarter apiece; of the great freshet of '73, when the river had risen into the lower town, and they had rowed old Sis Patsy Lowery to safety in a dugout canoe, she protesting all the while that the Lord would not let her drown, and that if He did, it was His own business. They laughed together over these recollections, as men laugh who have shared the follies and adventures of youth; and for a little while it seemed to Mr. Merrill that the twenty years had rolled away, and that he was once more a barefoot boy upon Pigeon Street, with nothing to conceal and no one to deceive.

When at length they rose to go in, Mr. Merrill took from his pocketbook a gold piece of the denomination of twenty dollars, and pressed it into his cousin's hand.

"That is for the five dollars you gave me when I went away," he said. "I have owed it to you for twenty years."

Thomas looked at the coin for a moment in the moonlight, and then handed it back.

"Keep it, Ham," he said gently. "I didn't lend you that money. I give it to you. An' besides, you've paid it back a'ready."

"How so?"

"By comin' home," said Thomas. "Aunt Viney's been waitin' for you five years. You've made her happy. That's worth mo' than twenty dollars to me."

Mr. Merrill remained in Dunmore three days, during which he settled the small business that had ostensibly brought him thither, visited the grave of his mother in the colored cemetery, called upon Sis Patsy Lowery, who knew him at once and asked him why he had not brought his wife, and spent many hours upon the porch with Aunt Viney, who talked to him sometimes as a grown man and sometimes as a child, and who called him, upon the last afternoon, by the name of his grandfather, who had been dead for half a century.

On the morning of his departure Thomas walked with him to the depot, as he had once walked with him to the stage-coach. They shook hands upon the platform, and the white men who stood about looked at them curiously, and one of them said something to another, and laughed. Mr. Merrill heard the laugh, and for once he did not care.

"Write to Aunt Viney, Ham," said Thomas. "It don't matter what you say. Jes' write."

"I will write," said Mr. Merrill; and he kept his word, though whether he ever told his wife the truth concerning the old servant of the family, the present chronicler is not in a position to state.

As the train drew away from the station, he looked back and saw his cousin standing upon the platform, hat in hand, a plain brown man in a worn black coat, against the background of the little town that had given them both their being. And it occurred to Mr. Merrill, not for the first time in those three days, that of the two grandsons of Nancy Merrill, it was by no means certain which had made the better bargain with the world; and that the one who had kept his name and his kindred had perhaps carried away from the old house on Pigeon Street the larger share of the inheritance.

The town of Ashbury, in the old North State, had in the years following the war settled back into the ways of its fathers with a facility that would have surprised those who imagined that a great conflict must leave great changes behind it. The courthouse still stood in the square, its columns somewhat in need of paint; the market-house still sheltered on Saturdays the same assortment of countrymen, mules, and watermelons; and the color line, though it had been rubbed out by statute, had been redrawn by custom with a firmer hand than ever. There were persons in Ashbury, however, whom this line did not so much divide as perplex, and of these Mrs. Laura Tolliver was one.

Mrs. Tolliver was the widow of a man who had kept a respectable shoe shop on Front Street and who had left her, at his death, a modest frame house on a quiet lane near the edge of town, a small sum in the savings bank, and a son named Robert, who at the time of which we write was in his eighth year. She was a woman of perhaps thirty, of a complexion so fair that strangers passing her on the street not infrequently lifted their hats, and of a carriage so erect that those who knew her history sometimes said she held her head too high. She taught a class of colored children in the little school maintained by the Northern missionary society, and she was accounted, by those competent to judge, a woman of uncommon refinement and good sense.

The household was completed by Mrs. Tolliver's mother, a woman whom the neighborhood knew as Aunt Viney. She was as dark as her daughter was fair, the difference being one of those freaks of descent which the institution of slavery had multiplied beyond the power of the genealogist to follow. She had been born on a plantation in the eastern part of the county, had been hired out in her youth as a cook in Ashbury, and by twenty years of labor and economy, of which her master had taken the greater share, had at length purchased her own freedom some time before the war made such purchases unnecessary. She was now past sixty, a little bent, much given to the smoking of a clay pipe in the evening, and devoted, with a devotion that asked nothing in return, to her daughter and her daughter's child.

Robert, or Robbie, as he was called by everyone but his mother when she was displeased with him, had inherited his mother's complexion and his father's gray eyes, with a head of soft brown hair which curled at the ends and which his grandmother brushed every morning with a pride she made no effort to conceal. He was a bright child, quick at his letters, and possessed of that capacity for observation which in children is often mistaken for innocence, and which is in reality the very faculty by which they learn the world's injustice. Of this capacity the events of a certain afternoon in early autumn afforded a melancholy illustration.

It happened that a family named Pettigrew had lately taken the large house at the head of the lane, a house which had stood empty since the death of its former owner, and which the Pettigrews, who had come down from Raleigh, had repaired and painted with an energy that was the talk of the neighborhood. Judge Pettigrew had been appointed to the bench of the district, and his grandson, a boy of about Robbie's age, named Clarence, had come to live with him. Clarence, finding the lane deficient in companions of his own station, and observing Robbie at play in his front yard with a top and string, had come down to the fence and proposed a game of marbles. Neither boy had asked the other any questions which boys do not ordinarily ask, and Robbie, it must be confessed, had volunteered no information. The game had gone forward for the better part of an hour, under the shade of a chinaberry tree, with great satisfaction on both sides.

Mrs. Tolliver, who had come home early from the school, was sitting at the open window of the front room with a basket of mending in her lap. She had observed the beginning of the acquaintance with a misgiving which she would have found it difficult to put into words. She knew the Pettigrews by reputation; she knew the judge's opinions, which he had expressed on more than one public occasion with a candor that left nothing to the imagination; and she knew, too, what was likely to happen when the discovery was made which must sooner or later be made. But she had not the heart to call the boy in. He had so few playmates, and he seemed so happy, and there is in every mother's heart a little corner where hope lingers against all the evidence.

Toward five o'clock Aunt Viney came round the corner of the house from the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron, and stood at the edge of the yard.

"Robbie, honey," she called, "you come 'long in now an' wash yo' han's. Supper 'mos' ready, an' I done made you some o' dem fritters you lak so well."

Robbie looked up from the ring of marbles. Clarence looked up also, and regarded the old woman with the frank curiosity of childhood.

"Who's that old darky?" he asked.

There was a pause, not long, but long enough for a great deal to be decided in it. Mrs. Tolliver, at the window, laid down her needle and waited. Aunt Viney, at the corner of the house, stood quite still.

"Oh," said Robbie, gathering up his marbles with somewhat more attention than the operation required, "she's just an old woman that works for us."

Clarence accepted the explanation without remark, as one which accorded entirely with the natural order of things, and announced that he would come again to-morrow. He went off up the lane, whistling. Aunt Viney turned without a word and went back into the kitchen. Robbie, having put his marbles in his pocket, came up the steps of the front porch, and found his mother standing in the doorway.

"Robert," she said, "come into the parlor."

The child knew at once, from the use of his full name and from the quality of his mother's voice, that something was amiss; and he knew also, with that instinct which conscience supplies even to the very young, precisely what it was. He followed her into the little parlor, which was used only on Sundays and on solemn occasions, and which smelled faintly of the furniture polish with which Aunt Viney rubbed the horsehair sofa every Saturday. On the wall above the mantel hung a crayon portrait of his father, and beside it a framed certificate attesting that Laura Tolliver had completed with credit the course of study at a normal school in Pennsylvania. Mrs. Tolliver sat down in the rocking-chair by the window and motioned the boy to stand before her.

For some moments she did not speak. She was a woman who had learned, in a hard school, the value of governing her tongue, and she did not wish to say anything in anger which she might afterwards regret. Robbie stood with his hands behind him, looking at the pattern of the carpet, and the silence grew so heavy that he would have welcomed a whipping as a relief from it.

"Robert," she said at length, "who was it that called you in to supper just now?"

"Granny," said the boy, in a very small voice.

"And who is Granny?"

The child did not answer.

"I asked you a question, Robert. Who is she?"

"She's—she's your mother."

"Yes," said Mrs. Tolliver, "she is my mother. And what did you tell that little boy she was?"

Robbie's lip began to tremble, but he made a brave effort to justify himself, as older and wiser persons have done in like case.

"I didn't say anything that wasn't true, mamma. She does work for us. She cooks, and she washes, and she—"

"Stop," said his mother, and the boy stopped. "You are old enough, Robert, to know that a thing may be true in every word and yet be a lie altogether. Your grandmother works for us, it is true. She works for us because she loves us, and because she has worked all her life, and does not know how to be idle. But you did not say that to the little Pettigrew boy. You said it so that he would think she was a servant who had nothing to do with you; you said it because you were ashamed of her. Look at me, Robert. Is not that why you said it?"

The boy raised his eyes to his mother's face, and what he saw there was not anger, as he had expected, but something which frightened him a great deal more. He burst into tears.

Mrs. Tolliver did not take him in her arms, as her heart prompted her to do. She knew that the lesson, if it was to be learned at all, must be learned now, and that the world would teach him the contrary lesson soon enough and with a heavier hand. She let him cry for a little while, and then she spoke again, more gently, but with no less firmness.

"I am going to tell you something, Robert, and I want you to listen to every word, and remember it as long as you live. When your grandmother was a young woman, not much older than I am now, she did not belong to herself. She belonged to a man named Colonel Fairley, who lived out on the Cape Fear road; and he could sell her, or hire her out, or do with her whatever he pleased, and there was no law in this State to say him nay. He hired her out to cook for a family here in town, and he took for himself nearly all the money she earned. But they let her keep a little, and she took in washing at night, after her day's work was done, and she sat up many a night till the roosters crowed, with her hands in the suds and her back aching, and she put by every penny she could save. It took her eighteen years, Robert. Eighteen years, and she bought herself, and paid for herself with her own hands, and then she began all over again to save money to buy me."

The child had stopped crying and was listening with wide eyes.

"The war came before she had saved enough," Mrs. Tolliver went on, "and so I was set free with the rest. But she did not stop working. She kept on washing and cooking and saving, and when the Northern ladies opened the school, and said that I was quick enough to be sent away to be trained as a teacher, it was your grandmother who paid my fare to Pennsylvania, and sent me money every month for my board, and went without shoes herself one whole winter so that I might have a decent dress to wear among the white girls at the normal school. Everything I am, Robert, I owe to her. Everything you have—this house, the clothes on your back, the books you read, the very name you bear without shame—you owe to her as much as to me or to your father. And to-day, when a little boy whom you never saw before last week asked you who she was, you were ashamed to own her."

She paused, and the boy, who had the quick sensibilities of his mixed inheritance, felt the full weight of what she had said. He hung his head, and the tears came again, but they were tears of a different kind.

"I know why you did it," said his mother, and her voice trembled a little in spite of her. "You did it because you have eyes, and you have seen how things are in this town. You have seen that the people who look like Clarence Pettigrew live in the big houses and ride in the carriages, and that the people who look like your grandmother live in the cabins and carry the bundles. You have seen that a white skin is a passport, and a dark one is a badge; and you thought, with a child's cunning, that if you could keep the badge out of sight you might travel on the passport. I do not blame you for seeing these things, Robert. God knows they are plain enough to see. But I will not have you building your life on a lie, and least of all on a lie which denies the woman who gave you everything."

"I didn't mean to, mamma," sobbed the boy. "I didn't think. It just came out."

"That is what I am afraid of," said Mrs. Tolliver, "that it just came out. A thing that comes out so easily must have been waiting inside a long while. I want you to understand, Robert, that there may come a time, when you are a man, when you will have to choose between your grandmother's people and the people who would take you in only if you denied her. Some men in your position have made the one choice, and some the other. I cannot make it for you; but I can tell you that no man ever yet bought anything worth having at the price of his own mother's blood. And if you begin by denying her before a child in a dirt yard, for a game of marbles, what will you do when the stake is larger?"

The boy did not wholly understand this; but he understood enough, and the rest he would understand later, as children do, when the words came back to him out of the past at moments of trial.

Mrs. Tolliver rose from her chair.

"Now," she said, "you will go into the kitchen and tell your grandmother that you are sorry. You will tell her what you said and why you said it, and you will ask her to forgive you. I will not go with you. This is between you and her."

Robbie went slowly down the narrow hall, past the dining-room where the table was already laid for supper, and pushed open the door of the kitchen. Aunt Viney was standing at the stove with her back to him, turning the fritters in the skillet. The kitchen was warm and fragrant, and the late sun came in at the western window and fell across the scrubbed boards of the floor. She did not turn round when he came in, but he could see, from the set of her shoulders, that she knew who it was.

"Granny," he said.

"Yas, honey," said the old woman, still without turning.

"Granny, I'm sorry. I'm sorry for what I said to Clarence. I said you were just an old woman that worked for us, and I said it because—because I didn't want him to know you were my granny. Mamma says it was a lie, and it was. I'm sorry, Granny. Please forgive me."

Aunt Viney set the skillet back on the stove and turned round. Her face, which was seamed with a hundred fine wrinkles, was perfectly composed, but her eyes were wet. She wiped her hands deliberately upon her apron and sat down in the split-bottomed chair by the window.

"Come heah, chile," she said.

Robbie went to her, and she drew him between her knees and looked at him for a long moment.

"Lawd, honey," she said at last, "you ain' got no call ter cry lak dat. I ain' hol'in' nuffin' 'g'inst you. I knowed w'at you was gwine ter say 'fo' you said it. I 'lowed it 'u'd come some day, an' I'd ruther it come now, w'en you's little, dan latah, w'en you's growed an' it 'u'd hurt wuss. Yo' ma's a good 'oman, an' a smart 'oman, an' she knows w'at's right; but she don' know ez much ez I does 'bout how de worl' is. Dis is a hard worl' fer folks lak us, honey, an' it's a hard worl' fer folks lak you, w'at's half one thing an' half de yuther, an' don' rightly b'long nowhar. You's gwine ter be tempted mo' times dan you kin count."

She smoothed back the brown curls from his forehead with her rough hand.

"But I tells you w'at, chile," she went on, with a shrewd twinkle that belied the tears in her eyes, "dat little Pettigrew boy, he gwine fin' out who I is sooner er latah, 'caze dey ain' nuffin' in dis town dat stays hid fer long. His gran'pappy de jedge, he knows a'ready, sho' ez you bawn. Dey ain' a w'ite man in Ashbury dat don' know de pedigree er ev'y cullud fambly in de county better'n dey knows dey own. An' w'en dat chile fin's out, he gwine stop playin' marbles wid you, whether you owns me er whether you don'. So you see, honey, you'd 'a' sol' yo' ole granny fer nuffin' at all, an' dat's de wust kin' er bargain dey is. Ef you's gwine ter sell yo' folks, you mought ez well git a good price fer 'em; but I 'lows you ain' never gwine fin' no buyer dat'll pay what dey's wuth."

Robbie did not quite follow the irony of this observation, but he understood that he was forgiven, and he flung his arms round the old woman's neck and hid his face against her shoulder. Aunt Viney held him close, and over his head she looked out of the window at the big house at the head of the lane, where the new paint glistened white in the last of the sunlight.

"Now you run 'long an' wash yo' han's," she said presently, putting him away from her, "an' tell yo' ma supper's ready. Dem fritters done got col' w'iles we been talkin', but I reckon dey'll eat."

Mrs. Tolliver, who had remained in the parlor, heard the boy's footsteps in the hall and his voice calling her to supper, and she knew from the tone of it that the reconciliation had been effected. She sat for a moment longer in the rocking-chair, looking up at the crayon portrait of her husband, who had been nearly as fair as herself, and who had chosen, when he might have chosen otherwise, to cast in his lot with his mother's people. She wondered whether her son would have the strength to make the same choice when the time came; and she wondered, too, with a bitterness she did not often permit herself, by what right a world which had made the choice so hard should demand of a child of seven that he make it rightly.

It may be recorded, for the satisfaction of those who like to know the sequel of such matters, that Clarence Pettigrew did not come down the lane the next day, nor on any day thereafter. Whether some servant in the judge's household had enlightened him, or whether the judge himself, observing the direction of his grandson's rambles, had administered such instruction as he deemed suitable, was never known in the Tolliver household. Robbie watched for him at the fence for several afternoons, and then ceased to watch. He said nothing to his mother about it, nor she to him; but that evening, when Aunt Viney sat on the back step with her clay pipe, the boy came and sat down beside her, and leaned his head against her arm, and asked her to tell him again about Colonel Fairley and the eighteen years. And the old woman, who had told the story many times before to no one in particular, told it now to an audience that listened as if every word were being written down in a book that would one day be opened in judgment.

Candor compels the admission that it was not an impressive sheet in any respect, except when regarded as the first local effort of a struggling people to make public expression of their life and aspirations. From this point of view it did not speak at all badly for a class to whom, a generation before, newspapers, books, and learning had been forbidden fruit.

"It's an elegant specimen of journalism, isn't it?" laughed the general, airily. "Listen to this 'ad':— "'Kinky, curly hair made straight by one application of our specific. Our face bleach will turn the skin of a black or brown person four or five shades lighter, and of a mulatto perfectly white. When you get the color you wish, stop using the preparation.' "Just look at those heads!—'Before using' and 'After using.' We'd better hurry, or there'll be no negroes to disfranchise! If they don't stop till they get the color they desire, and the stuff works according to contract, they'll all be white. Ah! what have we here? This looks as though it might be serious." Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.

"Gentlemen," interposed the general, "would you mind suspending the discussion for a moment, while I mind Jerry across the street? I think I can then suggest a better plan." Carteret rang the bell for Jerry, who answered promptly. He had been expecting such a call ever since the gentlemen had gone in.

"Jerry," said the general, "step across to Brown's and tell him to send me three Calhoun cocktails. Wait for them,—here's the money."

"Yas, suh," replied Jerry, taking the proffered coin.

"And make has'e, charcoal," added McBane, "for we're gettin' damn dry." A momentary cloud of annoyance darkened Carteret's brow. McBane had always grated upon his aristocratic susceptibilities. The captain was an upstart, a product of the democratic idea operating upon the poor white man, the descendant of the indentured bondservant and the socially unfit. He had wealth and energy, however, and it was necessary to make use of him; but the example of such men was a strong incentive to Carteret in his campaign against the negro. It was distasteful enough to rub elbows with an illiterate and vulgar white man of no ancestry,—the risk of similar contact with negroes was to be avoided at any cost. He could hardly expect McBane to be a gentleman, but when among men of that class he might at least try to imitate their manners. A gentleman did not order his own servants around offensively, to say nothing of another's. The general had observed Carteret's annoyance, and remarked pleasantly while they waited for the servant's return:— "Jerry, now, is a very good negro. He's not one of your new negroes, who think themselves as good as white men, and want to run the government. Jerry knows his place,—he is respectful, humble, obedient, and content with the face and place assigned to him by nature."

"Yes, he's one of the best of 'em," sneered McBane. "He'll call any man 'master' for a quarter, or 'God' for half a dollar; for a dollar he'll grovel at your feet, and for a cast-off coat you can buy an option on his immortal soul,—if he has one! I've handled niggers for ten years, and I know 'em from the ground up. They're all alike,—they're a scrub race, an affliction to the country, and the quicker we're rid of 'em all the better." Carteret had nothing to say by way of dissent. McBane's sentiments, in their last analysis, were much the same as his, though he would have expressed them less brutally. "The negro," observed the general, daintily flicking the ash from his cigar, "is all right in his place and very useful to the community. We lived on his labor for quite a long time, and lived very well. Nevertheless we are better off without slavery, for we can get more out of the free negro, and with less responsibility. I really do not see how we could get along without the negroes. If they were all like Jerry, we'd have no trouble with them." Having procured the drinks, Jerry, the momentary subject of the race discussion which goes on eternally in the South, was making his way back across the street, somewhat disturbed in mind.

"O Lawd!" he groaned, "I never troubles trouble till trouble troubles me; but w'en I got dem drinks befo', Gin'l Belmont gimme half a dollar an' tol' me ter keep de change. Dis time he didn' say nothin' 'bout de change. I s'pose he jes' fergot erbout it, but w'at is a po' nigger gwine ter do w'en he has ter conten' wid w'ite folks's fergitfulniss? I don' see no way but ter do some fergittin' myse'f. I'll jes' stan' outside de do' here till dey gits so wrop' up in deir talk dat dey won' 'member nothin' e'se, an' den at de right minute I'll ban' de glasses 'roun, an' moa' lackly de gin'l 'll fergit all 'bout de change." While Jerry stood outside, the conversation within was plainly audible, and some inkling of its purport filtered through his mind.

"Now, gentlemen," the general was saying, "here's my plan. That editorial in the negro newspaper is good campaign matter, but we should reserve it until it will be most effective. Suppose we just stick it in a pigeon-hole, and let the editor,—what's his name?"

"The nigger's name is Barber," replied McBane. "I'd like to have him under me for a month or two; he'd write no more editorials."

"Let Barber have all the rope he wants," resumed the general, "and he'll be sure to hang himself. In the mean time we will continue to work up public opinion,—we can use this letter privately for that purpose,—and when the state campaign opens we'll print the editorial, with suitable comment, scatter it broadcast throughout the state, fire the Southern heart, organize the white people on the color line, have a little demonstration with red shirts and shotguns, scare the negroes into fits, win the state for white supremacy, and teach our colored fellow citizens that we are tired of negro domination and have put an end to it forever. The Afro-American Banner will doubtless die about the same time."

"And so will the editor!" exclaimed McBane ferociously; "I'll see to that. But I wonder where that nigger is with them cocktails? I'm so thirsty I could swallow blue blazes."

"Here's yo' drinks, gin'l," announced Jerry, entering with the glasses on a tray. The gentlemen exchanged compliments and imbibed—McBane at a gulp, Carteret with more deliberation, leaving about half the contents of his glass. The general drank slowly, with every sign of appreciation.
