The house of Henry Mabry stood on the upper side of Locust Street, at the point where that thoroughfare, having passed the last of the brick residences of the white gentry, began to lose something of its dignity and to straggle off toward the pine barrens in a succession of frame cottages, each a little smaller and a little less freshly painted than its neighbor. Mabry's house, however, was neither small nor shabby. He was a builder by trade, and had put up with his own hands, or under his own eye, a good third of the dwellings in which the better people of Clarendon ate, slept, and discussed the shortcomings of the colored race. It was natural, therefore, that his own roof should be sound, his own porch level, and his own pickets straight; and if the house was somewhat plainer than those he had built for others, it was because a long and not always pleasant experience had taught him that a colored man who builds too handsomely for himself is apt to be thought by his white neighbors to have forgotten his place.

On a certain evening in the early autumn, Mabry sat in the little room which his wife called the library, because it contained a bookcase, and which he called the office, because it contained his desk. The lamp had been lit, though the dusk was not yet complete, and in its yellow circle lay a letter, which had come by the afternoon mail and had been read, by one or the other of them, perhaps a dozen times since. Mrs. Mabry sat opposite her husband, with some sewing in her lap which she did not sew. She was a woman of forty or thereabouts, of a complexion so fair that strangers from the North, meeting her upon the street, sometimes lifted their hats to her, and were afterwards informed by their hosts, with a smile at Northern simplicity, of the mistake they had made. She had been educated at a seminary in Ohio, in the years immediately following the war, when the enthusiasm of the North for the freedman had not yet cooled into indifference, and she had brought back to Clarendon a certain refinement of speech and manner, and a certain restlessness of spirit, which her husband had admired in the days of their courtship and had since learned to regard with a respect not unmixed with apprehension.

"You have read it again, Henry," she said, breaking a silence which had lasted for some minutes.

"I have read it again," he replied, laying it down. "It says the same thing it said the first time."

"And what do you think of it?"

"I think," said Mabry slowly, "that your cousin Julia means well, as she has always meant well, and that she has always had a gift for meaning well in the wrong direction."

Mrs. Mabry's lips tightened. The letter was from her cousin, Mrs. Julia Haskell, who had gone North many years before, had married there a man of whose antecedents her neighbors knew nothing and inquired less, and had risen with him to a position of comfort and some consideration in a thriving city on the shore of Lake Erie. Mr. Haskell was now upon the board of education of that city, and there was, so the letter ran, a vacancy in one of the grammar schools,—a good school, in a good ward, at a salary which seemed to Mrs. Mabry, accustomed to the wages paid colored teachers in the South, little short of princely. The place might be had for Marian, if Marian would come; Mr. Haskell would see to it. There was but one condition, and it was set down with a delicacy which did credit to Mrs. Haskell's tact, if not to her candor: it would be as well, all things considered, if nothing were said about Clarendon, or about Marian's people, beyond what was necessary; and it was not necessary, Mrs. Haskell was sure, to say anything at all.

"She does not mean it in the wrong direction," said Mrs. Mabry. "She means it in the only direction there is. What is there for Marian here?"

"There is her home," returned Mabry, "and her father and mother, and her own people."

"Her own people!" echoed his wife, with a little gesture of impatience. "Who are her own people, Henry? She is as white as Judge Pembroke's daughter,—whiter, for the Pembroke girl is freckled. She reads French, which the Pembroke girl does not. She plays the piano better than anyone in Clarendon. And when she walks down Front Street she must step off the sidewalk if two white ladies are coming abreast, and when she goes to the depot she must sit in a car with drunken field hands and tobacco juice on the floor, and when she wants a new pair of gloves the clerk at Wheeler's hands them to her across the counter as though she might be carrying the smallpox. That is what her own people have made for her here."

Mabry was silent for a moment. He was a man of a darker hue than his wife,—not dark, as the term is understood in the South, but of that warm brown which is unmistakable and which makes no pretension. He had been born a slave, the son of a white man whom he had never been permitted to call father, and he had come through the war and the hard years after it with no capital save a pair of skilled hands and a disposition to use them. What he had, he had earned; and the earning of it had given him a certain stubbornness of character which his friends called independence and his enemies, when they troubled to call it anything, called impudence.

"I know all that, Ellen," he said at length. "I have known it longer than you, and felt it harder. But it isn't the sidewalk and the car and the gloves that you are asking her to run away from. It's me. It's you. It's every one of us that ever had a drop of black blood. Read that letter again, and see if it isn't so. 'It would be as well if nothing were said.' Nothing about her father, who is a colored man. Nothing about her mother, who is a colored woman, however white she may look. Nothing about her grandmother, who is lying out yonder in the Baptist burying ground, and who cooked for the Pembrokes forty years. Marian is to go up there and be born over again, without any father or mother at all, like Melchizedek in the Scriptures."

"You are unjust, Henry. She would write to us. She would come home in the summers—"

"Would she?" he asked, not harshly, but with a quiet persistence that was harder to bear than harshness. "And when she came home, would she bring her friends? And when her friends came to call, would she introduce them to her father? Or would she tell them I was the man who looked after the place?"

Mrs. Mabry rose and went to the window. The street outside had grown dim, and the figures that passed along it were scarcely more than shadows,—a white man on horseback, going home from his store; two colored women with baskets on their heads, returning from the day's washing; a small boy driving a cow. It was a scene so familiar that she did not see it; and yet, had she been asked, she might have said that it summed up, in its quiet and unconscious way, the whole social order of the South, in which every soul had its fixed station, and in which the only sin past forgiveness was to wish to change it.

It may be remarked here, for the benefit of those readers who have not given much thought to such matters, that the question which Mr. and Mrs. Mabry were debating was by no means a novel one, nor were they the first couple in Clarendon to debate it. There were, in that town as in every town of the South, a number of families whose blood had been so long and so thoroughly mingled with that of the dominant race that the line which the law drew about them was invisible to every eye but that of the law, and of the neighbors, who knew. From these families, quietly, and without any announcement in the newspapers, a son or a daughter would now and then disappear, and would be heard of afterward, vaguely, as doing well in the West, or in the North, or abroad; and if the family missed them, the family did not say so, and if the town knew where they had gone, the town, with a discretion that was not always the product of charity, kept its own counsel. It is a curious commentary upon the logic of race prejudice that it should thus continually drain away from the despised class the very elements which, by its own standards, it ought most to have desired to retain; but logic has never been the strong point of prejudice, which, if it could reason, would cease to exist.

"You talk," said Mrs. Mabry, turning from the window, "as though I wanted to lose her. Do you think it costs me nothing? She is my only child. I have hardly let her out of my sight for nineteen years. But I would rather lose her into happiness than keep her here in this,—this prison, and watch her eat her heart out. Do you know what happened to her last week?"

"She told me something about the Sunday school picnic."

"She did not tell you all of it, because she knew it would make you angry, and she is afraid of your anger, Henry, as I am sometimes. The Wilkins boy,—young Fred Wilkins, whose father you built the new house for,—followed her halfway home from the church grove and spoke to her as no decent man would speak to a decent woman. And when she would not answer him, he laughed, and said that he supposed she thought she was white. That is what she has to look forward to here, if she stays. Either to marry some colored man who will never be able to give her what she is fitted for,—"

"As her mother did," interposed Mabry quietly.

Mrs. Mabry flushed to the roots of her hair. "That is not fair, and you know it. I have never complained."

"No, Ellen, you have never complained. I will say that for you. You have never complained, and you have never been satisfied." He stood up, and for a moment the two looked at each other across the lamp, with that peculiar wretchedness which comes when two persons who love each other have said, in anger, things which they have long thought in silence. Then Mabry sat down again, heavily, and passed his hand across his eyes. "I beg your pardon," he said. "I had no right to say that."

"You had a right to say it if you believe it."

"I don't know what I believe. I know that I have lived in this town fifty years, man and boy, and that I have tried to do right by it. I have built its houses and its churches, and I built the very schoolhouse where they won't let our children go. I have paid my taxes and kept out of the courts, and when there was yellow fever in seventy-eight I nailed up coffins for white and colored alike and never asked which was which. And I thought,—God help me, I thought,—that if a colored man lived like that, and his children after him, then some day, maybe not in my time but in Marian's, the white folks would have to own that we were men and women like themselves. And now you tell me that the only way for Marian to be counted a woman is to stop being my daughter."

There was a knock upon the door, and before either could answer, it opened to admit the broad and comfortable person of Aunt Hagar, who had cooked for the Mabrys since before Marian was born, and who regarded the household with that proprietary affection which old servants of her class bestow upon the families they serve, whatever the color of those families may be.

"'Scuse me, Mis' Ellen," she said, "but supper's been settin' on de stove dis half-hour, an' de biscuits is gittin' ez hard ez de Jedgment Day. Miss Ma'ian say she ain' hongry, an' she done gone up ter her room an' shet de do'. I tol' her she better eat somethin', but she say no'm, she gwine set up dere an' study. I don' know w'at she studyin' 'bout. Seem lak dat chile studyin' all de time, here lately. Studyin' an' studyin', an' lookin' out de winder, lak she 'spectin' somebody ter come an' fetch her erway."

Mr. and Mrs. Mabry exchanged a glance.

"We will come presently, Aunt Hagar," said Mrs. Mabry. "Keep it warm a little longer."

"Yas'm. But I ain' promisin' nothin' 'bout dem biscuits." The old woman lingered in the doorway, her shrewd eyes passing from one face to the other. Whatever she had heard through the door,—and it is to be feared that she had heard a good deal, for the walls of Mabry's house, though well built, were not soundproof,—she made no further reference to it, except to remark, as she withdrew, and to nobody in particular, "W'en de Lawd made folks diffe'nt colors, I reckon He knowed w'at He wuz doin'. But I ain' so sho' 'bout some er de folks w'at's be'n sortin' 'em out sence."

When the door had closed behind her, Mrs. Mabry came back to her chair and sat down, and for a little while neither spoke. The clock upon the mantel, which Mabry had bought in Richmond the year they were married, ticked loudly in the silence, and a moth, attracted by the lamp, beat its soft wings against the chimney with a persistence that seemed, to Mrs. Mabry's overwrought fancy, not unlike her own.

"Henry," she said at last, more gently, "I know what you have done, and what you have hoped. I have hoped it too. But look about you. Is it coming any nearer? When we were married, colored men sat on the juries in this county, and there were two of them on the board of aldermen. Where are they now? The juries are white, and the aldermen are white, and they are talking at the courthouse, Mr. Dudley told me, of a new registration law that will leave not a colored voter in the county except those the white men choose to let stay. The schools are worse than they were twenty years ago. The very preachers have stopped preaching that things will be better. And you would have Marian wait, and be good, and hope, while the door is closing in her face? There is a door open for her now, Henry, this one time. It may never open again."

"It is not a door," said Mabry. "It is a window. And she must climb out of it in the night, and leave her name behind her."

"What is a name?" asked his wife, with a touch of bitterness. "Your own father would not give you his."

Mabry winced, as a man winces at the touch of an old wound. "No," he said, "he would not. And I have made the one he did not give me into something that is mine, and that I am not ashamed of. That is the difference, Ellen. I would rather Marian had that than the finest name in Ohio, if she must get it by pretending she never had any other."

"And if she wishes to go?"

The question fell between them like a stone into still water. It was, in truth, the question which both had been avoiding, for both knew the answer. Marian had seen the letter; it had been addressed, in fact, to her mother, but Mrs. Haskell, with the thoughtlessness of the prosperous, had enclosed a separate note for Marian herself, full of descriptions of the lake, and the shops, and the theaters, and the young people's reading circle at the Congregational church, where everyone was so cultivated and so kind. Marian had read it at the dinner table, and had said nothing; but her father had seen her face, and had understood, and the understanding had been with him all the afternoon, like a weight upon his chest.

"If she wishes to go," he said slowly, after a long pause, "I suppose I cannot stop her. She is a woman grown, or near enough. I could forbid it, and she would stay, because she is a good girl and an obedient one; and she would hate me for it, maybe not out loud, but in her heart, every time she had to step off the sidewalk. I have seen what that kind of hating does to people. I would not have her live with it." He looked down at his hands, broad, scarred, and capable, which had never yet failed him at any task they had been set. "But I will not tell her to go, Ellen. If she goes, she will go without my telling."

"That is no answer."

"It is the only one I have."

Mrs. Mabry rose and stood beside him, and after a moment's hesitation laid her hand upon his shoulder. It was the first gesture of tenderness that had passed between them that evening, and he did not move, though she felt the muscles of his shoulder grow rigid beneath her touch, as though he feared that any yielding might betray him.

"I will go up to her," she said. "I will not tell her to go, either, if that is what you wish. I will only tell her that she must choose for herself, and that whatever she chooses, her father and mother will love her."

"Tell her that," said Mabry, without looking up. "And tell her,—tell her that if she goes, and it is ever found out, as it is found out sometimes, and they turn her off, she is to come home. Tell her there will always be a place here, whatever happens. A colored man's house, but a place."

Mrs. Mabry went out, and her husband heard her light step upon the stair, and then the low murmur of voices from the room above. He sat for a long time without moving, while the moth beat against the lamp and the clock ticked off the minutes, and the biscuits in Aunt Hagar's oven grew harder and harder, until they might well have rivaled the Judgment Day itself. He was thinking, perhaps, of the house he had built for the Wilkinses, with its broad veranda and its fanlight over the door; of the schoolhouse with its neat belfry, into which no child of his might enter; of the coffins he had nailed in the fever year, and of the white men and women who had lain in them; and of the curious arithmetic of a civilization which could reckon a drop of blood as weightier than a lifetime of service. Or perhaps he was thinking of nothing at all, but only feeling, as men feel in such moments, the slow and silent ebbing of something which he had thought his own, and which was going from him by a law he had not made and could not alter.

Whether Marian Mabry went North that autumn, and what befell her there, and whether the window through which she climbed opened upon happiness or upon something else, are matters which belong to another chapter. It is enough to say here that in the town of Clarendon, where such things were known without being spoken, it was remarked by some of the colored people that Henry Mabry seemed to have grown older that winter, and by some of the white people that Mabry's girl had gone off somewhere and that it was just as well, for she had always been too stuck up for her station. And neither the one remark nor the other, it is safe to say, came within a thousand miles of the truth.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

It was late in the afternoon of an October day, when the shadows of the great oaks lay long across the sandy streets of Dorchester, that Robert Wade alighted from the northbound train, which, by one of those curious dispensations of Southern railroad management, arrived from the south. He had been absent from his native town for something more than fourteen years. He had left it a lad of nineteen, with a cardboard valise, a letter of introduction to a minister in Ohio, and a resolution, formed in the bitterness of youth, never to return. He came back a man of thirty-three, with a leather portmanteau, a practice at the bar of a Northern city, and a resolution which, like most resolutions formed in youth, had not survived the test of years.

The station platform had not changed, except that it had grown older and somewhat more dilapidated, as is the habit of things which are expected to last forever and are never repaired. The same sign, divided by a painted line, directed the traveler to one waiting-room or the other, according as nature or the law had determined his complexion; and Wade, whose complexion was of that indeterminate shade which left the question largely to the discretion of the observer, paused for a moment with the old familiar hesitation before turning his steps toward the door which, in the South, he had always used, and which, he reflected with a certain grim humor, he would doubtless always use there, so long as there remained in the town a single man who remembered his grandmother.

He had sent no word of his coming. The impulse which brought him had been sudden, and he had half feared that, if he announced it, he would find some reason for changing his mind. Leaving his portmanteau with the station-master, a stout white man who looked at him twice and seemed upon the point of addressing him as "sir," and then, upon some subtle indication not apparent to the casual eye, thought better of it, he set out on foot toward the lower part of the town.

The street along which he walked had been, in his boyhood, an unpaved road bordered by straggling cabins. He found it now, to his surprise, lined for a considerable distance with neat cottages, painted white or gray, with flower-gardens before them and here and there a picket fence. The colored people of Dorchester, he perceived, had not stood still during his absence. They had bought land, built houses, and planted roses, in sober confidence that the future would permit them to enjoy what they had made,—a confidence which, in view of the history of their race, may be regarded either as a sublime faith or as a pathetic delusion, according to the temperament of the observer.

At the corner of Market Street, where it crossed the old Wilmington road, stood a brick building of two stories, somewhat newer than its neighbors. Over the door hung a sign, lettered in gilt upon a black ground:—

I. WADE,
TONSORIAL PARLOR.
HOT AND COLD BATHS.

Wade stopped and read the sign twice, and something rose in his throat which he did not care to analyze. He had known that Isaac kept a barber-shop; his aunt had written it to him, in one of the infrequent letters which had followed him for a few years and had then ceased, as such letters do when they receive no answer. But he had pictured a shed with a single chair, and a cracked mirror, and a cousin grown old and humble in the service of other men's chins. The building before him spoke of quite another condition.

He opened the door and entered. The shop was long and clean, with four chairs of the latest pattern, a marble counter, and a row of shaving-mugs upon a shelf, each lettered with the name of a patron. Three of the chairs were occupied by white gentlemen in various stages of tonsorial undress, and three colored men in white jackets were attending them with that grave and deferential skill which had made the colored barber an institution of the South, and which, it may be observed, was at that very time beginning to make him a rarity in the North, where the free competition of races had brought in foreigners who would work for less. At the fourth chair, which was empty, stood a broad-shouldered, dark-skinned man of five and thirty or thereabouts, stropping a razor, with his back half turned to the door.

"Take a seat, suh," he said, without looking around. "I'll be wid you in a minute."

"I think," said Wade, in a voice not altogether steady, "that I would rather stand, Isaac."

The barber turned. For a moment he looked at the stranger with the polite blankness of a man trying to place a customer; then the razor stopped in its stroke, and his face underwent a series of changes, from doubt to wonder, from wonder to recognition, and from recognition to a joy so open and unguarded that the white gentleman in the nearest chair, whose face was half covered with lather, turned his head to see what had happened.

"Fo' de Lawd!" exclaimed Isaac. "Ef it ain' Bob! Ef it ain' Cousin Bob, come back fum de dead!"

He laid down the razor with the care of a craftsman, even in his excitement, and came forward with both hands outstretched. Wade took them, and the two men stood for a moment without speaking, while the three white gentlemen and the three colored barbers regarded them with varying degrees of curiosity.

"Gentlemen," said Isaac, turning to his customers with a dignity which sat well upon him, "dis is my cousin, Mr. Robert Wade, fum Cleveland, Ohio, whar he's a lawyer in de co'ts. We was raised in de same house, an' I ain' laid eyes on him in fo'teen years. Jim, you finish Mr. Pettigrew fer me. Henry, I'll leave de shop wid you till closin'."

The gentleman in the nearest chair, who was Mr. Pettigrew, a cotton broker of some local consequence, sat up and wiped the lather from one side of his mouth.

"A lawyer, eh?" he said, regarding Wade with an interest not wholly free from suspicion. "Practice in the courts up there, do you,—before white juries?"

"Before such juries as the law provides," replied Wade quietly.

Mr. Pettigrew lay back in his chair. "Well, well," he said to the ceiling, "times have changed. Isaac, you're a good barber; I hope your cousin's as good a lawyer." And he closed his eyes, as though to signify that the subject was exhausted, and that the proper relations of the universe had been sufficiently restored by this gracious compliment.

Isaac led his cousin through a door at the rear of the shop, and up a narrow flight of stairs to the floor above, where he had his living-rooms. They were plainly but comfortably furnished, with a carpet upon the floor, a few framed lithographs upon the walls, and in one corner a cabinet organ, upon which lay a hymnal and a volume of Dunbar's poems. A comely brown woman, who was sewing by the window, rose as they entered, and a little girl of six or seven, who had been playing with a doll upon the floor, regarded the visitor with round and serious eyes.

"Ma'y," said Isaac, "dis is Bob. You've heard me talk about Bob."

"I should think I had," said the woman, smiling and giving him her hand. "Isaac has talked about you ever since I've known him. He always said you'd come back some day. I had about made up my mind he was wrong."

"So had I," said Wade, with a candor which surprised himself.

Mrs. Wade, with that instinctive tact which is often found in women who have never heard the word, presently discovered that the supper required her attention, and withdrew to the kitchen, taking the child with her; and the two cousins were left alone, facing each other across the little sitting-room, each studying the other with the frank curiosity of men who had parted as boys and were meeting as strangers bound by a common memory.

They had been born within a year of each other, in the same small house on the edge of the town, the children of two brothers, and had been reared, after the death of both their fathers, by their grandmother, old Aunt Phoebe Wade, who had been a slave in the family of a judge and had borne him two sons. The judge, it may be remarked, had been a man of the highest character, a pillar of the church and the bar, and the author of a learned treatise upon the law of descent and distribution,—a subject upon which he was peculiarly qualified to speak, since he had so arranged his own affairs that his property descended to his white heirs and his blood was distributed elsewhere. One of his sons had married a woman nearly as fair as himself, and Robert was the fruit of that union; the other had married a woman of darker hue, and Isaac had inherited her complexion along with her patience and her strength. Thus the two boys, cousins in blood, and in all things else as close as brothers, had been divided from their cradles by that invisible line which the South draws with such confident precision, and which it so frequently has occasion to redraw.

"You've done well, Isaac," said Wade at length, glancing about the room. "Better than I had any idea of."

"I ain' done so bad," replied Isaac, with modest satisfaction. "I own dis buildin', an' de lot it stan's on, an' two houses on Chestnut Street dat I rents out, an' I got a little money in de bank,—not in de white folks' bank, but in our own. We got a bank now, Bob; did you know dat? Started it five years ago, an' it's never missed a dividen'. An' I'm a deacon in de church, an' secretary of de lodge, an' on de school board,—de colored school board, dat is, which ain' got much to say 'bout nothin', but we says it anyhow."

He laughed, and Wade laughed with him; but beneath the laughter Wade detected a note which he recognized, for it had been the undertone of his own boyhood.

"And the white people," he asked, "they let you alone?"

Isaac considered the question with the deliberation of a man who has given much thought to it.

"Dey lets me alone," he said slowly, "so long as I lets dem alone. I shaves de bes' white men in Dorchester, Bob. Judge Hollis comes in every mornin', an' de mayor, an' Mr. Pettigrew, an' half de lawyers on de co't-house square. Dey talks befo' me like I was a piece er furniture, an' I hears mo' 'bout what's gwine on in dis town dan de newspaper does. Dey trus' me wid a razor at dey th'oats, an' dey wouldn' trus' me wid a vote ef dey could he'p it. I've studied 'bout it a good deal, an' I ain' never been able to make it out. It looks to me like a man dat'll let you shave him had oughter let you vote; but I reckon dat's 'cause I ain' had de advantage of a white man's eddication."

Wade smiled at the irony, which was none the less keen for being so mildly delivered.

"And you, Bob?" said Isaac, leaning forward with his elbows upon his knees. "Tell me 'bout yo'se'f. Aunt Ca'line said you was a lawyer, an' den she didn' hear no mo', an' den she died, an' I didn' know whar to write. I been readin' de Cleveland paper sometimes, when a drummer'd leave one in de shop, lookin' fer yo' name. I seen it once, in a case 'bout a railroad. Was dat you?"

"It was I," said Wade. "I won that case, as it happened."

"I knowed it!" cried Isaac, slapping his knee. "I tol' Ma'y it was you. I tol' her de minute I seen it."

Wade was silent for a moment. The simple pride of his cousin in an achievement which he himself had almost forgotten touched him more deeply than he would have cared to admit; for in all the years of his absence no one had taken pride in him, except as a lawyer is valued by those who pay him, for what he can do and not for what he is.

"I have done well enough, in a way," he said at last. "I have a fair practice. I have a house, though it is rather too large for one man. I belong to a club or two. I go where I please, sit where I please, and eat where I please,—or nearly so. In Cleveland, Isaac, I am simply a lawyer. Nobody asks who my grandmother was."

"Do dey know?" asked Isaac, with a directness that was almost brutal in its innocence.

Wade looked out of the window, where the last red light of the sun was fading from the roofs across the way.

"Some of them know," he said. "Most of them do not. I have never told them, and I have never denied it. I have simply—not spoken of it. It is a curious thing, Isaac, how much a man can avoid saying, if he gives his mind to it. I have become rather expert in the art. It is, I suppose, the principal accomplishment of my profession."

Isaac said nothing, but his eyes rested upon his cousin with a look in which there was no reproach, but only a kind of grave pity, such as a man might feel for one who had purchased an estate and found the title clouded.

"I'm not complaining," Wade went on, with a slight hardening of the voice. "I made my choice, and I would make it again. I could not have stayed here. You remember how it was. I could not have stood at a chair and shaved Mr. Pettigrew, and listened to him talk about the negro problem, and said 'Yes, sir' when he finished. I should have cut his throat, or he would have had me hanged for looking as though I wanted to. You have the temper for it, Isaac. I never had."

"It ain' a matter er temper," replied Isaac quietly. "It's a matter er what you wants mos'. I wanted to stay whar my folks was. I wanted to be buried in de same graveyard wid granny, an' have my chillun know whar dey come from. An' I found out, Bob, dat a man can say 'Yes, suh' wid his mouf, an' keep his own counsel in his heart. Ole Judge Hollis thinks I'm de mos' contented nigger in Dorchester. Maybe I is. But I've put fo'teen boys th'ough school wid de money I made off'n his chin, an' two of 'em's teachin', an' one's studyin' medicine in Washin'ton. I reckon dat's my way er cuttin' his th'oat."

Wade looked at his cousin with a new respect. He had come South, if he had admitted it to himself, with some secret expectation of finding Isaac a humble and pitiable figure, whose condition would justify his own departure and sweeten the solitude of his Northern success. He found instead a man who had built, upon a foundation which the law itself sought daily to undermine, a structure of usefulness and honor which, in its own sphere, was quite as considerable as his own, and which had this advantage over it, that it rested upon the truth.

"Do you remember," said Isaac presently, in a softer tone, "de time we run off to go fishin' in de mill-pond, an' granny cotch us comin' home, an' whupped us bofe wid de same switch?"

"I remember," said Wade, and laughed. "She whipped me harder, because she said I was the older and ought to have known better. I was eleven months older, and I never knew better in my life."

"An' de time you fit dat white boy, Sam Hollis, fer callin' me a name, an' his daddy come down to de house an' raised sich a row, an' granny tol' him she'd whup you herse'f, an' den when he was gone she give you a piece er sweet-potato pie instid?"

"Sam Hollis," said Wade thoughtfully. "Is that the judge?"

"Dat's de judge," said Isaac, with a chuckle. "I shaves him every mornin'. He don' remember it. Or ef he do, he don' let on. White folks has got a mighty convenient memory, Bob. Dey remembers everything dat happened in de wah, an' nothin' dat happened befo' it."

They talked on as the dusk gathered, and Mrs. Wade came in and lighted the lamp, and they talked through the supper, which was abundant and excellent, and long after it, while the little girl fell asleep upon her mother's lap and was carried off to bed. They talked of their grandmother, who had died in the winter of the great freeze, with Isaac holding her hand and asking for Robert to the last; of the house on the edge of town, which had been sold to pay her burial and was now pulled down; of old friends, some prosperous, some dead, some gone to the cities of the North and swallowed up there, as a stream is lost in the sands; of the changes which had come over the town, and the greater changes which every intelligent man of their race foresaw, and which none could foresee with any comfort.

"Dey's talkin' 'bout a new constitution," said Isaac, his face clouding. "Gwine to fix it so a colored man can't vote 'less'n he can read an' write an' 'splain de constitution to de satisfaction er de registrar. I can read an' write as good as Mr. Pettigrew, an' better'n some. But I ain' never yit seen de registrar dat'd be satisfied wid a black man's 'splanation er anything."

"And you will stay," said Wade, "even so?"

"I'll stay," said Isaac simply. "Somebody's got to stay, Bob. Ef we all went off, dey wouldn' be nobody lef' to remember how it was, an' to tell de chillun dat it wa'n't always gwine ter be dis way. You went off, an' I reckon dat was right fer you. But dey's got to be some of us dat stays."

It was near midnight when Wade rose to go. Isaac would not hear of his returning to the hotel,—which, indeed, would not have received him, had his identity been known, and might not have received him even if it had not,—and a bed was made ready in the little room at the back. But before he retired, the two men stood for a while at the window, looking out upon the quiet street, where a single lamp burned at the corner and the shadows of the oaks lay black and motionless under the moon.

"Bob," said Isaac, "how long you gwine ter stay?"

"I had thought," said Wade, "of going back on Thursday."

"Stay till Sunday," urged Isaac. "Come to church wid us. I'd like de folks to see you. I'd like 'em to know dat one of us went off an' made a lawyer, an' wa'n't too proud to come back."

Wade hesitated. He thought of his office in Cleveland, of the cases awaiting him, of the club where no one asked who his grandmother was; and he thought, too, of what would follow if it became known in Dorchester that he had sat in a colored church, and how quickly such news travels, and how far, and how it might, by some malign chance, find its way into a Northern courtroom, where a lawyer's standing depends so much upon the color of his skin, and so little upon the color of his argument. It was the same choice he had made fourteen years before; and he perceived, with a sudden clearness, that he had been making it every day since, and that it had not grown easier with practice.

"I will stay till Sunday," he said.

Isaac grasped his hand, and said nothing; and it may be doubted whether, in all his practice at the bar, Robert Wade had ever pronounced a decision which gave him so much satisfaction, or which, in the larger court before which all men must at last appear, would have been more likely to be sustained.

Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. The house of Henry Ransom stood upon the corner of Mulberry and Front Streets, in that quarter of the town of Clarendon which the white people, with a fine indifference to the niceties of social distinction among those whom they regarded as all of one color, were pleased to call "Haiti." It was a neat frame cottage of five rooms, painted white, with green blinds and a porch across the front, and it was the visible fruit of fifteen years of patient industry. Ransom was a carpenter by trade, and by common report the best in the county. He had learned his craft under an old master builder who had owned him before the war, and had improved upon it since by such study as a man may give to books after a day's labor is done. He had built half the new houses on Second Street, where the white people lived, and could have built the other half, had he been asked. It was his habit to say, with a certain grim humor, that the white folks did not object to living in a house that a colored man had built, so long as they were not obliged to live next door to him.

He had married, at twenty-six, a young woman who had been one of the first graduates of the colored normal school at Fayetteville, and who had taught for three years in the public school before her marriage. She had brought to the union a small library of some forty volumes, a melodeon, and a set of convictions concerning the rearing of children which her husband had found it wise to respect. Of their three children, two had died in infancy, and the survivor, a boy named Robert, after his mother's father, was now in his ninth year. Upon this child, as is frequently the case where the parental affections have been narrowed to a single object, the hopes of the household were centered with an intensity which a disinterested observer might have thought excessive. He was a bright, sturdy, well-favored lad, of a complexion somewhat lighter than his father's and somewhat darker than his mother's, with a quick tongue, a quicker temper, and that perfect confidence in the justice of the world which is the birthright of all children, and which, in the case of children of his race, is usually forfeited at an early age.

On the afternoon in question, Mrs. Ransom had sent the boy to Pettigrew's grocery, at the foot of Market Street, for a pound of coffee and a cake of soap. She had given him a quarter, and had cautioned him, as she always did, to come straight home and not to loiter on the way. He was gone rather longer than the errand required, and when he returned he brought neither the coffee nor the soap, but a torn collar, a long scratch across one cheek, a swelling under the left eye, and the quarter, which he laid upon the kitchen table with an air of having discharged at least that portion of his trust.

"Robert!" exclaimed his mother, dropping the dish which she had been wiping, which, fortunately, was of tin. "What in the world has happened to you?"

The boy's account, delivered with more heat than order, was to the effect that he had gone into Pettigrew's and had waited by the counter until the clerk should be at leisure; that while he was waiting a white boy named Tillotson, whom he knew by sight, had come in after him and had been served first; that he, Robert, had said that he was there first, and that his money was as good as anybody's; that the white boy had called him a name which he would not repeat, because his mother had forbidden him to say such words; that the white boy had then pushed him; and that he had pushed the white boy back, with the result that the white boy had fallen against a barrel of crackers and upset it. What had followed was somewhat confused in the narration. It appeared that the clerk had put Robert out of the store, and that the white boy had followed him into the street, and that the encounter had been renewed there with varying fortune, until a colored drayman named Isham Bell had separated the combatants and sent Robert home.

Mrs. Ransom washed the scratch, applied a cold cloth to the eye, and, having satisfied herself that no serious injury had been done, sent the boy to his room to await his father. She did not reprove him herself. She was a wise woman, and she had perceived at once that the matter was one which went beyond the ordinary discipline of the household, and that it touched upon questions which she would rather have left to her husband, though she knew very well what he must say, and dreaded the saying of it almost as much as he would.

Ransom came home at six o'clock. He had already heard of the affair. Indeed, he had heard of it in a manner which left him in no doubt of its gravity, for he had been stopped on the corner of Market Street by Mr. James Tillotson himself, the father of the white boy, who was foreman at the cotton compress and a man of some local consequence among a class of white people whose consequence consisted largely in their being white. Mr. Tillotson had informed him, with a fluency of profanity which would have done credit to a larger vocabulary, that his boy had been assaulted by a young nigger, and that if Ransom did not take the hide off that young nigger, there were those in Clarendon who would save him the trouble, and take his father's along with it. Ransom had answered civilly, as it was his habit and his policy to answer white men, that he would look into the matter, and had walked home with the blood beating in his temples and his hands clenched in his pockets.

He did not go at once to his son. He sat for some minutes upon the back porch, looking out over the small garden which he had planted with his own hands, where the late tomatoes were reddening upon the vines and his wife's roses climbed over the fence of the neighbor's lot. His wife came out and stood beside him, and laid her hand upon his shoulder.

"You've heard, Henry?" she asked.

"Yes, I've heard. Tillotson stopped me on the street. He was good enough to say that if I didn't whip the boy, somebody else would whip us both."

"What are you going to do?"

"I don't know, Mary," he said, after a moment. "God help me, I don't know. I know what I ought to do, and I know what I must do, and the trouble is that they're not the same thing."

She said nothing more, for there was nothing to be said; and presently he rose and went into the house.

The boy's room was a small chamber at the back of the cottage, with one window looking upon the garden. He was sitting upon the edge of the bed when his father entered, and he rose at once, as he had been taught to do, and stood with his hands at his sides. The swelling under his eye had darkened somewhat, and gave to one side of his face a lopsided and rather comical expression which, at any other time, would have moved his father to laughter. There was no laughter in Ransom now. He sat down in the one chair which the room contained, and motioned the boy to stand before him.

"Robert," he said, "tell me what happened. Tell me all of it, and tell me the truth."

The boy told it again, more coherently this time, for he had had leisure to arrange his thoughts, and something in his father's manner warned him that the occasion was a serious one. Ransom listened without interruption. When the child had finished, he was silent for so long that the boy began to shift his weight from one foot to the other.

"You say you were there first?"

"Yes, sir. I was there a long time. Mr. Pettigrew's clerk saw me. He looked right at me."

"And the Tillotson boy came in after you?"

"Yes, sir. And the clerk asked him what he wanted, and he said a pound of sugar and a box of matches, and the clerk got them, and I said, 'I was here first,' and he said—" The boy hesitated.

"Never mind what he said. What did you say?"

"I said my money was as good as his. You said so, papa. You said it to Mr. Williams last Sunday on the church steps. You said a colored man's dollar was worth a hundred cents the same as a white man's, and anybody that said different was a liar."

Ransom winced. It is one of the trials of parenthood that children remember precisely those things which were not said for their instruction, and repeat them at the moment when they can do the most mischief. He had said that, and he had meant it; and he had said it, moreover, among his own people, where such sentiments might be safely uttered, and where they served to keep alive in men's breasts a self-respect which it was the whole effort of the community about them to extinguish.

"And then he pushed you?"

"Yes, sir. He pushed me hard, and called me that word again, and I pushed him back. I didn't hit him first, papa. Truly I didn't. I just pushed him, and he fell down on the crackers. And then the clerk put me out, and he came out after me, and he hit me in the eye, and I hit him back. I hit him a good one, papa," added the boy, with a certain pride which he could not altogether suppress. "Right on the nose. And he hollered."

It would be idle to pretend that the father heard this last statement without a responsive thrill. He was a man, and his son had stood up for his rights; and the instinct which bids a man rejoice when his offspring proves himself no coward is older and deeper than any lesson of prudence. For a moment his face relaxed, and the boy, quick to read the signs of the parental countenance, began to hope that he had come off well. But the moment passed. Ransom thought of Tillotson's face as he had seen it that afternoon, red and swollen with passion; he thought of certain things which had happened in Clarendon within his own memory, and of things which were happening, at that very time, in other towns not far away, of which the newspapers spoke with an indifference more terrible than any rage; and his heart grew cold within him.

"Robert," he said, "come here."

The boy came and stood at his knee. Ransom took him by both shoulders and looked into his face.

"You did wrong," he said.

The child's lip trembled. "But, papa—I was there first."

"I know you were."

"And he called me—"

"I know what he called you."

"And he pushed me first. You said a man oughtn't to let anybody push him around. You said that, papa. You said it about Uncle Isham, when the policeman—"

"Hush!" said Ransom sharply; and then, more gently, "Hush, son. Listen to me. I want you to listen to me now as you never listened before, and I want you to remember what I say as long as you live."

He paused, as if to gather his thoughts, or perhaps to summon his courage, for there are lessons which it is harder to teach than to learn, and this was one of them. It is a lesson which every colored parent in the South is called upon, sooner or later, to impart; and it may be doubted whether, in the whole range of human instruction, there is any other which so taxes the conscience of the teacher, since it requires him to inculcate, in the name of virtue, a submission which virtue itself condemns.

"There are two kinds of right in this world, Robert," he said slowly. "There is the right that God made, and the right that men make. God's right is the same for everybody, white and black. When you were there first, you had the right to be served first. When that boy called you a name, he did a wicked thing, and when he pushed you, he did another. By God's right you were not wrong. Do you understand that?"

"Yes, sir," said the boy, though his face showed that he understood nothing of the sort, but was waiting for the qualification which he felt was coming.

"But there is the other right, the one that men make, and in this town and in this state the men who make it are white men. And by their right, son, a colored boy is always wrong when he has trouble with a white boy. It doesn't matter who was there first. It doesn't matter who spoke first or who pushed first. If there is trouble, the colored boy is wrong, and the colored boy's father is wrong, and the colored boy's mother, and everybody that belongs to him. That's the law, son. It's not written in any book; you won't find it in the Constitution, or in the Bible, or in any of your mother's books in the parlor; but it's the law here, and it's stronger than any law that is written."

"But that ain't fair, papa," protested the boy.

"Isn't," corrected his father, from mere force of habit; and then, perceiving the absurdity of the correction in the face of so large a solecism in the moral order, he very nearly smiled. "No, it isn't fair. Nobody said it was fair. I'm not telling you what's fair; I'm telling you what is. And you've got to learn it, Robert, and you've got to learn it now, while you're young, because if you don't learn it now, you may not live long enough to learn it at all."

The child's eyes grew round. He had never heard his father speak in that tone before, and something of its meaning penetrated his understanding, though the full import of it was mercifully hidden from him.

"Do you know what Mr. Tillotson said to me today?" Ransom went on. "He said that if I didn't whip you, other people would whip both of us. He didn't mean whip, son. He meant something worse. And there are men in this town who would do it, and other men who would stand by and see it done, and nobody would ever be punished for it. You think about that. You think about your mother."

The boy began to cry, not loudly, but with the silent, shaking sobs of a child who is frightened by something he cannot see. His father's hands tightened upon his shoulders.

"I'm not going to whip you," Ransom said. "I ought to, maybe, if only so I could tell Tillotson I'd done it, and tell him the truth. But I'm not going to whip a boy for standing up for himself, God forgive me, even if I've got to teach him never to do it again. You'll stay in this room tonight without your supper. And tomorrow morning you and I will go together to Mr. Tillotson's house, and you'll tell him you're sorry you pushed his boy, and that you won't do it any more."

"But I ain't—I'm not sorry, papa."

"You'll be sorry," said Ransom, and his voice broke a little in spite of him, "when you're old enough to know what you've done. You'll say it whether you're sorry or not. That's part of the lesson, son. Sometimes a colored man has to say what he doesn't mean, and smile when he doesn't feel like smiling, and step off the sidewalk when he has as much right to it as anybody. You'll learn that too. I learned it. Your grandfather learned it before me, and he learned it harder than I did."

At this moment a voice was heard from the kitchen, where old Aunt Phoebe Ransom, the carpenter's mother, who had lived with them since her husband's death, had been preparing the supper, and from which point of vantage she had heard, without in the least intending to listen, the greater part of the colloquy.

"Henry," she called, "is you gwine ter starve dat chile?"

"He'll go without his supper tonight, mother," answered Ransom.

The old woman appeared in the doorway, a small, wrinkled figure in a gingham apron, with a turban wound about her head after the fashion of an earlier day. She looked at her son, and then at her grandson, and then back at her son again, and something in her face made Ransom drop his eyes.

"Henry," she said, "I ain't gwine ter meddle in yo' business. You is de man er dis house, an' you knows w'at's bes'. But I wants ter say one thing, an' den I'll hol' my peace. Dey tuck yo' daddy out'n de quarters one time fer sassin' de overseer, an' dey whupped 'im tel he couldn' stan'; an' w'en dey brung 'im back, he say ter me, 'Phoebe, I ain' sorry. Dey kin whup me ter def, but dey can't make me say I'm sorry.' An' dey couldn'. Dey sol' 'im down de country two years after, an' I ain' seed 'im fer six years, tel de war wuz over an' he walk back all de way fum Alabama. But dey never did make 'im say it."

"Times are different now, mother," said Ransom.

"Is dey?" said the old woman. "Is dey, sho' 'nuff? Den w'at fer you 'fraid er dat po' w'ite trash Tillotson? I 'members w'en his daddy wa'n't nothin' but a patteroller, ridin' roun' nights wid a whip, an' glad ter git de job. Times is diff'ent, is dey? Hit 'pears ter me de onlies' diff'ence is dat in dem days dey owned us, an' tuk some kinder keer of us fer de money we wuz wuth; an' now dey don' own us, an' don' keer w'at becomes of us, so long ez we keeps out'n deir way."

She turned and went back to the kitchen, and Ransom heard her setting the dishes upon the table with somewhat more noise than the operation required. He sat for a while longer with his son before him, and neither of them spoke. Then he drew the boy to him and held him close, as he had not done since the child was very small, and the boy, who had expected anything rather than this, clung to him and wept afresh.

"Papa," he whispered, when he could speak, "was I bad?"

It was a simple question, and it deserved a simple answer; but Ransom found that he could not give one. He thought of all the answers he might make, and none of them was true, or rather all of them were true and contradicted one another, as truths have a way of doing in a world not ordered by justice. At length he said, "You were brave, son. And being brave is a dangerous thing for a boy like you. Some day, maybe, it won't be. Some day, maybe, when you're a man, or when your children are men, a colored boy can stand in a store and say 'I was here first,' and nobody will think it anything but the plain truth. I've worked for that day all my life, and so has your mother. But it isn't here yet, and until it comes, I'd rather have you live than be right."

He put the boy from him, rose, and went out, closing the door behind him. In the kitchen his mother did not look up from the stove, and his wife, who stood by the window, came to him and took his hand without a word. He sat down at the table, but he did not eat, and presently, when the old woman had gone to her room and the dishes had been washed and put away, his wife took a plate of bread and a glass of milk and went softly to the boy's room, and Ransom, who saw her go, said nothing.

The next morning, father and son walked together to the Tillotson house on Chestnut Street, and the boy, standing upon the steps, with his cap in his hand and his eye still discolored, made his apology in a voice that could scarcely be heard. Mr. Tillotson received it with a magnanimity which cost him nothing. He remarked that the boy seemed to have been brought up right, after all, and that if all the niggers in Clarendon had as much sense as Henry Ransom there would be no trouble in the town; and he went so far as to say that he would remember Ransom when he came to build the new kitchen he had in contemplation. Ransom thanked him, and the two walked home again in silence.

It may be remarked that the lesson so painfully imparted was well learned. Robert Ransom grew to manhood in Clarendon, and in all the years that he lived there no white man ever had occasion to complain of his manners. He was civil, he was obliging, and he knew his place. He also became, in due course, a lawyer, and one not without distinction, in a Northern city to which he removed as soon as his education permitted; and it is related of him, by those who knew him there, that he was never known to yield a point which he believed to be just, nor to step aside for any man upon the public way. Whether this was in spite of his father's teaching or because of it is a question which the philosophers may determine. It is enough to record that the father, who lived to see the son's success, used to say that of all the work of his hands, the hardest he had ever done was not any house that he had built, but the half hour in the little room at the back of the cottage on Mulberry Street, when he had taught his child to be a coward in order that he might grow up to be a man.
