Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Stephen Crane, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
I

The train came down out of the hills with a long yell, as if it were angry at the country for having so many curves. It swept along the edge of the town of Ballard's Mills, and the little yellow station, which had the cowering air of a dog that expects to be kicked, received it with a shiver of all its windows. A cloud of black smoke went rolling over the roof of the freight-shed and broke upon the elms beyond, and the elms tossed their heads in a kind of outraged dignity.

Upon the platform stood Orrin Pike. He had put on his Sunday coat. It was a coat of a stern black, and it had been worn to the funerals of eleven persons, so that it carried itself with gloom and with a certain authority. Orrin was not easy in it. He had been standing there for forty minutes, and in that time he had twice gone to the end of the platform to look along the rails, and twice come back, as a man will who has nothing to do with his hands but cannot bear to let them be still.

Two loafers sat upon a truck near the baggage-room. They had observed the Sunday coat, and they had drawn their own conclusions. One of them now spat with deliberation upon the planks and said: "Orrin's waitin' fer somebody."

The other loafer considered this for a time. "I guess he is," he said at last.

The train halted with a great sigh of steam, and the passengers began to descend. There was a fat woman with a basket, who peered fearfully about her as if the town might presently attack her. There was a drummer in a gray suit, who whistled. And then, in the doorway of the second car, there appeared a figure that caused the two loafers to sit up straight upon their truck.

It was a man of perhaps thirty-five years, and he was dressed in a checked suit of a pattern so loud that it seemed to shout across the platform. Upon his head was a brown derby, and from his waistcoat there hung a chain of yellow metal which caught the late sun and flung it about. He carried a valise of new leather, and he stepped down from the car with the manner of one who conferred a favor upon the earth by touching it.

Orrin Pike went forward. His face had become suddenly red. He had prepared, during the forty minutes, a great many things to say, but now they had all fled from him, and he could think of nothing but that his cousin had grown a mustache.

"Well, Lafe," he said.

"Well, Orrin," said the other.

They shook hands. It was a long handshake and an awkward one, for each man was trying to read the other's face, and each was conscious of being read. Orrin saw a stranger of evident importance, a man who had been in the great city and had been touched and polished by it. Lafe Hollister saw a mild, stooped fellow with a little dust of meal in the creases of his knuckles, and he felt for him a sudden and agreeable pity.

"You ain't changed much," said Lafe generously.

"No," said Orrin. "I guess not." He looked at the checked suit. "You have," he added, and then was immediately afraid that this might be taken amiss.

But Lafe laughed. He laughed in a large, easy way, throwing back his head. "Well, a man can't stay in Chicago fourteen years and come out the same as he went in," he said. "It ain't possible. The town gets into him."

The two loafers had heard the word "Chicago," and they looked at each other with the eyes of men who have received an important communication.

II

They went up the main street of the town together. It was the hour when the sun, having finished with the day, was painting the upper windows of the brick block a furious crimson, and the dust of the road lay in long golden sheets. A wagon creaked by with a sleepy team. From the open door of the blacksmith shop came the clang of iron, steady and indifferent, like the beating of some slow heart.

Lafe walked with his chin up. He was looking at everything, and his glance had in it a kind of fond contempt. "There's old Dutcher's store," he said. "Lord, it's got smaller. I used to think that was a big store."

"It's the same size," said Orrin.

"Well, it looks smaller." Lafe flicked an ash from his cigar. "Everything does, after you been away. You ought to see Marshall Field's, Orrin. You could put this whole street into the front of it and have room left for a circus."

Orrin said that he would like to see it some time. He said this humbly. He was thinking of his own store, the feed store at the foot of Water Street, where the sacks of bran leaned against each other like weary old men and the rats held long conversations under the floor. He had been proud of the store that morning. He had swept it. But now it seemed to him a shabby thing, and he was glad that their road did not lead past it.

"What line are you in now, Lafe?" he asked.

"Hardware," said Lafe. "Wholesale. I got a position with Heilbronner and Strauss." He pronounced the names as if they were the names of kings. "Responsible position. I handle a whole territory practically by myself. They think a good deal of me there. Old Heilbronner, he says to me once, he says, 'Hollister, I don't know what we'd do without you.' That's what he said."

Orrin was silent. He was very much impressed. It seemed to him that his cousin had climbed a high mountain, and was now calling down to him from the peak, and that his own voice, if he raised it, would sound thin and foolish in such air.

At the bridge they paused. Below them the river went sliding over its stones with a low, continuous chuckling, as if it were telling itself an old joke. The willows along the bank hung their heads in the water. Beyond, the mill-race shot black and smooth under the wheel-house, and the great wheel itself stood still and dripping, a dark ruin against the burning sky.

Lafe leaned upon the rail. For a moment his face lost some of its confidence. "That's where we had the raft," he said.

"Yes," said Orrin.

"You remember the raft?"

"I remember it."

"We was going to float her clean down to St. Louis," said Lafe, and he laughed again, but this time the laugh was smaller. "Clean down to St. Louis. And then to New Orleans, and then I don't know where. China, I guess."

"You was going to China," said Orrin. "I was going to stop at St. Louis and be a pilot."

They looked down at the water. A little brown bird skipped from stone to stone, entirely occupied with its own affairs.

"She broke up on the dam," said Lafe.

"She broke up on the dam," Orrin agreed, "because you would steer."

Lafe turned his head. "Because I would steer? I never steered. You had the pole."

"I didn't have the pole. You took it away from me."

"I never took it away from you. You dropped it."

The two men regarded each other. It was suddenly apparent that a dispute twenty-two years old had come up out of the river and was standing between them, dripping, upon the bridge. Lafe's face had grown pink above his collar. Orrin's mouth had set itself in a line which his wife would have recognized.

Then Lafe laughed once more, and slapped his cousin upon the shoulder with a large hand. "Well, it don't matter now, does it?" he said. "It don't matter a continental."

"No," said Orrin. "It don't matter." But privately he was certain that Lafe had taken the pole.

III

Orrin's house stood upon a little rise at the edge of the town, a white house that had been white a long time ago. There was a picket fence in front of it, and several of the pickets were missing, so that the fence had the appearance of an old man grinning. In the yard a hen went about her business with an air of grievance.

Mrs. Pike met them at the door. She was a thin woman with a face that seemed to have been made for the purpose of expecting the worst, and she wore an apron which she had forgotten to take off. When she saw the checked suit she drew in her breath. Then she wiped her hands upon the apron and gave one of them to the visitor.

"Pleased to meet you, Mr. Hollister," she said.

"Call me Lafe, ma'am," said the cousin magnificently. "We're all one family here."

Behind her, in the dimness of the hall, there was a stirring and a whispering, and three children became visible, ranged in order of their heights like a set of jugs upon a shelf. They stared at the visitor with round and solemn eyes. They had been told that a cousin was coming from Chicago, and they had formed in their minds an image of something enormous and terrible, perhaps with feathers. They were now trying to make the man in the checked suit fit this image, and he was not fitting it very well, and they were disappointed, but also they were not sure.

"These are the young ones," said Orrin.

Lafe bent down. "Well, well," he said. "Well, well, well." He took a coin from his pocket and held it up so that it shone. The smallest child put her finger in her mouth. The largest, a boy of ten, regarded the coin with deep suspicion, as if he suspected that it would be the beginning of some obligation.

At supper Lafe talked. The lamp had been lit, and it threw a round yellow glow upon the table, upon the ham and the biscuits and the dish of preserved pears, and beyond this glow the room was full of brown shadows in which the faces of the children floated like little moons. Lafe talked of the city. He talked of buildings ten stories high, and of the cable cars that ran without horses, and of the lake that was like an ocean. He talked of a fire he had seen, and of a man who had been run over by a dray in front of his very eyes, and he described the incident with such care that Mrs. Pike put down her fork.

"Did you ever see any Indians?" asked the boy suddenly.

Lafe hesitated. It was an important moment. Six eyes were fixed upon him with a terrible hope. "Well," he said, "I seen a good many."

"Wild ones?"

"Some of 'em was pretty wild."

The boy breathed deeply. He looked at his father with something like pity. His father had never seen an Indian. His father sold bran.

Orrin sat at the head of his table and ate his supper. He ate it slowly. He was listening to his cousin and he was proud of him, for it is a fine thing to have a relative who has seen wild Indians and a man run over by a dray; and at the same time there was growing within him a dull and secret resentment, which he did not understand and of which he was ashamed. He observed that his children did not look at him at all.

Mrs. Pike, in the kitchen afterward, said to him in a low voice: "Orrin, that suit."

"What about it?"

"Nothing," she said. "Only it's a mighty loud suit."

"It's a city suit," said Orrin with some heat. "That's how they wear 'em in the city."

"I expect so," said Mrs. Pike, and she rattled the dishes in the pan in a way that conveyed a great deal.

IV

Later the two cousins sat upon the porch. The night had come down over the valley, soft and enormous, and the stars were out in such numbers that they seemed to crowd one another. From the marsh beyond the river the frogs had begun their chorus, a vast, shrill, unending argument in which every frog was certain he was right. Now and then a dog barked far off in the town, and another dog answered him, and then both were quiet, as if ashamed.

Lafe had offered a cigar, and Orrin had accepted it. It was a cigar with a gold band, but it did not draw well, and it had a taste which Orrin could not name. He smoked it doggedly. He would have smoked it if it had been made of hay.

For a time they did not speak. The great talk of the supper-table had worn itself out, and now there was only the dark and the frogs and the two red points of the cigars, which brightened and faded, brightened and faded, like the slow eyes of some watchful animal.

"Aunt Mattie's dead," said Orrin presently.

"I heard," said Lafe. "I got the letter." He was silent. "I meant to come," he said.

"It was in March," said Orrin. "The roads was bad."

"I meant to come," said Lafe again.

Orrin said nothing. He was thinking of the burying, of the gray rain that had come down all through it, and of the minister, who had a cold, and of the few people who had stood about the grave with their collars turned up. He remembered that he had looked once at the road, half believing that he would see a figure coming. He had not told anyone this.

"She used to give us them molasses cookies," said Lafe. His voice had changed. It had grown husky and low, and some of the city had gone out of it. "You remember? She kept 'em in the blue crock on the shelf. And you'd climb up and I'd hold the chair."

"I held the chair," said Orrin.

"Now, Orrin—"

"I held the chair. You was always the one to climb. You was lighter."

Lafe began to protest, and then he stopped. In the darkness he made a curious sound, and Orrin perceived that his cousin was laughing, not in the large, fine way of the afternoon, but quietly, with his shoulders shaking.

"Lord," said Lafe, "we never can agree on nothing, can we?"

"I guess not," said Orrin, and then he too began to laugh. They sat there laughing together on the dark porch, two men no longer young, while the frogs went on with their argument in the marsh. It was not a thing that could have been explained to anyone. Mrs. Pike, hearing it through the kitchen window, paused with a dish in her hand and frowned, for it seemed to her an unreasonable noise.

When they had done, there was another silence, and it was a different silence from the first. The air seemed to have loosened between them.

Lafe threw the end of his cigar out into the yard, where it lay glowing in the grass. "Orrin," he said.

"What?"

"About that position."

Orrin waited.

"It ain't—" Lafe began, and halted. "Well, old Heilbronner, he didn't exactly say what I told you. That is, he said something like it, but it was a man named Gersten he said it to. I was standing right there. I heard it." He cleared his throat. "I handle a territory all right. But it ain't such a big territory. It's mostly down around Joliet."

Orrin turned this over in his mind. He was conscious of a feeling that was not disappointment, and was not triumph, but was some third thing that warmed him oddly about the heart. He perceived that the mountain upon which his cousin had stood was not so high, after all, and that the voice calling down from it had been, perhaps, a little frightened of the height.

"And the suit," said Lafe. "I'm owing on the suit."

"It's a good suit," said Orrin.

"It's a fool suit," said Lafe bitterly. "I seen it in a window and I thought, I'll go home in that. I'll show 'em. And all the way on the cars I was proud of it, and then when I got down on the platform and seen them two loafers looking at me, I felt like a parrot in a cage."

Orrin considered. Then, slowly, as a man will lay down a card he has been holding a long while, he said: "The store's mortgaged."

Lafe turned his head.

"Since two years back," said Orrin. "When the river come up and spoiled the corn. Bank's got a paper on it. And on the house too, partly." He drew upon the evil cigar. "I didn't tell Ella how much. She'd fret."

"Well," said Lafe softly. "Well, I'll be darned."

They sat and looked out at the night. And it seemed to each of them, in that moment, that he had come into possession of something valuable, though he could not have said what it was. They had each laid down a burden of pretense, and found that the other did not think the less of him. It was a small thing. The stars, which had looked upon a great many porches, did not remark it. The frogs did not pause. But the two men felt it, and they were silent for a long time out of a kind of shyness, as if they had been caught in some act of tenderness that was not proper between grown men.

"That raft," said Lafe at last.

"What about it?"

"I guess maybe I did take the pole."

Orrin was a long while in answering. "No," he said finally. "I guess maybe I dropped it."

V

In the morning the sun came up clean and bright, and the hen in the yard resumed her grievance where she had left it. Lafe came down to breakfast in the checked suit, for he had no other, and the children looked at it again, and the boy asked him whether the Indians had tried to scalp him, and Lafe, after a glance at Orrin, said that they had not tried very hard.

The two cousins walked down to the station together. The street was full of wagons, and the blacksmith's iron rang out as before, steady and indifferent. At the bridge Lafe paused and looked down at the water, and Orrin paused beside him, and neither of them said anything.

There was a war in the vacant lot behind the Methodist church. It had been declared shortly after the noon meal, and by three o'clock it had become one of those vast and complicated struggles in which the original causes are lost and only the hatreds remain. Two armies of small boys faced each other across a stretch of burnt grass and broken bottles. Between them lay a ditch, and in this ditch the dead sometimes rested and argued with the living as to whether they had been properly killed.

Georgie Vane was a general. He had appointed himself to the post, and the appointment had been confirmed by the circumstance that he possessed ammunition. This ammunition he carried in a flour sack, which hung from his shoulder and swung against his knees in a manner both martial and inconvenient. It contained some threescore objects, brown and round and papery, which he had procured that morning from a certain bed of earth beside his mother's kitchen. He had not inquired into their nature. It had been sufficient that they were of a size to fit the hand and of a weight to carry well through the air. When they struck, they burst with a soft and satisfactory sound, and the enemy howled.

"Charge 'em!" he cried. "Charge 'em, fellers! They ain't got nothin' left but clods!"

His army consisted of three boys and a dog. The boys were named Pete Holloway, Arthur Fenn and a small cousin of Arthur's who had come visiting from Ohio and who had been pressed into service with the understanding that he was a private and would remain a private forever. The dog had no rank. He went where his heart directed him, and his heart directed him chiefly toward the enemy's lunch, which lay in a paper parcel behind a heap of bricks.

The enemy was commanded by a large, freckled youth named Sammie Dorr, who was in the fifth reader and who therefore carried with him the dignity of an older civilization. He fought from behind the bricks. His face appeared above them now and then like a red moon, and his voice issued forth in great bellows of contempt.

"Yah! Yah! Georgie Vane, you can't hit a barn!"

Georgie drew back his arm. He felt within himself a swelling, as if his chest had become too small for the thing that lived in it. The sky was very blue, and the grass was very yellow, and the bricks were the color of old blood. He threw. The missile sang across the field and broke upon the edge of the brick pile, and a spray of brown fragments went up like a puff of smoke from a cannon. Sammie Dorr's face vanished. There was a short silence, and then a wail of genuine anguish.

"It's in my eye! Aw, it's in my eye!"

The army of Georgie Vane set up a cheer. It was a thin and piping cheer, but to the general it sounded like the roar of multitudes. He stood upon the lip of the ditch and waved his sack, and in that moment he was conscious of the eyes of nations upon him. He was a figure of bronze. Somewhere, in a city he had never seen, men were already preparing his statue.

Then, from beyond the church, beyond the board fence and the row of currant bushes and the grape arbor with its sagging wires, there came a voice. It was a woman's voice. It rose in a long note, and broke, and rose again.

"Geor-gie! Geor-gie Vane!"

The effect upon the field of battle was singular. Both armies paused. Sammie Dorr, with one hand clapped to his eye, put his head up from behind the bricks and regarded his late adversary with a sudden and terrible interest. The cousin from Ohio sat down in the ditch. Pete Holloway began to walk away in a casual manner, whistling, as one who had merely been passing and had stopped to look at the weather.

"Your ma," said Arthur Fenn, in a hushed voice. "That's your ma."

Georgie said nothing. The bronze had gone out of him. He was again a small boy with a flour sack, and the flour sack had become very heavy. He looked down into it, and the brown round things looked back at him with a strange and accusing look, as if they had been waiting all afternoon for this moment.

"Geor-gie!"

The voice had in it a quality which he recognized. It was not the voice that called him to supper, nor the voice that called him to have his ears washed. It was another voice, and he had heard it perhaps three times in his life. Each time it had been followed by events which his mind now declined to remember.

"I got to go," he said hoarsely.

"Yeh," said Sammie Dorr from behind the bricks. "I guess you have." He spoke with deep satisfaction, and his uninjured eye glittered.

Georgie went. He did not run. To run would have been to admit that the summons had power over him, and he had a vague idea that a general, even a defeated general, should march. So he marched, very slowly, through the gap in the board fence and past the currant bushes, and his army watched him go as men watch a comrade led out to be shot. The dog followed him a little way, and then remembered the lunch behind the bricks, and turned back.

His mother stood in the side yard. She was a small woman, and ordinarily she had a soft and indefinite face, like a face seen through a window on a rainy day. But now it had become sharp. It had edges. She stood beside the bed of earth by the kitchen wall, and the bed of earth was full of holes. They were neat round holes, dug with a garden trowel, and there were a great many of them. They gaped at the sky. They resembled, to the guilty eye of Georgie, a little cemetery in which all the graves had been robbed.

"Georgie," said his mother, "what is in that sack?"

He looked at the sack as if he had never seen it before. He looked at it with honest wonder, as if some stranger had hung it upon his shoulder while he slept.

"It's—it's a sack," he said.

"I can see that it is a sack. What is in it?"

He opened his mouth. Several explanations presented themselves to his mind. He had found the sack. Pete Holloway had given it to him. It had been in the barn. A tramp had left it. Each of these explanations seemed, as it approached his tongue, to grow thin and transparent, so that he could see his mother's face through it. He closed his mouth.

His mother reached out and took the sack from him. She looked into it. She was silent for a long time. Then she said, in a low voice, "These came from Philadelphia. They came all the way from Philadelphia, in a box, with straw. Your father sent away for them in the winter. They were to be tulips. There were to be red ones and yellow ones and some that were striped."

Georgie stared at the ground. A small black beetle was walking across the path. It walked with great purpose, as if it had an appointment, and Georgie watched it with a kind of envy.

"They were to come up in the spring," said his mother. Her voice shook a little. "Mrs. Fitch was going to come and see them. I told her. I told the whole Missionary Society."

"I didn't know they was tulips," said Georgie. "I thought they was just—things."

"Things," repeated his mother.

"I thought they was onions," said Georgie, gaining a little courage. "Old onions. I thought you didn't want 'em."

"You thought I buried onions beside the kitchen door, in rows, with little sticks to mark them."

Georgie could find no answer to this. It seemed to him a very unfair thing to say. It was the kind of thing that grown persons said, and there was no answer to it, and they knew there was no answer, and they said it anyway.

His mother handed him back the sack. It was a curious gesture, and it frightened him more than anything she had yet done. "Go up to your room," she said. "Your father will be home at six o'clock. He will want to see you in the library."

The library. The word fell upon Georgie like a stone dropped into a well. He heard it go down and down.

He went into the house and up the stairs. The stairs were very long. He had never before noticed how long they were. At each step the house seemed to grow more silent, as if it, too, had learned of his crime and was holding its breath. In the hall above, the clock ticked with a dreadful deliberation. It said, "Six—o'clock. Six—o'clock." He went into his room and shut the door and sat upon the edge of his bed with his hands between his knees.

The window of his room looked out upon the side yard. By leaning a little he could see the bed of earth with its holes. He did not lean. He looked instead at the wallpaper, which was covered with small blue sailboats, all sailing in the same direction, toward the bureau. He had counted them many times. There were two hundred and eleven, not counting the half ones that went behind the door.

He began to construct the future.

In the first future, he ran away. He climbed down the lightning rod at midnight and went to the railroad yards and hid himself in a freight car full of cattle. He traveled to the West. He became a scout, and later a great Indian fighter, and his name appeared in the newspapers. Years afterward he came riding back into the town on a black horse, with a long mustache and silver spurs, and his father and mother stood on the porch, very old and bent, and his mother said, "Is it—can it be—Georgie?" And he said coldly, "Madam, I have brought you some tulips," and threw a great bag of them at her feet, and rode away forever.

This future pleased him a great deal for a time. Then it occurred to him that he did not know how to climb down a lightning rod, and that the railroad yards were a long way off, and that it would be dark, and he abandoned it.

In the second future, he died. He was not certain how he died, but it was a slow and beautiful death, and he lay upon this very bed, very white, and the whole town came to look at him. Sammie Dorr came, and wept, and said, "He was the best general there ever was." His mother came, and fell upon her knees, and cried, "Oh, my boy, my boy, what are tulips beside thee?" Down in the street a wagon went by, and its wheels made a sound like distant artillery. A bell rang somewhere. Presently there was the sound of the front gate. It was a particular sound, a click and then a creak, and Georgie had heard it every evening of his life without paying it any attention. He had them off now. He was holding the flour sack upon his knee. He had evidently been examining its contents, for one of the brown bulbs lay upon the table in the lamplight, and it looked very small and naked there, like a thing in a museum.

Georgie said nothing.

Georgie's throat worked. "We was having a war," he said. "Me and Pete and Arthur, against Sammie Dorr's gang. They had clods. We didn't have nothin'. So I—I got those."

"I see," said his father. "You used them for ammunition."

Georgie did not answer. A strange thing was happening to him. The vine on the carpet had begun to swim. It wavered and grew large and then small, and the red of it ran into the edges of things. He fought this with all his strength. He told himself that generals did not do it, that scouts did not do it, that men with silver spurs did not do it. He set his teeth.

He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. The man came up from the barn when the light was nearly gone. The snow in the lane had been trodden into a gray paste, and his boots made little sucking noises in it, as if the earth were reluctant to let him go. Over the hill the sky was a cold green, with a single bar of crimson laid across it like a welt. The house squatted before him. A window glowed. He paused at the gate and regarded this window for some time, as a man might regard the eye of a creature he had wronged.

He had resolved upon a speech. He had composed it in the barn, among the patient cattle, and it had seemed to him there a fine and manly speech, with a beginning that was firm and an end that was tender. He had recited portions of it to the gray mare. She had made no objection. But now, with the window staring at him, he found that the speech had grown thin and threadbare in his mind, and certain of its noblest phrases had fled away altogether.

He scraped his boots upon the step with great deliberation. It was a long scraping. He was aware that it was a long scraping, and that it was audible within, and he began to feel that the scraping was itself a kind of confession.

The kitchen was hot. The stove sat in its corner and glared at him with a red, eternal eye. The lamp upon the table made a little island of yellow, and beyond its shores the room went off into brown shadow, where the dresser loomed and the clock ticked with the dull insistence of a thing that had been wound for a purpose. The woman sat by the lamp. She was sewing. The needle went in and came out, went in and came out, and flashed at each emergence like a small fish leaping.

She did not look up.

He hung his coat upon the peg. He was very careful about the hanging of the coat. He straightened the shoulders of it. He then stood for a moment with his hands hanging, and he discovered that his hands were enormous, and that they had no business anywhere.

"Cold," he said.

"It's January," said the woman.

He sat down across from her and began to unlace his boots. The laces had frozen and would not give. He picked at them with his great fingers, and he bent so low over this labor that his face was hidden. He felt that his face was a thing to be hidden.

The needle went in and came out.

"Supper's on the back of the stove," she said presently. "It's been there some time."

"I ain't hungry."

"You'll eat it, though."

"I s'pose."

He got one boot off and set it upon the floor with a small, careful thud. Then he began upon the other. The clock ticked. The stove muttered. Somewhere above them, in the dark of the loft, the child turned over in her sleep, and the rope bed creaked, and both of them lifted their faces to the ceiling and listened, and then lowered them again, and neither had looked at the other.

"Mis' Hatcher was in to the store this afternoon," said the woman.

The man's fingers paused upon the lace. He felt the blood go up into his face in a hot tide. The speech, which had been waiting somewhere in the back of his skull, rose up all at once and fell over itself and lay in a confused heap.

"Was she?" he said.

"She was."

"Well, I s'pose she's got a right to go to the store."

The woman bit off her thread. She did it with a sharp, decisive motion, as one who severs a rope that has held a boat. She looked at him then for the first time. Her eyes in the lamplight were very dark, and there was in them something he could not name—a quality of waiting, like that of a hawk upon a dead limb.

"She said Hatcher told her you'd put your name down. With that man from Omaha. She said you was going in the spring."

He had his boot off now. He held it in his two hands and studied it. It was an old boot, cracked across the instep, and he regarded it with profound attention, as if within its leather lay some answer that had hitherto escaped him.

"I was going to tell you," he said.

"When?"

"Tonight. I was going to tell you tonight."

"Hatcher knew it Tuesday."

There was a silence. The clock seemed to grow louder in it. Each tick fell into the room like a pebble into a well, and he found himself waiting for the splash.

He had known, of course, that she would come to know. He had known it in the way a man knows that winter will come, which is to say that he had known it and had not believed it. He had told Hatcher because Hatcher had been there, leaning upon the rail of the feed lot with his pipe, and the man from Omaha had just driven off in his yellow buggy, and the thing had been so large and so new in his breast that it had forced itself out of his mouth. He had told Hatcher, and then he had driven home, and he had looked at his wife across the supper table, and the words had shrunk within him to the size of seeds, and he had swallowed them.

That had been Tuesday. Since Tuesday he had swallowed them three times a day.

"Well," he said heavily, "you know it now."

"Yes. I know it now."

She took up another piece of cloth. It was a small piece, blue, a child's garment. She held it up to the lamp and looked at it, turning it this way and that, and then she laid it in her lap and folded her hands upon it and did not sew.

"Tell me about it," she said.

He set the boot down. He felt that he must now make his speech or be forever a coward. He drew in his breath. He fixed his eyes upon a point somewhat above her head, where a calendar from the implement company hung upon a nail, displaying a picture of a red reaper in a field of impossible gold.

"There's silver out there," he began. "In the mountains. This man—Pruitt, his name is—he's got a claim staked, and he's took on four men already, and he needs two more, and he says a man that's willing to work can clear more in a summer than he'd clear here in five years. Five years. He showed me a paper from the assay office. It had a seal on it."

"A seal," said the woman.

"A gold seal. Stamped right into it." He made a little circle in the air with his forefinger. "I seen it."

She said nothing. He waited for her to say something. He had prepared himself for many things she might say, and he had ready an answer for each, as a soldier lays out cartridges upon a log. But she said nothing at all, and the cartridges lay there useless.

"We can't go on like this," he said. His voice rose a little. "You know we can't. The note's due in October. Gilfillan won't carry it another year; he as much as said so. And the wheat—you seen the wheat last summer. You seen it. Burnt up like it'd been set fire to. A man works and works and the sky just—" He made a gesture of helplessness, opening his great hands upward toward the ceiling, toward the loft, toward the cold green sky beyond it. "The sky don't care," he said. "It don't care nothing about it."

He was pleased with this sentence. It had not been in the speech. It had come to him new and whole, and it seemed to him that it held a great and terrible truth. He looked at her to see if she perceived it.

"No," said the woman. "I don't s'pose it does."

He felt rebuffed. The great truth had fallen upon the floor between them and lain there like a dropped spoon.

"So I'm going," he said. "That's all. I'm going in the spring and I'll send money back. Pruitt says the mail goes out regular from Leadville. I'll send it regular. And by fall, maybe—maybe sooner—"

"And who's going to plant?"

"Ed Sayre's boy. I'll get Ed Sayre's boy."

"Ed Sayre's boy is twelve years old."

"He's big for twelve."

"He's simple."

"He ain't simple. He's slow. There's a difference."

The woman smiled. It was not a good smile. It was thin and quick, like the crack that runs across a pond when a man steps too far out upon the ice, and he saw it and was afraid.

"You talked to Hatcher," she said, "and you talked to the man with the seal, and I s'pose you talked to Ed Sayre about his boy. Did you talk to Ed Sayre?"

He did not answer.

"You talked to everybody in the county," said the woman, "excepting me."

The stove ticked as its iron settled. A gust of wind came down off the hill and leaned against the house, and the window rattled in its frame, and a fine sifting of snow struck the glass with a sound like a whisper. The man listened to this whisper. It seemed to him that the whole night outside was listening also, crowding close to the panes, putting its great black ear against the walls.

He began to feel a deep and righteous anger. It came up in him slowly, out of some well of grievance he had not known he possessed. He had labored. He had broken his back upon this ground. He had stood in the burnt field in August with the dust rising about his knees, and he had not wept, though he had wished to. And now he was to be judged by this woman, who sat in the warm with her sewing, and who had never had to face Gilfillan across a desk with his hat in his hands. He considered that he had been very ill-used. He considered that there was no man in the township so ill-used as he.

"A man's got to do something," he said loudly. "A man can't set and wait for the sky. A man's got a right to try."

"I never said you hadn't a right."

"You're saying it now. You're setting there saying it."

"I'm setting here," said the woman, "and I ain't said nothing about rights at all."

This was true, and he knew it was true, and the knowledge enraged him further. He got up from his chair. He walked to the stove and lifted the lid of the pot that waited there, and looked into it, and saw a gray mass of potatoes and pork lying in congealed fat, and he set the lid down again with a clang. He walked to the window. He could see nothing in it but his own face, hung against the darkness, yellow and enormous, with the eyes sunk into it like two holes. He regarded this face with distaste. It seemed to him the face of a stranger, and not a stranger he would care to know.

"I thought you'd be glad," he said to the window.

Behind him the woman made a small sound. He did not know whether it was a laugh.

"Glad," she said.

"I thought—I thought you'd see it was for you. And for her." He jerked his head toward the ceiling. "I ain't going off to have a high time. It's work out there. It's hard work. Pruitt says men die of it sometimes. The cold, and the rock falls. He told me square. He didn't hide nothing."

"He told you men die of it."

"He told me square."

"And you told Hatcher, and you didn't tell me."

He turned from the window. She had risen. She stood by the table with the little blue garment crushed in one hand, and the lamplight came up under her chin and made her face strange, all hollows and high places, like a country seen from a hill at evening. He had known this face for nine years. He had seen it flushed at the dances at the Grange hall, and white upon the pillow when the child came, and brown and sweat-streaked under a sunbonnet in the hay. But he had never seen it as it was now. It seemed to him to be made of some hard pale substance, like the china dog upon the shelf in her mother's parlor, and he could not imagine that it had ever been soft.

"Why didn't you tell me?" she said.

He opened his mouth. The speech was gone. It had fled entirely, and in its place there was nothing but a great white silence, like a field after snowfall, without a track upon it anywhere.

"I don't know," he said.

And it was true. He did not know. He searched himself and found only a vague and shameful confusion, as of a boy discovered in the orchard with green apples in his shirt. He had been afraid. That was the whole of it. He had been afraid of this kitchen, and of this lamp, and of this woman with the needle that went in and came out. He had been less afraid of the mountains, and the rock falls, and the cold that killed men, than he had been of the moment when she would look up from her sewing. He perceived this now with a terrible clearness, and he was humiliated by it, and he hated her a little for having made him perceive it.

"I don't know," he said again.

The woman looked at him for a long moment. Then she sat down. She smoothed the blue garment upon her knee, pressing the wrinkles out of it with the flat of her hand, slowly, over and over, as one smooths the hair of a sick child.

"My father went to Californy," she said. "In 'forty-nine. Did I ever tell you?"

"No."

"He went. He had a paper too. I don't know if it had a seal on it." She smoothed the cloth. "Mother kept the place two years. She was smaller than me. She used to plow with a rope tied around her middle, so if the horse bolted it wouldn't run off with the plow. I used to watch her from the fence. I was six."

He waited.

"He come back," said the woman. "He come back the third spring. He walked in the door and set down at the table, just about where you're standing, and he didn't have nothing. Not a thing. He had a cough. And he set there and he looked at her, and she looked at him, and nobody said a word. And then she got up and give him his supper." She paused. "That's all. She give him his supper."

The wind leaned against the house again. The snow whispered at the glass.

"I ain't your father," said the man hoarsely.

"No," said the woman. "I know you ain't."

She did not say it unkindly. That was the worst of it. If she had flung it at him, he could have caught it and flung it back. But she laid it down very gently, like a cup set upon a table, and he did not know whether it was meant for an insult or for a mercy, and he stood there with his hands hanging and could not decide.

He came back to the table and sat down. The chair groaned under him. He put his elbows upon the oilcloth and looked at the lamp. A moth, wakened untimely by the heat, had come out of some crevice and was beating itself against the chimney with small, soft, tireless blows. He watched it. It seemed to him a very foolish creature. It seemed to him that there was no creature in all the earth so foolish as this moth, which could not see that the glass was there, and would batter itself to dust against it before it would turn away.

"I put my name down," he said at last. "I can't take it off. I give my word."

"I know."

"Pruitt's counting on me."

"I know."

"It wouldn't be honest."

"No," said the woman. "It wouldn't be honest."

They sat. The clock ticked. Above them the child murmured something in her sleep—a name, perhaps, or the fragment of a song—and was quiet.

"You'll want your heavy coat mended," said the woman. "The lining's gone at the shoulder."

He looked at her. Her head was bent. The needle had come up out of the blue cloth and was waiting in her fingers, catching the light.

"I'll do it in March," she said. "There ain't no hurry for it now."

He felt something rise in his throat, something enormous and formless, that might have been gratitude and might have been grief, and might have been merely the potatoes and pork, which he had not eaten. He swallowed it. He had grown expert in swallowing.

"All right," he said.

She went back to her sewing. The needle went in and came out, went in and came out. He sat and watched it. After a time he got up and went to the stove and took the pot from the back of it and spooned the gray mass into a bowl, and sat down again, and ate. It was cold. He ate all of it.

When he had finished, she rose and took the bowl from him without a word and carried it to the basin. He heard the dipper strike the bottom of the pail. He heard water poured. These were small sounds, homely sounds, and he had heard them every night for nine years, and he had never once listened to them before.

Outside, the crimson bar had long since gone from the sky over the hill. The night was black and very large. Far off, beyond the hill and beyond the next hill and beyond all the hills there were, the mountains stood up in the darkness, white and indifferent, with the silver locked in their hearts. They did not know his name. They did not know that he was coming. He thought of this as he sat in the hot kitchen with the lamp before him, and it seemed to him, for a moment, a very lonely thing.

Then the woman came back and wound the clock.

He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The train came to a halt with a long sigh, as if it were weary of the whole affair of travel and wished to lie down in the weeds beside the track. The young man descended with his valise. He stood for a moment upon the platform and arranged his face. He had been arranging it, with intervals of despair, since Albany.

It was seven years since he had seen his cousin. In that time he had gone to the city and become a clerk in a house that sold buttons, braid, and other small and necessary glories, and he had acquired a derby hat, a watch-chain of considerable pretension, and a manner. The manner had cost him the most. He had studied it from the floorwalkers and from certain young men who stood before cigar stores in the evening, and he believed that it was now nearly perfect. It consisted chiefly in a way of glancing at things as if they had been shown to him before, in another place, at a better price.

He had resolved that his cousin should see this manner at once. He had pictured the scene many times. There would be the cousin, a gawk in a straw hat, gaping at the derby. There would be a little embarrassment on the part of the gawk, and a large and generous ease on the part of himself. He would be kind. He had determined upon that. He would not crush his cousin with too much of the city at the first meeting. He would dole it out, as one doles sugar to a horse.

The station was a little gray building squatted beside the rails like a toad that had grown old waiting for flies. A man with a long beard sat upon a bench and regarded the young man without interest. Beyond the station a road went off between fences into a world of yellow stubble. There was no wagon.

The young man took out his watch and looked at it with a frown. He was not angry, but he felt that a man with a watch-chain of such quality ought to frown when kept waiting. Then he put the watch away, and, as nobody had observed the frown, he felt that it had been wasted.

Presently there came from along the road a sound of wheels and a cloud of dust which advanced with the deliberation of a cow. It resolved itself into a wagon, two brown horses, and a large man. The man pulled up with a jerk that made the horses throw their heads, and he climbed down. He came forward with long strides. His hands were huge and red. He had a short brown beard, and his shoulders seemed to fill the whole road behind him.

The young man stared. It was his cousin. He had remembered a thin boy with knees.

"Hello, Frank," said the large man. He held out one of the red hands.

"Why—hello, Asa," said the young man. His hand went into the other's and was lost there. It was squeezed and returned to him somewhat damaged. He had meant to say something easy and amused, something about the train. It went from his mind. He looked at the beard.

"You've growed," said Asa, and he looked the young man up and down with a long, slow, sober eye, the way he might have looked at a heifer offered for sale. The eye rested for a moment upon the derby hat. It contained no awe. It contained nothing at all that the young man could discover. Then Asa picked up the valise as if it were a pocketbook and slung it into the wagon.

"Hop in," he said.

The young man climbed to the seat. He was conscious that the derby hat had suddenly become a thing of tremendous size. It seemed to him to tower above the landscape like a steeple. He would have liked to take it off and sit upon it.

The horses moved. The wagon groaned and complained in all its joints. For some time neither cousin spoke. The fields went past them, wide and yellow and silent, with here and there a black crow walking in the stubble with the air of a deacon who disapproves. A wind came across the land and smelled of dry grass and of distance. The sky was enormous. The young man had forgotten that the sky could be so large. In the city it came to him in strips, between the cornices, like ribbon off a bolt.

He felt that he should begin. He cleared his throat.

"Things look about the same," he said.

"Yep," said Asa.

The young man waited, but there was nothing more. He tried again. "I s'pose you haven't heard much about the new elevated road they've got down in the city. It goes right up over the streets on iron legs, and the cars run along on top. You can sit in a car and look right into folks' second-story windows."

Asa considered this. "What for?" he said.

"Well—" said the young man. "Well, it ain't for that, exactly. That's just the way it runs."

"Huh," said Asa. He clucked to the horses. Then, after a time, he said, "That off horse is going lame, I guess. I'll have to look at him."

The young man felt that the elevated railroad had been destroyed. It had fallen down in the road behind them with all its iron legs in the air. He looked sideways at his cousin, and the big man was gazing at the off horse with a face of serene and complete absorption, as if there were no cities anywhere, and never had been.

A resentment began to grow in the young man. He had come three hundred miles bearing the city in his hands like a gift, and his cousin had not so much as looked at the wrapping. It was a sort of insolence. He began to assemble other wonders—the theaters, the great stores with their bright windows, the crowds that went along Broadway in the evening like a river with hats on it. He would bring these up, one by one, and lay them in his cousin's path. But each time he opened his mouth he saw the big red hand upon the reins and the slow eye fixed upon the off horse, and he closed it again.

The road went down a hill and across a little bridge. Under the bridge a creek ran brown and talkative over its stones. The young man looked at it, and suddenly a thing came into his mind from a great way off. It was a summer of long ago, and two boys were fighting on the bank of a creek over a jackknife with a bone handle. He remembered the smell of the mud and the sting of a blow upon his ear. He remembered that he had been beaten, and that he had wept, and that afterward his cousin had given him the knife.

He looked again at Asa. He wondered if the big man remembered. It seemed to him all at once a very important question. If Asa remembered, then there was a bond between them that no derby hat could alter. And if Asa did not remember—the young man felt a queer little chill. It would mean that he himself had been carrying about a thing for seven years that the other had thrown away.

"That's the old creek," he said, in a voice he tried to make careless.

"Yep," said Asa. "She run dry in August. First time in twenty years, Pa says."

The young man waited. The wagon rumbled off the bridge. The creek fell behind, chattering to itself. Asa said nothing more of it, and the young man, after a struggle, said nothing either. He would not be the first to speak of the knife. He felt that to do so would be a sort of surrender. He sat stiffly upon the seat and looked at the crows.

The farmhouse came into view at the top of a long rise. It was white, with a gray barn behind it that leaned slightly, as if listening for something in the next county. Smoke went up from the chimney straight and thin. A dog came out from under the porch and barked in a large and official manner, and then, upon recognizing the wagon, became ashamed and wagged its whole body.

On the porch stood a young woman with a child upon her arm.

The young man had known, in a vague way, from letters, that his cousin had married. But it had been a fact of the kind that is kept in a drawer. Now it stood upon the porch in a blue calico dress with its sleeves rolled to the elbows, and it smiled at him. And the child stared at him with round, hostile eyes, as at an invader.

"This here's Frank," said Asa. "Frank, this is Mary. And that's the boy."

"How do you do?" said the young man. He took off the derby hat. It was the first relief he had felt in an hour.

"My, but we've heard a lot about you," said the young woman. "Asa's always talking about his cousin Frank in New York. Come in, come in. You must be just about tuckered."

The young man was astonished. He glanced at his cousin, but Asa had gone to the head of the off horse and was lifting its foot and peering at it with the frown of a scholar. The young man felt a little warm flame of gratification. So the big man had talked of him. He had been a figure, then, in this house, a personage. He went up the steps with a better step than he had used upon the station platform.

At supper there was a great deal of food. It came out of the kitchen in heaps and mounds, as if the young woman wished to bury him in it. There were potatoes and ham and beans and hot biscuits and three kinds of preserves, and the young man ate until he felt that the chair was too small for him. The young woman questioned him with shining eyes. Was it true that the buildings went up ten stories? Was it true that a body could buy anything at all in the stores, anything in the world? Had he ever seen a great actor?

The young man expanded. He perceived that here at last was a proper audience. He told of the stores, the crowds, the lights at night. He made the buildings a little higher than they were, and when he spoke of a great actor he gave the impression, without exactly saying it, that he had met the man upon the street and been nodded to. He used his manner. He glanced at the kitchen walls as if he had been shown them before, at another price.

Gradually he became aware that his cousin had stopped eating.

Asa sat with his large hands lying upon the oilcloth on either side of his plate. He was looking at his wife. His face had in it nothing that could be named. It was simply a large, bearded, motionless face. But the young man felt something come across the table toward him, cold and heavy, like the shadow of a cloud upon a field.

He faltered in the middle of a sentence about a jeweler's window. He could not remember how the sentence was to end. He had a sudden vision of himself as his cousin must see him: a thin young man in a tight coat, talking very fast, with ham upon his fork. He put down the fork.

"I guess it ain't all like that," he said lamely. "Most of the time you just go to work and come home."

"Well, I'd like to see it, just once," said the young woman. "I'd just like to see it once." She looked out the window, where the sky had gone the color of a ripe peach, and there was in her voice a little wistful note that made the young man feel he had done something wrong, though he could not discover what.

Asa got up. "Got to see to the stock," he said, and went out. The door banged behind him.

The young woman looked at the door and then at her plate. The child, in a high chair by the stove, banged a spoon upon its tray and shouted a word that was not in any language. The young man felt that the supper had become a wreck, and that he was its author. He was angry with himself. Then he was angry with his cousin for being so easily wounded, like a girl. Then he was angry with himself again. The emotions went round in him like horses in a ring, and none of them would stop.

Later, when the dishes had been taken away and the lamp lit, the young man went out upon the porch. The night had come down over the land with a vast quiet. The stars were out in great multitudes, more of them than he had thought existed, crowding the sky like people at a fire. From somewhere in the low ground came the voices of frogs, steady and innumerable, as if a whole congregation were reciting something it had learned by heart. A light showed in the barn.

He sat upon the step and lit a cigar. It was a good cigar. He had bought two of them for this visit, one for himself and one for his cousin, and had carried them three hundred miles in his breast pocket. He felt the second one there now. It seemed a foolish thing, like a valentine.

The light in the barn went out. Presently he heard heavy feet upon the grass, and the big shape of his cousin came out of the darkness and sat down upon the step beside him. The step creaked.

For a long time neither spoke. Asa took a pipe from his pocket and filled it with slow, deliberate fingers and lit it. The match flared and showed his face for an instant, bronze and grave, and then the darkness took it back.

The young man drew upon his cigar. He wished to say something. He did not know what it was that he wished to say. It seemed to him that there was a great thing lying between them, a thing as large as the barn, and that they were sitting on either side of it, each pretending that it was not there.

"That horse all right?" he said at last.

"Stone bruise," said Asa. "He'll do."

The frogs went on. A late bird made a noise in the orchard like a rusty hinge.

"Mary's a good woman," said the young man, and then was horrified, for it sounded as if he had been appraising her.

But Asa only nodded. "She is," he said. And then, after a long pause, he said in a low voice, "She ain't never been further'n Utica."

The young man understood then, in a dim way, the shadow that had come across the supper table. He had thought it was jealousy. Now he was not sure. It seemed to him that it was a different thing, a sort of sorrow, and he did not know how to answer it. He sat silent and turned the cigar in his fingers.

"It ain't so much, the city," he said finally. "I made it out more than it is."

"I figured," said Asa.

The young man was stung. He had offered a confession, and it had been accepted too easily. He had expected it to be refused, and to be urged upon him, and to be at last allowed to take it back. Now it lay there on the step between them, and he could not recover it.

"What do you mean, you figured?" he demanded.

Asa puffed his pipe. "Well," he said slowly, "you was always a great one for telling things bigger. Recollect the time you said you'd seen a bear down in the swamp lot? Had the whole township out with guns. It was Hiram Pratt's black calf."

The young man felt his face grow hot in the darkness. He had forgotten the bear. He did not wish to remember it now. He had come here to be a man of affairs and a wearer of derby hats, and he was being shown a small boy in torn trousers pointing at a calf.

"I was a kid," he said stiffly.

"Sure," said Asa. "So was I."

There was another silence. The young man sat in it and suffered. He felt that the whole visit had been a failure, that he had come a great way to be laughed at, that he would take the morning train and go back to the buttons and the braid, where at least a man was known by his hat. He composed in his mind a cold and dignified farewell.

Then Asa spoke again, in a different voice.

"Recollect the jackknife?"

The young man turned his head quickly. He could see nothing of his cousin but the dull red glow of the pipe.

"The one with the bone handle," said Asa. "Down to the creek. We had a fight over it, and I licked you."

"I recollect," said the young man. His voice came out strangely. He cleared his throat. "You gave it to me after."

"I did," said Asa. "Pa tanned me for it. It was his knife."

The young man sat very still. He had never known this. For seven years, and for the years before them, he had carried that knife about in his memory as a token of something, of a large and careless generosity on the part of his cousin, and now it appeared that the generosity had been paid for behind the woodshed. He did not know whether he ought to feel grateful or ashamed. He felt both, and a third thing besides, which had no name, and which made his throat tight.

"I've still got it," he said.

"Have you?" said Asa. He seemed pleased. The pipe glowed brighter for a moment.

The young man put his hand into his breast pocket. His fingers found the second cigar. He drew it out and held it toward the darkness where his cousin was.

"Here," he said gruffly. "I brought you this. Brought it from the city."

There was a pause. Then the big red hand came out of the night and took the cigar, gently, as a man takes an egg from under a hen.

"Much obliged," said Asa. He turned it over in his fingers. He held it to his nose and smelled it. "Must've cost something."

"Oh, not much," said the young man, and for the first time that day he did not use his manner.

Asa put the cigar away in his shirt pocket with great care. "I'll save it," he said. "For Sunday."

They sat on. The frogs had not paused once in all this time. They went on with their recitation as if nothing had happened, as if two men had not just crossed a gulf of seven years upon the strength of a jackknife and a five-cent cigar. The stars wheeled slowly. The barn leaned and listened.

The young man felt a great warmth in him, and a great foolishness. He wished to say something large and fine to his cousin, something about blood, and boyhood, and the long years. He searched for it. He felt that he almost had it. It rose in him like a bubble in a pond.

"Asa," he began.

"Yep?"

The young man struggled. The fine thing hung just beyond his reach. The night waited for it.

"Do you still keep pigs?" he said.

"Four," said Asa. "And a sow due in a week."

"Oh," said the young man.

From within the house the child set up a sudden wail, thin and imperious, and the young woman's voice could be heard hushing it. Asa knocked his pipe out against the step. The sparks fell into the grass and went out one by one, like a little constellation dying.

"Well," said the big man, rising. "Guess we'd best turn in. Got to be up early."

The young man rose also. He looked out once more at the immense night, the crowded stars, the dark land rolling away under them toward places he had been and places he had not. He felt that something had been settled, though he could not have said what it was. He went in after his cousin, and the screen door clapped shut behind them, and the frogs, unmindful, went on.

In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.
