The sun had come over the roof of the Hollister barn and was laying long yellow bars upon the dust of the lane when the small boy came home. He came slowly. He walked with the air of one who has been upon a great expedition and has returned laden with secrets. His trousers were wet to the knee, and upon one cheek there was a smear of red clay like the paint of a savage. He carried a stick, which had lately been a sword, and before that a rifle, and before that a stick.

He paused at the gate. The house stood before him, white and square and full of windows. To the boy it seemed at this moment to wear an expression. The windows regarded him. The two upper ones, under the eaves, were like the eyes of an old man who sits in judgment and says nothing. The door, painted a stern green, was shut.

He looked down at his trousers. He had intended to dry them in the sun of the meadow, lying on his back upon a flat rock and watching the clouds go by like slow white cattle. But the clouds had been diverting, and the rock had been warm, and he had fallen into a contemplation of a hawk that wheeled and wheeled in the blue as if it were tied to a string, and when at last he arose the trousers were as wet as before. He had then made an elaborate plan of walking home by the long way, through the Pettibone pasture, so that the wind might do the work. But the Pettibone bull had been standing in the pasture, black and enormous, swinging its head in a manner that was plainly a threat to small boys with wet trousers, and he had come by the lane.

He lifted the latch of the gate with infinite caution. It squealed. The sound was like a cry of betrayal. He stood still, his heart making a great noise in him, and waited for the green door to open. It did not open. A hen walked across the yard with the gait of a disapproving old woman, and a bee went into the hollyhocks. He began to feel that he had perhaps escaped notice entirely, that the house was empty, that his mother had gone to the store, or to the church sewing circle, or to some far country from which she would not return before dark. He crept around to the side of the house, toward the kitchen, where there was a window with a sill low enough to climb.

He had his hands upon the sill when the kitchen door opened and his mother stood in it.

She was a tall woman, and from where the boy crouched she appeared tremendous. She seemed to fill the doorway from post to post and from sill to lintel. The light of the kitchen was behind her, so that her face was in shadow, but he could see the white of her apron and the flour upon her forearms, and he could see that her hands were folded. This was a bad sign. When her hands were busy there was hope. When they were folded there was none.

"Willie," she said.

The boy took his hands from the sill. He made a small movement which, had it been carried to its conclusion, would have been flight. But there was no place to fly to. Behind him was the yard, and the hen, and the lane, and beyond the lane the whole round world, and he perceived dimly that in all of it there was no refuge from the woman in the doorway.

"Come here," she said.

He came. He came with his eyes upon the ground and his stick trailing behind him, making a little furrow in the dust. He mounted the step. He passed under the arm of his mother, which she held up so that he might enter, and it seemed to him like a gate of a fortress closing at his back.

The kitchen was full of the smell of bread. On the table a row of loaves sat in their pans, brown and swollen and complacent. The stove ticked. Its iron front, with the little round draft holes, looked at him with a row of red eyes. The clock upon the shelf said "tock" with great deliberation, as if it were counting something and did not wish to lose its place.

His mother closed the door. She did not sit down. She stood by the table and looked at him, and the boy, after one swift glance at her face, studied the pattern of the oilcloth upon the floor. It was a pattern of small brown squares with yellow lines between, and he discovered that by looking hard at one square he could make the others swim. He looked very hard.

"Where have you been?" asked his mother.

The boy considered. He perceived that this was an important question and that a great deal depended upon the answer. He reviewed a number of answers. He had been to the store. He had been at the Hollisters'. He had been in the barn. He had been in the orchard. Each of these places rose before him, bright and plausible, and each one, as he examined it, developed a flaw. The store did not account for the trousers. The Hollisters would tell. The barn was dry. The orchard, he thought, might do, if there had been a rain, but the sky had been of an unbroken blue since morning, and his mother had been under it.

"Nowheres," he said at last.

"Nowhere," repeated his mother. "And did you get your legs wet in nowhere?"

The boy looked at his legs as if they belonged to another person and he had only now been introduced to them. He seemed astonished. He seemed to be wondering how in the world they had come to be in such a condition.

"I guess I must 'a' stepped in somethin'," he said.

"Willie, you have been to the creek."

He made no reply. The clock said "tock." Outside, the hen made a remark.

"You have been to the creek," said his mother again, "after I told you this very morning, and yesterday morning, and the morning before that, that you were not to go near it. After I told you about the Dorsey boy."

The Dorsey boy had drowned in the creek two summers past. The boy had a confused memory of the event. He remembered a great many men in their shirtsleeves walking along the bank and poking at the water with poles, and a woman screaming in a manner that had made him go behind the woodshed and stay there a long time. He remembered that afterward there had been a funeral, and that he had worn his Sunday shoes, which pinched. But the Dorsey boy himself he had never thought much of. The Dorsey boy had been big and slow and had once taken his top. The boy could not see what the Dorsey boy had to do with him.

"I never went in deep," he said. "I only went in to my knees. I was fishin' for crawdads."

"I don't care if you went in to your ankles. I told you not to go."

"Johnny Pettibone goes."

"I am not Johnny Pettibone's mother."

The boy regarded this as an unanswerable piece of logic, and for a moment he was silent before it. Then a sense of the vast injustice of the world began slowly to fill him. Johnny Pettibone went to the creek every day. Johnny Pettibone had caught a crawdad as long as a man's finger and had carried it about in a tomato can for a week, until it died and smelled, and was envied by every boy in the district. Johnny Pettibone had never been called into a kitchen. No green door had ever closed upon him. He went about the world free and wet and happy, while he, Willie, stood upon a brown oilcloth and was hounded for a few inches of water. He felt that he was the victim of a great conspiracy of grown persons, and that his mother was its chief.

"I don't see what's the harm," he muttered.

His mother unfolded her hands. The boy saw it from the corner of his eye, and he felt a sudden chill. He had gone too far. He had uttered rebellion in the very citadel of authority, and now the walls would fall upon him. He braced himself.

But his mother did not move toward him. She sat down in the chair by the table, heavily, as if she were tired, and she looked at him for a long time without speaking. The boy found this more terrible than any shouting. He would have welcomed shouting. Shouting was a storm that came and went. This silence was like the stillness before a battle, when the guns have stopped and no one knows from which quarter the next blow will fall.

"Willie," she said, "come here."

He came, one step and then another, and stood at her knee. She put out a hand and turned his face so that he must look at her. Her fingers were floury and smelled of yeast. He looked at her. Her eyes were gray, and there was something in them that he did not understand. It was not anger exactly. It was something else, something that troubled him because it did not belong to the world of switches and suppers and being sent upstairs.

"Do you know what I thought," she said, "when I went out to call you for your milk this afternoon and you weren't anywhere?"

The boy shook his head.

"I thought of the creek," she said. "I thought of the creek, and I thought of Mrs. Dorsey."

The boy was silent. He did not know what was expected of him. He perceived that his mother was speaking of something very large, something that loomed up behind her words like a mountain behind a fence, and he could not see the whole of it. He could see only the fence. And upon the fence there was written plainly that he had disobeyed, and that he was to be punished, and he fastened his attention upon this because it was a thing he could comprehend.

"I'm sorry," he said. He said it in the voice he used for saying his prayers.

"Are you sorry?" asked his mother. "Or are you sorry you were caught?"

This was an embarrassing question, and the boy examined it with great care. He discovered, upon reflection, that he was a little sorry for both reasons, but chiefly for the second, and he did not think it would be wise to say so. He looked at the loaves of bread. They sat in their row, brown and fat and indifferent, and he envied them. No one asked a loaf of bread whether it was sorry.

"Both," he said finally, which was nearer the truth than he had intended.

His mother's mouth moved at one corner. For an instant the boy had a wild hope that she was going to laugh. He had seen it happen before. He had seen his mother begin to scold him and then turn away suddenly toward the window, with her shoulders shaking, and when she turned back the storm had passed. He watched her face as a sailor watches the sky. But the corner of her mouth was still again, and she said, "Go and get me a switch from the lilac."

The words fell upon him like a sentence of death.

He went out of the kitchen. He went down the step. The hen, which had been standing by the step, regarded him with one round yellow eye and then walked away as if it wished to have nothing to do with criminals. The lilac bush stood at the corner of the house. It was a great bush, older than the boy, older than his mother perhaps, and in the spring it was covered with purple blossoms that smelled so sweet the bees went drunk among them. Now the blossoms were gone and the leaves were dark and dusty. It seemed to the boy that the bush had been planted there, long ago, for this one purpose. It was a gallows tree. It stood waiting.

He walked slowly around it. He studied each branch. He had a theory that a very thin switch, no thicker than a straw, would be less terrible than a thick one, and he looked for such a switch. But then another theory came to him, that a very thin switch would sting like a hornet, while a thick one would merely thump, and he began to search instead for a thick one. He found one and broke it off and then was seized by doubt. He threw it down and looked for another. He became absorbed in the problem. He walked around and around the lilac, bending and testing and discarding, until the ground at his feet was littered with branches like the field after a fight.

From the kitchen came his mother's voice. "Willie!"

He seized the nearest switch and went in. It was a switch of no particular character, neither thick nor thin, and he held it out before him as a defeated general holds out his sword.

His mother took it. She looked at it. She looked at the boy. Then she said, "Turn around."

The boy turned around. He faced the stove. The row of red eyes looked into his. He set his teeth and gripped the edge of the woodbox, and in that moment he was a martyr. He was a soldier taken by the enemy and put against a wall. He was a man in a story, tied to a stake while savages danced. He thought that when it was over he would go away. He would go away to the West, where there were buffaloes, and he would become very rich, and one day he would come back on a gigantic horse, and his mother would be standing in the doorway, and she would weep, and he would forgive her. He would forgive her nobly. He would get down from the gigantic horse and say, "Never mind, Ma." He was considering whether he would give her a buffalo robe when the switch fell.

It fell three times. It stung like a row of bees. The boy howled. He howled with a vigor that was out of all proportion to his injury, partly because it hurt and partly because some instinct told him that howling shortened these affairs. The buffaloes and the gigantic horse vanished entirely. The forgiveness vanished. There was nothing left in the world but the stove and the red eyes and the three hot stripes upon the backs of his legs.

Then it was over. His mother laid the switch upon the table beside the bread.

"Now go upstairs," she said, "and take off those wet things, and stay there until I call you."

The boy went. He went up the narrow stairs with great sobs that shook him like a cart going over stones. He made each sob as loud as possible, so that it might be heard in the kitchen. He wished his mother to know the full extent of what she had done. At the top of the stairs he paused and gave one sob of extraordinary magnitude, and then listened. From below came the sound of the oven door opening and the scrape of a pan. She was taking out the bread. She was taking out the bread as if nothing had happened, as if her son had not just been flogged nearly to death in her own kitchen. The boy was appalled at such callousness. He went into his room and shut the door very hard.

He took off his wet trousers and threw them into a corner, and he put on his other pair, which were too short and had a patch upon the knee. Then he lay down upon his bed on his stomach, because of the stripes, and buried his face in the pillow. The pillow smelled of soap and of sun. He lay there a long time and thought about his wrongs.

They were many. He reviewed them in order. There was the creek, which was the finest place in the world and which was denied to him alone of all boys. There was Johnny Pettibone and his crawdad. There was the Dorsey boy, who had taken his top and then had the effrontery to drown and become a reason. There was the lilac bush, which he resolved to cut down some day with an axe. There was his mother. He thought for a long time about his mother. He thought that she did not love him, and that perhaps she had never loved him, and that he was very likely not her son at all but a foundling left upon the doorstep in a basket. This idea pleased him greatly. He developed it. He imagined the basket and the storm and the mysterious stranger in a black cloak who had left it, and he imagined that one day the stranger would return and reveal that the boy was the son of a king. He was not certain which king. He decided it did not matter.

Through the window the light had changed. The yellow bars had climbed from the floor to the wall, and then up the wall, and now they had turned a deep orange and were lying across the ceiling. Outside, somewhere down the lane, he could hear boys shouting. They were playing at something. He could hear Johnny Pettibone's voice, high and shrill, crying, "You're dead! I got you! You're dead!" and another voice crying back, "I ain't neither!" The boy lifted his head and listened. He felt that the voices came to him from a great distance, from a lost and happy country to which he would never return. He was an exile. He was a prisoner in a tower. He put his head down again upon the pillow and was very sad, and the sadness was so large and so pleasant that he wallowed in it as a pig wallows in the cool mud of a summer afternoon.

After a time he grew tired of being sad. He turned over on his back, forgetting the stripes, and then remembered them and turned over again. He examined the wallpaper by the bed, which had a pattern of small blue baskets with flowers in them. He counted the baskets in one row. There were eleven. He counted the baskets in the next row and there were twelve, and this discrepancy occupied him for some time. He picked at a loose corner of the paper where it met the window frame, and then stopped, because he remembered that this also was forbidden, and he did not wish to give his enemies any further advantage.

Then, from below, there came up the stairs a smell. It was the smell of the new bread, and with it another smell, which the boy identified after a moment of intense concentration as fried ham. He sat up. The smell came in under the door and filled the room, warm and brown and wonderful, and it seemed to the boy that it was speaking to him. It said that the world was not perhaps so dark a place. It said that there might be eggs.

He went to the door and opened it a crack. He heard the clink of dishes and the sound of his mother moving about, and then he heard her begin to hum. She was humming a hymn, the one about the sweet by-and-by, and she hummed it slowly and a little out of tune, as she always did when she was setting the table.

The boy stood at the crack of the door and listened. Somewhere in him the grand edifice of his grievance began to tremble. He tried to hold it up. He reminded himself of the stripes, and of the lilac, and of the king who was his father. But the ham went on smelling, and his mother went on humming, and the edifice swayed and toppled and fell down, and there was nothing left of it but a small boy in short trousers who was very hungry.

"Willie," called his mother from the foot of the stairs. "Supper."

He did not answer at once. He felt that something was due to his dignity. He stood a moment longer, composing his face into an expression of cold and noble suffering. Then he went down the stairs. He went down slowly, one step at a time, with his chin up, like a prince who has been wronged but who will consent, out of the greatness of his heart, to eat.

His mother was standing by the stove. She did not look around. On his plate there was a slice of ham and a heel of the new bread, which was the part he liked best, spread thick with butter, and beside it a glass of milk. He sat down. He looked at the bread. It was the heel. She had given him the heel.

He ate it. He ate the ham and drank the milk, and when he had finished, his mother put another slice of bread before him without a word, and he ate that also. Outside, the orange light had gone to purple, and the voices of the boys in the lane had ceased. A whippoorwill began somewhere off in the Pettibone woods.

When at last he pushed back his chair his mother turned from the stove and looked at him, and he looked at her, and for a moment neither of them said anything. Then she came over and put her hand upon his hair, and it was the same floury hand, and he let it stay there.

"You won't go to the creek again?" she said.

"No'm," said the boy.

He meant it entirely. He meant it with his whole soul. He did not know that in four days the sun would be hot and the Pettibone bull would be in the far pasture and Johnny Pettibone would come whistling down the lane with a tomato can, and that the whole of this evening, the switch and the stripes and the tower and the king, would by then have shrunk to a small dim thing, no larger than a crawdad, and as easy to let go.

Pete took note of Maggie.

"Say, Mag, I'm stuck on yer shape. It's outa sight," he said, parenthetically, with an affable grin. As he became aware that she was listening closely, he grew still more eloquent in his descriptions of various happenings in his career. It appeared that he was invincible in fights.

"Why," he said, referring to a man with whom he had had a misunderstanding, "dat mug scrapped like a damn dago. Dat's right. He was dead easy. See? He tau't he was a scrapper. But he foun' out diff'ent! Hully gee." He walked to and fro in the small room, which seemed then to grow even smaller and unfit to hold his dignity, the attribute of a supreme warrior. That swing of the shoulders that had frozen the timid when he was but a lad had increased with his growth and education at the ratio of ten to one. It, combined with the sneer upon his mouth, told mankind that there was nothing in space which could appall him. Maggie marvelled at him and surrounded him with greatness. She vaguely tried to calculate the altitude of the pinnacle from which he must have looked down upon her.

"I met a chump deh odder day way up in deh city," he said. "I was goin' teh see a frien' of mine. When I was a-crossin' deh street deh chump runned plump inteh me, an' den he turns aroun' an' says, 'Yer insolen' ruffin,' he says, like dat. 'Oh, gee,' I says, 'oh, gee, go teh hell and git off deh eart',' I says, like dat. See? 'Go teh hell an' git off deh eart',' like dat. Den deh blokie he got wild. He says I was a contempt'ble scoun'el, er somet'ing like dat, an' he says I was doom' teh everlastin' pe'dition an' all like dat. 'Gee,' I says, 'gee! Deh hell I am,' I says. 'Deh hell I am,' like dat. An' den I slugged 'im. See?" With Jimmie in his company, Pete departed in a sort of a blaze of glory from the Johnson home. Maggie, leaning from the window, watched him as he walked down the street. Here was a formidable man who disdained the strength of a world full of fists. Here was one who had contempt for brass-clothed power; one whose knuckles could defiantly ring against the granite of law. He was a knight. The two men went from under the glimmering street-lamp and passed into shadows. Turning, Maggie contemplated the dark, dust-stained walls, and the scant and crude furniture of her home. A clock, in a splintered and battered oblong box of varnished wood, she suddenly regarded as an abomination. She noted that it ticked raspingly. The almost vanished flowers in the carpet-pattern, she conceived to be newly hideous. Some faint attempts she had made with blue ribbon, to freshen the appearance of a dingy curtain, she now saw to be piteous. She wondered what Pete dined on. She reflected upon the collar and cuff factory. It began to appear to her mind as a dreary place of endless grinding. Pete's elegant occupation brought him, no doubt, into contact with people who had money and manners. It was probable that he had a large acquaintance of pretty girls. He must have great sums of money to spend. To her the earth was composed of hardships and insults. She felt instant admiration for a man who openly defied it. She thought that if the grim angel of death should clutch his heart, Pete would shrug his shoulders and say: "Oh, ev'ryt'ing goes." She anticipated that he would come again shortly. She spent some of her week's pay in the purchase of flowered cretonne for a lambrequin. She made it with infinite care and hung it to the slightly-careening mantel, over the stove, in the kitchen. She studied it with painful anxiety from different points in the room. She wanted it to look well on Sunday night when, perhaps, Jimmie's friend would come. On Sunday night, however, Pete did not appear. Afterward the girl looked at it with a sense of humiliation. She was now convinced that Pete was superior to admiration for lambrequins. A few evenings later Pete entered with fascinating innovations in his apparel. As she had seen him twice and he had different suits on each time, Maggie had a dim impression that his wardrobe was prodigiously extensive.

"Say, Mag," he said, "put on yer bes' duds Friday night an' I'll take yehs teh deh show. See?" He spent a few moments in flourishing his clothes and then vanished, without having glanced at the lambrequin. Over the eternal collars and cuffs in the factory Maggie spent the most of three days in making imaginary sketches of Pete and his daily environment. She imagined some half dozen women in love with him and thought he must lean dangerously toward an indefinite one, whom she pictured with great charms of person, but with an altogether contemptible disposition. She thought he must live in a blare of pleasure. He had friends, and people who were afraid of him. She saw the golden glitter of the place where Pete was to take her. An entertainment of many hues and many melodies where she was afraid she might appear small and mouse-colored. Her mother drank whiskey all Friday morning. With lurid face and tossing hair she cursed and destroyed furniture all Friday afternoon. When Maggie came home at half-past six her mother lay asleep amidst the wreck of chairs and a table. Fragments of various household utensils were scattered about the floor. She had vented some phase of drunken fury upon the lambrequin. It lay in a bedraggled heap in the corner.

"Hah," she snorted, sitting up suddenly, "where deh hell yeh been? Why deh hell don' yeh come home earlier? Been loafin' 'round deh streets. Yer gettin' teh be a reg'lar devil." When Pete arrived Maggie, in a worn black dress, was waiting for him in the midst of a floor strewn with wreckage. The curtain at the window had been pulled by a heavy hand and hung by one tack, dangling to and fro in the draft through the cracks at the sash. The knots of blue ribbons appeared like violated flowers. The fire in the stove had gone out. The displaced lids and open doors showed heaps of sullen grey ashes. The remnants of a meal, ghastly, like dead flesh, lay in a corner. Maggie's red mother, stretched on the floor, blasphemed and gave her daughter a bad name.

An orchestra of yellow silk women and bald-headed men on an elevated stage near the centre of a great green-hued hall, played a popular waltz. The place was crowded with people grouped about little tables. A battalion of waiters slid among the throng, carrying trays of beer glasses and making change from the inexhaustible vaults of their trousers pockets. Little boys, in the costumes of French chefs, paraded up and down the irregular aisles vending fancy cakes. There was a low rumble of conversation and a subdued clinking of glasses. Clouds of tobacco smoke rolled and wavered high in air about the dull gilt of the chandeliers. The vast crowd had an air throughout of having just quitted labor. Men with calloused hands and attired in garments that showed the wear of an endless trudge for a living, smoked their pipes contentedly and spent five, ten, or perhaps fifteen cents for beer. There was a mere sprinkling of kid-gloved men who smoked cigars purchased elsewhere. The great body of the crowd was composed of people who showed that all day they strove with their hands. Quiet Germans, with maybe their wives and two or three children, sat listening to the music, with the expressions of happy cows. An occasional party of sailors from a war-ship, their faces pictures of sturdy health, spent the earlier hours of the evening at the small round tables. Very infrequent tipsy men, swollen with the value of their opinions, engaged their companions in earnest and confidential conversation. In the balcony, and here and there below, shone the impassive faces of women. The nationalities of the Bowery beamed upon the stage from all directions. Pete aggressively walked up a side aisle and took seats with Maggie at a table beneath the balcony.

"Two beehs!" Leaning back he regarded with eyes of superiority the scene before them. This attitude affected Maggie strongly. A man who could regard such a sight with indifference must be accustomed to very great things. It was obvious that Pete had been to this place many times before, and was very familiar with it. A knowledge of this fact made Maggie feel little and new. He was extremely gracious and attentive. He displayed the consideration of a cultured gentleman who knew what was due.

"Say, what deh hell? Bring deh lady a big glass! What deh hell use is dat pony?"

"Don't be fresh, now," said the waiter, with some warmth, as he departed.

"Ah, git off deh eart'," said Pete, after the other's retreating form. Maggie perceived that Pete brought forth all his elegance and all his knowledge of high-class customs for her benefit. Her heart warmed as she reflected upon his condescension. The orchestra of yellow silk women and bald-headed men gave vent to a few bars of anticipatory music and a girl, in a pink dress with short skirts, galloped upon the stage. She smiled upon the throng as if in acknowledgment of a warm welcome, and began to walk to and fro, making profuse gesticulations and singing, in brazen soprano tones, a song, the words of which were inaudible. When she broke into the swift rattling measures of a chorus some half-tipsy men near the stage joined in the rollicking refrain and glasses were pounded rhythmically upon the tables.

Excerpt 2: In a hall of irregular shape sat Pete and Maggie drinking beer. A submissive orchestra dictated to by a spectacled man with frowsy hair and a dress suit, industriously followed the bobs of his head and the waves of his baton. A ballad singer, in a dress of flaming scarlet, sang in the inevitable voice of brass. When she vanished, men seated at the tables near the front applauded loudly, pounding the polished wood with their beer glasses. She returned attired in less gown, and sang again. She received another enthusiastic encore. She reappeared in still less gown and danced. The deafening rumble of glasses and clapping of hands that followed her exit indicated an overwhelming desire to have her come on for the fourth time, but the curiosity of the audience was not gratified. Maggie was pale. From her eyes had been plucked all look of self-reliance. She leaned with a dependent air toward her companion. She was timid, as if fearing his anger or displeasure. She seemed to beseech tenderness of him. Pete's air of distinguished valor had grown upon him until it threatened stupendous dimensions. He was infinitely gracious to the girl. It was apparent to her that his condescension was a marvel. He could appear to strut even while sitting still and he showed that he was a lion of lordly characteristics by the air with which he spat. With Maggie gazing at him wonderingly, he took pride in commanding the waiters who were, however, indifferent or deaf.

"Hi, you, git a russle on yehs! What deh hell yehs lookin' at? Two more beehs, d'yeh hear?" He leaned back and critically regarded the person of a girl with a straw-colored wig who upon the stage was flinging her heels in somewhat awkward imitation of a well-known danseuse. At times Maggie told Pete long confidential tales of her former home life, dwelling upon the escapades of the other members of the family and the difficulties she had to combat in order to obtain a degree of comfort. He responded in tones of philanthropy. He pressed her arm with an air of reassuring proprietorship.

"Dey was damn jays," he said, denouncing the mother and brother. The sound of the music which, by the efforts of the frowsy-headed leader, drifted to her ears through the smoke-filled atmosphere, made the girl dream. She thought of her former Rum Alley environment and turned to regard Pete's strong protecting fists. She thought of the collar and cuff manufactory and the eternal moan of the proprietor: "What een hell do you sink I pie fife dolla a week for? Play? No, py damn." She contemplated Pete's man-subduing eyes and noted that wealth and prosperity was indicated by his clothes. She imagined a future, rose-tinted, because of its distance from all that she previously had experienced. As to the present she perceived only vague reasons to be miserable. Her life was Pete's and she considered him worthy of the charge. She would be disturbed by no particular apprehensions, so long as Pete adored her as he now said he did. She did not feel like a bad woman. To her knowledge she had never seen any better. At times men at other tables regarded the girl furtively. Pete, aware of it, nodded at her and grinned. He felt proud.

"Mag, yer a bloomin' good-looker," he remarked, studying her face through the haze. The men made Maggie fear, but she blushed at Pete's words as it became apparent to her that she was the apple of his eye. Grey-headed men, wonderfully pathetic in their dissipation, stared at her through clouds. Smooth-cheeked boys, some of them with faces of stone and mouths of sin, not nearly so pathetic as the grey heads, tried to find the girl's eyes in the smoke wreaths. Maggie considered she was not what they thought her. She confined her glances to Pete and the stage. The orchestra played negro melodies and a versatile drummer pounded, whacked, clattered and scratched on a dozen machines to make noise. Those glances of the men, shot at Maggie from under half-closed lids, made her tremble. She thought them all to be worse men than Pete.

"Come, let's go," she said. As they went out Maggie perceived two women seated at a table with some men. They were painted and their cheeks had lost their roundness. As she passed them the girl, with a shrinking movement, drew back her skirts.

Jimmie did not return home for a number of days after the fight with Pete in the saloon. When he did, he approached with extreme caution. He found his mother raving. Maggie had not returned home. The parent continually wondered how her daughter could come to such a pass. She had never considered Maggie as a pearl dropped unstained into Rum Alley from Heaven, but she could not conceive how it was possible for her daughter to fall so low as to bring disgrace upon her family. She was terrific in denunciation of the girl's wickedness. The fact that the neighbors talked of it, maddened her. When women came in, and in the course of their conversation casually asked, "Where's Maggie dese days?" the mother shook her fuzzy head at them and appalled them with curses. Cunning hints inviting confidence she rebuffed with violence.

"An' wid all deh bringin' up she had, how could she?" moaningly she asked of her son. "Wid all deh talkin' wid her I did an' deh t'ings I tol' her to remember? When a girl is bringed up deh way I bringed up Maggie, how kin she go teh deh devil?" Jimmie was transfixed by these questions. He could not conceive how under the circumstances his mother's daughter and his sister could have been so wicked. His mother took a drink from a squdgy bottle that sat on the table. She continued her lament.

"She had a bad heart, dat girl did, Jimmie. She was wicked teh deh heart an' we never knowed it." Jimmie nodded, admitting the fact.

"We lived in deh same house wid her an' I brought her up an' we never knowed how bad she was." Jimmie nodded again.

"Wid a home like dis an' a mudder like me, she went teh deh bad," cried the mother, raising her eyes. One day, Jimmie came home, sat down in a chair and began to wriggle about with a new and strange nervousness. At last he spoke shamefacedly.

"Well, look-a-here, dis t'ing queers us! See? We're queered! An' maybe it 'ud be better if I—well, I t'ink I kin look 'er up an'—maybe it 'ud be better if I fetched her home an'—" The mother started from her chair and broke forth into a storm of passionate anger.

"What! Let 'er come an' sleep under deh same roof wid her mudder agin! Oh, yes, I will, won't I? Sure? Shame on yehs, Jimmie Johnson, for sayin' such a t'ing teh yer own mudder—teh yer own mudder! Little did I t'ink when yehs was a babby playin' about me feet dat ye'd grow up teh say sech a t'ing teh yer mudder—yer own mudder. I never taut—" Sobs choked her and interrupted her reproaches.

"Dere ain't nottin' teh raise sech hell about," said Jimmie. "I on'y says it 'ud be better if we keep dis t'ing dark, see? It queers us! See?" His mother laughed a laugh that seemed to ring through the city and be echoed and re-echoed by countless other laughs. "Oh, yes, I will, won't I! Sure!"

"Well, yeh must take me fer a damn fool," said Jimmie, indignant at his mother for mocking him. "I didn't say we'd make 'er inteh a little tin angel, ner nottin', but deh way it is now she can queer us! Don' che see?"

"Aye, she'll git tired of deh life atter a while an' den she'll wanna be a-comin' home, won' she, deh beast! I'll let 'er in den, won' I?"

"Well, I didn' mean none of dis prod'gal bus'ness anyway," explained Jimmie.

"It wasn't no prod'gal dauter, yeh damn fool," said the mother. "It was prod'gal son, anyhow."

"I know dat," said Jimmie. For a time they sat in silence. The mother's eyes gloated on a scene her imagination could call before her. Her lips were set in a vindictive smile.

"Aye, she'll cry, won' she, an' carry on, an' tell how Pete, or some odder feller, beats 'er an' she'll say she's sorry an' all dat an' she ain't happy, she ain't, an' she wants to come home agin, she does." With grim humor, the mother imitated the possible wailing notes of the daughter's voice.

"Den I'll take 'er in, won't I, deh beast. She kin cry 'er two eyes out on deh stones of deh street before I'll dirty deh place wid her. She abused an' ill-treated her own mudder—her own mudder what loved her an' she'll never git anodder chance dis side of hell." Jimmie thought he had a great idea of women's frailty, but he could not understand why any of his kin should be victims.

"Damn her," he fervidly said. Again he wondered vaguely if some of the women of his acquaintance had brothers. Nevertheless, his mind did not for an instant confuse himself with those brothers nor his sister with theirs. After the mother had, with great difficulty, suppressed the neighbors, she went among them and proclaimed her grief. "May Gawd forgive dat girl," was her continual cry. To attentive ears she recited the whole length and breadth of her woes.

"I bringed 'er up deh way a dauter oughta be bringed up an' dis is how she served me! She went teh deh devil deh first chance she got! May Gawd forgive her." When arrested for drunkenness she used the story of her daughter's downfall with telling effect upon the police justices. Finally one of them said to her, peering down over his spectacles: "Mary, the records of this and other courts show that you are the mother of forty-two daughters who have been ruined. The case is unparalleled in the annals of this court, and this court thinks—" The mother went through life shedding large tears of sorrow. Her red face was a picture of agony. Of course Jimmie publicly damned his sister that he might appear on a higher social plane. But, arguing with himself, stumbling about in ways that he knew not, he, once, almost came to a conclusion that his sister would have been more firmly good had she better known why. However, he felt that he could not hold such a view. He threw it hastily aside.

In a hilarious hall there were twenty-eight tables and twenty-eight women and a crowd of smoking men. Valiant noise was made on a stage at the end of the hall by an orchestra composed of men who looked as if they had just happened in. Soiled waiters ran to and fro, swooping down like hawks on the unwary in the throng; clattering along the aisles with trays covered with glasses; stumbling over women's skirts and charging two prices for everything but beer, all with a swiftness that blurred the view of the cocoanut palms and dusty monstrosities painted upon the walls of the room. A bouncer, with an immense load of business upon his hands, plunged about in the crowd, dragging bashful strangers to prominent chairs, ordering waiters here and there and quarreling furiously with men who wanted to sing with the orchestra. The usual smoke cloud was present, but so dense that heads and arms seemed entangled in it. The rumble of conversation was replaced by a roar. Plenteous oaths heaved through the air. The room rang with the shrill voices of women bubbling o'er with drink-laughter. The chief element in the music of the orchestra was speed. The musicians played in intent fury. A woman was singing and smiling upon the stage, but no one took notice of her. The rate at which the piano, cornet and violins were going, seemed to impart wildness to the half-drunken crowd. Beer glasses were emptied at a gulp and conversation became a rapid chatter. The smoke eddied and swirled like a shadowy river hurrying toward some unseen falls. Pete and Maggie entered the hall and took chairs at a table near the door. The woman who was seated there made an attempt to occupy Pete's attention and, failing, went away. Three weeks had passed since the girl had left home. The air of spaniel-like dependence had been magnified and showed its direct effect in the peculiar off-handedness and ease of Pete's ways toward her. She followed Pete's eyes with hers, anticipating with smiles gracious looks from him. A woman of brilliance and audacity, accompanied by a mere boy, came into the place and took seats near them. At once Pete sprang to his feet, his face beaming with glad surprise.

"By Gawd, there's Nellie," he cried. He went over to the table and held out an eager hand to the woman.

"Why, hello, Pete, me boy, how are you," said she, giving him her fingers. Maggie took instant note of the woman. She perceived that her black dress fitted her to perfection. Her linen collar and cuffs were spotless. Tan gloves were stretched over her well-shaped hands. A hat of a prevailing fashion perched jauntily upon her dark hair. She wore no jewelry and was painted with no apparent paint. She looked clear-eyed through the stares of the men.

"Sit down, and call your lady-friend over," she said cordially to Pete. At his beckoning Maggie came and sat between Pete and the mere boy.

"I thought yeh were gone away fer good," began Pete, at once. "When did yeh git back? How did dat Buff'lo bus'ness turn out?" The woman shrugged her shoulders. "Well, he didn't have as many stamps as he tried to make out, so I shook him, that's all."

"Well, I'm glad teh see yehs back in deh city," said Pete, with awkward gallantry. He and the woman entered into a long conversation, exchanging reminiscences of days together. Maggie sat still, unable to formulate an intelligent sentence upon the conversation and painfully aware of it. She saw Pete's eyes sparkle as he gazed upon the handsome stranger. He listened smilingly to all she said. The woman was familiar with all his affairs, asked him about mutual friends, and knew the amount of his salary. She paid no attention to Maggie, looking toward her once or twice and apparently seeing the wall beyond. The mere boy was sulky. In the beginning he had welcomed with acclamations the additions.

"Let's all have a drink! What'll you take, Nell? And you, Miss what's-your-name. Have a drink, Mr. ——-, you, I mean." He had shown a sprightly desire to do the talking for the company and tell all about his family. In a loud voice he declaimed on various topics. He assumed a patronizing air toward Pete. As Maggie was silent, he paid no attention to her. He made a great show of lavishing wealth upon the woman of brilliance and audacity.

"Do keep still, Freddie! You gibber like an ape, dear," said the woman to him. She turned away and devoted her attention to Pete.

"We'll have many a good time together again, eh?"

"Sure, Mike," said Pete, enthusiastic at once.

"Say," whispered she, leaning forward, "let's go over to Billie's and have a heluva time."

"Well, it's dis way! See?" said Pete. "I got dis lady frien' here."

"Oh, t'hell with her," argued the woman. Pete appeared disturbed.

"All right," said she, nodding her head at him. "All right for you! We'll see the next time you ask me to go anywheres with you." Pete squirmed.

Excerpt 3: Pete did not consider that he had ruined Maggie. If he had thought that her soul could never smile again, he would have believed the mother and brother, who were pyrotechnic over the affair, to be responsible for it. Besides, in his world, souls did not insist upon being able to smile. "What deh hell?" He felt a trifle entangled. It distressed him. Revelations and scenes might bring upon him the wrath of the owner of the saloon, who insisted upon respectability of an advanced type.

"What deh hell do dey wanna raise such a smoke about it fer?" demanded he of himself, disgusted with the attitude of the family. He saw no necessity for anyone's losing their equilibrium merely because their sister or their daughter had stayed away from home. Searching about in his mind for possible reasons for their conduct, he came upon the conclusion that Maggie's motives were correct, but that the two others wished to snare him. He felt pursued. The woman of brilliance and audacity whom he had met in the hilarious hall showed a disposition to ridicule him.

"A little pale thing with no spirit," she said. "Did you note the expression of her eyes? There was something in them about pumpkin pie and virtue. That is a peculiar way the left corner of her mouth has of twitching, isn't it? Dear, dear, my cloud-compelling Pete, what are you coming to?" Pete asserted at once that he never was very much interested in the girl. The woman interrupted him, laughing.

"Oh, it's not of the slightest consequence to me, my dear young man. You needn't draw maps for my benefit. Why should I be concerned about it?" But Pete continued with his explanations. If he was laughed at for his tastes in women, he felt obliged to say that they were only temporary or indifferent ones. The morning after Maggie had departed from home, Pete stood behind the bar. He was immaculate in white jacket and apron and his hair was plastered over his brow with infinite correctness. No customers were in the place. Pete was twisting his napkined fist slowly in a beer glass, softly whistling to himself and occasionally holding the object of his attention between his eyes and a few weak beams of sunlight that had found their way over the thick screens and into the shaded room. With lingering thoughts of the woman of brilliance and audacity, the bartender raised his head and stared through the varying cracks between the swaying bamboo doors. Suddenly the whistling pucker faded from his lips. He saw Maggie walking slowly past. He gave a great start, fearing for the previously-mentioned eminent respectability of the place. He threw a swift, nervous glance about him, all at once feeling guilty. No one was in the room. He went hastily over to the side door. Opening it and looking out, he perceived Maggie standing, as if undecided, on the corner. She was searching the place with her eyes. As she turned her face toward him Pete beckoned to her hurriedly, intent upon returning with speed to a position behind the bar and to the atmosphere of respectability upon which the proprietor insisted. Maggie came to him, the anxious look disappearing from her face and a smile wreathing her lips.

"Oh, Pete—," she began brightly. The bartender made a violent gesture of impatience.

"Oh, my Gawd," cried he, vehemently. "What deh hell do yeh wanna hang aroun' here fer? Do yeh wanna git me inteh trouble?" he demanded with an air of injury. Astonishment swept over the girl's features. "Why, Pete! yehs tol' me—" Pete glanced profound irritation. His countenance reddened with the anger of a man whose respectability is being threatened.

"Say, yehs makes me tired. See? What deh hell deh yeh wanna tag aroun' atter me fer? Yeh'll git me inteh trouble wid deh ol' man an' dey'll be hell teh pay! If he sees a woman roun' here he'll go crazy an' I'll lose me job! See? Yer brudder come in here an' raised hell an' deh ol' man hada put up fer it! An' now I'm done! See? I'm done." The girl's eyes stared into his face. "Pete, don't yeh remem—" "Oh, hell," interrupted Pete, anticipating. The girl seemed to have a struggle with herself. She was apparently bewildered and could not find speech. Finally she asked in a low voice: "But where kin I go?" The question exasperated Pete beyond the powers of endurance. It was a direct attempt to give him some responsibility in a matter that did not concern him. In his indignation he volunteered information.

"Oh, go teh hell," cried he. He slammed the door furiously and returned, with an air of relief, to his respectability. Maggie went away. She wandered aimlessly for several blocks. She stopped once and asked aloud a question of herself: "Who?" A man who was passing near her shoulder, humorously took the questioning word as intended for him.

"Eh? What? Who? Nobody! I didn't say anything," he laughingly said, and continued his way. Soon the girl discovered that if she walked with such apparent aimlessness, some men looked at her with calculating eyes. She quickened her step, frightened. As a protection, she adopted a demeanor of intentness as if going somewhere. After a time she left rattling avenues and passed between rows of houses with sternness and stolidity stamped upon their features. She hung her head for she felt their eyes grimly upon her. Suddenly she came upon a stout gentleman in a silk hat and a chaste black coat, whose decorous row of buttons reached from his chin to his knees. The girl had heard of the Grace of God and she decided to approach this man. His beaming, chubby face was a picture of benevolence and kind-heartedness. His eyes shone good-will. But as the girl timidly accosted him, he gave a convulsive movement and saved his respectability by a vigorous side-step. He did not risk it to save a soul. For how was he to know that there was a soul before him that needed saving?

Upon a wet evening, several months after the last chapter, two interminable rows of cars, pulled by slipping horses, jangled along a prominent side-street. A dozen cabs, with coat-enshrouded drivers, clattered to and fro. Electric lights, whirring softly, shed a blurred radiance. A flower dealer, his feet tapping impatiently, his nose and his wares glistening with rain-drops, stood behind an array of roses and chrysanthemums. Two or three theatres emptied a crowd upon the storm-swept pavements. Men pulled their hats over their eyebrows and raised their collars to their ears. Women shrugged impatient shoulders in their warm cloaks and stopped to arrange their skirts for a walk through the storm. People having been comparatively silent for two hours burst into a roar of conversation, their hearts still kindling from the glowings of the stage. The pavements became tossing seas of umbrellas. Men stepped forth to hail cabs or cars, raising their fingers in varied forms of polite request or imperative demand. An endless procession wended toward elevated stations. An atmosphere of pleasure and prosperity seemed to hang over the throng, born, perhaps, of good clothes and of having just emerged from a place of forgetfulness. In the mingled light and gloom of an adjacent park, a handful of wet wanderers, in attitudes of chronic dejection, was scattered among the benches. A girl of the painted cohorts of the city went along the street. She threw changing glances at men who passed her, giving smiling invitations to men of rural or untaught pattern and usually seeming sedately unconscious of the men with a metropolitan seal upon their faces. Crossing glittering avenues, she went into the throng emerging from the places of forgetfulness. She hurried forward through the crowd as if intent upon reaching a distant home, bending forward in her handsome cloak, daintily lifting her skirts and picking for her well-shod feet the dryer spots upon the pavements. The restless doors of saloons, clashing to and fro, disclosed animated rows of men before bars and hurrying barkeepers. A concert hall gave to the street faint sounds of swift, machine-like music, as if a group of phantom musicians were hastening. A tall young man, smoking a cigarette with a sublime air, strolled near the girl. He had on evening dress, a moustache, a chrysanthemum, and a look of ennui, all of which he kept carefully under his eye. Seeing the girl walk on as if such a young man as he was not in existence, he looked back transfixed with interest. He stared glassily for a moment, but gave a slight convulsive start when he discerned that she was neither new, Parisian, nor theatrical. "Sure," again they chorused.

"Yessir," he cried, with deep earnestness, as if someone disputed him. "I'm damn goo' f'ler, an' w'en anyone trea's me ri', I allus trea's—le's have nozzer drink." He began to beat the wood with his glass.

"Shay," howled he again. The waiter appeared at the door.

"Bringsh drinksh," said the man. The waiter disappeared with the orders.

"Zat f'ler damn fool," cried the man. "He insul' me! I'm ge'man! Can' stan' be insul'! I'm goin' lickim when comes!"

"No, no," cried the women, crowding about and trying to subdue him. "He's all right! He didn't mean anything! Let it go! He's a good fellah!"

"Din' he insul' me?" asked the man earnestly.

"No," said they. "Of course he didn't! He's all right!"

"Sure he didn' insul' me?" demanded the man, with deep anxiety in his voice.

"No, no! We know him! He's a good fellah. He didn't mean anything."

"Well, zen," said the man, resolutely, "I'm go' 'pol'gize!" When the waiter came, the man struggled to the middle of the floor.

"Girlsh shed you insul' me! I shay damn lie! I 'pol'gize!"

"All right," said the waiter.

Twilight came down upon Mullen's Court like a soiled blanket thrown over a bed by a careless hand. The tenements, tall and shouldering one another, stood with their windows lighted here and there in a dim yellow, as if the buildings were blinking in a stupid effort to stay awake. From doorways came the smell of boiled cabbage and the noise of quarrels. Upon the fire-escapes hung garments of every shade of weariness, and these swung softly in the little wind from the river, like the ghosts of laborers who had been hanged for their sins.

On the fourth floor, at a window that looked down upon the cobbles, sat Kate Halloran, finishing vests. She sewed with the swift, small, ceaseless motion of a woman who is paid by the dozen. A pile of finished garments lay at her elbow and a larger pile of unfinished ones lay at her feet. The lamp on the table was turned low, for oil cost money, and she bent close to her work so that her face was lit from below with a sallow glare. It was a thin face. It had once been round, and the neighbors who remembered her wedding day said that she had been a fine, strapping girl. They said it now in the tone that is used at funerals.

Upon a heap of coats in the corner a small boy slept with his fist in his mouth. The room held a stove, a table, three chairs of varying degrees of infirmity, a bed with a mended quilt, and a clock. The clock sat upon a shelf over the stove. It was a cheap, black, solemn object with a cracked face, and it ticked with the loud, judicial air of a thing that had been appointed to keep accounts.

Kate looked at it often. She had been looking at it since six o'clock.

It was Saturday. On Saturday Dennis Halloran received his pay from the trucking company. On Monday the agent of the landlord would climb the four flights of stairs, wheezing and important, with a small book in his hand. He was a fat man with a waxed moustache and a soul composed entirely of arithmetic. He had told Kate, the month before, that he had his orders, and he had said it with the regret of a man who would very much enjoy obeying them.

The philosophers of the building had discussed the Hallorans. The woman across the hall, who had buried two husbands and therefore spoke with authority upon the whole subject, had declared that Dennis was not a bad man, but that he had a weakness. She did not say what the weakness was. She did not need to. The entire court had seen it, at various times, being carried home from Fogarty's place upon the shoulders of friends.

The clock said half-past eight. Kate bit off a thread and looked at the door.

Presently there came a sound of feet upon the stairs. They were heavy feet, but they climbed with a curious caution, as if each step were a separate negotiation. They paused upon the landing below. They paused again outside the door. Kate did not raise her head. She drove her needle through the cloth and drew it out, and drove it in again.

The door opened and Dennis Halloran came in.

He was a large man with a red neck and a brown moustache that drooped over his mouth like a curtain drawn upon a scene of guilt. His hat was pushed back from his forehead. His coat was open and showed a vest of a flowered pattern that had been, in its youth, the pride of a second-hand shop on Chatham Street. He brought with him into the room a strong smell of horses and a faint, sweet smell of whiskey, and an air of having been grievously wronged by the whole of creation.

He hung his hat on a nail. He did it slowly and with great attention, as if the hat were a delicate instrument. Then he sat down in the least infirm of the chairs and began to unlace his boots.

"Well," he said, "I'm home."

"I see yeh are," said Kate.

He worked at a knot in his lace. It resisted him. He swore at it in a low voice, briefly, as a general might swear at a disobedient private.

"Deh boss kep' us late," he said. "Dere was a load of hides come in off a boat, an' he says, 'Halloran, you take dem,' he says. Always me. Always it's Halloran. Dere's men in dat stable dat don' do nottin' but set on deh feed-box an' chew, an' it's always Halloran dat gits deh hides."

Kate sewed.

"I'm dead tired," said Dennis. He pulled off a boot and dropped it upon the floor with a thud that seemed meant to establish the fact. The boy in the corner stirred and muttered and was still.

"Where's deh money, Dennis?"

The other boot came off. Dennis regarded it. He turned it over in his hands as if he expected to find something written upon the sole.

"What money?"

Kate laid the vest down upon her knees. She did not look at him. She looked at the clock, which ticked.

"Deh money," she said. "Deh pay. It's Sattiday. Deh man's comin' Monday. Yeh know he's comin' Monday."

"Oh, deh rent," said Dennis, as if the matter had escaped him in the press of more considerable affairs. "Sure. Deh rent." He set the boot down carefully beside its fellow and placed his large hands upon his knees. He cleared his throat. He had the look of a man about to address a public meeting upon a subject of grave importance.

"Now, lookit here, Kate," he began. "Yeh don' unnerstan' about dese t'ings. A woman don' unnerstan' business. Dat's all right. Dat ain't nottin' against her. It ain't deh way she's made. But I'm tellin' yeh, an' yeh listen teh me. Dere was a man in deh stable, Mike Dolan, see, an' he's got a cousin dat's a sparrin' partner wid deh Brooklyn Swede. Yeh know who deh Brooklyn Swede is?"

"No."

"Well, he's a scrapper. He's deh best middle-weight dere is dis side of Chicago. Dat's what he is. An' he was goin' teh fight a mug from Philadelphy las' night down at deh club on Water Street, an' Dolan's cousin, he says it was a dead sure t'ing. Dead sure! He says deh Swede was goin' teh put deh Philadelphy mug teh sleep in deh t'ird round. He says he seen deh Swede hit a bag so hard deh bag busted. Dat's what he says."

He paused, as if expecting applause. The clock ticked.

"So me an' Dolan an' a couple of deh odder fellers, we puts our money togedder. See? It was a chanct, Kate. It was deh kind of chanct a man don' git but once. Two teh one, we got. Two teh one! I'd 'a' come home here wid twenty-two dollars in me pocket, an' paid dat fat mug his rent, an' had enough over teh buy yeh a hat. A hat wid a feather on it, like dem dat yeh see on Grand Street. I was t'inkin' about dat hat all day. Honest teh Gawd I was."

He looked at her with eyes that had grown moist at the vision of his own generosity. In his mind the hat was already purchased. He could see it upon her head. He felt that he deserved her gratitude for it.

"An' deh Swede lost," said Kate.

Dennis struck his knee with his fist. His face darkened with a righteous wrath.

"Lost! He laid down! He laid down like a dog in deh fift' round! Dere wasn't nottin' deh matter wid him. Deh Philadelphy mug hit him a little tap on deh ear, like dat, an' down he goes, an' he lays dere an' he don' git up. He was fixed. Dat's what it was. Somebody got teh him. Dolan says so. Everybody says so. Dere was men dere dat wanted teh go up an' kill him. I'd 'a' killed him meself if I could 'a' got trough deh crowd."

He breathed heavily. It was plain that he regarded himself as the victim of a vast conspiracy, in which the Brooklyn Swede, the man from Philadelphia, the club on Water Street, and possibly the police and the clergy had all combined against Dennis Halloran.

"How much?" said Kate.

"What?"

"How much of deh money?"

Dennis moved in his chair. He looked at the stove. He looked at the window, where the dark had come down entirely and the panes gave back a dim picture of the room, a lamp and a woman and a man with his boots off.

"Well," he said, "it was all of it. But I'm tellin' yeh it was a sure t'ing."

Kate took up the vest again. Her needle went in and came out. Her face did not alter, save that the corner of her mouth drew down, very slightly, as if pulled by a thread.

The silence grew in the room until it seemed to press against the walls. Dennis felt it. He shifted. It was not a silence he understood. He would have preferred that she scream at him. Screaming he could meet. He had met it before, and had roared it down, and had gone out afterward to Fogarty's with the comfortable sense of a man who has asserted himself. But this quiet sewing appeared to him a kind of insolence.

"Well, what deh hell?" he burst out. "Ain't yeh goin' teh say nottin'? I'm tellin' yeh it wasn't me fault! I'm tellin' yeh deh fight was fixed! What deh hell d'yeh want me teh do? Go down teh Water Street an' lick deh whole club?"

"I want deh rent," said Kate.

"Well, I ain't got it! See? I ain't got it! Yeh can' git blood out of a stone!"

"Yeh had it dis mornin'."

He rose from the chair. He was a large man and he made the room seem small. He stood in his stocking feet upon the bare boards and glared down at her, and she continued to sew.

"Lookit here," he said, in a voice that trembled with the injury of it, "I work like a horse. I'm up at five o'clock in deh mornin' an' I'm out in deh col' an' deh wet all day, haulin' hides an' barrels an' Gawd knows what, an' a man's got a right teh a little chanct now an' den. A man's got a right teh try an' better himself. Ain't he? Ain't he got a right?"

"Deh kid ain't had no shoes since deh first of deh month," said Kate.

"Dere yeh go! Dere yeh go! Throwin' deh kid in me face! Like I didn' know about deh kid! Like I wasn't t'inkin' about deh kid when I put deh money down! What d'yeh t'ink I was goin' teh do wid deh twenty-two dollars? Drink it? I was goin' teh buy deh kid shoes. An' you a hat. I tol' yeh about deh hat."

He had now entirely forgotten that until this moment he had not thought of the shoes. He believed fully in his own intention. He saw himself, a noble father, returning with shoes beneath his arm, and the picture moved him. He felt that his wife, by refusing to see it, was guilty of a deep ingratitude.

Kate laid the vest aside a second time. She folded her hands in her lap. They were red hands, with the needle-marks upon the fingers like the marks of a small and patient torture.

"I'll tell yeh somet'ing, Dennis," she said. "Two weeks ago dere wasn't no coal. Yeh remember? Yeh was out dat night. Yeh was out a good many nights. An' deh kid was cryin' wid deh col', an' I took me mudder's ring down teh deh place on deh corner, an' I got t'ree dollars fer it. An' I bought coal."

Dennis stared at her. His mouth opened beneath the curtain of his moustache.

"Yer mudder's ring?"

"Yes."

"Yeh pawned it? Widout tellin' me?"

"Yes."

Upon his face there came slowly an expression of profound and virtuous horror. He drew himself up. He seemed to swell. He had found, at last, solid ground on which a man could stand.

"Well, by Gawd!" he cried. "By Gawd! An' you settin' dere an' talkin' teh me about deh rent! You! Pawnin' t'ings behind a man's back! Yer own mudder's ring dat she left yeh when she died! Ain't yeh got no shame? Ain't yeh got no feelin's? What kind of a woman is it dat goes an' pawns her own mudder's ring an' don' say nottin' teh her husband? Dat's a fine t'ing! Dat's a fine t'ing teh do!"

His voice rose until it rang against the ceiling. Somewhere beyond the wall a door opened softly, and stayed open. The woman who had buried two husbands was listening, with her head on one side, as a connoisseur listens to music.

"Dat's deceivin'," roared Dennis. "Dat's what it is! It's deceivin' a man! An' den yeh set dere wid yer mout' shut like a preacher an' make out I'm deh one dat's done wrong!"

The boy on the coats awoke and sat up and began to wail, thinly, with his fists in his eyes. Neither of them looked at him.

"I didn' have no money," said Kate. "Yeh had deh money."

"Don' gimme none of dat! Don' gimme none of dat!" He raised his hand. It was a large hand, hardened by the reins. It hung in the air above her head, and the lamp threw its shadow upon the wall, huge and black and wavering, like the hand of some swollen god.

Kate looked up at it. She did not move. Her eyes, in the yellow glare, were very still. There was no fear in them, and no anger. There was only a vast fatigue, as if she had been looking at that hand for a hundred years and had grown weary of its never coming down nor ever going away.

The clock ticked. The boy wailed. Beyond the wall the open door creaked a little upon its hinges.

Dennis let his hand fall. He did not know why. He felt that he had been robbed of something, and he did not know of what. He turned away and began to search about the floor for his boots.

"I ain't goin' teh stay here an' be talked teh like dis," he said thickly. "A man comes home tired, an' dis is what he gits. Dis is what he gits." He found a boot and sat down and dragged it on, and the lace broke in his fingers. "Damn it! Look at dat! Everyt'ing in dis house is busted."

"Where yeh goin'?"

"I'm goin' teh see a frien' of mine. See? I'm goin' teh git deh money. Dere's men in dis world dat knows how teh treat a feller. Dere's men dat'll stan' by a feller when he's down. I ain't askin' you fer nottin'. I'll git deh money meself."

He got the other boot on. He took his hat from the nail and clapped it upon his head with a violence that expressed his opinion of women, of rent, of the Brooklyn Swede, and of the arrangement of the universe. At the door he turned.

"An' I'm tellin' yeh one t'ing," he said. "When I git dat money, yeh needn't t'ink yer goin' teh git no hat."

The door slammed. His feet went down the stairs, no longer cautious, but loud and hurried, as if each step were a separate blow struck in a just cause. Across the hall the other door closed softly.

Kate went over to the corner and lifted the boy and held him against her shoulder, swaying, until his wailing sank to a hiccough and then to silence. When he slept she laid him down again upon the coats. She stood for a moment looking at him. Then she went back to her chair by the window and turned the lamp a trifle lower, and took up the vest.

In Fogarty's place the gas burned with a warm and confidential glow. The mirror behind the bar reflected rows of bottles that shone like the jewels of a heathen idol. The sawdust upon the floor was fresh. A dozen men stood along the rail in attitudes of comfort, each with one foot raised, as though they were all upon the point of ascending a staircase into some better world and had paused here to fortify themselves for the climb.

Dennis Halloran came in and placed his elbows upon the bar. He looked about him with the air of a man who has escaped from a burning house.

"Gimme a short beer," he said.

Fogarty drew it. He was a silent man with a bald head and a white apron, and he had heard a great many speeches.

Dennis drank half the beer. He wiped his moustache with the back of his hand. Then he turned to the man at his left, who was a stevedore of his acquaintance named Corcoran.

"Women," said Dennis darkly.

Corcoran nodded. He did not need to be told more. He had a wife on Monroe Street.

"Yeh work like a horse," said Dennis, "an' yeh try teh better yerself, an' what d'yeh git? Dey don' unnerstan' a man. Dey can' see nottin' but deh rent. Deh rent, deh rent, deh rent. Dat's all a woman t'inks about."

"Sure," said Corcoran.

"An' all deh time," said Dennis, leaning closer and lowering his voice so that it might carry farther, "all deh time she's goin' around behind yer back an' pawnin' t'ings. Her own mudder's ring! I come home an' she tells me, cool as yeh please, settin' dere. Dat's deh kind of a woman she is."

Several men turned their heads. A murmur of sympathy went along the rail. It was evident to them all that Halloran was a deeply injured man. He felt their sympathy flow toward him and it warmed him more than the beer. He finished the glass.

"Have one on me, Dennis," said Corcoran.

"I don' mind," said Dennis.

He had another, and then he bought one for Corcoran, because a man who would not return a treat was no better than a dog, and the quarter that was left of his pay went across the bar to Fogarty, who rang it into the drawer without a word. The fact that this quarter existed had somehow not been mentioned in Mullen's Court. It did not now occur to Dennis that it might have been mentioned. He was among friends. He told them about the Brooklyn Swede, and they agreed that the fight had been fixed. He told them about the hat with the feather, and they agreed that he was a good husband. As the evening went on, he grew to regard himself as a sort of martyr, a large, brave, generous man broken upon the wheel of a woman's unreason. Tears stood in his eyes. He would have forgiven Kate everything, had she been there to receive his forgiveness.

High in the tenement, at the window above the cobbles, the lamp burned low. The pile of finished vests had grown, and the pile of unfinished ones had shrunk. The clock upon the shelf ticked on with its loud and judicial air, keeping its accounts, and the woman beneath it sewed with the small, swift, ceaseless motion of those who are paid by the dozen. Now and then she lifted her head and looked at the door. Then she bent again to the cloth.

Down in the court a drunken man was singing a song about a girl in Killarney. The tenements stood shouldering one another in the dark, and their few lit windows blinked stupidly, as if the buildings were trying to stay awake to see how it would all come out, and did not much care.
