"You eat," Helen said. "You eat it all."

"It's very good."

"Of course it's good."

"I mean it. I haven't eaten anything like this in a long time."

"Well, what did they feed you?"

"I don't know," Lewis said. "I don't remember. It all tasted the same."

Helen looked at him and then she looked at Joe and Joe was looking at his plate.

"There's pie," she said. "Apple. From the tree out back."

"The old tree?"

"It still bears. Not as much. But it bears."

After supper she would not let them help with the dishes and they went back into the front room and Joe put more wood on the fire. They did not drink any more whiskey. They sat and Joe smoked a pipe and Lewis watched the fire.

"How's the arm?" Joe said.

"It's all right."

"Can you use it?"

"Some. I can use it some. It gets better. They say it gets better."

"Can you cast?"

"I don't know. I haven't tried."

"Well," Joe said. "We'll find out."

"We'll find out."

"If you can't you can watch me."

"I'd rather fish."

"Sure. Everybody would rather fish."

Joe knocked his pipe out on the stone of the fireplace.

"I'm going to bed," he said. "You go when you want. Your room is the same room. Helen put the extra blankets on."

"Thanks."

"I'll wake you at five."

"I'll be up."

"I'll wake you anyway."

Joe went out and Lewis heard him on the stairs and then he heard the door close. He sat for a long time by the fire. When it burned down he did not put any more wood on. He sat and watched it go to coals and then he got up and went upstairs.

The room was the same room. It was the room he had slept in every summer from the time he was seven until he was seventeen. The bed was the same bed and the window looked out over the cottonwoods and down to the creek and the creek was silver now under the moon. He undressed in the dark and got into bed. The sheets were cold and then they warmed. He lay on his back and listened. He could hear the creek. He had forgotten that you could hear the creek from here. He lay and listened to it and after a while he slept and he did not dream.

---

Joe woke him at five but he was already awake. It was dark and cold in the room and he dressed quickly. Downstairs Joe had coffee on the stove and they drank it standing up. Then they took the rods from where they hung on the back porch and went out.

It was cold outside and their breath smoked and there was frost on the grass. They walked down through the pasture to the creek. The sky was getting light in the east over the hills and the stars were going out. By the time they reached the creek it was light enough to see the water.

They walked up along the bank. The grass was wet and soaked through their trousers below the knee. There were willows along the creek and the willows were bare and red and they had to push through them in places. A deer went crashing away through the brush ahead of them and they stopped and listened to it go.

"Doe," Joe said.

"I didn't see it."

"It was a doe. I saw the tail."

They came to the beaver dam. It was built of sticks and mud and it ran across the creek in a long low curve and the water came over the top of it in a smooth sheet and fell into the pool below. The pool was deep and green and the current moved slowly in it and turned back on itself at the edges.

"There," Joe said. "Under the far bank. Where the roots are."

"I see it."

"You take it. I'll go up above."

"No. You take it."

"I've fished it all fall," Joe said. "You take it."

Joe went on up around the dam. Lewis sat down on a log and took a fly from the box and tied it on. His right hand was slow with the knot and he had to do it twice. Then he stood up and walked down to the edge of the water.

He stripped line off the reel and let it lie in loops at his feet. He brought the rod back. His arm hurt when he brought it back but it was not a bad hurt. He brought it forward and the line went out and fell on the water too short and too heavy. He took it up and tried again. It was better. The third time the fly lit on the water just below the roots on the far bank and rode the current down and turned in the eddy.

Nothing came. He took it up and cast again. His arm hurt more now. He made himself be slow. The fly went out and lit and floated and then there was a swirl in the water under it and he lifted the rod and felt the trout.

It was a good trout. It went down and he could feel it shaking its head down there and then it ran upstream toward the dam and the line cut through the water and the reel made a noise. He held the rod up. His arm was shaking. The trout turned and came back down and he took in line with his left hand and then it jumped. It came all the way out of the water and he saw it in the light, heavy and spotted and bright, and it fell back with a splash.

"Keep him up," Joe called. He was standing on the dam. "Keep him out of the roots."

"I know."

"Keep him up."

The trout went for the roots and Lewis turned it. He did not know how he turned it. His arm was very bad now but he held the rod up and the trout came out from the bank and into the open water of the pool. It was tiring. He brought it in slowly. When it was close he could see it in the clear water, lying on its side and then righting itself and then lying on its side again.

Joe came down off the dam with the net. He waded into the shallow water at the tail of the pool and Lewis led the trout to him and Joe put the net under it and lifted it out.

"That's a fish," Joe said.

"It's a good one."

"It's the best one out of here all year."

"You're lying."

"I'm not lying. Look at him."

They looked at him. The trout lay in the net and its gills worked. It was dark on the back and silver on the sides and there were red spots along the sides with blue around them. Joe took it out and killed it with a blow against a rock and laid it in the grass.

Lewis sat down on the log. He held his right arm with his left hand. It was shaking and he could not make it stop.

"You all right?" Joe said.

"I'm fine."

"You're not fine."

"It's just the arm. It's just tired."

Joe sat down beside him on the log. He took out his pipe and filled it and lit it and they sat there. The sun had come up over the hills now and it was on the water and on the frost in the grass and the frost was beginning to melt.

"You can stay," Joe said. "If you want."

Lewis did not say anything.

"I mean it. There's work if you want it. There's the room. Helen would like it. I'd like it."

"I don't know what I'm going to do."

"You don't have to know. That's what I'm saying."

"I can't do much. With the arm."

"You did all right just now."

"That was a fish."

"It was a fish," Joe said. "It's a start."

Lewis looked at the water. A leaf came down the creek and went over the dam and into the pool and turned in the eddy where the trout had been and then went on.

"I used to think about this," he said. "In the hospital. I used to lie there and think about this creek. Every hole in it. I'd start at the bridge and go up. I'd fish every hole. Some nights I got all the way to the forks."

"Did you catch anything?"

"Every time. Every hole."

"Well," Joe said. "That's better than we ever did."

"That's what I'd think. I'd think, it was never this good."

"It's pretty good now."

"It's pretty good."

Joe stood up. "I'm going to go up above," he said. "You rest. Fish this again when he's settled. There's another one in there. I saw it."

"All right."

"You'll be all right?"

"I'll be fine."

Joe picked up his rod and went up along the bank and around the dam. Lewis watched him go. Then he sat on the log in the sun and looked at the trout lying in the wet grass. The color was going out of it already. He reached down and picked it up and wet it in the creek and laid it in the shade under the willows where it would keep.

His arm had stopped shaking. He flexed his hand and opened it and closed it. Then he sat a while longer in the sun. It was getting warm. He could hear Joe's reel up above the dam and he could hear the water coming over the dam and falling into the pool. After a while he got up and picked up his rod and stripped the line off the reel and let it lie in loops at his feet, and he looked across the water to the place under the roots where the other trout would be.

The wind came up in the night and in the morning it was still blowing. The man woke early and lay in the bed and listened to it in the pines behind the cabin. He could hear the water working against the rocks below the point. It was a steady sound and he knew it would blow all day. He lay there and did not think about anything and then he got up and put on his trousers and his shirt and went out to the kitchen.

The stove was cold. He put in paper and kindling and some of the split birch and lit it and stood there with his hands over it until the birch caught. Then he filled the coffee pot from the pail and put it on. The boy's door was open. He did not look in because he thought the boy was sleeping and he did not want to wake him. The boy was seven and he slept hard in the mornings.

When the coffee was boiling he took it off and let the grounds settle and poured a cup and went out onto the porch with it. The lake was dark and rough and the waves were white on top all the way across to the far shore. The sky was clear and very blue and the wind came down out of the northwest cold and clean. He drank the coffee and looked at the lake. He looked at the dock. The rowboat was not there.

He set the cup down on the rail. He looked along the shore toward Halvorsen's place and then out at the water. He did not see anything at first. Then he saw the boat. It was a long way out, past the point and well toward the middle, and it was riding broadside to the waves. There was someone in it. It was small in the boat and it was not doing anything.

He went down the path to the dock. He did not run on the path because the roots were bad and he knew if he fell it would be worse. At the dock he stood and looked out again. The boat was drifting southeast with the wind. He could see now that the boy was sitting in the bottom of it and holding onto the gunwales. There was only one oar in the boat. He could not see the other oar anywhere.

Halvorsen's canoe was pulled up on the beach a hundred yards down. He went along the shore to it, over the rocks, and turned it over and found the paddle under it. He dragged the canoe down into the water and the wind took the bow around and he had to wade out to his knees to hold it. The water was very cold. He got in and knelt in the middle and began to paddle.

It was hard going out past the point. The waves came at the canoe on the quarter and he had to keep the bow into them and paddle hard on the one side. Water came over the bow and he could feel it cold on his knees in the bottom. He did not look at the boat for a while. He looked at the waves coming and kept the bow into them and paddled. When he was past the point and out in the open it was rougher and he had to quarter more. Then he looked up and saw the boat and it was closer. The boy had seen him. The boy was not waving. He was just sitting and holding on.

The man paddled. His shoulders began to hurt and then they stopped hurting and he did not think about them. He thought about the waves and about keeping the canoe straight. He thought that if the canoe went over he would hold onto it and kick toward the boat. He thought that the water was too cold to be in for long. Then he did not think about that anymore and only paddled.

When he came up alongside the boat the boy looked at him. The boy's face was very white and his lips were blue and his hair was wet from the spray. He had on his sweater and his short pants and his shoes were off. The man did not know why his shoes were off.

"Hold the gunwale," the man said. "Hold it tight."

The boy did not say anything. He held on.

The man brought the canoe in against the side of the boat and caught the oarlock and held it. The two boats knocked together in the waves. He took the painter of the canoe and made it fast to the stern ring of the rowboat with two half hitches. Then he got over into the rowboat, careful, low, his weight in the middle, and the canoe swung off behind on the line.

"Are you hurt?" he said.

"No."

"Get in the bow. Sit down in the bottom. Hold on."

The boy went forward on his hands and knees and sat down in the bottom of the bow with his back against the seat. The man took the one oar and looked at the shore. They had drifted a long way. He put the oar over the stern and began to scull. It was slow. The wind was against them and the canoe dragged behind. He sculled and kept the stern into the wind and watched the point and after a long while the point began to come nearer. The boy sat in the bow and did not look at him. The boy looked at the bottom of the boat where there was some water and an old sinker and a piece of line.

When they came in behind the point the water was smoother and the man sculled easier. He brought the boat in to the dock and the boy got out first and stood on the dock. The man made the boat fast and then he pulled the canoe in and untied it and carried it down the beach to Halvorsen's and turned it over where it had been and put the paddle under it. Then he walked back to the dock. The boy was still standing there. He had not moved. The man's trousers were wet to the thighs and his hands were stiff and his arms felt light, as though there were nothing in them.

"Come up to the house," he said.

They went up the path. The boy went ahead. At the porch the man said, "Sit down there," and the boy sat on the bench against the wall of the cabin. The man went inside and got the blanket off the boy's bed and came out and put it around him. Then he sat down on the step below the boy and took out a cigarette and tried to light it. The wind blew the match out. He lit another one with his hands cupped and got the cigarette going. His hands were shaking a little. He looked at them and then he put them on his knees.

"All right," he said. "Tell me."

The boy did not say anything.

"Tell me what happened."

"I took the boat."

"I know you took the boat."

"I wanted to go to the island."

The man looked out at the lake. The island was a long way down, beyond the bay, a little island with three pines on it and a rock beach on the south side. You could not see it from the porch.

"Why did you want to go to the island?"

"I just wanted to."

"That isn't any reason."

The boy pulled the blanket around himself. "There were the big perch there. Off the rocks. Where we caught them before."

"That was a long time ago."

"It was last summer."

"All right. It was last summer." The man smoked the cigarette. "What happened to the oar?"

"It came out of the lock. I was pulling hard and it came out and then it went away."

"Why didn't you sit down and wait?"

"I did. I sat down."

"Why were your shoes off?"

The boy looked at his feet. They were red and wet. "I thought I might have to swim."

The man did not say anything for a while. He looked at the boy's feet. They were very small. He threw the cigarette off the porch into the needles and then he got up and stepped on it and came back and sat down again.

"Listen to me," he said. "Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"Look at me."

The boy looked at him. His eyes were very dark and they were wet now but he was not crying.

"You don't take the boat," the man said. "You don't ever take the boat alone. Not to the island and not to the point and not to anywhere. Do you understand that?"

"Yes."

"Say it."

"I don't take the boat alone."

"Not ever."

"Not ever."

"You could have died out there," the man said. "Do you know that? You don't know that. You think you know it but you don't. That water is cold. If the boat went over you would have been in that water and you would have been all right for a little while and then you would not have been all right. Your arms would stop working. Then you would go down. You would go down and nobody would find you. Do you understand?"

The boy was crying now. He was not making any sound but the tears were coming down and he did not wipe them.

"Do you understand?" the man said.

"Yes."

"I didn't know where you were. I came out and the boat was gone. Do you know what that is like?"

"No."

"No," the man said. "You don't."

They sat there. The wind blew in the pines and the needles came down on the porch roof with a small sound. Down below the water broke on the rocks and drew back and broke again.

"Mother let me take it," the boy said.

The man did not look at him.

"She let me take it to the end of the dock and back. On the rope. She let me."

"That was on the rope."

"She said I could go farther when I was bigger."

"Your mother isn't here," the man said.

He said it and then it was said and he could not do anything about it. The boy looked at him. Then the boy looked away, out at the lake, and pulled the blanket up over his mouth.

The man stood up. He went inside and stood in the kitchen. The stove was going well and the kitchen was warm. He poured another cup of coffee. It was strong now from sitting and he drank it standing up by the stove. He looked at the window. There was a fly on the inside of the glass walking up and falling down and walking up again. He watched it for a while. Then he went to the cupboard and took down the bottle and poured some of the whiskey into the coffee and drank it. It was good. It went down hot and he felt it in his chest and then in his stomach. He did not pour any more.

He went back out onto the porch. The boy was still sitting there in the blanket.

"Go in and get your dry things on," the man said. "Then come out to the kitchen."

The boy got up and went in. The man stood on the porch and looked at the lake. The wind was still strong. It would blow all day and maybe tomorrow. He thought about the oar. It was out there somewhere going southeast, and it would come up on the far shore in a day or two, or it would not. It was a good oar. He had bought the pair in the town at the beginning of the summer. It did not matter about the oar.

In the kitchen he cut bacon and put it in the big pan. When it was cooking he cut bread and laid the slices out on the board. The boy came in. He had on his other trousers and a dry shirt and his wool socks and he stood in the doorway.

"Sit down," the man said.

The boy sat at the table. The man turned the bacon. When it was done he took it out and laid it on a paper and put the bread in the fat and fried it brown on both sides. He put the bread and the bacon on two plates and brought them to the table and sat down. He poured milk into a cup for the boy.

"Eat," he said.

The boy ate. He ate slowly at first and then he ate faster. The man watched him and then he ate too. The bread was good fried in the bacon fat and the bacon was crisp. They did not say anything while they ate.

When they were done the man took the plates to the basin. He stood with his back to the boy.

"For a week you don't go to the dock," he said. "Not without me. You don't go down the path. You stay up here at the house and you split the kindling and you carry the water. You do that every day."

"Yes."

"And after a week we will see."

"Yes."

The man washed the plates in the basin and dried them and put them in the cupboard. Then he turned around. The boy was sitting at the table looking at the oilcloth. There was a burn on it from a pan once and the boy was running his finger around the edge of the burn.

"You did one thing right," the man said.

The boy looked up.

"You sat down in the boat. You didn't stand up. That was right. And you held on. That was right too."

"I wanted to stand up. To see better."

"But you didn't."

"No."

"That was right," the man said.

The boy looked at the burn on the oilcloth again. "Would you have come if I didn't have the shoes off?"

"I would have come."

"Even if I went in?"

"Even then."

"But you said my arms would stop."

"I would have come anyway," the man said.

The boy nodded. He seemed to be thinking about it. Then he said, "Is the oar gone?"

"I guess it's gone."

"I'm sorry about the oar."

"It doesn't matter about the oar."

"Was it expensive?"

"It doesn't matter," the man said. "We will get another oar."

In the afternoon the boy split kindling on the block behind the cabin. He was not strong enough to split anything big and the man gave him the small hatchet and set up the pieces of dry cedar for him and showed him again how to hold it, short, with his other hand well back. The boy split the cedar into long thin pieces and stacked them in the box by the back door. The man sat on the back step and cleaned the shotgun, which did not need cleaning, and watched him. The wind came over the ridge and moved the tops of the pines but it was quiet behind the cabin and the sun was warm there. The boy worked carefully. When he had split all the cedar he came and stood by the step.

"I'm done."

"Good. Now the water."

The boy took the pail and went down the other path to the spring. It was not the lake path. The man watched him go down through the trees and then he could not see him and he listened. He heard the pail knock against a rock and then he heard it filling and then he heard the boy coming back up. The boy carried it with both hands and some of it slopped over and he came around the corner of the cabin with the front of his trousers wet.

"You spilled some."

"It's heavy."

"Carry it on one side. Change hands when you're tired."

"All right."

"Put it on the bench."

The boy put it on the bench and stood there. The man put the gun down across his knees.

"Come here," he said.

The boy came. The man put his hand on the back of the boy's neck. It was a very small neck and it was warm from the work.

"You did good with the kindling."

"Did I do it right?"

"You did it fine."

In the evening the wind began to go down. They sat on the porch after supper and watched the lake. The whitecaps were gone and the waves were long and slow now, and the light went yellow on the far shore and then red and then it was gone and the water was gray. The boy sat on the bench next to the man. He had the blanket again because it was cold. The man smoked.

"Tomorrow will it be calm?" the boy said.

"Maybe. I think it will be calm."

"Can we go to the island?"

The man looked at him.

"Both of us," the boy said. "In the boat. You row."

"With one oar?"

"Oh," the boy said.

"I can make one, I guess," the man said. "There's that ash board in the shed. I can make one out of that."

"Can I help?"

"You can hold the board."

"And then can we go?"

"Not tomorrow. You have a week."

"A week," the boy said. He did not argue. He pulled the blanket up. "After a week, can we go?"

"After a week we will see."

"The perch will still be there."

"They'll be there."

"Off the rocks."

"Off the rocks on the south side," the man said. "Where the deep water comes in."

"That's where Mother caught the big one."

"That's right," the man said. "That's where."

The boy did not say anything else. The man sat and smoked and after a while he felt the boy lean against him and then the boy's head was against his arm and he was asleep. The man did not move. It was dark now and the lake was flat and black and he could hear a loon out past the point. It called once and then it was quiet and then it called again farther off. The man sat and listened to it. His arms ached now, both of them, from the shoulders all the way down, and his back ached, and he did not mind it. He finished the cigarette and dropped it and put it out with his shoe. Then he sat there in the dark with the boy against him and did not get up for a long time.

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

“You ought to have let me know, darling.” We were off the driveway, walking under the trees. I took her hands, then stopped and kissed her.

“Isn’t there anywhere we can go?”

“No,” she said. “We have to just walk here. You’ve been away a long time.”

“This is the third day. But I’m back now.” She looked at me, “And you do love me?”

“Yes.”

“You did say you loved me, didn’t you?”

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

“And you don’t have to say you love me. That’s all over for a while.” She stood up and put out her hand. “Good-night.” I wanted to kiss her.

“No,” she said. “I’m awfully tired.”

“Kiss me, though,” I said.

“I’m awfully tired, darling.”

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

“Ah, ha!” he said. “It does not go so well. Baby is puzzled.”

“Where have you been?”

“At the Villa Rossa. It was very edifying, baby. We all sang. Where have you been?”

“Calling on the British.”

“Thank God I did not become involved with the British.” I came back the next afternoon from our first mountain post and stopped the car at the smistimento where the wounded and sick were sorted by their papers and the papers marked for the different hospitals. I had been driving and I sat in the car and the driver took the papers in. It was a hot day and the sky was very bright and blue and the road was white and dusty. I sat in the high seat of the Fiat and thought about nothing. A regiment went by in the road and I watched them pass. The men were hot and sweating. "All right," he said.

She put her hand on his arm. He could feel it through the sweater. She did not hold on. She only rested it there and then took it away.

The train came in late and Paul got down from the last car with his bag and stood on the platform. It was a small station with a water tank and a low red building and there was nobody on the platform but the agent. The agent took the mail sack off and went inside. Paul set his bag down. Beyond the station there was a road and beyond the road there were fields of cut hay and beyond the fields were the woods. The woods were dark and the sun was low over them. He had not seen the woods in nine years.

"Hello, Ned," Paul said.

"Hello, kid." They shook hands. Ned's hand was hard and dry. He looked at Paul and Paul looked at him.

"You got old," Ned said.

"So did you."

"I got fat. You got old. That's different." He picked up the bag. "Is this all you brought?"

"That's all."

"You travel light."

"I learned to."

They went down the steps and Ned put the bag in the bed of the truck and they got in. The seat was torn and there was a coil of rope on the floor and a box of shells. Ned started the truck and they went out along the road. The dust came up behind them and hung in the air and the sun was in it.

"How was the trip?"

"Long."

"I bet it was long. Where'd you come from?"

"New York. Before that Paris."

"That's fine."

"I want a chicken," Paul said.

"I remember this," Paul said.

"It hasn't changed."

"No. I can see it hasn't."

"I remember the creek."

"He looks all right. He won't hunt though. Come on."

"I got beer," Ned said. "I figured you'd want a beer."

"I want a beer."

"It's good beer," Paul said.

"It's from Marquette. It's not bad."

"It's good."

"I guess you've had better."

"Not as cold."

"He's been dead six years."

"I know. I got the letter."

"No."

"I don't think I'd like a country without trees."

"It's the same kitchen."

"That's what's fine about it."

"It's better than Paris."

"It's different."

"Is it better?"

"It's very good," Paul said. "Leave it at that."

"Where'd you get this?"

"A man in town."

"It's not bad."

"It's terrible. But it's what there is."

They drank. The stars were very thick over the lake now and there was no moon. The frogs were loud. Somewhere up the shore a dog was barking and Jack lifted his head on the porch and then put it down again.

"You were in the war," Ned said.

"Not really. I was with the ambulances. Then I was with a newspaper."

"Ma said you got hurt."

"She worried."

"I wrote her it was nothing."

"That's a hell of a thing."

"That's how she is."

"I know how she is."

"You were lucky."

"I know. But I wanted to go anyway."

"There wasn't anything to it."

"There was."

"Oh," Ned said.

"I see."

"It wasn't anything. It was just a thing that happened."

"Sure."

"I bet she was."

"I'm not talking about it."

"All right."

"All right, kid."

"We stood on it and we were up to our knees."

"It was out," Ned said. "God, that was a summer."

"That was a fine summer."

"I was ten. You were twelve."

"I was always the little one."

"It's good you came," he said.

"It's good to be here."

"I mean it. It's good you came. I didn't think you'd come."

"I said I would."

"I know."

"Good-night, Ned."

The ice had gone dark along the shore in the last week of March and there was open water now at the mouth of the creek where it came in from the swamp. Out in the middle the lake was still white but it was not a good white. It was gray under the white and in the afternoons when the sun was on it you could see the water standing in the low places. The man had been splitting wood behind the house and he stopped to rest and wipe his face and he looked down past the boathouse and saw the boy out on the ice.

The boy was a long way out. He was nearly to the old fish shanty that Halvorsen had left on the ice too late in the season and that would go down when the ice went. The boy was walking carefully the way he had been taught to walk on a log across the creek, with his arms out a little from his sides. He had on his red mackinaw and the cap with the ear flaps and he looked very small out there.

The man put down the axe. He did not run. He walked down through the snow to the boathouse and out onto the end of the dock and stood there. The dock was still in the ice and the boards were wet and soft and black. He did not call out at first. He watched the boy. The boy had reached the shanty and was looking at something on the ice beside it. Then he squatted down and looked at it.

The man cupped his hands.

"Luke," he called. He did not call it loudly. His voice went out across the ice and the boy stood up and turned around.

"Come back in," the man called. "Come in the way you went out. Walk in your own tracks."

The boy stood there. Then he waved. The man did not wave back.

"Walk in your own tracks," he called again. "Slowly."

The boy started back. The man could see him looking down at the ice and stepping and looking and stepping. Once the boy stopped and looked back at the shanty and the man said nothing and the boy came on again. It took a long time. The sun was low and there was no wind and the man could hear a crow somewhere back in the hemlocks and he could hear the water running under the ice at the creek mouth. He stood on the end of the dock with his hands in the pockets of his coat and his hands were closed and he watched the boy come in.

When the boy was close the man could see the ice was wet where he walked. There was water in the tracks. The boy came up to the edge of the dock and the man reached down and took him under the arms and lifted him up onto the boards. The boy was not heavy. His face was red from the cold and his eyes were very bright.

"There's a fox," the boy said. "There's a dead fox out by the shanty. It's frozen in. You can see all its teeth."

"Go up to the house."

"It's a red fox. Its tail is all—"

"Go up to the house," the man said. "Go in the kitchen and take your boots off and sit at the table."

The boy looked at him. Then he went up the path through the snow. The man stood on the dock and looked out at the tracks going out across the ice to the shanty. The tracks were dark now all the way out. He looked at them for a while. Then he went up to the house.

---

The kitchen was warm from the range and the boy was sitting at the table in his stockings. His boots were by the door where water was coming off them onto the floor. He had not taken off his mackinaw. The man took off his own coat and hung it on the hook by the door. There was another coat on the hook, a woman's coat of green wool, and he moved it over to make room. He did not look at it.

He sat down at the table across from the boy.

"Take off your coat," he said.

The boy took it off. He put it on the back of the chair.

"Now," the man said. "Where were you?"

"On the lake."

"Where on the lake?"

"At the shanty."

"Who said you could go out on the lake?"

The boy did not say anything. He looked at the oilcloth on the table. There was a burn mark in the oilcloth shaped like a horseshoe where somebody had once put down a pan that was too hot. The boy put his finger on it.

"Look at me," the man said.

The boy looked at him.

"Who said you could go out on the lake?"

"Nobody."

"What did I tell you about the lake?"

"Not to go out on it."

"When did I tell you?"

"I don't know."

"You know."

"Sunday."

"That's right. Sunday. What else did I tell you on Sunday?"

"That the ice was rotten."

"What does rotten mean?"

"It means it's no good."

"What else does it mean?"

The boy took his finger off the burn mark. "It means you can go through."

"That's right," the man said. "It means you can go through. And if you go through what happens?"

The boy did not answer.

"I asked you a question."

"You drown."

"That's right. You go through and the water is so cold you can't breathe and you can't get your arms to work and you go under and the ice is over you. And you can't find the hole. It's dark under there and you can't find the hole you went in by. And nobody can get to you because the ice won't hold anybody. Do you understand that?"

"Yes."

"No you don't. You don't understand it. If you understood it you wouldn't have gone out."

"I walked careful," the boy said. "I walked like on the log."

"It doesn't matter how you walk. The ice doesn't care how you walk."

"It held me."

"It held you this time."

"It held me all the way out and all the way back."

The man put his hands flat on the table. They were big hands and there was pitch on them from the wood and a cut on the back of one knuckle that had opened up again. He looked at his hands and then he looked at the boy.

"Don't argue with me," he said.

"I wasn't arguing."

The boy shook his head.

"No," the man said. "You don't."

He got up from the table and went to the range and lifted the lid off the front and looked in at the fire and put the lid back on. He did not need to look at the fire. "It's not the same."

"No," the man said. "It's not the same."

"Here is what I want you to understand," he said. "I don't care about the shanty. I don't care about the fox. I don't care if you wanted to see them. You can want to see anything you like. "Why?"

"Because I'm telling you. That's why. Because I know about the ice and you don't. I've been on this lake thirty years. I've seen the ice go out thirty times. I know how it goes and you don't."

"It goes all at once," the man said. "It looks all right and then it goes all at once."

The boy looked at him.

"No."

"Well, he did. Not on this lake. On the big lake. A long time ago, when I was a boy. He went out after the ice was bad to get his nets in. He knew the ice. He'd been on the ice his whole life. He went through and they didn't find him till May."

"Was he dead?" the boy said.

"Yes. He was dead."

"What did he look like?"

"Never mind what he looked like."

"I'm sorry, though."

"Yes."

"Say it back to me."

"I'm not to go down to the lake."

"Until when?"

"Until the ice is out."

"Without who?"

"Without you."

"All right," the man said. "And you're not to go outside at all tomorrow. You'll stay in the house."

"All day?"

"All day."

"What about the next day?"

"We'll see about the next day."

The boy wiped his face again with the towel. He folded the towel and put it on the table and smoothed it out with his hands. The man watched him do it. The boy's hands were red and the knuckles were cracked from the cold and the man looked at the hands and something went through him that he did not want and he looked away from them out the window.

"Your hands are cold," he said.

"No they're not."

"Give them here."

The boy held out his hands across the table and the man came and sat down again and took them. They were very cold. He held them between his own hands. The boy's hands were small inside his and he could feel the bones in them.

"You should have had your mittens," he said.

"I forgot them."

"Where are they?"

"On the porch."

"That's a fine place for them."

"I forgot."

"I know you forgot." He held the hands. They were beginning to get warm. "You don't forget mittens in March. You don't go out without mittens in March."

"I won't."

"Your mother—" the man said, and stopped.

The boy looked at him and waited. The man did not go on. He held the boy's hands and looked at the burn mark on the oilcloth. The kettle had begun to boil on the back of the range and he heard it and did not get up. Then he got up.

"Do you want cocoa?" he said.

"Am I allowed?"

"Yes. You're allowed."

He took the tin down from the shelf and the boy watched him make it. He put in too much cocoa and too much sugar and he poured the water from the kettle and stirred it and then he put in some of the canned milk and stirred it again. He put it in front of the boy in the white cup with the chip on the handle. The boy held the cup with both hands and blew on it.

"It's hot," the man said. "Wait for it."

"I'm waiting."

The man poured himself a cup of coffee from the pot that had been on the range since morning. It was black and bitter and he drank it standing up. The light outside had gone from yellow to a kind of rose and then it was going gray. He could not see the lake from the kitchen. He was glad he could not see it.

"Is the fox going to go down too?" the boy said.

"Yes."

"When the shanty goes?"

"When the ice goes. It'll all go together."

"Where will it go?"

"To the bottom."

"Will it stay there?"

"Some of it will."

The boy drank some of the cocoa. "It had all its teeth," he said. "You could see them all. It looked like it was going to bite something."

"They look like that."

"Why?"

"The cold does it. It pulls the lips back."

"Does it hurt?"

"No. It doesn't hurt. It's dead. It doesn't feel anything."

The boy thought about that. He drank more of the cocoa and there was a brown mark on his upper lip.

"Did Halvorsen's brother look like that?"

"I told you never mind about that."

"I just wanted to know."

"Well, you don't need to know."

They were quiet. The fire ticked in the range. The man finished his coffee and put the cup in the sink and stood there with his hands on the edge of the sink. Then he went to the door and took his coat off the hook. The green coat swung on its hook when he took his own down and he put out his hand and stopped it.

"Where are you going?" the boy said.

"To get the wood in. I left the axe out."

"Can I come?"

"No."

"I'll wear my mittens."

"No. You stay here. Finish your cocoa."

"I'm finished."

"Then sit there."

He went around behind the house to the chopping block and the axe was there where he had put it down and he picked it up and looked at the edge and then he stuck it in the block. He did not get the wood. He stood there. From the chopping block you could see down through the birches to the boathouse and past the boathouse to the lake and the shanty out on the lake, very small and dark now in the gray light. He could not see the tracks. It was too dark to see the tracks.

He thought about the boy squatting by the fox. He thought about the boy walking with his arms out. He thought about how far it was from the dock to the shanty and how long it would take to get out there on a ladder pushed ahead of you on the ice, and whether the ladder in the boathouse was long enough, and he knew it was not long enough. He had thought all of that while he was standing on the dock. He had thought it all very clearly and calmly. He had thought where the rope was and how much rope there was and he had known it was not enough rope either. He had thought all of that and had not let any of it into his voice. That was the thing. You did not let it into your voice.

He took a deep breath of the cold air and let it out.

It was all right now. The boy was in the kitchen and the boy was warm and the boy had cocoa on his lip. It was all right. He had been hard with him but he had needed to be hard and it was all right to be hard. The boy would not go out again. He was fairly sure the boy would not go out again. You could never be sure. But he was fairly sure.

He stood there until his hands got cold. Then he took an armload of wood off the pile and went in.

The boy was still at the table. He had put his head down on his arms again but he was not crying now. He was asleep. The man put the wood down quietly in the box by the range and stood and looked at him. The boy's hair had dried funny from the cap and there was a crease on his cheek from his sleeve. The cocoa cup was empty.

The man went and sat down across from him. He did not wake him. He sat and looked at him for a long time while the kitchen got dark. He did not light the lamp. Once the boy said something in his sleep that the man could not hear and he leaned forward to hear it but the boy did not say it again.

Outside, very far off, there was a sound from the lake like a gun going off. It was the ice. It made that sound in the spring when it was getting ready. The boy did not wake. The man sat and listened and it did not come again.

After a while he got up and lit the lamp and turned it low. He took the green coat down off the hook and held it for a moment and then he folded it over his arm and took it into the other room and put it in the closet there, in the back, behind the other things. Then he came back into the kitchen and put more wood in the range and started to make supper. He made it quietly so the boy could sleep. It was going to be a cold night. There would be ice again in the tracks by morning, thin ice over the water in each track, all the way out to the shanty. And in another week it would all be gone.

This is the smell I love. This and fresh-cut clover, the crushed sage as you ride after cattle, wood-smoke and the burning leaves of autumn. That must be the odor of nostalgia, the smell of the smoke from the piles of raked leaves burning in the streets in the fall in Missoula. Which would you rather smell? Sweet grass the Indians used in their baskets? Smoked leather? The odor of the ground in the spring after rain? The smell of the sea as you walk through the gorse on a headland in Galicia? Or the wind from the land as you come in toward Cuba in the dark? That was the odor of the cactus flowers, mimosa and the sea-grape shrubs. Or would you rather smell frying bacon in the morning when you are hungry? Or coffee in the morning? Or a Jonathan apple as you bit into it? Or a cider mill in the grinding, or bread fresh from the oven? You must be hungry, he thought, and he lay on his side and watched the entrance of the cave in the light that the stars reflected from the snow. Some one came out from under the blanket and he could see whoever it was standing by the break in the rock that made the entrance. Then he heard a slithering sound in the snow and then whoever it was ducked down and went back in. I suppose she won’t come until they are all asleep, he thought. It is a waste of time. The night is half gone. Oh, Maria. Come now quickly, Maria, for there is little time. He heard the soft sound of snow falling from a branch onto the snow on the ground. A little wind was rising. He felt it on his face. Suddenly he felt a panic that she might not come. The wind rising now reminded him how soon it would be morning. More snow fell from the branches as he heard the wind now moving the pine tops. Come now, Maria. Please come here now quickly, he thought. Oh, come here now. Do not wait. There is no importance any more to your waiting until they are asleep. Then he saw her coming out from under the blanket that covered the cave mouth. She stood there a moment and he knew it was she but he could not see what she was doing. He whistled a low whistle and she was still at the cave mouth doing something in the darkness of the rock shadow. Then she came running, carrying something in her hands and he saw her running long-legged through the snow. Then she was kneeling by the robe, her head pushed hard against him, slapping the snow from her feet. She kissed him and handed him her bundle.

“Put it with thy pillow,” she said. “I took these off there to save time.”

“You came barefoot through the snow?”

“Yes,” she said, “and wearing only my wedding shirt.” He held her close and tight in his arms and she rubbed her head against his chin.

“Avoid the feet,” she said. “They are very cold, Roberto.”

“Put them here and warm them.”

“Nay,” she said. “They will warm quickly. But say quickly now that you love me.”

“I love thee.”

“Good. Good. Good.”

“I love thee, little rabbit.”

“Do you love my wedding shirt?”

“It is the same one as always.”

“Yes. As last night. It is my wedding shirt.”

“Put thy feet here.”

“Nay, that would be abusive. They will warm of themselves. They are warm to me. It is only that the snow has made them cold toward thee. Say it again.”

“I love thee, my little rabbit.”

“I love thee, too, and I am thy wife.”

“Were they asleep?”

“No,” she said. “But I could support it no longer. And what importance has it?”

“None,” he said, and felt her against him, slim and long and warmly lovely. “No other thing has importance.”

“Put thy hand on my head,” she said, “and then let me see if I can kiss thee.”

“Was it well?” she asked.

“Yes,” he said. “Take off thy wedding shirt.”

“You think I should?”

“Yes, if thou wilt not be cold.”

“Qué va, cold. I am on fire.”

“I, too. But afterwards thou wilt not be cold?”

“No. Afterwards we will be as one animal of the forest and be so close that neither one can tell that one of us is one and not the other. Can you not feel my heart be your heart?”

“Yes. There is no difference.”

“Now, feel. I am thee and thou art me and all of one is the other. And I love thee, oh, I love thee so. Are we not truly one? Canst thou not feel it?”

“Yes,” he said. “It is true.”

“And feel now. Thou hast no heart but mine.”

“Nor any other legs, nor feet, nor of the body.”

“But we are different,” she said. “I would have us exactly the same.”

“You do not mean that.”

“Yes I do. I do. That is a thing I had to tell thee.”

“You do not mean that.”

“Perhaps I do not,” she said speaking softly with her lips against his shoulder. “But I wished to say it. Since we are different I am glad that thou art Roberto and I Maria. But if thou should ever wish to change I would be glad to change. I would be thee because I love thee so.”

“I do not wish to change. It is better to be one and each one to be the one he is.”

“But we will be one now and there will never be a separate one.” Then she said, “I will be thee when thou art not there. Oh, I love thee so and I must care well for thee.”

“Maria.”

“Yes.”

“Maria.”

“Yes.”

“Maria.”

“Oh, yes. Please.”

“Art thou not cold?”

“Oh, no. Pull the robe over thy shoulders.”

“Maria.”

“I cannot speak.”

“Oh, Maria. Maria. Maria.” Then afterwards, close, with the night cold outside, in the long warmth of the robe, her head touching his cheek, she lay quiet and happy against him and then said softly, “And thou?”

“Como tu,” he said.

“Yes,” she said. “But it was not as this afternoon.”

“No.”

“But I loved it more. One does not need to die.”

“Ojala no,” he said. “I hope not.”

“I did not mean that.”

“I know. I know what thou meanest. We mean the same.”

“Then why did you say that instead of what I meant?”

“With a man there is a difference.”

“Then I am glad that we are different.”

“And so am I,” he said. “But I understood about the dying. I only spoke thus, as a man, from habit. I feel the same as thee.”

“However thou art and however thou speakest is how I would have thee be.”

“And I love thee and I love thy name, Maria.”

“It is a common name.”

“No,” he said. “It is not common.”

“Now should we sleep?” she said. “I could sleep easily.”

“Let us sleep,” he said, and he felt the long light body, warm against him, comforting against him, abolishing loneliness against him, magically, by a simple touching of flanks, of shoulders and of feet, making an alliance against death with him, and he said, “Sleep well, little long rabbit.” She said, “I am asleep already.”

“I am going to sleep,” he said. “Sleep well, beloved.” Then he was asleep and happy as he slept. But in the night he woke and held her tight as though she were all of life and it was being taken from him. He held her feeling she was all of life there was and it was true. But she was sleeping well and soundly and she did not wake. So he rolled away onto his side and pulled the robe over her head and kissed her once on her neck under the robe and then pulled the pistol lanyard up and put the pistol by his side where he could reach it handily and then he lay there in the night thinking. A warm wind came with daylight and he could hear the snow melting in the trees and the heavy sound of its falling. It was a late spring morning. He knew with the first breath he drew that the snow had been only a freak storm in the mountains and it would be gone by noon. Then he heard a horse coming, the hoofs balled with the wet snow thumping dully as the horseman trotted. He heard the noise of a carbine scabbard slapping loosely and the creak of leather.

“Maria,” he said, and shook the girl’s shoulder to waken her. “Keep thyself under the robe,” and he buttoned his shirt with one hand and held the automatic pistol in the other, loosening the safety catch with his thumb. He saw the girl’s cropped head disappear with a jerk under the robe and then he saw the horseman coming through the trees. He crouched now in the robe and holding the pistol in both hands aimed it at the man as he rode toward him. He had never seen this man before. The horseman was almost opposite him now. He was riding a big gray gelding and he wore a khaki beret, a blanket cape like a poncho, and heavy black boots. From the scabbard on the right of his saddle projected the stock and the long oblong clip of a short automatic rifle. He had a young, hard face and at this moment he saw Robert Jordan. He reached his hand down toward the scabbard and as he swung low, turning and jerking at the scabbard, Robert Jordan saw the scarlet of the formalized device he wore on the left breast of his khaki blanket cape. Aiming at the center of his chest, a little lower than the device, Robert Jordan fired. The pistol roared in the snowy woods. The horse plunged as though he had been spurred and the young man, still tugging at the scabbard, slid over toward the ground, his right foot caught in the stirrup. The horse broke off through the trees dragging him, bumping, face downward, and Robert Jordan stood up holding the pistol now in one hand. The big gray horse was galloping through the pines. There was a broad swath in the snow where the man dragged with a scarlet streak along one side of it. People were coming out of the mouth of the cave. Robert Jordan reached down and unrolled his trousers from the pillow and began to put them on.

“Get thee dressed,” he said to Maria. Overhead he heard the noise of a plane flying very high. Through the trees he saw where the gray horse had stopped and was standing, his rider still hanging face down from the stirrup.

“Go catch that horse,” he called to Primitivo who had started over toward him. Then, “Who was on guard at the top?”

“Rafael,” Pilar said from the cave. She stood there, her hair still down her back in two braids.

“There’s cavalry out,” Robert Jordan said. “Get your damned gun up there.” He heard Pilar call, “Agustín,” into the cave. Then she went into the cave and then two men came running out, one with the automatic rifle with its tripod swung on his shoulder; the other with a sackful of the pans.

“Get up there with them,” Robert Jordan said to Anselmo. “You lie beside the gun and hold the legs still,” he said. The three of them went up the trail through the woods at a run. The sun had not yet come up over the tops of the mountains and Robert Jordan stood straight buttoning his trousers and tightening his belt, the big pistol hanging from the lanyard on his wrist. He put the pistol in its holster on his belt and slipped the knot down on the lanyard and passed the loop over his head.

Excerpt 2: Anselmo was crouched in the lee of the trunk of a big tree and the snow blew past on either side. He was pressed close against the tree and his hands were inside of the sleeves of his jacket, each hand shoved up into the opposite sleeve, and his head was pulled as far down into the jacket as it would go. If I stay here much longer I will freeze, he thought, and that will be of no value. The Inglés told me to stay until I was relieved but he did not know then about this storm. There has been no abnormal movement on the road and I know the dispositions and the habits of this post at the sawmill across the road. I should go now to the camp. Anybody with sense would be expecting me to return to the camp. I will stay a little longer, he thought, and then go to the camp. It is the fault of the orders, which are too rigid. There is no allowance for a change in circumstance. He rubbed his feet together and then took his hands out of the jacket sleeves and bent over and rubbed his legs with them and patted his feet together to keep the circulation going. It was less cold there, out of the wind in the shelter of the tree, but he would have to start walking shortly. As he crouched, rubbing his feet, he heard a motorcar on the road. It had on chains and one link of chain was slapping and, as he watched, it came up the snow-covered road, green and brown painted, in broken patches of daubed color, the windows blued over so that you could not see in, with only a half circle left clear in the blue for the occupants to look out through. It was a two-year-old Rolls Royce town car camouflaged for the use of the General Staff but Anselmo did not know that. He could not see into the car where three officers sat wrapped in their capes. Two were on the back seat and one sat on the folding chair. The officer on the folding chair was looking out of the slit in the blue of the window as the car passed but Anselmo did not know this. Neither of them saw the other. The car passed in the snow directly below him. Anselmo saw the chauffeur, red-faced and steel-helmeted, his face and helmet projecting out of the blanket cape he wore and he saw the forward jut of the automatic rifle the orderly who sat beside the chauffeur carried. Then the car was gone up the road and Anselmo reached into the inside of his jacket and took out from his shirt pocket the two sheets torn from Robert Jordan’s notebook and made a mark after the drawing of a motorcar. It was the tenth car up for the day. Six had come down. Four were still up. It was not an unusual amount of cars to move upon that road but Anselmo did not distinguish between the Fords, Fiats, Opels, Renaults, and Citroens of the staff of the Division that held the passes and the line of the mountain and the Rolls-Royces, Lancias, Mercedes, and Isottas of the General Staff. This was the sort of distinction that Robert Jordan should have made and, if he had been there instead of the old man, he would have appreciated the significance of these cars which had gone up. But he was not there and the old man simply made a mark for a motorcar going up the road, on the sheet of note paper. Anselmo was now so cold that he decided he had best go to camp before it was dark. He had no fear of missing the way, but he thought it was useless to stay longer and the wind was blowing colder all the time and there was no lessening of the snow. But when he stood up and stamped his feet and looked through the driving snow at the road he did not start off up the hillside but stayed leaning against the sheltered side of the pine tree. The Inglés told me to stay, he thought. Even now he may be on the way here and, if I leave this place, he may lose himself in the snow searching for me. All through this war we have suffered from a lack of discipline and from the disobeying of orders and I will wait a while still for the Inglés. But if he does not come soon I must go in spite of all orders for I have a report to make now, and I have much to do in these days, and to freeze here is an exaggeration and without utility. Across the road at the sawmill smoke was coming out of the chimney and Anselmo could smell it blown toward him through the snow. The fascists are warm, he thought, and they are comfortable, and tomorrow night we will kill them. It is a strange thing and I do not like to think of it. I have watched them all day and they are the same men that we are. I believe that I could walk up to the mill and knock on the door and I would be welcome except that they have orders to challenge all travellers and ask to see their papers. It is only orders that come between us. Those men are not fascists. I call them so, but they are not. They are poor men as we are. They should never be fighting against us and I do not like to think of the killing. These at this post are Gallegos. I know that from hearing them talk this afternoon. They cannot desert because if they do their families will be shot. Gallegos are either very intelligent or very dumb and brutal. I have known both kinds. Lister is a Gallego from the same town as Franco. I wonder what these Gallegos think of this snow now at this time of year. They have no high mountains such as these and in their country it always rains and it is always green. A light showed in the window of the sawmill and Anselmo shivered and thought, damn that Inglés! There are the Gallegos warm and in a house here in our country, and I am freezing behind a tree and we live in a hole in the rocks like beasts in the mountain. But tomorrow, he thought, the beasts will come out of their hole and these that are now so comfortable will die warm in their blankets. As those died in the night when we raided Otero, he thought. He did not like to remember Otero. In Otero, that night, was when he first killed and he hoped he would not have to kill in this of the suppressing of these posts. It was in Otero that Pablo knifed the sentry when Anselmo pulled the blanket over his head and the sentry caught Anselmo’s foot and held it, smothered as he was in the blanket, and made a crying noise in the blanket and Anselmo had to feel in the blanket and knife him until he let go of the foot and was still. He had his knee across the man’s throat to keep him silent and he was knifing into the bundle when Pablo tossed the bomb through the window into the room where the men of the post were all sleeping. And when the flash came it was as though the whole world burst red and yellow before your eyes and two more bombs were in already. Pablo had pulled the pins and tossed them quickly through the window, and those who were not killed in their beds were killed as they rose from bed when the second bomb exploded. That was in the great days of Pablo when he scourged the country like a tartar and no fascist post was safe at night. And now, he is as finished and as ended as a boar that has been altered, Anselmo thought, and, when the altering has been accomplished and the squealing is over you cast the two stones away and the boar, that is a boar no longer, goes snouting and rooting up to them and eats them. No, he is not that bad, Anselmo grinned, one can think too badly even of Pablo. But he is ugly enough and changed enough. It is too cold, he thought. That the Inglés should come and that I should not have to kill in this of the posts. These four Gallegos and their corporal are for those who like the killing. The Inglés said that. I will do it if it is my duty but the Inglés said that I would be with him at the bridge and that this would be left to others. At the bridge there will be a battle and, if I am able to endure the battle, then I will have done all that an old man may do in this war. But let the Inglés come now, for I am cold and to see the light in the mill where I know that the Gallegos are warm makes me colder still. I wish that I were in my own house again and that this war were over. But you have no house now, he thought. We must win this war before you can ever return to your house. Inside the sawmill one of the soldiers was sitting on his bunk and greasing his boots. Another lay in his bunk sleeping. The third was cooking and the corporal was reading a paper. Their helmets hung on nails driven into the wall and their rifles leaned against the plank wall.

“What kind of country is this where it snows when it is almost June?” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said.

“It is a phenomenon,” the corporal said.

“We are in the moon of May,” the soldier who was cooking said. “The moon of May has not yet terminated.”

“What kind of a country is it where it snows in May?” the soldier on the bunk insisted.

“In May snow is no rarity in these mountains,” the corporal said. “I have been colder in Madrid in the month of May than in any other month.”

“And hotter, too,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“May is a month of great contrasts in temperature,” the corporal said. “Here, in Castile, May is a month of great heat but it can have much cold.”

“Or rain,” the soldier on the bunk said. “In this past May it rained almost every day.”

“It did not,” the soldier who was cooking said. “And anyway this past May was the moon of April.”

“One could go crazy listening to thee and thy moons,” the corporal said. “Leave this of the moons alone.”

“Any one who lives either by the sea or by the land knows that it is the moon and not the month which counts,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Now for example, we have just started the moon of May. Yet it is coming on June.”

“Why then do we not get definitely behind in the seasons?” the corporal said. “The whole proposition gives me a headache.”

“You are from a town,” the soldier who was cooking said. “You are from Lugo. What would you know of the sea or of the land?”

“One learns more in a town than you analfabetos learn in thy sea or thy land.”

“In this moon the first of the big schools of sardines come,” the soldier who was cooking said. “In this moon the sardine boats will be outfitting and the mackerel will have gone north.”

“Why are you not in the navy if you come from Noya?” the corporal asked.

“Because I am not inscribed from Noya but from Negreira, where I was born. And from Negreira, which is up the river Tambre, they take you for the army.”

“Worse luck,” said the corporal.

“Do not think the navy is without peril,” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said. “Even without the possibility of combat that is a dangerous coast in the winter.”

“Nothing can be worse than the army,” the corporal said.

“And you a corporal,” the soldier who was cooking said. “What a way of speaking is that?”

“Nay,” the corporal said. “I mean for dangers. I mean the endurance of bombardments, the necessity to attack, the life of the parapet.”

“Here we have little of that,” the soldier on the bunk said.

“By the Grace of God,” the corporal said. “But who knows when we will be subject to it again? Certainly we will not have something as easy as this forever!”

“How much longer do you think we will have this detail?”

“I don’t know,” the corporal said. “But I wish we could have it for all of the war.”

“Six hours is too long to be on guard,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“We will have three-hour watches as long as this storm holds,” the corporal said. “That is only normal.”

“What about all those staff cars?” the soldier on the bunk asked. “I did not like the look of all those staff cars.”

“Nor I,” the corporal said. “All such things are of evil omen.”

“And aviation,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Aviation is another bad sign.”

“But we have formidable aviation,” the corporal said. “The reds have no aviation such as we have. Those planes this morning were something to make any man happy.”

“I have seen the red planes when they were something serious,” the soldier on the bunk said. “I have seen those two motor bombers when they were a horror to endure.”

“Yes. But they are not as formidable as our aviation,” the corporal said. “We have an aviation that is insuperable.” This was how they were talking in the sawmill while Anselmo waited in the snow watching the road and the light in the sawmill window. I hope I am not for the killing, Anselmo was thinking. I think that after the war there will have to be some great penance done for the killing. If we no longer have religion after the war then I think there must be some form of civic penance organized that all may be cleansed from the killing or else we will never have a true and human basis for living. The killing is necessary, I know, but still the doing of it is very bad for a man and I think that, after all this is over and we have won the war, there must be a penance of some kind for the cleansing of us all. Anselmo was a very good man and whenever he was alone for long, and he was alone much of the time, this problem of the killing returned to him. I wonder about the Inglés, he thought. He told me that he did not mind it. Yet he seems to be both sensitive and kind. It may be that in the younger people it does not have an importance. It may be that in foreigners, or in those who have not had our religion, there is not the same attitude. But I think any one doing it will be brutalized in time and I think that even though necessary, it is a great sin and that afterwards we must do something very strong to atone for it. It was dark now and he looked at the light across the road and shook his arms against his chest to warm them. Now, he thought, he would certainly leave for the camp; but something kept him there beside the tree above the road. It was snowing harder and Anselmo thought: if only we could blow the bridge tonight. On a night like this it would be nothing to take the posts and blow the bridge and it would be all over and done with. On a night like this you could do anything. Then he stood there against the tree stamping his feet softly and he did not think any more about the bridge. The coming of the dark always made him feel lonely and tonight he felt so lonely that there was a hollowness in him as of hunger. In the old days he could help this loneliness by saying of prayers and often coming home from hunting he would repeat a great number of the same prayer and it made him feel better. But he had not prayed once since the movement. He missed the prayers but he thought it would be unfair and hypocritical to say them and he did not wish to ask any favors or for any different treatment than all the men were receiving.

Excerpt 3: So now everything had been done that there was to do that night. All orders had been given. Every one knew exactly what he was to do in the morning. Andrés had been gone three hours. Either it would come now with the coming of the daylight or it would not come. I believe that it will come, Robert Jordan told himself, walking back down from the upper post where he had gone to speak to Primitivo. Golz makes the attack but he has not the power to cancel it. Permission to cancel it will have to come from Madrid. The chances are they won’t be able to wake anybody up there and if they do wake up they will be too sleepy to think. I should have gotten word to Golz sooner of the preparations they have made to meet the attack, but how could I send word about something until it happened? They did not move up that stuff until just at dark. They did not want to have any movement on the road spotted by planes. But what about all their planes? What about those fascist planes? Surely our people must have been warned by them. But perhaps the fascists were faking for another offensive down through Guadalajara with them. There were supposed to be Italian troops concentrated in Soria, and at Siguenza again besides those operating in the North. They haven’t enough troops or material to run two major offensives at the same time though. That is impossible; so it must be just a bluff. But we know how many troops the Italians have landed all last month and the month before at Cádiz. It is always possible they will try again at Guadalajara, not stupidly as before, but with three main fingers coming down to broaden it out and carry it along the railway to the west of the plateau. There was a way that they could do it all right. Hans had shown him. They made many mistakes the first time. The whole conception was unsound. They had not used any of the same troops in the Arganda offensive against the Madrid-Valencia road that they used at Guadalajara. Why had they not made those same drives simultaneously? Why? Why? When would we know why? Yet we had stopped them both times with the very same troops. We never could have stopped them if they had pulled both drives at once. Don’t worry, he told himself. Look at the miracles that have happened before this. Either you will have to blow that bridge in the morning or you will not have to. But do not start deceiving yourself into thinking you won’t have to blow it. You will blow it one day or you will blow it another. Or if it is not this bridge it will be some other bridge. It is not you who decides what shall be done. You follow orders. Follow them and do not try to think beyond them. The orders on this are very clear. Too very clear. But you must not worry nor must you be frightened. For if you allow yourself the luxury of normal fear that fear will infect those who must work with you. But that heads business was quite a thing all the same, he told himself. And the old man running onto them on the hilltop alone. How would you have liked to run onto them like that? That impressed you, didn’t it? Yes, that impressed you, Jordan. You have been quite impressed more than once today. But you have behaved O.K. So far you have behaved all right. You do very well for an instructor in Spanish at the University of Montana, he joked at himself. You do all right for that. But do not start to thinking that you are anything very special. You haven’t gotten very far in this business. Just remember Durán, who never had any military training and who was a composer and lad about town before the movement and is now a damned good general commanding a brigade. It was all as simple and easy to learn and understand to Durán as chess to a child chess prodigy. You had read on and studied the art of war ever since you were a boy and your grandfather had started you on the American Civil War. Except that Grandfather always called it the War of the Rebellion. But compared with Durán you were like a good sound chess player against a boy prodigy. Old Durán. It would be good to see Durán again. He would see him at Gaylord’s after this was over. Yes. After this was over. See how well he was behaving? I’ll see him at Gaylord’s, he said to himself again, after this is over. Don’t kid yourself, he said. You do it all perfectly O.K. Cold. Without kidding yourself. You aren’t going to see Durán any more and it is of no importance. Don’t be that way either, he told himself. Don’t go in for any of those luxuries. Nor for heroic resignation either. We do not want any citizens full of heroic resignation in these hills. Your grandfather fought four years in our Civil War and you are just finishing your first year in this war. You have a long time to go yet and you are very well fitted for the work. And now you have Maria, too. Why, you’ve got everything. You shouldn’t worry. What is a little brush between a guerilla band and a squadron of cavalry? That isn’t anything. What if they took the heads? Does that make any difference? None at all. The Indians always took the scalps when Grandfather was at Fort Kearny after the war. Do you remember the cabinet in your father’s office with the arrowheads spread out on a shelf, and the eagle feathers of the war bonnets that hung on the wall, their plumes slanting, the smoked buckskin smell of the leggings and the shirts and the feel of the beaded moccasins? Do you remember the great stave of the buffalo bow that leaned in a corner of the cabinet and the two quivers of hunting and war arrows, and how the bundle of shafts felt when you closed your hand around them? Remember something like that. Remember something concrete and practical. Remember Grandfather’s saber, bright and well oiled in its dented scabbard and Grandfather showed you how the blade had beer thinned from the many times it had been to the grinder’s. Remember Grandfather’s Smith and Wesson. It was a single action, officer’s model .32 caliber and there was no trigger guard. It had the softest, sweetest trigger pull you had ever felt and it was always well oiled and the bore was clean although the finish was all worn off and the brown metal of the barrel and the cylinder was worn smooth from the leather of the holster.
