The train was nearly an hour late, and the afternoon had gone gold and long by the time it drew in to Ellery. Helen Morrow stood on the platform of the car with her bag in her hand and looked out across the country while the brakes ground and the bell rang. She had been looking at it since morning, since the train crossed the Missouri. All day it had been unrolling past the window, and all day she had been telling herself that she did not remember it, that it was a new country to her. But when the train stopped and the wind came up against her face, warm and dry and smelling of ripened grass and dust, she knew that she had been mistaken. That wind she remembered. She had carried it with her for twenty-two years without knowing it.

There were only a few people on the platform: a drummer with his sample cases, two farmers waiting for freight, and a stout woman in a brown dress and a hat that had been trimmed over at least once. The woman was shading her eyes and looking along the cars. Helen stepped down, and the woman turned, and for a moment neither of them moved.

"Well, Helen," said the woman at last. "Well, here you are."

"Della," Helen said. "Oh, Della, I wouldn't have known you, and yet I would have known you anywhere."

They kissed awkwardly, as people do who were children together and have not touched since, and then Della took her by both arms and held her off and looked at her frankly, the way country people look at things they mean to remember.

"You've kept your figure," she said. "And your hands. I always said you would keep your hands. Look at mine." She held them out, broad and brown, the knuckles large. There was a wedding ring sunk deep in the flesh of one finger. "I couldn't get that off now if I wanted to. Peter says it's grown on like bark on a tree. Come along. The team don't like the engine."

The buggy was drawn up at the end of the platform, and the horses, a pair of bays, were stamping and switching at the flies. Della untied them and climbed up with an ease that surprised Helen, for she had grown heavy, and Helen handed up her bag and followed. They drove out past the grain elevator and the lumberyard and the two churches, down a main street that Helen thought she would have recognized if it had not been so much longer and so much better built than she remembered. There were brick fronts now, and a bank with a stone cornice, and a hotel with a wide porch where men sat tipped back in chairs.

"It's grown," Helen said.

"Everything's grown," said Della. "You'll see."

Beyond the town the road ran straight to the west between fields of corn. The corn stood higher than the horses' heads, and the tassels had gone brown, and the long leaves rattled together when the wind went through them. When Helen was a child this had been open country, red grass to the horizon, with here and there a sod house or a dugout or a little frame shanty no bigger than a henhouse. There had been no fences then, only the wagon tracks wandering off across the prairie, and the sunflowers growing tall along them where the wheels had broken the sod. Now there were fences everywhere, and windmills turning, and groves of trees about the farmhouses, cottonwoods and box elders and ash, so that the land seemed to have been gathered in and made small, like a quilt pieced together from many squares.

"I don't know where I am," Helen said. "I used to know every draw and every hill along here."

"There's not so many hills as you'd think," Della told her. "They've plowed most of them down. That's the Kovar place, where the big barn is. You remember old Mrs. Kovar, who used to bring us poppy-seed bread? Her grandsons have it now. They're doing well. Everybody is doing well, these last years. It's hard to believe, after what it was."

She spoke without bitterness, as she might have spoken of the weather of some other country. Helen looked at her profile under the old hat. It was a broad, ruddy face, deeply lined at the eyes from squinting into the sun, and the mouth had grown firm and a little grim at the corners. But when Della turned and smiled, it was the same smile that Helen had carried away with her when she was twenty-two and Della was nineteen: slow, a little crooked, beginning in the eyes before it reached the lips.

"You're staring at me," Della said.

"I'm trying to find you."

"Oh, I'm here. There's just more of me." She laughed and touched up the horses. "Seven children will do that. And forty acres of garden."

"Seven," Helen said. "You wrote me about the first four. I'm afraid I lost track after that."

"So did I, nearly." Della was silent for a little while. "There were eight. We lost the second boy when he was two. Diphtheria, the winter of ninety-six. I wrote you about that, too, but maybe the letter never came. Letters went astray, in those days."

Helen said that she had had the letter. She remembered it very well, a single sheet written in pencil, the lines running crookedly downhill. She remembered that she had read it in her room on Pinckney Street in Boston, with the snow coming down outside and someone practicing scales in the room below, and that she had not been able to think what to write back, and that in the end she had written something stiff and correct that she had been ashamed of ever since.

"I didn't answer it properly," she said.

"I didn't expect you to. What was there to say?" Della shook her head. "Nobody can say anything about a thing like that. I know that now. I didn't know it then."

The sun was going down when they turned in at the lane. The farmhouse stood on a low rise with a grove of cottonwoods behind it to the north, and the leaves of the cottonwoods were already turning, so that the whole grove shone yellow against the sky. It was a square white house with a porch across the front, and there was a big red barn and a windmill and a row of hives along the garden fence. A great many children seemed to come out of it all at once, and a collie dog, and a tall stooped man in overalls who came last and stood a little apart, wiping his hands on a cloth.

"That's Peter," Della said. "He won't talk much. He never does. Don't think it's you."

Peter Hanek took Helen's hand in his own, which was enormous and very hard, and said, "You are welcome," with great seriousness, and then took her bag and carried it into the house. The children were introduced in order of their ages, from Mary, who was eighteen and had her mother's slow smile, down to the baby, whom Mary carried on her hip. They looked at Helen's gray traveling suit and her gloves and her hat with the single wing on it, and the smaller ones hid their faces against their sisters' skirts, but they did not go away.

Supper was laid in the kitchen, which was the largest room in the house. There was a long table covered with oilcloth, and a range that took up half of one wall, and a cupboard with glass doors where Della kept her good dishes. Helen had forgotten what farm suppers were. There was fried chicken and new potatoes and sweet corn and sliced tomatoes, and bread that Mary had baked that morning, and three kinds of preserves, and a plum pie, and coffee so strong that Helen could only drink half a cup of it. Peter sat at the head of the table and ate steadily and said almost nothing. Once, when the second boy, Frank, began to tell a story about a coyote he had seen in the pasture, his father looked at him, and Frank stopped and finished his supper in silence. But afterward, when Helen praised the pie, Peter lifted his eyes to his wife and said, in his slow careful English, "She makes the best. Always, in the whole country," and Della colored like a girl and told him not to be foolish.

When the dishes were washed, and the little children put to bed, and Mary sent upstairs with the baby, Della took a shawl from the hook behind the door and said, "Come out. It's too fine a night to sit in."

They went out across the yard and through the gate and along a cowpath that ran beside the cornfield. The sky was still light in the west, a clear deep green above the place where the sun had gone down, and one star had come out low over the horizon. The air had turned cool. Somewhere a long way off a dog was barking, and nearer at hand the crickets were going in the grass.

"Do you know where we're going?" Della asked.

Helen said she did not.

"Over that rise, and down, and across the draw. It isn't far. A mile and a half, maybe. You used to walk it twice a day."

Then Helen knew. She stopped in the path. "Grandmother's place," she said.

"What's left of it."

They walked on without speaking. The cornfield ended and there was pasture land, still in native grass, and the grass was red and bronze in the twilight, and it moved under the wind like the hide of a living animal. Helen felt something tighten in her throat. She had not seen that color anywhere else in the world. She had looked for it, without quite knowing that she looked, in the autumn marshes along the coast below Boston and in the hills of New Hampshire, and once, years ago, in a field in the south of France where she had gone with a party of other teachers. But it had never been there.

"It's the only quarter that's never been broken," Della said. "Peter bought it from the Swedes who had it after your folks went back East. He says he'll never plow it. I don't know why. He's not a man to waste land. But he says a person ought to keep a piece of the old country, just to remember what it was."

"I'm grateful to him."

"I'll tell him. He'll be pleased. He won't say so."

They came down into the draw. There was a little creek at the bottom, nearly dry at this season, and a thicket of wild plum along its banks, and beyond the creek, on a shelf of level ground, stood three old cottonwoods. They were very big now, their trunks rough and furrowed, their tops ragged where the wind had broken them. There was nothing else. The house had been sod, and the sod had long ago melted back into the earth. Where it had stood there was only a low mound overgrown with grass and buckbrush, and a hollow beside it where the cellar had been.

"We planted those," Helen said. She went up to the nearest cottonwood and laid her hand against it. The bark was still warm from the sun. "You and I and Walter. Grandmother sent us down to the river for the slips, and we carried them back in a bucket, and Walter dropped one on the way and cried because he thought it would die."

"It was that one," said Della, pointing. "The smallest. It lived, though."

"Yes. It lived."

Della spread her shawl on the grass at the foot of the trees and they sat down together, as they had sat there when they were children, with their backs against the same trunk. The draw was in shadow now, but up above them the sky was still bright, and the tops of the cottonwoods caught the last of the light.

"I think about Walter more than I'd have believed," Della said after a while. "More than I did when it happened. Isn't that strange? You'd think it would wear off."

Walter was Della's brother. He had been fifteen the summer he went down to the river with the hired man to water the horses and did not come back. They found him two days later, three miles downstream, caught in the roots of a willow. Helen had gone East that same autumn. She had always believed, though she never said so to anyone, that she would not have had the courage to go if it had not been for Walter. After Walter, everything at home had seemed already finished.

"I think about him, too," she said. "I used to dream about him. He was always carrying that bucket."

"He'd be forty-two this winter. Can you think of Walter at forty-two? With a bald spot, maybe, and a paunch?"

"No," said Helen. "I can't."

"No more can I. He'll always be just a boy. Sometimes I think he's the lucky one, and then I'm ashamed of thinking it." Della pulled a stem of grass and began to chew it. "Tell me about yourself now. Your letters never told anything. They were nice letters, but they never told anything. You wrote about concerts and the pictures you saw and the weather in Boston. I used to read them out loud to Peter, and he'd listen, and afterward he'd say, 'But how is she?' And I never could tell him."

Helen laughed a little. "I suppose I didn't know how I was."

"Are you happy?"

It was a question that nobody had asked her in a great many years, and she found she could not answer it at once. She looked up at the cottonwood leaves moving against the sky.

"I have my work," she said at last. "I have forty pupils, and some of them are good, and one or two are better than good. There's a girl now, a little Italian girl from the North End, who plays Chopin as if she'd been born knowing it. When I hear her play, I think that's enough. I think it's worth having gone away for. And I have friends, and a room with a view of the river, and I go abroad every third summer. I have a good many things."

"But you never married."

"No. There was someone once. He was a lawyer, a widower. He was very kind. He wanted me to give up teaching, and I couldn't make up my mind to it, and while I was making up my mind he married someone else. I don't think I minded as much as I ought to have. That's the dreadful part, Della. I don't think I minded much at all."

Della said nothing for a while. Then she reached over and took Helen's hand in her own rough one and held it on her knee.

"I used to envy you," she said. "Oh, you don't know how I envied you. Those first years, when the drought came and the corn burned up in the fields, and we lived on cornmeal and sorghum, and Peter went off to work on the railroad and left me alone with the babies, I used to think about you in Boston with your music and your fine clothes, and I'd cry myself to sleep. I'd think, that could have been me. I could have gone, too. Aunt Sarah would have taken me if I'd asked. And I'd think I'd thrown my whole life away on a quarter section of sand and a man who couldn't speak English."

"And now?"

"Now I don't know. I don't think about it the same way." She turned Helen's hand over and looked at the palm, as if she might read something there. "I've had a hard life. I won't pretend I haven't. But it's been a full one. Every year there was something that had to be done, and I did it, and when I look back I can see it all, every bit of it, like rows in a field. The house, and the trees, and the children. Mary, and Frank, and the baby. Even little Joe, that we lost. He's part of it, too. I wouldn't give up having had him, not for anything, though I've grieved for him every day since." She paused. "I guess what I mean is, I wouldn't trade. Not now. But I'm glad one of us went. I'm glad it was you. Somebody had to go and see the world for both of us, and you were always the one who could."

Helen found that she was crying, quietly, the tears running down her cheeks in the dark. She did not try to stop them. Della did not seem to notice, or if she noticed she gave no sign, but went on holding her hand and looking out across the draw.

It was quite dark now. The stars had come out thick overhead, and down in the plum thicket a whippoorwill had begun to call. The wind had dropped, and the cottonwood leaves hung still. Far off to the east, across the fields, they could see the lights of the farmhouse, a lamp in the kitchen and another in an upstairs window where Mary was putting the baby to sleep.

"We ought to go back," Della said at last. "Peter will be wondering. He worries, though he won't say."

They got up stiffly, and Della shook out her shawl and put it around Helen's shoulders, because the night had grown cold and Helen was in her thin traveling suit. They climbed up out of the draw and stood for a moment on the rise, looking back. The three cottonwoods were only a darker shape against the sky now, and the mound where the house had been could not be seen at all.

"I'm glad you came," said Della. "I didn't think you would. I'd about given up."

"So had I," Helen said. "I don't know why I waited so long. I suppose I was afraid."

"Of what?"

"Of finding it all gone."

Della considered this. "Some of it's gone," she said. "Most of it. But not all. Not the part that matters. That stays."

They walked back along the cowpath together, the grass wet now with dew and brushing against their skirts. Neither of them spoke. When they came into the yard, Peter was standing on the porch with a lantern in his hand. He did not say anything when he saw them, only nodded and turned and went into the house ahead of them, holding the lantern high so that they could see the steps.

That night Helen lay awake for a long time in the spare room under the eaves. The window was open, and the white curtain stirred in a wind that had come up again out of the west, and through it she could hear the windmill creaking and the cottonwood leaves stirring in the grove. She thought of the little Italian girl in Boston, bent over the piano in the gray winter light. She thought of Walter carrying the bucket of slips up from the river, his face red with crying, and of Della at nineteen, standing in the door of the sod house with her hand raised against the sun. It seemed to her that all these things were part of one thing, and that she had only now begun to understand it. She did not know what it was. But she lay very still, listening to the wind, and for the first time in many years she was not lonely; and presently, toward morning, she slept.

The Rybar farm lay in a shallow draw, eight miles north of the town of Wilber, where the land fell away from the high prairie and made a little hollow sheltered from the worst of the winds. In the autumn, when the sunflowers along the section lines had gone brown and rattled on their stalks, the hollow held the afternoon light longer than the open country did. The grass on the slopes turned the colour of a fox's back, and the willows by the creek were yellow as old brass. From the kitchen window Josefa Rybar could see the whole of it: the corral and the cattle shed with its roof of straw, the windmill turning slowly over the stock tank, the long field where her husband was husking corn with the hired boy, and beyond that the sky, which in that country was always the largest thing one looked at.

On this October afternoon she was baking. She had set her bread before daylight, and now the loaves stood in a row on the shelf by the stove, brown and shining where she had brushed them with lard. She was a tall woman, broad in the shoulders, with a strong brown neck and grey eyes that were set wide apart. She had been handsome when she was a girl in Bohemia, and she was still handsome in a way people did not often remark upon, because she was always working and never sat still long enough to be looked at. Her hands were red from the lye soap, and there was a burn on one wrist from the oven door. She did not mind it. She had been burned many times.

The children came home from the schoolhouse a little after four. The two boys went straight to the barn to help with the milking, but Lida, who was seven, came in alone and stood just inside the door, holding her dinner pail against her apron. She was a small, quick child, with her father's black hair and a pointed chin, and as a rule she came into the house like a sparrow into a hedge, all noise and flutter. Today she said nothing at all. She put her pail on the bench and hung her shawl on its nail and went to the corner by the woodbox, where she sat down on the low stool and began to pick at a scab on her knee.

Her mother glanced at her once and went on with her work. Josefa had borne five children and buried one of them, and she had learned that a child who is quiet without being sick has usually done something. She did not ask. She thought it better to let the thing come out of its own weight, as a stone works up through a field after frost.

It came out sooner than she expected. Before the sun was down she heard the gate by the road creak, and when she went to the window she saw old Mrs. Kessler coming up the path. The old woman walked slowly, leaning a little to one side, and she carried something in her arms wrapped in a piece of grey blanket. She wore, as she always did, a man's felt hat tied under her chin with a strip of calico, and a long black skirt that had gone green at the hem with age and weather.

Mrs. Kessler lived alone in a sod house a mile and a half to the west, on a quarter section that her husband had taken up when the country was first opened. He had died in the third year, of a fever he got from drinking slough water, and she had stayed on. Nobody knew exactly how old she was. She spoke no English, only a German that even the German settlers said was hard to follow, and she kept a flock of grey geese that she drove out every morning to feed along the creek, walking behind them with a long willow switch. The children of the neighbourhood called her the Goose Woman, and some of the older ones said she was a witch, because she talked to her geese and because there was a dried snakeskin nailed over her door.

Josefa opened the door before the old woman could knock. "Good evening, Mrs. Kessler," she said in German, for she had worked a year in a German household in Prague before she was married, and she could make herself understood.

The old woman did not answer the greeting. She drew back the corner of the blanket, and Josefa saw that she was holding a grey gander, one of the big ones, with its long neck lying limp across her arm. One wing hung down at a wrong angle, and the feathers along it were stuck together with blood. The bird's eye was open and very bright, and when Josefa bent over it, it hissed feebly and tried to raise its head.

Mrs. Kessler began to speak. She spoke quickly and in a high, cracked voice, and Josefa could not catch all of it, but she caught enough. Children had come along the creek at noon, at the dinner hour when they were let out of the schoolhouse. They had thrown clods of dirt at the geese and chased them, and they had shouted things. When the old woman came out of her house with her switch, they had run away laughing, and one of them, a little girl with black hair, had turned at the top of the bank and thrown a stone. The stone had struck the gander. The old woman held the bird out a little, as if it were a piece of evidence before a magistrate, and her chin trembled. She had raised that gander from an egg, she said. He was eleven years old. He was the one who led the others home in the evening.

Josefa stood very still in the doorway. Behind her she could feel the silence from the corner by the woodbox, and she knew without turning that her daughter had heard everything and understood the meaning of it, even if she did not understand the words.

"I am sorry," she said at last. "I am very sorry. I will see to it. You will not be troubled again."

She asked the old woman to come in and sit down, to have coffee and bread, but Mrs. Kessler shook her head. She wrapped the blanket about the gander again with great care, tucking it under the bird's feet, and turned and went back down the path. Josefa watched her go through the gate and out along the road, a small, dark, bent figure against the red light, until she went down into the dip by the culvert and was gone.

Then she shut the door and turned around.

Lida had not moved from the stool. Her face was white, and her hands were holding each other very tightly in her lap. Her mother came and stood over her, and for a long moment said nothing at all. The kettle ticked on the stove. Out by the barn one of the boys was whistling.

"Stand up," Josefa said.

The child stood up.

"Did you throw the stone?"

Lida's lips moved, but no sound came from them. Then she said, very fast, "It was the Nygaard boys. They threw first. Ole Nygaard threw first, and Knut, and they said she was a witch and would put a spell on the corn, and everybody was throwing, and I only threw one, I didn't mean to hit anything, I only—"

"I did not ask about Ole Nygaard," her mother said. "Ole Nygaard has a mother of his own. Did you throw the stone?"

"Yes."

"Did you hit the gander?"

The child's eyes filled, and her chin began to shake. "I didn't know it would break," she said. "I didn't know it would."

Josefa did not raise her voice. Lida would have been less afraid if she had. When the children were naughty in small ways, about chores or quarrelling, their mother scolded them loudly and in a mixture of two languages, and sometimes she boxed their ears, and it was over in a minute, like a summer storm. But now she spoke low and slowly, and her face had a stillness in it that the child had seen only once before, on the day the little brother died.

"Sit down at the table," she said.

Lida sat down. Her mother drew out the chair across from her and sat too, with her red hands folded on the oilcloth. The light from the west window fell across the table between them and lay there in a long yellow bar.

"Now you will listen to me," Josefa said. "When we came to this country, you were not born. Your brother Frank was a baby, and your father and I came on the train from New York with everything we owned in two boxes and a feather bed tied up in a sheet. We got off the train at Wilber in the snow. It was February. We did not know anybody. We did not know how to say anything but 'yes' and 'thank you,' and we did not always know when to say which. Your father had a coat from the old country, a long coat with a fur collar, that his father had given him. It was the best thing he had. And when we walked through the town, carrying the boxes, there were boys on the sidewalk in front of the store, big boys, and they laughed at that coat. They laughed and pointed and walked behind your father like this"—she lifted her shoulders and threw back her head in a stiff, foolish way—"and one of them threw snow at him. Your father did not say anything. He did not know the words. He only walked on, carrying the box. But I saw his face."

She stopped. Lida was looking at her with wide eyes, the tears running down her cheeks unheeded.

"That first winter," her mother went on, "we lived in a dugout by the creek, on this place, before your father built the house. It was a hole in the bank with a door on it. The snow came over the top of it, and we had to dig out every morning. We had no cow. We had a little flour and some potatoes, and when they were gone we had nothing. And in March, when Frank was sick and I thought he would die, a woman came across the snow from the west with a can of milk under her shawl. She walked a mile and a half in the snow. She did not speak our language and we did not speak hers. She came in and looked at the baby and put the milk on the table and went away again. She came every day for two weeks, until the snow went off and your father could get to town."

The child said in a whisper, "Was it—"

"It was Mrs. Kessler," her mother said. "Her husband was alive then. They had a cow. They had only the one."

Lida put her head down on her arms and began to cry aloud, with the hard, tearing sobs of a child who has seen all at once the size of something she did not know was there. Josefa let her cry. She did not reach across the table. She sat looking out of the window at the hollow, where the light was going out of the willows and the creek had turned to a thread of pale silver, and she waited until the crying had worn itself down.

"In this country," she said then, "there are people who have had a hard life and people who have had a harder one. You do not know yet which you will be. Nobody knows. But I will not have a child of mine throwing stones at an old woman because she is poor and talks strange and lives alone. I will not have it. You hear me?"

"Yes," said Lida into her sleeve.

"Look at me when I speak to you."

The child raised her face. It was swollen and blotched, and her black hair stuck to her forehead.

"You will go to Mrs. Kessler now," her mother said. "Before your father comes in. You will take her a loaf of the bread and the jar of plum butter from the cellar, and you will tell her you are sorry. I will teach you what to say. You will say it to her face, and then you will come home. And on Saturday you will go again and help her with whatever she wants done, and the Saturday after, until the gander is well or until I say."

Lida's eyes went to the window, where the sky was already turning the colour of a ripe apricot. "It will be dark," she said.

"Then you had better go quickly."

Josefa got up and went down into the cellar and came back with the jar of plum butter, dark as wine, and wrapped it in a clean cloth. She took the best of the loaves from the shelf, the one that had risen highest, and wrapped that too, and put them both in a willow basket. Then she knelt down in front of the child and buttoned her coat to the chin and tied the shawl over her head, and while she did it she said the German words over and over, slowly, until Lida could say them back. *Es tut mir leid. Ich bitte um Verzeihung.* It does me sorrow. I ask your pardon.

"Again," her mother said.

"*Es tut mir leid. Ich bitte um Verzeihung.*"

"Good. Go now."

Lida went out with the basket on her arm. The air had turned cold, and there was a smell of frost in it, and of burnt grass from a fire somewhere far off to the south. She went down the path and through the gate and out along the road, and when she came to the top of the rise beyond the culvert she stopped and looked back. Her mother was standing in the lighted doorway, a tall dark shape with the kitchen glowing behind her. She did not wave. She only stood there, and the child understood that she would stand there until she could no longer see her.

The road ran west along the section line, straight toward the sunset. On either side the prairie stretched away, rolling and empty, the tall red grass moving in the wind with a sound like water. The whole sky was on fire. Long bars of crimson and gold lay along the horizon, and above them the sky deepened to green and then to a clear, cold blue, in which the first star had come out, very small and white. A flock of sandhill cranes went over high up, going south, calling to one another in their strange, rusty voices. Lida had heard the cranes all her life, but tonight they sounded lonely to her, and she walked faster.

She thought about the gander. She thought about the sound the stone had made, a soft, dull sound, not at all what she had expected, and how the bird had fallen over sideways in the shallow water and flapped one wing and could not get up. The Nygaard boys had been laughing so hard that they did not see it. She had seen it. She had run away with the others, laughing too, because she did not know what else to do, but all afternoon in the schoolhouse, while the teacher heard the spelling lesson, she had seen it again every time she shut her eyes.

Mrs. Kessler's sod house stood on a little rise above the creek, with a stand of box-elder trees behind it that her husband had planted. In the dusk it looked like a part of the hill itself, low and dark, with grass growing on the roof. There was a light in the one window. The geese were shut up for the night in a pen made of willow poles, and as Lida came up the path they set up a great clamour, honking and hissing, so that the door opened before she reached it.

The old woman stood there with a lamp in her hand. She had taken off her hat, and her hair was thin and white and braided close to her head. She looked down at the child for a long time without speaking.

Lida held out the basket. Her throat had closed up, and for a moment she could not remember any of the words at all. Then they came back to her in her mother's voice, and she said them, stumbling: "*Es tut mir leid. Ich bitte um Verzeihung.*" And then, because the German was not enough, she said in English, "I'm sorry. I'm sorry about the goose," and began to cry again.

The old woman stepped back and held the door wide.

Inside, the sod house was warm and smelled of earth and woodsmoke and something sour, like cabbage. The walls had been plastered and whitewashed, and there was a picture of a saint over the bed, and a clock with a painted face that ticked loudly on a shelf. In a box beside the stove, on a bed of hay, lay the gander. Someone had bound his wing to his side with strips of cloth, and he was sitting up with his neck curved and his eyes half closed. When the child came near, he opened them and looked at her, but he did not hiss.

Mrs. Kessler set the lamp on the table and took the bread and the plum butter out of the basket and looked at them. She unwrapped the loaf and held it up to the light, turning it, and nodded slowly, as if she were judging a piece of cloth. Then she cut two slices from the end, and spread them thick with the plum butter, and gave one to Lida and kept one for herself. They ate standing up, by the stove, without a word between them, while the clock ticked and the gander dozed in his box. When they had finished, the old woman bent down and put her hand on the child's head, just for a moment, and said something in German that Lida did not understand. Then she opened the door again.

It was full dark when Lida came home. The stars were out over the whole sky, thick and near, and the windmill stood up black against them. Her father had come in from the field, and he was washing at the bench by the door, splashing water over his face and neck. He looked up as she came into the light, and then he looked at his wife, and something passed between them that the child did not see. He said only, "So. You are back," and went on washing.

Her mother was setting the table. She did not ask how it had gone. She took the empty basket from Lida's arm and hung it on its hook, and unwound the shawl, and unbuttoned the coat, and then, still kneeling, she put her arms around the child and held her hard against her breast for as long as it takes to count ten. She smelled of bread and woodsmoke. Then she got up and said, "Wash your hands. Supper is ready," in her ordinary voice, and it was over.

Many years afterward, when Lida Rybar was a grown woman with children of her own, living in a frame house in Omaha with a furnace in the cellar and a piano in the parlour, she would sometimes think of that evening. She would remember the road running west into the burning sky, and the cranes going over, and the sound of the old woman's clock. She could not remember a single word of the German that Mrs. Kessler had spoken to her at the door. But she remembered her mother's face across the kitchen table in the yellow light, and the stillness of it, and she came to believe that it was on that evening, and not on any other, that she had first understood what her parents had come through to give her the life she had. It seemed to her that everything she knew about being good, whatever little it was, she had learned in the time it took to walk a mile and a half across the prairie in the dusk, carrying a loaf of bread.

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? People say sometimes he runs about the country howling at night because he is afraid the Lord will destroy him. Mother thinks he must have done something awful wicked.” Lou looked back and winked at Carl. “What would you do, Emil, if you was out on the prairie by yourself and seen him coming?” Emil stared. “Maybe I could hide in a badger-hole,” he suggested doubtfully.

“But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

The wind had gone down with the sun, as it often did in late August, and the stillness that came after it was almost a sound in itself. Henrik Sorensen sat on the bench outside his kitchen door, his boots unlaced and his elbows on his knees, and looked out over the stubble fields toward the west, where a long bar of copper-colored cloud lay along the edge of the world. The wheat was in, and it had been a fair crop; not so good as the year the rains came every week in June, but better than his neighbors had expected, and much better than he himself had feared. He had paid the thresher that morning in cash, counting the bills out upon the wagon-box, and he had felt, while he did it, something that was very like contentment.

Inside, his wife was washing the supper dishes. He could hear the clink of the plates and the splash of the dipper in the reservoir of the range. Marta was a slow, thorough worker, and she did not like to be hurried or spoken to while her hands were in the water. In twenty-two years he had learned that, along with a good many other things about her, and he waited.

Henrik had come out from Denmark at nineteen, with a cousin who had gone back after the first hard winter. He had worked for other men in Iowa for four years, saving everything, and then he had come farther west to take up land of his own. He had been a lean, red-haired young fellow then, with a quick temper and a great deal of faith in his own two arms. The temper had cooled and the hair had faded to the color of dry grass, but the faith remained, though it had shifted its ground a little. He believed now not so much in his arms as in the land itself, in its patience and its long memory. He had seen men come and go on the Divide, had seen them break their hearts and their plowshares on it and give it up; and he had stayed, and the land had been good to him, in its fashion. He owned three hundred and twenty acres free and clear, and a good frame house with a parlor, and a windmill, and eleven head of cattle. For a man who had crossed the ocean with a wooden box and a pair of extra shirts, it was not so little.

The door creaked behind him, and Marta came out, drying her hands on her apron. She was a large woman, broad in the shoulders and the hips, with a calm face and very clear gray eyes that had a way of resting on things a long time before she spoke of them. She did not sit down beside him, but stood against the door-frame, looking where he looked.

"Erik has gone to bed?" Henrik asked.

"He is up in the loft with his lamp. Reading."

"Always reading." Henrik said it without unkindness, as a man might remark that a colt was always running. "He will put his eyes out, that boy."

Marta did not answer. She folded her apron over her arm and smoothed it, and then she said, in the even voice she used for the most important things as well as the least, "I want to talk to you about Erik, Henrik."

He looked up at her quickly. Something in the stillness of her face made him straighten on the bench.

"Well, what about him? He is a good boy. He worked well this harvest. Nyquist said to me he never saw a boy of seventeen pitch bundles so steady."

"He is a good boy," Marta agreed. "That is why I want to talk about him."

She came and sat down at the other end of the bench, leaving a space between them, and put her hands together in her lap. They were red from the dishwater, and the knuckles were swollen a little, as her mother's had been. Henrik noticed them, and noticed, too, that she was holding them very tightly.

"The teacher came to see me last week," she said, "while you were at Nyquist's helping with the stacking. Miss Corliss."

"I know Miss Corliss."

"She says Erik is the best scholar she has ever had in that school. She says he has learned everything she knows how to teach him, and some things she does not know herself. She says he ought to go to the university in Lincoln."

Henrik was silent. A meadowlark, late at its business, sang once from the fence-post by the road, and then was quiet. Out in the corral one of the horses blew through its nose and stamped.

"Miss Corliss is a young woman from town," he said at last. "She has ideas. Town people think everybody ought to go to school until they are thirty years old. Who will run the place when I am old? Who will the land go to?"

"There is Nils. Nils does not care for books. He will stay on the land and be glad to."

"Nils is twelve years old."

"He will not always be twelve."

Henrik turned and looked at her fully now. He was beginning to understand that she had not come out to him by chance, that she had been thinking about this for a long time, perhaps for longer than a week, and that she had made up her mind about it before ever she opened her mouth. That was her way. She was not a woman who argued; she decided, slowly and alone, and afterward she held to what she had decided as a tree holds to a hillside.

"And where is the money to come from?" he asked. "Do you know what it costs, to keep a boy in Lincoln? Board and books and clothes and I don't know what all. Four years of it. You have to buy everything in town. You know I have been talking to Johnson about the Nyberg quarter. The old woman wants to sell, and she will let it go cheap, because the sons are all in Omaha and don't care. That is good land, Marta. It lies right against ours. There is water on it. If I don't buy it, some Englishman from the east will, and put a tenant on it who will let it go to weeds."

"I know about the Nyberg quarter."

"Then you know where the money is going."

Marta looked down at her hands. When she spoke again her voice was lower, but it had not lost its evenness.

"There is money for Erik," she said. "I have it. I have been putting it by."

Henrik stared at her. For a moment he did not understand, and then, quite suddenly, he understood altogether, and a slow heat came up into his face.

"What money?"

"The butter money. The eggs. What I got for the turkeys every fall. Some of it I gave to the house, you know that. But some of it I kept back. I have kept it back for six years, ever since Erik finished the fourth reader in one winter and Miss Hadley told me then he was not like other children." She drew a breath. "There is four hundred and twelve dollars. It is in the blue coffee tin, on the top shelf of the cave, behind the crocks of lard."

The copper bar in the west had gone dull now, the color of an old kettle, and above it the sky was turning that clear, deep green which comes only on the high prairie, and only for a little while. Henrik looked at it without seeing it. He was thinking of the blue coffee tin. He had seen it a hundred times, going down into the cave for potatoes or a jar of pickles. He had thought it held buttons, or seeds.

"Six years," he said.

"Yes."

"Six years you have been hiding money in my cellar, and never said a word."

"It is not hiding. It is saving."

"You did not tell me. That is hiding." He stood up, as if he could not sit still under it, and walked a few steps into the yard and turned around. "What kind of a wife is it who keeps money from her husband? Behind the lard! Like a hired girl who steals sugar!"

Marta did not flinch, but the color left her face, and her mouth set in a straight line. She had always been a fair-skinned woman, and in the dusk her face looked almost white.

"I did not steal it, Henrik. I made it. I churned that butter. I raised those turkeys from the egg, and sat up nights with them when they had the gapes, and carried them into the kitchen in the hail that time. You never once fed them. You never once looked at them, except to say they made too much noise."

"And who bought the feed? Who built the coop?"

"You did. And I did not keep that money. I gave it to the flour and the coffee and the children's shoes and the doctor when Anna was sick. I kept back only what was left over, a little at a time. Sometimes it was only a quarter. One whole year it was only nine dollars."

He stood before her with his hands hanging. He was not an unjust man, and in the part of his mind that stood apart from his anger he knew that what she said was so. But his pride had been touched in a tender place, and pride is slower than justice to come to terms.

"Why didn't you tell me?" he said again, and this time it was not so much an accusation as a question, and there was hurt in it.

Marta was a long time in answering. She looked out past him, at the windmill standing black against the green sky, its wheel quite still.

"Because I knew what you would say," she said at last. "You would say, 'That is good, Marta, now we can buy the Nyberg quarter a year sooner.' Or the new binder. Or the heifers from Kearney. You would not mean any harm by it. You would think it was the right thing, and maybe for you it would be the right thing. And I would let you have it, because you are my husband. So I did not tell you."

Henrik opened his mouth and closed it again. There was nothing he could say to that, because he knew that it was true. He could hear himself saying those very words.

He came back and sat down heavily on the bench, closer to her this time. For a while neither of them spoke. The dusk was thickening fast now, and the first stars had come out over the cornfield to the east, small and far apart. Somewhere over toward the creek a coyote set up its thin, wavering cry, and another answered it.

"You think I care more for the land than for my own boy," Henrik said finally, in a low voice.

"No. I do not think that." Marta turned toward him. "I think you care for the land because of the boys. Because you want them to have what you never had at home. I know that. I have always known it. But Erik does not want what you want for him, Henrik. He is not like you, and he is not like Nils. When he goes out with the team he takes a book in his shirt, and when the horses rest he reads. When he went with you to the river last spring he came back and told me the names of all the birds, and where they go in the winter, and how far. I did not know them. You did not know them. Where did he learn that?"

"From books," Henrik said shortly.

"From books. And from looking. He looks at everything, that boy. He looks at the land the way you look at it, only he sees different things in it. He sees what it is made of, and what was here before us, and why the grass grows one way on the north slope and another way on the south. Miss Corliss says there are men in Lincoln who study only that, their whole lives long. She says Erik could be one of them."

Henrik rubbed his hand over his face. He was tired; he had been up since four, and the day's work and the day's satisfaction seemed to have drained away all at once, leaving only weariness behind.

"I don't understand such things," he said. "A man should work with his hands. A man should make something come out of the ground. What is a man who only looks?"

"Maybe he will find out something that helps men like you make more come out of the ground," Marta said. "There are such men now. The county agent who came last winter, who told you about the alfalfa. He went to school for that."

Henrik was silent. He remembered the county agent, a thin young man with spectacles and a soft voice, whom he had privately thought a fool until the alfalfa came up thick and green on the low forty that had never grown anything but sunflowers.

"You remember my father?" Marta asked suddenly.

He looked at her in surprise. "I never saw your father. He died before you came over."

"I mean, you remember what I told you of him. He was a schoolmaster in Ribe. A poor one; we had nothing. But he had books, two whole walls of them, and when I was a little girl he used to read to me in the evenings, out of the old sagas and out of Holberg, and sometimes out of books about the stars. I did not understand much. But I remember how his face looked. It was like a lamp was lit in it." She stopped, and her voice, for the first time, was not quite steady. "When I see Erik up in the loft with his book, his face looks like that. I have watched it for six years. I would like for him to have that, Henrik. I would like for one of us to have it."

Henrik did not answer at once. He was thinking of her, not as she was now, broad and slow and gray at the temples, but as she had been the first time he saw her, at a dance in the schoolhouse on Plum Creek, a tall, fair girl in a dark blue dress, standing against the wall and watching the dancers with those same clear, grave eyes. She had been working out for the Pedersens then, scrubbing their floors and minding their children. He had thought her proud, because she did not laugh and chatter like the other girls. It was a long time before he found out that she was only shy, and homesick, and that she had left behind her in the old country a life which she would never speak of except, as now, in a word or two, and then not again for years.

He had brought her out to this place when there was nothing on it but a sod house and a well. She had borne him five children there, and buried one of them, little Anna, under the cottonwood by the draw. She had never once complained to him of the wind, or the loneliness, or the grasshoppers that came the second summer and ate the very washing off the line. He had always taken it for granted that she was content. Now, sitting beside her in the dark, he wondered for the first time whether she had been content, or whether she had only been patient, and whether, all these years, she had been putting by something of herself, a little at a time, as she had put by the quarters and dimes in the blue coffee tin.

"You should have told me," he said, but gently now.

"Yes. Maybe I should have. I was afraid."

"Afraid of me?"

"Afraid of how much you want the land. It is a strong thing, Henrik. Sometimes I think it is stronger than you are."

He laughed a little, without much mirth in it. "Maybe it is. Maybe it is stronger than all of us. It has had its way with plenty of men out here." He was quiet a moment. "Ole Nyberg wanted land, too. He wanted it so bad he worked himself into the ground at fifty-two. And now his boys are in Omaha selling shoes, and the old woman sits alone in that house and talks to the cat. And it is his land I want to buy." He shook his head slowly. "It is a strange thing, when you think of it."

Marta said nothing. She had said what she had to say, and she was waiting now, as she had waited six years. Henrik knew that if he told her the money must go to the Nyberg quarter, she would go down into the cave tomorrow and bring up the blue tin and set it on the kitchen table in front of him, and never speak of the matter again. And he knew, too, that something would be gone out of the house after that which would not come back, however many quarter-sections he added to it.

The coyotes had stopped their crying. The night had come down altogether now, soft and enormous, and the stars were thick overhead, the great river of them flowing from north to south across the sky. Up in the gable end of the house a square of yellow light still showed where Erik's lamp was burning. Henrik looked up at it for a long while.

"What is he reading up there, that he stays awake so late?" he asked.

"I don't know. Something Miss Corliss lent him. About the rocks, I think. How the country was made."

"How the country was made," Henrik repeated. He seemed to turn the words over, as he might turn a clod in his hand to see what was in it. "Well. Somebody ought to know that, I suppose. God knows I don't."

He sat a while longer. Then he bent and began to lace up his boots again, slowly, pulling each lace tight.

"Where are you going?" Marta asked.

"Only to look at the stock before I go to bed." He stood up, and then he paused, standing over her in the dark, a big, stooped shape against the stars. "Johnson can wait a year for his answer about the Nyberg place," he said. "The old woman is not going anywhere. Maybe in a year we will see." He hesitated. "You keep your coffee tin, Marta. It is yours. You did right to keep it."

He walked away toward the corral before she could answer, and she heard him speak to the horses in Danish, in the low, coaxing voice he had always used with them and seldom with people. She sat on alone on the bench, her red hands open now in her lap, and looked up at the square of light in the gable. She did not go in until it had gone out.

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar.
