When Frank Hronek wrote that he would stop off at Hanover on his way to the coast, his cousin Marie read the letter three times standing by the mailbox, and then folded it into her apron pocket and carried it about with her all that day, as if it were something warm. She had not seen him for fourteen years. He had gone away the spring he was seventeen, the year of the hard frost in May, when the wheat came up black and her uncle's mill on the Little Blue was sold at a sheriff's sale. Frank had been the kind of boy who was always looking down the railroad track. He went first to Omaha, where he worked in a packing house, and then to Denver, and after that his letters came from places Marie had to find on the map in the children's geography: Pueblo, Cheyenne, Ogden. Now he was a conductor on the Union Pacific, and he was going to take a run between Salt Lake and Sacramento, and he wanted, he wrote, to see the old country once before he went so far.

By "the old country" he did not mean Bohemia, which neither of them could remember, but the Divide south of Hanover, where they had both been children.

Marie had married Joe Pokorny when she was nineteen. Joe was a steady, silent man, a good deal older than she, who had come over from Moravia alone and had broken out his quarter-section with a team of oxen and a walking plow. He had prospered slowly, as such men do, by never buying anything he could do without. They had five children now, a frame house painted white, a windmill, and a grove of cottonwoods that Marie had set out herself, carrying water to the slips in pails the first two summers. She was thirty-one, a strong, brown woman with heavy braids wound about her head, and the quick gray eyes that ran in her mother's family. She did not often think about herself. There was always too much to do.

The train was due at four o'clock in the afternoon. Marie hitched the bays to the spring wagon herself, because Joe was cutting corn and could not be spared, and she drove the eleven miles into Hanover with her best hat in a paper bag on the seat beside her, so that the dust would not spoil it. It was the end of October. The cornfields stood brown and rustling on either side of the road, and the pastures had gone the color of a lion's hide. Here and there a sumac patch in a draw burned red as a coal. The sky was very high and very blue, and the wind came steadily out of the northwest, smelling of dry grass and far-off rain that would not come. Marie loved the country best at this time of year, when the work of the summer had been gathered in and the land lay resting, tawny and open, as if it had nothing more to hide.

She reached the depot half an hour early and put on her hat in the shelter of the freight shed. The station agent, a young man with a waxed mustache, came out to look at her and went back in again. She walked up and down the platform. She was afraid, suddenly, that she would not know him, or that he would not know her, or, worse than either, that they would know each other perfectly and have nothing to say.

When the train came in, smoking and grinding, only one passenger got down. He was a tall man in a dark blue overcoat and a hard hat, and he carried a leather grip. He stood still a moment on the step, looking about him at the elevator and the lumber yard and the single street running away toward the bank, and Marie saw that his face was thinner than she remembered and that he had a mustache, fair like his hair. Then he saw her, and he laughed, and she knew him by the laugh. It was exactly the same. It had always come out of him all at once, as if something had been let go.

"Marie! Is it you? You've grown up on me."

"I was grown up when you left," she said. "You were the one that was a boy."

He took both her hands and held them, looking at her, and she felt her face grow hot under his eyes, as it had not done for years.

"No," he said, "you were fifteen. You had a pink dress and you cried at the station. I remember it very well."

"I never cried," said Marie stoutly; but she had, and they both knew it.

He put his grip into the back of the wagon and climbed up beside her, and she turned the horses out of town. For a while neither of them spoke. Frank sat with his hat pushed back, looking at everything. The road ran straight south between the section lines, rising and falling with the long swells of the land, and at the top of each rise the whole country opened out before them, mile upon mile of it, with the farmhouses set down here and there like toys and the windmills turning.

"It's all fenced," he said at last. "When I went away you could drive clear to the river and never open a gate."

"Most of it's fenced now. The Lindquists have put in hedges of Osage orange. And there's a church at Prague Corner, with a steeple. You'll see it from the hill."

"And the Kucera place? Where the dugout was?"

"Old Kucera died. The boys sold out and went to Oklahoma. A German family has it now. They've built a big red barn, bigger than the house."

Frank nodded slowly. "That would be a German," he said, and Marie laughed. She had forgotten how he could make her laugh, and the forgetting seemed to her, all at once, like a loss she had never counted.

He asked about everyone, and she told him: who had married and who had gone away, who had made money and who had been foreclosed. Old Mrs. Vavra was still living, ninety-two years old and nearly blind, and still smoked a clay pipe behind the kitchen stove when she thought no one was looking. The Fuchs boy who used to fight them at the schoolhouse had become a lawyer in Lincoln and had been to the legislature. The schoolhouse itself had burned down one winter, when a tramp built a fire in the stove and went to sleep.

"And Aunt Anna?" he asked, more quietly.

"Mother has been dead six years. I wrote you."

"Yes, you wrote me. I was in Wyoming then. I got your letter in a section house at Rawlins, two months after. I read it out on the platform in a snowstorm." He was silent a little. "She was good to me, Marie. After my father lost the mill, she was the only one who didn't look at me as if I were a calamity."

"She always said you would come back some day and buy the mill again."

Frank smiled, but not as he had smiled before. "Well, I haven't bought anything yet. A man on the railroad doesn't get rich. He gets to see the country, and that's about all he gets."

They came to the top of the long hill above Prague Corner, and Marie stopped the horses to let them breathe. Below them the land fell away to the creek, where the willows were yellow and the cottonwoods had already dropped most of their leaves, so that the white trunks showed through. Beyond the creek the country rose again, gently, in field after field, to the far edge of the sky. The little church stood on the near slope with its new steeple, and its graveyard behind it, where the iron crosses leaned a little in the wind.

Frank looked at it a long while. "I used to think about this," he said. "Out in the desert, in Nevada, where there's nothing but sagebrush and alkali, I'd lie in my bunk at night and try to remember how it looked from here. But I could never get it right. I'd always make the hills too high."

"They aren't hills at all, really," said Marie. "Joe says in Moravia they would just call it level ground."

"That's the trouble," said Frank. "It looks level until you've been away."

---

It was nearly dark when they drove into the Pokorny yard. The children had been watching from the windmill and came running, all five of them, in a body, and then stopped short a little way off and stood staring, the smallest one holding to the skirt of the oldest girl. Frank got down and shook hands with each of them gravely, asking their names, and he gave the boys each a silver dollar and the girls each a little gold locket, which he had brought in his pocket wrapped in tissue paper. The children did not know what to say. Little Anna, who was six, looked at her locket and then at the strange man and then burst into tears, and had to be carried into the house.

Joe came up from the cornfield with his shirt dark with sweat and his hands bleeding a little from the husks. He shook hands with Frank in the Moravian way, looking him straight in the eye, and said he was glad to see him, and went off to wash at the pump. Marie saw that he liked Frank, though another woman might not have seen anything at all.

Supper was a great occasion. Marie had killed two young roosters that morning and had baked kolaches with poppyseed and apricot, and there were noodles in the chicken broth, and pickled beets, and a crock of new sauerkraut, and plum butter made from the wild plums along the creek. Frank ate as if he had been starved for years. He said there was nothing fit to eat west of North Platte; the railroad eating houses gave you beefsteak fried till it curled up at the edges, and pie made out of dried apples and sawdust. The children giggled at this and grew bold. The oldest boy, Charley, who was twelve and wanted to be an engineer, asked him how fast the trains went in the mountains, and whether he had ever seen a wreck, and whether there were still Indians. Frank told them about a snowslide in the Wasatch that had buried a whole train for three days, and how the passengers had burned the seats to keep warm, and how a German woman had given birth to a baby in the smoking car, and they had named it after the conductor.

"After you?" cried Charley.

"After me," said Frank. "Somewhere in Utah there's a little Frank Hronek Schmidt. I suppose he's six years old now and doesn't know what he's missed."

Joe laughed at that, which he seldom did at table, and Marie looked at him in surprise.

---

After the children had been put to bed, Joe sat a while with them in the kitchen, smoking his pipe and asking Frank about wages on the railroad and the price of land in California, which he had heard was very high. Then he knocked out his pipe against the stove and said that he must be up at four, and that a man who cut corn all day was not good for much talking at night. He shook hands with Frank again, and went into the bedroom and shut the door.

Marie put on a shawl, and she and Frank went out and sat on the step of the porch. The wind had gone down with the sun, as it does in that country, and the night was very still and cold. There was no moon yet. The stars came down close all around the edge of the sky, and the cornfields were dark and whispering. Away off to the east, a dog barked at some farmhouse, and another answered it, and then there was no sound at all but the windmill creaking now and then as it swung a little in some breath of air that did not reach them.

"Your man is a good man," Frank said.

"Yes," said Marie. "He is a good man."

She said it simply, as one states a fact about the weather, and Frank did not reply. He took out a cigar and lit it, and in the light of the match she saw his face, and it seemed to her older than it had looked by day, and more tired.

"Do you remember the plum thicket?" she asked. "Below the mill dam?"

"Remember it! We used to go there every August with lard pails. And you fell in the race once, reaching for a branch, and I pulled you out by your braids."

"You pulled so hard I had a sore head for a week. Mother thought you'd scalped me."

"I'd have let you drown if I'd known." He laughed, and then he was quiet. "Is it still there?"

"The mill's gone. They took the machinery out and used the timbers for a barn. But the dam is there, all washed out at one end, and the plums are there. I take the children every summer. Charley climbs out on the old wheel-shaft where you used to sit."

"I used to sit there and think about going away," said Frank. "I'd watch the trains go by on the trestle, way off across the bottom, and count the cars. I thought anybody who got on a train like that went straight into some kind of glory." He drew on his cigar. "I've ridden a good many trains since, Marie. Thousands of miles. I've been over the Sierra and down to the Gulf, and once clear to New York, on a pass. And I'll tell you something funny. I never yet got off one into any glory. You get off into a depot, and there's a lunch counter and a newsstand and a fellow sweeping, and it's always the same depot, whatever the name on the sign."

Marie did not know how to answer this. She looked out at the dark fields and thought about the trains crossing the trestle long ago, and about herself at fifteen, watching him watch them, and knowing, as girls know such things, that he would go.

"I used to envy you," she said at last. "When your letters came. I'd read them over and over, about the mountains and the big cities. I thought you were living the way people live in books. And here I was, just having babies and putting up plums."

"And now?"

She considered. She was an honest woman and did not answer quickly.

"Now I don't know. I don't think I'd change. I like to see things grow. When I set out those cottonwoods, Joe said they would never live, the ground was too dry. Every evening I carried water from the well, and some nights I was so tired I cried while I did it. And now they're higher than the house, and the orioles nest in them. I couldn't have that on a train." She laughed a little at herself. "That sounds foolish."

"No," said Frank slowly, "it doesn't sound foolish."

They sat a long while without speaking. A late cricket was singing somewhere under the porch, slowly, as if the cold had got into it. The moon came up over the eastern rim of the land, red and enormous, and climbed and grew pale, and the fields came out of the darkness, gray and silver, as far as they could see. The windmill threw a long, thin shadow across the yard.

"Grandmother used to say," said Marie, "that when she came over on the ship, she sat up on the deck all one night and watched the moon on the water, and that was the night she knew she would never go home. She said she didn't cry. She just knew it, the way you know a thing in your bones."

"I remember her saying that. She said it every Christmas." Frank threw away the end of his cigar and watched it glow in the dust. "I suppose that's what we've all got in us. She left Bohemia, and my father left the mill, and I left the Divide. We're a family that keeps going away."

"I didn't go away."

"No," he said, turning to look at her. "You didn't. You stayed and put your roots down. I've thought about that, Marie, out there. There's nobody in this world but you that remembers me when I was a boy. When you go, there won't be anybody. A man doesn't think of that when he's young. He thinks there's always going to be somebody back home who knows him."

He said it lightly, but Marie heard what was under it. She put out her hand in the dark and laid it on his sleeve, as she had sometimes done when they were children and he had been beaten by his father, and they had hidden together in the haymow until the storm was over.

"You'll come back again," she said. "Not in fourteen years. Sooner."

"California is a long way."

"It's not as far as Bohemia was."

He laughed at that, his old laugh, and put his hand over hers for a moment. Then they both felt the cold and went in.

---

He left on the morning train. Joe had gone to the field before daylight, but he had harnessed the bays and left them standing at the post, which was his way of saying good-bye. The children were at school. Marie drove Frank to Hanover alone, through a gray, still morning with frost on the fence wires and a thin haze lying over the creek bottoms. They talked very little. Once, at the top of the long hill, he asked her to stop, and he sat and looked down at the church and the creek and the far fields again, as if he were trying this time to get it right, so that he would remember.

At the depot he kissed her on the cheek and climbed up onto the step of the coach with his grip, and stood there as the train began to move, holding his hat in his hand. Marie waved to him until the last car had passed the elevator and the smoke was only a gray smudge against the sky, and then she stood a little longer, looking down the track, which ran away straight and shining to the west until it narrowed to nothing.

Driving home, she found that she was crying, and she let herself cry, for there was nobody on the road to see. She did not altogether know why. She was not unhappy. She thought of the white house and the cottonwoods and the five children, and of Joe coming in from the field at noon, who would ask nothing and would know everything. She thought of the corn that must be finished before the snow came. But she thought too of the girl in the pink dress, standing on that same platform, and it seemed to her that the girl was standing there still, and always would be, watching a train that had never come back.

By the time the windmill came in sight above the brown fields, her eyes were dry. The smoke was going up straight from her own chimney, where the oldest girl had built the fire for dinner, and the bays quickened their pace without being told, because they knew the way home.

Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. The Hruby place lay four miles west of the town of Black Hawk, on a rise of ground where the road bent to go around a draw. In June the draw was full of wild plum bushes, and the wheat came up to the very edge of them on the north side, so that from the kitchen door one looked out across a sea of green that rippled and changed color all day long with the wind. There were no trees on the place except the young cottonwoods Frank Hruby had set out along the lane the first spring, and these were not yet tall enough to throw a shade. The house was a frame house, painted white on the side that faced the road and not painted at all on the other three sides, because the paint had given out. Frank Hruby always meant to finish it, and every fall he put it off until the next year.

He had been a harness-maker in a little town near Pilsen, and he had come to Nebraska because his wife's brother had written that a man could get land for nothing there. That was nine years ago. He had found out since that land is never got for nothing, but he did not regret coming. He liked the country. He liked the long roads that ran straight to the edge of the sky, and the way the clouds moved over the wheat, and the larks that sang from the fence posts in the early morning. He was not a very good farmer; his neighbors said he spent too much time looking at things. But he was clever with his hands, and in the winter he mended harness for half the township, sitting by the kitchen stove with his spectacles pushed down on his nose and his pipe going out every few minutes because he forgot to draw on it.

Mrs. Hruby was a short, black-haired woman with quick eyes and a sharp tongue, who could do the work of two women and often did. She had never cared about the larks. She cared about her chickens and her turkeys and her garden, and about keeping her children clean and decent in a country where, as she said, nobody seemed to care whether their children went barefoot to church or not. She had three children living and one buried in the little graveyard on the hill by the Catholic church. Marie, the eldest, was fourteen and already as good a cook as her mother. Rudolph was twelve and worked in the fields with his father. The youngest was Joe, who was seven, and who was, everyone agreed, the most like his father.

Joe had his father's light-brown hair and his father's way of standing still and staring at things until he forgot what he had been sent to do. He would go out to bring in the cows and come back an hour later without them, because he had found a gopher hole and had lain on his stomach waiting for the gopher to come out. His mother scolded him and his sister laughed at him, but his father seldom said anything. Frank Hruby understood very well what it was to forget the cows.

That spring Rudolph had made a slingshot out of a forked stick of plum wood and a strip of old inner tube that a man in town had given him, and Joe had wanted it more than he had ever wanted anything. He begged for it every day for two weeks. At last Rudolph, who had grown tired of the slingshot and was beginning to think about a gun, traded it to him for a jackknife with a broken blade and three agates. Joe carried the slingshot everywhere. He slept with it under his pillow. He shot at tin cans set up on the fence and at knots in the side of the barn, and he grew very skillful; he could hit a can at twenty paces four times out of five.

One afternoon in the middle of June, his mother sent him to take a jug of cold coffee to his father, who was cultivating corn in the field beyond the draw. It was a hot, still day. The sky was white with heat, and the wheat stood motionless, as if it were holding its breath. Joe walked along the edge of the field with the jug in one hand and the slingshot in the other, and his pockets heavy with pebbles he had picked out of the creek bed. Halfway across, a meadowlark flew up from the grass at his feet and lit on a fence post not ten yards away. It sat there with its yellow breast puffed out, and the black crescent on it shining like something polished, and it threw back its head and began to sing.

Joe did not think about it at all. He set the jug down in the grass, fitted a pebble to the leather, drew back, and let go. He had hardly expected to hit it. The song stopped in the middle, and the bird dropped off the post on the far side, like a stone falling. For a moment he stood quite still. Then he ran to the fence and crawled under the wire.

The lark lay on its back in the grass. One wing was spread out, and its feet were drawn up tight against its body. Its eyes were open. Joe knelt down and touched it with one finger, and it did not move. He had thought he would feel proud, but he did not feel proud. He felt hot all over, and a little sick, as he had felt once when he ate too many green plums. He looked around quickly, but there was no one anywhere; only the wheat, and the white sky, and the heat shimmering over the road. He picked up the bird by one wing, carried it a little way off, and pushed it under a tangle of grass. Then he went back for the jug and went on to the cornfield.

His father had stopped the horses at the end of a row and was sitting in the shade of the cultivator, wiping his face with a red handkerchief. He drank the coffee in long swallows, tilting the jug up over his arm, and when he set it down he looked at Joe and smiled.

"Hot, eh? You walk slow in the heat, like the old men. What have you been doing all the way?"

"Nothing," said Joe.

"Nothing? That is a long time to do nothing." His father put the cork back in the jug. "You go home now and tell your mother I come in at six. Tell her the corn is looking good on this side. She likes to hear that."

Joe went home the long way, by the road, so that he would not have to pass the fence post. He told his mother what his father had said, and then he went out behind the barn and sat in the shade with his back against the boards. He took the slingshot out of his pocket and looked at it. After a while he put it back.

He did not know that his father, coming home at six o'clock across the wheat with the horses, had seen something yellow in the grass beyond the fence, and had stopped, and had gone to look. Frank Hruby stood over the bird a long time. Then he took it up carefully in his big hand and carried it home inside his hat.

At supper he said nothing. They got up and went back under the wire. The light was almost gone. Over the draw a nighthawk was flying, crying its harsh little cry, and the first fireflies had come out above the wheat and were drifting there like sparks blown from a fire. "We bury her tomorrow," his father said, "under the cottonwoods. You will dig the hole. It does not need to be deep."

"Yes, father."

"And you will tell your mother what you did. Not I. You."

Joe swallowed. His mother would scold, he knew; she would scold loud and long, and Marie would hear, and perhaps Rudolph. But somehow that did not seem so bad now. It did not seem so bad as the hat on the shelf in the harness shed, or the four yellow mouths in the grass.

"I will tell her," he said.

She saw how the boy's face was swollen, and she saw how her husband held his hand, and she was a wise enough woman to ask no questions just then. Joe went out to the nest every morning and every evening for eleven days. On the second morning he saw the father bird come with something in his beak, a green worm, and stand on the edge of the nest while the four mouths went up; and he ran all the way home across the wet grass, so fast that he could hardly get his breath to tell it, and his father put down his coffee cup and laughed out loud. On the sixth day one of the young birds was gone, and there was nothing to show where. Joe told that too, standing by his father's chair with his hands behind him, and his father nodded and said nothing. On the eleventh evening the nest was empty, and the grass around it was trodden flat, and from somewhere out in the wheat, very faint and unsteady, came a little broken scrap of song, as if someone were trying to remember a tune and could not get the whole of it.

Joe stood by the fence a long time, listening. Then he went home to supper. He did not ask for the slingshot that summer, nor the next. The groom had the best team and his sledge was lightest—all the others carried from six to a dozen people. Another driver lost control. The screams of the horses were more terrible to hear than the cries of the men and women. Nothing seemed to check the wolves. It was hard to tell what was happening in the rear; the people who were falling behind shrieked as piteously as those who were already lost. The little bride hid her face on the groom’s shoulder and sobbed. Pavel sat still and watched his horses. The road was clear and white, and the groom’s three blacks went like the wind. It was only necessary to be calm and to guide them carefully. At length, as they breasted a long hill, Peter rose cautiously and looked back. “There are only three sledges left,” he whispered.

“And the wolves?” Pavel asked.

“Enough! Enough for all of us.” Pavel reached the brow of the hill, but only two sledges followed him down the other side. In that moment on the hilltop, they saw behind them a whirling black group on the snow. Presently the groom screamed. He saw his father’s sledge overturned, with his mother and sisters. He sprang up as if he meant to jump, but the girl shrieked and held him back. It was even then too late. The black ground-shadows were already crowding over the heap in the road, and one horse ran out across the fields, his harness hanging to him, wolves at his heels. But the groom’s movement had given Pavel an idea. They were within a few miles of their village now. The only sledge left out of six was not very far behind them, and Pavel’s middle horse was failing. Beside a frozen pond something happened to the other sledge; Peter saw it plainly. Three big wolves got abreast of the horses, and the horses went crazy. They tried to jump over each other, got tangled up in the harness, and overturned the sledge. When the shrieking behind them died away, Pavel realized that he was alone upon the familiar road. “They still come?” he asked Peter.

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Twenty, thirty—enough.” Now his middle horse was being almost dragged by the other two. Pavel gave Peter the reins and stepped carefully into the back of the sledge. He called to the groom that they must lighten—and pointed to the bride. The young man cursed him and held her tighter. Pavel tried to drag her away. In the struggle, the groom rose. Pavel knocked him over the side of the sledge and threw the girl after him. He said he never remembered exactly how he did it, or what happened afterward. Peter, crouching in the front seat, saw nothing. The first thing either of them noticed was a new sound that broke into the clear air, louder than they had ever heard it before—the bell of the monastery of their own village, ringing for early prayers. Pavel and Peter drove into the village alone, and they had been alone ever since. They were run out of their village. Pavel’s own mother would not look at him. They went away to strange towns, but when people learned where they came from, they were always asked if they knew the two men who had fed the bride to the wolves. Wherever they went, the story followed them. It took them five years to save money enough to come to America. They worked in Chicago, Des Moines, Fort Wayne, but they were always unfortunate. When Pavel’s health grew so bad, they decided to try farming. Pavel died a few days after he unburdened his mind to Mr. Shimerda, and was buried in the Norwegian graveyard. Peter sold off everything, and left the country—went to be cook in a railway construction camp where gangs of Russians were employed. At his sale we bought Peter’s wheelbarrow and some of his harness. During the auction he went about with his head down, and never lifted his eyes. He seemed not to care about anything. The Black Hawk money-lender who held mortgages on Peter’s live-stock was there, and he bought in the sale notes at about fifty cents on the dollar. Every one said Peter kissed the cow before she was led away by her new owner. I did not see him do it, but this I know: after all his furniture and his cook-stove and pots and pans had been hauled off by the purchasers, when his house was stripped and bare, he sat down on the floor with his clasp-knife and ate all the melons that he had put away for winter. When Mr. Shimerda and Krajiek drove up in their wagon to take Peter to the train, they found him with a dripping beard, surrounded by heaps of melon rinds. The loss of his two friends had a depressing effect upon old Mr. Shimerda. When he was out hunting, he used to go into the empty log house and sit there, brooding. This cabin was his hermitage until the winter snows penned him in his cave. For Ántonia and me, the story of the wedding party was never at an end. We did not tell Pavel’s secret to any one, but guarded it jealously—as if the wolves of the Ukraine had gathered that night long ago, and the wedding party been sacrificed, to give us a painful and peculiar pleasure. At night, before I went to sleep, I often found myself in a sledge drawn by three horses, dashing through a country that looked something like Nebraska and something like Virginia.

The first snowfall came early in December. I remember how the world looked from our sitting-room window as I dressed behind the stove that morning: the low sky was like a sheet of metal; the blond cornfields had faded out into ghostliness at last; the little pond was frozen under its stiff willow bushes. Big white flakes were whirling over everything and disappearing in the red grass.

Excerpt 3: We knew that things were hard for our Bohemian neighbors, but the two girls were light-hearted and never complained. They were always ready to forget their troubles at home, and to run away with me over the prairie, scaring rabbits or starting up flocks of quail. I remember Ántonia’s excitement when she came into our kitchen one afternoon and announced: “My papa find friends up north, with Russian mans. Last night he take me for see, and I can understand very much talk. Nice mans, Mrs. Burden. One is fat and all the time laugh. Everybody laugh. The first time I see my papa laugh in this kawn-tree. Oh, very nice!” I asked her if she meant the two Russians who lived up by the big dog-town. I had often been tempted to go to see them when I was riding in that direction, but one of them was a wild-looking fellow and I was a little afraid of him. Russia seemed to me more remote than any other country—farther away than China, almost as far as the North Pole. Of all the strange, uprooted people among the first settlers, those two men were the strangest and the most aloof. Their last names were unpronounceable, so they were called Pavel and Peter. They went about making signs to people, and until the Shimerdas came they had no friends. Krajiek could understand them a little, but he had cheated them in a trade, so they avoided him. Pavel, the tall one, was said to be an anarchist; since he had no means of imparting his opinions, probably his wild gesticulations and his generally excited and rebellious manner gave rise to this supposition. He must once have been a very strong man, but now his great frame, with big, knotty joints, had a wasted look, and the skin was drawn tight over his high cheek-bones. His breathing was hoarse, and he always had a cough. Peter, his companion, was a very different sort of fellow; short, bow-legged, and as fat as butter. He always seemed pleased when he met people on the road, smiled and took off his cap to every one, men as well as women. At a distance, on his wagon, he looked like an old man; his hair and beard were of such a pale flaxen color that they seemed white in the sun. They were as thick and curly as carded wool. His rosy face, with its snub nose, set in this fleece, was like a melon among its leaves. He was usually called “Curly Peter,” or “Rooshian Peter.” The two Russians made good farmhands, and in summer they worked out together. I had heard our neighbors laughing when they told how Peter always had to go home at night to milk his cow. Other bachelor homesteaders used canned milk, to save trouble. Sometimes Peter came to church at the sod schoolhouse. It was there I first saw him, sitting on a low bench by the door, his plush cap in his hands, his bare feet tucked apologetically under the seat. After Mr. Shimerda discovered the Russians, he went to see them almost every evening, and sometimes took Ántonia with him. She said they came from a part of Russia where the language was not very different from Bohemian, and if I wanted to go to their place, she could talk to them for me. One afternoon, before the heavy frosts began, we rode up there together on my pony. The Russians had a neat log house built on a grassy slope, with a windlass well beside the door. As we rode up the draw we skirted a big melon patch, and a garden where squashes and yellow cucumbers lay about on the sod. We found Peter out behind his kitchen, bending over a washtub. He was working so hard that he did not hear us coming. His whole body moved up and down as he rubbed, and he was a funny sight from the rear, with his shaggy head and bandy legs. When he straightened himself up to greet us, drops of perspiration were rolling from his thick nose down on to his curly beard. Peter dried his hands and seemed glad to leave his washing. He took us down to see his chickens, and his cow that was grazing on the hillside. He told Ántonia that in his country only rich people had cows, but here any man could have one who would take care of her. The milk was good for Pavel, who was often sick, and he could make butter by beating sour cream with a wooden spoon. Peter was very fond of his cow. He patted her flanks and talked to her in Russian while he pulled up her lariat pin and set it in a new place. After he had shown us his garden, Peter trundled a load of watermelons up the hill in his wheelbarrow. Pavel was not at home. He was off somewhere helping to dig a well. The house I thought very comfortable for two men who were “batching.” Besides the kitchen, there was a living-room, with a wide double bed built against the wall, properly made up with blue gingham sheets and pillows. There was a little storeroom, too, with a window, where they kept guns and saddles and tools, and old coats and boots. That day the floor was covered with garden things, drying for winter; corn and beans and fat yellow cucumbers. There were no screens or window-blinds in the house, and all the doors and windows stood wide open, letting in flies and sunshine alike. Peter put the melons in a row on the oilcloth-covered table and stood over them, brandishing a butcher knife. Before the blade got fairly into them, they split of their own ripeness, with a delicious sound. He gave us knives, but no plates, and the top of the table was soon swimming with juice and seeds. I had never seen any one eat so many melons as Peter ate. He assured us that they were good for one—better than medicine; in his country people lived on them at this time of year. He was very hospitable and jolly. Once, while he was looking at Ántonia, he sighed and told us that if he had stayed at home in Russia perhaps by this time he would have had a pretty daughter of his own to cook and keep house for him. He said he had left his country because of a “great trouble.” When we got up to go, Peter looked about in perplexity for something that would entertain us. He ran into the storeroom and brought out a gaudily painted harmonica, sat down on a bench, and spreading his fat legs apart began to play like a whole band. The tunes were either very lively or very doleful, and he sang words to some of them. Before we left, Peter put ripe cucumbers into a sack for Mrs. Shimerda and gave us a lard-pail full of milk to cook them in. I had never heard of cooking cucumbers, but Ántonia assured me they were very good. We had to walk the pony all the way home to keep from spilling the milk.

One afternoon we were having our reading lesson on the warm, grassy bank where the badger lived. It was a day of amber sunlight, but there was a shiver of coming winter in the air. I had seen ice on the little horse-pond that morning, and as we went through the garden we found the tall asparagus, with its red berries, lying on the ground, a mass of slimy green. Tony was barefooted, and she shivered in her cotton dress and was comfortable only when we were tucked down on the baked earth, in the full blaze of the sun. She could talk to me about almost anything by this time. That afternoon she was telling me how highly esteemed our friend the badger was in her part of the world, and how men kept a special kind of dog, with very short legs, to hunt him. Those dogs, she said, went down into the hole after the badger and killed him there in a terrific struggle underground; you could hear the barks and yelps outside. Then the dog dragged himself back, covered with bites and scratches, to be rewarded and petted by his master. She knew a dog who had a star on his collar for every badger he had killed. The rabbits were unusually spry that afternoon. They kept starting up all about us, and dashing off down the draw as if they were playing a game of some kind. But the little buzzing things that lived in the grass were all dead—all but one. While we were lying there against the warm bank, a little insect of the palest, frailest green hopped painfully out of the buffalo grass and tried to leap into a bunch of bluestem. He missed it, fell back, and sat with his head sunk between his long legs, his antennæ quivering, as if he were waiting for something to come and finish him. Tony made a warm nest for him in her hands; talked to him gayly and indulgently in Bohemian. Presently he began to sing for us—a thin, rusty little chirp. She held him close to her ear and laughed, but a moment afterward I saw there were tears in her eyes. She told me that in her village at home there was an old beggar woman who went about selling herbs and roots she had dug up in the forest. If you took her in and gave her a warm place by the fire, she sang old songs to the children in a cracked voice, like this. Old Hata, she was called, and the children loved to see her coming and saved their cakes and sweets for her. When the bank on the other side of the draw began to throw a narrow shelf of shadow, we knew we ought to be starting homeward; the chill came on quickly when the sun got low, and Ántonia’s dress was thin. What were we to do with the frail little creature we had lured back to life by false pretenses? I offered my pockets, but Tony shook her head and carefully put the green insect in her hair, tying her big handkerchief down loosely over her curls. I said I would go with her until we could see Squaw Creek, and then turn and run home. We drifted along lazily, very happy, through the magical light of the late afternoon. All those fall afternoons were the same, but I never got used to them. As far as we could see, the miles of copper-red grass were drenched in sunlight that was stronger and fiercer than at any other time of the day. The blond cornfields were red gold, the haystacks turned rosy and threw long shadows. The whole prairie was like the bush that burned with fire and was not consumed. That hour always had the exultation of victory, of triumphant ending, like a hero’s death—heroes who died young and gloriously. It was a sudden transfiguration, a lifting-up of day. How many an afternoon Ántonia and I have trailed along the prairie under that magnificence! And always two long black shadows flitted before us or followed after, dark spots on the ruddy grass. We had been silent a long time, and the edge of the sun sank nearer and nearer the prairie floor, when we saw a figure moving on the edge of the upland, a gun over his shoulder. He was walking slowly, dragging his feet along as if he had no purpose. We broke into a run to overtake him.

“My papa sick all the time,” Tony panted as we flew. “He not look good, Jim.” As we neared Mr. Shimerda she shouted, and he lifted his head and peered about. Tony ran up to him, caught his hand and pressed it against her cheek. She was the only one of his family who could rouse the old man from the torpor in which he seemed to live. He took the bag from his belt and showed us three rabbits he had shot, looked at Ántonia with a wintry flicker of a smile and began to tell her something. She turned to me.

“My tatinek make me little hat with the skins, little hat for win-ter!” she exclaimed joyfully. “Meat for eat, skin for hat,”—she told off these benefits on her fingers. Her father put his hand on her hair, but she caught his wrist and lifted it carefully away, talking to him rapidly. I heard the name of old Hata. He untied the handkerchief, separated her hair with his fingers, and stood looking down at the green insect. When it began to chirp faintly, he listened as if it were a beautiful sound. I picked up the gun he had dropped; a queer piece from the old country, short and heavy, with a stag’s head on the cock. When he saw me examining it, he turned to me with his far-away look that always made me feel as if I were down at the bottom of a well. He spoke kindly and gravely, and Ántonia translated:— “My tatinek say when you are big boy, he give you his gun. Very fine, from Bohemie. It was belong to a great man, very rich, like what you not got here; many fields, many forests, many big house. My papa play for his wedding, and he give my papa fine gun, and my papa give you.”

I was glad that this project was one of futurity. There never were such people as the Shimerdas for wanting to give away everything they had. Even the mother was always offering me things, though I knew she expected substantial presents in return. We stood there in friendly silence, while the feeble minstrel sheltered in Ántonia’s hair went on with its scratchy chirp. The old man’s smile, as he listened, was so full of sadness, of pity for things, that I never afterward forgot it. As the sun sank there came a sudden coolness and the strong smell of earth and drying grass. Ántonia and her father went off hand in hand, and I buttoned up my jacket and raced my shadow home.

The hot wind had been blowing for three days when Thomas Doane came in from the north field and laid the letter on the kitchen table. He did not say anything about it. He went to the wash-bench outside the door and poured water into the tin basin, and Margaret, who was frying potatoes at the stove, heard him splashing and blowing for a long while, as if he meant to wash away more than the dust. The letter lay where he had put it, beside the sugar bowl. She knew the handwriting. It was from his brother Henry, in Ohio, and it had been in Thomas's coat pocket since Saturday, when he drove to Harlan Junction for the mail.

She set the potatoes on the back of the stove and went to the door. The sun was going down red and enormous behind the windmill, and the whole west was the color of a heated stove-lid. All day the wind had come up out of the southwest as steadily as if it were blown from a furnace door, and now, with evening, it had not slackened at all. The leaves of the corn, which a week ago had stood up green and shining, hung twisted and gray along the stalks, like rags hung out to dry. Down in the draw the cottonwoods kept up a dry, papery rustling. There was no other sound anywhere, except the creak of the windmill wheel, turning and turning, and bringing up so little water now that the tank was green and scummed at the bottom.

Thomas dried his face on the roller towel and stood looking at the field. He was a tall man, gaunt in the jaw, with a short brown beard that the sun had bleached at the ends. His shoulders had grown heavier in the eight years they had lived on this place, and he had begun to stoop a little, as men do who are always bending over the ground. When he turned and saw her in the doorway, he smiled, but only with his mouth.

"It's done for," he said. "The corn. Another day of this and there won't be a green blade on the place."

"There may be rain."

"There may be." He came past her into the kitchen and sat down at the table. He did not look at the letter, but she saw that he had placed himself so that it lay between his plate and hers.

They ate their supper without much talk. The kitchen was hot, for the stove had to be kept up for the cooking, and the lamp, which Margaret lit early because the dust made a kind of twilight in the room, drew millers in through the screen door. They circled the chimney and dropped scorched upon the oilcloth. Thomas brushed them away absently with the back of his hand. He ate slowly, as he always did when he had something on his mind, cutting his meat into small pieces and laying down his fork between mouthfuls. Margaret watched him and waited. She had learned that it was of no use to hurry him; he was like the slow, deep-rooted grass of that country, which would not be pulled up all at once.

When he had finished his coffee he pushed the cup away and took up the letter, unfolding it carefully, though she was sure he knew every word of it.

"Henry's written again," he said. "About the store."

"I know. I saw it was from him."

"He's made it plain this time. Mr. Ashby is getting old and wants to sell his half. Henry says if I'll come in with him, he'll carry me until I can pay my share out of the profits. He says there's a house on Mulberry Street, near the church, that we could rent cheap. Brick, with a cistern and a grape arbor." He looked up at her. "It's a good offer, Maggie. It's better than we have any right to expect."

She did not answer at once. She took up the plates and carried them to the dishpan, and stood there with her back to him, looking out of the little window over the wash-shelf. From there she could see the rise beyond the garden, where the wild plum bushes grew, and the white paling fence that Thomas had built around the small mound under the plum bushes the spring their boy died. The fence showed pale and clear against the red sky. Every evening of her life she looked at it from that window while she washed the dishes; she did not have to think about it any more than she had to think about drawing breath.

"Henry has always been generous," she said at last.

"He has. And he's done well. He says the store cleared nearly two thousand dollars last year." Thomas folded the letter and smoothed it on his knee. "Two thousand dollars, Maggie. I haven't seen two hundred clear in any year since we came here."

"We had a good year in 'eighty-two."

"One good year." He laughed shortly. "One good year in eight. And we put every cent of it into the new house and the windmill, and the next summer the hail came."

She began to wash the plates, slowly, and set them one by one in the rack. The water was warm and greasy, and the soft soap had a sharp smell of lye. She found that her hands were not quite steady, and she held them under the water so that he should not see.

"You've decided, then," she said.

"I haven't decided anything. I wanted to talk to you first. That's why I've kept the letter since Saturday."

"You've kept it because you knew what I would say."

He was silent. The windmill wheel creaked outside, and somewhere off in the dark a cow lowed thirstily. Margaret dried her hands on her apron and turned round. Thomas was sitting with his elbows on the table and his chin in his hands, looking at the lamp, and in that light his face seemed older than she had ever seen it, older than his thirty-eight years—worn down, like a stone that water has run over for a long time.

"I suppose I did," he said. "But I thought—this summer, with everything going the way it is—I thought you might have come round to it."

"Come round to leaving?"

"To seeing that there's no sense in staying." He got up and went to the screen door and stood looking out. "Look at it. You can see it as well as I can. We've worked this place eight years. I've broke every foot of sod on it with my own hands. And what have we got? A frame house with a mortgage on it, and a windmill that pumps more air than water, and forty acres of corn that's burning up while we stand here. A man can't fight the sky, Maggie. I used to think he could. I don't think so any more."

She came and stood beside him at the door. The red had gone out of the west, and the sky above the horizon was a clear, hard green, with one star showing in it. The fields stretched away on every side, gray and featureless in the dusk, rolling off to the edge of the world like a sea that had been stilled. There was not a light anywhere; their nearest neighbors, the Kubiceks, lived four miles to the east, behind a swell of land. The wind blew hot against their faces and stirred the hair on Margaret's forehead.

"When we first came out," she said, "you used to stand at the door of the old soddy in the evenings, just like this, and tell me what the place would be. You said there would be an orchard down by the draw, and a grove of box-elders along the road, and a red barn, and that some day our children would ride to school in a buggy instead of walking. Do you remember?"

"I remember. I was a fool."

"You weren't a fool. We have the box-elders. They're higher than the house now."

"Box-elders," he said bitterly. "We can't eat box-elders."

She did not reply to that. It was a thing that had often surprised her, in their life together, how a man who could be so patient with a balky horse or a sick calf, who could sit up all night in the barn with a cow that was calving, could be so impatient with his own hopes. It was as though he could not bear to have hoped for anything; as though the hoping itself shamed him, once it had failed.

"I didn't want to come out here," she said slowly. "You know that. When you first talked of it, back in Ohio, I cried for a week. I thought it would be the end of me. I'd never been farther from home than Zanesville. And that first winter in the soddy, when the snow drifted over the window and we didn't see a living soul from Christmas until March—I used to lie awake and think that if I died, nobody would ever know what had become of me. I thought this country was the loneliest place God ever made."

"Then why—"

"Let me finish, Tom." She put her hand on his arm. "I don't know when it changed. It wasn't any one day. It came on gradually, the way the grass greens up in the spring, so you don't notice until all at once the whole country is green. I began to look forward to things. The first meadowlark. The wild roses along the section line in June. The way the wheat looks just before harvest, when the wind goes over it and it's like silk being stroked. I used to think there was nothing out here to look at. Now I think there's too much. I can't take it all in."

He looked down at her, puzzled, and a little hurt. "You never told me any of this."

"You never asked. And I didn't know how to say it." She smiled faintly. "I don't know how to say it now."

They stood together in the doorway. The star in the west had grown brighter, and others had come out above it, faint at first, then sharp and many. The wind had a different sound now that it was dark; it seemed to come from farther away, and to go on farther, across a country that had no end. Margaret thought, as she had often thought on such nights, that she could feel the size of the land pressing upon her, not as a weight, but as a kind of largeness that entered into her and made her larger too.

Thomas cleared his throat. "That's all very well," he said, "for a woman. A woman can stand in the door and look at the stars and the wild roses. But I'm the one has to go out every morning and see the crops die. I'm the one has to go to Wick Hollister at the bank in the fall and ask him to carry us another year, and watch him smile while he writes it down. I'm the one has to think what we'll do if he won't." His voice had grown rough. "You don't know what it is, Maggie, to fail and fail, and to know it's in front of everybody. The Kubiceks are making out. The Larsens are making out. Half the Bohemians in this county came out here with nothing but a feather-bed and a coffee-grinder, and they're making out. And I came with a team and a wagon and three hundred dollars, and I'm worse off than any of them."

"The Kubiceks lost their whole crop to the hail in 'eighty-four. You helped Joe Kubicek replant."

"That's different."

"It isn't different. It's the same for all of us. The Bohemians aren't any better farmers than you are, Tom. They're only more used to being poor. They don't expect so much."

He turned away from her abruptly and went back to the table and sat down. He took up the letter again and held it without looking at it. The lamp flickered, for the oil was low, and the shadows of the millers wheeled huge across the ceiling.

"Henry says the schools are good in Millersburg," he said, in a low voice. "There's an academy, too, for later on. If we had more children—" He stopped.

Margaret stood very still in the doorway. She knew what he had not said, and she knew that it had cost him something to come so near it. In the four years since the boy died, they had not had another child, and it had become one of the silences between them, like the little fenced mound under the plum bushes—a thing always present, and never spoken of.

"If we had more children," she said quietly, "they could go to the school at the Corners, the way Davy did. It's a good school. Miss Thorsen is a good teacher."

"Miss Thorsen is a Swede girl of eighteen who can hardly spell."

"She taught Davy to read. He could read the whole of the Second Reader before he was six."

Thomas put his face in his hands. Margaret had not meant to say the boy's name; it had come out of her before she could stop it, and now it hung in the hot room between them like something that had been dropped and broken. She came and sat down across from him. For a long time neither of them spoke. The windmill creaked outside. The clock on the shelf ticked loudly, the way clocks do in a silent house.

"That's it, isn't it," Thomas said at last, without lifting his head. "That's the real reason. You won't leave him."

She did not answer.

"Maggie, he isn't there. You know he isn't there. Whatever was Davy is gone to God. What's under those plum bushes is—" His voice broke. "I can't stay here on his account. I can't. It's like living on a grave. Every time I go out to the barn I pass it. Every time I plow the south field I see that fence out of the corner of my eye. Sometimes I think if I could get away from this place I could begin to forget."

"I don't want to forget."

"I don't mean forget him. I mean forget—the rest of it. The winter. The fever. The way he looked at the end, and the doctor not coming, and the roads drifted shut." He raised his head, and she saw that his eyes were wet, and that he was ashamed of it. "I've never said this to you, Maggie, but I've always thought if we'd been in a town, with a doctor near, he'd have lived. I've thought it every day for four years. It was this country killed him. And now you want me to stay here and let it kill everything else."

Margaret sat with her hands folded on the oilcloth. She looked at her husband's face, and it seemed to her that she was seeing it for the first time in a long while—that she had looked at it every day without seeing it at all. She understood now many things that had puzzled her: why he had grown so silent, why he worked so late in the fields, why he had never once in four years gone up the rise to the plum bushes, though she went there every Sunday afternoon. She had thought he did not care. She saw now that he had cared too much, and that his grief had turned inward and become a kind of anger against the land itself, as if the land had been a living enemy that had taken his son from him.

"It wasn't the country, Tom," she said gently. "Children die in towns, too. The Ashby girl died of diphtheria in Millersburg, with three doctors in the house. You read it in Henry's letter, the year before we lost Davy."

"I know that."

"You know it, but you don't believe it."

He made no answer. Margaret reached across the table and took the letter out of his hand, and laid it down between them, and put her own hand over his. His fingers were rough and cracked, the nails worn short and stained with earth, and she thought of the white, clean hands of the clerks she remembered in the stores at home, measuring out calico and weighing nails. She tried to imagine Thomas behind a counter in a brick store on a shaded street, wearing a collar every day, saying "Good morning, Mrs. So-and-so" to the ladies who came in to buy stove-blacking. It was not that she could not imagine it; she could imagine it very well. It was that she could not imagine him happy in it.

"If you want to go," she said, "I'll go with you. I won't make it hard for you. You've a right to say. It's your work, more than mine, that went into this place."

He looked at her quickly. "You mean that?"

"I mean it. But I want you to be sure. I want you to be sure it's what you want, and not only what you're afraid of." She pressed his hand. "You were happy here once, Tom. I remember it. The year the box-elders first leafed out, you carried Davy down the row on your shoulders and made him count them. You were happy then."

"That was a long time ago."

"Not so long. Eight years isn't long, for land. Old Mr. Larsen says it takes a man ten years to learn a piece of ground, and another ten before the ground learns him." She smiled a little. "We're only beginning."

Thomas pushed back his chair and got up. He stood for a moment irresolutely in the middle of the kitchen, then took his hat from the nail by the door.

"I'm going out to look at the stock," he said.

She knew that the stock did not need looking at; he had watered and fed them before supper. But she did not say anything. She watched him go out, and heard his boots on the step, and then saw his figure pass the window, dark against the starlit sky. He did not go toward the barn. He went along the garden fence, slowly, with his head bent, and she saw him stop at the corner where the path turned up the rise. He stood there a long time. Then, to her great astonishment, he went on up the path, through the dry grass, toward the plum bushes and the white paling fence.

Margaret blew out the lamp, so that he should not feel himself watched, and sat down by the window in the dark. The wind was still blowing, but it had begun to change; she could feel it on her cheek through the screen, and it was not so hot as it had been. Far off in the northwest, low on the horizon, there was a faint flickering, so faint that at first she thought she had imagined it. Then it came again—a pale, soundless light that ran along the rim of the sky and went out. Heat lightning, perhaps; it had come every night that week and brought nothing. And yet she sat very still and watched it, scarcely breathing, as she had watched so many skies before.

Up on the rise, she could just make out her husband's figure beside the little fence. He had taken off his hat. He was standing with his hand on the top rail of the paling, the way she had seen him stand with his hand on the neck of a horse he was fond of, and the wind was blowing his hair about. She could not see his face. She did not need to. She knew that whatever he decided, he would not decide it tonight, nor tomorrow; that the letter would lie on the shelf beside the clock for many days, and that they would not speak of it again until something—the rain, or the lack of it—spoke for them. She knew, too, that something had been given back to her in that hot kitchen which she had thought lost, and that it did not depend upon the corn, or the bank, or the brick house on Mulberry Street.

The lightning came again in the northwest, nearer now, and after a long moment there was a low mutter, so low that it seemed to come up out of the ground rather than down from the sky. Up on the rise, Thomas lifted his head and turned toward it. Margaret leaned forward against the screen. The smell came first, before anything else—the smell that all who have lived in a dry country know and wait for and cannot describe: the smell of dust that is about to be wet, of far-off rain falling on far-off grass, sweet and raw and full of promise, like the breath of the earth itself turning in its sleep.

Soon we could see the broken, grassy clay cliffs which indicated the windings of the stream, and the glittering tops of the cottonwoods and ash trees that grew down in the ravine. Some of the cottonwoods had already turned, and the yellow leaves and shining white bark made them look like the gold and silver trees in fairy tales. As we approached the Shimerdas’ dwelling, I could still see nothing but rough red hillocks, and draws with shelving banks and long roots hanging out where the earth had crumbled away. Presently, against one of those banks, I saw a sort of shed, thatched with the same wine-colored grass that grew everywhere. Near it tilted a shattered windmill-frame, that had no wheel. We drove up to this skeleton to tie our horses, and then I saw a door and window sunk deep in the draw-bank. The door stood open, and a woman and a girl of fourteen ran out and looked up at us hopefully. A little girl trailed along behind them. The woman had on her head the same embroidered shawl with silk fringes that she wore when she had alighted from the train at Black Hawk. She was not old, but she was certainly not young. Her face was alert and lively, with a sharp chin and shrewd little eyes. She shook grandmother’s hand energetically.

“Very glad, very glad!” she ejaculated. Immediately she pointed to the bank out of which she had emerged and said, “House no good, house no good!” Grandmother nodded consolingly. “You’ll get fixed up comfortable after while, Mrs. Shimerda; make good house.” My grandmother always spoke in a very loud tone to foreigners, as if they were deaf. She made Mrs. Shimerda understand the friendly intention of our visit, and the Bohemian woman handled the loaves of bread and even smelled them, and examined the pies with lively curiosity, exclaiming, “Much good, much thank!”—and again she wrung grandmother’s hand. The oldest son, Ambrož,—they called it Ambrosch,—came out of the cave and stood beside his mother. He was nineteen years old, short and broad-backed, with a close-cropped, flat head, and a wide, flat face. His hazel eyes were little and shrewd, like his mother’s, but more sly and suspicious; they fairly snapped at the food. The family had been living on corncakes and sorghum molasses for three days. The little girl was pretty, but Án-tonia— they accented the name thus, strongly, when they spoke to her—was still prettier. I remembered what the conductor had said about her eyes. They were big and warm and full of light, like the sun shining on brown pools in the wood. Her skin was brown, too, and in her cheeks she had a glow of rich, dark color. Her brown hair was curly and wild-looking. The little sister, whom they called Yulka (Julka), was fair, and seemed mild and obedient. While I stood awkwardly confronting the two girls, Krajiek came up from the barn to see what was going on. With him was another Shimerda son. Even from a distance one could see that there was something strange about this boy. As he approached us, he began to make uncouth noises, and held up his hands to show us his fingers, which were webbed to the first knuckle, like a duck’s foot. When he saw me draw back, he began to crow delightedly, “Hoo, hoo-hoo, hoo-hoo!” like a rooster. His mother scowled and said sternly, “Marek!” then spoke rapidly to Krajiek in Bohemian.

“She wants me to tell you he won’t hurt nobody, Mrs. Burden. He was born like that. The others are smart. Ambrosch, he make good farmer.” He struck Ambrosch on the back, and the boy smiled knowingly. At that moment the father came out of the hole in the bank. He wore no hat, and his thick, iron-gray hair was brushed straight back from his forehead. It was so long that it bushed out behind his ears, and made him look like the old portraits I remembered in Virginia. He was tall and slender, and his thin shoulders stooped. He looked at us understandingly, then took grandmother’s hand and bent over it. I noticed how white and well-shaped his own hands were. They looked calm, somehow, and skilled. His eyes were melancholy, and were set back deep under his brow. His face was ruggedly formed, but it looked like ashes—like something from which all the warmth and light had died out. Everything about this old man was in keeping with his dignified manner. He was neatly dressed. Under his coat he wore a knitted gray vest, and, instead of a collar, a silk scarf of a dark bronze-green, carefully crossed and held together by a red coral pin. While Krajiek was translating for Mr. Shimerda, Ántonia came up to me and held out her hand coaxingly. In a moment we were running up the steep drawside together, Yulka trotting after us. When we reached the level and could see the gold tree-tops, I pointed toward them, and Ántonia laughed and squeezed my hand as if to tell me how glad she was I had come. We raced off toward Squaw Creek and did not stop until the ground itself stopped—fell away before us so abruptly that the next step would have been out into the tree-tops. We stood panting on the edge of the ravine, looking down at the trees and bushes that grew below us. The wind was so strong that I had to hold my hat on, and the girls’ skirts were blown out before them. Ántonia seemed to like it; she held her little sister by the hand and chattered away in that language which seemed to me spoken so much more rapidly than mine. She looked at me, her eyes fairly blazing with things she could not say.

“Name? What name?” she asked, touching me on the shoulder. I told her my name, and she repeated it after me and made Yulka say it. She pointed into the gold cottonwood tree behind whose top we stood and said again, “What name?” We sat down and made a nest in the long red grass. Yulka curled up like a baby rabbit and played with a grasshopper. Ántonia pointed up to the sky and questioned me with her glance. I gave her the word, but she was not satisfied and pointed to my eyes. I told her, and she repeated the word, making it sound like “ice.” She pointed up to the sky, then to my eyes, then back to the sky, with movements so quick and impulsive that she distracted me, and I had no idea what she wanted. She got up on her knees and wrung her hands. She pointed to her own eyes and shook her head, then to mine and to the sky, nodding violently.

“Oh,” I exclaimed, “blue; blue sky.” She clapped her hands and murmured, “Blue sky, blue eyes,” as if it amused her. While we snuggled down there out of the wind she learned a score of words. She was quick, and very eager. We were so deep in the grass that we could see nothing but the blue sky over us and the gold tree in front of us. It was wonderfully pleasant. After Ántonia had said the new words over and over, she wanted to give me a little chased silver ring she wore on her middle finger. When she coaxed and insisted, I repulsed her quite sternly. I did n’t want her ring, and I felt there was something reckless and extravagant about her wishing to give it away to a boy she had never seen before. No wonder Krajiek got the better of these people, if this was how they behaved. While we were disputing about the ring, I heard a mournful voice calling, “Án-tonia, Án-tonia!” She sprang up like a hare. “Tatinek, Tatinek!” she shouted, and we ran to meet the old man who was coming toward us. Ántonia reached him first, took his hand and kissed it. When I came up, he touched my shoulder and looked searchingly down into my face for several seconds. I became somewhat embarrassed, for I was used to being taken for granted by my elders. We went with Mr. Shimerda back to the dugout, where grandmother was waiting for me. Before I got into the wagon, he took a book out of his pocket, opened it, and showed me a page with two alphabets, one English and the other Bohemian. He placed this book in my grandmother’s hands, looked at her entreatingly, and said with an earnestness which I shall never forget, “Te-e-ach, te-e-ach my Án-tonia!”

On the afternoon of that same Sunday I took my first long ride on my pony, under Otto’s direction. After that Dude and I went twice a week to the post-office, six miles east of us, and I saved the men a good deal of time by riding on errands to our neighbors. When we had to borrow anything, or to send about word that there would be preaching at the sod schoolhouse, I was always the messenger. Formerly Fuchs attended to such things after working hours. All the years that have passed have not dimmed my memory of that first glorious autumn. The new country lay open before me: there were no fences in those days, and I could choose my own way over the grass uplands, trusting the pony to get me home again. Sometimes I followed the sunflower-bordered roads. Fuchs told me that the sunflowers were introduced into that country by the Mormons; that at the time of the persecution, when they left Missouri and struck out into the wilderness to find a place where they could worship God in their own way, the members of the first exploring party, crossing the plains to Utah, scattered sunflower seed as they went. The next summer, when the long trains of wagons came through with all the women and children, they had the sunflower trail to follow. I believe that botanists do not confirm Jake’s story, but insist that the sunflower was native to those plains. Nevertheless, that legend has stuck in my mind, and sunflower-bordered roads always seem to me the roads to freedom. I used to love to drift along the pale yellow cornfields, looking for the damp spots one sometimes found at their edges, where the smartweed soon turned a rich copper color and the narrow brown leaves hung curled like cocoons about the swollen joints of the stem. Sometimes I went south to visit our German neighbors and to admire their catalpa grove, or to see the big elm tree that grew up out of a deep crack in the earth and had a hawk’s nest in its branches. Trees were so rare in that country, and they had to make such a hard fight to grow, that we used to feel anxious about them, and visit them as if they were persons. It must have been the scarcity of detail in that tawny landscape that made detail so precious. Sometimes I rode north to the big prairie-dog town to watch the brown, earth-owls fly home in the late afternoon and go down to their nests underground with the dogs. Ántonia Shimerda liked to go with me, and we used to wonder a great deal about these birds of subterranean habit. We had to be on our guard there, for rattlesnakes were always lurking about. They came to pick up an easy living among the dogs and owls, which were quite defenseless against them; took possession of their comfortable houses and ate the eggs and puppies. We felt sorry for the owls. It was always mournful to see them come flying home at sunset and disappear under the earth. But, after all, we felt, winged things who would live like that must be rather degraded creatures. The dog-town was a long way from any pond or creek. Otto Fuchs said he had seen populous dog-towns in the desert where there was no surface water for fifty miles; he insisted that some of the holes must go down to water—nearly two hundred feet, hereabouts. Ántonia said she did n’t believe it; that the dogs probably lapped up the dew in the early morning, like the rabbits. Ántonia had opinions about everything, and she was soon able to make them known. Almost every day she came running across the prairie to have her reading lesson with me. Mrs. Shimerda grumbled, but realized it was important that one member of the family should learn English. When the lesson was over, we used to go up to the watermelon patch behind the garden. I split the melons with an old corn-knife, and we lifted out the hearts and ate them with the juice trickling through our fingers. The white Christmas melons we did not touch, but we watched them with curiosity. They were to be picked late, when the hard frosts had set in, and put away for winter use. After weeks on the ocean, the Shimerdas were famished for fruit. The two girls would wander for miles along the edge of the cornfields, hunting for ground-cherries. Ántonia loved to help grandmother in the kitchen and to learn about cooking and housekeeping. She would stand beside her, watching her every movement. We were willing to believe that Mrs. Shimerda was a good housewife in her own country, but she managed poorly under new conditions: the conditions were bad enough, certainly! I remember how horrified we were at the sour, ashy-gray bread she gave her family to eat. She mixed her dough, we discovered, in an old tin peck-measure that Krajiek had used about the barn. They hated Krajiek, but they clung to him because he was the only human being with whom they could talk or from whom they could get information. He slept with the old man and the two boys in the dugout barn, along with the oxen. They kept him in their hole and fed him for the same reason that the prairie dogs and the brown owls housed the rattlesnakes—because they did not know how to get rid of him.

Excerpt 2: While the autumn color was growing pale on the grass and cornfields, things went badly with our friends the Russians.
