The Holm place lay on the high Divide, where the land rolled away in long, low swells toward the river, and where, in June, the wheat came up so evenly that a man standing at the edge of his field could believe the whole country had been laid out with a rule. Anders Holm had broken that ground himself, the first year, with a borrowed team and a plough that kept throwing him off its handles, and he had never since been able to look at it without a kind of wonder. Now it was green, going gray-green at the tops, and when the wind ran over it the field moved all one way, like water.

Kristian was seven that summer, and it was his work to herd the cows. There were five of them, and a yearling heifer who had not yet learned to behave herself, and every morning after breakfast he drove them down into the draw west of the house, where the grass grew rank along the dry creek-bed and there was a buffalo wallow that held rain until July. He had a willow switch and an old shepherd dog named Bonde, who had come with his father from the old country and was gray about the muzzle. The dog did most of the work. Kristian's part was to stay with the cattle and to keep them out of the wheat, which bordered the pasture on two sides with nothing between but a plough furrow. His father had promised him that when he was eight he should have a pony to herd on, and he thought about that pony a great deal, and had already named it, and changed its name several times.

The boy was small for his age, fair, with his mother's wide-set gray eyes and a way of standing very still when anything interested him, so that he seemed to have forgotten he had a body at all. His mother said he would stand so in front of an ant-hill until the ants carried him away. She was a large, quick woman, Marta Holm, with red forearms and hair the color of oat-straw, and she had a sharp tongue that she used freely and without much effect. Her husband she seldom scolded. He was a quiet man, slow in his speech, who had learned his English from the railroad section where he worked the first winter, and who still put his words together as if he were laying stones in a wall, each one carefully, so that it would not fall.

That year the railroad was building a branch line up from the river, to run across the corner of the Divide and on to the new towns farther west. All spring the neighbors had talked of nothing else. The grade had been thrown up the winter before, a long raw scar of yellow clay running straight as a furrow over hill and hollow, and now, in June, the track-laying crew was coming. One could hear them from the Holm place on still mornings: the ring of iron on iron, very faint and clear, like a bell struck far off, and sometimes a man's voice singing. Kristian heard it every day from the draw. It came to him over the wheat, and he would stop whatever he was doing and turn his head toward it, as a horse turns toward a sound in the night.

On the morning of the trouble the air was very still and bright, and the sound came nearer than it had ever come before. He judged that the crew could not be more than a mile away, just over the second rise, where the grade crossed the Lindquist pasture. The cows were lying down in the wallow, chewing, with their eyes half-shut. Bonde lay beside them. Kristian told himself that he would only go to the top of the rise and look, and come straight back; and he set off with his switch in his hand, walking at first, then running, through the short grass where the larks went up before him.

From the top of the rise he could see them. It was a sight he never forgot. The work train stood on the finished track, a long string of flat-cars piled with ties and rails, and an engine at the end of it, breathing softly, with a thin gray plume going straight up into the sky. Ahead of it, on the bare grade, the men were swarming: forty or fifty of them, he thought, in faded blue shirts and red handkerchiefs, their backs bent and shining. Two men would carry a tie forward and drop it in its place; then a little gang ran up with a rail between them, and laid it down; then the spikers came behind, swinging their long hammers high over their heads and bringing them down with that ringing stroke he had heard so often, and the sound reached him a moment after he saw the hammer fall, as if it had been delayed somewhere on the way. Every few minutes the engine crept forward a little, and the whole train moved after it, and the men moved ahead of it, and the shining track grew longer under the sun.

He did not go back. He went down the slope instead and sat on a pile of discarded ties a little way from the grade, where the earth smelled of creosote and hot iron, and watched. Most of the men were foreigners, darker than any people he had ever seen, and they called to each other in a language that sounded to him like quarrelling and singing at once. Nobody minded him. At noon, when a whistle blew and the men sat down in the scant shade of the flat-cars to eat, one of them came over and looked at him. He was a short, thick man with a black mustache and a gold ring in one ear, and he had a heavy, good-natured face.

"You live here?" he asked, and waved his arm at the whole empty country.

Kristian nodded.

The man sat down beside him on the ties and opened a cloth bundle. He had bread, and a long, dark sausage, and an onion, and he cut off a piece of each with his clasp-knife and gave them to the boy without asking whether he wanted them. The sausage was full of garlic and burned his tongue, but he ate it all. The man talked to him a good deal, half in English and half in his own speech. He had a boy at home, he said, in a village in the mountains, a boy just so big; and he held his hand flat at Kristian's height. He had not seen this boy for three years. When the railroad was finished he would have money enough to bring him over, and the mother, too. He took a photograph out of his shirt, wrapped in oiled paper, and showed it: a woman in a dark dress, standing very stiffly, and a child beside her in a white collar, scowling at the camera. The man looked at it for a long time himself before he put it away. Then the whistle blew again, and he got up, and touched Kristian on the head, and went back to his hammer.

The boy stayed. He meant every moment to go, and every moment he stayed. The sun moved over to the west, and the shadows of the flat-cars stretched out across the grade, and still the track went on, and the hammers rang, and the engine breathed and crept forward. It was as if he had been put under a spell. Afterward, when he tried to think how so much of the day had gone by, he could not account for it at all.

It was the sound of Bonde barking that broke the spell, very far away, hoarse and frantic, the bark the old dog used only when something was wrong. Kristian jumped up as if he had been struck. He ran back up the rise with his heart pounding in his ears, and from the top of it he saw what he had known he would see.

The cows were in the wheat. All five of them, and the heifer, had wandered out of the draw and across the furrow and far into the field, and they were feeding there contentedly, with the green stalks hanging out of their mouths. Behind them, where they had come in, there was a long, crooked track of broken grain, and another where the heifer had gone off by herself and run in circles. Bonde was dashing back and forth at the edge of the field, barking, afraid to go in. And coming down from the house, walking steadily, not running, was his father.

Kristian ran the whole way. By the time he reached the field his father had already turned the cattle and was driving them out, walking behind them through the wheat with his arms spread, speaking to them quietly in Danish. He did not look up at the boy. The cows came out one by one across the furrow, and Bonde fell in behind them, and Kristian, because he did not know what else to do, took his switch and followed them down into the draw and stood there with them until his father came.

Anders Holm came down the slope slowly. He was a tall man, a little stooped in the shoulders, and his face, burned dark by the sun, was very quiet. He had taken off his hat, and his hair, which was quite thin on top, stood up in the wind. He stopped a few feet from the boy and looked at him for a long moment without speaking. Kristian waited for him to shout, or to take the switch out of his hand and use it; he would have been glad of either. His father did neither.

"Where you go?" he asked at last.

"To the railroad," Kristian said. His voice came out very small.

"All day?"

The boy nodded. He could not say anything more.

His father turned and looked out over the field. The sun was getting low, and the long light came across the wheat and lay along the broken places, so that they showed plainly, darker than the rest, like wounds. Swallows were dipping over the field, very low. The wind had come up a little, as it always did toward evening, and the standing grain bowed and rose again; but the trampled grain lay flat and did not rise.

"Come," his father said.

He walked into the wheat, and Kristian followed him. They went along the track the cows had made, and his father walked slowly and stopped often. He would stoop down and lift a broken stalk in his hand and look at the head of it, not yet filled, soft and green; and then he would lay it down again, carefully, as if it could still feel. Once he stood up and pointed to the place where the heifer had run in circles, a ragged round patch where nothing was left standing at all, and said, "There," and nothing else. They went on to the end of the track, where the cows had been feeding when he found them, and there he stopped and turned to the boy.

"You know what this is?" he asked, and opened his hand toward the field.

"Wheat," Kristian said.

His father shook his head. "No. This is shoes for you, in winter. This is coat for your mother. This is flour for bread, all winter, when the snow comes. This is money for the man in town who has paper on our land. You know about that paper?"

The boy did not know about the paper, but he nodded.

"All this," said his father. "I plough it. I plant it. Every day I look at it. And today you let the cows eat it, because you go to look at the railroad." He said the word *railroad* slowly, with a kind of weariness, as if it were a thing he had known all his life and had no great opinion of.

Kristian began to cry. He had not meant to; he had been holding it back all the way up from the draw. His father let him cry and did not try to stop him, nor comfort him either. He stood and looked away over the wheat until the boy was quiet.

"When I was little boy like you," Anders Holm said, "in the old country, my father had sheep. Not many. Fourteen sheep. We lived by the sea, where the sand is, and the grass is very poor, and every sheep was like a person to us. My father gave me the sheep to watch. One day I go down to the shore, because a ship is broke on the rocks, and everybody goes to look. I look all day, like you. When I come back, three sheep are gone in the sand-hills. We never find them. That winter we eat very little."

He was silent a while, and Kristian looked up at him. He had never heard his father talk so much at one time, nor ever before about the old country. He tried to imagine the sea, and the sand-hills, and his father little, like himself, but he could not; he could only see his father as he stood there now, tall and stooped, with the wind blowing his thin hair.

"My father did not beat me," Anders went on. "I wish he beat me. He only did not talk to me, a long time. And every day when we eat I know why there is so little." He looked down at the boy, and his eyes, which were a pale, washed blue, seemed to see something a long way off. "I don't want that you feel like that. But you must know. When you are given something to take care of, you take care of it. Not some of the time. All the time. This is what makes a man. Not to be big and strong. Anybody can be strong. To be there, when you say you will be there."

The boy nodded. His throat hurt too much to speak.

"Tonight," his father said, "you stay here in the field until the sun goes down. You stand here and you look at what the cows did. You think about it. Then you come in."

He turned and walked away through the wheat toward the house, and did not look back.

Kristian stood where he had been left. The sun was very low now, just above the edge of the world, and it had turned the whole field to red gold, and the long shadows of the wheat lay all one way across it, fine as hair. The broken places were dark and gray. He looked at them, as he had been told to do, and they seemed to grow larger the longer he looked. He thought of the shoes, and the flour, and the paper in town, which he imagined as a long white sheet with black writing on it, very terrible; and he thought of his father as a little boy coming home over the sand-hills and counting the sheep. Far off to the east, the hammers on the railroad had stopped for the day. There was no sound but the wind in the wheat and, once, the cry of a killdeer going over. It seemed to him that he had never been so alone, nor ever been in so large a place.

From where he stood he could see the house, small and gray on its rise, with the kitchen chimney smoking. His mother came out once and stood in the doorway with her hand over her eyes, looking toward the field. He knew she wanted to call him; she was never able to keep from calling anybody. But she did not call. Presently his father came and stood behind her and said something, and she went in again.

The sun touched the earth and seemed to flatten there, as if it were too heavy to sink, and then it went down quickly, all at once, and the red went out of the wheat and left it gray and cool. A little chill came up from the ground. In the draw the cows were lowing to be milked. Kristian waited until the last bright edge of the sky had faded behind the rim of the prairie, because he did not want there to be any doubt about it, and then he turned and walked toward the house.

His father was at the barn, milking, with a lantern hung on a nail above him. The boy went in and stood by the stall without saying anything. After a moment his father moved over on the box and made room for him, and handed him the pail, and Kristian sat down and put his forehead against the warm flank of the cow, as his father had taught him, and began to milk. His hands were small and he was slow at it. The lantern swung a little on its nail, and the shadows of the two of them went back and forth on the boards of the stall. Neither of them spoke. When the pail was full his father took it from him, and looked into it, and nodded; and then he put his hand on the back of the boy's neck for a moment, and held it there, and took it away.

They went up to the house together. The lamp was lit in the kitchen window, and through it they could see Marta moving about the stove, setting out the supper she had kept warm for them. Behind them, in the dark, the wind was getting up again, and all over the Divide the wheat was bowing and lifting under it, the broken and the whole together, with a sound like a long breath let out.

All his life afterward, whenever Kristian Holm heard the sound of a hammer ringing on iron, far off on a still morning, he thought of that field at sundown, and of his father standing in it with the broken stalks in his hand. He grew up to have wheat of his own, and children, and a great deal of land; but he never learned anything, he used to say, that he had not learned that evening in the wheat, while the light went out of the sky.

There is a kind of quiet that comes down on the mesa between the going of the sun and the first stir of the night wind. It is not silence, for the sage keeps up its small dry talk and the doves go over to water in the dusk, but it is a waiting, and people who have lived long in that country learn to put off whatever they have to say until it is past. It is not a good time for speaking. The land seems to listen, and what is said in it has a way of being remembered by the hills.

Anson Yerby had lived nine years at Willow Springs, which is a day's drive out of Agua Mala on the road to nowhere in particular, and he knew this as well as any man. Nevertheless it was in that hour, with the light going brown on the Coso range and the cattle bawling at the trough below the corral, that he chose to tell his wife he had sold the water.

Willow Springs is not much to look at. There are perhaps a dozen willows, and these are of the gray, stooping, unthrifty sort that grow where water is sure but scant, and below them a reach of salt grass, and a cabin of adobe with a ramada of brush along the south side. The spring itself rises out of a fissure in the black rock at the foot of a little hill, and runs perhaps a hundred yards before the sand drinks it. But in that country a hundred yards of running water is a kingdom, and there is no measuring the worth of it by acres. Every trail for thirty miles bends toward Willow Springs as the needle bends to the north. The Shoshones came to it before there were any white men to call it by a name, and the rocks above the fissure are pecked with their signs, rings and wavy lines and the figures of sheep with their horns curled back, which nobody now can read. It was the water and not the land the company wanted, and they had paid well for it, as such things go.

Anson had come in from Agua Mala that afternoon with the paper in his pocket, and had unhitched and fed and watered, and had walked twice around the corral looking at nothing, which is a thing men do when there is something to be put off; and Mertie had watched him from the door and said nothing at all. She had been a long time in the desert, and the desert teaches a woman, if it teaches her anything, to let a thing come to her in its own time. So she waited, and set out the supper, and when they had eaten it she took her chair out under the ramada as she did of evenings, and he came and sat on the edge of the water bench with his hat between his knees.

"I seen Bassett in town," he said at last.

"I thought likely you would."

"He had the papers drawed up. I signed them."

She did not answer for a while. Down at the trough a cow lifted her head and let the water run out of her mouth, and the sound of it came up clear and small through the dusk. Mertie Yerby was not a large woman, and the sun had dried her as it dries all things in that country, so that there was no telling her age within ten years. She had come to Willow Springs a bride out of a wet green valley in Missouri, and the first summer she had cried every day of it. There are people in Agua Mala who remember that. They remember how she would stand in the door of the adobe looking out at the long white levels of the Sink with her hand at her throat, as if the very size of the country were choking her; and how Anson, who was a big gentle man with a slow voice, would come up from the corral and stand beside her and not know what to say. He had loved the desert from the first day he saw it, with the kind of love a man has for a thing he does not understand and does not need to, and it was a long time before he could believe that it frightened her.

"How much?" she said.

He told her. It was more money than either of them had ever seen in one place.

"That's a good deal of money," said Mertie.

"It's enough to go back on. It's enough to buy into a place where things grow without you carry every drop to them in a bucket. I been thinking of the Ozarks. Or Oregon, maybe. Bassett says there's good land in Oregon. It rains there."

"I've heard it does."

"You used to talk about rain."

"I used to," she said.

The edge of the night wind came over the mesa then, very lightly, and set the willow leaves turning so that they showed their pale undersides in the dusk, and was gone again. There was a smell in it of sage and of the far, bitter alkali of the Sink. Anson turned his hat around in his hands.

"I done it for you, Mertie," he said.

It is a thing men say, and it is generally true as far as it goes, and it generally does not go far enough. Mertie knew this. She had known it for some years, though she could not have said when the knowledge came to her. Knowledge in the desert does not come as it comes in the towns, out of books and the talk of neighbors; it comes up through the soles of the feet, like the heat out of the ground, and one day it is simply there, and there is no remembering a time when it was not.

"You might have asked me," she said.

"I did ask you. Three years back, when Bassett first come out. You said you didn't care. You said it was all one to you."

"That was three years back."

"Well," said Anson, "it ain't changed none that I can see."

That was the trouble, and both of them knew it. He could not see. He had brought her into the country and watched her weep for it, and then watched her go silent, and he had taken the silence for a kind of patient enduring, which was what it had been at first. What he had not seen was the slow turning of it into something else. It is not a thing that happens all at once. The desert does not take hold of people by violence; it waits for them. It lies out under the sun day after day, the same, and asks nothing, and one morning a woman goes out to the clothesline and stops with a wet sheet in her hands and looks at the long blue shadows lying across the mesa from the hills, and something in her that was clenched lets go. After that she belongs to it, whether she will or no.

Mertie could have told him the very day. It was in her fourth spring, a wet year, when the rains had come early and soft in February and the whole floor of the valley, that had been the color of ashes, broke out in a little while into gold and white and a blue like a child's eyes. She had walked out alone along the wash, farther than she had ever gone, and had sat down on a rock with the flowers going away from her on every side as far as she could look, and had cried as hard as ever she did the first summer. Only it was not the same crying. She did not tell Anson about it. There are things there are no words for between a man and a woman, and the more they have lived together the fewer the words become.

After that she began to go about the land as he did, but in her own way. He went looking for things: for strayed stock, for float in the washes, for the trail of the bighorn up on the Coso ridges. She went looking at things, which is a different matter. She learned where the quail came down at evening and where the coyotes laid up in the heat of the day under the rabbit-brush. She learned the plants the old Shoshone woman Pahutsie showed her, which was good for fever and which for the bite of the red ant, and how to roast the pods of the mesquite in the ashes. She learned to know when it was going to blow by the look of the dust devils walking out on the Sink in the forenoon, tall and slow like old men going to a burying. She learned the way the hills changed color through the day, from the rose of morning to the hard white of noon and then through all the purples and blues of the afternoon to that last brown that was on them now. She had a name for every one of them, in her own mind, that Anson had never heard.

And all this while he had been learning something else, though she did not rightly understand it until this minute, sitting under the ramada with the paper in his pocket between them. He had been learning that the country would not give him anything. Nine years he had worked it, and run cattle on it, and prospected over every ledge within two days' ride, and it had given him exactly what it gave him the first year, which was enough to live on and not a dollar more. He was a man who liked to see a thing come of his labor, and nothing came. The desert does not reward; it only permits. Some can live under that and some cannot, and it is not always the ones you would suppose.

"Anson," she said, "do you want to go?"

"I want what's best for us."

"That isn't what I asked you."

He stood up and walked to the end of the ramada and stood looking out toward the spring, where the water ran dark now among the dark willows. He was a long time answering.

"I'm tired, Mert," he said. "That's the God's truth. I'm tired of it. A man gets so he can't look at them hills without they're laughing at him. I go out of a morning and there it all is, the same as yesterday, and the same as it'll be when I'm dead and gone, and nothing I do makes no more mark on it than a lizard's tail in the sand. I want to go someplace where there's a fence I built that'll stand, and a tree I planted that'll grow up taller than me. I want to see green out the window. That's all. It ain't much to want."

"No," said Mertie. "It isn't much."

"I thought you'd be glad," he said, and there was something in his voice now, a kind of hurt bewilderment, like a child that has brought a present and seen it put aside. "All them years you hated it. I used to lay awake nights thinking how I done wrong to bring you here. And now I got the money to take you out, and you set there like I'd took something away from you."

"You have," she said.

She had not meant to say it. It came out of her flat and quiet, the way a stone drops into a well, and they both stood listening to it go down.

There is a saying among the Shoshones that a word once spoken goes out over the land and does not come back, but walks forever in the empty places looking for the one it was meant for. Pahutsie had told her that, sitting in the door of her brush hut at the rancheria with her old hands working the willow withes into a basket. Mertie had thought it a pretty fancy at the time. She did not think so now. She could feel the word going out from her across the mesa in the dark, and she knew she could not call it back, and she was not sure that she wished to.

Anson came back and sat down again on the water bench, heavily, as though his legs had given out.

"I don't understand you," he said.

"I know you don't. I didn't expect you would. I didn't understand it myself for a long time." She leaned forward in her chair, and her voice was low and even, and only the way her hands held each other in her lap would have told anyone how much it cost her. "When you brought me here I thought it was the end of the world. I thought there wasn't anything in it but heat and sand and things that stung. I wanted to die, Anson. You never knew how much. But I didn't die, and after a while I got so I could look at it, and after a while more I got so I couldn't look at anything else. I don't know how to say it to you. It's like it got into my blood. When I think of Missouri now, I think of it all shut in with trees, and the sky just a little piece up over the top of them, and the air so thick you could cut it, and I can't breathe. I'd smother there. I would. I know I would."

"You was raised there."

"I was born there. I was raised here. It's different."

He was silent. The wind had come up in earnest now, the long steady night wind off the high Sierra that blows down across all that country from dark until near morning, and the brush of the ramada rattled with it, and somewhere a loose board on the corral gate began to knock, slow and patient, like someone asking to be let in.

"I signed the papers," he said finally. "It's done, Mertie. Bassett's men come out the first of the month to put in the pipe."

"I know."

"I can't undo it."

"I know that, too."

"Well, then." He turned his hat over once more and set it on his head and pulled it down, as a man does who is going out to face weather. "Well, then, there ain't nothing more to say."

But it was plain there was, and neither of them moved. The lamp was not lit in the cabin behind them, and the dark had come down so close that they could no longer see each other's faces, only the shapes of them against the paler dark of the sky where the stars were coming out thick and white the way they do in that dry air, with no softness about them, every one as sharp as a needle's point. It is easier to say some things in the dark. Perhaps that is why so much that matters in that country is said there.

"Anson," she said. "You go."

He did not answer.

"You take the money and go to Oregon, or wherever you've a mind to. Buy your green place. Plant your trees. You've earned it. Nine years you've given this country, and it's given you nothing back, and you've a right to go. I won't hold you."

"And you?"

"There's the old Hatfield claim up at Burro Tanks. There's a seep there. It isn't much of one, but it's enough for a woman and a garden and a few goats. Nobody wants it. Bassett don't want it. I could file on it."

"Alone? Up there? Mertie, you're crazy. It's twenty mile to the nearest living soul."

"Pahutsie's people come down by there every fall for the piñon nuts. And the sheepmen go through in the spring. I wouldn't be so alone as you think."

"A woman can't live like that."

"Women have," she said. "There was that one used to walk the country between here and Lone Pine, before your time. Folks called her crazy too. She lived to be old."

He got up then, and she heard him walking, out from under the ramada and into the yard, and then back, and then out again, his boots grinding in the coarse sand. When he spoke it was from a little distance off, out in the dark, and his voice was not steady.

"Nine years," he said. "Nine years I been thinking you only stayed on account of me."

"I did, at first."

"And now?"

She did not answer that, because there was no answer that would not hurt him worse than the silence, and she was not a cruel woman. Only the desert had made her honest, as it makes all who stay in it long enough honest, because there is nothing out there to hide behind. Anson understood the silence. That much the country had taught him, if nothing else.

After a long while he came back and stood before her chair, a darker shape against the dark.

"You don't have to decide nothing tonight," he said. "There's three weeks yet before the first of the month."

"No," she agreed. "There's three weeks."

"Maybe you'll feel different when you've slept on it."

"Maybe."

But they both knew she would not. And they both knew, too, though neither of them would have said it, that it was not the selling of the water that lay between them, nor Oregon, nor Burro Tanks, nor anything that had to do with money or land. It was only that the same country which had broken him had made her, and there was no help for that, and no blame in it either. It is the way of that land to sort people out. It takes those it can use and spends the rest, and it does not ask leave of either.

Anson went in and lit the lamp. She saw the yellow square of the window spring out on the sand beside her, with his shadow moving across it. She did not go in. She sat on under the ramada with the wind pulling at her skirts and the loose board knocking at the corral, and looked out past the willows to where the black rock of the little hill rose up against the stars. She could not see the spring, but she could hear it, the small steady talk of it going out over the stones and losing itself in the sand, as it had been doing since long before the Shoshones pecked their sheep and their wavy lines into the rock above it, and as it would go on doing, she supposed, until Bassett's men came with their pipe and carried it off in the dark to some town she would never see.

She thought that she would go up to the spring in the morning, early, before Anson was about, and sit a while by the rocks and look at the old signs. She had never been able to read them. Nobody could. But she had come to believe that they said something like what she would have said herself, if there had been anyone to say it to; and that the people who made them had known, as she knew now, that a country can be loved in a way that has nothing to do with what it gives.

In Agua Mala they tell it both ways. Some say that Mertie Yerby went to Oregon with her husband after all, and grew fat and contented among the apple trees, and never spoke of the desert again. Others say she was seen years afterward at Burro Tanks, a little dried brown woman with a garden of squash and a flock of goats, who talked to the Shoshones in their own tongue and would not come down to the town even for the Fourth of July. It does not much matter which is true. The desert keeps its own counsel in these matters, and it is not for the towns to know.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Mary Austin, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
There is a kind of meeting that happens only in the desert, where people who have not seen one another for a long term of years come together without any of the softening of the town between them; no parlor, no tea things, no neighbors coming in, only the two of them and the wide, uncommenting land. Such meetings are apt to be more honest than either party intends. The country sees to that. It is not possible to keep up a pretense very long under a sky so large and so entirely without opinion.

Letitia Garland went down to the stage station at Coyote Holes on a morning in late April to meet her cousin Clare, whom she had not seen for nineteen years. She drove the light wagon herself, with the bay mare that was going a little blind in the off eye, and she started early, before the sun had got over the Inyo wall, for it is eleven miles from the Garland place to the station and the road is mostly sand. All the way down she was thinking what she should say first, and she did not settle it, so that when the stage came rocking in out of the south, trailing its long pale banner of dust, she found she had nothing ready at all.

You are to understand that these two had been brought up together on a ranch in the lower San Joaquin, in the time when it was still a ranch and not a subdivision, and that they had been more like sisters than cousins, sleeping in one bed and quarreling over one hair ribbon. Then Clare's people had gone to San Francisco, and from there Clare had gone farther, to Chicago and to New York and once, it was said, to Paris; and Letitia had married Ben Garland, who ran cattle on the east side of the Sierras, and gone with him into the country of the long valleys, where she had stayed. There had been letters, at first many and then fewer, and then only at Christmas. Neither of them could have told you why. It is the way of letters, which are like water in a ditch that is not kept up; they go on running a while from habit, and then the sand drifts in.

Clare got down from the stage stiffly, as people do who have come a long way through heat, and stood looking about her with a hand up against the glare. She was a tall woman still, with the same carriage of the head, but thinner than Letitia remembered, and she wore a gray traveling suit of a cut that had never before been seen at Coyote Holes. The hostler stopped with the bucket in his hand to look at it. Then she saw Letitia, and the two of them came toward each other across the trampled yard, slowly, the way you would go toward a horse you were not sure of.

"Lettie," said Clare. "Why, Lettie."

"You've come, then," said Letitia, which was not at all what she had meant to say, and then they had their arms about one another, and the hostler went on to the trough.

---

They did not talk much on the drive home. The heat had come up by that time, standing over the valley floor in a kind of trembling, and the mare walked heavily in the sand. Clare sat with her hands in her lap and looked. Letitia, watching her sidelong, saw her eyes go out across the flat to where the creosote stood in its endless, even ranks, each bush at its decent distance from the next, as if they had been set out by a careful hand; and up to the bajadas, where the color changed from gray to tawny; and up again to the mountains, which at that hour were without any shadow at all, flat as if they had been cut out of paper and stood up against the sky.

"It's very bare," Clare said at last.

"It's full," said Letitia, "when you know it."

She could have said a great deal more. She could have told how, in a wet spring, the whole of that gray flat goes gold and purple for a week with the little annual flowers that wait in the sand, sometimes for years together, for rain enough to make it worth their while; or how the cactus wrens build in the cholla where nothing can get at them, and the shrike hangs his meat on the thorns of the same bush; or how the mesquite will put its root down sixty feet to find water and live a hundred years on the finding. But she had learned long since that this is a country which will not be explained to anybody. It must be lived into, the way a foot is lived into a new boot, and there is no hurrying it. So she said only that it was full, and Clare looked at her a moment and was silent.

At noon they stopped at the Willow Springs, where there is a little seep coming out from under a black ledge, and a patch of wiregrass and a dozen ragged willows that the cattle have browsed to the height of a man's shoulder. Letitia watered the mare and got out the lunch she had brought, cold mutton and biscuits and a jar of plum preserves, and they ate it sitting in the thin willow shade with the flies humming about them. A pair of doves came down to the seep and drank, lifting their heads after every sip in the way doves have, as if they were giving thanks for it.

"Do you remember," said Clare, "the doves in the eucalyptus at home? We used to lie awake and listen to them in the mornings."

"And Grandmother would call up the stairs that we were a pair of lazy-bones."

"And you'd always get up first, so as not to be scolded, and I'd lie there and let her scold."

They both laughed, and something that had been held tight between them since the station let go a little. It is a curious thing that the oldest memories are the safest to handle. People who have nothing to say to each other about the last twenty years can go on very comfortably about the first ten, as if the years in between were a stretch of bad road that both had agreed not to mention.

---

The Garland place lies at the mouth of a cañon on the east slope of the Sierras, where the creek comes down out of the snow and spreads itself in a fan of meadow before it is lost in the sand of the valley floor. Ben Garland's father had taken it up in the sixties and had built a house of stone, low and thick-walled, with the windows set deep, and a long porch on the side toward the mountains. There was an orchard of apples and apricots, gone somewhat to neglect, and a row of poplars that the old man had planted for a windbreak, and the corrals and the long sheds, and beyond the corrals the meadow, green with wiregrass and blue flags, where the saddle horses stood switching their tails. It is the kind of place that looks, from a little distance, like the only living thing in the world.

Clare walked through the house slowly, touching things. She touched the Navajo blanket on the settle, and the shelf of books, mostly old agricultural reports and a set of Scott in a broken binding, and the basket that stood by the hearth. She stopped before the basket a long time.

"That was made by a woman on the reservation below," said Letitia. "Mrs. Tom, they call her. She brings me one every few years, and I give her flour and a dress length. She's very old now. She says the young women won't learn the patterns any more, they'd rather buy pails at the store."

"It's beautiful."

"It holds water," said Letitia, "if you wet it first."

Clare turned the basket in her hands. It was of willow and the black fiber of the devil's-claw, woven so close you could not have put a needle between the stitches, with a pattern going round it of little stepped figures like a flight of birds.

"What does the pattern mean?"

"I asked her once. She said it meant the basket was finished." Letitia smiled a little. "She meant I had no business asking."

Ben was away with the cattle on the summer range; he would be gone till the end of May. There was a man on the place, a Basque named Ignacio who did the chores and kept mostly to himself, and there was Letitia's boy, Tom, who was fourteen, all elbows and silence, and who shook hands with his mother's cousin and fled to the corrals as soon as it was decent. That was the whole household. Clare noticed, without remarking it, that there was a photograph on the shelf of a little girl in a white dress, and that nobody spoke of her.

---

It was not until evening that they began to talk in earnest. They sat on the porch after supper, in the long, slow failing of the light, which in that country is the best part of the day. The sun goes down early behind the Sierra wall, and for an hour after, the whole east side of the valley stays lit, the Inyos burning rose and then amber and then a pale, unearthly violet, while the near slopes are already in shadow and the air comes down cold off the snow. The poplars had begun to whisper. Somewhere up the cañon a poorwill was saying his one word over and over, and out on the meadow the frogs had started.

Clare had a cigarette, which she asked leave to smoke, and Letitia gave it with a slight lift of the eyebrows that she was ashamed of afterward. They watched the smoke go up straight in the still air.

"You haven't asked me anything," said Clare.

"I didn't know what you'd want asked."

"No. I suppose not." She was quiet a while. "I left him, you know. Harold. Four years ago. I don't think I wrote you."

"You wrote that you were traveling."

"That was the year. I traveled. I had a little money of my own, from Mother, and I went about from place to place like a cat that's been moved and can't find the right corner to settle in. Italy for a while. Then New York again. There's nothing to tell, really. He wasn't unkind. It was only that one day I looked at my life and there was nothing in it that I had chosen. Everything had been chosen for me, so nicely, so suitably, and I had gone along. I thought, if I die now I shall have been a sort of very well dressed furniture." She laughed, not happily. "That sounds ridiculous, said out loud, here."

"It doesn't sound ridiculous."

"Doesn't it? I thought it would. I thought you'd think I was a fool. You always had so much sense, Lettie."

Letitia did not answer at once. She was looking out over the meadow, where the light was going, and the horses had become dark shapes, and the line of the creek showed only by the paler mist that had begun to lie along it. There is a saying among the people of that country that the desert does not care what you do, and this is true; but it is also true that the desert has a way of showing you very plainly what it is you have done. Things stand out there with their edges sharp. There is no shelter of other people's opinion to stand behind.

"Ben and I lost a little girl," she said. "Seven years ago in the fall. Diphtheria. There was no doctor nearer than Bishop, and the creek was up, and by the time Ben got through it was too late." She said it quite evenly, in the voice one uses to tell the price of hay. "I didn't write that either."

"Oh, Lettie."

"I'm not telling you for you to be sorry. I'm telling you because I thought, after, that I'd go. Away from here. I hated it. I hated the mountains and the sand and the wind and the way nothing changes, the way the sage just stands there, year after year, and doesn't care. I used to go out and look at it and hate it so I could hardly breathe." She stopped. "I had a trunk packed. I was going to my sister Ellen's, in Sacramento."

"What happened?"

"Nothing happened. That's the thing. I went out one morning, early, to get the horse up, and it was just after a rain, which isn't often, and the whole flat below there smelled of sage. You've never smelled it after rain. It's like nothing else. And the light was coming over the Inyos, and a meadowlark was sitting on the corral post, and I thought, well, it doesn't care. It doesn't care about Annie and it doesn't care about me. But it's here. It goes on being here. And if I stay I can go on being here with it." She turned her hands over in her lap, looking at them. "I unpacked the trunk that night. I don't know that I could tell it any better than that."

Clare had let her cigarette go out. She sat holding it.

"I think," she said slowly, "that I've never in my life been anywhere that I could say that about. Anywhere that just went on being there."

"It isn't always comfortable."

"No. I don't suppose comfort is the thing."

---

It had grown quite dark. The stars had come out in that close, crowding way they have in the dry air, so many that the sky seemed lit rather than spotted, and the Milky Way went over like a drift of smoke from some fire beyond the mountains. A coyote began on the bench above the house, and was answered by another far out on the flat, and then the whole chorus took it up, that wild, broken, quavering yell that sounds like a dozen voices and is very likely three. Clare started at it, and Letitia laughed.

"They come down to the orchard for the windfalls," she said. "Ben shoots at them sometimes, but he never hits any. I think he doesn't try very hard. He says they were here first."

"Do you love him?" said Clare suddenly. "Ben? I've always wondered. You were so young."

Letitia considered the question as she would have considered a horse offered for sale, honestly, from all sides.

"I don't know that I'd have the word for it, the way you mean," she said. "He's like the place. I don't think about him much when he's here. When he's gone I notice the shape of where he isn't. When the creek was up that time and he went through it, I stood on the bank and watched him, and I knew if he didn't come back up out of it I'd have no reason to keep on breathing. But he did come back up. I suppose that's what it is. I never thought to ask."

"I asked all the time," said Clare. "I asked so much I never found out."

They were quiet then for a long while. There are silences between people that are like an empty room, and silences that are like a room full of furniture that both know the place of, so that neither need light a lamp to move about in it. This was coming to be the second kind. The years that had lain between them like bad road were not mended, but they had been looked at, which is something; and each had come to see that the other had been traveling too, and had not found it easy.

Presently Letitia got up and went inside and came back with a shawl, an old one of gray wool that had been their grandmother's, and put it round Clare's shoulders.

"You'll take cold," she said. "People from outside always do. They think because it's hot all day it must be warm at night. It never is."

Clare drew the shawl close and put her face down to it a moment.

"It still smells of her," she said. "Of lavender. How can that be, after all this time?"

"I keep it in the cedar chest. With some of the lavender she gave me when I married. It's mostly dust now, but the smell stays."

"Things stay with you," said Clare. "You keep them."

"There's not so much to keep, out here. You learn to hold on to what there is."

---

Clare stayed three weeks, which was longer than either had planned. She rode out with Letitia to the reservation below and sat in the shade of a brush shelter while Mrs. Tom, who was very old indeed and nearly blind, worked at a basket with her fingers and would not say a word in English. She walked up the cañon alone in the mornings, as far as the first falls, and came back with her skirts torn by the wild rose and her hands full of things she could not name, which Letitia named for her: the mariposa, the paintbrush, the little purple pentstemon that grows in the cracks of the granite. She got sunburned. She stopped wearing the gray suit and borrowed Letitia's calico, which was too short for her, and Tom, who had lost his shyness by the second week, taught her to throw a loop over a fence post and laughed at her without mercy.

On the last evening they sat again on the porch, as on the first, and watched the light go off the Inyos.

"I shan't stay out here," said Clare. "You know that. I'd go mad. I haven't your patience, or whatever it is."

"I didn't think you would."

"But I'll go somewhere. I'll find somewhere. A place that goes on being there, and I'll stay in it, and let it not care about me." She laughed. "I don't know where. Maybe the coast. Maybe nowhere you'd ever have heard of. But I shan't be furniture any more."

"No," said Letitia. "I don't think you will."

She had a feeling, which she did not express, that Clare would very likely go on moving for some years yet, like the cat she had spoken of, trying one corner and another; and that this was not a thing to be sorry about. There are people made to strike root, as the mesquite does, and go down sixty feet for water and stand a hundred years in one place, and there are people made like the seeds of the little desert flowers, to blow about and lie dormant and wait, sometimes a long while, for the one right rain. The land has room for both, and does not think the less of either. It is only people who make a virtue of one kind and a reproach of the other.

In the morning Letitia drove her down to Coyote Holes, the eleven miles through the sand, with the bay mare that was going blind in the off eye. The stage came in out of the north this time, trailing its dust, and the hostler stopped with his bucket to stare, though there was nothing now to stare at, Clare being dressed in the gray suit again and looking very much as she had looked getting down. Only her face was brown, and her hands.

"Write to me," she said, at the step. "Write to me properly. Not Christmas."

"I'll write," said Letitia.

They did not embrace this time, but stood a moment holding each other's hands, and looked at each other plainly, the way one looks at a country one has come to know. Then Clare got in, and the driver gathered his lines, and the stage went rocking away to the north, growing smaller, until it was only a moving point at the head of its banner of dust, and then not that.

Letitia stood a while longer, watching where it had gone. A shrike sat on the top of a creosote bush near the road and regarded her with its black-masked face, as shrikes do, as if it were sizing her up for the thorn. The heat was coming up. Away to the west the Sierras stood, as they had stood the morning she unpacked her trunk, entirely without opinion.

She turned the mare toward home. It was a long drive, and she had the whole of it to herself, and the country to keep her company, which is to say no company at all, and all the company in the world.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
Water in that country is not a thing to be had, but a thing to be gone after. Whoever lives between the Coso hills and the long white glare of the borax flats learns this first or learns it last, and there is no third way. The creatures know it; their trails, which begin anywhere among the creosote, all bend at last toward the one wet place, as the spokes of a wheel bend toward the hub. The Indians know it, and keep their campoodies within a morning's walk of the springs, moving when the springs move, which they do, though not so often as the white settlers suppose. It is only the newcomer who thinks of water as he thinks of air, something laid on by Providence and not to be counted, and it is the business of the land to correct him. The land is very patient about this, and very thorough.

The Burdicks had been two years on the mesa below Black Mountain when the thing happened that I am to tell, which is not much of a thing as the world reckons, but was a great deal to the parties concerned. Burdick had taken up a quarter section there in a wet spring, when the wild hay stood to a horse's knees along the wash and the sheepmen had not yet come down from the north with their bands. He had built a board house with a lean-to, and a brush shed for the team, and he had dug where a willow grew and got a little seepage that filled a barrel in the night and was gone again by noon. In the second summer the seep failed altogether, as such seeps will when the snow on the high ridges has been light; and after that Burdick hauled water in casks from the spring at the head of Little Lake Cañon, two miles up, a load every third day, and in between hauled freight for the borax works across the flats to make the living that the quarter section would not make.

There was a woman, of course. There is always a woman in such places, and she is generally the one who pays for them. Ellen Burdick was a tall, spare, quiet person out of the Iowa country, who had come to the desert with the notion, common enough among women of her sort, that hardship was a thing one met with the jaw set and got through. It had not yet come to her, as it comes to most who stay, that hardship in that country is not an event but a condition, like the weather, and that one does not get through it so much as grow to the shape of it. She was learning, though. The land had begun with her as it begins with everyone, by taking away the small softnesses one by one, the green thing in the window, the clean apron on weekdays, the habit of talking much; and she had let them go with less complaint than might have been expected, because she had the boy.

The boy was called David after her father, and was six that summer. He was a brown, square, silent child with his mother's long upper lip and a trick of standing quite still to look at things, which is the beginning of wisdom in the desert, though his parents did not know it. He had been born in Iowa and remembered nothing of it. The mesa was all the world he had, and he had made himself free of it as a lizard is free of a rock, so that he knew where the horned toads lay flattened in the sand at noon, and which of the burrows under the rabbit brush belonged to the kangaroo rats and which to the little striped ground squirrels, and how the quail went down the wash in the cool of the morning in a long chattering file with their topknots bobbing. These things are the proper schooling of a child in that country, and he had them all. What he had not yet learned was the one thing that underlies them, and the mesa, which teaches nothing by halves, was preparing to teach it.

It was the end of July, when the heat stands on the flats like a wall and the far mountains swim in it with no bottoms to them. Burdick had gone out before daylight with the big wagon to the borax works and would not be back until the next noon. He had hauled water the evening before; the two casks stood full under the brush shed with wet sacking over them, and the olla hung in the lean-to door sweating and cool, and there was in all perhaps sixty gallons, which with care, and with the team away, would do the house three days. Ellen Burdick had reckoned it out as she reckoned everything now, so much for drinking and so much for the cooking and so much, a very little, for washing, and none at all for the two slips of tamarisk that she had set out by the doorstep in the spring and had been keeping alive, against her better judgment, with the dishwater.

In the forenoon she lay down in the shade of the lean-to with a wet cloth on her face, because the heat had given her one of her headaches, and she told the boy to keep within call. He kept within call. That is to say, he went no farther than the shed, where he had found a thing that interested him extremely.

The wash below the house ran dry ten months of the twelve, but in the spring there had been a little water in it for a week, and the boy had seen the water go down the channel, carrying sticks and bits of dead brush, turning about, catching, going on again. He had not forgotten it. Children do not forget the first running water they ever saw in a dry country, any more than grown men forget it; I have known old prospectors to speak of a flash flood they saw in their youth as other men speak of their first love. And now, under the brush shed, here were the casks, and here was the bung in the lower side of the near one, which his father knocked out with the flat of the hatchet when he drew water, and here was the hatchet leaning against the post.

He did not think of it as wrong. He did not think of it at all, which is the whole history of mischief. He had in his head the picture of the wash running, and the sticks going down, and it seemed to him the most natural thing in the world to make it run again. He scooped a little channel in the dust from the foot of the cask out past the shed and down the slope toward the wash, and laid sticks along it for boats, and then he took the hatchet in both hands and struck the bung as he had seen his father strike it.

The bung came out. The water came after it, much faster and fuller than he had looked for, a thick bright rope of it that hit his little channel and overran it and spread out in a dark fan over the dust, and the dust drank it, as that dust will drink anything, with a kind of hiss. The sticks went bobbing. He shouted with delight. He ran beside them as far as the slope, and the water ran with him a little way and then sank, and he ran back for more boats, and the cask went on emptying itself with a sound like a creek.

It was the sound that woke his mother.

She came out of the lean-to with the cloth still in her hand and stood a moment not understanding, because the noise of running water was so strange in that place that she thought for one wild instant that the seep had come back. Then she saw. She did not cry out. She went across the yard in four long strides and caught up the bung out of the dust and drove it home with the heel of her hand, and the water stopped. Then she stood with her hand flat against the wet staves and looked at the cask, and down at the dark stain spreading on the ground and already beginning to pale at the edges, and then at the boy.

He had stopped running. He stood at the end of his little channel with a stick in each hand, and he knew now. He knew it by the way she stood. Children in a lonely place learn their parents as the Indians learn the sky, by signs too small for strangers to read; and he had never seen her stand like that.

She knocked on the cask with her knuckles, low down and then higher, listening, as Burdick did when he would know how much was left. It rang hollow nearly to the bottom. Out of thirty gallons there might be four.

There is a kind of anger that comes up in women of her make, that have been schooled all their lives to keep it down, which is not hot but cold, and is the more dreadful to a child for that. Ellen Burdick felt it rise in her and was afraid of it. She had a sudden clear picture of herself crossing the yard and taking the boy by the arm and shaking him, and she saw her own hand do it, and she held the hand still against the cask until the picture went away. It was not the water only. It was the two years; it was the tamarisk slips and the clean aprons and the window with nothing green in it; it was Burdick gone across the flats every second day and the house so silent you could hear the sand tick against the boards; it was all of it, and it had found a door to come out by, and the door was a child of six with a stick in each hand. She knew that, standing there. That she knew it was the beginning of her own schooling in that country, and it went further with her afterward than anything she taught the boy.

"Come here, David," she said.

He came, dragging his feet in the wet dust.

"Do you know what you have done?"

He looked at the cask and at the ground, and his lip came down over his teeth, but he did not cry. He was not a crying child. "I made it run," he said.

"You made it run. Where did it run to?"

He looked at the ground again, where the dark fan was now no more than a dim mottle, drying from the edges inward as you watched. There was nothing to say to that, and he said nothing.

"That was our water," said his mother. "That was the water for today, and tomorrow, and the next day. Your father is gone with the team. There is no more until he brings it. Do you understand me?"

He nodded, but she saw that he did not understand, not as she meant it, and she saw too that he could not, not by being told. One cannot tell a child what thirst is, any more than one can tell him what grief is; it must be laid on him. The Paiute women, who had been at this business of raising children in that land a thousand years before the Burdicks came, did not tell. Ellen Burdick had seen them, at the campoodie by the spring, with their little ones; she had thought them careless mothers, letting the children go hungry when the pine nuts were short and cold when the wood was scarce, and never a word of scolding. It came to her now, standing by the empty cask, that it was not carelessness, but something she had not had the wit to see.

She went into the house and came out again with her sunbonnet on, and the two-gallon pail, and the little canteen that Burdick carried on the wagon seat, and the boy's straw hat. She put the hat on his head and tied the string under his chin.

"We are going to the spring," she said.

He looked up the long slope of the mesa toward the cañon mouth, where the heat stood in a shaking sheet over the greasewood and the black rocks of the hills seemed to float above it with nothing under them. It was two miles. He had been there with his father on the wagon, but never afoot.

"You will carry the canteen," she said, "going and coming. And when we get there you will fill it yourself."

She did not wait to see if he would follow. She went out of the yard and up the faint wheel track toward the hills, and after a moment she heard his feet behind her.

It was past noon. There is no shade on the mesa at that hour; the creosote throws a shadow no bigger than a plate, and the rocks are too hot to touch. The ground underfoot was the coarse grey granite sand that slips back half a step for every step you take, and the air came off it in a breath like an oven door. Ellen Burdick went slowly, because she was not a fool, but she did not stop, and she did not look back except now and then from the side of her bonnet to see that he was there. He was always there. He walked with his head down and the canteen bumping on his hip, and after the first half mile he stopped looking at anything.

She would have had him look. That was the pity of it, that the lesson was all about him and he was too hot and too unhappy to read it. For the whole mesa was writ over with water as a page is writ with words. Here a cottontail had gone up the track in the early morning, and here a coyote after it, and both trails bore to the left toward the cañon; and here was the fine double stitching of quail feet going the same way, and the long sweeping scrawl of a snake, and the little pricked dots of the kangaroo rat, all going one way, toward the one wet place. Every live thing on the mesa went to that spring or to the dew or to the green pith of some plant that had gone to it before them, and spent its life between, and no creature of them all was so foolish as to pour it on the ground. Ellen Burdick saw this, walking, as she had never seen it before in two years of looking out of the window, and she was ashamed, and the shame took the last of her anger away, but she did not stop.

At the cañon mouth the boy sat down in the sand.

She came back and stood over him. His face under the straw hat was dark red and his mouth was open.

"I'm thirsty," he said.

"So am I," said his mother. "It is a mile yet."

He looked at the canteen on his hip, and she saw what was in his mind, and she shook her head.

"It is empty," she said. "We are going to fill it. That is what we came for."

He got up. He did not cry even then, though she saw his chin go, and she thought him a better child than she had known, and was prouder of him in that minute than she had ever been, and showed it not at all.

The last mile was up the cañon, among the black boulders, where the heat came off the rock walls on both sides and there was no wind. Then the cañon turned, and there were the willows.

You must have come upon a desert spring in July to know what that green is. It is not the green of other countries. It is a green that hurts, that strikes the eye like a cry; it is a green that has fought for every inch of itself against the sand and the sun and won, and knows it. There was a clump of willows and a wild grape tangled through them, and under the willows a pool no bigger than a washtub, very clear, with the water welling up through clean sand at the bottom so that the grains danced in little fountains, and a thread of overflow that ran a few yards down the cañon and was swallowed. Doves went up out of the willows with a clatter as they came. There were wet tracks of every kind at the edge of the pool, crossing and recrossing, and a little way off on the rocks a scatter of grinding holes where the Indian women had pounded mesquite beans in some other summer.

The boy ran forward and dropped flat at the edge of the water and would have put his face in it, and his mother let him. She knelt beside him and drank too, from her hand. Then she sat back on her heels and waited until he lifted his head.

"Fill the canteen," she said.

He did it. It took a long while, because the neck was narrow and his hands were clumsy and the pool was shallow, and twice the water ran out over his fingers back into the spring, and she did not help him. When it was full she showed him how to drive the cork, and hung it on his shoulder, and filled her own pail, and they sat a little in the willow shade until the worst of the heat had gone off the walls of the cañon.

"Now," she said, "we will carry it home."

They came down the cañon in the late afternoon with the shadows reaching after them, and out onto the mesa where the long light lay level across the greasewood and every bush had a blue shadow twenty times its own length. The canteen was heavy for him. It was a little more than half a gallon, and he shifted it from shoulder to shoulder, and at last carried it in both arms against his chest like something alive. His mother carried the pail, and walked with her free hand held a little out from her side to balance it, and never let it spill a drop, and he watched her, and after a while he walked the same way.

Halfway across the mesa he stopped, and she stopped with him, thinking he was spent. But he was only looking down at the canteen in his arms.

"Is this all the water?" he said.

"That is all, until your father comes."

He said nothing more, but she saw his face, and she knew that it had gone into him, not as a thing told, but as a thing known; that he had walked the two miles and the two miles back and had felt the weight of it in his arms, and that he would never again see water in that country without feeling the weight of it. It was as much as the land could teach him in one day, and it was enough. It was, she thought, more than she had learned in two years.

It was dusk when they came into the yard, and the first coyote had begun on the ridge. The boy set the canteen down very carefully on the bench by the lean-to door, and stood looking at it. His mother poured the pail into the olla, and then she stood and looked at the two tamarisk slips by the doorstep, drooping a little in the dusk, and she did not water them that night, nor ever again, and in a week they were dead. She did not grieve for them as she had thought she would.

When Burdick came in the next noon with the wagon, he found the near cask empty, and asked how it came so. The boy told him, standing very straight, before his mother could speak. Burdick looked at his wife over the boy's head, and she shook her head a little, and he said nothing at all, which in that country is often the kindest thing and the most just.

It is a saying among the Paiutes that the land does not punish; it only shows. I suppose that is true. The Burdicks stayed on the mesa eleven years, until the borax works shut down and the freighting failed, and in all that time the boy never wasted so much as a dipperful. When he was a grown man, and had a ranch of his own in a better-watered country, it was remarked by his neighbors that he would go down every evening to look at his ditch head as another man might look in at a sleeping child, and that he could not bear to see a gate left open on a running flume. They thought him close. They did not know he had once carried the water for a whole house in his arms across two miles of sand, nor that a woman had walked beside him and let him carry it, and had loved him enough not to help.

The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" "But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

It was not until the lamp had been lighted and the supper things cleared away, in that hour which had come, by twelve years of use, to stand for whatever there was of leisure between them, that Lucy Wheelock found herself able to put to her husband the question which had lain all afternoon at the bottom of her mind like a stone at the bottom of a spring. That it should have waited so long was, she perceived, the measure of her fear of it. She had wished, with a kind of desperate fastidiousness, to have him eat his supper first.
