It was a better offer than we'll ever get again, the way things are going in the valley."

"But you didn't tell me." She had not meant it to come out so; she had meant to begin with the meadow, with the spring under the cottonwoods, with all the reasons that were so clear to her and must, she thought, be clear to anybody who had lived beside them; but it was that, after all, that had worked its way to the top, and having said it she understood that it was the whole of her grievance, and that the meadow was, for the moment, only the ground on which it stood.

"I meant to," he said again. "I wanted it settled first. You'd have——" He stopped, and she finished it for him with a quickness that surprised her.

"I'd have talked you out of it. That is what you thought, isn't it? That if I knew in time I'd have found some way to stop you."

"No, Lucy, I thought you'd have worried. You take things so hard."

It was the old note, the note that had sounded through so many of their differences that she had come to wait for it as one waits, on a long road, for the turn that is known to be coming; that she took things hard, that she was excitable, that she felt more than the occasion warranted. He had used it with tenderness, in the beginning, as one shields a child from a draught; and she had accepted it, as a young wife will, half flattered to be thought so fine a thing as to need shielding. It was only of late that she had begun to perceive the walls it set about her, the way in which, by being spared, she was shut out.

"I am not worried," she said. "I am not in the least worried. I only want to know why, when it is my home as much as yours, and the meadow——" Her voice failed her there, not from tears, for she was dry enough, but from the sheer impossibility of saying in any words that he would accept what the meadow had been to her. She saw it as she sat there, the long sweep of it running down from the foot of the hills, the wild iris coming purple in May along the runnels, the old Paiute woman who had come every year, until she died, to dig the brodiæa bulbs in the hollow by the spring, and who had told her, squatting on her heels in the sun, the names of things in the speech that was older than any deed. She saw the evening she had gone there alone the first summer, homesick and young and shamed to be homesick, and had lain in the grass with her face against the earth and felt the land take her as a mother takes a child, not asking whether it was deserved. It was not a thing one could put to a man across the lamp with the Register folded on his knees. She knew that he had been there a thousand times and had seen, on every one of them, the feed for the stock and the water for the alfalfa.

"I know you're fond of it," he said gently. "I know you like to walk there. But you can walk there just the same, Lucy, for a while anyway. They won't be doing anything with it for a year or two."

"And after the year or two?"

"Well——" He looked at the stove. "They'll take the water out. That's what they want it for. They'll put a ditch down and carry it off to the south."

"And the meadow will dry up."

"I suppose it will, in time."

"And the cottonwoods will die."

"Lucy, there's no use going on like that. Things change. The whole valley's changing. You can't hold back a thing like that by being fond of a few trees."

She put down her mending then, and looked at him fairly for the first time since she had begun, and saw with a pang that he was not hard, that there was nothing in his face but a kind of anxious honesty, a wish, even, to be understood, which made it all the more terrible that he did not understand. If he had been grasping, if there had been in him any of that heat of acquisition which she had seen in Clancy's red neck and small bright eyes, she would have known how to fight it. But what she had against her was only the plain sense of a plain man, who had looked at his account book and his mortgage and the price that was offered, and had done what any man of his kind in the valley would have called the reasonable thing.

"It isn't the trees," she said. "Or it isn't only the trees. It's that you went and did it, and sat at the table with me, and ate what I cooked for you, Monday and Tuesday and to-day, and said nothing. Didn't you think, Henry, didn't it come to you at all, that I'd have wanted to know?"

"I've told you I meant to tell you."

"After."

"Well, after. What difference would it have made, before?" He rose, as if the chair had become too small for the thing he had to say, and stood with one hand on the shelf beside the clock, a big man made awkward by the low room. "I'll tell you plainly, Lucy, since you want it plain. I didn't tell you because I knew how you'd take it. I knew you'd set yourself against it, and I'd have had to choose between going against you and losing the best chance we've had since we came here. I didn't want to have to choose. I thought if it was done, you'd see after a while it was for the best, and we'd neither of us have to go through—this."

He made a small gesture with his free hand that took in the lamp and the mending and herself, and she understood that by "this" he meant the conversation, the having of it at all, the necessity of feeling across the space between them for a meeting place that neither of them had ever been at the pains to mark. It came to her with a curious clearness, as things will in moments of strain, that he had spared himself, quite as much as he had spared her; that the walls he had built about her had been built, in part, to keep out the sound of her.

"So you decided for both of us," she said slowly, "what I would think, and how long it would take me to think it."

"Somebody has to decide things."

"Yes," said Lucy. "Somebody has to." She had not known, until she heard herself say it, how much was in it. It was not that she wished to decide everything, nor even most things; there had been years when she had been glad enough to have him take the burden of the ranch, the buying and selling and the dealings with men in town, and to keep for herself the house and the garden and the little secret commerce with the land that was her own. But she saw now that she had kept it only by sufferance, and that the moment it crossed his reckoning it would be put aside, not cruelly, but as one puts aside a child's toy that has got in the way of the furniture. She felt herself diminished by it, as if some part of the stature she had supposed herself to have had been quietly taken off, an inch at a time, through all the years she had not been looking.

He must have seen something of it in her face, for he came and stood over her, with that slow heaviness of approach which in the early days she had loved for its very clumsiness, and laid his hand upon her shoulder.

"Lucy, you know I wouldn't do anything to hurt you. You know that."

"I know you wouldn't mean to."

"Then what is it? It's only a piece of land."

She sat very still under his hand, feeling the warmth of it come through her dress, and with it the old impulse to yield, to let the thing go under the comfortable surface of their life as so many other things had gone, and be at peace. It would be so easy. He would be kind to her for a week, a little shamefaced, and bring her something from town; and in a month neither of them would speak of it; and in two years the water would go south in Clancy's ditch, and she would walk in the dry grass under the dying cottonwoods and say nothing, because it would have been agreed, without any saying, that there was nothing to be said. She had seen it happen to other women in the valley. She had seen it in Mrs. Saltonstall's eyes, that bright, avid interest in another woman's hurt which is the last refuge of those who have long since given up their own.

"It isn't only a piece of land," she said, and moved a little so that his hand slipped from her. "Not to me. And you knew it wasn't. That's why you didn't tell me."

He took a turn down the room, to the door and back, and she heard the boards complain under him, and the wind try the pane again with a long sighing pressure as of something that had waited a great while.

"I don't know what you want me to say," he said at last. "It's done. The papers are signed. I can't go back on it now, if I wanted to."

"Do you want to?"

He did not answer, and in his silence she had her answer, and found, strangely, that she had expected nothing else, and that it was not the meadow, after all, she had been asking him to give back to her.

"No," she said. "No, I didn't suppose you did."

"There's the mortgage, Lucy. You know how we've been fixed. There's the boy to think of, going to school down below, and the new barn. I've been carrying it all alone, and I've never complained to you——"

"You've never told me," she said. "That's not the same thing."

"I didn't want you troubled."

"I know. You've never wanted me troubled. You've kept everything from me that might trouble me, and that is the thing I can't——" She caught at her breath. "Henry, don't you see? It isn't that I'd have stopped you. Maybe I wouldn't. Maybe if you'd come to me and said, here's the mortgage, here's what it costs to keep Robert at school, here's what Clancy offers, maybe I'd have said yes. I don't know what I'd have said. But I'd have been there. I'd have been in it with you. And you went and left me out, as if I was—as if I was one of the things on the place."

It was out now, the thing she had not known was in her to say, and having said it she felt a great hollowness, as if it had been the very core of her that had gone out with the words, and left her light and empty and a little cold. He stood looking at her in a kind of slow dismay, and she saw the words go into him and not find any place to lodge, as rain falls on hard ground and runs off without soaking in.

"I never thought of you like that," he said. "Lucy, you know I never did."

"No," she said wearily. "You never thought of me at all, in that way. That's what I mean."

She took up her mending again because she could not bear to have her hands empty any longer, and bent her head over it, and the lamp made a little circle of light upon the coarse blue cloth of his work shirt where the elbow had gone through. It came to her with a sense almost of comedy that she would mend it, that whatever happened she would sit here and mend it, and he would wear it to-morrow to the corral, and nothing would be outwardly altered by so much as a thread. And yet she knew, sitting there with the needle going in and out, that something had been altered past mending; that she had seen, for one clear moment, the shape of her life as it stood under the comfortable furniture of habit, and that she could never again quite fail to see it.

He came back, presently, and stood by the stove, rubbing his hands before it though the evening was not cold, and she understood by the very helplessness of the gesture that he was suffering too, after his fashion, and that his suffering was the more bewildering to him because he had no name for it.

"I'll tell you what," he said, with an effort at heartiness that wrung her. "When the money comes through, we'll take a trip. We'll go down to Los Angeles, the two of us, and see Robert, and you can get yourself some things. You've wanted to go for a long time."

She looked up at him then, and something in her face must have stopped him, for he did not go on. She had wanted to go, once; she had spoken of it often in the early years, until she perceived that it was one of the things to be put by. And now it was offered her, out of the price of the meadow, as one offers a sweet to a child that has been hurt; and she saw that he meant it kindly, that he meant it with all his heart, and that he would never understand why she could not take it.

"That's good of you, Henry," she said.

"Then you'll go?"

"I'll think about it."

He seemed to take that, after his fashion, as the end of the matter, the first easing of the strain, the place from which they might begin again to be comfortable; and she let him take it so, because she was too tired to do otherwise, and because she perceived that there was no use, now or ever, in trying to make him see what she saw. He went back to his chair and took up the Register, and this time she heard him turn the page.

She sat a long while after that, until the fire burned down and the wind fell off, as it does toward midnight in that country, and the stillness came up out of the land and filled the room. She thought of the meadow lying out there under the stars, the water going softly through the grass in the dark as it had gone for a thousand years, not knowing that it was sold. She thought of the old Paiute woman, and of what she would have said, and was half ashamed to find that she envied her, who had owned nothing and so could lose nothing, and had gone into the earth at last with the names of things still on her tongue. And she thought of herself as she had been at twenty, lying with her face in the grass, believing that there was a place in the world that would take her as she was; and it came to her, not with bitterness, for she was past that, but with a kind of grave and quiet wonder, that she had never in all those years thought to ask whether the man beside her was such a place, or only a man who had been kind.

When at last he rose and wound the clock and said, as he had said every night for twelve years, "Well, I guess it's bedtime," she folded the shirt and laid it on the table, and put out the lamp, and followed him up the narrow stair in the dark, her hand upon the rail worn smooth by their two hands going up and down; and she knew, as surely as she knew the turn of the stair, that she would go on following him, and mending his shirts, and keeping his house, and that he would never know that anything had happened to her at all.

It had been, he recalled on some one of those occasions of social approval by which it appeared engagements in the Best Society proceeded, that he had sat thus, waiting until the clock ticked on the moment when he might properly join her, sat so full of the sense of her that for the instant he accepted her unannounced appearance at the darkened doorway as the mere extension of his white-heated fancy. The next moment as she charged into the circle of the lamp he saw that the umbra of some strange electrical excitement hung about her. It fairly crackled between them as he rose hurriedly to his feet.

"You have come, Eunice! You have come——" But he saw well enough what she had come for. She laid the case on the table, but as she tugged impatiently at her glove, the fringe of her wrap caught the clasp of it and scattered the jewels on the cloth. She tried then to put the ring beside them, but her hand shook so that it fell and rolled upon the floor behind them. Peter picked it up quietly, but he did not offer it to her hand again.

"I have come," said Eunice, "to say what in my mother's house I was afraid of being interrupted in saying; what you must see, what my mother won't see."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. But she was too thin for their severity—and if he married her he would have insisted on her wearing them now and then as a tender way to prevent her suspecting that it was on their account he had thought of not marrying her. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. He told himself afterward that he would not have done it if he had recalled in time the friendly seaman's romantic appreciation of the situation between himself and Miss Dassonville. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. To see the way he was going and to go on in it, had for him the fascination of the abyss. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. "When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

It was not until the train had drawn out from the last of the little prairie stations, where the elevators stood up against the flat rim of the world like the stopped fingers of a clock, that Lydia Marchbanks began to be aware of how much, in the twelve years of her absence, she had depended on Fenwick remaining exactly as she had left it. She had carried it about with her, through all the shifting camps and the long, white silences of the desert country, as a kind of inner furniture: the square brick house with the iron fence, the catalpa that dropped its long pods on the walk, and her cousin Emmeline at the gate, perpetually nineteen, in the blue lawn with the tucked yoke which Lydia herself had helped to stitch. That Emmeline would have gone on being nineteen, while she had come through a marriage and a widowhood and the loss of the greater part of what Royal had left her, was a thing so foolish when she looked at it squarely that she had not looked at it at all. It came upon her now, as the conductor put his head in at the door to call the town, with something of the shock of finding that one has been talking aloud in an empty room.

She saw Emmeline before the train had well stopped, standing a little apart from the knot of loungers on the platform as if she had been set there by somebody who meant to come back for her presently. She had on a dark stuff gown of no particular period and a hat that Lydia remembered—or thought she remembered—as having belonged to Aunt Phoebe; and she was thinner, or perhaps only straighter, with the Thrale nose come out on her face as the family features have a way of doing when the softer flesh of girlhood has gone down from about them. Lydia had a moment, with her foot on the step, of wishing herself back on the train, of being afraid not so much of Emmeline as of what Emmeline would see in her; and then her cousin had turned and found her and come forward with both hands, and it was all, for the instant, quite simple.

"Lyddy! You've come, then. I was afraid at the last——"

"Afraid I wouldn't? Oh, Em, after you wrote...." She did not finish that, for it was in the nature of Emmeline's letter, the one that had brought her, that it should not be finished. Aunt Phoebe had died in March, and the house, the letter had said, would have to be "seen to," and there were things of her mother's—Lydia's mother's—which had been put away in the attic against the time she should come for them. That was all; but Lydia, reading it at her table in the boarding-house in Los Angeles with the pepper trees rattling outside, had heard under it something which had not been said in twelve years, and had packed her trunk that same night.

They went up from the station in a hired motor whose driver Emmeline addressed as Albert and inquired after the health of his wife's mother, and Lydia, sitting very upright beside her, had leisure to perceive that the town had not stood still for her any more than her cousin had. There were new cement walks laid along Main Street, and the Odd Fellows had put up a building of yellow pressed brick where the livery stable had been; but these were less disturbing to her than the discovery that everything which had remained was smaller. The courthouse square, which had seemed to her as a child as wide as the world, could be crossed, she saw, in thirty steps; the catalpas were only trees. It was as though, in all those years of looking at mountains, she had mislaid some instrument of measure, and she felt herself, absurdly, a little hurt by it, as if Fenwick had shrunk on purpose to put her out of countenance.

"You'll find it changed," said Emmeline, who seemed to have been following her thought.

"Not you, Em. You haven't changed at all."

"Oh, Lyddy, I have." She said it without any coquetry, rather with an air of having considered the matter and come to a sober finding on it, and Lydia felt the speech she had made fall back upon her, cheap and a little vulgar, like a coin rung on a counter and found to be lead. She had acquired, she supposed, in the West, a habit of saying the easy thing; there had been so many people out there whom one met only once.

The house, when they came to it, had at least the grace to be exactly the size she had remembered. It stood back from the street in its square of shabby lawn, with the shutters closed on the parlour side as they had always been closed, and the iron deer on the terrace, from whose antlers she and Emmeline had once hung daisy chains, looking out over the fence with the same stiff, foolish dignity. Lydia had a sudden sense, as she went up the walk, of the house having waited for her; and then, more sharply, of its having waited for someone else, who had not come, so that she was received into it rather as a substitute than as a guest.

It was not until they had had supper—Emmeline would not hear of her helping, but moved about the kitchen in a kind of grave competence, as one who has long been the only hands in a house—and had gone into the sitting-room where the lamp stood on the marble-topped table between their two chairs, that they came, by degrees, to talk. It had been, up to then, all about Aunt Phoebe: how she had gone, quite quietly, between one breath and the next, with her knitting still in her lap; how the minister had been very kind; how the Ladies' Aid had sent in more cake than two women could have eaten in a month. Lydia listened, and asked the right questions, and was all the time aware of something gathering under the surface of their talk as water gathers under ice, which neither of them was ready to put a foot upon.

"And you, Lyddy," said Emmeline at last, folding her hands on her knee in a gesture that was so entirely Aunt Phoebe's that Lydia had to look away from it, "you've had such a life. I used to read your letters ... oh, over and over."

"I didn't write you many."

"You wrote me enough." There was no reproach in it, or none that came to the surface; but Lydia, who had grown in the desert country very quick at hearing what was under the ground, heard the dry trickle of it a long way down. "I used to take them to the Circle, sometimes, when there was a description—of the mountains, I mean, and the Indians, and that time you were caught in the sandstorm at—what was it?—Coso. Mrs. Pettibone said you ought to write for the magazines. They all asked after you. You don't mind, do you, Lyddy? It was all we had in Fenwick, you see. You were our ... well, our romance."

Lydia did mind, for an instant very sharply, as one minds having one's clothes worn by another person, however kindly; and then she did not mind at all, but felt a hot pressure behind her eyes at the picture it gave her, of her letters, written at the end of long, dusty days on whatever came to hand, carried about and read aloud in the stuffy parlours of Fenwick to women who had never seen anything higher than the courthouse dome. It had never occurred to her that she had been, all that time, a figure in anybody's imagination; she had thought of herself, when she thought at all, as someone who had dropped quite out of the world in which she had begun.

"It wasn't so very romantic," she said. "Not most of it. Royal was ... he was a good man, Em, but he wasn't, you know, lucky. We were always just about to strike it. There's a kind of man that's always just about to strike it." She heard her own voice going on, flat and a little hurried, as if it had been wound up and must run down. "And then when he did, at the Little Antelope, it was only enough to pay what we owed, and then he took sick, and that was all of it. Three years ago. I didn't write you about that."

"No," said Emmeline. "You didn't."

"I couldn't, somehow. I kept thinking I would when I had something to put with it ... something to show for it all, I mean. But there wasn't anything. There was only me."

She had not meant to say so much, and having said it, sat looking at the lamp with a kind of surprise at herself, as if she had turned out her pocket and found in it something she had forgotten putting there. It was odd, considering that she had come all this way chiefly, as she had told herself on the train, to see to her mother's things, that she should be so shaken by the mere relief of having said it to somebody who had known her before.

Emmeline did not move or put out a hand; that was not the Thrale way. But she said, after an interval in which the clock on the mantel seemed to Lydia to be counting something off against them both, "I'm glad you've come home, Lyddy," and it was as though she had laid a shawl over her.

It came out a little later—perhaps when Emmeline had gone to the kitchen to see to the fire and come back with two cups of the cambric tea which Aunt Phoebe used to give them as children when they could not sleep—that there was something on her cousin's side, too, which had been waiting. Lydia perceived it first in the very care with which Emmeline set down the cups, as if they had been fuller than they were; and then in the way she began to talk, too lightly, of the people they had known. The Hobarts had gone to Chicago. Nettie Shriver had married a dentist in Galesburg and had four children. Old Judge Dysart had died the winter after Lydia left, and the house on Locust Street had been sold.

"And Walter?" said Lydia. She had not meant to ask it; it slipped out of her with the ease of a thing that has been kept so long at the edge of the mind that it has worn smooth. "What became of Walter Dysart?"

Emmeline drank her tea. "He's in St. Louis," she said, "with a firm of lawyers. He's done very well, they say. He never married."

"Never?"

"No." And then, as if the word had been a door she had opened and found she could not shut again, "He asked me to, Lyddy. The spring after you went."

Lydia sat quite still. She had a sensation, which she could only have described as physical, of the room tilting a little under her, so that the lamp, the marble table, the worn figures in the carpet, slid all a few inches out of the places where she had been keeping them. For it had been on account of Walter Dysart—though she had never said so, even to herself, in so many words—that she had gone West at all. She had been so sure, that last summer, that it was Emmeline he cared for: Emmeline, with her quietness and her good sense and her way of making a room comfortable merely by sitting in it, who was so evidently, by every measure Fenwick knew, the better wife for a judge's son. And Lydia, who had been restless and sharp-tongued and inclined to say things that set the Circle buzzing, had taken her restlessness off to Colorado to visit a school friend, and had met Royal there, and married him in six weeks, in a kind of fierce determination to have her life go somewhere, since it could not go where she had wished.

"And you refused him," she said. It was not a question; she knew it by the set of Emmeline's shoulders, by the very carefulness with which she held her cup.

"There was Mother," said Emmeline. "She'd had her first stroke that winter, you remember. Somebody had to stay. And Walter wanted ... he was going to St. Louis even then. He couldn't have been tied to Fenwick."

"Oh, Em!" Lydia leaned forward. "Oh, Em, and you let him go for that—for Aunt Phoebe? And all these years——"

"It wasn't only Mother." Emmeline put down the cup now, and looked at her across the lamp, and Lydia saw that her face had gone quite white about the mouth, with that pallor which in the Thrales stood for what in other people might have been tears. "I'd have liked you to think it was. I meant you always to think it was. But I'm forty, Lyddy, and you've come home, and I don't know that it matters any more what anybody thinks. He asked me because you'd gone. He'd have asked you, if you'd stayed. He told me so, the night he asked me—not meaning to, I think. He'd been to the Shrivers' that evening, and Nettie had read out one of your letters ... the first one, from Colorado, about the man you'd met who was going into the mines. And he walked home with me afterward and asked me, all of a sudden, at the gate, and I knew. I knew it was because he couldn't stand Fenwick without one of us."

The clock went on counting. Outside, the wind had risen a little and a catalpa pod knocked against the window with a dry, small sound, like someone who had been a long time at a door and had almost given up expecting it to open. Lydia found that she could not speak. She was thinking—it rose up in her with a bitterness which surprised her by being directed not at Emmeline, nor at Walter, nor even at Royal, who had been so kind and so unlucky, but at herself—of all those nights in the desert when she had lain awake under the enormous stars, telling herself the story of her sacrifice; of how she had gone away so that Emmeline might have what she herself could not; of how, at the very least, one of them had been made happy by it. She had leaned her whole weight upon that story; it had been, she saw now, the single beam that held up the roof of those twelve years. And it had never been true at all. There had been nobody made happy by it, not anywhere.

"Why didn't you tell me?" she got out at last.

"How could I? You were married. You wrote me how happy you were—you did write that, Lyddy, the first year. What good would it have done?" Emmeline was silent a moment; then, with a little, dry laugh that had nothing of mirth in it, "Besides, I was so jealous of you. You don't know. Going off like that, and seeing everything, and having a husband and a life ... and me here reading your letters out to the Circle, as if they'd been written to all of us. I used to think you'd taken everything there was, and left me Fenwick. I used to sit in this chair and hate you, Lyddy. Not for long at a time. But I did."

It was the strangest thing in the world to Lydia, who had so often, in the alkali flats or the bare cabins of the mining camps, with the stove smoking and Royal off for a week at a time, thought of this very room, of the lamp and the quiet and the smell of Aunt Phoebe's geraniums on the sill, as the one fixed and gracious place in a world that would not stand still under her—it was the strangest thing to learn that she had been envied in it. She felt, for the moment, as one does who after a long journey turns to look back at the road and finds it running in quite another direction from the one he had supposed.

"I used to think of you here," she said slowly. "Oh, Em, I used to think of you here as if you'd had the only real thing. A house, and your mother, and people who knew you ... and Walter, I thought. I thought you had Walter. I used to be so glad and so miserable about it, both at once, that I couldn't sleep."

They looked at each other across the lamp, and it seemed to Lydia that it was the first time in twelve years, perhaps in all their lives, that they had looked at each other at all; that before, there had always been between them some figure, some third person whom each had dressed up out of her own longing and set in the other's place. It was not a comfortable look. There was in it too much of what each had missed, and of how much of the missing had been their own doing. But it was, she thought, honest; and she was surprised to find how much, after all those years of being merely kind to people, she had been hungry for that.

Emmeline got up presently and stood a moment with her hand on the back of her chair, as if she were not quite sure of her footing.

"There's the trunk," she said, "of your mother's. In the attic. I don't suppose you want to see it to-night."

"Yes," said Lydia, rising also. "I think I do."

They went up together, Emmeline carrying the lamp, by the narrow back stairs that smelled of cedar and old rain, and the shadows went before them up the slanting walls in a kind of procession, as if all the people who had ever lived in the house were going up too, to see what would be found. The trunk stood under the eaves, with a quilt thrown over it, and when Emmeline had set the lamp on a box and turned back the lid, the first thing that lay on top, folded with careful creases gone yellow at the edges, was a blue lawn dress with a tucked yoke.

"Why—it's yours," said Lydia. "It's the one we made, Em, the summer before—— What's it doing in Mother's trunk?"

"I put it there." Emmeline knelt down and touched it, not lifting it out. "After you'd gone. I couldn't wear it, somehow. And I couldn't give it away. I thought ... I don't know what I thought. That you'd come back, maybe, and we'd laugh about it."

Lydia knelt too, on the dusty boards, and it was not the dress she looked at but her cousin's hand lying on it—a thin hand, roughened at the knuckles, with the nails cut short, the hand of a woman who for twelve years had done everything in a house that a house requires—and she saw, with a kind of grave astonishment, that Emmeline too had had a life: that it had been lived, every day of it, here, under this roof, with as much of pain and of patience in it as any of the days she herself had lived under the open sky; and that it was not less a life because nobody had read it aloud to the Circle.

She put her own hand over her cousin's, as she had not done since they were children, and they stayed so, neither of them saying anything, while the wind went round the eaves and the lamp drew its small, steady circle about them in the dark.

"We'll laugh about it, Em," she said at last. "Not to-night. But we will."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! "Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. "I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. He decided that she made them very well. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. "When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

The occasion of it, when Adam Fairlie came afterward to turn it over, appeared to him so incommensurate with the figure he had been made to cut, that he could account for it only as one of those small explosions by which a household, too long kept at the pitch of decorum, finds relief. It was the clock that had done it, the little French clock with the gilt shepherdess, which had stood on his mother's mantel in Hartford and on his own ever since, and which, as he came in from the office a little after five with the light going thin and saffron behind the pepper trees, he discovered lying face downward on the hearth with its glass in a spray of splinters about it and the shepherdess, who had leaned for forty years upon her crook in an attitude of perpetual and gilded expectancy, snapped clean off at the ankles. He stood looking at it for an appreciable interval with his gloves in his hand. He was not a man to whom things mattered greatly; he had trained himself in that, as a kind of armour against the disappointments which he had learned early to expect of them. He came, by the sound, with that dragging, sidelong progress by which children manage to protract to the last possible moment the interval between the summons and the reckoning, stopping on the stairs to examine something, stopping again in the hall, so that when at last he stood in the doorway with one hand trailing along the jamb, Adam had had time to compose and abandon three several openings. He was a slight, fair child of six, with his mother's way of holding his head a little on one side, and a mouth that, in the moment of his appearance, was set in a line of such small and obstinate defence that Adam was reminded, absurdly, of the shepherdess clinging to her rock.

"Come here, Robin."

Robin came, not directly, but by a detour of the furniture, touching the back of the sofa and the corner of the bookcase as he passed, as if he would assure himself in the face of whatever was impending of the continued solidity of things. He brought up at last at the farther side of the table where the clock lay, and fixed upon it a look in which there was no guilt whatever, but only a grave and absorbed interest, as one might look at an accident in the street.

"Do you know what this is?"

"It's the clock," said Robin. And then, after a considering pause, "It's broke."

"It is broken. And Aunt Martha tells me that you broke it."

"I didn't." It came out on the instant, flat and final, with no colour of evasion in it, and with his eyes still on the shepherdess. "I didn't break it. It was him."

"Robin," said his father, and was dismayed to hear his voice take on, in spite of him, the very tone of Mrs. Bassett, "you know there is no one. You know quite well that there is no one but yourself."

The child lifted his eyes then, and Adam saw in them, so plainly that it struck him like a blow, the thing which he had seen in Ellen's when he had come upon the two of them laughing together: the look of being shut out by a dullness that could not be helped. Only in the child it was not laughing. It was, if anything, a kind of patient pity.

"There is," said Robin. "He was up on the mantel. He wanted to see if the lady could walk. He said she'd been standing there so long she must be tired."

It was so precisely the thought which had passed through Adam's own mind as he stooped over the hearth, that the long-standing shepherdess must have been weary of her post, that he was for a moment quite put out of his course by it. He took refuge, as he was apt to do when his feelings outran him, in a deliberate formality.

"Sit down, Robin. No, here, where I can see you." He drew up the little footstool which had been Ellen's, and the child sat upon it with his knees drawn up and his arms about them, so that his face came barely above the level of the table. "I want you to listen to me carefully, because this is a very serious matter. It is not the clock. The clock can be mended, perhaps, or if it can't, why——" he paused, aware that it could not, and that the loss of it was not, after all, so small to him, "why, we shall have to do without it. But when you tell me that some one else did a thing that you did yourself, you are telling me what is not true. And that is a great deal worse than breaking a clock. Do you understand that?"

"Yes," said Robin. He said it so readily that Adam perceived he had understood nothing, or rather, had understood something altogether different, which had nothing to do with the matter in hand; that he was being agreed with merely as children agree with the weather.

"What is it you understand?"

"That you think I did it."

"I know you did it."

"No," said Robin, with that terrible gentleness, "you only think you know."

Adam got up and walked to the window. The pepper trees had gone black against a sky the colour of the inside of a shell, and in the lower town the lights were coming out one by one, like a slow counting. He stood there with his hands behind him, conscious of the small figure on the footstool at his back, and of an extraordinary sense of being himself, rather than the child, on trial. It came to him, as such things will at the moment when they are least serviceable, that he had once, at about Robin's age, been shut into a closet for a whole afternoon for telling his mother that the Indians had taken the preserves. There had been no Indians in Hartford for a hundred years; he had known that, of course, as Robin no doubt knew that there was no one on the mantel. But he had known also, with a knowledge that went deeper than the closet and outlasted it, that the preserves had gone in the course of an expedition in which the Indians had been as indisputably present to him as the shelves and the stone crock, and that nothing which his mother could have said to him would have persuaded him otherwise. He had come out of the closet at supper time with his conviction unshaken and a new and bitter understanding that it was not a thing to be spoken of to grown people. He had never spoken of anything of the kind again. He had grown up, he supposed, in that very silence; it was perhaps the beginning of the walled and solitary habit by which he had kept his life about him ever since, and which Ellen, in the first year of their marriage, had beaten upon with such a bright impatience, and then, as he had seen too late, given over.

He turned round. Robin had not moved, except to put out one finger and lay it, very lightly, upon the broken feet of the shepherdess, where they still clung to the gilded rock.

"Don't touch the glass," said Adam sharply. "You'll cut yourself."

The finger withdrew. But the action had told him something, he could not have said precisely what: that the child was sorry, perhaps, for the shepherdess, as he himself was sorry, and that there was between them, across the ruin of the clock, a community of feeling which the matter of who had broken it had somehow shouldered out of the way. He came back and sat down again, nearer this time, so that he could have put out his hand and touched the fair head, had he been a man who did such things readily.

"Robin," he began again, and this time he found that he was feeling his way, "suppose—just suppose, you know—that there was some one. Some one that you could see and I couldn't. Do you think he would want you to be punished for what he did?"

The child considered this with his chin upon his knees. It was evident that it had not occurred to him before, and that it presented itself now as a genuine difficulty.

"He doesn't care," he said at last. "He doesn't ever get punished. Nobody can see him to do it."

"Then isn't it rather hard on you?"

"Yes," said Robin, and his voice for the first time wavered. "But he didn't mean to. He only wanted to see if she could walk."

"And so did you, I think."

There was a long silence. Adam could hear the clock in the hall, the tall one, ticking away with its heavy, indifferent beat, and from somewhere overhead the faint creak of Mrs. Bassett's rocker, which went always faster when she was listening. He was aware that he was holding his breath, and that it was absurd of him to be holding it, as if more hung upon what the child would say next than upon any word that had been said to him in a long time.

"I only touched her," Robin said, very low. "I only touched her a little, to see. And then she fell."

It was out, and Adam, who had been bracing himself for it as the end and object of the whole proceeding, found that he took no satisfaction in it whatever. He saw that the child was crying, not noisily, but with the slow, abundant tears of a grief that had been a long while gathering, and that it was not for the clock, nor even for having been found out, but for something which had gone down along with the shepherdess and which neither of them could have named. He saw too, with a perception that went through him like the cold of the evening, that what he had got out of Robin was not the truth, or not the whole of it; that the Other One had been as present on the mantel as the child himself, and that in bringing him to confess the touch, he had obliged him to deny the companion. He had won; and he had won exactly as his mother had won, by shutting the door upon something.

"Robin," he said, and found that his own voice was not altogether steady, "come here."

The child got up from the footstool and came, as he had come into the room, a little sidelong, as if he were not sure of what was to be done to him. Adam took him upon his knee. He had not done it, he realized, since the baby days, when Ellen had used to put him there and stand back laughing to see the two of them together; and he was surprised at the slightness of the body, at the way the bones of the shoulder came through the blouse, and at the dampness of the face which, after a moment's stiffness, was turned against his coat.

"I'm not going to punish you," he said. "Not this time. You see, I think you have been punished enough." He was aware that this was a departure from every principle he had laid down for himself, and that Mrs. Bassett, overhead, would have her own opinion of it, and he did not care. "But I want you to promise me something. When things happen—when you touch things and they fall—I want you to come and tell me. Even if the Other One was there too. You can tell me that he was there. Only tell me about yourself first."

He felt the child stir against him with what seemed a kind of incredulous relief.

"Can I tell you about him?"

"If you like."

"Mother lets me," said Robin. "Only she's sick now." And then, as if he had been turning it over: "He's sorry about the lady too. He told me."

"Is he?" said Adam gravely. "Then we're all three sorry together." And he was astonished at the sudden lightness that came into the room with the admission, as if it had been the opening of a window.

They sat so for some time, while the fire burned down and the last of the colour went out of the sky behind the pepper trees. Presently Robin, with his head still against his father's coat, put out his hand toward the table and drew the shepherdess, very carefully, away from the heap of glass.

"Could we glue her?" he asked.

"We might try. Not to-night, though. To-night you must go up to supper."

"Will you show me how?"

"Yes," said Adam, "I'll show you how." He had no idea how. But it seemed to him, as he set the child down and watched him go out through the door with his hand once more trailing along the jamb, that he would find out; that there were a great many things, in fact, which it was not too late to find out. He gathered up the fragments of the clock and laid them in the drawer of the table, the shepherdess on top, and stood a moment with his hand on the drawer, looking at the empty place on the mantel.

It was odd, considering how little he had ever let himself be moved by the loss of things, that he should feel the gap so keenly; and odder still that the feeling should have in it, along with the pang, something which was very like the beginning of a hope. He found himself, before he went up, pausing at Ellen's door, and then, upon a sudden impulse which he did not stop to examine, knocking upon it softly.

"Ellen," he said, when her voice came to him faintly from within, "I've been talking with Robin. About the Other One." He hesitated, and then went on, to his own surprise, with a little catch of laughter. "It seems he wanted to see if the shepherdess could walk."

There was a pause, and then he heard her laugh too, low and tired but with the old ring in it, the ring which he had heard so often from outside, and which now, for the first time, seemed to admit him.

"Come in, Adam," she said. "Come in and tell me."
