The Treadwell house stood upon that part of Sycamore Street which had once been thought the very summit of the town's ambition and was now thought, by those who had moved farther north, to be "still perfectly respectable." This phrase, when it is applied to a street, is like a kindly word spoken over an elderly relative who has begun to repeat himself at table; it is meant generously, and it is the beginning of the end. The house itself was of brick painted the colour of a robin's breast in a poor light. It had a cupola, which nobody ever entered, and a cast-iron deer upon the lawn, which nobody ever looked at. Mr. Treadwell had several times proposed removing the deer, and Mrs. Treadwell had several times replied that it had been her father's, and so the deer remained, gazing northward over the hedge with an expression of mild reproach, as if it, too, had noticed where the better families were going.

Upon a certain evening in October, at about the hour when the street lamps came on and the smoke from the new factories beyond the river settled down upon Sycamore Street like a damp grey shawl, Mr. Royce Treadwell let himself in at his front door with a care that would have been instructive to any observer acquainted with husbands. He closed the door softly; he hung his hat upon the rack without permitting it to knock against the mirror; and he stood for a moment in the hall, breathing as quietly as a man of fifty-three and somewhat more than a hundred and ninety pounds is able to breathe, and listening.

He heard nothing. That is to say, he heard the clock upon the landing, which had a cough in its works and seemed always to be clearing its throat before it struck; he heard the cook in the kitchen saying something bitter to the furnace; and he heard, faintly from upstairs, the sound of his daughter Lucy singing a song about the moon while she dressed for the Assembly dance. But he did not hear his wife, and this silence he found more ominous than any sound could have been.

"Ellen?" he said, not loudly.

"I'm in the library, Royce."

The voice was perfectly pleasant. It was, if anything, a little more pleasant than usual, and Mr. Treadwell, who had been married twenty-six years, received it as a sea captain receives a sudden fall of the barometer. He passed one hand over the top of his head, where the hair had long since gone the way of the better families, and went into the library.

Mrs. Treadwell was seated beside the lamp with her sewing. She was a small woman, still pretty in the manner of women who have been pretty all their lives and have never quite been told to stop, and she wore a grey silk that she had made over twice and that looked, as she intended it to look, as though it had never been made over at all. She did not glance up when he entered. She drew her needle through the cloth, examined the stitch, and said, "You're late."

"Was I? I stopped at the club a minute."

"Yes," said Mrs. Treadwell. "I supposed you might have."

He lowered himself into the leather chair across from her, the chair that had taken the shape of him over a quarter of a century so faithfully that it seemed sometimes to be a second and more comfortable Mr. Treadwell, and he took up the evening paper. He did not read it. He held it before him in the manner of a man who has been taught, by long experience, that a newspaper is not a wall but may serve for a little while as a hedge.

"Mrs. Corliss called this afternoon," said his wife.

The newspaper made a slight sound, as if a breeze had passed through it, although the windows were closed.

"Did she?" said Mr. Treadwell. "Well, that's nice. How is Mrs. Corliss?"

"She's very well. She is always very well. She said Mr. Corliss had been at the bank yesterday."

"Corliss is at the bank a good deal. He's a director."

"Yes," said Mrs. Treadwell. "That's what she said."

There followed a silence, during which the clock on the landing cleared its throat, thought better of it, and went on ticking. Mr. Treadwell turned a page, though he had not read the page before it, and Mrs. Treadwell bit off a thread with a small, decisive motion of her pretty teeth.

Now it is one of the curious properties of a married couple that they can conduct an entire quarrel without either party having yet said what the quarrel is about. They are like two duellists who have measured off the ground, examined the pistols, and taken their places, all in the most courteous silence, and who stand now waiting only for someone to drop the handkerchief. The Treadwells had arrived at precisely this stage, and both of them knew it; and Mr. Treadwell, who had a sound instinct in such matters if not a very bold one, understood that whoever spoke first would be at a disadvantage, and he resolved to read the paper until midnight if necessary.

He was spared this ordeal. "Royce," said his wife, laying her sewing in her lap, "did you lend Henry Mapes four thousand dollars?"

Mr. Treadwell lowered the paper. He looked at his wife over the top of it, and then he looked at the fire, and then at the cast-iron andirons, which were also her father's, and finally at the ceiling, where a crack in the plaster had for several years been slowly tracing out what Lucy insisted was the coastline of Norway.

"Well," he said, "in a manner of speaking."

"In what manner of speaking?"

"Why, it wasn't exactly a loan, Ellen. It was more in the nature of an—an accommodation. Henry's going to pay it back. He's got that contract with the railroad people coming in next spring, and the minute it comes in—"

"Henry Mapes," said Mrs. Treadwell, "has had a contract with the railroad people coming in next spring every spring since eighteen ninety-one."

"That isn't quite fair. He's had bad luck."

"He has had the same bad luck for twenty years. One would think he would have grown tired of it by now. I should have. Royce, is it true?"

"I told you it was, in a manner—"

"Was it Lucy's money?"

He did not answer at once, and his silence answered for him. Mrs. Treadwell sat very still, with her hands folded upon the grey silk, and two small spots of colour came up into her cheeks and stayed there, like the lights of a house seen from a distance at night.

The money in question had a history, and the history is necessary. For six years Mr. and Mrs. Treadwell had been putting aside, out of an income that was not large and that had lately begun to feel smaller every year, for no reason either of them could name except that everything else in town had grown larger, a sum against the day when Lucy should be twenty. It was understood that she was then to go abroad for a year with her Aunt Amelia, who knew the right pensions in Florence, and see the pictures, and learn to say things about them. Mrs. Treadwell had never been abroad. Neither, for that matter, had Mr. Treadwell, who did not wish to go and who privately suspected that the pictures were very much like the pictures at the Art Association, only older. But Mrs. Treadwell had wanted Lucy to go with a wanting that was not altogether on Lucy's account. It is the habit of mothers to send their daughters into the countries they themselves were prevented from visiting, and to receive, in the letters that come home, a kind of delayed and borrowed travelling, as a person who cannot afford a garden will sometimes take a deep satisfaction in a neighbour's roses.

"I meant to tell you," said Mr. Treadwell.

"When?"

"Why, I meant to tell you right along. I was just waiting for a good time."

"And when," inquired Mrs. Treadwell with dangerous gentleness, "did you suppose a good time would come? Did you imagine that some evening I should be sitting here, and you would say, 'Ellen, I have given away our daughter's year in Italy to Henry Mapes,' and I should look up and say, 'How very nice, dear; did you remember to wind the clock?'"

"Now, Ellen."

"Don't say 'Now, Ellen' to me, Royce. You always say 'Now, Ellen' when you know perfectly well you're in the wrong. You said it when you bought the mare that went lame, and you said it when you let the Fosdicks have the corner lot for a song, and you said it the day you told Mr. Brainard that his new house looked like a railroad station, at his own dinner table."

"Well, it did look like a railroad station."

"That," said Mrs. Treadwell, "is not the point."

Mr. Treadwell folded the newspaper and laid it on the floor beside his chair, a gesture of surrender, or perhaps only of a man who perceives that the hedge has been trampled flat. He leaned forward, his hands upon his knees.

"See here, Ellen," he said. "You don't know how it was. Henry came into the office Tuesday afternoon. I hadn't seen him for a month. He looked—well, he looked bad. You know how Henry always used to be, always laughing, always with some new idea or other. He wasn't laughing Tuesday. He sat down in that chair by my desk, and he didn't say anything for a minute, and then he said, 'Royce, they're going to take the shop.' Just like that. He'd borrowed on it, you see, to carry over till the contract—"

"Till the contract comes in next spring."

"Yes, well—it might, you know. It might, this time. Anyway, they were going to foreclose on the first, and he had nothing else. Nothing. And there's Clara, and the two boys still in school, and that house of theirs out on Walnut Street isn't paid for either. I couldn't sit there and let him go under, Ellen. Henry and I were boys together. He pulled me out of the river at the old mill dam when I was eleven years old; you've heard me tell it."

"I have heard you tell it," said Mrs. Treadwell, "a great many times."

"Well, it happened every time," said her husband, with a flicker of spirit. "It isn't any less true for being told."

She did not smile; but something in the set of her mouth altered a very little, as the surface of a pond alters when a breath of wind goes over it and is gone. She took up her sewing again, looked at it as though she had never seen it before, and put it down.

"You might have asked me," she said.

"I know it."

"You might have come home and asked me. I am your wife, Royce. It was my money as much as yours. I put by out of the housekeeping, every month, for six years. I made over this dress so that I could put by. I didn't have a new hat last spring; did you notice that? No, you didn't notice it. Men never do. I wore the old blue one with the feather turned, and Mrs. Corliss said, 'How clever of you, Ellen, to make that feather go the other way; one would hardly know it,' which meant, of course, that she knew it perfectly well, and wanted me to know she knew it. I didn't mind. I said to myself, 'It is for Lucy; it is for Florence and the pictures,' and I didn't mind anything. And now Mrs. Corliss knows that you have given it to Henry Mapes before I know it myself. She sat in that chair, Royce—in your chair—and told me, and I had to say, 'Oh, yes, Royce mentioned something of the sort,' and smile at her, and give her more tea. I gave her three cups. I didn't know what else to do."

Mr. Treadwell had nothing to say to this. He had a vague sense, as men frequently have in these conversations, that he was being charged not only with the offence he had committed but with several others he had not, and that these others—the hat, the feather, the three cups of tea—were in some obscure way the worst of the lot. Yet he could not deny any of them. A husband standing before his wife's reproaches is in the position of a man caught in the rain without an umbrella; he may argue that he did not cause the rain, but he is wet all the same.

"I ought to have asked you," he said humbly. "I knew you'd say no."

"How did you know I'd say no?"

He looked at her in genuine surprise. "Well—wouldn't you?"

Mrs. Treadwell opened her lips to reply and then closed them again. She looked away from him into the fire, where a log had burned through in the middle and lay in two glowing pieces, each leaning a little toward the other.

"I don't know," she said at last. "I suppose I should have. I suppose I should have said that Henry Mapes has always been a fool about money and always will be, and that Clara Mapes has had her drawing-room re-papered twice in four years, and that it was none of our affair. I suppose I should have said all that."

"That's what I thought you'd say."

"And then," said Mrs. Treadwell, "I suppose you'd have gone and done it anyway."

Mr. Treadwell considered this honestly. "I expect I would," he admitted.

"Then you might just as well have asked me."

To this piece of logic, which is peculiar to wives and which no husband in recorded history has ever been able to refute, Mr. Treadwell made no answer. He sat looking at his large hands, and his wife sat looking at the fire, and for a little while neither of them said anything at all. Upstairs, Lucy had stopped singing about the moon and begun singing about a girl named Rosie who lived somewhere down a lane, and the cheerful, careless sound of it came down to them through the ceiling, by way of the coastline of Norway.

"What are we going to tell her?" said Mrs. Treadwell.

"I've been thinking about that."

"Have you? I hope you've been thinking hard. She's talked of nothing else since summer. She has a list of the churches in Florence. She has a book about them with a green cover. She reads it in bed; I've seen the light under her door at midnight."

"I could make some of it up," said Mr. Treadwell. "I've been figuring. If I don't take that new office downtown—Halloway says the old one's good enough, after all, it's only that everybody else is moving to the Fletcher Building—and if we let the cupola go one more year without the new roof—"

"The cupola leaks, Royce."

"Well, nobody goes up there."

"The water comes down, though. It comes down into the linen closet."

"Then we'll move the linen," said Mr. Treadwell with an air of having solved a problem that had baffled engineers. "And there's the deer."

"What about the deer?"

He hesitated. "Fellow named Schermerhorn, out on the new boulevard, has been after me twice to sell it to him. He's building one of those big stone places, and he says it would give the grounds a—what did he call it?—an 'old established look.' He offered me a hundred and fifty dollars."

Mrs. Treadwell turned from the fire and looked at her husband for a long moment, and there came into her face an expression that he could not altogether read and that he had not seen there, perhaps, for a good many years.

"You'd sell my father's deer," she said slowly, "to a man named Schermerhorn, so that his house would look as though he had always lived in it?"

"I'd hate to. I'd hate to on your account, Ellen. But it's a hundred and fifty dollars."

There was another pause. And then a curious thing happened—curious, at least, to Mr. Treadwell, who never understood afterward how it came about, although his wife understood it perfectly and did not choose to explain. Mrs. Treadwell put her handkerchief to her mouth, and her shoulders moved, and for an alarmed instant her husband thought that she was crying. But she was not crying; or if she was, it was the sort of crying that has laughter mixed into it so thoroughly that no chemist could separate the two.

"Oh, Royce," she said. "Oh, Royce, you are the most absurd man. You'd sell the deer. You'd let the cupola rain into the linen. You'd sit in that dreadful old office with the gas brackets till you were ninety, and everybody laughing at you from the Fletcher Building, and all on account of Henry Mapes, who pulled you out of a mill pond forty years ago and has been pulling you into one ever since."

"It wasn't a pond. It was a dam."

"It doesn't matter what it was!" She wiped her eyes. "Do you know what Mrs. Corliss said? Before she went? She stood up and drew on her gloves, and she said, 'Of course, Ellen, Edward would never dream of doing such a thing. Edward is so sensible.' And I thought, sitting there with the teapot, I thought—Edward Corliss is so sensible that if his own brother were drowning, he'd send him a pamphlet on the art of swimming, and charge him interest on the postage. And I was angry with you, Royce, I was angrier than I've been since we were married, but I was angrier with her for being right, and angriest of all because I knew that I'd sooner have you than Edward Corliss if you gave away every penny we had."

Mr. Treadwell did not entirely follow this, but he understood the last part of it, and the last part was what mattered. He got up out of his chair, an operation that required some little effort and was accompanied by an expiring sigh from the leather, and he crossed the hearth rug and stood beside her, rather awkwardly, with one large hand upon the back of her chair.

"We won't sell the deer," he said.

"No, we won't. We'll sell my mother's garnets. I never wear them; they make me look like a funeral at Christmastime." She folded her handkerchief into a small, neat square, which was the way she folded everything, including, upon occasion, her husband. "And you will take the new office, Royce, because I won't have the Corliss people laughing at you. And the cupola will be roofed, because I won't have the linen ruined. And Lucy will go to Florence a year late, and she will be twenty-one instead of twenty, and she will be just as pretty, and the churches will still be there. I don't believe they're going anywhere."

"Then where's the money coming from for all of that?"

"From Henry Mapes," said Mrs. Treadwell, "next spring, when the contract comes in."

He stared at her. She met his gaze with perfect gravity for as long as she could manage it, which was about three seconds, and then they both laughed together, as they had not laughed together in a long time; and the sound of it went up through the ceiling, by way of Norway, and caused Lucy, in her room above, to stop singing about Rosie and say to her looking-glass, "Well! What on earth's got into them?"

She came down presently in her new pink dress, which her mother had made from a pattern in a magazine and which looked, as it was intended to look, as though it had come from somewhere a great deal farther off than the sewing-room; and she found her parents sitting on opposite sides of the lamp, her father reading the paper and her mother sewing, exactly as they had sat on every evening of her life. Nothing was in any way changed, except that her father was holding the paper upside down and appeared not to have noticed it, and that her mother looked up at her with eyes that were unusually bright.

"You look lovely, dear," said Mrs. Treadwell. "Doesn't she look lovely, Royce?"

"Like a picture," said Mr. Treadwell, and then, after a moment, added with peculiar emphasis, "Like one of those Italian pictures."

Lucy glanced from one of them to the other, decided that the ways of the old were past finding out, and went to the window to watch for the young man who was to take her to the Assembly. Outside, the smoke lay low over Sycamore Street, and the lamps made blurred gold rings in it, and the cast-iron deer stood upon the lawn with its head lifted, gazing northward as it always had toward the new boulevard and the great stone houses and the better families. But whether it was reproaching them, or only wondering what they had that Sycamore Street had not, nobody could have said; and nobody, that evening, thought to ask.

response:
Mr. Amos Croyle, of the firm of Croyle & Haverstick, Wholesale Hardware, Cutlery and Builders' Supplies, received the telegram at eleven o'clock on a Tuesday morning. He read it twice, laid it face downward upon his desk as though it might be indelicate to leave it staring at the ceiling, and then took it up and read it a third time. It said:

ARRIVE THURSDAY FOUR-TEN WILL KNOW YOU ANYWHERE HATTIE

Mr. Croyle was fifty-two years old, and he had not been called "anywhere" by anybody in a great while. He sat back in his swivel-chair, which complained, and looked out of the window at the soot that came drifting down over the roofs of the wholesale district like a slow, perpetual black snow. It is a curious property of the human mind that a single word upon a yellow slip of paper may unseat thirty-five years as easily as a boy upsets a sled. For the word "Hattie" did not bring before Mr. Croyle the image of any woman at all. It brought before him a little girl in a pinafore that had once been white, with a great many freckles and two braids that stuck out behind her ears like the handles of a sugar-bowl. This little girl was standing upon the curb of his grandmother's cistern, in the side yard of the old house on Delamater Street, and she was saying, with the serene assurance of a bishop, "Amos Croyle, if you don't give me that jackknife I'll push you in."

And she had. That was the strange thing about it; at fifty-two Mr. Croyle could still feel the cold of that water upon the back of his neck, and the outrage of it, and the iron taste of the bucket-chain he had clutched. He had never got the jackknife back, either. Hattie had gone away to California with her father two summers afterward, when she was seventeen and he was eighteen, and had taken the jackknife with her, so far as anybody knew. There had been letters at first, and then Christmas cards, and then, for a long time, nothing but the occasional report of a relative at a funeral: Hattie had married; Hattie had a boy; Hattie's husband was "in oranges," a phrase which had always suggested to Mr. Croyle a man standing up to his waist in fruit.

He put the telegram in his pocket and went home to lunch, which was a habit he had kept up against the advice of his partner, his physician, and the general tendency of the age.

"Ella," he said to his wife, "Hattie's coming."

Mrs. Croyle was a comfortable lady with a manner of mild and permanent forbearance, as of one who has long lived next door to a brass band. "Hattie who?"

"Why, Hattie! My cousin Hattie. Hattie Pettibone. Hattie Pettibone that was."

"Oh," said Mrs. Croyle. "The one that pushed you in the cistern."

Mr. Croyle was a little annoyed. He had told this story perhaps more often than was strictly necessary during twenty-six years of married life, but it seemed to him that his wife need not have seized upon it so promptly as the single distinguishing mark of a human being. "She was a very remarkable girl," he said, with dignity. "Very high-spirited. Everybody said so."

"I'm sure she was," said Mrs. Croyle. "Where shall I put her? In the blue room or in Marjorie's room?"

"Put her in the blue room," Mr. Croyle said. "Put her in the best room we've got." And then, after a moment, with an odd shyness, "Ella, I wonder what she looks like."

---

He wondered about it a good deal during the next two days. He wondered about it in the bathroom on Thursday morning, where he stood longer than usual before the mirror, inspecting the top of his head with a hand-glass held at an angle. The inspection was not encouraging. What hair Mr. Croyle retained had withdrawn to the sides and back of his skull, in the manner of a garrison that has abandoned the citadel but still holds the outer walls; and he was conscious, too, of a certain amplitude about the middle of his waistcoat that had not been there when he was eighteen. "Will know you anywhere," he muttered. "Well, she won't."

He was at the Union Station by a quarter to four, which was twenty-five minutes too early, and he spent the interval walking up and down the platform with his hands behind him, like a man who has a great deal on his mind and is not going to tell anybody what it is. The station was new since Hattie's day; so was nearly everything else. When she had gone away the town had been a place of maple trees and picket fences, of cows pastured on vacant lots within six blocks of the courthouse, and of a public square where farmers hitched their teams on Saturday afternoons and their wives went into Gossett's Dry Goods to finger calico. Now the maples were mostly gone, and the picket fences altogether, and the public square was a place where a policeman in white gloves stood upon a little platform and blew a whistle at motor-cars. There were tall buildings, and the smoke from them, and a great roar of traffic that never quite stopped, even at night; and the people who lived in the city were very proud of all this and called it Progress, and Mr. Croyle was proud of it too, as a rule. It was only on the platform that afternoon, waiting for a train out of the West, that it occurred to him to wonder whether Hattie would be proud of it.

The train came in at four-sixteen. Mr. Croyle stationed himself near the steps of the Pullman and peered with a kind of anxious ferocity into the face of every woman who descended. He was looking, though he would not have admitted it, for a slender person with braids; and so it happened that his gaze passed over and beyond a large lady in a plum-colored traveling suit and a hat with a great deal of ostrich upon it, who stood upon the lowest step with a lorgnette raised to her eyes, surveying the platform as a general surveys an indifferent battlefield.

The lorgnette came to rest upon Mr. Croyle.

"Amos Croyle!" said the large lady, in a voice that caused two porters to turn round. "You haven't changed one particle!"

Mr. Croyle was so taken aback that he removed his hat, thereby exhibiting precisely that region of himself which had changed most; and the large lady, descending from the step, embraced him with a heartiness that bent his collar.

"Hattie?" he said, when he could. "Is it—why, Hattie!"

"Well, who'd you think it was? The Queen of Sheba?" She held him off at arm's length and looked him up and down. "I'd have known you in the dark. You still stick your chin out when you don't know what to say. You always did. You did it the day I pushed you in the cistern."

"You remember that?"

"Remember it! I've told it at every dinner party in Pasadena for thirty years. It's my best story."

Mr. Croyle experienced a sensation both gratifying and obscurely injured, as of a man who learns that his property has been doing a profitable business under another's name. He took her bags from the porter, who seemed to think he was being robbed, and conducted her through the station to where his automobile waited at the curb, and all the way she talked, and all the way he listened, and every now and then he looked sidelong at her and tried to find the little girl somewhere inside the plum-colored traveling suit. He could not find her at all for a long while. Then, as he was handing her into the car, she wrinkled her nose at the smoke and said, "My land, Amos, what have you all been doing to the sky?" And the nose wrinkled exactly as it used to when Grandmother Croyle made them eat boiled greens; and he found her.

---

"I want to go past the house," she said, before they had gone a block. "Grandma's house. On Delamater Street. Drive past it slow, Amos, I want to look at it."

Mr. Croyle cleared his throat. "Well, now, Hattie—"

"Is it torn down?"

"Not exactly torn down."

"Then drive past it."

He drove past it. That is to say, he drove past the place where it had been; for where Grandmother Croyle's tall, narrow brick house had stood, with its iron deer upon the lawn and its cupola that nobody was ever permitted to enter, there was now a gasoline filling station, painted green and orange and decorated with a large sign bearing the likeness of a smiling tiger. A young man in overalls was squirting water upon the windshield of a delivery truck.

Mrs. Bellows—for Hattie was Mrs. Bellows now, and had been for twenty-nine years—looked at it for some moments through her lorgnette.

"Well," she said finally, "I always did think that cupola was silly."

"They took the house down in nineteen-twelve," Mr. Croyle said apologetically, as though it were his fault. "After Aunt Libby died. There wasn't anybody to live in it. And the street went to business, Hattie; all the streets around here went to business."

"Where's the cistern?"

"Why, I suppose it's under there somewhere. Under the tiger."

Mrs. Bellows lowered the lorgnette. "Amos," she said, "I don't know whether to laugh or cry."

"Well, don't cry," said Mr. Croyle hastily.

"I'm not going to. I'm going to laugh." And she did; she laughed in a great, rich, unexpected peal, so that the young man with the hose looked up, startled, and Mr. Croyle, after a moment's uncertainty, laughed too. He could not have said what they were laughing at. It may have been the tiger.

"Drive on," she said, wiping her eyes. "Drive on, Amos. I want to see the Sloane place. Is the Sloane place still there? And the Methodist church with the crooked steeple? And the bridge where Willis Endicott fell through the ice and you pulled him out by his comforter?"

"I didn't pull him out," said Mr. Croyle. "You did."

"I never did any such thing. You did. You went out on your stomach."

"Hattie, I give you my word—"

"Amos Croyle, I was standing on the bank. I was holding Willis Endicott's sled. I saw you go out on your stomach."

Mr. Croyle opened his mouth and then closed it again. He had for thirty-five years possessed an image of Hattie Pettibone, aged twelve, lying flat upon the ice of Pogue's Run with her braids spread out behind her, hauling Willis Endicott into the light of day by a red woolen comforter; and he had been privately a little ashamed, all that while, that it was not himself. To have this image now abruptly taken from him and replaced with one in which he was the hero was a dislocation not easily borne at fifty-two. He found himself unable to accept it.

"Well, I don't remember it that way," he said.

"Nobody ever remembers anything the right way but me," said Mrs. Bellows comfortably. "Ezra used to say so."

Ezra was the husband in oranges. Mr. Croyle stole another glance at her. "How is Ezra?" he asked, and then wished he had not, for she was quiet a moment.

"Ezra died in March," she said. "I wrote you. Didn't you get my letter?"

Mr. Croyle had not got any letter. He said so, and was dismayed, and began to say he was sorry, and she patted his arm and said, "There, Amos. It's all right. Show me the Methodist church."

The Methodist church was still there, but the steeple had been straightened in nineteen-hundred-and-four by a committee of progressive young men, and Mrs. Bellows said it looked "plain foolish" without its crook, as if a man had had his nose fixed. The Sloane place was a boarding house. The bridge over Pogue's Run was gone, and so was Pogue's Run itself, which had been put into a sewer by an ordinance of the city council; and Mr. Croyle found himself, as he drove from one vanished landmark to another, explaining and apologizing and defending, now with a kind of civic pride and now with a sheepishness he could not account for, until it seemed to him that he had personally arranged the growth of the city from a town of thirty thousand to one of three hundred thousand for the express purpose of disappointing his cousin.

"You needn't keep saying it's very convenient," Mrs. Bellows said at last. "I can see it's convenient. Everything's convenient nowadays. In Pasadena they've made everything so convenient you can't find a place to stand still."

---

At dinner Mrs. Croyle was gracious and Mrs. Bellows was voluble, and Marjorie Croyle, aged nineteen and home from college for the Easter recess, sat in a condition of silent and mounting astonishment. She had never before seen her father as anybody's junior. Mr. Croyle was a deacon and a director of the Second National Bank, a man whose opinions on the tariff were listened to at the Commercial Club; and here was this large lady from California calling him "Amos" in a tone that implied she had seen him with jam on his face, and telling the table how he had once tried to run away to join a circus and had got as far as the Pennsylvania freight yards before he became hungry and came home. Worse, her father did not seem to mind. He laughed. He interrupted. He contradicted, and was contradicted in turn, and pounded the table so that the gravy-boat trembled, and at one point he so far forgot himself as to tell the story of the jackknife.

"You never gave it back," he said.

"Gave what back?"

"The knife. My Barlow knife. The one I had in my pocket when you pushed me in."

"Why, Amos," said Mrs. Bellows, "I never had your knife."

"You certainly did! That's what it was about! You said if I didn't give it to you—"

"I said if you didn't give it back. It was mine. Uncle Ben gave it to me for my birthday, and you took it out of my workbasket to whittle a whistle, and you wouldn't give it back, so I pushed you in." She regarded him with large, round, perfectly honest eyes. "Didn't you know that?"

There was a silence. Mrs. Croyle looked down at her plate, and her shoulders moved slightly. Marjorie looked at her father with a new and terrible interest.

"Well," said Mr. Croyle finally, in a voice not altogether firm, "I must say—I must say, after thirty-five years—"

"You always did take things out of my workbasket," said Mrs. Bellows. "Pass the pickles, Amos."

He passed the pickles.

Later, when Mrs. Croyle had gone upstairs, and Marjorie had gone out with a young man in a roadster, and the house had settled into that particular quiet which follows company, the two cousins sat on the side porch in the April dark. The air was soft, and somewhere down the street somebody's phonograph was playing a fox-trot, faintly and over and over, as if it could not remember how the end went. The smoke had thinned with nightfall, and here and there a star showed above the roofs, dim but authentic.

Neither of them said anything for a long while. Then Mrs. Bellows said, "I'm going to sell the grove, Amos."

"The orange grove?"

"Ezra's. Ours. Nobody to run it. Our boy's in Chicago, in insurance, doing very well; he doesn't want it. I don't want it. I never did like oranges, if you want to know. Thirty years I looked at them, and I never got so I liked them."

Mr. Croyle did not quite know what to say, and so he said nothing, which was perhaps the best thing.

"I thought I'd come back here," she went on. "I thought I'd just come back and look. I don't know what I thought I'd find. Grandma's house, I suppose. The cistern." She laughed a little, not so loud as before. "Silly, at my age. I knew it would all be changed. Folks wrote me. But you don't believe a thing like that till you see the tiger."

"No," said Mr. Croyle. "No, I guess you don't."

"Everybody's gone," she said. "Aunt Libby. Uncle Ben. Willis Endicott—is Willis gone?"

"Willis is a judge," Mr. Croyle said. "Circuit court. He weighs two hundred and forty pounds."

"My land," said Mrs. Bellows softly. "Little Willis Endicott." And then, after a moment, "Well, he never would have been anything if you hadn't pulled him out."

Mr. Croyle stirred in his chair. "Hattie," he said, "I've thought for thirty-five years that you pulled him out."

"I know you have. You looked so surprised this afternoon. You always did give other folks the credit, Amos. You gave me the credit for the knife, too, and it wasn't mine to take, being it was mine already." She laughed again. "You were the best boy in the world. Did you know that? I used to tell Ezra. I used to say, 'Ezra, I've got a cousin back home that was the best boy in the world, and I treated him like a dog.'"

Mr. Croyle was glad of the darkness. Something had happened to his throat; it seemed to have been stopped up with a quantity of old and unexpected material, and he coughed twice before he could clear it.

"Pshaw," he said. "You didn't treat me like a dog."

"I pushed you in the cistern."

"Well," said Mr. Croyle, "I expect I had it coming."

They sat there a while longer. The phonograph down the street gave up its fox-trot at last, defeated, and in the stillness a streetcar went grinding by on the avenue, two blocks over, with a long blue spark that lit the underside of the trees for an instant and was gone. Presently Mr. Croyle became aware that a low, tuneless sound was issuing from somewhere close at hand; and he was considering whether it might be a cricket, or the wind in the porch screens, when Mrs. Bellows said:

"You still whistle through your teeth when you're thinking."

He stopped. "I don't whistle through my teeth."

"You were doing it just now."

"I was not."

"You were, Amos. You did it at Grandma's table when you were nine, and she used to rap your knuckles with a spoon. You were doing it just now." She rose, in a great rustle of plum-colored silk, and stood a moment looking down at him, a large, dim, ostrich-plumed shape against the light of the doorway; and Mr. Croyle, looking up, saw for the second time that day the small girl with the braids, standing on the cistern-curb, regarding him with an expression of entire and affectionate certainty. "I'm going up to bed," she said. "We'll go see Willis Endicott tomorrow. I want to see a judge that weighs two hundred and forty pounds. Good night, Amos."

"Good night, Hattie."

She went in, and he heard her heavy, cheerful tread upon the stairs, and a door close somewhere overhead. Mr. Croyle sat on alone in the dark for a time, his hands folded upon the amplitude of his waistcoat, looking out at the faint and smoky stars. He was not thinking of anything in particular. He was not thinking, for instance, of a cold, iron-tasting chain, or a red woolen comforter, or a tall brick house with a cupola nobody was allowed to enter; he was simply sitting there, a director of the Second National Bank, at peace in the April night.

And after a while, very softly, through his teeth, he began to whistle.

At about half-past five o'clock of a June afternoon there is no being upon this earth so wholly at peace with the scheme of things as a boy of nine who does not yet know that he has been found out. He may have done much that day; he may, indeed, have done things which, could he but view them through the eyes of his elders, would cause him to grow pale and seek the protection of the cellar. But he does not so view them. To him the day has been merely a long and agreeable sequence of events, each arising naturally from the one before, and if any of them has left behind it a residue of consequence, that residue lies, in his mind, somewhere in a misty and improbable future, like old age or the Day of Judgment.

Such was the condition of Roderick Mays as he sat upon the edge of the rain-barrel behind his father's stable, swinging his heels against its staves and whittling, with a knife of great age and little edge, a stick which he had not yet decided to make into anything. He was a lean, brown, scratched, and freckled boy, with a cowlick that no application of water or of maternal palms had ever subdued, and upon his face there rested at this moment an expression of such benign vacancy that a stranger, coming upon him, might have supposed him to be thinking about the angels. He was, in fact, thinking about nothing at all, which is the most restful of all occupations and the one most commonly practised by boys upon rain-barrels.

Then, from the direction of the house, there came his mother's voice.

"Ro-*der*-ick!"

It is a peculiarity of the human ear, and particularly of that ear when it is attached to the head of a boy, that it can distinguish among a hundred shadings of a single word. Roddy had been called by his mother many thousands of times in his life, and he had learned to know, without conscious thought, the call that meant supper, the call that meant an errand to the grocery, the call that meant his Aunt Clara had come and he must wash his neck and be kissed. But this was none of these. This was his whole name, all three syllables of it, delivered with a kind of terrible evenness, the middle syllable lifted and held, as though his mother had paused upon it to steady herself. It was the voice of a woman who has seen something.

Roddy stopped whittling. His heels ceased to drum upon the barrel. Into his face there came, not alarm precisely, for he had as yet no notion of what he ought to be alarmed about, but a sort of thoughtfulness, a turning inward of the eye, as of one who rapidly reviews the events of a long day and finds them, now that he looks closely, more numerous than he had supposed.

"Ro-*der*-ick! You come here this minute!"

"Yes'm," said Roddy, but in a voice so small that it could not have been heard at a distance of six feet, and he did not move. He had, at that instant, remembered the hat.

It must be explained that at about eleven o'clock of that morning Roddy and his friend Elmer Vogel, who lived in the next street but one, had discovered beneath the Mays's back porch the body of a rat. It was a large rat, and it was beyond question dead, and it presented to the two boys an opportunity which they were not of a temperament to let pass. Elmer, whose family were Methodists of a fervent sort, had recently attended the funeral of an elderly relative and had been greatly impressed by it, and he was of the opinion that the rat should be buried with every circumstance of dignity. Roddy concurred. It was agreed that there should be a procession, a hymn, a sermon, and a coffin; and it was in the matter of the coffin that the difficulty arose, for a shoe-box, which Roddy first proposed, was held by Elmer to be beneath the station of so large a rat. What was wanted, Elmer said, was something black and shiny, like what his Great-uncle Ezra had had.

Now, in the hall closet of the Mays house, upon the topmost shelf, there reposed in a pasteboard box lined with tissue-paper the silk hat which Mr. Mays wore upon occasions of the gravest public and social import—to weddings, to the funerals of bank directors, and once, memorably, to shake the hand of a Vice-President of the United States who had passed through the town upon a special train. It was black. It was extremely shiny. And by means of a kitchen chair, a stool placed upon the chair, and a degree of acrobatic daring which, had it been exercised upon the trapeze, would have brought him fame, Roddy had got it down.

The obsequies had been conducted in the side yard, behind the lilac bushes. The deceased, wrapped in a lace antimacassar from the back of the parlor sofa, had been placed in the hat, which was then borne about the yard upon a coal-shovel while Elmer sang "Shall We Gather at the River" and Roddy, in a sheet, walked behind making a noise which he believed resembled the tolling of a bell. Elmer had then preached, taking for his text the words "He was a good rat," which he repeated a number of times, with variations, until he could think of nothing more; and the hat, with its contents, had been lowered into a grave dug with a garden trowel in the soft earth of Mrs. Mays's pansy bed. Here, however, a misunderstanding had arisen, for the grave, though deep enough for the rat, was not deep enough for the hat; and the two mourners, after some argument as to whether it was more fitting to dig deeper or to stamp the hat down level, had decided upon the latter course, and had carried it out with great thoroughness. Then they had gone off to Elmer's house to see a dog that was said to be able to count.

All this returned to Roddy now, not as a chain of reasoning but all at once, in a single vivid picture, as the drowning are said to behold the whole of their past lives; and with it came the comprehension, cold and complete, that his mother had been working in her pansy bed.

He got down from the rain-barrel. He put the knife in his pocket and threw the stick away. He looked at the alley gate, and for a moment there flickered across his mind the thought of the open road, the far horizon, the life of a cabin boy upon a whaler. But the thought did not stay with him, for the open road leads nowhere for a boy of nine except, eventually, back to supper; and besides, his mother was now standing upon the back porch, and she could see him.

"Roderick," she said, "come into this house."

He came. He came slowly, by a route which carried him around the stable and along the fence and past the grape arbor, as though by approaching indirectly he might somehow arrive at a different destination. His mother waited. She was a pretty woman, with a gentle face, and at most times she looked upon her son with an indulgence which her husband held to be excessive; but she was not looking upon him with indulgence now. In her hand, held at arm's length and by the extreme edge of its brim, was an object which no one who had not been told would ever have recognized as having once been a hat. It was flattened, it was creased, it was caked with earth, and from it there depended a fragment of lace antimacassar. It was, in short, a ruin; and as Roddy mounted the steps and stood before it, it seemed to him to regard him with a dreadful reproach, as though it knew him.

"Do you know what this is?" said his mother.

Roddy looked at it with every appearance of honest perplexity.

"Well, I—it looks kind of like—"

"It is your father's hat," said Mrs. Mays. "His silk hat."

"Is it?" said Roddy.

"Roderick, look at me."

He looked at her, but only for a moment, and then his eyes slid away and fixed themselves upon a knot in the porch floor, which they examined with deep scientific interest.

"I am not going to say anything to you," said his mother. "I am going to leave this entirely to your father. He will be home in fifteen minutes. You will go up to your room and wash, and put on a clean waist, and then you will go and sit in the library until he comes. And you will not leave it."

"Yes'm," said Roddy; and he went.

Mr. Herbert Mays, who was in the wholesale hardware business and a deacon of the Second Presbyterian Church, reached home that evening at a quarter before six, as he had reached it every evening for eleven years; and he was met in the front hall by his wife, who drew him into the dining room and closed the door and talked to him for some time in a low voice. When he came out he was carrying the hat. He carried it into the library, where his son sat upon the extreme forward edge of a horsehair chair, with his hands folded in his lap and his feet together, in an attitude so suggestive of meekness and so remarkably clean that it could only have been the product of design.

Mr. Mays sat down at his desk. He placed the hat upon the blotter before him, where it lay like evidence before a magistrate. Then he took off his eyeglasses and wiped them, and put them on again, and looked at his son for a long time without speaking.

It should be said that Mr. Mays, though a man of firm opinions, was also a man who believed in progress. He had lately been reading, in a magazine of serious purpose which his wife's cousin had sent them, an article entitled "The Child as a Reasoning Being," by a professor at an Eastern university; and this article had made a considerable impression upon him. It held that the rod was the relic of a barbarous age; that a child was a small rational creature who, if his errors were patiently explained to him, would of his own accord perceive their wrongness and amend them; and that the parent who struck in anger was but confessing his own failure as a teacher. Mr. Mays had read it twice. He had said to his wife that there was a great deal in it. And he resolved now, as he sat looking at the hat and at his son, that he would conduct this interview upon the principles laid down by the professor, calmly, judicially, and in the light of reason.

"Roderick," he said, in a voice of great mildness, "do you know why you are here?"

Roddy considered the question with care. He had learned that it is never wise to admit to more than is already known.

"Mamma said to come," he said.

"Yes. And do you know why she said to come?"

"Well," said Roddy, "I guess it's about that hat."

"It is about that hat," said Mr. Mays. "Now, Roderick, I am not going to be angry with you." He paused, a little surprised to observe that his hand had closed upon a paper-weight, and set it down again. "I want you to tell me, quite honestly, in your own words, how this happened."

Roddy drew a long breath. It was not, perhaps, that he wished to deceive his father; it was rather that he perceived, with the instinct of his kind, that the truth, baldly stated, would not sound well, and that some arrangement of it was required.

"Well," he said, "there was this rat."

"A rat."

"Yes, sir. It was dead. It was under the porch. And Elmer Vogel, he said it would be a sin not to bury it right, because it was a living creature, like it says in Sunday school, and he said a person ought to be buried respectful, and this was a pretty near as big as a person—well, it was pretty big, anyway—and so we had a funeral."

"I see," said Mr. Mays. "And the hat?"

"Well, Elmer said there had to be a coffin."

Mr. Mays closed his eyes briefly. When he opened them his voice was still mild, but there had come into it a certain tightness, as of a violin string drawn a half-turn higher.

"And it did not occur to you, Roderick—I am asking you only to reason with me now—it did not occur to you that a silk hat which cost me eleven dollars at Bostwick and Hale's, and which I have worn upon perhaps nine occasions in six years, was not a suitable coffin for a rat?"

"Elmer said it had to be black," said Roddy.

"Elmer said!" Mr. Mays caught himself, and laid both hands flat upon the desk, and regarded them until they were quite still. "Never mind what Elmer said. I am asking what *you* thought."

Roddy looked at the ceiling, as though the answer might be written there. It was not. He had not, in point of fact, thought anything at all about the hat except that it was black and shiny and that Elmer would be impressed by it; but he felt dimly that this would not be a satisfactory reply, and he cast about for a better one.

"Well," he said, at last, "I thought maybe it was an old one."

"An *old* one!"

"Yes, sir. I thought—it was way up on the top shelf, and you never wear it hardly, and I thought maybe you were through with it."

"Through with it!" said Mr. Mays. "Through with it! Roderick, that is the only silk hat I possess! That is the hat I wore to shake the hand of the Vice-President of the United States!"

"Yes, sir," said Roddy, and he added, by way of consolation, "Well, but he's not Vice-President any more, is he?"

There was a silence in the library. It was a long silence, and in the course of it Mr. Mays rose from his chair and walked to the window and stood looking out at the street with his hands clasped behind him, and the back of his neck, which was all that Roddy could see of him, gradually assumed a color which Roddy had seen it assume before, and which he did not like. Roddy shifted upon the horsehair, which pricked him through his clean stockings, and wished that he had been born an orphan.

When Mr. Mays turned around he had evidently been engaged in a struggle with himself, and it was not apparent from his face which side had won.

"Roderick," he said, "I am going to try once more. I want you to understand. I want you to *see*. Do you understand that this hat was not yours? That it belonged to me? That you had no right to take it?"

"Yes, sir."

"Then why did you take it?"

"I don't know," said Roddy.

It is the answer of all boys in all ages, and it has driven more fathers to despair than all the taxes and wars of history. It is the more maddening for being, as a rule, perfectly true. Mr. Mays heard it and felt the professor from the Eastern university slip quietly from his grasp.

"You don't know!" he said. "You don't know! You climb up to the top shelf of the hall closet—you might have broken your neck, do you understand that?—you take down your father's best hat, you put a dead rat in it, you march it all over the yard, you bury it in your mother's flower bed, and then you stand on it—"

"We didn't stand on it hardly," said Roddy. "Just Elmer, mostly."

"—you *stand* on it," said Mr. Mays, his voice rising, "and you sit there and tell me you don't know why! And this is not the first time, Roderick! This is not the first time by a great deal! Who was it put the molasses in the piano? Who was it took the clothes-wringer apart to make a cannon? Who was it painted the Haskells' cat?"

"That was a long time ago," said Roddy, feeling that he was being dealt with unjustly. "That was last *summer*."

"I don't care if it was in the Garden of Eden!" cried Mr. Mays; and then, remembering, he stopped and passed a hand across his brow, and sat down heavily in his chair. For a moment he said nothing at all, and there was in his face an expression which, if Roddy had been older, he might have recognized as that of a man contemplating the gulf between theory and practice.

"Very well," said Mr. Mays at last, and his voice was quiet again, but it was a different quiet, a quiet without hope in it. "Very well. You will go up to your room. You will stay there for the rest of this evening. You will have no supper. And tomorrow you will not go to Elmer Vogel's, nor will Elmer Vogel come here, and you will spend the morning weeding your mother's pansy bed, and replanting what you have destroyed, and you will do it with your own hands and your own allowance. Is that understood?"

"Yes, sir," said Roddy. He got down from the horsehair chair with alacrity, for he had expected worse, and it is one of the mercies of boyhood that a sentence of exile without supper, when one has eaten four doughnuts and a pickle at Elmer Vogel's at half-past four, is not so terrible as it sounds. He went to the door. And there, with his hand upon the knob, he turned, moved by some obscure impulse toward justice, and spoke once more.

"Papa," he said, "it was a real good funeral, though. Elmer said it was better'n his Great-uncle Ezra's."

Then he went out, and closed the door behind him, and could be heard ascending the stairs, slowly at first, and then, as he gained the upper hall and the distance from the library increased, with a lightness that was very nearly cheerful.

Mr. Mays remained at his desk. He looked at the hat. He took it up and turned it about in his hands, and brushed some of the earth from its crown, and lifted away with two fingers the last remnant of lace antimacassar. Then, for no reason that he could afterward explain, there came into his mind a picture that he had not thought of in thirty years: a hot afternoon in a little Ohio town, a dead blue jay, a cigar box stolen from the counter of his father's store, and a small boy in a nightshirt walking behind it down an alley, chanting what he believed to be Latin. He remembered the cigar box very well. It had been full of cigars.

The corners of Mr. Mays's mouth moved. He pressed them firmly together. They moved again; and a curious sound, like a cough that had gone astray, escaped him, and then another, and he bent his head over the ruined hat, and his shoulders began, slightly but unmistakably, to shake.

At this moment the door opened, and Mrs. Mays looked in.

"Herbert," she said, "I heard you shouting. Was it very dreadful? Did you—are you *ill*?"

Mr. Mays straightened himself at once. He set the hat down upon the blotter. He took off his eyeglasses and wiped them with great deliberation, and when he looked up at his wife his countenance was that of a deacon and a man of affairs, stern, composed, and wholly without levity.

"I have dealt with him," he said. "He will have no supper. And Martha, I have been thinking. That article of your cousin's—the one about the reasoning child—you may as well throw it out. There is nothing in it whatever."

But later that evening, when Mrs. Mays had gone up to bed, and the house was quiet, the cook, coming through the back hall, was astonished to encounter her employer upon the kitchen stairs, in his slippers, carrying a plate upon which were two slices of cold chicken, a piece of bread and butter, and a wedge of cherry pie; and he looked at her with such a fierce and silent dignity that she never mentioned it to anyone, as long as she lived in that house.

George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mrs. Henry Croft had a way of removing her gloves, after an evening abroad, which her husband had long ago learned to read as a sailor reads the sky. When she drew them off briskly, finger by finger, and tossed them upon the hall table with a little laugh, the weather was fair. When she drew them off slowly, with her lips pressed together, and laid them down side by side as if she meant to have them identified later by the police, a storm was making up somewhere beyond the horizon. To-night she drew them off very slowly indeed, and Henry, hanging his overcoat upon the walnut rack that had been her mother's, perceived that he would do well to look to his rigging.

"It was a pleasant dinner," he ventured, which was a mistake, as he knew the moment he had said it.

"Was it?" said Mrs. Croft. "I'm glad you thought so. I'm sure you seemed to enjoy yourself."

"Well, the Bannings always do things handsomely."

"Handsomely!" She turned from the table and went into the parlour, where the gas had been left burning low, and turned it up with a decisive hand. "Yes, I should say they did things handsomely. I should say they could afford to. I should say, too, that some people might take a lesson from them, if some people weren't too stubborn to learn anything from anybody."

Henry followed her, but not too closely. He was a mild, broad, greyish man of fifty, with a moustache that drooped at the ends as if it, too, had been worn down by years of domestic weather, and he had been for twenty-two years the proprietor of Croft's Hardware and Implement Store on Washington Street, which was the most respectable hardware store in the town and, as Mrs. Croft had lately begun to observe, also the most old-fashioned. He sat down in his own chair by the base-burner, and, there being nothing else to do with his hands, he took up the evening paper, which he had already read.

"Henry, will you put that down?"

He put it down.

"I want to talk to you," said Mrs. Croft, "and I don't intend to talk to a newspaper. I've talked to newspapers long enough. I've talked to the back of one every evening since we were married, and I'm tired of it."

"Why, Addie, I only—"

"Never mind what you only. Did you see Mrs. Banning's face to-night, when Mrs. Fenwick asked us whether we'd decided on our lot in the Elmhurst Addition?"

Henry said he had not noticed Mrs. Banning's face particularly.

"No, you wouldn't. You never notice anything that a person with ordinary perceptions would see in a minute. Well, I noticed it. She looked at Mrs. Fenwick, and Mrs. Fenwick looked at her, and then they both looked at their plates. And I sat there and smiled, Henry Croft, and said we hadn't quite made up our minds between the corner lot on Linden Avenue and the one facing the little park—and I had to say it with every one of them knowing perfectly well that you've been putting me off about it since last March!"

There is a kind of husband who, being accused, defends himself, and there is another kind who, being accused, examines the pattern of the carpet. Henry Croft belonged to the second kind; and it may be said for the carpet, which was a Brussels of large red roses upon a ground of a green no longer to be found in nature, that it rewarded examination. He examined it now.

"I don't see that it's anybody's business but ours," he said at last.

"Oh, you don't! Then I'll tell you whose business it is. It's Edith's business. Edith is nineteen years old, and every girl she knows is either living out in Elmhurst already or going to be living there by next fall. The Fenwicks are building. The Bannings have built. Even the Pruitts—the Pruitts, Henry!—have bought a lot, and everybody knows Sam Pruitt never had a dollar he didn't owe to somebody. And here we sit in this house on Mercer Street with the smoke from the round-house coming in at every window, and the boarding-houses creeping up from the other end of the block, and a saloon—a saloon, Henry—not three doors from where your daughter has to walk to get the street-car!"

"It isn't a saloon, exactly," Henry said. "Schaefer calls it a sample-room."

"I don't care what he calls it! I know what it is, and so does every young man who comes to call on Edith, and so does every young man who doesn't come because of it!"

This was a new consideration, and Henry looked up from the roses. "Why, Addie, I didn't know any young man had stopped coming."

"Of course you didn't. You don't know anything that goes on in this house. You come home, and you eat your supper, and you read your paper, and you go to bed; and you'd think the whole world was a hardware store with a family attached to it for the convenience of the proprietor." Mrs. Croft's voice trembled slightly upon this, for it was a phrase she had been composing, at intervals, for several weeks, and she was moved by it herself. "Harvey Fenwick hasn't been here since Easter."

"Well, I never thought much of Harvey Fenwick."

"That's not the point! The point is that he doesn't come, and the reason he doesn't come is that his mother says Mercer Street isn't what it used to be—and she said it, Henry, she said it in my hearing at the Woman's Club, and pretended she didn't know I was standing right behind her!"

Henry was silent. He was thinking, not of Harvey Fenwick, whom he considered a young man of inferior character because he parted his hair in the middle and had once asked Henry, in a tone of light raillery, whether he still kept horseshoe nails, but of something else—something which had been lying at the bottom of his mind, like a stone at the bottom of a well, for the better part of a year. He had grown used to its being there. He had even, at times, contrived to forget it for an hour together. But it was there now, very large and cold, and his wife's voice seemed to be drawing a bucket down toward it.

"Addie," he said, "there's no use getting excited."

"Excited!" said Mrs. Croft. "Excited! I've never been calmer in my life."

It is a curious law of the domestic universe that no woman ever announces her calmness except at the precise moment when it has departed from her; and Henry, who had been married long enough to know this law, though he had never thought to formulate it, rose and went to the window, where he stood looking out at the dark shapes of the maples along Mercer Street and the yellow lamp of Schaefer's sample-room glimmering beyond them.

"I'm only asking you," his wife went on, "for a plain answer. Are we going to build in Elmhurst, or are we not?"

"I haven't said we weren't."

"You haven't said we were. You've said 'we'll see' and 'there's plenty of time' and 'let's wait till the spring trade's over' and 'let's wait till the fall trade's started,' and now it's November and the Linden Avenue lot is the only good one left, and Mr. Ormsby told me himself, on the street, that he had an offer for it from a man in Chicago. A man in Chicago, Henry!"

"Ormsby always has an offer from a man in Chicago," said Henry. "It's his way of doing business."

"I don't care whether it is or not. I want that lot." She came and stood beside him, and for a moment her voice softened, and she put her hand upon his sleeve—a hand that was still small and still pretty, though it had kept house for twenty-two years with one hired girl and sometimes none. "Henry, I've never asked for much. You know I haven't. When the Bannings had their carriage, I didn't say a word. When everybody put in electric light, I said gas was good enough for me, because you said it was cheaper. I've made over Edith's dresses and my own, and I've done it gladly, because I knew you were saving—and I've always thought, all these years, that when the time came, when Edith was grown and it really mattered, we'd have something to show for it. And now the time's come. It's come, Henry. And I don't understand why you won't—"

She stopped, for her husband had turned from the window, and something in his face, under the full light of the gas, arrested her.

"Henry," she said in a different voice, "what is it?"

"Nothing," said Henry.

"It isn't nothing. You look sick."

"I'm not sick." He went back to his chair and sat down heavily, and the springs of the chair, which had known his weight for a dozen years and were well acquainted with its customary manner of descent, complained at this one as at a stranger. "Sit down, Addie."

She did not sit down. She stood where he had left her, by the window, with her hands clasped before her, and the little ornamental clock upon the mantel, a wedding present from an aunt who had long since gone to her reward, ticked into the silence with an air of tactless cheerfulness.

"Henry, you'd better tell me."

"I've been meaning to tell you," he said. "I've been meaning to, for a long time. I—it's the Midland Traction stock."

"The what?"

"The Midland Traction Company. The interurban line they were going to build out to Bentonville and Meade's Crossing. You remember. Everybody was going into it, a year ago last summer. Banning was in it. Fenwick was in it. Judge Hollister was one of the directors."

"I remember there was talk about it," she said slowly. "I remember you said it was a speculation, and you didn't believe in speculations. You said it at this very table."

"Yes," said Henry. "I did say that." He looked at the base-burner, through whose little isinglass windows the fire glowed redly, as if he hoped to find some counsel there. "I said it in June. In August I put eleven thousand dollars into it."

Mrs. Croft did not cry out. For a moment, indeed, she did not say anything whatever, and when at last she spoke it was in a tone so quiet that Henry would almost have preferred the other.

"Eleven thousand dollars," she said. "That's—Henry, that's nearly all of it."

"It's all but about eighteen hundred," he said. "And the store, of course. The store's clear."

"And the Midland Traction Company—"

"There isn't any Midland Traction Company," said Henry. "Not any more. There was a receiver appointed in February. They'd laid about four miles of track out past the fair-grounds, and then the money gave out, and it turned out some of the money had given out before it ever got to the track. Judge Hollister's resigned. There's talk of an indictment, but there's always talk. The stockholders might get eight or nine cents on the dollar, some day, if the court ever gets through with it. I don't count on it."

"In February," Mrs. Croft repeated. "In February. And this is November."

"Yes."

"And all through the spring, and all through the summer, when I was talking about the lot, and the plans, and showing you the pictures out of the magazines, and asking you whether you liked the house with the round tower or the one with the porch all the way across—all that time you knew."

"Yes," said Henry. "I knew."

She sat down then, not in her own chair, but upon the end of the horsehair sofa nearest the window, as if she had been walking a long way and had come upon it by chance. Henry did not look at her. He had made his confession to the base-burner, and he went on addressing himself to that unresponsive object, because it was easier.

"I don't know why I did it," he said. "That's the truth, Addie. I've been in business twenty-two years and I never did a foolish thing with money in my life—not one. I used to laugh at men who did. And then everybody was talking about it, at the Commercial Club, and on the street, and Banning came into the store one day and said, 'Well, Henry, I suppose you're too old-fashioned for anything like this,' and laughed, and I—well, I didn't like it. I didn't like being old-fashioned. I'd been hearing it a good deal." He paused. "I'd been hearing it at home, too, some."

Mrs. Croft made a slight movement, but did not speak.

"I thought," Henry went on, "that if it went the way they all said it would, we'd have enough to build in Elmhurst and not touch the savings at all. I thought I'd surprise you. I used to think about how I'd tell you—how I'd come home some evening and say, 'Addie, you go and pick out any lot you want.' I used to think about it on the way home from the store. That's the fool part of it." He laughed, without much success. "And then when it went the other way, I couldn't tell you. I kept thinking something would turn up. I kept thinking the receiver might find something. And every time you'd bring out those magazine pictures—"

He stopped, because his voice had become unreliable, and Henry Croft was of a generation and a place which held that a man's voice should under no circumstances become unreliable in the presence of his wife.

There followed a silence of some length, during which the clock upon the mantel continued its tactless observations, and a street-car went clanging by at the end of the block, and somewhere beyond the maples a voice, presumably issuing from Schaefer's sample-room, lifted itself in fragmentary and uncertain song. Mrs. Croft sat looking at her husband. She was seeing, it may be, a number of things at once: the house with the round tower, and the house with the porch all the way across, and Mrs. Banning's face, and Mrs. Fenwick's; but she was also seeing a broad greyish man, a little stooped now, walking home from Washington Street in the summer dusk and composing, with laborious happiness, a speech that would never be delivered. It was this last picture, perhaps, that lingered.

"Henry," she said at length, "does anybody know?"

"Banning knows I was in it. I don't know whether he knows how much."

"Does Edith know?"

"No."

"Then nobody's to know," said Mrs. Croft, and her voice had in it something which Henry had not heard there for a long time—something brisk and capable and very nearly cheerful, such as it had held twenty years ago, when they had moved into the house on Mercer Street with a borrowed dray and four dollars and sixty cents between them. "Nobody's to know anything about it, do you hear? Not Edith, and not the Bannings, and certainly not Cora Fenwick."

"But the lot—what'll you tell them about the lot?"

"I'll tell them," said Mrs. Croft, rising and smoothing her skirt with a gesture that was almost martial, "that we've decided Elmhurst is too far out. I'll tell them the Addition's going to be overbuilt, and that the drainage is bad, and that anybody with any judgment can see the town's going to grow the other way, toward the river. I'll tell them we think it's very sensible of them to have built there, and that we hope they'll be comfortable, and that we've decided to keep this house and put in electric light and a new furnace and have the front porch widened. And I'll say it so that every one of them will go home wondering if they haven't made a mistake."

Henry stared at her. "Addie, can we afford—"

"We can afford the electric light," said Mrs. Croft. "The porch can wait. They won't know whether it's waiting or not." She came over to his chair and stood looking down at him, and her mouth, which had been pressed so firmly together when she laid down her gloves, now relaxed into an expression which he could not altogether interpret, though it was not unkind. "And as for Harvey Fenwick," she added, "if a sample-room three doors away is enough to keep him from calling on Edith, then I think Edith is well rid of him. I never did like the way he parts his hair."

"Why, that's just what I always—" Henry began, and then stopped, overcome by the singularity of the coincidence.

"I know it is," said his wife. "You've said it at least fifty times." She touched his shoulder lightly, as one might touch a child who has been brought home late and unexpectedly unpunished. "Now I'm going up to bed. You turn down the gas when you come, and see that the base-burner's shut. And Henry—"

"Yes, Addie?"

She hesitated in the doorway, and for a moment it seemed that she might say something tender, or something reproachful, or possibly both. But she was a woman of her time and place, as he was a man of his; and in the end she merely said:

"You might have told me in February. I'd have liked to have known in February."

Then she went upstairs, and Henry sat for a long while by the base-burner, watching the red glow behind the little isinglass windows and listening to the clock. Once he picked up the evening paper, and once he laid it down again. He felt that something had happened to him which he did not wholly understand; that he had expected to be struck, and had been struck, but not where he had braced himself, nor in the manner he had feared. He had dreaded her anger, and her anger had been brief. What he had not foreseen, and what remained with him now, was the quiet sentence in the doorway, which had in it neither anger nor forgiveness but only a kind of grave surprise, as if, after twenty-two years, she had found a door in the house that she had not known was there.

He was still turning it over when he rose at last, and shut the damper of the base-burner, and turned down the gas, and went up the dark stairs, treading carefully upon the third step, which creaked, so as not to wake his daughter.

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”
