Mrs. Croft had made the announcement at breakfast, between the oatmeal and the eggs, in the manner of a woman who has long held a piece of news in reserve and believes its effect will be heightened by a casual delivery.

"Your Aunt Lavinia is coming on the Thursday train," she said, "and she's bringing Harriet."

Lindley Croft, aged seventeen and some months, laid down his spoon with deliberation. He had lately adopted deliberation as a principle, having observed it in a travelling elocutionist who recited "The Wreck of the Hesperus" at the Second Presbyterian Church and who had seemed to him, in the pauses before his more striking lines, to carry the weight of a whole world's experience.

"Harriet?" he said. "Oh, yes. Harriet."

"Your cousin Harriet," said his mother, as if there might be some confusion with other Harriets in his life. "You haven't seen her since she was eleven. You were ten. She pushed you into Shaler's Creek the summer before they went East. You surely remember that."

Lindley did remember it, and he remembered as well that the push had been unprovoked, that the creek had been colder than anyone would have supposed in August, and that he had afterwards been made to apologize for losing his temper, while Harriet, who began it, was given a peach. Of Harriet herself he retained a picture both distinct and unflattering: a lean, brown, peremptory creature, all knees and elbows and pigtails, with a nose that peeled in summer and a voice that carried to the next block. That this person should now be coming back, presumably to be fussed over and introduced and taken to the band concerts in the park, seemed to him an imposition upon his time.

"I shall be pretty busy Thursday," he said.

"Busy with what?" his father asked, looking up from the Daily Courier.

Lindley found that he had not decided. "Things," he answered, with dignity; and Mr. Croft, who had been seventeen himself at a period so remote that he no longer believed it, returned to his newspaper with a short sound through the nose which his son preferred not to interpret.

It is one of the mercies of youth that its resolutions, however firmly taken at breakfast, are seldom binding by afternoon, and it is one of its torments that it never perceives this mercy at the time. By Thursday noon Lindley had arrived at a fixed plan for the reception of his cousin. He would be present, since his mother required it; but he would be present in the manner of a man who has outgrown family occasions and attends them out of courtesy. He would be civil, even kind. He would make it plain, without unpleasantness, that the boy who had been pushed into Shaler's Creek no longer existed, and that in his place stood one who had read a good deal of Bulwer-Lytton, had smoked four cigarettes (only one of them disagreeably), and had danced twice with Miss Mabel Rennick, who was nineteen.

With this in view he spent a considerable part of the afternoon before his mirror. He put on his new waistcoat, which was of a pale fawn shade and had been chosen in defiance of his mother's opinion that it made him look "like a bookmaker." He put on the highest of his collars, which held his chin at an angle of perpetual mild surprise, and he arranged his hair in the style then favoured by the more advanced young men of the town: parted precisely in the middle and drawn down on either side in two wings, with an effect, as his father once remarked, "of a gentleman peering out between a pair of curtains." Then, having found a book of essays by Mr. Emerson upon the parlour table, he carried it out to the porch and opened it at random, so that he might be discovered reading when the carriage arrived.

The carriage was late. Lindley read the same paragraph about Self-Reliance eleven times without learning what it said, and was beginning to feel that Mr. Emerson must have been a tiresome man to sit next to at dinner, when he heard wheels at the corner and his mother's voice calling from the hall. He did not look up. He turned a page, and frowned at it thoughtfully, and permitted himself to become aware of the visitors only when the gate clicked and his aunt's voice, which he recognized at once, exclaimed upon the size of the maples.

"My land, Ellen, how those trees have grown! And the Hollisters have painted their house yellow. Whatever possessed them?"

Lindley rose, closing his book upon one finger to keep the place, and descended the steps with what he intended to be the unhurried courtesy of a host. He shook hands with Aunt Lavinia, who was stouter than he remembered and who kissed him in spite of the collar, and then he turned, with his speech of welcome ready, toward the cousin.

The speech did not come.

There was nobody in front of him whom he could identify as Harriet. There was a tall young lady in a grey travelling dress and a hat with a curving plume, who was paying the driver from a small purse and laughing at something he had said. When she turned, he saw a face that was pale where he had expected brown, composed where he had expected peremptory, and possessed of a pair of grey eyes which regarded him for a moment with frank inquiry and then filled, slowly and unmistakably, with amusement.

"Why, it's Lindy!" she said. "Mamma, look—it's Lindy, and he's grown a moustache!"

He had not grown a moustache. He had grown something on his upper lip, and had been cultivating it with secret care for upward of six weeks, but he had not supposed it was yet visible to the public; and the discovery that it was visible, and that its first public notice should take the form of this announcement in the front yard, before the driver and very probably before Mrs. Hollister in her yellow house across the way, struck him dumb. He shook the hand she offered him and said, "How do you do, Harriet," in a voice that began in one register and ended in another, and then he followed the party into the house, carrying a hatbox and Mr. Emerson together, and not knowing what to do with either.

There followed that interval, familiar to every household that has ever received relatives, in which nobody listens to anybody and everybody talks at once. Aunt Lavinia had to be shown her room and had to say it was exactly the same, and then had to say it was not the same at all, because the wallpaper was new; Mrs. Croft had to apologize for the wallpaper; the hired girl had to be introduced and had to be told that Miss Harriet took no sugar in her tea; and through it all Lindley stood in the hall with the hatbox, until his mother took it from him with an absent-minded "Thank you, dear," and he found himself with nothing in his hands but Emerson, who did not help.

It was Harriet who rescued him, though he would not have described it so. She came down the stairs alone, presently, having taken off her hat, and he saw that her hair, which he remembered as two tight ropes of an indeterminate colour, was in reality a soft brown, done up in a manner that he did not understand but felt to be very becoming.

"Mamma and Aunt Ellen have begun on the Pruitt family," she said, "and they'll be at it till supper. Let's go out on the porch where it's cool. Unless you're too busy reading," she added, glancing at the book. "What is it?"

"Emerson," said Lindley.

"Oh dear," said Harriet. "Do you like him?"

He had meant to say that he found Emerson a profound thinker, but there was something in her tone that suggested she would not be impressed by this, and he heard himself saying instead, "Well, parts of him."

"Which parts?"

"The—the parts about self-reliance."

"I never could get through those," she said cheerfully. "I always wanted to tell him he'd been self-reliant long enough and might let somebody else talk." And she went out to the porch and settled herself in the wicker rocker, which had been his grandfather's, and looked out over the lawn and the street with an expression he could not read.

Lindley took the porch swing, which he had not intended; it was a seat for children and couples, and a man of the world would have chosen the steps. But he found the steps too far away, for some reason, and so he sat in the swing, and it moved under him with a faint creak of chains, and he was obliged to brace one foot against the floor to keep from drifting.

"It's queer," Harriet said, after a while. "Everything is smaller."

"Smaller?"

"The houses. The street. Even the trees, though Mamma says they're bigger. I suppose it's because I was smaller. When we left I thought the Hollister house was a palace. I used to make up stories that a princess lived in it." She laughed. "And now it's yellow."

"They only painted it last spring," Lindley said, feeling vaguely that the town ought to be defended. "Lots of things are new. They've got the trolley line clear out to the fairgrounds now, and there's a new opera house on Main Street that seats nine hundred. And they've cut up the Harbaugh orchard into lots."

"Not the Harbaugh orchard!"

"Yes. There's going to be a street through it. They're going to call it Fairview Avenue."

Harriet was silent for a moment. "We used to steal apples there," she said. "Don't you remember? You and I and Tommy Pruitt, and old Mr. Harbaugh came out with a buggy whip and you fell out of the tree and he was so frightened he gave us each a whole basket to take home."

Lindley did remember; he remembered it with a sudden and complete vividness that took him by surprise—the smell of the grass under the trees, and the bark scraping his knees, and the old man's face going from purple to white when he saw that the boy on the ground was not moving. He had not been badly hurt; he had only had the wind knocked out of him; but he had lain there with his eyes shut a little longer than was strictly necessary, because it was interesting to hear what people said about him while they thought him unconscious.

"I wasn't really hurt," he said now, a little stiffly.

"I know you weren't," said Harriet. "I saw you peeking. I didn't tell."

He looked at her. She was rocking gently, with her eyes on the street, and there was nothing in her face but a kind of peaceful reminiscence; and yet he had an uncomfortable conviction that she was laughing at him somewhere underneath. It was a conviction that would come to him a good many times in the course of the summer, and he never learned whether it was justified, which is perhaps the chief thing that a cousin a year older can do for a cousin a year younger.

"Well," he said, adjusting his collar, "a person grows out of that sort of thing."

"Out of stealing apples?"

"Out of—oh, the whole business. Children's games." He leaned back in the swing, which unfortunately carried him backward farther than he had intended, so that he had to recover with a jerk. "I suppose you've found the same thing, back East. I suppose you've seen a good deal of society."

"Some," said Harriet.

"I've been going out a good deal myself, lately," he went on, with an air of reluctant confession. "Dances and so on. Of course this isn't Philadelphia, but there's a pretty lively set here, among the older crowd. I don't care for most of it, though. I find most people pretty shallow, when you get to know them."

"Do you?" said Harriet. "I find most people pretty deep, when I get to know them. That's what makes them so hard to talk to at dances."

He did not know how to answer this, and so he let it pass, as one lets pass a remark in a foreign language that one has not quite caught; and he was relieved when she turned the conversation herself.

"Tell me about everybody," she said. "Tell me about Tommy Pruitt. Is he still horrid?"

"He's at the State University," said Lindley. "He's on the football team. He weighs a hundred and eighty pounds."

"Tommy Pruitt! He was the littlest boy in the Sunday school. He used to cry when they made him say the Golden Text."

"Well, he doesn't cry now," Lindley said, with some feeling; for Tommy Pruitt, in the season just past, had developed a habit of greeting him on Main Street by lifting him clear of the sidewalk, which was not a thing a man of the world could easily forgive. "And Bessie Lamb is married. She married a dentist from Terre Haute. And old Dr. Ruggles died, and they put up a drinking fountain for him in the courthouse square, only the water doesn't work."

"And Grandfather?" Harriet said.

The swing stopped. Lindley had known, of course, that she would ask; Aunt Lavinia had come back for the reading of the papers and the dividing of the house on Locust Street, and that was the real reason for the visit, though nobody had said so at breakfast. But he had somehow supposed that she would ask it of his mother, in the parlour, with lowered voices, and not of him, out here.

"It was in March," he said. "He wasn't sick long. He sat right there, mostly—in that chair you're in—up till about two weeks before. He used to tell me to sit up straight."

Harriet stopped rocking. She did not look at the chair, but he saw her hands, which had been lying in her lap, close upon each other.

"He used to tell me that, too," she said. "He used to say, 'Hattie, a lady may slump in her own bedroom, but nowhere else in the Republic.' And then he would give me a peppermint, because he thought he'd been too stern." She was quiet for a little. "He wrote to me every month, all the time we were away. Did you know that? Long letters, about everything—about the weather, and the price of wheat, and how the Hollisters' cow got into the Methodist church. I have all of them. Mamma thinks I'm silly to keep them."

"He wrote to you?" said Lindley. It was not jealousy that he felt; it was something stranger, a sense that he had been living for six years beside a man who had a whole correspondence he knew nothing about, and that the old gentleman in the wicker chair, who had seemed to him chiefly a source of admonitions about posture, had been a person of more resources than he had suspected.

"Every month," Harriet said. "He said he wanted me to know what was going on at home, so I wouldn't come back a stranger." She smiled, though not very steadily. "And here I am, and everything's smaller, and the Harbaugh orchard is Fairview Avenue, and Tommy Pruitt weighs a hundred and eighty pounds. I'm a stranger anyhow."

Lindley was aware that something was required of him, and that it was not anything he had learned from Bulwer-Lytton. He sat in the swing with his foot braced against the floor and his chin held up by his collar, and he searched his mind for the right thing to say, and found nothing in it but a recollection of the creek.

"You pushed me in Shaler's Creek," he said.

Harriet turned and looked at him.

"I mean," said Lindley, reddening, "I mean you can't be a stranger. Strangers don't push people in creeks. I remember it perfectly. It was the eleventh of August. You said I was a baby because I wouldn't wade out to the big rock, and then you pushed me, and I got a peach and you didn't—no, wait—you got a peach and I didn't. That's how it was. It was the most unjust thing that ever happened to me."

For a moment Harriet only looked at him, and then she began to laugh—not the amused, superior laugh he had been bracing against all afternoon, but a laugh of a different kind, helpless and warm, which made her put her hand over her eyes.

"Oh, Lindy," she said. "Oh, Lindy, you're exactly the same."

He was not sure this was a compliment, and he was quite sure it was not true; but he found, somewhat to his own surprise, that he did not mind. He let the swing move a little, and the chains creaked, and down the street the lamplighter came by on his bicycle, touching the posts with his long pole one after another, so that a row of small flames bloomed along the dusk.

"I'm not the same," he said, after a time, but without much conviction. "I've changed a good deal."

"I know," said Harriet, wiping her eyes. "You've got a moustache."

"It's not a moustache," he said. "Not yet."

"It's a very nice beginning of one."

He considered this. "Mabel Rennick says it makes me look older."

"Who is Mabel Rennick?"

"Oh, just a girl," said Lindley carelessly; and then, because the dusk was kind and the swing was moving and his cousin seemed to be listening with a real and friendly interest, he told her all about Mabel Rennick—her age, her accomplishments upon the mandolin, the two dances, and the deplorable fact that she had afterwards been seen at the Elks' picnic in the company of a druggist's clerk from Indianapolis who wore yellow shoes. It was a long recital and not altogether coherent, but Harriet heard it through without once laughing, and at the end of it she said, very gravely, that she thought Miss Rennick had shown poor judgment, and that it was probably the yellow shoes, which some girls could not resist.

They were still sitting there, talking about the druggist's clerk and Tommy Pruitt and the drinking fountain that would not work, when Mrs. Croft came to the screen door to call them in to supper. She stood a moment looking out at them, unseen—her son in the porch swing, with his collar wilted at last and one wing of his hair fallen down over his forehead as it used to fall when he was ten, and her niece in the old wicker chair, leaning forward, with her chin on her hand.

"Well," said Aunt Lavinia, coming up behind her, "they seem to be getting on."

"Yes," said Mrs. Croft; and something in her voice made her sister glance at her. "It's the chair, I think. Father always liked company on the porch in the evening."

Supper was a long affair, as such suppers are, and the talk at it was all of the house on Locust Street and the Pruitt family and the price of lots on Fairview Avenue. Lindley ate a great deal and said very little. Once, when his father asked him whether he had got much good out of Mr. Emerson that afternoon, he replied that Emerson was all right in parts, but that a man could be too self-reliant; and Mr. Croft, who had been about to make the short sound through his nose, looked at his son over his spectacles instead and said nothing at all.

Later, in his own room, with the high collar thrown across the back of a chair, Lindley sat for some time at the window, looking down at the porch roof and the dark lawn and the row of lamps along the street. He had kept a diary since January, in a leather book with a lock, and in it he had recorded, at intervals, his views on life, on society, and on the general shallowness of the feminine character. He opened it now and wet his pencil and considered.

"My cousin Harriet arrived to-day from Philadelphia," he wrote at last. "She is much changed in appearance. She is fairly intelligent for a girl." He looked at this for a while and frowned at it, as he had frowned at Emerson, and then he crossed out the last sentence with three heavy lines and wrote beneath it: "She remembered about the creek."

And that, though he could not have told you why, seemed to him to say everything.

Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. “Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. “But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. Mr. Albert Crane came home that Thursday evening at a quarter past six, which was his hour, and set his umbrella in the rack, which was its place, and hung his hat upon the third peg of the hall-tree, which was its peg; for he was a man who believed that a household, like a bank, should be conducted upon principles, and he had been cashier of the Second National for eleven years without once permitting a principle to be overdrawn. He was of a moderate size, with a moderate moustache, and he wore the expression of patient rectitude which comes upon men who are obliged to say no to their neighbours across a brass grille six days in the week. It was an expression he had not intended to bring home with him; but, as Mrs. Crane had once observed to her sister, it was a little like his rubbers: he forgot to take it off at the door.

On this particular evening he found his wife waiting for him at the foot of the stairs, and there was that in her attitude which warned him. She was a small, pretty woman, inclined to plumpness and to laughter, and she was not laughing now. She had, instead, the look of one who carries a parcel that may go off.

"Albert," she said, "I want you to come into the sitting-room a moment before supper. Don't go upstairs."

"Why not?"

"Because he's up there."

Mr. Crane did not need to ask who was meant. In that house there was only one person who was ever referred to by the pronoun alone, and in a tone that implied capital letters. He was seven years old, he was named Wendell after his maternal grandfather, and he had been sent to his room at half-past three that afternoon, where, according to report, he had since been engaged in making a noise like a steam-calliope at intervals of about four minutes.

"What has he done now?" asked Mr. Crane, and followed his wife into the sitting-room, where she closed the door with a care that seemed excessive for so domestic an occasion.

Mrs. Crane did not answer at once. She went to the centre-table and took up from it, with both hands and a certain reverence, an object which she held out to her husband in silence. He looked at it for some moments before he recognized it, and when he did so his countenance underwent a change.

It was, or it had been, his silk hat. It was the hat he had bought in Chicago at the time of his brother-in-law's wedding; the hat he wore to funerals of directors and to the annual dinner of the Bankers' Association of the Fourth District; a hat of such lustre that Mrs. Crane had once said she could do her hair in it. It was now of a shape not readily described. The crown had been pushed down into the brim and then, apparently, hauled out again by main force, so that it rose in a series of terraces, like a pagoda; there was a long rent in the silk upon one side; and around the band, secured by what seemed to be several yards of the pink ribbon from Mrs. Crane's work-basket, there had been fastened a quantity of feathers which Mr. Crane, being a man of some experience, identified without difficulty as having come from the Wyandotte rooster belonging to Mrs. Purcell next door.

"Good heavens!" said Mr. Crane.

"That isn't all," said his wife.

"Isn't all!"

"He gave a circus," Mrs. Crane explained, in a voice that wavered a little, though whether toward tears or toward the other thing her husband could not be sure. "In the carriage-house. He charged two pins admission, and five pins for the reserved seats, which were the oat-bin. All the children on the street came. Albert, they say there were twenty-two. And he was the ringmaster, and he wore that, and he had your—your riding-crop——"

"I haven't ridden in nine years."

"Well, he had it. And the Purcell rooster was the Great Bird of Paradise from the Jungles of Borneo, only it got away, and they chased it through the Purcells' grape-arbour, and that's how the feathers—and then little Ethel Purcell's kitten was the Blue Tiger of India."

"The *blue* tiger?"

"He dipped it in the bluing," said Mrs. Crane faintly. "Bridget's tub was standing right there. It isn't hurt, Albert. It's only blue. Mrs. Purcell brought it over to show me. She said she thought I ought to see it." Here Mrs. Crane took out her handkerchief and applied it to her eyes; and her husband, observing that her shoulders shook, laid a hand upon one of them with a gentleness he did not feel.

"There, there, Laura. Don't cry. I'll attend to it."

"I'm not crying," said Mrs. Crane in a muffled tone; and went on not crying, so far as he could tell, with considerable vehemence.

Now, it may be said at once that Mr. Albert Crane had very definite views upon the rearing of children, and that these views, like most views upon that subject, had been formed largely in the years before he had any children to rear. He believed in firmness. He believed that a boy should be reasoned with, but reasoned with from a height; that justice should be swift and quiet and adapted to the offence; and that the great error of the age—he had read an article about it in a magazine—was the modern parent's weakness, his habit of laughing at what should be punished, and of punishing, afterward and inconsistently, what he had laughed at before. Mr. Crane did not intend to be a modern parent. He had told his wife so, upon several occasions; and she had agreed with him, upon several occasions, with an air of being entertained by something not visible to him.

He went now to the foot of the stairs and called up them, in the voice he used for refusing extensions of credit:

"Wendell! Come down here, please. I wish to see you in the library."

The steam-calliope, which had been in the midst of an ambitious passage, stopped abruptly. There followed a silence of the kind that is thoughtful; then a door opened, and footsteps began to descend—slowly, one step at a time, with a pause upon each, as of a man going to the scaffold who wishes the crowd to have its full money's worth.

Mr. Crane did not wait to watch. He went into the library and seated himself behind the walnut desk, and, after a moment's consideration, moved the green-shaded lamp so that its light would fall upon the chair opposite rather than upon himself. He laid the ruined hat upon the blotter before him, where it rose in its terraces, gay with its rooster plumes, like a monument to some barbaric and forgotten victory. Then he folded his hands upon the desk, composed his features, and waited.

The door opened, and Wendell came in.

He was not a large boy for his age, but he gave an impression of solidity, as though he had been packed tightly by a manufacturer who did not wish to waste space. He had his mother's round face and his grandfather's chin, which was a chin that had once held out for three weeks against a whole Methodist conference; and he had, at the moment, a long streak of something dark upon one cheek, the nature of which could only be guessed at. His stockings had come down. One of his shoe-laces trailed after him like the painter of a skiff. His expression was one of perfect and unclouded innocence, and his father, who had been a boy himself, found it the most alarming thing about him.

"Close the door, Wendell."

Wendell closed it, and stood by it.

"Come here and sit down."

Wendell came and sat, upon the edge of the chair, with his feet not quite reaching the floor. His eyes went at once to the hat upon the blotter, and rested there with an interest that seemed almost professional. Then they came back to his father's face, and waited, respectfully, for the proceedings to begin.

Mr. Crane allowed the silence to continue for what he judged to be a sufficient period. He had observed that it was effective with borrowers. It did not seem to be effective with Wendell, who employed the interval in an attempt to scratch the back of one knee with the toe of the opposite shoe, and achieved it.

"Wendell," said Mr. Crane at last, "do you know what this is?"

"Yes, sir. It's your hat."

"It *was* my hat," said Mr. Crane, with an emphasis he thought rather good.

Wendell looked at the hat again, and seemed to consider the point honestly. "Well, it's mostly still your hat," he said. "Except the feathers. The feathers are Mrs. Purcell's."

Mr. Crane was conscious that the conversation had taken a direction he had not planned for it. He brought it back.

"Wendell, do you know what that hat cost?"

"No, sir."

"It cost eight dollars."

The figure appeared to impress Wendell profoundly. His eyes widened, and he looked at the hat with a new respect, as one might look at a stranger upon learning that he has been in jail.

"Eight dollars!" he said. "*Gee!*"

"Don't say 'gee.' Yes, eight dollars. That is more money than you will have in your bank until you are a great deal older than you are now. And you took it without asking anybody, out of my closet, where you know perfectly well you are not allowed to go, and you wore it in a—a circus, and you allowed it to be ruined. Did you ever stop to think, even for one moment, that it was not yours?"

"Yes, sir," said Wendell.

His father had expected a denial, or an evasion, or at least the beginning of tears; for each of these he had prepared a suitable rejoinder. Against a simple affirmative he had no defences ready. He was obliged to fall back upon the obvious.

"You did? Then why did you take it?"

Wendell drew a long breath, as a man does who is about to present a case he believes to be unanswerable.

"Well, a ringmaster has *got* to have a tall hat. Everybody knows that. When Sells Brothers came, the ringmaster had a tall hat, and he had a whip, and he had a red coat, only I couldn't find any red coat, so I wore Mamma's shawl. And I asked Georgie Purcell's father if I could borrow *his* tall hat, and he laughed and said I better ask you for yours, so then I thought it would be all right." He paused, and added, with an air of producing the decisive document: "Besides, you said, yourself, a man ought always to look the part."

Mr. Crane had said this. He remembered saying it, some two weeks before, at the supper table, in connection with a young man who had applied for a position at the bank wearing a plaid waistcoat. He had said it with emphasis, and he had elaborated it at some length, for the benefit of his family; and it now occurred to him, with that peculiar chill which the doctrines of the fathers produce when they return upon the fathers in the mouths of the children, that Wendell had been listening.

"That," he said, a little hastily, "is not at all the same thing."

"Why isn't it?"

Mr. Crane opened his mouth to explain why it was not, and discovered, as cashiers and philosophers have discovered before him, that the distinction, though perfectly clear to his own mind, did not lend itself readily to words of one syllable. He closed his mouth again, and took up another line of attack.

"And the rooster," he said. "Mrs. Purcell's rooster. Did you think that was yours, too?"

"No, sir. That was Georgie's idea. Georgie said his mother wouldn't mind, because it was only for a little while, and then we'd put it back. Only it didn't want to be the Bird of Paradise. It wanted to go home. And it went." Wendell's face clouded for the first time, at the memory of this professional disappointment. "It went right through the arbour. Georgie got some of its tail, and I got some, and Ethel Purcell got the rest, and then it went under the porch and wouldn't come out, and Mrs. Purcell came out, and she was pretty mad."

"I should think she might have been."

"Yes, sir, she was." Wendell nodded gravely, as one who acknowledges the justice of an opponent's position without in any way yielding his own. "But we didn't *hurt* it. It's all right. It's just not so long behind as it was."

There is a certain point in every reprimand at which the reprimander, if he be honest with himself, becomes aware that the case is slipping from his hands, and that a stern face, maintained much longer, will require more muscular exertion than he is prepared to give it. Mr. Crane felt that point approaching, and he set his jaw against it. He thought of the magazine article. He thought of the modern parent and his weakness. He thought of eight dollars. He thought, unfortunately, of Mrs. Purcell, a large and determined woman who sang alto in the church choir with a power that had more than once drowned out the organ, pursuing a tailless rooster under her own porch—and he looked very hard at the inkwell.

"And the kitten," he said, when he had mastered the inkwell. "Ethel Purcell's kitten. Your mother tells me you dipped it in the bluing."

"Yes, sir."

"Why?"

Wendell regarded his father with mild surprise, as though the question disclosed a gap in his education which it would be kindly to fill.

"Because it was the Blue Tiger of India," he said patiently. "We couldn't have a Blue Tiger of India that was just *yellow*. People wouldn't have paid five pins for that. They can see yellow cats every day."

"And did you think it was kind," said Mr. Crane, rallying, "to take a poor little helpless animal and plunge it into a tub of cold water?"

"It wasn't so cold. Bridget had just put it in." Wendell considered. "Besides, Ethel said it was all right. She said she'd always wanted a blue cat, and now she's got one, and nobody else in the whole town has. She's *glad*. It was her mother that cried."

At this Mr. Crane rose abruptly from the desk and went to the window, where he stood for some time with his back to the room, looking out at the Purcells' grape-arbour in the dusk. His shoulders, like his wife's an hour earlier, were not altogether steady; and Wendell, watching them with the deep, unblinking attention of the young, may have drawn his own conclusions, though he was wise enough to keep them to himself. When Mr. Crane turned round again, his face was entirely grave, and rather red.

"Wendell," he said, "I want you to listen to me very carefully."

"Yes, sir."

"You have done three wrong things to-day. You took what was not yours. You allowed someone else's property to be damaged, and you frightened Mrs. Purcell. And you treated a little animal in a way that—well, that might have hurt it, even if it didn't. Do you understand why those things are wrong?"

Wendell looked at the floor, and at the hat, and at the lamp, and finally at his father.

"Yes, sir," he said in a lower voice. "I guess I do. Only it was a pretty good circus."

"That," said Mr. Crane, "has nothing whatever to do with it."

"No, sir," Wendell agreed, though without conviction; and there was a pause.

It was during this pause that the father became aware of something he had not foreseen in all his theorizing, and which no magazine article had ever warned him of: namely, that the small culprit before him, with the smear upon his cheek and his stockings about his ankles, was regarding him not with fear, nor with resentment, but with a kind of hopeful and expectant trust—as though Mr. Crane were not the judge at all, but some older and more experienced member of the same profession, who would naturally understand, when all was said and done, that a ringmaster must have a tall hat. And, in a remote and long-closed chamber of his memory, Mr. Albert Crane, cashier of the Second National, beheld another carriage-house, in another town, and a boy of eight in his own father's Prince Albert coat, collecting pins at the door for an exhibition of the Wild Man of Patagonia; and he recollected, with uncomfortable clearness, that the Wild Man had been his little cousin Harriet, painted with stove-blacking, and that the coat had never been the same.

He cleared his throat.

"You will go to bed without your supper to-night," he said. "To-morrow you will go over to Mrs. Purcell's, and you will tell her you are sorry, and you will offer to weed her pansy bed every afternoon for a week. And you will give Ethel Purcell's mother—not Ethel—you will give her mother the pins you took in."

"All of them?" asked Wendell, in real anguish. "There's a hundred and sixty-three."

"All of them."

Wendell bowed his head beneath this sentence with the fortitude of a Roman. He slid from the chair and went to the door, and there he turned.

"Papa?"

"Well?"

"Can I keep the feathers?"

"No," said Mr. Crane. "Go to bed."

And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

There is a kind of silence known only to people who have been married a long while. It is not the silence of strangers, which is merely empty, nor that of lovers, which is full. It is a furnished silence, crowded with old grievances and older habits, and either party may walk about in it at will, bumping into things. Mr. and Mrs. Lamar Dorsey had been married nineteen years, and they had furnished their silence handsomely.

They sat in it now, upon a warm evening in early September, in the front sitting-room of the frame house on Pennington Street which Mr. Dorsey had bought, "on very reasonable terms," the year their daughter Florence was born. He was reading the *Evening News*, or appeared to be; and she was rocking. The rocker had a squeak in it which Mr. Dorsey had promised to oil some time during the second Cleveland administration. Mrs. Dorsey had never reminded him of the promise. She preferred to rock.

Neighbours who passed the lighted window, and glanced in as neighbours will, would have seen nothing more than a pleasant domestic picture: a stoutish, sandy, middle-aged man in his shirt-sleeves, a newspaper held well up before his face, and a handsome woman of forty-odd in a lilac house-gown, her hands folded in her lap, gazing at the gas-log. They might have envied the Dorseys their peace. They would have been mistaken about it. Mrs. Dorsey had come home at half-past five from Mrs. J. Hartley Teague's card party, and she had not yet said one word about it. In nineteen years she had never before returned from a card party without saying a great many words about it, so Mr. Dorsey's newspaper was not so much a newspaper as a fortification.

"Lamar," she said at last.

"Mm?"

"Is there anything in the paper?"

"Nothing much. They're going to pave Hazel Avenue again."

"Again?" said Mrs. Dorsey. "I didn't know they'd ever paved it once."

"Well, they did. That was the trouble." He turned a page, rattling it with what he hoped was an air of absorption. "This fellow says the asphalt was half sawdust. I guess there's been considerable graft in it somewhere."

"I shouldn't wonder," said Mrs. Dorsey. "People are so deceitful nowadays."

The paper did not lower, but it ceased, for an instant, to rattle; and Mr. Dorsey, behind it, cleared his throat with elaborate unconcern. He was a man who had never in his life been able to clear his throat with any unconcern whatever. His wife knew this, and the knowledge was in her voice when she spoke again.

"Mrs. Teague's rooms looked lovely. She had them all done in yellow chrysanthemums. They came from Pfaffinger's, and I suppose they cost a fortune; but then the Teagues can afford it, I suppose. At least they can afford it *now*."

"Well, Hartley's always done pretty well," Mr. Dorsey said, from his entrenchment.

"Yes. And he's going to do better, Mrs. Teague says. A great deal better." She rocked twice; the chair squeaked twice. "She told me all about it, Lamar. She thought I knew. She took it for granted I knew. She said, 'Of course you and Mr. Dorsey must be so relieved it's all settled at last,' and then she said, 'I do think Lamar has been perfectly splendid about it.' Those were her words. 'Perfectly splendid.' And I sat there with my cards in my hand and said, 'Oh, yes, indeed!' like a parrot—like a perfect *parrot*—because I didn't have the faintest idea in the world what the woman was talking about!"

Mr. Dorsey slowly lowered his newspaper and folded it across his knee, smoothing it with a care that might have been bestowed upon a valuable document. He did not look at his wife; he looked at the gas-log. It was as if both of them expected the gas-log to say something.

"I was going to tell you, Addie," he said.

"When?"

"Why, pretty soon. I was just waiting till things got more—more settled."

"Mrs. Teague seems to think they're settled. Mrs. Teague seems to think they've been settled for two weeks. Mrs. Teague knew all about it, and Mrs. Teague's sister-in-law knew all about it, and I shouldn't be surprised if Mrs. Teague's hired girl knew all about it! Everybody in this town knew about it except me!"

"Now, Addie—"

"Don't 'now, Addie' me, Lamar Dorsey! I want to know what it is. I want to hear it from you. I think I have that much right, at least—to hear it from my own husband, instead of having it handed to me over a card table between the third and fourth rubbers, by a woman who used to be glad enough to borrow my egg-beater!"

The egg-beater, though it had been returned these twelve years, evidently still rankled; and Mr. Dorsey, who knew something of the long memory of women for kitchen utensils lent in times of adversity, perceived that the situation was even graver than he had feared. He drew a breath.

"Well," he said, "it's this way. You know old Mr. Pruett died in March."

"Of course I know. We sent flowers."

"Well, his heirs didn't want to keep in the woodenware business. They wanted to sell out his interest, and Hartley and I couldn't buy it—not without mortgaging everything we had, and then some. So this Chicago concern, the Consolidated Kitchen Supply Company, they made an offer for the whole business. They're buying up houses all over the Middle West."

"I know that, too," Mrs. Dorsey said. "You told me that much in June. You said it was 'only a rumour.'"

"Well, it was a rumour then. It got to be more than a rumour along about August." Mr. Dorsey shifted in his chair. "They bought it, Addie. They bought the whole thing—Pruett's share and Hartley's share and mine. It's not Dorsey & Teague any more. It's going to be 'The Consolidated Kitchen Supply Company, Southern Indiana Branch.' They're going to have the sign painted next week."

Mrs. Dorsey stopped rocking.

"Then you've sold out," she said. "Then we've got the money?"

"We've got some money. Not as much as you might think. Pruett's estate got the biggest share, and there were some notes to take up." He cleared his throat again, and this time it was clearly a bad sign. "And they're keeping me on."

"Keeping you on? What do you mean, keeping you on?"

"They want me to stay with the business. They need somebody that knows the trade in this territory, and I guess I know it about as well as anybody. They're giving me a salary. It's a pretty fair salary, too, Addie. It's more than some men in this town get, I can tell you."

"And Hartley Teague?" said Mrs. Dorsey, and her voice had grown very quiet, which was the most ominous thing about it. "Are they 'keeping Hartley on,' too?"

Mr. Dorsey looked at the gas-log with great earnestness.

"No," he said. "Hartley's going to Chicago. They've made him one of the vice-presidents."

The silence that followed was no longer furnished; it was bare as a barn. Mrs. Dorsey sat perfectly still, her hands now gripped together rather than folded, and her handsome face, which had a fine high colour at all times, became of a colour much finer and higher.

"A vice-president!" she said. "Hartley Teague! And you—*you*—you're to be a clerk!"

"I am not to be a clerk! I'm to be branch manager."

"Branch manager! For a company in Chicago! Taking orders from Hartley Teague! Lamar, I never in my life—when I think how that man used to come to *you* for every last thing—when I think how it was always 'I'll have to ask Dorsey' and 'Dorsey'll know about that'—and his wife sitting there this afternoon in a gown that she must have got from Indianapolis if she got it anywhere, telling me how 'perfectly splendid' you'd been! *Splendid!* No wonder she thought you'd been splendid! I should think she would! She meant you'd been splendid about letting her husband walk right over you!"

"Hartley didn't walk over anybody," said Mr. Dorsey, with some heat of his own. "He's got a brother-in-law in the Consolidated, that's all. That's how it goes, in these big concerns. It's who you know."

"Then why didn't you know somebody?"

This was unanswerable, and Mr. Dorsey did not attempt it. He took up the folded newspaper again, looked at it as though he had never before seen such an object, and put it down.

"There's no use your getting all worked up," he said. "I'm getting a good salary and I've got a sure thing. Lots of men my age would be glad of it. I'm not going to have to worry about bad debts any more, nor take inventory with my own two hands, nor lie awake nights wondering whether that Evansville bunch is going to pay up. I'm going to draw my money every month, regular, and the company takes all the risk. I don't see what's so terrible about that."

"You don't see!" cried Mrs. Dorsey. "No, you don't, Lamar! That's just it—you never have! You never *see*! You'd go along for the rest of your life drawing your money every month, regular, and never once think what people were saying!"

"What are people saying?"

"They're saying," said Mrs. Dorsey, rising from the rocker in her agitation, so that it continued to rock and squeak without her, as if in sympathy, "they're saying that Hartley Teague is a big man and Lamar Dorsey is a little one! That's what they're saying! Or they will be, by to-morrow noon. And I'll have to go to the Fortnightly Club on Thursday and sit there and listen to Mrs. Teague read her paper on 'The Women of Shakespeare,' and have every woman in the room looking sideways at me to see how I'm taking it!"

"Well, I don't see that it matters much how a lot of women look at you sideways."

"You wouldn't. It's not you they'll be looking at."

Mr. Dorsey rose, also. He was a mild man, as a rule, but there are limits even to mildness, and he had come upon one of them.

"See here, Addie," he said. "I'd like to know something. I'd like to know just one thing. What were you really mad about when you came in that front door to-night? Were you mad because I'm not going to be a vice-president, or were you mad because I didn't tell you?"

Mrs. Dorsey opened her lips to reply, and then closed them again. She was an honest woman, at bottom; and the question, as is the way with such questions, had gone to the bottom. She turned and walked to the window, where she stood with her back to him, gazing out at the dim street and the maple-leaves stirring under the arc-light at the corner.

"Both," she said finally, in a muffled voice.

"Well, which most?"

She was silent so long that he thought she did not mean to answer. Then she said, without turning round:

"Why didn't you tell me, Lamar?"

He did not answer at once. He walked over to the mantelpiece, picked up a china shepherdess that had stood there since their wedding, examined it with deep attention, and set it down again an inch to the left of its accustomed place, where it looked uneasy for the rest of the evening.

"I guess," he said slowly, "I guess I didn't want to see you look the way you're looking right now."

"How am I looking?"

"Why—disappointed," said Mr. Dorsey. "In me, I mean."

Something in this simple statement produced a change in the back of Mrs. Dorsey's head, though it would have been difficult to say just what the change was. Her shoulders, which had been held very high and straight, lowered a little; and she lifted one hand and touched the lace curtain, absently, as women do when they wish to be doing something with their hands.

"I'm not disappointed in you," she said.

"Yes, you are, Addie."

"I'm not! I'm disappointed in—in *things*. That's different."

"I don't know that it's so very different," said Mr. Dorsey. "Things are mostly people, when you come down to it." He paused, and then added, with an awkwardness that made the words sound as though they were being pried out of him: "You always did think I'd amount to more than I have."

"Lamar!"

"Well, you did. I knew it right from the start. When you married me you thought I'd be like your father, or better. I knew you did. I guess every girl thinks that." He picked up the shepherdess again, found it offered no help, and put it back. "I tried, Addie. I tried pretty hard. But I never was the kind that pushes. Hartley pushes. He always did. Even when we were boys in school, Hartley used to push. I'm not built that way."

Mrs. Dorsey turned from the window. Her eyes were bright, and she was biting her lower lip, which was a thing she had not done since she was a girl, and which her daughter Florence had been told, many times, was a vulgar habit.

"I never asked you to push," she said. "I never asked you for a thing!"

He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. “Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“Well, but look how she’s thrown him over for it.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. She’s probably mistaken, but that’s what she thinks, and it’s too late for her to think anything else now, because she’s going to be married right away—the invitations will be out next week. It’ll be a big Amberson-style thing, raw oysters floating in scooped-out blocks of ice and a band from out-of-town—champagne, showy presents; a colossal present from the Major. The wedding was of Ambersonian magnificence, even to the floating oysters; and the Major’s colossal present was a set of architect’s designs for a house almost as elaborate and impressive as the Mansion, the house to be built in Amberson Addition by the Major. The orchestra was certainly not that local one which had suffered the loss of a bass viol; the musicians came, according to the prophecy and next morning’s paper, from afar; and at midnight the bride was still being toasted in champagne, though she had departed upon her wedding journey at ten. He did not, however, come again to the Major’s Sunday evening dinner, even when George Amberson returned. Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. When Lucy came home the autumn was far enough advanced to smell of burning leaves, and for the annual editorials, in the papers, on the purple haze, the golden branches, the ruddy fruit, and the pleasure of long tramps in the brown forest. George had not heard of her arrival, and he met her, on the afternoon following that event, at the Sharons’, where he had gone in the secret hope that he might hear something about her. Janie Sharon had just begun to tell him that she heard Lucy was expected home soon, after having “a perfectly gorgeous time”—information which George received with no responsive enthusiasm—when Lucy came demurely in, a proper little autumn figure in green and brown. Her cheeks were flushed, and her dark eyes were bright indeed; evidences, as George supposed, of the excitement incidental to the perfectly gorgeous time just concluded; though Janie and Mary Sharon both thought they were the effect of Lucy’s having seen George’s runabout in front of the house as she came in. George took on colour, himself, as, he rose and nodded indifferently; and the hot suffusion to which he became subject extended its area to include his neck and ears. Nothing could have made him much more indignant than his consciousness of these symptoms of the icy indifference which it was his purpose not only to show but to feel. She kissed her cousins, gave George her hand, said “How d’you do,” and took a chair beside Janie with a composure which augmented George’s indignation.

“How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Then, to cover his awkwardness, he coughed, and even to his own rosy ears his cough was ostentatiously a false one. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage. He drove into the Major’s stable too fast, the sagacious Pendennis saving himself from going through a partition by a swerve which splintered a shaft of the runabout and almost threw the driver to the floor. George swore, and then swore again at the fat old darkey, Tom, for giggling at his swearing.

“Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.
