However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

The return of Mr. Thomas Ridgely Carmody to the town of his boyhood was not, in the strict sense, an event; yet it was treated as one by a number of ladies whose windows commanded a view of Linden Street, and by at least one gentleman, old Judge Henley, who had sat behind young Thomas in church for nine years and still recalled, with no softening, the boy's habit of dropping hymnals. Eleven years had passed since the Carmodys removed to the East. The town had grown in that time, as towns of the Middle West were then growing, rapidly and somewhat carelessly, like a boy who outgrows his trousers before anyone has noticed the trousers were getting short. A trolley line now ran where the mule-car had dawdled. The old Bream place on Harrison Street had been "cut up into lots," and a row of narrow frame houses stood upon what had once been the finest strawberry bed in the county. These were matters of no great consequence to anybody except the people who had eaten the strawberries.

Mr. Carmody arrived upon the noon train. He descended with a walking-stick, a pair of pearl-gray spats, and an expression intended to convey that he had seen a great many railway stations and found this one, upon the whole, about what he had expected. The hackman who drove him to Linden Street reported afterward that the young man had addressed him as "my good fellow," and had asked whether the town "still had that rather jolly little park by the courthouse," as though the park were something a town might mislay. The hackman, a literal person, replied that it did, so far as he knew, unless somebody had took it in the night.

His cousin, who had been Adelaide Bream and was now Mrs. Lucius Pruett, was waiting for him on her front porch. She had been waiting there for some time; she had, in fact, put on and taken off two different shirtwaists before settling upon the third, which she considered the least likely to look as though she had thought about it. Her two children, Lucius Junior, aged seven, and a smaller person called Bunny, were stationed beside her under strict instructions to be good, and were already showing the strain. When the hack stopped at the gate, Lucius Junior was heard to inquire, in a voice that carried with great clarity to the Kessler house next door, "Is that him? What's he got on his feet?"

"Hush!" said his mother. "Those are spats."

"What are spats for?"

"Hush, I say! Go and shake hands with your Cousin Thomas."

But Lucius Junior did not go; he remained rooted, regarding the visitor's ankles with the profound and unwinking attention which children reserve for very large dogs and very small funerals. Mrs. Pruett, therefore, went down the walk herself; and the two cousins met halfway between the gate and the steps, under the maple tree, where, for an instant, neither appeared to know quite what to do. Then Adelaide laughed, and put both hands on his shoulders, and kissed him upon the cheek, a proceeding which Mr. Carmody received with an air of slightly alarmed gallantry.

"Why, Tod!" she cried. "Why, Toddles Carmody! I'd never have known you, never in this world!"

"My dear Adelaide," he said, and bowed a little over her hand, though she had already withdrawn it. "Charmed—really charmed. You're looking remarkably well. Remarkably."

"Remarkably!" she repeated, and laughed again. "Listen to him! 'Remarkably!' Well, I suppose I ought to be, at my age. Come up on the porch and be introduced. Lucius isn't home yet; he never gets away from the store before half-past five, and if there's a farmer in town wanting a pump he doesn't get away then. Children, this is your Cousin Thomas, that I've told you about."

Bunny, who was four, immediately put her thumb into her mouth and went behind her mother's skirt. Lucius Junior, however, advanced one step, and offered a remark which he had evidently been preparing.

"Mamma says you fell in the rain barrel."

"Lucius!"

"Well, you did say it. You said he fell in the rain barrel at Grandpa Bream's, and you had to pull him out by the legs, and he hollered."

Mr. Carmody's colour rose perceptibly above the line of his very high collar. "I'm afraid," he said, with a laugh that he intended to be easy, "that your mother's memory is—ah—somewhat more vivid than accurate."

"It is not!" said Adelaide. "You did fall in, and I did pull you out, and you did holler. You hollered so that Mrs. Gilpin came running all the way from across the alley with her apron full of clothespins. Don't you remember?"

"I can't say that I do," said Mr. Carmody. "It's so very long ago, you know. One forgets these—these rustic episodes."

"Rustic!" said Adelaide. "Oh, Tod!"

It was perhaps unfortunate for the young man that his cousin possessed a sense of humour, for nothing is so trying to a person of elegance as a relative who remembers him without it. Adelaide had been, in childhood, the elder by a year and the larger by several inches; she had been the leader of every expedition, the arbiter of every dispute, and the inventor of most of the punishments; and it was plain, even in this first moment, that she had never quite ceased to regard him as a small boy in short trousers who would get into difficulties if not watched. Mr. Carmody, on the other hand, had spent eleven years in becoming a person of whom nothing of the kind could be suspected, and he had brought these eleven years with him, together with his spats, as evidence.

They sat upon the porch, in two wicker rockers, and Adelaide sent Lucius Junior to the kitchen with instructions to tell Hilda to bring the lemonade. The order was received without enthusiasm, but obeyed, because Lucius Junior hoped to be present when the visitor took off his spats, and feared that he might do it while unobserved.

"Well," said Adelaide, folding her hands and looking at her cousin with frank delight, "tell me everything. Tell me all about yourself. Aunt Margaret writes to Mother, of course, but Aunt Margaret never tells anything except who's been sick. What have you been doing all these years?"

Mr. Carmody crossed his knees, laid his walking-stick across them, and contemplated the maple tree.

"Oh, one keeps busy," he said. "Business, you know—and a certain amount of the other thing. One has one's obligations. I'm associated with a rather large concern in New York—bonds and that sort of thing. Rather a responsible position, in its way. One can't always get off when one likes; I had the greatest difficulty in arranging this little trip."

"Bonds!" said Adelaide respectfully. "My! Lucius will be interested. He bought a bond once—a waterworks bond, from a man that came through here. It was the waterworks at some town in Kansas, and it turned out there wasn't any waterworks. Lucius always said afterward there wasn't any town either, but I think there was a town; I think it was just the waterworks that wasn't."

"Ah," said Mr. Carmody, with a slight compression of the lips. "Our concern doesn't deal in that class of security, I assure you."

"Oh, I'm sure it doesn't," she said hastily. "I didn't mean—Do you go out a great deal? Aunt Margaret said once you'd been to Newport."

"Not exactly," said Mr. Carmody.

"I do now," he said, and laughed; and this time he did not check himself.

A sign in the front window said "Rooms—Table Board," and a young man in a celluloid collar was sitting on the steps, picking his teeth with an air of permanent residence. They did not go in. They went instead along the side, by the alley, to where a fragment of the old barn still stood, now used, evidently, for the storage of coal; and beside it, at the corner where the downspout came off the roof, there was a barrel.

It was not the same barrel. It could not have been the same barrel, after eleven years; it was a newer, meaner barrel, and it stood on a slant upon two loose bricks, and there was a dead leaf floating in it. "It came up to here on me," said Mr. Carmody at last, and held his hand at about the level of his waistcoat pocket. "I was standing on the chopping-block, trying to sail a shingle in it. And you said I couldn't reach the middle, and I said I could."

"And you couldn't," said Adelaide.

"You said so," said Adelaide softly. "When I got you out. You were all over mud, and crying, and you said, 'Now I won't ever see the elephant.' And I told you you would, and I gave you my circus money so you could, because you'd spent yours on a mouth-organ."

"You never knew it," she said. "I told you I'd found a quarter."

There was another silence. Mr. Carmody poked at the dead leaf in the barrel with the ferrule of his stick.

"I'm a clerk. In the bond department. There are forty of us. I sit on a stool and add up columns, and the case was given me by the fellows in the office when I'd been there five years, and it isn't silver; it's plated. And I went to Newport once, last August, for four days, because one of the junior partners wanted somebody to help carry things for his mother. There! I don't know why I'm telling you. I suppose you think I'm a fearful ass."

Adelaide did not answer immediately. She was looking at the barrel too; and when at last she spoke, her voice had in it that quality, maddening to all men and to small boys particularly, of a person who has known a thing all along and is being kind about it.

"Aunt Margaret writes to Mother every two weeks, Tod," she said. "She tells who's been sick. But she tells everything else too."

He stared at her. "You knew? All the time you knew?"

"Of course I knew."

"Then why on earth," he demanded, with mounting indignation, "did you let me go on? About Newport, and the—and dining out every evening, and all of it? Why didn't you say something?"

"Because you were having such a good time," said Adelaide simply. "And because—oh, I don't know. Because you'd come all this way, and you looked so nice, and I didn't want to be the one to pull you out of the barrel this time. I thought maybe you'd climb out by yourself." She laughed, and put her hand through his arm. "And you did, didn't you?"

Mr. Carmody opened his mouth to reply, and found that he had nothing ready; and so, for the first time in a number of years, he said nothing at all, but merely stood there beside his cousin, a young man of twenty-nine in pearl-gray spats, feeling remarkably like a boy of eight who has been fished out of something and is not yet certain whether to be grateful or furious. It is an uncomfortable sensation; and it is, perhaps, the nearest approach to wisdom that most of us are permitted.

"Come home to supper," said Adelaide. "Lucius will be back, and Hilda's made a chicken pie, and you can tell him about bonds. He won't know whether you're a clerk or a partner; he only wants to know whether they're any good."

"They're not, most of them," said Mr. Carmody, and laughed.

They walked back under the elms, arm in arm, and it was observed by Mrs. Kessler, who happened to be examining her own rosebush when they returned, that the visitor had his hat pushed back upon his head and was swinging his walking-stick like a boy with a switch. "He's not so stuck-up as he looked," she reported that evening to Mrs. Purdy, whose husband had watered her. "I guess it was just the spats."

Mrs. Purdy, whose views upon the human race had been somewhat dampened, said that in her experience it was never just the spats.

Both ladies were partly right, as both ladies usually were. Mr. Carmody stayed three days, ate four of Hilda's chicken pies in succession, mended a kite for Lucius Junior, and permitted Bunny to unbutton his spats and wear them upon her arms as cuffs, a privilege she exercised with great solemnity throughout an entire afternoon. He departed upon the Thursday morning train with a shoebox of fried chicken under his arm and a promise to come again at Christmas. But he looked out of the window, after that, for a long while, as the town and its elms slid away behind him; and once, unaccountably, he laughed aloud.

You’ve probably got plenty of friends, for instance, that don’t care much about your son—” “No, indeed!” she protested quickly. “And if I knew anybody who felt like that, I wouldn’t—” “Never mind,” he interrupted. “I’ll try to explain a little more. If I have a friend, I don’t see that it’s incumbent upon me to like that friend’s relatives. If I didn’t like them, and pretended to, I’d be a hypocrite. If that friend likes me and wants to stay my friend he’ll have to stand my not liking his relatives, or else he can quit. I decline to be a hypocrite about it; that’s all. Now, suppose I have certain ideas or ideals which I have chosen for the regulation of my own conduct in life. Suppose some friend of mine has a relative with ideals directly the opposite of mine, and my friend believes more in the relative’s ideals than in mine: Do you think I ought to give up my own just to please a person who’s taken up ideals that I really despise?”

“No, dear; of course people can’t give up their ideals; but I don’t see what this has to do with dear little Lucy and—” “I didn’t say it had anything to do with them,” he interrupted. “I was merely putting a case to show how a person would be justified in being a friend of one member of a family, and feeling anything but friendly toward another. I don’t say, though, that I feel unfriendly to Mr. Morgan. I don’t say that I feel friendly to him, and I don’t say that I feel unfriendly; but if you really think that I was rude to him to-night—” “Just thoughtless, dear. You didn’t see that what you said to-night—” “Well, I’ll not say anything of that sort again where he can hear it. There, isn’t that enough?” This question, delivered with large indulgence, met with no response; for Isabel, still searching his face with her troubled and perplexed gaze, seemed not to have heard it. On that account, George repeated it, and rising, went to her and patted her reassuringly upon the shoulder. “There, old lady, you needn’t fear my tactlessness will worry you again. I can’t quite promise to like people I don’t care about one way or another, but you can be sure I’ll be careful, after this, not to let them see it. It’s all right, and you’d better toddle along to bed, because I want to undress.”

“But, George,” she said earnestly, “you would like him, if you’d just let yourself. You say you don’t dislike him. Why don’t you like him? I can’t understand at all. What is it that you don’t—” “There, there!” he said. “It’s all right, and you toddle along.”

“But, George, dear—” “Now, now! I really do want to get into bed. Good-night, old lady.”

“Good-night, dear. But—” “Let’s not talk of it any more,” he said. “It’s all right, and nothing in the world to worry about. So good-night, old lady. I’ll be polite enough to him, never fear—if we happen to be thrown together. So good-night!”

“But, George, dear—” “I’m going to bed, old lady; so good-night.” Thus the interview closed perforce. She kissed him again before going slowly to her own room, her perplexity evidently not dispersed; but the subject was not renewed between them the next day or subsequently. Nor did Fanny make any allusion to the cryptic approbation she had bestowed upon her nephew after the Major’s “not very successful little dinner”; though she annoyed George by looking at him oftener and longer than he cared to be looked at by an aunt. He could not glance her way, it seemed, without finding her red-rimmed eyes fixed upon him eagerly, with an alert and hopeful calculation in them which he declared would send a nervous man into fits. For thus, one day, he broke out, in protest: “It would!” he repeated vehemently. “Given time it would—straight into fits! What do you find the matter with me? Is my tie always slipping up behind? Can’t you look at something else? My Lord! We’d better buy a cat for you to stare at, Aunt Fanny! A cat could stand it, maybe. What in the name of goodness do you expect to see?” But Fanny laughed good-naturedly, and was not offended. “It’s more as if I expected you to see something, isn’t it?” she said quietly, still laughing.

“Now, what do you mean by that?”

“Never mind!”

“All right, I don’t. But for heaven’s sake stare at somebody else awhile. Try it on the house-maid!”

“Well, well,” Fanny said indulgently, and then chose to be more obscure in her meaning than ever, for she adopted a tone of deep sympathy for her final remark, as she left him: “I don’t wonder you’re nervous these days, poor boy!” And George indignantly supposed that she referred to the ordeal of Lucy’s continued absence. During this period he successfully avoided contact with Lucy’s father, though Eugene came frequently to the house, and spent several evenings with Isabel and Fanny; and sometimes persuaded them and the Major to go for an afternoon’s motoring. He did not, however, come again to the Major’s Sunday evening dinner, even when George Amberson returned. Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. When Lucy came home the autumn was far enough advanced to smell of burning leaves, and for the annual editorials, in the papers, on the purple haze, the golden branches, the ruddy fruit, and the pleasure of long tramps in the brown forest. George had not heard of her arrival, and he met her, on the afternoon following that event, at the Sharons’, where he had gone in the secret hope that he might hear something about her. Janie Sharon had just begun to tell him that she heard Lucy was expected home soon, after having “a perfectly gorgeous time”—information which George received with no responsive enthusiasm—when Lucy came demurely in, a proper little autumn figure in green and brown. Her cheeks were flushed, and her dark eyes were bright indeed; evidences, as George supposed, of the excitement incidental to the perfectly gorgeous time just concluded; though Janie and Mary Sharon both thought they were the effect of Lucy’s having seen George’s runabout in front of the house as she came in. George took on colour, himself, as, he rose and nodded indifferently; and the hot suffusion to which he became subject extended its area to include his neck and ears. Nothing could have made him much more indignant than his consciousness of these symptoms of the icy indifference which it was his purpose not only to show but to feel. She kissed her cousins, gave George her hand, said “How d’you do,” and took a chair beside Janie with a composure which augmented George’s indignation.

“How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Then, to cover his awkwardness, he coughed, and even to his own rosy ears his cough was ostentatiously a false one. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage. He drove into the Major’s stable too fast, the sagacious Pendennis saving himself from going through a partition by a swerve which splintered a shaft of the runabout and almost threw the driver to the floor. George swore, and then swore again at the fat old darkey, Tom, for giggling at his swearing.

“Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mr. Lucius Pell, of the Pell Hardware & Cutlery Company, was a man who had given a great deal of thought to the bringing up of children, and had arrived, at the age of forty-one, at a set of conclusions upon the subject so firm and so thoroughly considered that he was able to state them, upon request or without it, in less than a minute. A boy, according to Mr. Pell, was to be reasoned with; he was to be shown, calmly and with dignity, the error of his course; he was never to be struck in anger, nor shouted at, nor threatened with the bogey-man, nor bribed with doughnuts; and, above all, he was to be made to understand that his father was not his enemy but his best friend. These principles Mr. Pell had read, in substance, in a little book called "The Parent's Lamp," which a travelling gentleman had sold him one afternoon at the store, and he had improved upon them since by long reflection. He had, moreover, the great advantage of possessing a son upon whom to test them, and the even greater advantage, common to most theorists, of not having tested them very often.

The son was named Herbert Lucius Pell, and was eight years old, though there were times when the neighbourhood estimated him at somewhat higher. He was a sturdy, freckled, innocent-eyed person, with a cowlick that no water could subdue and a habit of looking straight at grown people while they talked to him, an attention which they usually mistook for respect. His mother called him "Bertie"; the boys of Sycamore Street called him "Pelly," or, in moments of strong feeling, "Ole Pell-mell"; and his father, upon formal occasions, called him "Herbert," which was a sign to the boy, as clear as a storm-flag over a lake steamer's office, that something was about to "happen."

On a certain warm evening in May, Mr. Pell came home from the store a little later than usual, set his umbrella in the rack in the front hall, hung up his alpaca coat, and went upstairs to his bedroom to brush himself for supper. He was a precise man, and it was his custom, before descending, to open the door of his wardrobe and glance at the round leather box upon its upper shelf. The box contained his silk hat. It was the only silk hat on Sycamore Street, and Mr. Pell had worn it upon nine occasions in four years: six funerals, two weddings, and the dedication of the new Odd Fellows' Hall. He was to wear it again on the following Thursday, when, as Past Grand of his lodge, he would ride in an open carriage at the head of the Decoration Day procession, directly behind the band; and it may be said that he looked at the leather box, these evenings, somewhat as a bride looks at her veil.

He looked at it now. Then, for no reason he could afterward name, except that a man sometimes has a premonition, he lifted it down and raised the lid.

The box was empty, except for a horned toad.

The horned toad looked up at Mr. Pell, and Mr. Pell looked down at the horned toad, and for some moments neither of them did anything at all. The creature was alive, and appeared to be comfortable; it had been furnished with a saucer of water and a lettuce leaf, and someone had thoughtfully punched a number of holes in the lid with a nail. Mr. Pell observed these holes, and the expression of his face underwent a change. He replaced the lid with great care, set the box upon the bed, and went to the head of the stairs.

"Mother," he called, in a voice of remarkable evenness, "will you ask Herbert to step up here a moment?"

There was a pause below. Mrs. Pell had been married to Mr. Pell for eleven years, and she knew the difference between "Bertie" and "Herbert" quite as well as did her son.

"Why, what is it, Lucius?"

"I should like to see Herbert," said Mr. Pell, "for a moment. Up here."

"He's out in the yard. Lucius, has he done something?"

"That," said Mr. Pell, "is what I propose to ascertain."

Mrs. Pell went to the kitchen door and called, and presently, after the interval which is necessary to any boy who hears his name spoken in an unfamiliar tone, and who must first finish what he is doing in order to be in a proper frame of mind, Herbert came in from the back yard. He had been occupied, with two friends named Orville Stamm and Daisy Mulhall's little brother, in digging what was to be a cave, and he brought a good deal of it with him. His mother looked at him anxiously.

"Bertie, your father wants you upstairs. Bertie, what have you done?"

"Nothin'," said Herbert promptly. It was the answer he always gave, and it had the merit, from his point of view, of being comprehensive; for it is a fact well established among boys that most of what grown people call doing something is, properly considered, doing nothing in particular.

"Well, go wash your hands first," his mother said; and then, with a sudden misgiving, "No—go right up. Don't keep him waiting."

Herbert went up the stairs one at a time, and slowly, holding to the banister in a manner that suggested he had lately been taken very ill. At the top he found his father seated in the rocking-chair by the bedroom window, his hands folded upon his waistcoat; and upon the bed, plainly visible in the slanting light, lay the leather hat-box. Herbert looked at it, and then looked at his father, and his face assumed that expression of grave and courteous interest with which a well-bred stranger regards a monument in a town he is passing through.

"Close the door, Herbert," said Mr. Pell.

Herbert closed the door.

"Now come here and stand before me."

Herbert came and stood before him. He stood with his feet wide apart and his hands behind him, which was the attitude of Napoleon in a picture at school, and it gave him a certain comfort.

Mr. Pell regarded him for some time in silence. This silence was in accordance with the third chapter of "The Parent's Lamp," which advised that the erring child be allowed a few moments in which "to collect his thoughts and feel the weight of the occasion." Herbert, however, made use of the few moments chiefly to observe that his father had a small piece of court-plaster on his chin where he had cut himself shaving, and to wonder whether it would come off if he talked very hard.

"Herbert," said Mr. Pell at last, "do you know what is in that box?"

Herbert considered the question. It seemed to him a fair one, and he wished to answer it accurately.

"Yes, sir."

"What is in it?"

"Horned toad."

"Whose horned toad?"

"Mine," said Herbert, and added, with some pride, "His name's General Grant."

"I see," said Mr. Pell. He unfolded his hands and folded them again the other way. "And what, Herbert, was in that box before General Grant was put into it?"

A shadow of difficulty passed over Herbert's face, as of one who perceives that a conversation is taking a turn he had not anticipated. "Well," he said, "there was a hat in it."

"Whose hat?"

"Your hat, papa."

"And where," said Mr. Pell, "is that hat now?"

Herbert shifted his weight from one foot to the other, and the Napoleonic attitude suffered somewhat. "Well, I guess—I guess prob'ly Mr. Isaacs has got it."

"Mr. Isaacs?"

"The rag man," Herbert explained helpfully. "The one that's got the wagon with the bells on, an' the horse that's blind in one eye. Not the other one, the one that hollers 'Rags-a-bottles.' Mr. Isaacs doesn't holler. He just rings."

Mr. Pell closed his eyes for a moment. When he opened them, his voice was still level, though it had begun to resemble a level which has been set upon a slight incline.

"Do you mean to tell me, Herbert, that you gave my silk hat to a rag man?"

"No, sir," said Herbert, relieved to be able to correct a misapprehension. "I didn't give it to him. I traded it."

"You traded it."

"Yes, sir. He gave me General Grant for it, an' a whistle." He brought one hand from behind him and displayed, as evidence of good faith, a tin whistle painted red. "It's a good whistle," he said earnestly. "It's got two notes. Listen—"

"Do not blow that whistle!"

Herbert did not blow it. He returned it to its place behind his back, and looked at his father with the patient, slightly wounded air of a merchant whose goods have not been appreciated.

It is here necessary to record that Mr. Pell, at this point, very nearly abandoned "The Parent's Lamp" altogether, and reverted to the methods of his own father, a blacksmith of Clark County who had not read any books on the subject and had reared seven sons with notable success. The impulse passed, however; Mr. Pell was a man of principle, and he was conscious, moreover, that his wife was almost certainly standing at the foot of the stairs, listening. He drew a long breath through his nose.

"Herbert," he said, "I am not going to punish you."

Herbert's face brightened.

"Not yet," said Mr. Pell; and the face clouded again. "I am going to reason with you. I want you to understand, Herbert, that I am your friend. I am not your enemy. I am your best friend. Do you understand that?"

"Yes, sir," said Herbert, without conviction.

"Very well. Then as your friend, I want to ask you a question, and I want you to answer it truthfully, because a boy who tells the truth to his best friend has nothing to fear. Why did you trade my hat to Mr. Isaacs?"

Herbert's expression became one of honest surprise, as if the reason were so evident that it could hardly need stating. "Why, so's you wouldn't haf to wear it."

"So that I—what?"

"So's you wouldn't haf to wear it in the p'rade," said Herbert. "You said you didn't want to."

"I said nothing of the kind!"

"Yes, you did, papa. You said it at supper. You said it Sunday. Mamma said you'd have to wear your silk hat in the p'rade, an' you said, 'Oh, Lord, that ole stovepipe!' An' you said it made you look like a undertaker. An' you said you'd give five dollars not to haf to wear it, only you'd haf to, on account of bein' Past Grand. You said it, papa," he concluded, with the quiet firmness of a witness who has the court record on his side. "Mamma heard you."

Mr. Pell opened his mouth, and then, after a moment, shut it again. It was true. He remembered now, with a peculiar sinking of the spirit, that he had said precisely these things, on Sunday, over the roast chicken, in a moment of what he had considered harmless humour. He had even, he recalled, made a little face, which his son had admired and attempted to reproduce. It is one of the minor tragedies of fatherhood that a man may say a hundred wise things at his table and have every one of them forgotten before the pie, while the single foolish thing he says will be remembered, word for word, and acted upon.

"That," said Mr. Pell, recovering himself, "was a joke."

"Was it?" said Herbert, interested. "It didn't sound like one."

"It was a joke," Mr. Pell repeated, more firmly, "and you should have known it was a joke. Grown people often say things they don't mean."

Herbert received this information thoughtfully, and it was evident that he was filing it away for future use; but at the moment he had a further point to make.

"Well, anyway," he said, "Mr. Isaacs said it wasn't worth much. He said it was all wore out inside, an' had a dent. I showed him where the dent was. He said he wouldn't hardly give a nickel for it, only he liked me. He said he'd give me General Grant an' the whistle just because I was a nice little feller. So I guess," Herbert finished generously, "I guess I didn't do so bad."

Mr. Pell, who had paid eleven dollars for the hat at Fenstermaker's in the year of the Odd Fellows' Hall, and who knew perfectly well where the dent was, and how it had got there (at the Sloane funeral, when the carriage door had been closed too quickly), now experienced sensations which "The Parent's Lamp" had not anticipated in any of its chapters. He rose from the rocking-chair and walked to the window and back again.

"Herbert," he said, "where did you get the idea that you could trade away things that don't belong to you?"

"Well, Orville Stamm traded his father's ole razor strop for a jew's-harp," said Herbert, "an' nothin' happened to him."

"I am not Orville Stamm's father."

"No, sir," Herbert agreed. "Mr. Stamm's fatter."

Mr. Pell turned away abruptly and looked out of the window. There was nothing to be seen there except the Kesslers' woodshed and the back of the Kesslers' cow; but he looked at them for some time, and his shoulders made a slight motion which might have been caused by a draught. When he turned again his face was very stern indeed—sterner, Herbert thought, than it had been at any previous point in the interview.

"Do you know what that hat cost, Herbert?"

"No, sir."

"It cost eleven dollars."

Herbert was impressed. Eleven dollars was a sum without definite meaning to him, but it was larger than any sum he had ever heard of in connection with a hat, and he looked at the leather box with new respect.

"Golly!" he said softly. "Then I guess Mr. Isaacs cheated me."

"Mr. Isaacs," said Mr. Pell, "did nothing of the sort. Mr. Isaacs has no idea what—never mind Mr. Isaacs! The point is, Herbert, that you have taken something that was not yours and disposed of it without permission. Do you know what that is called?"

Herbert thought. "Tradin'?"

"It is called," said Mr. Pell slowly, "something very much worse than trading. And if you were a grown man, you might be sent to a place where you would not like to be sent. Do you understand?"

Herbert's eyes grew very round. He had heard of this place; there had been a man in it once who used to drive the ice wagon, and the boys of Sycamore Street spoke of him in whispers. For the first time in the interview he appeared genuinely moved, and his lower lip, which had been very steady, began to behave in a manner of its own.

"I didn't mean to," he said. "I thought—I thought you'd be glad, papa. I thought you'd come home an' say, 'Where's that ole stovepipe?' an' I'd say, 'It's gone, papa, you don't haf to wear it,' an' you'd—you'd—" Here the lip got entirely out of hand, and Herbert, who had resolved under no circumstances to cry, since Orville Stamm and Daisy Mulhall's little brother were almost certainly listening beneath the window, cried.

It was a short cry, but a thorough one; and it had upon Mr. Pell the effect which such things have upon most fathers who have been reasoning with their sons according to a system. All at once he was aware that the room was very warm, that his collar was too tight, and that he did not feel at all like a man who has been firm and judicious, but rather like one who has kicked a small dog that had brought him a present. He put out his hand, and, after a moment's hesitation, laid it upon the cowlick, which immediately sprang up again between his fingers.

"There, there," he said gruffly. "There, there. That'll do. Stop it now."

Herbert stopped it, or very nearly, and wiped his face upon his sleeve, thereby distributing the cave more evenly over his features.

"Now, listen to me, Herbert," said Mr. Pell, sitting down again in the rocking-chair, but this time drawing the boy toward him. "You meant well. I can see you meant well. But meaning well isn't enough. A man has to think, too. You can't go doing things for people without asking them whether they want them done. Do you see that?"

"Yes, sir."

"And you mustn't ever—ever—trade away anything in this house again without asking your mother or me. Not anything. Not a spool of thread. Do you promise me that?"

"Yes, sir," said Herbert, and added, after due reflection, "Can I trade my own things?"

"Your own things," said Mr. Pell, "are your own affair."

Herbert seemed comforted by this, and his glance strayed, not without a certain proprietary affection, toward the leather box upon the bed.

"Then I can keep General Grant?"

Mr. Pell looked at the box, and then at his son, and it occurred to him, not for the first time in his life, that there are moments when a principle, however carefully thought out, does not quite cover the facts.

"We will discuss General Grant," he said, "at some later time. Now go downstairs and wash your face and tell your mother I'll be down directly. And, Herbert—"

"Yes, sir?"

"You will go without dessert to-night."

Herbert accepted this sentence with the composure of one who has expected the gallows and been let off with a fine. He went to the door, opened it, and then paused upon the threshold, with his hand upon the knob.

"Papa?"

"Well?"

"Will you haf to wear your ole derby in the p'rade now?"

"I don't know," said Mr. Pell shortly. "Go on downstairs."

Herbert went, and his father heard him descending in a rapid series of thumps quite unlike the halting progress by which he had come up; then the back screen door slammed, and from beneath the window there arose an eager murmur of young voices, through which one voice could be distinguished above the rest.

"Gee, he talked to me somep'm terrible! He said I'd go to jail if I was growed up. He said it was worth eleven dollars. Eleven dollars! An' I never got licked at all—only no pie."

"Golly!" said the voice of Orville Stamm, in which envy and respect were mingled. "My pa'd 'a' licked me."

"Well, my papa doesn't believe in it," said Herbert, with lofty indifference. "He's got a book."

Mr. Pell sat for some time in the rocking-chair after the voices had moved off toward the cave. Then he rose, took his alpaca coat from the hook where his wife had hung it, put it on, and went quietly down the front stairs and out of the front door, avoiding the dining-room, from which there came an odour of fried ham and the sound of Mrs. Pell asking Herbert, in a low and anxious voice, what his father had said.

It was nearly dark when he found Mr. Isaacs' wagon, in the alley behind the Methodist church, with the blind-eyed horse eating out of a nose-bag and Mr. Isaacs himself seated upon the tailboard, smoking a short pipe in the twilight. Mr. Pell's silk hat was upon his head. It sat a little far back, and the dent was plainly visible; but there was something in the angle at which Mr. Isaacs wore it, a certain dreamy contentment, that gave Mr. Pell pause.

"Evening," said Mr. Pell.

"Good evening, Mr. Pell," said the rag man, and, perceiving the direction of his visitor's gaze, he removed the hat and turned it slowly in his hands, with the air of a man who has been expecting a call and is not surprised to receive it. "A nice little feller, your boy," he said. "Very nice. He makes a hard bargain."

The terms upon which the hat was recovered were never made public. Mr. Pell, upon his return, said only that he had "fixed it up," and it was observed that he was a little short with the change when the paper boy came on Saturday. But on Decoration Day, when the procession went by the Pell house behind the band, the boys of Sycamore Street saw the Past Grand riding in his open carriage, very upright, in his silk hat; and those who looked closely remarked that the dent was gone, Mr. Isaacs having knocked it out with his thumb as a courtesy, by way of discount.

And Herbert, watching from the front steps, with General Grant in a cigar box under his arm, blew the red whistle twice, both notes, as his father passed; and Mr. Pell, it was afterward reported by Mrs. Pell, who had been standing behind the screen door, very nearly touched his hat.
