The cold had come down out of the north in the night, and by morning the spirit thermometer nailed outside the door of the cabin stood at sixty-three below. It was the kind of cold that does not bite so much as it crushes, settling upon the land like a weight, so that the spruce trees stood rigid and motionless, and the very smoke from the chimney rose straight as a ramrod into the pale air before it lost heart and spread out thinly and hung there, a gray roof above a white world. There was no wind. There was no sound. There was only the cold and the silence, and the long twilight that passed for day in that latitude at that season of the year.

Inside the cabin it was warm enough, for the stove was red and Jim Hollister had seen to it that the woodpile outside was high. He sat on an upturned box near the stove, mending a dog harness with a sail needle and a length of sinew, and his big hands moved slowly and with care, for there was nothing in all the Northland a man needed to hurry over in the dead of winter except dying. He was a large man, broad in the shoulder and deep in the chest, with a face that the frost and the wind had worked upon until it was the color of old saddle leather. His beard was short and red. His eyes were blue and very steady, and when he looked at a thing he looked at it a long time.

His wife stood at the table across from him, kneading sourdough in a pan. She was a small woman, but there was nothing of weakness in her smallness. Her forearms, bared to the elbow, were lean and corded, and the hands at the ends of them had done a man's work on the trail and at the windlass. She had come into the country with him three years before, over the Chilcoot in the spring rush, packing her own outfit on her own back, and the men who had sneered at her at Dyea had stopped sneering before they reached Lake Lindeman. Her name was Agnes, and she had been a schoolteacher in Ohio once, in a white frame schoolhouse with a bell on its roof, and sometimes, in the long nights, she remembered the sound of that bell.

In the bunk against the far wall a man lay sleeping. He was a stranger to them. Jim had found him two days before on the river trail, crawling on his hands and knees through the snow, his feet frozen to the ankles, his face black with frostbite, and his mind wandering among things that were not there. He had no dogs, no sled, no outfit. He had had them once, he said in his raving, but the dogs had gone through the ice at an air hole below the Hootalinqua, and the sled with them, and he had come on alone, for he did not know how far, eating nothing. Jim had put him across his shoulders and carried him three miles to the cabin. Agnes had thawed his feet in snow water and cut away the dead flesh from two of his toes with a skinning knife, and now he slept the sleep of a man who has been very close to the edge and has been pulled back and does not yet know it.

Jim laid the harness across his knees and looked at the sleeping man for a long while. Then he looked at his wife.

"How much flour is there?" he asked. He spoke low, so as not to wake the stranger.

Agnes did not look up from the pan. "You know how much flour there is."

"I want to hear you say it."

She worked the dough a little longer, pressing it down with the heels of her hands and folding it over. "Forty pounds," she said. "A little more, maybe. And the beans. And the side of bacon. And what's left of the dried apples."

"And it's the middle of January."

"I know what month it is, Jim."

"The ice won't go out till May. The first steamer won't come up from St. Michael till June. That's four months, and the caribou have gone over the divide and won't be back, and there's not a moose within thirty miles that I haven't already run down and eaten." He spoke without heat, laying the facts one beside the other, as a man lays logs in a wall. "Forty pounds of flour don't go far for two. For three it don't go at all."

Agnes stopped kneading. She wiped her hands upon her apron, slowly, finger by finger, and then she raised her eyes and met his. They were gray eyes, and there was something in them now that he had seen there before, on the summit of the Chilcoot when the guides had told her to turn back, and on the Box Canyon when the boat had swung broadside to the current and he had shouted to her to jump and she had not jumped.

"Say what you mean," she said.

He was silent for a time. The stove ticked and crackled. Somewhere outside, far off, a dog howled, and the howl went up and up into the cold and broke at the top of it, and the other dogs took it up, one after another, until the whole team was singing the old song of their wolf forebears, the song that is older than men and older than fire. Then it died away, and the silence came back, heavier than before.

"I mean he'll have to go," Jim said.

"Go where?"

"Down to Sixty Mile. There's a post there. They've got grub there, or they had in the fall."

"Sixty Mile is a hundred and ten miles," she said. "On those feet he couldn't walk a hundred and ten yards."

"I'd take him on the sled, then. When he's fit to travel."

"And when will that be? A week? Two weeks? And you'd eat on the trail, going and coming back, the two of you and the dogs, and you'd come back to find the flour no farther along than if he'd stayed here." She shook her head. "That's not what you mean, Jim. You've thought this through. You always think things through. Say what you mean."

He picked up the harness again and turned it over in his hands, and he did not look at her when he spoke.

"I mean that the North don't care," he said. "I mean that up here there's a law, and it's an old law, older than the one they've got outside, and it's the law of meat. There's so much meat, and there's so many mouths, and when there's more mouths than meat, some of the mouths go hungry, and the ones that go hungry die. That's the law. I didn't make it. You didn't make it. But it's here, and it's sitting on this cabin right now as sure as that cold is sitting on it. I've seen it work before. I saw it work on the Koyukuk the winter of 'ninety-four, and I saw it work at Circle when the boats didn't come. Men don't talk about it after. But it worked."

"And you'd have it work here."

"I'd have us live," he said. "That's all. I'd have you live."

She came around the table then and stood before him, and because he was seated and she was standing, she looked down upon him, and he had to raise his head to see her face. Her hands were at her sides, and they were closed.

"You carried him in," she said. "You put him over your shoulders and carried him three miles at fifty below, and you were near done when you came through that door. I saw your face. Why did you carry him in, Jim, if you were only going to put him out again?"

"I didn't know how bad it was. I didn't think."

"You always think."

"Not then," he said. "Not out there. Out there a man don't think, he just does. You see a man crawling in the snow, you pick him up. It's what your hands do. But now I've had two days to sit by this stove and do my thinking, and the thinking comes out different from what the hands did."

"Then I'll trust your hands," she said, "before I'll trust your thinking."

He laughed at that, a short laugh without much mirth in it, and he put the harness down on the floor beside the box and leaned forward with his elbows upon his knees.

"Agnes," he said, "listen to me. You know what I am. I'm not a hard man, not hard the way some of them are. I've shared grub on the trail. I've given my last matches to a Siwash at Pelly Crossing that I'd never seen before and never saw again. But this is different. This is you and me. This is the two of us, and this country has been trying to kill us for three years, and it hasn't done it yet, and I don't aim to let it now. I don't aim to let it because of a stranger whose name we don't even know, a chechaquo who didn't have sense enough to stay off the river ice in January."

"His name is Danforth," she said. "He told me, yesterday, when you were out at the traps. Ned Danforth. He's from Michigan. He has a mother in Grand Rapids, and he came in to make a stake so she wouldn't have to take in washing anymore. He's twenty-two years old."

Jim said nothing.

"He's a boy, Jim. He's somebody's boy."

"Everybody's somebody's boy," he said, but he said it less certainly than he had said the other things, and he looked over at the bunk where the stranger lay, at the thin face with the black patches on it and the yellow hair falling over the forehead, and he looked away again.

"You talk about the law of meat," Agnes said. Her voice had gone low and hard, and it trembled a little, though not with fear. "I know about the law of meat. I've lived under it as long as you have. I've watched the dogs fight over a fish, and I've watched the strong ones eat and the weak ones starve, and I've watched the wolves follow a cow moose that was heavy with calf until she couldn't run anymore. I know all that. But I'll tell you something, Jim Hollister. We're not dogs. We're not wolves. We came into this country with something the dogs and the wolves didn't have, and if we let the country take it away from us, then we might as well be dead, because we'll have nothing left worth keeping alive."

"And what's that?" he said. "What is it we've got that's worth starving for?"

She did not answer at once. She turned away from him and went to the window, which was a square of glass from an old lantern frame let into the logs, and she stood looking out through it, though there was nothing to be seen through it but frost, thick and white and patterned like the fronds of some strange sea fern. Her back was very straight.

"I don't know what to call it," she said at last. "They'd have a word for it, outside. In church they'd have a word for it. But I don't have the word. I only know that when I took that knife to his feet, and he held onto the side of the bunk and didn't cry out, and afterward he looked up at me and said thank you, ma'am, as polite as if I'd poured him a cup of tea, I knew there was something in him that was the same as in me, and the same as in you. And if I put him out to die, I'd be killing that thing in me as well as in him."

The stove ticked. The man in the bunk stirred and muttered something and was still again.

"You'd be dead, too," Jim said quietly. "You'd be dead by April. That's what I can't get past. I can see it as plain as I see you now. I can see it the way I can see a trail laid out ahead of me over a summit. The flour going down. The beans going. Then the bacon. Then the dogs, one by one. Then the harness leather, boiled. I've eaten harness leather. You haven't. Then nothing. And you lying there in that bunk with your face gone thin like his, and me sitting here by this stove watching it happen and not able to do one damned thing about it." His voice roughened, and he stopped and swallowed. "I'll not watch that. I'll not."

She turned from the window and looked at him, and for a moment the hardness went out of her face, and she was only a woman looking at a man she loved, who loved her, and who was afraid. For he was afraid. She saw it now. She had never seen it before, not on the Chilcoot, not in the rapids, not on the long trail down from Forty Mile when the dogs had given out and they had pulled the sled themselves for three days. But she saw it now, sitting on that upturned box by the stove with his big hands hanging between his knees, and she understood that it was not for himself he was afraid.

She came to him and knelt on the floor beside the box and took one of his hands in both of hers. The palm was rough as bark.

"Jim," she said. "Look at me."

He looked at her.

"There's the trapline," she said. "There's the ptarmigan in the willows along the creek. You haven't been hunting them because they're not worth the powder, you said. They're worth the powder now. And there's the snowshoe rabbits. They're coming up this year, you said so yourself, you've seen the tracks. And there's the Indian camp on the Stewart. Old Kakatah has meat. He has dried salmon, a whole cache of it. We could trade the rifle for it. The extra rifle, the Winchester."

"Kakatah'd want the Winchester and the blankets both."

"Then he'll have the blankets both. We can sleep under the bearskin." She held his hand tighter. "It's not forty pounds of flour against three mouths, Jim. It's never just that. It's forty pounds of flour and the two of us and everything we know how to do. And now it's him besides, and when his feet are healed, his hands too. Two men can run more traps than one. Two men can cut more wood. You know that."

"And if the rabbits don't come up? And if Kakatah's people have eaten their cache already, or won't trade? And if the ptarmigan go over the mountain like the caribou?"

"Then we'll go hungry," she said. "And maybe we'll die. But we'll die the three of us, inside this cabin, and not the one of us out in the snow by himself. And if it comes to that, Jim, I'd sooner die with you as the man who carried him in than live with you as the man who carried him out."

He drew his hand away from hers, not roughly, and stood up and went to the door and opened it. The cold came in like a living thing, white and smoking, and rolled across the floor and over her knees, and the flame in the stove shrank down and then roared up again. He stood there in the open doorway with his back to her, looking out at the frozen world, at the spruce trees standing black and still against the snow, at the low hills beyond, and the gray sky beyond the hills, and the vast indifference of it all, that did not know or care that there was a cabin there, or people in it, or a question being decided. It was a country that had been old when the first men came into it, and it would be old when the last of them had gone, and in all its ages it had never once turned aside from its way for the sake of any living thing.

He stood there so long that she thought he would freeze, and she got to her feet. But before she could speak he shut the door and came back into the warmth and stood by the stove, holding out his hands to it.

"It's sixty-five now," he said. "Maybe more. The glass is pretty near to the bottom." He rubbed his hands together slowly. "The ptarmigan will be roosting in the willows on a day like this. They don't fly much when it's that cold. A man could get close to them."

She did not say anything. She did not dare.

"I'll set snares on the creek tomorrow," he said. "And I'll go up to the Stewart at the end of the week, if it warms some, and see what Kakatah has." He turned his head and looked at her, and there was something in his face that had not been in it before, or that had been in it once and gone away and come back. "You're a hard woman, Agnes."

"I had to be," she said, "to keep up with you."

He grunted, and the corner of his mouth moved under the red beard. Then he looked at the bunk again, and the stranger was lying with his eyes open, looking at the two of them. How long they had been open, there was no telling. He was very pale where the frost had not blackened him, and his lips moved, and at first no sound came. Then he said, in a cracked voice, "I heard."

Jim looked at him a long time, in the way he had of looking at things.

"How much did you hear?"

"Enough." The young man wet his lips. "I'll go, mister. When I can stand. I'll go. I don't want to be the cause of it."

"You'll not go anywhere," Jim said, "till your feet are mended. And then you'll go out on the creek with me and run snares, and we'll see what kind of man Grand Rapids sends into this country." He picked up the harness from the floor and sat down again on the box and took up the needle. "Can you shoot?"

"Some."

"You'll learn to shoot better. Ptarmigan don't hold still forever." He drew the sinew through the leather and pulled it tight. "Go back to sleep. A man heals sleeping."

The stranger closed his eyes. Agnes went back to the table and to the sourdough in the pan, and she began to knead it again, pressing it down with the heels of her hands and folding it over, and she found that her hands were shaking, and she kneaded harder until they stopped.

Outside, the cold held the land in its grip and did not loosen it. The smoke went straight up from the chimney and spread and hung. Far off, the dogs began to howl again, all together, the long wolf-howl rising and rising into the twilight, a song of hunger and of the dark and of the endless struggle of the living to go on living. But inside the cabin the stove burned red, and the man mended the harness, and the woman kneaded the bread, and the stranger slept, and none of them listened.

Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Jack London, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
The roadhouse at Sixty Mile squatted on the bank of the frozen river like some beast that had crawled out of the forest to die and had frozen in the dying. It was built of spruce logs, chinked with moss and banked to the eaves with snow, and from its single stovepipe a thin thread of smoke went straight up into the windless air, for it was fifty below, and at fifty below even the smoke has not the heart to stray. Behind it the hills rose white and silent; before it the Yukon lay in its winter sleep, a vast and rugged highway of ice that ran north to the Bering Sea and south to the lakes and the passes, and on all its length, for days' travel either way, there was nothing that moved save the occasional dog-team and the men who drove them.

Inside, the air was thick and warm and foul with the smell of drying socks and moccasins, of bacon grease and tobacco and wet dog. A dozen men lounged about the big sheet-iron stove, or sprawled in their blankets on the pole bunks along the walls, and talked in the slow, half-hearted fashion of men who have nothing to do but wait for the cold to break. They were of the breed that the gold had drawn into the North, men of many races and many lands, and the North had laid its mark upon each of them, so that they looked alike, as soldiers look alike after a long campaign. Their faces were gaunt and frost-bitten, their beards ragged, their eyes narrowed from the glare of the snow.

Among them, and yet somehow not of them, sat Billy Coffin. He was young, two-and-twenty perhaps, broad of shoulder and deep of chest, and his face, though it had been burned brown by tropic suns and whipped raw by the gales of the North Pacific, had not yet taken on the haggard, hungry look of the men about him. He had come in over the Chilcoot in the fall, with the last of the boats, and he was still a chechaquo, a tenderfoot, and he knew it, and the men knew it, and because he was quick to laugh and slow to boast they had let him be.

It was near to noon, which in that latitude and at that season meant a pale glimmer of light on the southern horizon and nothing more, when the dogs set up a howling outside. The men at the stove lifted their heads. A moment later the door was flung open and a cloud of frost rolled in across the floor, and out of the frost came a man.

He was a tall man, but he walked bent, as men walk who have spent many days in the harness, and he was clad from head to foot in furs that were worn and patched and stiff with ice. His beard and mustache were a solid mass of frozen breath, so that his mouth was a mere hole in the ice, and his eyelashes were white with rime. He pulled off his mittens with his teeth and stood a moment at the stove, holding his hands to the heat, and the men watched him and said nothing, for it was the custom of the country to let a man thaw before you spoke to him.

"Cold," he said at last, and the word came out of him cracked and harsh, like a sound that had not been used in a long while.

"Sixty-two at the bend this morning," said one of the loungers. "Where you from?"

"Stewart River."

"Bad trail?"

"Bad enough." He began to break the ice from his beard, picking it away in chunks and dropping it hissing on the stove. "Lost two dogs at the Rink Rapids. Went through the ice. Couldn't get 'em out."

There was a grunt of sympathy from the stove. Dogs were worth more than men in that country, that winter, and a man who lost two dogs had lost a good deal.

Billy Coffin had been watching the newcomer with a vague and growing interest. There was something in the set of the man's shoulders, in the way he held his head cocked a little to one side as he worked at his beard, that stirred some old memory in him. And when the last of the ice came away, and the man turned his face to the light of the candle, Billy came up off the bench as though a spring had been released beneath him.

"Dave!" he cried. "Dave Harnish!"

The tall man swung about, and his hand went, swift and instinctive, to his hip, where the butt of a revolver showed beneath the fur. Then he saw the young face before him, and he stared, and his hand fell away.

"Who the hell are you?" he said.

"Billy. Billy Coffin. Aunt Martha's sister's boy. Don't you know me, Dave?"

For a long moment the older man did not answer. He looked at Billy as a man might look at a ghost, or at something he had lost and forgotten that he had lost, and had come upon again in a strange place. Then a slow smile broke the hard lines of his face, and it was not a pleasant smile to see, for his lips were cracked and bleeding from the frost, and the smile pulled them open.

"Little Billy," he said. "Little Billy Coffin, that used to steal the eggs out of the hen-house and lay it on the hired man. By God."

They gripped hands, and the grip of the older man was like iron, and Billy winced under it and laughed. The men at the stove looked on with mild curiosity, then turned back to their own talk, for meetings of this sort were not uncommon in the North. Men came into the country from all the corners of the earth, and the trails were long, and sooner or later every man met someone he had known in another life.

They sat together at the end of the long plank table, and the roadhouse-keeper, a squat, silent Swede, brought them beans and bacon and sourdough bread and a pot of tea black as tar. Dave Harnish ate as the starved eat, wolfishly, bending low over his plate and shoveling the food in with his knife, and he did not speak until the plate was clean and he had wiped it with a crust of bread and eaten the crust. Billy watched him, and as he watched he felt a strange pain rise in him, for he remembered this man as he had been.

He remembered him, seven years before, on the ranch in the Sonoma hills—a big, laughing, golden-haired young giant of twenty, who could pitch hay from dawn to dark and dance till midnight after, who could ride anything on four legs and outwrestle any man in the valley, and who had been to Billy, a lad of fifteen, something very like a god. He remembered the morning Dave had gone away, standing in the dust of the road with a carpet-bag in his hand and his hat pushed back on his head, laughing at Aunt Martha's tears and promising to come home rich. Alaska, he had said then; there was gold up there, and he meant to have it. And Billy had stood by the gate and watched him go down the road, and had hated the ranch and the hills and the slow round of the seasons, and had sworn that some day he too would go.

And here was the god. Here was what the North had made of him. The golden hair was dull and matted and streaked with gray, though he was not yet thirty. The great frame was there still, but the flesh had been stripped from it, so that the bones of the face stood out like the ribs of a wreck on a beach, and the eyes had sunk back into the skull, and there was a look in them that Billy had seen before only in the eyes of men who had been long adrift in open boats.

"Well," said Dave, pushing back his plate and reaching for his pipe, "how's the folks?"

Billy had been dreading the question. He had known, from the moment he recognized the man, that it must come. He looked down at the table.

"Your mother's dead, Dave," he said. "Two years back, in the spring. It was her heart. She went quick, they said. She didn't suffer."

Dave Harnish filled his pipe with slow, careful fingers, and tamped the tobacco down with his thumb, and lit it with a splinter from the stove, and drew on it till the coal glowed red. Not a muscle of his face moved.

"I figured as much," he said. "Didn't get no letters for a long time. Figured something had happened." He drew on the pipe again. "Two years. I was up the Koyukuk two years back. Starving, about that time. Eating our moccasins. Funny. I was thinking about her a lot that spring. Thought it was because I was hungry and remembering her biscuits." He was silent a moment. "And the ranch?"

"Sold. Uncle Ed couldn't work it alone, after. He's in Petaluma now, keeping books for the creamery."

"Ed Harnish keeping books." Dave laughed, a short, harsh bark of a laugh. "He couldn't add two and two without taking off his boots."

"He's learned, I guess."

"I guess we all learn." Dave stared into the stove, where the fire showed red through a crack in the iron. "What about Nellie Waring?"

Billy hesitated. "She married Hank Strother. The one that has the store at the crossroads. They've got two kids."

This time something did move in the older man's face, a flicker, gone almost before it came, like the shadow of a bird crossing snow. Then it was gone, and the face was hard and still again.

"Hank Strother," he said. "Hank was all right. Fat, but all right. She'd have been a fool to wait." He took the pipe from his mouth and looked at it. "Seven years is a long time for a girl to wait. It's a long time for anybody to wait, for anything."

They were silent then, the two of them, while the stove roared and the men about it talked of claims and creeks and the price of flour at Dawson, which was a dollar a pound and climbing. Outside the dogs had ceased their howling and lay curled in the snow, their noses tucked under their tails, and the cold settled down upon the land as a hand settles down upon a struggling thing and holds it still.

"And you, kid," Dave said at last. "What fetched you up here?"

So Billy told him. He told of how he had run away from the ranch at sixteen, and shipped before the mast out of San Francisco on a lumber schooner bound for the Sound; of three years in the sealing fleet, hunting the herds from the Bonins to the Commanders, of fights in the forecastle and fights ashore, of a typhoon off the coast of Japan when the schooner had lain on her beam ends for a night and a day and two men had been washed from the deck and never seen again. He told it simply, as a sailor tells such things, without much heat; but as he talked his eyes brightened and his voice quickened, for he was young, and the blood ran hot in him, and the world was still to him a great adventure. And he told how, when the news of the Klondike strike had come down to the coast in the summer, and the whole Pacific had gone gold-mad, he had drawn his pay at Victoria and outfitted and come north with the rush.

"I've got a ton of grub cached at the head of Lake Bennett," he said, "and four hundred dollars in my belt, and I'm going to stake on Bonanza or Eldorado or some creek nobody's heard of yet, and I'm going to make my pile. And then—"

"And then what?" Dave said.

"And then I'll go home rich," said Billy, and laughed, and the laugh died, for he heard the words as he said them, and he remembered the morning by the gate.

Dave Harnish looked at him a long while, and there was no mockery in his look, only a great weariness, and something else that might have been pity.

"Listen to me, kid," he said, and he leaned forward across the table, and his voice was low. "Seven years I've been in this country. I come up through Dyea before there was any trail to speak of, and I've been on the Fortymile and the Birch Creek and the Koyukuk and the Tanana, and I've been on a dozen creeks that ain't got names yet and maybe never will. I've froze and I've starved and I've et my dogs and I've buried my partners. Three partners I've buried. Jack Kearney went through the ice on the Tanana, and we never found him. Swede Larsen got the scurvy on the Koyukuk and died in the cabin, and we couldn't dig a grave because the ground was froze like iron, so we laid him out in the snow and piled rocks on him, and the wolverines got to him anyhow before spring. And Tom Peckham—" he stopped, and drew on the dead pipe, and did not seem to notice it was dead. "Never mind about Tom Peckham.

"Twice I've had gold. Once on the Fortymile I took out eleven thousand in a season, and I come down to Circle City and I lost it in two weeks at faro, and I was glad to get the stake back to go out again. And the second time—the second time I had a claim on Hunker Creek this fall that would've gone a hundred thousand, maybe more. I'd staked it fair and recorded it fair, and I come back from Dawson and found three men working it, and they had papers, and they had the Gold Commissioner's office behind 'em, and I had nothing but my word. So I went off up the Stewart, because there was a rumor, and the rumor was a lie, and now I'm going back to Dawson with nothing but my dogs, and two of them dead in the Rink Rapids."

He leaned back. "That's what this country is, kid. It ain't a place. It's a—a thing. It's alive, and it's hungry, and it eats men. It don't hate 'em. It don't care about 'em one way or the other. It just eats 'em, the way a wolf eats a rabbit, because that's what it is and that's what they are. The weak ones it eats quick, the first winter, the scurvy and the cold and the ice. The strong ones it takes longer about. It wears 'em down. It takes a little each winter. And you don't even know it's taking, till one day you look at yourself in a pan of water and you see a stranger."

Billy said nothing. He looked at the gaunt face before him, at the gray-streaked hair and the sunken eyes, and he knew that what his cousin said was true, for the proof of it sat across the table from him. And yet even as he knew it, something in him rose up and refused it—the same thing, perhaps, that had driven him from the ranch at sixteen and sent him into the fo'c'sles and onto the sealing grounds; the stubborn, blind, insatiable thing that lives in the young of the race and drives them forth over the edge of the world, to conquer or to perish, and does not much care which.

"Then why don't you go out, Dave?" he said. "Why don't you go back?"

Dave Harnish laughed again, that short, harsh bark.

"Back to what? To Petaluma? To keep books for the creamery alongside Uncle Ed? To go to church of a Sunday and tip my hat to Mrs. Hank Strother?" He shook his head slowly. "No, kid. That's the joke of it. That's the thing nobody tells you. This country eats you, but once it's had a taste of you, you can't leave it. You go out, and you sit in a soft chair in a warm room, and you eat fresh meat and green vegetables every day, and you sleep in a bed with sheets on it. And a month goes by, and two months, and then one night you wake up and you hear the wind, and it ain't the same wind, it's too soft, it ain't got no teeth in it, and you lay there and you think about the trail, and the dogs, and the cold, and the long dark, and the creek that nobody's ever panned. And you know you're going back. I seen it happen to a dozen men. Big men. Men that had made their pile and swore they was through. Every one of 'em come back. Some of 'em come back to die."

He knocked the dead ashes from his pipe against the table edge.

"I'm in it, kid. I'm in it till it gets me. That's all."

The candle had burned low, and the roadhouse-keeper came and lit another from its stub. Most of the men about the stove had crawled into their blankets, and the room was filled with their snoring, and with the creak of the logs as the cold worked into them. Somewhere outside, far off in the hills, a wolf howled, a long, quavering cry that rose and fell and rose again and died away into the stillness, and the dogs about the roadhouse lifted their heads and answered it.

Billy Coffin sat a long while staring at the table. Then he looked up.

"Dave," he said, "I've got four hundred dollars and a ton of grub, and you know this country, and I don't. I'm strong, and I can work, and I'll learn. Let's go in together. Partners. Fair halves."

The older man's eyes narrowed. "I ain't asking for charity," he said.

"It ain't charity. It's a trade. I've got the grub and the stake, and you've got the savvy. Without you I'll likely go through the ice my first month, like that Kearney fellow. Without me you'll go into Dawson broke, and it's a long time till spring." Billy grinned suddenly, the old boyish grin. "Besides, somebody's got to keep you out of the faro games."

For a long moment Dave Harnish did not answer. He sat with his big, scarred hands lying on the table before him, and stared at them as though they belonged to someone else. And Billy, watching him, saw a strange thing; for he saw the hard, gaunt face soften, ever so little, and he saw a light come into the sunken eyes that had not been there before—a faint light, a mere spark, but a light nonetheless. It was as though, deep down beneath the frost and the hunger and the seven years of the trail, some ember of the laughing young giant who had gone down the road with his carpet-bag still lived, and had been stirred.

"You're a damned fool, kid," Dave said at last, slowly.

"I guess I am."

"The country'll eat you, same as me."

"Maybe. Maybe it'll choke on me."

And at that Dave Harnish laughed, and it was not the harsh bark of before, but a real laugh, deep and rumbling and rusty with disuse; and one of the sleepers in the bunks stirred and cursed and turned over. Dave reached across the table and gripped his cousin's hand, and this time the grip was not iron, but something warmer.

"Fair halves," he said. "We pull out at six, cold or no cold. We'll go up to Bennett for your outfit, and then we'll go over to the Klondike, and we'll find a creek. I've got a notion about a creek on the far side of the Dome. Never told nobody. Figured I'd die before I got to it." He stood up, stretching his long frame until the joints cracked. "Get some sleep. You'll need it. You ain't never seen a trail like the one I'm going to show you."

They lay down side by side on the floor before the stove, rolled in their blankets as they had lain once, long years before, in the haymow of the old barn in the Sonoma hills, when Billy was a small boy and Dave a big one, and the world beyond the hills was a thing to be wondered at and dreamed about. The fire roared low in the stove. The logs creaked and groaned with the cold. And outside, in the long arctic night, the land lay white and still and waiting, patient as death, ancient as the stars; and it did not care that two men slept within its grip, nor that they dreamed of gold, nor that they would rise at six and go forth into it with their small strength and their great hope. It had waited for men before. It would wait for these. And in the end, as always, it would take what it was owed.

But that was in the end; and the end was a long way off; and the two cousins slept.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
The cold had come down upon the land in the night, and with the morning it lay over everything, heavy and motionless, like the hand of some vast and indifferent god pressing the earth flat and holding it so. There was no wind. There was no sound save the occasional sharp report of a spruce trunk splitting in the frost, and that sound, when it came, was swallowed instantly by the silence. The silence closed over it the way water closes over a dropped stone. The sun had not shown itself for many weeks. Away to the south, at midday, a pale flush stained the sky above the ridges, then faded, and the long twilight drew back into night.

In the cabin on the bank of the Little Pelly, a man named Andrew Ross sat on a sawed block of spruce by the stove and looked at his son. He did not speak. He had not spoken for some minutes, and the boy, who was seven years old and small for his age, stood before him with his hands at his sides and his eyes upon the floor. The floor was of hewn logs, worn smooth by moccasins, and the boy studied the grain of it as though there were some salvation written there.

The woman, Ellen, was at the far end of the cabin, mending a mitten by the light of the slush lamp. She did not look up. Her needle went in and out, in and out, steadily, and she did not look up, though her lips were pressed together in a thin line, and once the needle missed and pricked her finger, and she put the finger to her mouth and sucked it and went on sewing.

Andrew Ross was a big man, broad in the shoulder and long in the arm, with a beard grown thick and ragged through three winters in the North. His face, where the beard did not cover it, was dark and seamed and scarred white in patches where the frost had bitten it. He had come into the country in the rush of '97, over the Chilkoot with a hundred and fifty pounds on his back and the woman beside him carrying fifty, and he had seen what the country did to men. He had seen it break them and he had seen it kill them. He had seen strong men, men stronger than himself, lie down in the snow and not rise up again because they had been careless in some small matter, a wet foot, a lost match, a dog team ill-fed. The North was not cruel. He had learned that. Cruelty implied a will, and the North had no will. It simply was. It made its laws, and the laws were few and very simple, and they did not bend. A man obeyed them or a man died. There was no third way, and there was no appeal.

And now his son had broken one of them.

"Look at me, Davy," he said at last.

The boy raised his eyes. They were blue eyes, his mother's eyes, and they were wet, but the tears had not yet fallen. He was fighting them. Andrew Ross saw that, and something moved in him, but he did not let it come into his face.

"You know what you did?"

"Yes, sir."

"Tell me."

The boy swallowed. "I left the cache open."

"You left the cache open," the man repeated slowly, as though he were weighing each word upon a gold scale. "And what came of it?"

"The wolverine got in."

"The wolverine got in," said Andrew Ross. "Aye. The wolverine got in."

He was silent again, and the stove ticked and muttered, and outside, far off, a dog lifted its voice in a long, quavering howl, the old wolf-cry, the cry of the wild that the dogs of the North had never forgotten, and the other dogs took it up, one by one, until the whole team was howling in the darkness under the cold stars. Then, as suddenly as it had begun, the howling ceased.

It had happened in the forenoon. The man had gone up the creek to look at his trap line, and he had told the boy to bring down a slab of bacon and a measure of beans from the cache for the noon meal. The cache stood fifty yards back from the cabin among the spruce, a little log house perched high on four peeled poles, with tin wrapped about the poles so that no creature might climb them. A ladder leaned against it, and the boy had climbed the ladder, as he had climbed it many times before, and lifted the bar from the door and gone in. And then a whiskey-jack, a camp robber, one of those bold grey birds that haunt the camps of men, had lit upon a spruce bough not ten feet from him and cocked its head and scolded him, and the boy, who loved all wild things and had been trying all winter to make one of these birds eat from his hand, had forgotten the bacon and forgotten the beans and forgotten the door. He had come down the ladder with a fistful of crumbs and followed the bird into the timber, holding out his hand and calling softly to it. The bird had led him on, as such birds will, from tree to tree, scolding and flirting its tail, and he had followed it a long way. When he came back, cold and empty-handed and laughing at his own foolishness, the ladder still leaned against the cache and the door still stood open.

He had thought nothing of it. He had climbed up again and fetched the bacon and the beans and barred the door behind him. And in the afternoon, when the man came down from the trap line and went to the cache for a sack of flour, he had found the wolverine.

It had come while the boy was in the timber. It had come up the ladder, that thick-furred, low-slung, evil-smelling robber of the North, that creature which fears nothing that walks and which will follow a trapper's line for a hundred miles, springing his traps and devouring his catch, for the sheer malignant joy of the thing. It had found the door open and gone in, and it had done what wolverines do. It had not merely eaten. It had destroyed. It had torn open the flour sacks and scattered the flour and fouled it. It had ripped the sugar and the dried apples and trampled them. It had gnawed through the canvas that wrapped the bacon and dragged two great slabs of it out the door and down into the snow. And over everything that it could not eat or carry away it had left its musk, that rank, abominable scent which no washing can remove and which renders food unfit for man or dog. And then, when the boy came back and closed the door, the beast was gone, slipped off into the timber with its belly full, and the boy had climbed into that wrecked place in the gloom and taken down his bacon and his beans and seen nothing, for the light was poor and he was thinking of the whiskey-jack.

Andrew Ross had stood in the doorway of the cache for a long time. He had not cursed. He was not a cursing man. He had simply stood there and looked, and reckoned, and the reckoning was not good.

"How many sacks of flour did we have?" he asked the boy now.

"Eight, sir."

"How many are left?"

The boy did not answer.

"Two," said the man. "Two sacks. The rest is spoiled. And the sugar is spoiled, and the fruit is spoiled, and half the bacon is gone. It's the first of January, Davy. The ice won't go out of the Yukon till the middle of May. That's four months and a half. Can you reckon how long two sacks of flour will last three people?"

"No, sir."

"Nor can I," said the man, "for they won't."

The woman at the end of the cabin put down her mending. "Andrew," she said quietly.

He did not turn his head. "Let me be, Ellen. This is a thing the lad must know."

She took up the mitten again, but she did not sew.

The man leaned forward, his elbows upon his knees, his great scarred hands hanging between them. When he spoke again his voice was lower, but there was iron in it still.

"I'm going to tell you a thing, Davy, and I want you to listen, for you'll not hear me tell it twice. You're a little lad. You're seven years old. Back in the States, back in the soft country where you were born, a little lad can forget a thing and no great harm comes of it. He leaves the gate open and the cow gets out and he gets a whipping and that's the end of it. The cow comes home. There's a store at the crossroads and there's flour in the store. There's a neighbor down the road. There's always somebody, somewhere, to make it right."

He paused, and the boy watched him, and the tears stood in the boy's eyes and did not fall.

"There's nobody here," said Andrew Ross. "Do you understand that? There's nobody. The nearest post is Selkirk, and that's a hundred and forty miles, and it's sixty below on the trail, and like as not they've no flour to sell when I get there, for it was a short year on the river and the boats came late. There's nobody to make it right. There's only us. There's only you and me and your mother, and what we've got, and what we can kill. And the country doesn't care. The country doesn't care if you're seven years old or seventy. It doesn't care if you meant no harm. It doesn't care that you were following a bird. It doesn't know about the bird and it wouldn't care if it did. It only knows that the door was open. That's all it knows. The door was open, and the wolverine came in."

The boy's lip trembled. He set his teeth upon it.

"Do you know what scurvy is?" asked the man.

The boy shook his head.

"I'll tell you. On Thirty Mile, the first winter, there was a man named Haskell camped below us. A good man. A strong man. He'd come up from Seattle with an outfit that ought to have seen him through, but he'd had bad luck on the lakes and lost the half of it when his scow went over in the rapids. So he wintered on short grub. Bacon and beans and no potatoes, no fruit, nothing green. And along in February his gums began to go soft and his teeth to loosen, and his legs swelled and turned black, and the old scars on him, scars from when he was a boy, opened up again and wouldn't close. I went down to his cabin in March. He couldn't get up from his bunk. He couldn't chew. He lay there and looked at me, and he knew, and I knew, and there wasn't a thing in the world either of us could do. He lasted till April. We put him under the snow because the ground was too hard to dig, and in the spring the river took him."

The cabin was very still. The slush lamp sputtered and the shadows leaped upon the walls and settled again.

"I'm not telling you this to frighten you," said the man, though he knew that he was frightening the boy and meant to. "I'm telling you because it's true, and because you're old enough to know what's true. I'll not let it come to that with us. I'll go down to Selkirk. I'll go tomorrow, and I'll buy what I can, and if there's nothing to buy at Selkirk I'll go on to Five Fingers. And I'll kill a moose if I can find one, and I'll set more snares for rabbits, and we'll pull through. We'll pull through, Davy. But it'll be a long trail and a hard one, and it needn't have been. Do you hear me? It needn't have been. And that's on you."

Then at last the tears came. They spilled over and ran down the boy's cheeks, and he made no sound, but his shoulders shook, and he stood there and wept silently with his hands clenched at his sides. He did not run to his mother. He did not try to hide his face. Something in him, some small hard core of pride that he had from his father and from his father's fathers, kept him standing there before the man, taking what came.

Andrew Ross watched him weep and did not stop him. It was a hard thing to do. It was perhaps the hardest thing he had done in three years in the North, harder than the Chilkoot, harder than the White Horse Rapids, harder than the burying of Haskell. Every instinct in him cried out to reach forward and gather the boy into his arms. But he had a deeper instinct than that, an instinct older than tenderness, the instinct of the creature that must teach its young to live in a world that will kill them if they do not learn. The she-wolf does not spare her cub when it strays too near the lynx's den. The mother grouse does not spare her chick. Life is a stern teacher, and the parent who would have the child survive must sometimes be as stern as life itself, that the child may learn the lesson in the warmth of the cabin and not in the white death of the trail, where the lesson comes but once.

So he sat and watched, and his face was like the face of a man carved out of spruce, and only the woman at the end of the cabin, who knew him, saw his hands tighten upon each other until the knuckles stood out white.

When the boy's weeping had spent itself somewhat, the man spoke again.

"There'll be no whipping," he said. "A whipping's for a thing that's done and finished. This isn't finished. You'll carry this one, Davy. Every time we sit down to a short meal this winter, and there'll be many, you'll know why it's short. That's punishment enough, and more than enough. But there's another thing."

The boy lifted his wet face.

"Tomorrow, before I leave, you'll go up to the cache with me. And you'll take every sack that's spoiled and every tin that's fouled, and you'll carry it down and bury it in the snow below the bank, so the dogs don't get at it, for it would sicken them. It'll take you the whole of the morning, and your hands will freeze, and you'll stink of wolverine for a week. And while you're doing it, you'll think about the door. And when it's done you'll climb up into that cache and you'll look at what's left, and you'll remember how much there was before."

"Yes, sir," said the boy, very low.

"And from this day," said Andrew Ross, "you'll never leave a door open. Not the cache door. Not the cabin door. Not any door, anywhere, as long as you live. You'll never leave a thing half done. You'll never go off after a bird, or a squirrel, or anything else, till the thing you were sent to do is done. Do you hear me?"

"Yes, sir."

"Say it."

The boy drew a long, shuddering breath. "I'll never leave a door open," he said. "I'll never leave a thing half done."

"Again."

"I'll never leave a door open. I'll never leave a thing half done."

The man looked at him a long moment. Then he nodded, once, and leaned back upon his block of spruce, and it was as though some great weight had been lifted from him, or as though he had set it down for a little while.

"Go to bed," he said.

The boy turned and went to the bunk at the back of the cabin, the low bunk built against the logs beneath his parents' bunk, and crawled in among the rabbit-skin robes, and drew them over his head. The woman rose and went to him, and knelt beside the bunk, and put her hand upon the robes where his shoulder was, and said nothing. After a time she rose and came back to the stove and stood by her husband.

"You were hard with him, Andrew," she said.

"Aye," he said. "I was hard."

"He's only a baby."

"He's not a baby, Ellen. Not here. There's no room for babies here." He stared at the stove, at the red glow through the cracks of the iron. "If it had been the cabin door, and in the night, and the fire gone out—"

He did not finish. He did not need to. She had lived three winters in the North as he had, and she knew.

"I know," she said. She put her hand upon his shoulder, and he reached up and covered it with his own, and they stayed that way for a while, neither speaking.

After a time the man rose and went to the door and opened it a crack and looked out. The cold came in upon him like a living thing, and the breath froze in his beard. Overhead the aurora had come out, great wavering curtains of green and rose and pale violet, sweeping and folding across the heavens in utter silence, vast and splendid and remote, caring nothing for the little cabin and the three human lives within it, caring nothing for flour sacks or wolverines or the tears of a small boy. The man looked up at it, and he felt, as he had felt many times before, how small a thing a man is in the face of that immensity, how frail and brief and soon forgotten. And he felt, too, how fierce a thing it is, that smallness, that frailty, that holds on and will not let go, that builds its cabins and lays in its grub and teaches its young, generation upon generation, in the teeth of the cold and the dark.

He closed the door and barred it, and tried the bar with his hand to see that it held.

Later, when the lamp was out and the stove had died down to a dull red eye in the darkness, the man lay awake in his bunk and listened. Below him, in the low bunk, he could hear the boy's breathing, and he knew by the sound of it that the boy was not asleep. Once he heard a small, choked sob, quickly smothered. Andrew Ross lay still and stared up into the blackness under the roof logs, and his jaw was set, and his eyes were wet.

Then, very softly, so softly that the woman sleeping beside him did not stir, he reached down over the edge of the bunk in the darkness. His hand found the boy's hand, groping upward. The small fingers closed upon his big ones and held them tightly, and neither of them spoke. Outside, the frost cracked in the spruce, and the dogs were silent, and the great cold lay upon the land. And after a while the boy's breathing grew slow and even, and his fingers loosened, and he slept. But the man did not draw his hand away. He left it there, hanging down into the dark, until the grey light of the short day crept in under the door.

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.
