The cabin stood on a bench above the frozen creek, a squat thing of unbarked spruce logs chinked with moss, and around it the land lay dead under the cold. It was the dead time of the year, when the sun no more than peeped above the southern hills at midday and then fled as though afraid of what it saw. The spirit thermometer nailed outside the door had sunk past sixty and stood there sullenly. At such a temperature the very air seemed to grow thick and brittle, and a man's breath, as it left his lips, crackled faintly like the rustle of dry paper. Nothing moved upon the face of the land. The spruce trees stood rigid, their branches bowed with burdens of frost. The creek had long since ceased to murmur, and lay locked and silent under six feet of ice. Only the smoke from the stovepipe moved, rising straight up in a slender grey column, and even this seemed to rise reluctantly, as though it, too, felt the weight of the cold pressing down from the stars.

Inside, Matt Corliss knelt upon the floor and laced his moccasins. He was a big man, heavy in the shoulders and long in the arm, with a face burned dark by sun and frost alike. A short beard, rusty in colour, covered his jaw, and above it the skin of his cheekbones was scarred with old frostbite, black patches that had healed badly. He did the lacing slowly and with great care, for he knew, as all men of the North know, that a wrinkle in the sock or a careless knot might cost him a foot before the day was out.

His wife sat on the edge of the bunk and watched him. She had been watching him for some time, and she had not spoken. Her hands lay in her lap, the fingers interlaced and very still, and that stillness of her hands was the only sign she gave of what was going on within her. She was a slender woman, younger than her husband by a dozen years, and the two winters she had spent on Henderson Creek had drawn the flesh tight across the fine bones of her face. Her eyes were grey, and they were steady eyes.

"You'll not be told, then," she said at last.

He did not look up. "I've told you how it is, Ellen. There's no use goin' over it again."

"There is every use. It is the only use there is left to us."

He finished the lacing of one moccasin and began upon the other. A stick of spruce settled in the stove with a soft sound, and the sheet-iron ticked as it expanded. Outside, one of the dogs, curled in the snow beneath the cache, lifted its muzzle and gave voice to a long and quavering howl, and the others took it up, one after another, until the whole team was wailing at the frosty sky. It was the old song of the wolf, the song of hunger and of the long dark, and it went out over the dead land and was swallowed up. Then the dogs were quiet again.

"Sixty-two below this morning," Ellen said. "I looked at the glass when I went for the water. Sixty-two, Matt. And it is falling."

"It'll break. It can't hold like this forever."

"It held for eleven days last January. You told me so yourself. You said it was the worst you had seen since 'ninety-six."

He grunted and drew the thong tight. "I've travelled at sixty-two."

"With a partner. You have always said that no man should travel alone below fifty. It was one of the first things you told me when we came in. I wrote it down in my book, I remember, because it seemed such a strange thing to have to know. No man should travel alone below fifty. Those were your words."

He looked up at her then, and for a moment there was something hard in his face, something that came and went swiftly, like the glint of ice under a passing light. It was the look of a man who has had his own wisdom flung back at him and does not relish the taste of it.

"There ain't no partner to be had," he said. "Every man on the creek's holed up for the winter. And there ain't no time to go lookin' for one, neither. If that strike on the Sixty Mile is what Beaudry says it is, every claim along the left fork will be staked inside two weeks. You know what that means. You know what it means to us."

"I know what Beaudry says. Beaudry has said a great many things."

"He's never lied to me."

"He has never had to. You have always been too ready to believe him."

The words were sharper than she had intended, and she saw them strike home. He rose to his feet, his head nearly brushing the ridgepole, and stood looking down at her, and the cabin seemed suddenly too small to hold the two of them. He was not a man given to violence, and she had never once been afraid of him, but there was in his great body at that moment a tension that was like the tension of a hauled rope, and she could feel it from where she sat.

"Say it out," he said. "Say what you're thinkin'."

"I am thinking that you mean to go out alone into that cold on the word of a half-breed who was drunk when he told it, and that you mean to travel seventy miles over an unbroken trail with five dogs and a fifty-pound sack of flour, and that Lafferty went out on the same trail nine days ago and has not come back. That is what I am thinking."

He turned from her and went to the shelf where the cartridges were kept, and began to count them out into his palm. He counted them twice. She knew that he was not counting at all, that he was merely giving his hands something to do the while he mastered himself, and she waited.

"Lafferty's a fool," he said at last. "Lafferty never knew how to make a fire when his fingers was gone. I've seen him try. He'd waste half a box of matches before he got a blaze. A man like that has no business on the trail in the winter, and the North'll tell him so quick enough. It's told plenty of his kind before him."

"And what will it tell you?"

"It'll tell me I'm a better man than Lafferty."

He said it simply, without boasting, as a man might say that the sun would rise in the morning. And she knew, looking at him, that he believed it utterly; that in all his thirty-six years he had never yet met the thing that could break him; that he had come through the Chilkoot in the rush and through the scurvy winter on the Stewart and through the ice-jam at Five Fingers when the boats went down by the dozen; and that out of all this he had built a faith in his own strength that was like a religion. It was a fine faith. She had loved him for it once. She loved him for it still. But she had lived two winters on Henderson Creek, and she had learned that the North cared nothing for the faith of men. It was not cruel, the North. Cruelty implies a purpose, a will, and the North had no will. It was merely cold, and vast, and patient, and it waited. It could afford to wait. It had waited before ever there were men, and it would be waiting still when the last of them had crawled into his last bed of spruce boughs and let the frost have its way with him.

"Matt," she said, and her voice was lower now. "Sit down a minute. Please."

He hesitated, and then he sat down upon the stool by the stove, the cartridges still clenched in his fist. The firelight came through the cracks of the stove door and lay in thin red bars across his face.

"How much flour is left in the cache?" she asked.

"You know how much."

"I want you to say it."

"Ninety pounds, near enough. And the beans. And the side of bacon."

"And it is the middle of December."

"I know what month it is."

"Ninety pounds of flour to last two people until the river goes out in May. And the claim has given us nothing. Forty feet of shaft and nothing but muck and gravel. You thawed it all last winter, and this winter you have thawed it again, and there is nothing in it. You said so yourself, three weeks ago. You came in from the shaft and sat where you are sitting now, and you said, 'She's a blank, Ellen. We've drawn a blank.' I have never seen you look so old as you looked that night."

He made no answer. The muscles were working along his jaw beneath the beard.

"We owe Sullivan at the post four hundred dollars," she went on steadily. "He will carry us until spring, because he is a decent man and because he knows you. But he will not carry us another year. You know he will not. And so you have made up your mind that there is only one throw left, and that this is the throw, and that you will make it now, in the dead of the winter, with the glass falling, alone. Because if you wait, the throw is gone. Because if you wait, the other men will have it. That is the whole of it, is it not?"

"That's the whole of it," he said heavily.

"Then I will tell you the rest of it, the part you have not said."

He looked at her quickly, and she saw a wariness come into his eyes.

"You are not going because of the flour," she said. "And you are not going because of Sullivan. You are going because you cannot bear to go Outside in the spring with empty pockets. You cannot bear to walk down the street in Seattle and have men look at you and know that you went into the Klondike in 'ninety-seven and came out again in nineteen-hundred and one with nothing to show for it but frozen cheeks and a wife who has forgotten how to wear a hat. That is why you are going. It is your pride that is going, Matt. You are only carrying it."

He came up off the stool as though he had been struck. The cartridges spilled from his fist and rolled across the floor, rattling on the rough boards, and one of them fetched up against the leg of the bunk at her feet. Neither of them looked at it.

"By God," he said. "By God, Ellen."

"It is true. You know it is true."

"And what if it is?" He was standing over her again, and his voice had gone hoarse and thick. "What if it is? Is a man to have nothin'? Is he to come crawlin' back like a whipped cur and take a job swampin' in some saloon on Front Street, and thank the man that gives it to him? I've seen 'em. I've seen the men that came out busted. I've seen the look on 'em. They ain't men anymore. Something's gone out of 'em, something the North took and never give back. I'd sooner lie down in the snow. I would, by God. I'd sooner lie down in the snow and be done with it."

"Yes," she said quietly. "I believe you would. That is what frightens me."

The words fell into the silence of the cabin and lay there. He stood very still. Outside, far off down the creek, there was a sharp report like a rifle shot, and then another; it was the ice, contracting in the bitter cold, splitting along its length with the sound of artillery. The dogs stirred and whimpered and were still.

When he spoke again his voice had changed. The anger had gone out of it, leaving something dull and tired behind.

"What would you have me do, then?"

"Wait. Wait until the cold breaks. If it breaks in three days, go then, and take Henderson's boy with you. He would go. He has said so."

"Three days may be too long."

"Then it is too long. Then the claims are gone, and we go Outside in the spring with nothing, and you swamp in a saloon on Front Street, and I take in sewing, and we live. We live, Matt. Do you understand? We are alive, the two of us, and that is the only claim worth the staking. It is the only one that has never yet come up blank."

He looked at her as though he were seeing her for the first time. And indeed it may have been so, for men are slow to see the things that live beside them day by day, and it is often only in the moment of crisis that the veils fall away. What he saw was a woman who was no longer the pale schoolteacher he had married in a Seattle boarding house three years before, a woman who had wept the first time she saw a dog beaten and had fainted the first time she saw a man's frozen foot cut off with a skinning knife. That woman was gone. The North had taken her, too, as it took all things, and had worked upon her with its cold and its hunger and its long, unending dark; and what it had left in her place was something harder and more enduring, something that had learned, as the wolf learns and the wolverine, that life was the one thing, that all else was vanity and wind. She was not pleading with him. He saw that now. She was not pleading at all. She was fighting him, fighting for his life against his own mad pride, as fiercely and as coldly as ever he had fought the ice-jam at Five Fingers; and he had the strange sensation, which he could not have put into words, that in this battle she was the stronger of the two.

"And if I go anyway?" he said slowly. "If I harness the dogs and go?"

She did not answer at once. She looked down at her hands, still interlaced in her lap, and he saw the knuckles whiten.

"The mail carrier comes through on the twentieth," she said. "He goes out by way of the Pass. He has a place on his sled for a passenger, if the passenger can pay, and I have the forty dollars that was my mother's. I have never told you about it. I kept it against the day I might need it." She raised her eyes to his. "If you go, Matt, I will not be here when you come back. If you come back."

"You'd do that?"

"I would do that."

"You'd leave me?"

"I would not be leaving you. You would have left me first. You would have left me this morning, when you went out that door with your pride on your back and your face to the Sixty Mile. I will not sit in this cabin for three weeks and listen for the dogs and know, every hour of every day, that you are lying somewhere on the trail with your matches spilled in the snow, like Lafferty. I will not do it. I have done everything else this country has asked of me, but I will not do that."

He stood a long time without moving. The fire had burned low, and the cold was creeping in already through the chinks of the logs, a thin and searching cold that found the floor first and then began to climb. He could feel it about his ankles. It was always so, he thought. The moment a man let his fire die, the cold was there, waiting, as it had been waiting all along, patient and without malice, merely there, merely waiting for the warmth to fail.

He thought of the trail to the Sixty Mile. He knew it well, every turn and every portage of it. He thought of the long climb out of the valley of the Henderson, and the windswept divide beyond, where no tree grew, and where a man caught by the dark could not find so much as a stick to burn. He thought of the overflow on the creeks, the treacherous water that welled up beneath the snow and lay hidden there, waiting for the unwary foot. A man who broke through at sixty below had perhaps ten minutes to build his fire. If his fingers failed him, or his matches, or the birch bark was damp, there was no second chance. He had known men who had had no second chance. He had found one of them once, sitting with his back against a spruce, his mittens off and his dead hands curled about a bundle of matches, his face peaceful, almost smiling, as though at the last he had found the cold to be a kind of comfort.

He thought of all this, and he thought of the good gravel on the left fork, the gravel that might run a dollar to the pan or might run nothing at all; and then he looked at his wife, sitting upright on the edge of the bunk with her white knuckles and her steady grey eyes; and something gave way within him. It did not break. It was not so violent as that. It gave way slowly, as the ice gives way in the spring, with a groaning and a grinding deep beneath the surface, and a long, reluctant yielding.

He went down on his knees upon the floor and began to gather up the scattered cartridges. He did it slowly, one by one, searching them out in the dimness beneath the bunk and the stool. When he had found them all he rose and put them back upon the shelf, and then he went to the stove and opened the door and fed it three sticks of spruce. The fire caught with a roar, and the red light leaped out and filled the cabin.

"I'll see to the dogs," he said, and his voice was rough. "They'll be wantin' their fish."

He took his parka from the peg and went out, and the door swung shut behind him, and a breath of frost came rolling across the floor like smoke. Ellen sat where she was. She did not move for a long time. Then, very slowly, she unlaced her fingers and looked at them. They were trembling now, trembling so that she could not still them; and she put her face down into them, and her shoulders shook, but she made no sound.

Outside, under the cold stars, Matt Corliss stood beside the cache with the frozen salmon in his arms and the dogs leaping and snarling about his knees. He did not throw them their fish at once. He stood looking off toward the south, toward the divide and the unseen Sixty Mile beyond it, and his breath went up before him in a cloud and crackled as it froze. He stood so until the cold began to bite through his moccasins, until his cheekbones stung and then went numb. Then he threw the fish to the dogs, and turned, and went back into the warmth and the light.

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

Arthur Lyle had arrived first, and for a quarter of an hour he sat at the corner table of the chophouse with his hat upon his knee and his eyes upon the door, composing in his mind the several sentences with which he would greet his cousin. It was not that he lacked words. Words were his trade, after a fashion, for he was chief clerk in the law offices of Bradbury and Coyle, and there was scarcely a day in which he did not frame some careful paragraph upon the transfer of a lot or the settlement of an estate. But these were words of a particular kind, nicely measured and precisely fitted, and he felt, with a vague discomfort he could not have explained, that they would be of little service to him now. Seven years is a long time. It had been seven years since Jim Haskell walked down the Oakland mole with a blanket roll upon his shoulder and a grin upon his face, bound for Seattle and the Chilkoot and the gold that every newspaper in the land declared was lying in the creek-beds of the North for any man with the stomach to dig it out. Arthur had stood upon the mole and waved his hat. He remembered that it had been raining, and that his mother, who had come with him, had wept a little and called Jim a wild boy, and that Jim had kissed her and laughed and told her he would bring her back a nugget as big as a hen's egg. She was dead now, three years dead, and the nugget had never come.

The chophouse was a low-ceilinged place near the foot of Broadway, frequented by teamsters and longshoremen and the masters of bay scows, and Arthur, in his stiff collar and his grey business suit, was conscious of being out of his element. It had been Jim's choosing. "I don't want any of your swell joints," he had written in the scrawled note that came to the office. "I want a steak and I want it thick, and I want to sit where a man can put his elbows on the table." Arthur had smiled at that, and then, curiously, had not smiled; for he had suddenly realized that he could not remember the last time he had put his elbows on a table.

The door swung open, letting in a gust of wind off the estuary and the smell of tide-flats and tar, and a man came in and stood looking about him. Arthur half rose, then hesitated. He had been watching for a boy of twenty-two, lean and freckled and quick-moving, and this was not a boy. This was a man, broad through the shoulders and thick through the chest, with a face burned to the colour of old saddle-leather and creased about the eyes as though from long squinting into great distances. His hair was cropped close, and there was grey in it at the temples, though he could not have been thirty. He wore a pea-jacket buttoned to the throat, and his hands, which hung at his sides, were enormous and scarred and knotted at the knuckles. Yet it was the eyes that gave Arthur pause. They were the same blue eyes, but there was something in them now, a stillness, a watchfulness, as of an animal that has learned the trick of waiting.

Then the eyes found him, and the stillness broke, and the old grin split the leathery face from ear to ear.

"Art! Art, you son of a gun!" And the man was across the room in three strides, scattering a waiter from his path, and Arthur's hand was seized in a grip that ground the bones together and his shoulder was pounded until he staggered. "Look at you! Look at the collar on you! By the Lord, you look like a parson—like a bank president!"

"Jim," was all Arthur could say, and all the careful sentences he had composed went out of his head like water from a sieve. "Jim. Good Lord, Jim."

They sat down, and for a long moment neither spoke, but only looked at each other across the scarred table with that hungry, searching scrutiny which men bestow upon the faces of those they have known in boyhood, seeking the old lines beneath the new ones. Arthur saw that a white seam ran from Jim's left cheekbone into his hairline, and that the tip of one ear was gone, and that two fingers of the left hand ended at the second joint. Jim, for his part, was looking at Arthur's soft white hands lying upon the table, and at the slight thickening beneath his waistcoat, and at the spectacles which had not been there seven years before.

"You've got fat, Art," Jim said at last, and he said it without malice, in the tone of a man stating a fact about the weather.

"And you've got—" Arthur cast about for the word. "Hard," he finished lamely.

Jim laughed, a short bark of a laugh. "Hard? Well, I guess maybe. The North does that. It takes what's soft in a man and freezes it off him, the way it froze off them fingers. And what's left, why, what's left is hard, or else there ain't nothing left at all." He beckoned to the waiter. "Steak," he said. "Two of 'em. Thick as your fist, and don't burn the life out of 'em. And coffee, a big pot, black as the inside of a cow."

When the waiter had gone, Arthur leaned forward. "We heard so little, Jim. A letter from Dawson the first winter, and then nothing for nearly two years, and then that one from Nome. Mother—" he stopped.

"I know," Jim said, and his face changed. "I got your letter. It caught up with me in Unalaska, eight months after it was wrote. I was on a sealing schooner then, the *Mary Thomas*, and we'd put in for water. I read it standing on the beach with the fog coming in, and I'll tell you, Art, I sat down on a rock and bawled like a calf. Aunt Martha was the only mother I ever had, near enough." He turned his coffee cup slowly between his great scarred hands. "I never did bring her that nugget."

"She didn't care about the nugget."

"No. She'd have cared I came back, though. And I didn't come back. I was too busy getting hard." He said it bitterly, and then shook himself as a dog shakes off water. "Well, there's no use crying over it now. A man does what he does. Tell me about yourself. You married that Hendricks girl? The one with the yellow hair that used to sing in the choir?"

"Clara. Yes. Five years ago this June." Arthur felt a warmth of pride, and with it, oddly, a faint embarrassment, as though he were showing a small and ordinary coin to a man who had handled bullion. "We have a boy. Three years old. We named him James."

Jim stared at him. Then he set down the cup, very carefully, and looked away toward the window, where the masts of the scow schooners swayed against the grey sky. When he looked back, his eyes were wet, and he made no attempt to hide it.

"James," he said. "After me?"

"After you."

"Well, I'll be damned." He was silent a moment. "I'll be everlastingly damned. A kid with my name on him, and me freezing my feet off on the Stewart River and never knowing a thing about it." He reached across and gripped Arthur's arm. "I'll see him, Art. I'll see him before I go."

"Before you go?" Arthur's heart sank a little. "You've only just come."

But the steaks arrived then, great slabs of meat swimming in their own juices, and Jim fell upon his as a wolf falls upon a kill. He ate as Arthur had never seen a man eat, swiftly and silently and with an absolute concentration, his elbows upon the table and his head bent low over his plate, and Arthur, picking at his own portion with knife and fork, watched him with a fascination that was almost fear. Here was hunger, the real thing, not the polite appetite of the dining-room but the old, primordial hunger that had driven men since the first of them crawled up out of the slime—the hunger that knows meat is life and that no man can tell when he will eat again.

When the plate was clean, Jim sat back and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand and laughed at the expression on his cousin's face.

"You'll have to excuse me," he said. "I ain't been around white tablecloths. Up there you eat when you can and as much as you can, because tomorrow there mayn't be any. There was a winter, Art—the second winter—when me and my partner, a Swede named Olaf Lindquist, was holed up in a cabin on Henderson Creek with forty pounds of flour and a side of bacon gone green, and the thermometer at sixty-five below. Sixty-five below! You don't know what that means. Nobody down here knows what that means. You spit, and the spit crackles in the air before it hits the snow. You breathe, and your breath freezes in your beard till you've got a mask of ice over your face, and you've got to break it off with your fingers. We ate the bacon, green and all. We ate the flour, a cupful a day between the two of us, mixed with snow-water. Then we ate our moccasins, boiled. Then we ate the dogs."

He spoke flatly, without emphasis, and somehow this was more terrible to Arthur than any amount of passion would have been.

"And Olaf?" Arthur asked.

"Olaf died in February. Scurvy, mostly, and the cold, and something else besides—something I don't know the name of. He just quit. One morning he sat up in his bunk and looked at me and said, 'Yim, I tink I go now,' and lay down again and turned his face to the wall. I talked to him. I cussed him. I told him he was a yellow-bellied Swede and a quitter. It didn't do no good. He was dead by night." Jim was silent a moment. "I couldn't bury him. The ground was froze like iron. I put him up in a cache on poles, the way the Indians do, to keep him from the wolverines, and in the spring I came back and dug a hole. He was a good man, Olaf. Strong as a horse, and never a growl out of him. But he quit, and the North don't forgive a man that quits."

The waiter cleared the plates, and Jim poured himself a fresh cup of the black coffee and drank it scalding. Arthur found that his own hands were trembling, and he hid them beneath the table.

"I don't know how you stood it," he said.

"You stand it or you don't. That's all there is to it." Jim shrugged his great shoulders. "There ain't any secret. It's the law, Art—the law of the whole blamed universe, only up there it's laid bare, with all the frills stripped off it. Down here you've got your laws and your courts and your policemen, and you think that's what keeps a man alive. It ain't. It's just a kind of padding. Up there the padding's gone, and you see the thing itself. The strong live and the weak die, and the cold don't care which you are. It just waits."

Arthur was silent. He thought of his office, with its green-shaded lamp and its rows of calf-bound volumes; of the brass rail along which the clients passed; of the clock upon the wall that ticked away the hours between eight and six; of the streetcar that carried him home each evening to the little white house on Telegraph Avenue, with its mortgage held by the very bank whose papers he drew up. Padding. He had never thought of it that way. He had thought of it as civilization, as order, as the fruit of a thousand generations of human striving. And yet—and here was the strange thing—sitting across from this scarred and weathered man, he felt something stir in him that he had not felt since boyhood, a restlessness, a discontent, a kind of envy that shamed him even as he felt it.

"Do you remember the creek?" he said suddenly. "Back of Grandfather's place, in the valley?"

Jim's face lit up. "Alamo Creek! Lord, yes! The swimming hole under the big sycamore. And the time you jumped off the high branch on a dare and like to broke your neck."

"You dared me."

"Sure I did. And you did it, too, and come up spitting mud and blood with your nose all bent over to one side. I never was so proud of anybody in my life." Jim laughed, and the laugh rolled through the low room so that the longshoremen at the bar turned their heads. "And Grandfather came down with his razor-strop and lit into the both of us, and you never said a word about it being my dare. Took your licking like a man."

"I remember," Arthur said softly. He had not thought of it in years. He had not thought of himself, in years, as a boy who would leap from a high branch into a muddy pool on a dare. He had become, without ever quite deciding to become it, a careful man, a man who weighed consequences and drew up contracts against contingencies, a man who did not leap from anything.

"And the time we fought," Jim went on. "Over that Portuguese girl from the dairy, what was her name—Rosa?"

"Maria."

"Maria. That's it. We went at it behind the hay barn for an hour, and neither of us would quit, and at the end of it we was both too tuckered to stand up and just lay there in the straw laughing like a pair of loons. And she married the blacksmith's boy anyhow." Jim shook his head, still smiling. "We was a couple of young wolves then, Art. Both of us. I used to think you had more sand in you than I did, only you kept it hid."

Arthur looked down at his soft hands. "I don't think I have much sand left," he said.

Jim regarded him for a long moment with those still, watchful eyes. Then he leaned forward and spoke in a low voice, almost gently.

"Don't you go thinking that, now. I know what you're thinking. You're thinking you sat down here in a soft chair while I was up there freezing and starving and fighting, and that makes me more of a man than you. Well, it don't. I've seen the soft fellows go North—the counter-jumpers and the bank clerks and the college boys—and I've seen some of 'em die, sure, and I've seen some of 'em turn out the hardest men in the country. It ain't what you've done, Art. It's what's in you. And I've seen what's in you. I seen it behind the hay barn and I seen it under the sycamore." He sat back. "Besides, you got a wife and a kid and a house. What've I got? A poke of dust that'll be gone in six months, and a pair of feet that ache every time the wind shifts, and nothing to come home to. Which of us has done better?"

"But you're going back," Arthur said.

Jim was silent. He turned his head and looked again out the window, where the light was fading over the estuary and the riding lights of the scows were beginning to wink on, one by one, along the water. When he spoke, it was more to himself than to his cousin.

"I got to," he said. "I don't know why. I can't make you understand it, because I don't understand it myself. I been down here two weeks now, and every night I lay in my bed at the hotel and listen to the streetcars and the people going by, and I can't sleep. It's too close. It's too soft. I feel like I'm smothering. And then I shut my eyes, and I see the big white silence stretching away for a thousand miles, and the Northern Lights a-dancing over it, and I hear the dogs howling at the moon, and something in me just aches to be there, like a man aches for drink. It nearly killed me, the North. It killed Olaf, and a dozen other men I knew. And I want to go back to it worse than I ever wanted anything." He laughed shortly. "That's a fool thing, ain't it?"

"No," Arthur said. "No, I don't think it's a fool thing at all."

And he did not. For in that moment he understood his cousin as he had never understood him before—understood that the hardness he had seen in Jim's face was not the whole of the man, that beneath it lay something restless and hungering and unappeasable, the same thing that had driven men out of caves and across oceans and over mountains since the beginning of time, the thing that would not let them rest. And he understood, too, with a pang that was half sorrow and half relief, that this thing was in himself also, buried deep beneath the stiff collars and the calf-bound volumes and the ticking clock, and that he would never let it out. He had chosen. He had made his peace with the padding. And he would go home tonight to Clara and the boy, and he would be glad to go.

They sat a while longer, talking of small things—of uncles and aunts and the old ranch, which had been sold to a Chinese truck-gardener; of the price of gold and the price of land; of Arthur's prospects with the firm and Jim's plans for a claim on the Koyukuk. Then Jim drew a buckskin pouch from inside his pea-jacket and loosened the drawstring and shook out upon the table a single nugget, rough and lumpish and dull yellow, about the size of a hazelnut.

"It ain't as big as a hen's egg," he said. "But I been carrying it for her for five years. I want the kid to have it. Little Jim."

Arthur picked it up. It was heavier than he expected, and warm from the body that had carried it.

"I'll give it to him," he said, and his voice was not quite steady. "And you'll come to supper Sunday. You'll see him yourself."

"I'll come," Jim said.

They went out together into the dusk, and the wind off the bay struck them full in the face, cold and wet and smelling of salt. At the corner they shook hands, and Jim's grip ground the bones of Arthur's hand together once more, and neither of them winced. Then Jim turned and walked away toward the waterfront, with that slow, rolling, deliberate stride of a man who has walked many miles on snowshoes, and Arthur turned toward the streetcar line. Halfway down the block he stopped and looked back. Jim had stopped, too, at the edge of the wharf, and was standing there with his hands in his pockets and his head lifted, gazing out over the darkening water toward the Golden Gate and the great sea beyond it—gazing, Arthur knew, still farther, past the sea and the fog and the rim of the world, into the white silence that was calling him home.

Arthur stood watching until the streetcar came clanging up behind him. Then he climbed aboard and paid his nickel and sat down among the clerks and shopgirls going home, and he held the nugget tight in his soft white hand the whole way.

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.
