response:
It was after nine o'clock when Andrej Hudak came home from the mill, and the street was black and silent, except for the roar that never ceased from beyond the railroad tracks, where the furnaces of the Keystone Steel Company sent up their glare against the low clouds. The roar went on day and night, Sunday and weekday, Christmas and Easter; the people of the Flats had heard it so long that they no longer knew it was there, any more than they knew the smell of sulphur in the air they breathed, or the gray grit that settled upon their window sills and their bread and the faces of their sleeping children. It was only when the furnaces were banked, in a time of slack trade, that the silence came down upon the town like a blow, and men lay awake listening to it, and knew that there would be no wages that week.

Andrej climbed the three wooden steps of the house that was not his house, though he paid for it, and opened the door that was not his door. The house belonged to the Keystone Land and Improvement Company, which was the same thing as the Keystone Steel Company under another name, the lawyers having found it convenient that there should be two names. There were four rooms, and a cellar that filled with water in the spring, and the rent was eleven dollars a month, which was taken out of Andrej's pay before he ever saw it. In the lease, which he had signed with his mark six years before, there was a clause that the tenancy should end upon the day the tenant ceased to be employed by the company; and Andrej had not known that this clause was there, for he could not read English, and no one had troubled to tell him. He knew it now, however. Everyone in the Flats knew it now.

His wife was sitting by the kitchen stove, with the lamp turned low to save oil, and a heap of mending in her lap. She did not get up when he came in. She looked at him, and he saw at once that she had been waiting for him, and that she had been crying, and that she had stopped crying a long time ago and was now something worse than tearful. Zuzana was a small woman, and she had been pretty when he married her in the village near Presov, with her round cheeks and her yellow braids and her laugh that could be heard across the whole of the market square. She was twenty-seven years old now, and she had borne four children in this country, and buried two of them, and there was a fifth coming; and the cheeks were not round any more, and the laugh was a thing that Andrej could hardly remember.

"You are late," she said.

"There was a meeting," he answered, and hung his cap upon the nail, and sat down heavily upon the bench to unlace his boots. His hands were burned in a dozen places, and the backs of them were seamed with old scars, white against the grime; for he was a helper at the open hearth, and a man who worked at the open hearth for twelve hours a night, with the molten steel spitting at him and the heat striking his face like the flat of a shovel, did not keep his skin whole for long.

"I know there was a meeting," said Zuzana. "Mrs. Kovac told me. Mrs. Kovac told me who was there, and who spoke, and that you stood up at the end with the others. She told me before the store closed. The whole street knows it. Do you think the company does not know it?"

Andrej did not answer for a while. He got one boot off, and then the other, and set them side by side near the stove, where they began to steam. Then he said, "Let the company know. They will know soon enough anyway."

"Andrej," she said, and her voice shook, "you have signed the paper?"

"I have signed it."

She put the mending down upon the floor, very carefully, as if it were something that might break; and then she put her face in her hands.

---

Let it be understood what this paper was, and what it meant, for the reader who has never lived in a mill town will not know. For eleven years the men of the Keystone works had labored without any organization whatever. There had been a union once, in the old days, when most of the men were Welsh and Irish and spoke English and knew their rights; and the company had broken it, with Pinkerton detectives and with a regiment of the state militia, and with a long winter in which the Welsh and the Irish had starved and then gone away. After that the company had sent agents to the old countries of Europe, to the villages of Galicia and Slovakia and the Carpathian hills, and had brought over a new kind of labor—men who did not speak English, and who could not read the notices posted upon the walls, and who were grateful for a dollar and sixty cents a day because they had never in their lives seen so much money. These men had been divided carefully, so many of one race in this department and so many of another in that, so that they could not talk to one another; and the foremen had been instructed to set the Slovaks against the Poles and the Poles against the Italians, and to see that the hatred of one people for another was kept warm. It was a scientific system, devised by educated men in offices in Pittsburgh and New York, and it had worked admirably for eleven years, so that the dividends of the Keystone Steel Company had never once fallen below eight per cent.

But a strange thing had happened in the last year, which the educated men had not foreseen. The workers had begun to learn English. They had learned it from one another, in the boarding houses and the saloons, and they had learned it from the night school which a young woman from the settlement house had started in the basement of the Lutheran church; and with the English they had learned other things, which the company had not intended them to learn. They had learned that the men in the union mills at Wheeling were paid two dollars and forty cents for the same work. They had learned that there were mills where men worked eight hours instead of twelve, and did not work twenty-four hours straight through on the Sunday when the shifts changed over. They had learned that the son of the president of the Keystone Steel Company had given a dinner at a hotel in New York at which each guest had found a pearl in his oyster; and they had sat in their kitchens at night and thought about the pearl, and about the long turn, and about the children who were buried in the cemetery on the hill.

And so a man had come from the union in Pittsburgh, quietly, and had gone from house to house; and there had been meetings in the back room of Gorski's saloon, and in a barn outside the town limits where the company police had no authority; and now there was a paper, upon which a man put his name, or his mark, to say that when the call came he would lay down his tools and walk out of the mill with his brothers. Andrej Hudak had put his name upon that paper this night. He could write his name now; the young woman from the settlement house had taught him.

---

"You have signed it," Zuzana said again, through her fingers. "You have signed it, and you did not ask me. You did not even tell me you were going."

"If I had told you, you would have cried, the way you are crying now."

"And what if I would cry? Am I not your wife? Is it not my house, too, that they will put us out of? Are they not my children who will sleep in the street?"

"Nobody will sleep in the street," said Andrej. "The union will take care of that. There will be tents. There will be a relief fund. The man from Pittsburgh said so."

She lifted her face then, and he saw it wet and white in the lamplight, and his heart turned over within him; but there was a wildness in it, too, that frightened him.

"Tents!" she cried. "Tents, in November! Do you know what month it is, Andrej? Do you know that the baby will come in January? Shall I have it in a tent, then, on the ground, with the snow coming through? Shall I bring it into the world the way the Kovac woman brought hers, in the strike of the coal mines, when she was a girl in Scranton, and it died the third day, blue, with the cold? She has told me that story. She has told it to me many times."

"That was the coal mines. That was another time."

"It is always another time! It is always the same time!" She was standing now, her hands clenched at her sides, and her voice was rising, so that he glanced at the door of the bedroom where the children were sleeping. "Do you know how much we owe at the store? Do you know? I will tell you, since you do not trouble to know such things. We owe forty-three dollars and seventy cents. I went today to get the flour, and Mr. Bauer showed me the book. Forty-three dollars and seventy cents! And when the strike comes, do you think he will give us credit? He will give us nothing. He will give us a paper to say we must leave the house, and the constable will come with it, and we will owe the forty-three dollars still, and they will take the stove and the beds for it."

It was true, all of it, and Andrej knew that it was true. The store was the Keystone Mercantile Company, which was the steel company under a third name; and it charged twenty and thirty per cent more than the stores in the town across the river, where the workers were not permitted to trade, upon pain of being marked by the foremen as troublemakers. The wages were paid every two weeks, and a family could not live two weeks without food; and so there was a book at the store, in which everything was written down, and on payday the amount in the book was taken out of the envelope before the envelope was handed across the counter; and somehow, no matter how carefully Zuzana managed, no matter how many times she made the soup with nothing but potatoes and the bones from the butcher, no matter how she mended the children's shoes with pieces of an old harness and stuffed them with newspaper against the cold, the amount in the book grew a little larger every month, and never once grew smaller. Zuzana had tried to understand it; she had sat with a pencil and the back of a calendar, and added up what they earned and what they spent; but she had never been able to make the figures come out, and in the end she had concluded that she was stupid, and that it was her fault. She did not know that it was not meant to come out—that the debt at the company store was a chain, forged with as much care as any chain that ever bound a galley slave to his oar, and that there were men in Pittsburgh who knew the exact weight of it to a penny.

"I know about the store," said Andrej, in a low voice.

"You know nothing! You come home and you eat what I put in front of you, and you sleep, and you go back to the mill. It is I who stand at the counter while Mr. Bauer looks at the book and makes the clucking noise with his tongue. It is I who tell Mikulas there is no milk today, maybe tomorrow. Do you know what he said to me this morning? He said, 'Mama, why are we always tomorrow?' A child of five years! And now you go and sign a paper, and there will be no tomorrow at all."

She sat down again, all at once, as if her legs had given way; and the anger went out of her, and she began to cry in earnest, in long shuddering sobs that she tried to stifle with her apron, so as not to wake the children.

---

Andrej sat for a long time without speaking. He was not a man of words; he had been a peasant and the son of peasants, and the habit of his people was to endure in silence, as the oxen endure, and as the fields endure under the rain. But something had changed in him in the last year, as something had changed in all the men at the Keystone works; and he found now that there were words in him, struggling to get out, and that he could not keep them back.

"Zuzka," he said, using the name he had called her by in the old village, when they had walked home together from the dancing, "listen to me. I will tell you something I have not told you. You remember Stefan Ondrus?"

She nodded, without looking up. Everyone remembered Stefan Ondrus. He had been killed in the summer.

"You know how they said he died? They said he was careless. They said he walked under the crane when he was told not to. The company paper said it, and the coroner said it, and the company gave his wife fifty dollars, out of kindness, they said, because it was not their fault. Fifty dollars! I was there, Zuzka. I was ten feet from him. The chain on the crane was bad. It had been bad for a month. We told the foreman, Kessler, three times we told him. He said there was no time to stop the crane, the furnace was behind, the superintendent wanted the tonnage. And then the chain broke, and the ladle came down, and Stefan—" He stopped, and passed his burned hand across his eyes. "There was not enough of him to put in the box. They put in his boots, and some of the iron with him, because it was all one thing."

Zuzana had stopped crying. She was staring at him, her apron twisted in her two hands.

"And afterward," he went on, "they put a new man in Stefan's place. A boy from the boat, a Croatian, who did not speak anything. And Kessler showed him where to stand, under the same crane, with a new link in the chain, and the whole thing went on. The furnace did not stop. The tonnage did not stop. The next day, in the office, they sent a telegram to Pittsburgh, I suppose, and in Pittsburgh they wrote down so many tons, and in New York a man who owns the stock, he read in his newspaper that Keystone is a good company, it makes much money. And that man, Zuzka, I think he does not know there was a Stefan Ondrus. I think he does not know there is an Andrej Hudak. He knows only the tons."

"What has that to do with the paper?" she whispered. "Will the paper bring Stefan back?"

"No. But it is the only thing that will make them see us. One man, they do not see. One man says, the chain is bad, and Kessler says, shut your mouth, there are a hundred men at the gate who want your job. And it is true, there are. But if all the men at the gate are with us—if there is nobody to take the job—then they must listen. That is the whole thing, Zuzka. That is what the union is. It is that they cannot see one, so we must be a thousand."

"And if they bring in men from outside? They did it before. Mrs. Kovac's husband says they did it before. They brought in Negroes from the South, and men from the jails, and they put them in the mill behind a fence, with soldiers."

"Maybe they will do it again," said Andrej. "Maybe we will lose. I do not say we will not lose. But Zuzka, I am thirty-one years old. I have worked at the hearth for six years. You know how long a man lasts at the hearth? Look at old Brezina. He is forty-four, and he looks like a man of seventy, and he coughs all night so the whole house cannot sleep, and next year they will tell him he is too slow, and they will put him out, and then what? There is no pension. There is nothing. We are like the coal they put in the furnace. When we are burned up they shovel out the ashes and put in more. If I do not fight now, when I am strong, when will I fight? When I am Brezina?"

---

There was a long silence in the kitchen. The lamp sputtered, and Zuzana reached out mechanically and turned the wick a little lower, for oil was nine cents a quart at the company store. Outside, across the tracks, the roar of the mill went on, steady and pitiless, and a long red glare swept across the window as they tapped one of the furnaces, so that for a moment the kitchen was lit up like a scene from the inferno, and then fell back into gloom.

"You think I do not know all that," Zuzana said at last, very low. "You think because I am a woman I do not understand. I understand. I wash your shirts, Andrej. I see the holes the steel burns in them. I see the blood on them, some nights. I lie awake when you are on the long turn and I count the hours and I think, now maybe, now maybe they are carrying him home. Every time there is a knock on the door in the night, my heart stops. You think I want you to stay in that place forever?"

"Then why—"

"Because I am afraid!" she cried. "Because I am afraid, and you are not afraid enough! You are a man, you go to the meeting, a man from Pittsburgh makes a speech, everybody shouts, everybody is brave. It is very fine. But it is not the man from Pittsburgh who will be hungry. It is not his children. He will go back to Pittsburgh, to his hotel, and if it goes bad, he will make a speech somewhere else. And the women of the Flats will be standing in the snow with the furniture on the sidewalk. That is how it always is. The men are brave and the women pay."

Andrej had no answer to this, for there was a part of him that knew it to be true. He had seen the man from Pittsburgh, in his good overcoat and his clean collar; and though the man had spoken well, and though Andrej believed that he was honest, there had been a moment, in the barn, when the man had looked at his watch, and Andrej had thought: he has a train to catch.

"And yet," said Zuzana, more quietly, and with a strange new note in her voice that made her husband look up, "and yet I think maybe you are right. That is the worst of it. I think maybe you are right, and it does not help at all."

She got up and came across the kitchen to where he sat, and stood before him; and he saw that her face had changed again, and that it was no longer wild, but only very tired, and very old, older than her twenty-seven years.

"Mrs. Ondrus came to the store today," she said. "Stefan's wife. She had the baby with her. She is going back to the old country, she told me; her brother has sent the money for the ship. She had a paper from the company, very nice, with a seal on it, that says how sorry they are, and that her husband was a good worker. She showed it to everybody. She does not read English, so she does not know it says also that she has taken the fifty dollars and will not make any claim. Mr. Bauer read it to me after she was gone. He laughed, Andrej. He thought it was very funny, that she was so proud of it."

She put her hand upon his shoulder, upon the rough cloth of his work shirt that smelled of smoke and sweat and iron.

"I do not want to go back to the old country with a paper," she said. "I do not want to show people a paper with a seal on it. So—" Her voice broke, and she was silent a moment, and then she went on, "So you have signed it. All right. It is signed. I cannot unsign it. But you will listen to me now, Andrej Hudak, and you will do what I say. Tomorrow I will go to my cousin Anna in Braddock, and I will ask her, if it comes, can she take the children for a while. And you will not go to the meetings at Gorski's any more, because Gorski talks to the company police, everybody knows it but the men. And when the strike comes, if it comes, you will not be in the front. You will not be the one who throws the stone. You will not be the one they make an example of. There are men who want to be heroes. Let them. I want a husband."

He reached up and put his scarred hand over hers, and held it there; and for a while neither of them said anything at all.

It was a small thing, this conversation in a kitchen in the Flats, and no one would ever write of it in any newspaper. There were a thousand such conversations in the town that night, behind a thousand dim windows, and ten thousand more in other towns, in the coal fields and the textile mills and the lumber camps, wherever the great machine of industry had gathered up the poor of the earth and set them to toil for the profit of others. In each of them a man and a woman sat and weighed their hunger against their hope, and their fear against their dignity, and counted the pennies in the cracked sugar bowl on the shelf; and they did it alone, each pair of them, believing that no one else in the world had ever been so troubled. And in Pittsburgh, at that same hour, in a house upon a hill above the smoke, a man with a gold watch chain upon his waistcoat was reading the report of his spies, and making a list of names; and one of the names upon the list was the name of Andrej Hudak.

Hugh Raymond came back to Calder Falls on a Saturday afternoon in March, when the snow had gone to slush in the gutters and the sky over the valley was the color of an old iron kettle. He had been gone eleven years. He had left a boy of seventeen, with one pair of shoes and a cardboard valise tied up with clothesline, and he came back a man of twenty-eight, with a cheap overcoat and a bundle of pamphlets under his arm, and a look in his eyes that the people of the town did not understand, and would not have liked if they had.

He walked up from the depot by way of Furnace Street, because that was the way he remembered, and he found that it was still there, only blacker. Everything in Calder Falls was blacker. The smoke of the Keystone Steel Company's eleven stacks had been settling upon the town for forty years, and there was no paint made by the hand of man that could stand against it. The houses were company houses, two stories high and two rooms deep, set in rows along the hillside like teeth in a comb; and each one had been painted, once, a color that the company's agent called "slate," and which the smoke had long since turned to the color of nothing at all. In the yards there were cinders instead of grass, and the children who played in the cinders had faces as gray as the houses.

Hugh had a slip of paper with an address upon it, but he did not need it. He knew Number 41 Mill Row as soon as he saw it, for it was the house in which his Aunt Nora had died, and in which his cousin Ned had been born, and it had not changed except to grow more crooked. The porch sagged at one end where the post had rotted out, and somebody had propped it up with a length of railroad tie.

He knocked, and a woman opened the door—a thin woman with a baby on her hip and another child clinging to her skirt. She looked at him with the quick, frightened look which the poor give to every stranger, for a stranger may be the rent collector, or the company doctor, or the man from the store come about the bill.

"Is Ned Callahan here?" Hugh asked.

"He's sleeping," said the woman. "He's on nights."

"I'm his cousin. I'm Hugh. Hugh Raymond—Nora's sister's boy."

The woman's face changed. "Oh, my God!" she said. "Hugh! The one that went west! He's talked about you, Mister—he's talked about you a thousand times. Come in, come in. I'm Mary. I'm his wife. You'll have to excuse the place." She stood aside, and Hugh came into the front room, which was kitchen and parlor and dining room in one, and which smelled of boiled cabbage and wet wool and the coal smoke that leaked from the cracks in the stove.

"Don't wake him," Hugh said. "Let the man sleep."

But it was too late, for Ned had heard the voices through the thin board partition, and presently the door of the back room opened, and he came out in his undershirt, rubbing his eyes. Hugh stood up, and the two men looked at each other.

It is a strange thing to see a face one has known in childhood, after many years; for the mind keeps the old picture, and will not give it up, and so there is a moment of struggle, while the old face and the new one fight together. Hugh remembered Ned Callahan as a red-haired, freckled, laughing boy, the best swimmer in the river and the best pitcher on the Mill Row nine, a boy who could climb anything and was afraid of nothing. And here before him stood a stooped man with a gray face and pale eyes rimmed with red, and hair that was no longer red but a sort of faded rust, thinning at the temples. He was thirty-one years old, and he might have been forty-five.

"Hughie!" he said. "Is it you, Hughie?"

"It's me, Ned."

And then they had their arms about each other, and were pounding each other upon the back, and Ned was laughing, and there were tears on his cheeks, though he would have denied them to the end of his days. Mary stood by with the baby, smiling, and the older child, a boy of five or six, stared from behind her skirts at this strange man who had made his father cry.

They sat down at the oilcloth-covered table, and Mary made coffee, which was mostly chicory, and set out a plate of bread and a little dish of lard, apologizing all the while, so that Hugh had to beg her to stop. And then the questions began, tumbling over one another—where had he been, and what had he done, and why had he never written, and was he married, and was he rich?

"Rich!" laughed Hugh. "Look at this coat, Ned!"

He told them his story, so far as it could be told across a kitchen table. He had gone first to Chicago, and worked in a freight yard, and then he had gone farther west, to the lumber camps of Washington and Oregon, and had felled timber in the rain for four years. He had seen men crushed by falling trees and drowned in the log booms; he had slept in bunkhouses where the lice were so thick that the men burned their blankets in the spring; he had eaten food that a farmer would have been ashamed to give his hogs. And then there had been a strike, and he had been in it, and had been beaten by deputies and thrown into a jail in Everett, and it was there, in a cell with nine other men, that he had first heard the things that had changed his life.

"What things?" asked Ned.

Hugh hesitated, looking at his cousin's tired face. "Never mind that now," he said. "Tell me about yourself. Tell me about everybody. What's happened to the old crowd?"

And so Ned told him. He told it in a flat voice, without complaint, as a man reads off a list of goods from an invoice; and that was the most terrible thing about it, to Hugh, who listened. It was as if these things were the weather—as if they came out of the sky, and there was nothing to be done about them, and no one was to blame.

Did Hugh remember Johnny Sheehan, who used to play shortstop? Well, Johnny was dead—he had been caught by a ladle of hot metal in the open-hearth, seven years ago, and there had not been enough of him left to fill a coffin. The company had paid his mother a hundred and fifty dollars, after she signed a paper saying that it was Johnny's own carelessness. And Pete Kowalski, the big Polack who lived at the end of the row? He had lost both his legs under a train of ingot cars, and he sat now on a little wheeled board in front of the saloon on Furnace Street, and sold shoestrings. And the Murphy twins—one had gone to the penitentiary for breaking into the company store, and the other had the consumption, and was coughing his life out in a shack down by the river.

"And Aunt Nora?" said Hugh, in a low voice. "I heard she was gone. I got the letter in a camp, months after."

Ned looked down at the table. "It was the pneumonia," he said. "The winter of nineteen-five. The house was cold—we couldn't get coal. There was a strike that year, and they shut off our credit at the store, and the company wouldn't sell us coal. Their own coal, Hughie—from their own mines, that we could see piled up in the yards! And Ma got sick, and the company doctor wouldn't come because Pa was out on strike, and so—" He stopped, and turned his coffee cup around and around in his fingers. "She was fifty-two," he said.

Hugh said nothing. There was nothing to be said. He sat and looked at the cup going around in his cousin's fingers, and he noticed what he had not noticed before—that two of those fingers were missing at the first joint, and that the hand was seamed with white scars, like a map of rivers.

"What happened to your hand, Ned?"

"Oh, that." Ned laughed, a little shamefacedly, and put the hand in his lap. "That was the rolls, in the blooming mill. Eight years ago. I was lucky. A fellow named Hruska got his whole arm took off the same month."

"Did they pay you?"

"They gave me two weeks off. And they took me back after—they didn't have to do that. A lot of places wouldn't."

Hugh felt the blood come into his face, but he held his tongue. He looked about him at the room—at the cracked plaster and the stained ceiling, at the one window patched with cardboard, at the pallet in the corner where the older child slept; and he looked at Mary, who was perhaps twenty-six, and who had the eyes of a woman of fifty. He had seen many such homes in the last eleven years; he had seen them in Chicago and in Spokane and in the mill towns of the Willamette; but somehow this one was worse than all the rest, because it was his own blood that lived in it.

"What are you getting now, Ned?" he asked. "What's the pay?"

"Seventeen and a half cents an hour," said Ned. "I'm a second helper on Number Four open-hearth."

"And the hours?"

"Twelve. Seven days. We change shifts every two weeks—days to nights. When we change, we work the long turn."

"The long turn?"

"Twenty-four hours," said Ned. "Straight through. Then you get twenty-four off." And he added, with a kind of pride, as a soldier might speak of a battle, "I've done it a hundred times, Hughie. More."

Hugh sat back in his chair. He knew these figures; he had read them in the reports, and had quoted them himself from soapboxes in a dozen cities. But it was one thing to read them, printed in cold type in a pamphlet, and another thing to hear them from the lips of a man he loved, a man who had once been the best pitcher on the Mill Row nine. Twenty-four hours! He thought of what that meant—a man standing before the mouth of a furnace, in a heat that would wither a leaf, shoveling manganese and dolomite into a bath of molten steel, his eyes burning, his throat parched, his body streaming sweat until his clothes were soaked through; and then going out into the winter air, and walking home through the snow with the sweat freezing upon him; and doing this, not once, but every second Sunday of his life, year after year, until he died, or until the furnace took him, or until he became too old and slow to be of use, and was thrown upon the street like a worn-out shovel.

And all of this for what? Hugh knew that too. In the previous year, the Keystone Steel Company had paid its stockholders a dividend of eleven per cent; and its president, a gentleman named Thaddeus Marlowe, who lived in a marble house on Fifth Avenue and had never set foot in Calder Falls, had given half a million dollars to build a library at a university, and had been praised in all the newspapers of the land as a friend of learning and a benefactor of mankind. Hugh had seen a picture of the library in a magazine; it had a dome of white marble, and bronze doors, and a reading room with a ceiling painted by an Italian artist. And Ned Callahan, whose sweat had paid for it, did not have a book in his house, nor time to read one if he had.

"Ned," said Hugh, "do you ever think about it? About how it's all fixed?"

"Fixed?"

"Fixed, I mean, so that you work and they take. So that you make the steel, and they get the money for it. So that Marlowe has his marble house, and you have this."

Ned looked at him uneasily, and then glanced at the window, as if someone might be listening there. "Hughie," he said, "you'd better not talk like that around here."

"Why not?"

"Because they've got spotters. Everybody knows it. Men that work right beside you, and go to the office and tell. A fellow named Duffy got fired last year just for saying in the saloon that he thought the union ought to come back. They put him and his family out of their house in two days—right out in the street, in the rain, with their furniture. And his name went on the list. He couldn't get a job anywhere in the valley. He went to Ohio, they say."

"And you think that's right?"

"I didn't say it was right." Ned's voice had risen a little, and Mary looked over at him anxiously. "I didn't say anything was right. But what's a man going to do? I've got two kids, and another one coming." Mary flushed and turned away to the stove. "I've got to have a job. I've got to have a roof. Where would I go? What do I know how to do, except this? I've been in the mill since I was fourteen."

"I know that, Ned. I know it." Hugh leaned across the table and put his hand upon his cousin's scarred one. "I'm not blaming you. God knows I'm not blaming you. I'm only trying to tell you that it doesn't have to be this way. That's what I learned in that jail in Everett. That's what I've been doing these last four years—going around and telling men what I learned."

"What did you learn?"

And so Hugh told him. He spoke quietly at first, because of the window and because of Mary; but as he went on his voice grew warmer, and his eyes began to shine, and Ned, watching him, saw something come into his face that he had never seen in the face of any man in Calder Falls. He told how the mills and the mines and the railroads of the country had been built by the labor of men like Ned, and how they had been seized by a handful of men like Marlowe, who had done no labor at all; how those men owned not only the mills, but the courts and the legislatures and the newspapers and the churches, so that every voice in the land was raised to tell the worker that his lot was ordained by God and could never be changed; and how it could be changed, nevertheless, if only the workers would open their eyes, and stand together, and vote together, and take back what was theirs. He told how in Germany there were millions of men who believed this, and in England and France and Italy, and how there were hundreds of thousands in America already, and more every day; and how the time was coming—it was coming, Ned, as surely as the sun comes up over that ridge!—when the mills would belong to the men who worked in them, and there would be no more twelve-hour days, and no more long turns, and no more Johnny Sheehans burned to nothing in the open-hearth for the sake of an eleven per cent dividend.

When he had finished, there was a long silence in the little room. The baby had fallen asleep on Mary's shoulder, and the boy had crept out from behind her skirts and was sitting on the floor, staring up at the stranger with his mouth open. Outside, a switch engine was clanging in the yards, and far off, over the roofs, came the dull, endless roar of the mill, which never stopped, by day or by night, Sunday or weekday, and which the people of Calder Falls no longer heard, any more than they heard the beating of their own hearts.

"Hughie," said Ned at last, slowly, "it sounds fine. It sounds fine the way you tell it. But I'm tired."

And that was the whole of it—that was the answer that Hugh had heard from a thousand men, in a thousand towns, and that he would hear from a thousand more. *I'm tired.* They were too tired to think, too tired to hope, too tired even to be angry. The System had seen to that. It was not by accident that the Keystone Steel Company worked its men twelve hours a day and seven days a week; it was by design, though the gentlemen in the offices would never have admitted it, even to themselves. A man who works twelve hours a day does not read pamphlets, nor go to meetings, nor talk with his neighbors about the injustice of things; he eats his supper, and falls into bed, and gets up and goes back to the furnace. The weariness was a wall, higher and stronger than any wall of stone, and the men of Calder Falls lived inside it, and did not even know that it was there.

"I know you're tired, Ned," said Hugh gently. "That's what they count on."

Ned looked at him for a long time. Then he looked at his son on the floor—a thin, gray-faced little fellow, with his father's freckles and his father's rusty hair.

"He'll be in the mill in eight years," Ned said, as if speaking to himself. "Maybe less. They take them at twelve if the family needs it, and lie about the age."

"Does it have to be that way?"

Ned did not answer. But after a while he reached across the table, and drew toward him one of the pamphlets that Hugh had laid down beside his cup; and he turned it over in his maimed hand, and looked at the title, spelling out the words with his lips, for he had left school in the fourth grade. Then he folded it carefully, twice, and put it inside his undershirt, against his chest.

"Don't let anybody see that, Ned," whispered Mary, from the stove.

"I won't," said Ned.

Hugh stayed to supper, which was potatoes and the rest of the cabbage, and he slept that night on the floor of the front room, wrapped in his overcoat, while Ned went off to the mill at six o'clock with his dinner pail. Hugh walked with him as far as the gate, and they stood there for a minute in the dark, with the glare of the furnaces flaming up red against the clouds, and the men streaming past them in the thousands—gray men with gray faces, Irish and Slovak and Hungarian and Italian, men who could not speak one another's language, and who had been set against one another by the company for that very reason, so that they would never learn that they had a language in common.

"Will you come back, Hughie?" asked Ned.

"I'll come back," said Hugh. "And maybe next time I won't come alone."

Ned gripped his hand, and then turned and went in through the gate, and was swallowed up in the crowd and the smoke and the roaring glare. And Hugh stood looking after him, and thought of the red-haired boy who had been the best swimmer in the river; and he swore to himself, as he had sworn before in other places, before other gates, that he would not rest until the gates were opened, and the furnaces belonged to the men who fed them, and no child in all America had to follow his father into that fiery mouth.

It was a little after four o'clock in the afternoon when Anna Voytek discovered that the dime was gone, and for the space of perhaps half a minute she did not move at all, but stood in the middle of the kitchen with her hand still thrust into the cracked sugar bowl upon the shelf, as if by holding it there long enough she might cause the coin to come back again. Then she drew the hand out and looked at it, empty and red from the washtub, and the blood went out of her face, and she turned to the corner by the stove where her son was sitting upon the floor.

The boy's name was Mikolai, but in the street they called him Mickey, because the street was half Irish and half everything else, and the children of all nations had made among themselves a language of their own, out of which the parents were shut. He was six years old, and small for that age, as were most of the children of the Flats. He had a round head with hair the color of dry straw, which his mother cut with the bread knife, and great pale eyes, and a nose that was perpetually running, for he had had a cold since October, and it was now the end of February. He wore a pair of trousers which had once been his father's, cut down and sewn up again by lamplight, and a shirt of flour sacking upon which, if one looked closely, one could still read the words "PATENT ROLLER PROCESS." At the present moment he was engaged in building a house out of four clothespins and a sardine tin, and he did not look up, for he had heard the sugar bowl lid rattle, and he knew.

"Mikolai," said his mother.

He did not answer.

"Mikolai, come here to me."

He got up slowly and came, holding his hands behind his back as though they had done the thing without him, and stood before her upon the boards of the floor, which she had scrubbed white that morning with lye that ate the skin from her knuckles. She looked down at him, and he looked at the floor.

"Where is the money that was in the bowl?"

The child said nothing. His lower lip had begun to tremble, and he caught it with his teeth.

"I ask you a question! Where is the money? The ten cents, the money for the lard, the money for your father's dinner pail—where is it?"

And then, because she could see it in his face, and because something rose up in her throat that she could not keep down, she seized him by the shoulder with her wet hand and shook him, so that his head went back and forth like the head of a doll; and she cried out at him in the tongue of the old country, the words tumbling over one another, so that the little Irish boy who was passing beneath the window stopped and listened with his mouth open, not understanding one word in ten, but understanding perfectly what was taking place.

---

Now the reader who has been brought up in comfort, and who has never had occasion to count the price of lard, will be tempted at this point to pass judgment upon Anna Voytek. He will say that she is a hard woman, and an ignorant one, and that it is a shameful thing for a mother to lay hands upon a child for the sake of ten cents. He will perhaps recall that in his own nursery, when he had broken a vase or told a falsehood, he was reasoned with gently, and sent to sit upon a chair, and given to understand that his conduct had grieved his mother; and he will reflect that the foreign element in our industrial towns is sadly in need of instruction in the principles of modern child-rearing. And all this is very well; but before he settles himself in that opinion, let him consider for a moment what the ten cents was, and where it had come from, and what it stood for in that kitchen.

Stefan Voytek, the father of the boy, worked as a third helper on Number Six open-hearth furnace at the Carrick works of the Allegheny Valley Steel Company, which was in turn a subsidiary of a larger concern whose name was printed in the financial pages of every newspaper in the land, and whose stock had that year paid a dividend of seven per cent upon a capitalization of which, by the estimate of persons who had looked into the matter, something more than one half was water. For his services Stefan received the sum of sixteen and one half cents an hour. He worked twelve hours a day, seven days in the week, one week upon the day turn and the next upon the night; and at the end of every second week, when the shifts changed over, he worked what was known as the "long turn," which was twenty-four hours without stopping, from six o'clock on Sunday morning until six o'clock on Monday, in the heat of the furnaces, carrying and shoveling and raking, with the sweat running into his boots. There were men in the department who had done this for eleven years, and some of them were still alive.

Out of his wages, which came to something less than fourteen dollars a week when there was no lay-off, Stefan paid nine dollars a month for the three rooms in which the family lived. These rooms were in a frame house which leaned toward the river, and which had been built by a man who did not live in it, upon land that belonged to the company, and they were rented through an agent who also sold insurance, and who came every Saturday to collect a quarter upon a policy that was to pay for Stefan's funeral. There was a dollar a month for coal, for though the family could see the coal barges go down the river every day, and the great piles of it lying upon the company's wharves, they had to buy it by the bucket from a dealer who bought it from the company. There was the doctor, who came when the baby had the croup in December, and who had to be paid two dollars, which they had not finished paying yet. There was the money which Stefan sent home every quarter to his mother in the village beyond the Carpathians, because she had sold her cow to buy his steamship ticket. And the rest of it was for food.

Anna had learned, in the three years since she had come to America, the price of every article of food that was sold in the Flats, and the price of it in every one of the four stores, and the days of the week upon which it was a little cheaper. She knew that the butcher on Fourth Street put his thumb upon the scale, and that the grocer at the corner sold milk which had been watered and then whitened with chalk, and that the sausage in the window of the Hungarian's shop was made of things which it was better not to think about. She knew that the bread which was sold at five cents the loaf weighed less every month, though the loaf was baked to the same size, so that it was swollen and full of air; and she baked her own when she could get the flour, getting up at three in the morning to knead it, when Stefan was on the day turn, so that the stove would be cold again before the heat of the house became unbearable to the sleeping children. She knew how many potatoes could be got for a nickel, and how many onions, and how long a ham bone could be boiled before there was nothing left in it; and she knew, with a certainty which was like a pain in her side, exactly how far ten cents worth of lard would go.

It would go a week. It would go into the pan in which Stefan's potatoes were fried, and onto the bread that went into his dinner pail, and without it the bread was dry, and the potatoes stuck and burned, and a man who swung a shovel for twelve hours before an open furnace, in a heat that was a hundred and thirty degrees in the summer and not much less in the winter, could not keep up his strength upon dry bread and burned potatoes. And if he could not keep up his strength, the boss would see it; for the boss was always watching, and there were always men at the gate in the morning, Croatians and Slovaks and Italians and Negroes from the South, standing in the slush with their hands in their pockets, waiting for the chance to take Stefan's place at sixteen and a half cents an hour—or at fifteen, if the company should find that it could get them for fifteen. All this Anna knew, not as a thing reasoned out, but as a thing she had learned in her flesh; and it was all of this, and not the ten cents merely, that had come up into her throat when she put her hand into the sugar bowl and found it empty.

---

"Where is it?" she cried again. "Tell me, or I will beat you until you cannot stand!"

The boy began to cry. He did it silently at first, with his face screwed up and the tears running down into the dirt upon his cheeks; and then, as his mother shook him again, it burst out of him all at once, a wail that rose and filled the little room, and he gasped out the story between his sobs.

It had been the big boys from Second Street. There was one named Danny Mahon, who was ten, and who had a cap with a broken visor, and who could spit farther than anyone in the Flats; and he had come along the alley that morning, while Anna was hanging the wash in the yard, and had shown Mikolai a wonderful game. It was played with pennies, which one threw against the wall of the saloon, and whoever's penny landed nearest to the wall took all the others. Danny Mahon had won a whole handful of pennies that way, he said, and he had shown them, jingling in his pocket; and he had said that a little feller could win just as good as a big feller, because it was all luck, and if Mickey had a penny he could try. And Mickey had not had a penny, but he had known where there was a dime; and he had thought—he had truly thought, with the whole of his six-year-old heart—that he would win, and win a great deal, and come home with his pockets full of pennies, and give them to his mother, so that she would not have to sit up at night at the kitchen table, with the lamp turned low to save the oil, counting coins over and over and moving her lips.

So he had taken the dime, and Danny Mahon had changed it for him into ten pennies, taking one for his trouble; and they had pitched them against the wall of the saloon, and Danny Mahon had won them all, every one, in less time than it takes to tell. And when Mickey had cried, Danny had given him a shove into the gutter and gone away whistling, and the other boys had laughed. That was all.

Anna let go of his shoulder. She stood looking at him, and for a moment it seemed as if she were going to strike him; her hand was raised, and the child shrank from it, putting up his arms over his face. But the hand did not fall. Instead, she turned away and sat down heavily upon the one chair in the kitchen that had all its legs, and put her red hands over her eyes, and began to rock back and forth.

"Gambling," she said, in a low voice. "My son. Six years old, and already a gambler. Already they have taught him. Oh, Holy Mother!"

---

It was a fact which Anna Voytek did not know, and which, had she known it, she could not have put into words, that her son had that morning received his first lesson in the economic system of the country to which she had brought him. He had been told, by one who was older and stronger and more experienced than he, that if he would risk what little he had, he might come away with a great deal more; that it was all a matter of luck; that the big fellow and the little fellow stood equal before the wall. He had believed this, as millions of grown men believe it, and he had put down his ten cents, and the older and stronger one had taken it, together with a commission for the service of taking it. And when he had protested, he had been knocked into the gutter, and the bystanders had laughed.

There were men in the city of Pittsburgh, thirty miles up the river, who had played this same game upon a larger scale, and who lived in houses of carved stone with iron fences around them, and who gave libraries to towns like Carrick, with their names cut over the doors. There was one such library at the top of the hill, and Anna had once climbed up to look at it, holding the baby in her arms, and had stood upon the marble steps and looked in through the glass at the long rows of books and the electric lamps with green shades; but she had not gone in, because she could not read English, and because her shoes were not good enough, and because a man in a uniform had come to the door and looked at her. The money that had built that library had come out of the long turn, and the sixteen and a half cents an hour, and the burned potatoes in the dinner pails; but nobody in Carrick put it that way, and if anybody had put it that way in the hearing of the company's police, he would have found himself upon the other side of the river by nightfall, with his name upon a list that went to every mill in the valley.

---

Presently the child, finding that he was not to be beaten, crept toward his mother and laid his head against her knee. He was still sobbing, but quietly now, with long shuddering breaths; and he said, in the language of the street, which she did not like to hear in her house, "I'm sorry, Ma. I'm awful sorry. I won't never do it again."

She took her hands from her face and looked at him. And then her anger came back to her, for she was frightened, and fear in the very poor goes always by the name of anger. She took him by both arms and held him away from her and made him look at her.

"Listen to me," she said. "Listen, Mikolai, and remember, because I will say it only once. You know what your father does? You know where he goes, at night, when you are asleep? He goes into the fire. Into the fire, like the souls in the pictures in the church! He stands before the furnace all night, and the fire comes out at him, and the iron runs like water, and if he steps wrong, if he is tired and his foot slips, the iron will take him, and there will be nothing left to bury. You remember Jozef Kral, who lived across the alley, who gave you the wooden horse? That is what happened to Jozef Kral. They did not find enough of him to put into the box. And for that, for going into the fire, your father gets money, a little money, and he gives it to me, and I put it in the bowl, and every penny of it is his sweat. Every penny of it is his blood. And you took it, and you gave it to that Irish thief to throw against the wall of the saloon!"

The boy stared at her, his eyes wide with horror. He had not known about the fire; he had known only that his father came home black, and slept like a dead man, and must not be awakened.

"Tomorrow," said Anna, "your father will have dry bread in his pail. He will eat it, and he will not say anything, because he never says anything. And you will look at him, and you will remember why."

She stood up. Her face was set and hard, and her voice was hard; but there was a trembling under it that the child could feel, though he did not understand.

"Now you will go into the corner," she said, "and you will kneel there on the floor, and you will say your prayers, all of them, the Our Father and the Hail Mary and the Act of Contrition, and you will ask God to forgive you. And you will not get up until I tell you. And there will be no supper for you tonight. Go!"

---

He went. He knelt down in the corner by the stove, upon the boards which were cold despite the fire, because the wind came up between them from the space beneath the house, where the river mist lay; and he folded his hands, and began to whisper the prayers in a high, broken voice, stumbling over the words, which he did not understand, for they were in Latin and in Polish, and he thought now mostly in English. His mother turned back to the washtub, and plunged her arms into the gray water, and began to scrub at one of Stefan's shirts, which was so stiff with sweat and grime that it stood up by itself when it was dry; and she scrubbed it with a violence that tore the skin upon her knuckles anew, and did not feel it.

From the next room there came a sound of movement, and the creaking of the bed; and then the door opened, and Stefan Voytek stood in the doorway in his undershirt, his eyes red and swollen with sleep, his face still gray around the eyes and in the creases of the neck with the dust that would not wash out. He was a big man, broad in the shoulders, but he stooped, as all the open-hearth men stooped after a few years, and when he moved, it was slowly, as though every muscle had been separately bruised. He was twenty-nine years old.

"What is it?" he said. "What is the noise?"

Anna told him, in a few words, without turning from the tub. He listened, rubbing his eyes with the heels of his hands; and then he looked across the kitchen at the small figure kneeling in the corner, its shoulders shaking. For a long moment he said nothing. Then he went to the shelf and took down his coat, which hung upon a nail beside the sugar bowl, and felt in the pocket of it, and brought out a piece of tobacco wrapped in paper, and looked at it, and put it back.

"I will chew less this week," he said.

Anna turned upon him. "You will not! You need it, in the heat—you have said so yourself, it keeps the mouth wet—"

"I will chew less," said Stefan, and sat down upon the chair, and put his elbows upon his knees, and looked at the floor.

The boy in the corner had stopped praying. He was watching his father with eyes that were enormous in his small white face; and something was happening in him that was not in the catechism, and that the priest had never told him about. He was learning that what he had done did not fall upon himself alone, but upon all of them; that in that house there was nothing which belonged to one person, not a penny, nor a crust of bread, nor a moment of sleep; that each of them was bound to the others by a chain whose links were made of dimes and nickels and the hours of the night shift; and that when he had pulled upon that chain, it had pulled upon his father, who had gone into the fire. It was a lesson that the children of the rich are never taught, and that the children of the poor are taught early, and do not forget.

He began to cry again, but differently now, not for himself; and Stefan, hearing it, got up from the chair and crossed the kitchen and stood over him. Anna watched from the tub, her hands motionless in the water. The big man looked down at his son for a while; and then he put out one hand, black in the cracks and calloused like the hide of an animal, and laid it upon the straw-colored head.

"Pray," he said, gently. "Pray, Mikolai. And when you are a man, you will not go into the fire. You will go to school, and you will learn the English, and you will work in an office with a white collar. That is why we came."

Then he went back into the other room and lay down again upon the bed, for he had to be at the gate at a quarter before six; and in a few minutes they could hear his breathing, heavy and harsh, the breathing of a man whose lungs were full of the dust of the furnaces.

And the boy knelt in the corner and said his prayers, all of them, twice over; and his mother scrubbed the shirt, and the twilight came down over the Flats, and the sky above the Carrick works turned red with the glare of the open hearths, as it turned red every night, so that people who rode past in the trains of the Pennsylvania Railroad looked out of their windows and said to one another what a magnificent sight it was, and what an evidence of the industrial greatness of the nation.

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. It was necessary to call house-movers, and take the Bankside homestead to another lot; but that didn’t trouble Mr. Bankside, who had already moved himself to an ocean-front palace near Dad, and bought himself a whole outfit of furniture, and a big new limousine, also a “sport-car,” in which to drive himself to the country club to play golf every afternoon. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Dad and Bunny made another trip to Lobos River, and not without some difficulty they conquered the “jinx” in Number Two, and brought in a very good well. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. Right in the midst of his other triumphs it had occurred to him to take one of his old Antelope wells and go a little lower, and see what he found; he tried it—and lo and behold, at eight hundred feet farther down the darn thing went and blew its head off. Dad wanted some of the other operators to go in with him, and he was going up there and make a deal. “You promised we were going quail-shooting this year.”

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.
