The Haskell bungalow stood on Magnolia Avenue in the town of San Isidro, and it was exactly like the bungalows on either side of it, and like the hundred others that a real-estater named Mr. Fogarty had set out in rows upon what had been, three years before, a bean-field. It had five rooms and a screened porch, and a little patch of lawn in front that Ed Haskell watered every evening with a hose, and a pepper tree that had been planted at the same time as the house and was now about as high as Ed's shoulder. There was a mortgage on the bungalow, and a second mortgage, which was the way you bought a home in Southern California in those days. You paid three hundred dollars down, and the rest at so much a month, and if you missed two payments running, Mr. Fogarty's lawyer would write you a letter, very polite, and the third time he would not be polite at all. It was a fine system for Mr. Fogarty, who had sold some of these bungalows three or four times over, and every time had kept what had been paid in.

Ed Haskell was a timekeeper at the Golden State Packing Company, which put up apricots and peaches in cans with bright-colored labels, and shipped them all over the world, so that people in London and Chicago might know what a wonderful country California was. Ed had a little booth by the gate of the plant, and a big clock, and a rack full of cards, and it was his job to know when every man and woman came in and went out, and to dock them a quarter of an hour's pay if they were three minutes late. He did not like this part of his work, but somebody had to do it, and he was thirty-four years old and had a wife and a little girl, and the payments on the bungalow, and on the piano, and on the Ford.

On this particular evening in July he came home later than usual, and he did not water the lawn. He came up the walk slowly, and sat down on the porch steps, and Nora, who had been watching for him through the curtains, knew right away that something had happened. She had been married to Ed for nine years, and could read him like the morning paper; better, in fact, because Ed did not have big headlines put in to fool you.

"Supper's been ready half an hour," she said, coming out. "What kept you?"

"Mr. Durfee wanted to see me."

Mr. Durfee was the general superintendent, and nobody at the plant was called in to see him unless it meant either a raise or the sack. Nora's hand went to her throat. "Ed! He didn't—you haven't lost your job?"

"No," said Ed. "Nothin' like that. Jist the opposite."

"The opposite? What do you mean?"

"He offered me Hoyt's place. Assistant superintendent. Hoyt's goin' up to the new plant at Fresno."

Nora stood staring at him; and then she gave a little cry, and sat down on the step beside him and threw her arms around him. "Oh, Ed! Oh, honey! Why, that's wonderful! Why didn't you tell me right off? And here you sit lookin' like it was a funeral!" She drew back to look at him. "How much does it pay?"

"Two hundred and twenty-five."

"A month?" Ed was getting a hundred and thirty-five, and Nora began right away to do sums in her head, the way every wife in America had learned to do. They could pay off the piano by Christmas; they could get the new linoleum for the kitchen; they could maybe even trade in the Ford, which had been bought second-hand and was falling to pieces, for one of those new sedans with glass windows that you could roll up and down. Her sister Myrtle's husband had one, and Myrtle never let her forget it. "Ed, I can't believe it! When do you start?"

"I ain't said I'd take it."

She looked at him, and the joy went out of her face, and something hard and watchful came into it. "What do you mean, you ain't said you'd take it? Are you crazy?"

"Let's go in and eat," said Ed. "I'll tell you about it."

So they went in, and little Alice was put to bed—she was six, and had already had her supper, and had to be told a story about a rabbit before she would close her eyes. Then Nora put the warmed-over pot-roast on the table, and sat down across from her husband, and folded her hands, and waited. Ed ate for a while without saying anything, and she watched him, and the clock on the shelf ticked very loud.

"Well?" she said at last.

"It's this way," said Ed. "You know there's been talk at the plant about the union."

Nora knew. Everybody in San Isidro knew. There had been men going around among the cannery workers, and holding meetings in a hall over a pool-room on Second Street, and handing out little papers printed in English and Spanish and Italian. The San Isidro *Herald* had a piece about it nearly every day; it said the men were outside agitators, and Reds, and paid by Moscow, and that they wanted to destroy the American home. The *Herald* belonged to the same man who owned the biggest bank in town, and the bank held the paper of the Golden State Packing Company; but Nora did not know that, and if she had known it, it would not have meant anything to her.

"What's the union got to do with you?" she asked.

"Mr. Durfee says the company ain't goin' to stand for it. He says they're operatin' on the American Plan, and they always will." The American Plan, it should be explained, was a name which the Chamber of Commerce and the Merchants' and Manufacturers' Association had thought up, meaning that you could not have a union; and it was a very clever name, because if you were against it, that made you un-American. "He says there was a meetin' last Thursday night, over at the hall, and some of our people was there. He wants to know which ones."

"Well, what of it?"

"He thinks I know. Bein' timekeeper, I know all the men, and I hear what's goin' on. He says if I'll give him the names, the job's mine."

Nora was silent for a moment. "And do you know?"

Ed put down his fork. "I know some of 'em."

"Well, then!" said Nora. She said it as if that settled everything; and to her mind, it did. Here was a simple matter: a man had a chance to better himself, and all he had to do was to tell his employer something which the employer had a perfect right to know. She could not see where the difficulty lay; and the fact that Ed could see a difficulty filled her with alarm, as if she had discovered a crack in the foundation of the house.

"It ain't so simple as that, Nora."

"I don't see why not. It's Mr. Durfee's plant, ain't it? He's payin' them. If they don't like the way they're treated, they can quit."

"Quit and go where? There ain't another cannery in fifty miles that ain't run the same way. And you know what happens. The company'll fire every one of 'em, and put 'em on the black-list, so they can't get a job in the whole valley. There's Joe Martinez, with seven kids. There's old Mrs. Pruitt, that's worked on the peelin' line since before I come there; her husband's laid up with his back. There's Tony Scalia—"

"Tony Scalia's a Red, everybody knows that! He talks it right out on the street!"

"Tony's a good feller," said Ed, stubbornly. "He jist thinks the folks on the line ought to get more'n thirty cents an hour, and I don't know as I blame him. You try standin' over a vat of lye fer ten hours in this heat, with the steam comin' up in your face—"

"Ed Haskell!" Nora's voice went up sharp. "Are you tellin' me you're on their side?"

"I ain't on nobody's side. I'm jist sayin'—"

"You're sayin' you'd throw away two hundred and twenty-five dollars a month to protect a lot of dagoes and Mexicans that would cut your throat tomorrow if it'd do 'em any good!"

"They wouldn't, though," said Ed. "That's jist it. They been decent to me, Nora. When Alice had the croup that time, and I was off work, it was Joe Martinez' wife come over and sat up with her so you could sleep. You remember that."

Nora remembered it, and it made her angrier, because it was a thing that could not be answered. She got up and began to clear away the dishes, making a great deal of noise with them. She was a pretty woman, or had been when Ed married her; she had soft brown hair that she wore bobbed now, because all the women were wearing it bobbed, and a round face that was beginning to show little lines at the corners of the mouth. Those lines had come from nine years of figuring—of making over dresses, and cutting coupons out of the paper, and saying no to Alice when she wanted things in the store windows. Nora had been brought up on a dry-farm in Kansas, where her father had lost everything in a drought, and the thing she was afraid of more than anything in the world was to be poor again. When you have once seen your mother crying over an auctioneer's notice, it stays with you; and Nora would come awake in the night sometimes, and lie there thinking about the payments, and listening to Ed breathe, and wondering what would happen to them if he got sick.

She came back and stood over him, with a dish-towel in her hands.

"Ed, listen to me. I want you to think about this sensible. Do you know what Myrtle said to me last Sunday? She said Harold was gettin' a raise, and they were thinkin' of movin' up to Alta Vista Heights. And she looked at this house like—like it was a chicken-coop. And I had to sit there and smile."

"I don't care what Myrtle thinks."

"Well, I do! I'm sick of it! I'm sick of bein' the poor relation! I'm sick of makin' over my old clothes and pretendin' they're new, and havin' everybody know! I want Alice to grow up and have nice things, and go to the high school with her head up, and maybe go to the university. Don't you want that?"

"Sure, I want it."

"Then what's the matter with you?"

Ed sat looking at the oilcloth on the table. It had a pattern of little blue windmills, and there was a place where the pattern was worn through, from his elbow resting on it every night. He was a slow man, and words did not come easy to him; he felt things a long time before he could say them, and sometimes he could never say them at all. But he made a try now.

"It's this way, Nora. I been sittin' in that booth for six years. I see 'em come in every mornin', and I see 'em go out every night. I see the women that's been on the line all day, and their hands is all cracked and bleedin' from the fruit acid, and they ain't allowed to wear gloves because it slows 'em down. I see the kids that's sixteen, and says they're eighteen, because their folks needs the money. I punch their cards, and I dock 'em when they're late, and I don't say nothin'. That's my job. But this here is different. This is—" he hunted for the word—"this is like I was a stool-pigeon."

"Don't you say that word in this house!"

"Well, that's what it is. That's what they'd call me. And that's what I'd be."

"Who'd call you? Them Reds? What do you care what they call you? They'll all be gone in a month!"

"I'd call myself," said Ed, in a low voice.

There was a silence. Out on the street a car went by with its cut-out open, making a noise like a machine-gun, and some young people in it were laughing and singing a song from the movies. Nora sat down again, slowly, and the dish-towel lay in her lap, and she twisted it in her hands.

She was not a bad woman, you understand; she was a woman who had been taught, by every voice she had ever listened to, that the thing which mattered in life was to get ahead. The preacher at the First Methodist Church said it on Sundays, in a roundabout way, telling about the parable of the talents; the *Herald* said it every day, in the stories about the poor boy who had become a millionaire; the movies said it, with their pictures of shop-girls who married the boss's son and lived in marble palaces; the advertisements said it, on every bill-board along the highway. Nora had never heard anybody say anything else, except the Reds, and they were wicked people who wanted to take away everything you had. And now here was her own husband, talking like them! It was as if he had come home and told her he had taken to drink.

"Ed," she said, and her voice had changed; it was soft now, and pleading, and there were tears in it. "Ed, honey, you know I ain't hard-hearted. I'm sorry for those people, same as you. He thought about the hundred and thirty-five dollars, and the two hundred and twenty-five, and the difference, which was ninety dollars a month; and he thought how strange it was that a man's soul should come to have a price on it, like a can of peaches, and be marked up and down according to the market. Nobody had ever told him that this was the way the world was run. They had told him in Sunday-school that you should love your neighbor, and they had told him in the high-school civics class that this was a free country, where every man had the right to speak his mind; and he had believed them both. Across the street Mr. Bascomb's pipe glowed red in the dark, and went dim, and glowed again. Somewhere down the block a radio was playing a dance tune. It was eight years since Philip Ashby had seen his cousin Ruth, and he had grown so accustomed to not seeing her that the matter had ceased to trouble him. There had been a quarrel in the family; it had to do with Grandfather Mercer's will, and with a strip of land along the Arroyo Seco which Grandfather had left to his son, Philip's father, and which Aunt Margaret had claimed was promised to her. Philip had been eleven at the time, and had understood nothing about it, except that there were no more Sunday dinners at Aunt Margaret's cottage in Highland Park, and that when her name came up at table, his mother would look at his father, and his father would look at his plate. Afterward the strip of land had been cut up into building lots, and a company had been formed, and the lots had been sold to people from Iowa and Kansas at prices which made Philip's father a man of consequence in Pasadena. And so the quarrel had paid for itself, you might say; that was the way it went with quarrels among the well-to-do. The ones who won could afford to forget, and generally did.

But now Philip was twenty, and home from the university for the summer, and he had a roadster of his own, and a great deal of time on his hands. One day he was driving down Spring Street, in the heart of the city, and he saw a young woman waiting for a street-car at the corner of Fifth, and something about the set of her head made him turn and look again. She was slender and straight, in a plain blue dress, with a straw hat pulled down over brown hair, and she was holding a bundle of papers under her arm. Philip pulled over to the curb, and the motorist behind him blew his horn in a rage, but Philip didn't care. He leaned out and called, "Ruth! Ruth Mercer!" And the young woman turned, and stared at him for a moment, and then her face broke into a smile which was the very same smile he remembered from the orange grove behind Grandfather's house, when they had been eight and nine years old and had hidden together from the Japanese gardener.

"Why, Phil!" she said. "Is it really you? You've grown up!"

"So have you," he said. "Get in, won't you? I'll take you wherever you're going."

She hesitated, and he saw her glance at the roadster, which was a bright yellow one, and very new, with nickel trimmings that flashed in the sun. Then she laughed, and said, "All right; but I'm only going to Boyle Heights, and you'll be sorry you asked."

"I won't be sorry," he said. "I've been wanting to see you for years." This was not quite true, but it seemed true while he said it; and Ruth climbed in beside him, and put her bundle of papers on her lap, and they were off.

---

It is a strange thing, meeting a relative after a long absence; for you have known each other in a way that no stranger can know you, and yet you are strangers. You remember a little girl with skinned knees who cried because a bee had stung her, and here is a grown woman who has lived a whole life you know nothing about. Philip found himself searching her face for the little girl, and every now and then he would catch a glimpse of her, in a gesture, or a turn of speech, and then she would be gone again, and there would be this capable, self-possessed young person, who seemed in some way older than himself, though she was really a year younger.

"Tell me about yourself," he said. "What are you doing? How is Aunt Margaret?"

"Mother is well enough," said Ruth. "She takes in sewing. Didn't you know?"

He hadn't known; and he felt a little shock of embarrassment, as if he had been caught at something. "And Uncle Dan?"

"Father was hurt," she said. "Three years ago. He was a brakeman on the Southern Pacific, you remember, and he was crushed between two cars in the yards at Colton. He can walk now, with a crutch, but he can't work. The company paid him four hundred dollars, and their lawyer made him sign a paper saying it was his own fault."

"Good Lord!" said Philip. "Was it his own fault?"

"They had cut down the crews," said Ruth, quite matter-of-factly. "There used to be three men to do the work, and they made it two. Father was working his fourteenth hour that day. So you can say it was his fault, if you like; he ought to have been more wide awake."

Philip did not know what to answer. He drove for a while in silence, dodging a wagon loaded with crates of cantaloupes, and a jitney bus, and a Mexican boy selling newspapers. He was thinking that nobody had ever told him about Uncle Dan; and then he was thinking that perhaps somebody had known, and had not told him. That was a disquieting idea, and he put it away, to be taken out and examined later.

"And you?" he asked. "What are you doing?"

"I work in a cannery," said Ruth. "At least, I did until last week. I was a forelady on the packing line. Now I'm doing something else."

She looked at him with a kind of amused defiance, and tapped the bundle of papers on her lap. "I'm organizing," she said.

Philip had heard of organizing, of course; everybody had. In the city of Los Angeles there was a great association of business men, which had decided many years ago that this was to be an "open shop" town, and which spent a great deal of money every year to keep it so. Philip's father belonged to this association, and gave money to it, and talked about it at the dinner table; and from these conversations Philip had gathered that a labor organizer was a sort of foreign agitator, who stirred up contented workingmen with lies, and lived on their dues, and probably threw bombs on the side. There had been a newspaper building dynamited once, long ago, before Philip was born, and the business men of the city had never let anybody forget it.

So here was a strange thing: his own cousin, with whom he had made mud pies under the pepper tree, was a labor organizer! Philip glanced at her sidewise, half expecting her to look different, now that he knew; but she looked just the same, with the sun on her cheek and a little wisp of brown hair blowing loose from under her hat.

They came out upon the bridge over the river, which in summer was nothing but a broad bed of sand and stones, with a trickle of water down the middle, and a few willows; and beyond it lay Boyle Heights, where the poorer people lived—Russians and Jews and Mexicans, and the families of railroad men. "I'm only joshin' him," said Uncle Dan. "Set down, boy, set down. Ma, ain't there some of that lemonade left?"

So they sat in the little front room, which was very clean, and very crowded, with a horsehair sofa and a table covered with an oilcloth, and a picture of Grandfather Mercer on the wall—the same picture which hung in Philip's father's library, only there it had a gilt frame and here it had a plain black one. Aunt Margaret brought lemonade from the lemon tree, and they talked; or rather, the older people asked questions, and Philip answered them. How was his mother? Was it true they had a swimming pool? What was he studying at the university? Did he play football?

Philip told them that he was studying economics, because his father wished him to go into the business; and that he did not play football, but he was on the tennis team; and that he belonged to a fraternity, which was a sort of club where the fellows lived together. He found himself making these things sound less grand than they were; he did not mention that the fraternity house had a Steinway grand piano, or that the fellows kept a colored man to wait on table. He did not quite know why he left these things out; it was some instinct, some sense of the fitness of things, which told him that a Steinway piano would not go well with the horsehair sofa and the mended cushion on the porch.

"Economics," said Uncle Dan, thoughtfully. "That's the science of money, ain't it? What do they teach you about it?"

"Well," said Philip, "they teach you about supply and demand, and how prices are fixed, and about wages—"

"Wages!" said Uncle Dan. "Now that's interestin'. What do they say about wages?"

Philip tried to remember; it had been in the second semester, and there had been a long chapter about it, with graphs. "They say," he said, "that wages are fixed by the law of supply and demand, the same as anything else. If there are a lot of workers and not many jobs, wages go down; and if there are a lot of jobs and not many workers, they go up. And the professor says that it's no use trying to interfere with it, because it's a natural law, like gravitation."

Uncle Dan nodded slowly, and looked at Ruth, and Ruth looked at the ceiling. "Like gravitation," said Uncle Dan. "Well, now, I'll tell you somethin', son. When the railroad cut our crews from three men to two, there wasn't no fewer men wantin' to work. There was jist as many as before. What there was, was a feller in an office in San Francisco who figgered he could save so many thousand dollars a year if he got two men to do the work of three. Now maybe that's gravitation, I don't know. I never went to college. But it come down on my leg mighty heavy, whatever it was."

---

Philip did not argue; he had no argument ready, and besides, it did not seem the place for one. He drank his lemonade, which was sour, because sugar cost money; and presently Ruth said she must go to a meeting, and he offered to drive her, and she accepted. Aunt Margaret kissed him again at the door, and made him promise to come back, and Uncle Dan shook his hand and said, "No hard feelin's, boy. You tell your pa I said howdy." And Philip promised that he would, though he knew very well that he would not; there were some messages you did not carry into a house in Pasadena.

In the car, Ruth was silent for a while, and then she said, "I'm sorry about Father. He gets bitter sometimes. You can't blame him."

"I don't blame him," said Philip. "I—I didn't know about any of it, Ruth. Honestly I didn't. Nobody ever told me."

"No," she said. "I suppose nobody did."

He drove on, and he was thinking hard. He was thinking about the strip of land along the Arroyo Seco, and the building lots, and the people from Iowa; and about the four hundred dollars, and the paper Uncle Dan had signed; and about his own roadster, which had cost two thousand. He was not a stupid young man, though nobody had ever asked him to use his mind for anything more than passing examinations; and now, all at once, his mind was working of its own accord, putting things together and taking them apart, the way you take apart a watch to see what makes it go. It was not a comfortable sensation.

"Ruth," he said, "what was it really about? The quarrel, I mean. Between your mother and my father."

She looked at him. "Do you want the truth?"

"Of course I do."

"Grandfather meant the land for Mother. He said so, many times; he said it before witnesses. But he never put it in writing, and when he was sick at the end, your father was the one who looked after his affairs, and the will that came out was the will your father's lawyer drew. Mother could have gone to court, but she hadn't any money for lawyers, and Father said it would only make bad blood. So she let it go." Ruth paused, and then she added, quite gently, "I don't say your father did anything that wasn't legal, Phil. I'm sure it was all legal. That's the way things are done."

Philip said nothing. He was remembering the way his mother looked at his father, and his father looked at his plate.

---

The meeting was in a hall over a bakery on First Street, and there were women going up the stairs—Mexican women with black shawls, and Italian women, and some American girls in cheap bright dresses, and they all spoke to Ruth, and some of them looked at Philip and his yellow roadster with frank curiosity. Ruth got out, and gathered up her papers, and then she stood on the curb and looked at him.

"Thank you for the ride, Phil," she said. "It was nice to see you. Truly it was."

"Ruth," he said, "is there anything—I mean, could I help somehow? I've got some money of my own, an allowance, and I don't need half of it—"

She shook her head, and the smile came again, the old smile from the orange grove. "That's sweet of you. But it isn't money we need, not that kind. Do you know what these women earn in the cannery? Twenty cents an hour, in the rush season, standing ten hours on a cement floor, with their hands in brine till the skin comes off. If you gave every one of them a hundred dollars, it would be gone in a few months, and they'd be right back where they were. What they need is to stand together, so they can ask for what they've earned. You can't give them that. Nobody can give it to them. They have to take it."

"Take it!" said Philip. "That sounds like—"

"Like a Red? Yes, I know. That's what they'll call me in the papers, if they ever bother to call me anything." She laughed. "But you come to a meeting some time, and see for yourself whether these women look like Reds. Most of them go to Mass every morning."

"I will," said Philip, and he meant it, though he did not know how he could possibly explain it at home.

She turned to go, and then turned back. "Phil, do you still remember the time we buried the dead bird under the pepper tree, and you said a prayer over it, and you'd forgotten the words, so you said the multiplication table instead?"

"I'd forgotten that," he said. "Did I really?"

"You got as far as seven times eight," said Ruth, "and then you couldn't remember that either, so you said 'Amen.' I've thought of it lots of times." And she ran up the stairs, and was gone.

---

Philip drove home to Pasadena slowly, through the long golden afternoon, past miles of orange groves, and miles of new bungalows with their little lawns and their palm trees, all exactly alike, and all with signs on them saying "For Sale" or "Sold." He passed the place along the Arroyo where the strip of land had been; there were houses on it now, and a filling station, and a sign with his father's name in letters two feet high. He had passed it a thousand times, and had always felt a little glow of pride at the sign; now he looked at it, and felt something which was not pride, and which he could not have named.

When he got home, his mother was on the terrace, in a white dress, having tea with two ladies from the Shakespeare Club; and she called to him, and asked him where he had been all day, and he said, "Oh, just driving around." He went up to his room, and lay on the bed with his hands behind his head, and looked at the ceiling for a long time.

It is a curious thing about the minds of young people: they are full of locked rooms, which the grown-ups have locked for them, with signs on the doors saying "Not Your Business" and "Don't Ask." And mostly the young people obey, because it is easier, and because there is always tennis to be played, and dances to go to, and examinations to pass. But every now and then something happens, and one of the doors swings open, just a crack; and after that, no matter how hard you push against it, you can never quite get it shut again. That was what had happened to Philip Ashby this afternoon, on a street corner in Los Angeles, with the motorists blowing their horns behind him. He did not know it yet; he only knew that he was restless and unhappy, and that he did not want to go down to dinner. But the door was open, and the wind was blowing through.

Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. “Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. “But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. “Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. Ned Harlowe was eight years old when he learned that there are two kinds of wrong-doing in the world: the kind that grown-ups punish you for, and the kind that they do themselves and call business. He did not learn it all at once, of course; nobody does. It came to him the way the frost comes into the ground in the fall—a little at a time, so that you do not notice until one morning the earth is hard under your feet, and you cannot remember when it was soft.

His father was Mr. Walter Harlowe, who owned the Harlowe Box and Crate Company, down by the river at the lower end of Millbridge. Everybody in town knew the Harlowe mill; you could hear its whistle at six in the morning and again at six at night, and in between you could hear the scream of the big saws, which went on all day like some creature in pain that never got tired of complaining. The mill made boxes for the fruit-growers up the valley, and crates for the furniture factories in Grand Junction, and cheese-boxes for the creameries; and since everything in America had to be shipped somewhere in something, there was always plenty of work, and Mr. Harlowe had a big brick house on Elm Street, with a porch that went around three sides, and a cook named Hilda, and a Pierce-Arrow car with a man to drive it.

Ned loved his father; it would be well to say that at the outset, so that what follows may not be misunderstood. Mr. Harlowe was a large, ruddy man with a voice that filled up a room, and when he laughed you felt it in the floor. He had come up from nothing—he liked to tell about it; he had started as a tally-boy in a lumber yard at four dollars a week, and had saved his money and bought a second-hand saw, and so on, step by step, the way it is told in the books which they give to boys in Sunday school. He believed in hard work, and in thrift, and in the Republican party, and in the Methodist church, in about that order; and he believed that any man who would do what he had done could have what he had got. That was the whole of his philosophy, and it seemed to him so plain that he could not understand how anyone could think otherwise—except, of course, the agitators, who were a special kind of person, like snakes, and not to be argued with.

Now it happened that in the spring of that year there was an accident at the mill. A man named Stanislaus Wojcik, who worked at the cut-off saw, got his hand caught in the carriage, and lost three fingers and part of the palm. Ned heard about it at the supper-table; his father mentioned it the way he mentioned the price of spruce, or the trouble with the freight cars on the Northern line. "Fellow got careless down at the cut-off," he said. "Lost part of his hand. They will do it—you can tell 'em and tell 'em." And Ned's mother said, "Oh, how dreadful!" and then asked whether the Andersons were coming on Thursday, and the matter was closed.

But it was not closed for Ned, because Ned knew Joey Wojcik. Joey was in the third grade at the Lincoln School, where Ned went too—Mr. Harlowe believed in the public schools, and said a boy ought to rub elbows with all kinds; it would make a man of him. Joey was a thin, freckled boy with pale hair that stuck up in back, and he could throw a ball farther than anybody in the class, and he had shown Ned how to make a whistle out of a willow stick. Next day Joey was not in school, and the day after that he was not in school either; and on the third day Ned walked home by way of Front Street, which was a way he was not supposed to go, and found the Wojcik house.

It was one of a row of houses that the mill had put up years ago and rented to its hands; they were all alike, with tar-paper on the sides that had once been meant to look like brick, and little porches that sagged in the middle, as if they were tired. There was a smell of cabbage, and of the river, and of something sour that Ned did not know the name of. Joey was sitting on the step, whittling at nothing in particular, and when he saw Ned he did not get up.

"Hello," said Ned.

"Hello," said Joey.

Ned did not know what to say next, so he asked about the hand; and Joey told him, in a flat voice, that his father was home in bed, and that the doctor had been twice, and that the doctor wanted to be paid, and that the company had said the accident was his father's own fault and so there wasn't anything coming to him. His mother was taking in washing, but she had the baby, and there was a younger girl with the croup, and Joey himself was going to quit school and go to work at the mill, if they would take him—he was ten, though he was small for it, and you could get on as a sweeper if you said you were twelve and nobody asked.

"But you can't quit school!" said Ned. "You're the best one at long division!"

Joey looked at him in a way that Ned remembered for a long time afterward—not angry exactly, but the way you might look at a little dog that had wandered into the house and was making a puddle on the rug. "Long division don't buy no bread," he said.

Ned went home with something heavy inside him, like a stone he had swallowed. He sat on the back steps while Hilda was getting the supper, and thought about it. It was plain to him that there was a mistake somewhere. His father was a good man, and the mill was his father's mill; therefore, if his father knew that Joey was going to have to quit school, he would surely do something about it. But then, his father did know—he had said it at the table. Perhaps he did not know about the doctor, and the baby, and the croup? That must be it; grown-ups were always busy, and they did not get to hear about such things. Ned considered telling him; but there was the difficulty that he would have to explain how he knew, and that would mean Front Street. And besides, there was something in the way his father had said, "They will do it," which made Ned feel that the subject was not a good one to bring up.

So Ned did what seemed to him the simplest thing. In the top drawer of his father's desk, in the library, there was a japanned tin box in which Mr. Harlowe kept loose money—bills and silver for paying the iceman, and the boy who brought the papers, and such matters. Ned knew where the key was; it hung on a little nail behind the clock, and he had seen his mother use it a hundred times. Next afternoon, when his mother was at the Ladies' Aid, and Hilda was in the kitchen with the door shut, he went into the library and took out a ten-dollar bill. It was the largest sum of money he had ever held in his hand, and it seemed to him enough to pay a dozen doctors. He put it in his shoe, where it rubbed against his heel all the way down to Front Street, and he gave it to Joey; and Joey stared at it, and then at him, and then ran into the house without saying a word. Ned walked home feeling very light, as though the stone inside him had turned into a balloon.

It was Hilda who gave him away; not on purpose—Hilda would have cut off her own hand first, for she loved Ned, and slipped him cookies out of the jar when his mother was not looking. But Mrs. Wojcik, being an honest woman, and frightened half out of her wits at the sight of so much money in the hands of her son, came up to Elm Street that same evening, by the back way, with her shawl over her head, to find out whether it was all right. She stood in the kitchen and twisted the bill in her red hands, and talked to Hilda in a mixture of Polish and English, and Hilda went to get Mrs. Harlowe; and Mrs. Harlowe went to get Mr. Harlowe; and so the whole thing came out, like a rabbit out of a hat, except that nobody applauded.

Ned was upstairs in his room, supposedly doing his spelling. It was true, all three of them; Ned could not deny it. He had been told not to go to Front Street, though nobody had ever told him why, except that it was "not a nice place"—which was the reason grown-ups gave for most things they did not want you to know about. He saw now, dimly, that perhaps the reason they did not want you to go there was that you would see things you were not supposed to see, and then you would ask questions they did not want to answer. But this thought was too large for him to hold all at once; he put it away to look at later, the way he put away the pieces of a puzzle that would not fit.

"I'm sorry, Papa," he said. And he was sorry—sorry for making his father angry, sorry for the word "thief," sorry that Mrs. Wojcik had had to come up the back way with her shawl over her head. Mr. Harlowe looked at him for a while, and then he sighed, and some of the red went out of his face. He was not a cruel man; he did not believe in whipping, the way his own father had—his own father had used a harness-strap, and Mr. Harlowe could still remember it, and had sworn that no child of his would ever feel such a thing. So instead he laid down the law: Ned was to have no allowance for ten weeks, until the ten dollars was paid back; he was to stay in the yard after school for a month; and he was to go to Mrs. Wojcik, with his father, and apologize for having frightened her.

"But you'll let Joey keep it?" said Ned quickly. "You won't take it back?"

There was another of those hesitations. Mr. Harlowe had in fact already taken it back; the bill was at that moment folded in his vest pocket, where he had put it after Mrs. Wojcik handed it over, and she had gone back down the hill with her shawl over her head and her hands empty. He had not thought very much about it; it was his money, and naturally you took back what was yours. But now he looked at his son's face, and something stirred in him which he did not altogether understand, and did not altogether like.

"We'll see about that," he said gruffly. "I'll talk to the foreman. Maybe there's a light job they can find for the fellow—sweeping, or tallying, or something of the sort. I'm not a hard man, Ned; you know that. But it's got to be done the right way, through the proper channels. You can't just go handing out money right and left—you'd have every hunky in Millbridge lined up at the back door. You've got to think about these things. You've got to look at the whole situation."

Ned said, "Yes, sir." He understood that the interview was over, and that in some way he had won something, though he could not have said what, and that in some other way he had lost something, which he could not have named either. His father got up from the bed, and it creaked again, and he stood at the door with his hand on the knob.

"And Ned," he said, "you learn to spell that word. 'Obedient.' I saw it there. It's a good word for you to know."

Then he went out, and Ned heard him going down the stairs, slower than he had come up.

Ned sat a long time looking at the book. Outside, the evening whistle had long since blown, and the saws had stopped their screaming, and the light was going red over the river, where the mill stood dark against the sky with its tall stack and its piles of lumber. Down at the foot of the hill, on Front Street, there would be lamps being lit in the tar-paper houses, and Mrs. Wojcik would be bending over the wash-tub, and the girl with the croup would be coughing, and Joey would be sitting on the step, whittling at nothing in particular. Ned could see it all as plain as if he were there; and he understood, in the way that children understand things before they have the words for them, that there was a line running between the big house on Elm Street and the little houses on Front Street, and that the line had a great deal to do with money, and that his father stood on one side of it and did not like to be asked what was on the other.

He did not hold it against his father; not then, and not for many years. But he took the thing and hid it away in that secret place in his mind where children keep the things they cannot ask about, and there it lay, like a seed in the frozen ground, waiting for the spring. And as for the word "obedient"—he learned to spell it that night, getting the "ie" right at last; but somehow it never seemed to him again quite so simple a word as it had looked on the page.

There being no more to be done that day, the shop was left under the care of Lucija, and her husband sallied forth to show his friends the sights of Packingtown. Jokubas did this with the air of a country gentleman escorting a party of visitors over his estate; he was an old-time resident, and all these wonders had grown up under his eyes, and he had a personal pride in them. The packers might own the land, but he claimed the landscape, and there was no one to say nay to this. They passed down the busy street that led to the yards. It was still early morning, and everything was at its high tide of activity. A steady stream of employees was pouring through the gate—employees of the higher sort, at this hour, clerks and stenographers and such. For the women there were waiting big two-horse wagons, which set off at a gallop as fast as they were filled. In the distance there was heard again the lowing of the cattle, a sound as of a far-off ocean calling. They followed it, this time, as eager as children in sight of a circus menagerie—which, indeed, the scene a good deal resembled. They crossed the railroad tracks, and then on each side of the street were the pens full of cattle; they would have stopped to look, but Jokubas hurried them on, to where there was a stairway and a raised gallery, from which everything could be seen. Here they stood, staring, breathless with wonder. There is over a square mile of space in the yards, and more than half of it is occupied by cattle pens; north and south as far as the eye can reach there stretches a sea of pens. And they were all filled—so many cattle no one had ever dreamed existed in the world. Red cattle, black, white, and yellow cattle; old cattle and young cattle; great bellowing bulls and little calves not an hour born; meek-eyed milch cows and fierce, long-horned Texas steers. The sound of them here was as of all the barnyards of the universe; and as for counting them—it would have taken all day simply to count the pens. Here and there ran long alleys, blocked at intervals by gates; and Jokubas told them that the number of these gates was twenty-five thousand. Jokubas had recently been reading a newspaper article which was full of statistics such as that, and he was very proud as he repeated them and made his guests cry out with wonder. Jurgis too had a little of this sense of pride. Had he not just gotten a job, and become a sharer in all this activity, a cog in this marvelous machine? Here and there about the alleys galloped men upon horseback, booted, and carrying long whips; they were very busy, calling to each other, and to those who were driving the cattle. They were drovers and stock raisers, who had come from far states, and brokers and commission merchants, and buyers for all the big packing houses. Here and there they would stop to inspect a bunch of cattle, and there would be a parley, brief and businesslike. The buyer would nod or drop his whip, and that would mean a bargain; and he would note it in his little book, along with hundreds of others he had made that morning. Then Jokubas pointed out the place where the cattle were driven to be weighed, upon a great scale that would weigh a hundred thousand pounds at once and record it automatically. It was near to the east entrance that they stood, and all along this east side of the yards ran the railroad tracks, into which the cars were run, loaded with cattle. All night long this had been going on, and now the pens were full; by tonight they would all be empty, and the same thing would be done again.

“And what will become of all these creatures?” cried Teta Elzbieta.

“By tonight,” Jokubas answered, “they will all be killed and cut up; and over there on the other side of the packing houses are more railroad tracks, where the cars come to take them away.” There were two hundred and fifty miles of track within the yards, their guide went on to tell them. They brought about ten thousand head of cattle every day, and as many hogs, and half as many sheep—which meant some eight or ten million live creatures turned into food every year. One stood and watched, and little by little caught the drift of the tide, as it set in the direction of the packing houses. There were groups of cattle being driven to the chutes, which were roadways about fifteen feet wide, raised high above the pens. In these chutes the stream of animals was continuous; it was quite uncanny to watch them, pressing on to their fate, all unsuspicious a very river of death. Our friends were not poetical, and the sight suggested to them no metaphors of human destiny; they thought only of the wonderful efficiency of it all. The chutes into which the hogs went climbed high up—to the very top of the distant buildings; and Jokubas explained that the hogs went up by the power of their own legs, and then their weight carried them back through all the processes necessary to make them into pork.

“They don’t waste anything here,” said the guide, and then he laughed and added a witticism, which he was pleased that his unsophisticated friends should take to be his own: “They use everything about the hog except the squeal.” In front of Brown’s General Office building there grows a tiny plot of grass, and this, you may learn, is the only bit of green thing in Packingtown; likewise this jest about the hog and his squeal, the stock in trade of all the guides, is the one gleam of humor that you will find there. After they had seen enough of the pens, the party went up the street, to the mass of buildings which occupy the center of the yards. These buildings, made of brick and stained with innumerable layers of Packingtown smoke, were painted all over with advertising signs, from which the visitor realized suddenly that he had come to the home of many of the torments of his life. It was here that they made those products with the wonders of which they pestered him so—by placards that defaced the landscape when he traveled, and by staring advertisements in the newspapers and magazines—by silly little jingles that he could not get out of his mind, and gaudy pictures that lurked for him around every street corner. Here was where they made Brown’s Imperial Hams and Bacon, Brown’s Dressed Beef, Brown’s Excelsior Sausages! Here was the headquarters of Durham’s Pure Leaf Lard, of Durham’s Breakfast Bacon, Durham’s Canned Beef, Potted Ham, Deviled Chicken, Peerless Fertilizer! Entering one of the Durham buildings, they found a number of other visitors waiting; and before long there came a guide, to escort them through the place. They make a great feature of showing strangers through the packing plants, for it is a good advertisement. But Ponas Jokubas whispered maliciously that the visitors did not see any more than the packers wanted them to. They climbed a long series of stairways outside of the building, to the top of its five or six stories. Here was the chute, with its river of hogs, all patiently toiling upward; there was a place for them to rest to cool off, and then through another passageway they went into a room from which there is no returning for hogs. It was a long, narrow room, with a gallery along it for visitors. At the head there was a great iron wheel, about twenty feet in circumference, with rings here and there along its edge. Upon both sides of this wheel there was a narrow space, into which came the hogs at the end of their journey; in the midst of them stood a great burly Negro, bare-armed and bare-chested. He was resting for the moment, for the wheel had stopped while men were cleaning up. In a minute or two, however, it began slowly to revolve, and then the men upon each side of it sprang to work. They had chains which they fastened about the leg of the nearest hog, and the other end of the chain they hooked into one of the rings upon the wheel. So, as the wheel turned, a hog was suddenly jerked off his feet and borne aloft. At the same instant the car was assailed by a most terrifying shriek; the visitors started in alarm, the women turned pale and shrank back. The shriek was followed by another, louder and yet more agonizing—for once started upon that journey, the hog never came back; at the top of the wheel he was shunted off upon a trolley, and went sailing down the room. And meantime another was swung up, and then another, and another, until there was a double line of them, each dangling by a foot and kicking in frenzy—and squealing. The uproar was appalling, perilous to the eardrums; one feared there was too much sound for the room to hold—that the walls must give way or the ceiling crack. There were high squeals and low squeals, grunts, and wails of agony; there would come a momentary lull, and then a fresh outburst, louder than ever, surging up to a deafening climax. It was too much for some of the visitors—the men would look at each other, laughing nervously, and the women would stand with hands clenched, and the blood rushing to their faces, and the tears starting in their eyes. Meantime, heedless of all these things, the men upon the floor were going about their work. Neither squeals of hogs nor tears of visitors made any difference to them; one by one they hooked up the hogs, and one by one with a swift stroke they slit their throats. There was a long line of hogs, with squeals and lifeblood ebbing away together; until at last each started again, and vanished with a splash into a huge vat of boiling water. It was all so very businesslike that one watched it fascinated. It was porkmaking by machinery, porkmaking by applied mathematics. And yet somehow the most matter-of-fact person could not help thinking of the hogs; they were so innocent, they came so very trustingly; and they were so very human in their protests—and so perfectly within their rights! They had done nothing to deserve it; and it was adding insult to injury, as the thing was done here, swinging them up in this cold-blooded, impersonal way, without a pretense of apology, without the homage of a tear. Now and then a visitor wept, to be sure; but this slaughtering machine ran on, visitors or no visitors. It was like some horrible crime committed in a dungeon, all unseen and unheeded, buried out of sight and of memory. One could not stand and watch very long without becoming philosophical, without beginning to deal in symbols and similes, and to hear the hog squeal of the universe. Was it permitted to believe that there was nowhere upon the earth, or above the earth, a heaven for hogs, where they were requited for all this suffering? Each one of these hogs was a separate creature. Some were white hogs, some were black; some were brown, some were spotted; some were old, some young; some were long and lean, some were monstrous. And each of them had an individuality of his own, a will of his own, a hope and a heart’s desire; each was full of self-confidence, of self-importance, and a sense of dignity. And trusting and strong in faith he had gone about his business, the while a black shadow hung over him and a horrid Fate waited in his pathway. Now suddenly it had swooped upon him, and had seized him by the leg. Relentless, remorseless, it was; all his protests, his screams, were nothing to it—it did its cruel will with him, as if his wishes, his feelings, had simply no existence at all; it cut his throat and watched him gasp out his life. He brought out the placard, which was quite a work of art. It was nearly two feet long, printed on calendered paper, with a selection of colors so bright that they shone even in the moonlight.
