So there was only old Dede Antanas; Jurgis would have had him rest too, but he was forced to acknowledge that this was not possible, and, besides, the old man would not hear it spoken of—it was his whim to insist that he was as lively as any boy. He had come to America as full of hope as the best of them; and now he was the chief problem that worried his son. For every one that Jurgis spoke to assured him that it was a waste of time to seek employment for the old man in Packingtown. Szedvilas told him that the packers did not even keep the men who had grown old in their own service—to say nothing of taking on new ones. And not only was it the rule here, it was the rule everywhere in America, so far as he knew. To satisfy Jurgis he had asked the policeman, and brought back the message that the thing was not to be thought of. They had not told this to old Anthony, who had consequently spent the two days wandering about from one part of the yards to another, and had now come home to hear about the triumph of the others, smiling bravely and saying that it would be his turn another day. Their good luck, they felt, had given them the right to think about a home; and sitting out on the doorstep that summer evening, they held consultation about it, and Jurgis took occasion to broach a weighty subject. Passing down the avenue to work that morning he had seen two boys leaving an advertisement from house to house; and seeing that there were pictures upon it, Jurgis had asked for one, and had rolled it up and tucked it into his shirt. At noontime a man with whom he had been talking had read it to him and told him a little about it, with the result that Jurgis had conceived a wild idea. He brought out the placard, which was quite a work of art. It was nearly two feet long, printed on calendered paper, with a selection of colors so bright that they shone even in the moonlight. The center of the placard was occupied by a house, brilliantly painted, new, and dazzling. The roof of it was of a purple hue, and trimmed with gold; the house itself was silvery, and the doors and windows red. It was a two-story building, with a porch in front, and a very fancy scrollwork around the edges; it was complete in every tiniest detail, even the doorknob, and there was a hammock on the porch and white lace curtains in the windows. Underneath this, in one corner, was a picture of a husband and wife in loving embrace; in the opposite corner was a cradle, with fluffy curtains drawn over it, and a smiling cherub hovering upon silver-colored wings. For fear that the significance of all this should be lost, there was a label, in Polish, Lithuanian, and German—“Dom. Namai. Heim.” “Why pay rent?” the linguistic circular went on to demand. “Why not own your own home? Do you know that you can buy one for less than your rent? We have built thousands of homes which are now occupied by happy families.”—So it became eloquent, picturing the blissfulness of married life in a house with nothing to pay. It even quoted “Home, Sweet Home,” and made bold to translate it into Polish—though for some reason it omitted the Lithuanian of this. Perhaps the translator found it a difficult matter to be sentimental in a language in which a sob is known as a gukcziojimas and a smile as a nusiszypsojimas. Over this document the family pored long, while Ona spelled out its contents. It appeared that this house contained four rooms, besides a basement, and that it might be bought for fifteen hundred dollars, the lot and all. Of this, only three hundred dollars had to be paid down, the balance being paid at the rate of twelve dollars a month. These were frightful sums, but then they were in America, where people talked about such without fear. They had learned that they would have to pay a rent of nine dollars a month for a flat, and there was no way of doing better, unless the family of twelve was to exist in one or two rooms, as at present. If they paid rent, of course, they might pay forever, and be no better off; whereas, if they could only meet the extra expense in the beginning, there would at last come a time when they would not have any rent to pay for the rest of their lives. They figured it up. There was a little left of the money belonging to Teta Elzbieta, and there was a little left to Jurgis. Marija had about fifty dollars pinned up somewhere in her stockings, and Grandfather Anthony had part of the money he had gotten for his farm. If they all combined, they would have enough to make the first payment; and if they had employment, so that they could be sure of the future, it might really prove the best plan. It was, of course, not a thing even to be talked of lightly; it was a thing they would have to sift to the bottom. And yet, on the other hand, if they were going to make the venture, the sooner they did it the better, for were they not paying rent all the time, and living in a most horrible way besides? Jurgis was used to dirt—there was nothing could scare a man who had been with a railroad gang, where one could gather up the fleas off the floor of the sleeping room by the handful. But that sort of thing would not do for Ona. They must have a better place of some sort soon—Jurgis said it with all the assurance of a man who had just made a dollar and fifty-seven cents in a single day. Jurgis was at a loss to understand why, with wages as they were, so many of the people of this district should live the way they did. The next day Marija went to see her “forelady,” and was told to report the first of the week, and learn the business of can-painter. Marija went home, singing out loud all the way, and was just in time to join Ona and her stepmother as they were setting out to go and make inquiry concerning the house. That evening the three made their report to the men—the thing was altogether as represented in the circular, or at any rate so the agent had said. The houses lay to the south, about a mile and a half from the yards; they were wonderful bargains, the gentleman had assured them—personally, and for their own good. He could do this, so he explained to them, for the reason that he had himself no interest in their sale—he was merely the agent for a company that had built them. These were the last, and the company was going out of business, so if any one wished to take advantage of this wonderful no-rent plan, he would have to be very quick. As a matter of fact there was just a little uncertainty as to whether there was a single house left; for the agent had taken so many people to see them, and for all he knew the company might have parted with the last. Seeing Teta Elzbieta’s evident grief at this news, he added, after some hesitation, that if they really intended to make a purchase, he would send a telephone message at his own expense, and have one of the houses kept. So it had finally been arranged—and they were to go and make an inspection the following Sunday morning. That was Thursday; and all the rest of the week the killing gang at Brown’s worked at full pressure, and Jurgis cleared a dollar seventy-five every day. That was at the rate of ten and one-half dollars a week, or forty-five a month. Jurgis was not able to figure, except it was a very simple sum, but Ona was like lightning at such things, and she worked out the problem for the family. Marija and Jonas were each to pay sixteen dollars a month board, and the old man insisted that he could do the same as soon as he got a place—which might be any day now. That would make ninety-three dollars. Then Marija and Jonas were between them to take a third share in the house, which would leave only eight dollars a month for Jurgis to contribute to the payment. So they would have eighty-five dollars a month—or, supposing that Dede Antanas did not get work at once, seventy dollars a month—which ought surely to be sufficient for the support of a family of twelve. An hour before the time on Sunday morning the entire party set out. They had the address written on a piece of paper, which they showed to some one now and then. It proved to be a long mile and a half, but they walked it, and half an hour or so later the agent put in an appearance. He was a smooth and florid personage, elegantly dressed, and he spoke their language freely, which gave him a great advantage in dealing with them. He escorted them to the house, which was one of a long row of the typical frame dwellings of the neighborhood, where architecture is a luxury that is dispensed with. Ona’s heart sank, for the house was not as it was shown in the picture; the color scheme was different, for one thing, and then it did not seem quite so big. Still, it was freshly painted, and made a considerable show. It was all brand-new, so the agent told them, but he talked so incessantly that they were quite confused, and did not have time to ask many questions. There were all sorts of things they had made up their minds to inquire about, but when the time came, they either forgot them or lacked the courage. The other houses in the row did not seem to be new, and few of them seemed to be occupied. When they ventured to hint at this, the agent’s reply was that the purchasers would be moving in shortly. To press the matter would have seemed to be doubting his word, and never in their lives had any one of them ever spoken to a person of the class called “gentleman” except with deference and humility. The house had a basement, about two feet below the street line, and a single story, about six feet above it, reached by a flight of steps. In addition there was an attic, made by the peak of the roof, and having one small window in each end. The street in front of the house was unpaved and unlighted, and the view from it consisted of a few exactly similar houses, scattered here and there upon lots grown up with dingy brown weeds. The house inside contained four rooms, plastered white; the basement was but a frame, the walls being unplastered and the floor not laid. The agent explained that the houses were built that way, as the purchasers generally preferred to finish the basements to suit their own taste. The attic was also unfinished—the family had been figuring that in case of an emergency they could rent this attic, but they found that there was not even a floor, nothing but joists, and beneath them the lath and plaster of the ceiling below. All of this, however, did not chill their ardor as much as might have been expected, because of the volubility of the agent. There was no end to the advantages of the house, as he set them forth, and he was not silent for an instant; he showed them everything, down to the locks on the doors and the catches on the windows, and how to work them. He showed them the sink in the kitchen, with running water and a faucet, something which Teta Elzbieta had never in her wildest dreams hoped to possess. After a discovery such as that it would have seemed ungrateful to find any fault, and so they tried to shut their eyes to other defects.

Excerpt 3: It was four o’clock when the ceremony was over and the carriages began to arrive. There had been a crowd following all the way, owing to the exuberance of Marija Berczynskas. The occasion rested heavily upon Marija’s broad shoulders—it was her task to see that all things went in due form, and after the best home traditions; and, flying wildly hither and thither, bowling every one out of the way, and scolding and exhorting all day with her tremendous voice, Marija was too eager to see that others conformed to the proprieties to consider them herself. She had left the church last of all, and, desiring to arrive first at the hall, had issued orders to the coachman to drive faster. When that personage had developed a will of his own in the matter, Marija had flung up the window of the carriage, and, leaning out, proceeded to tell him her opinion of him, first in Lithuanian, which he did not understand, and then in Polish, which he did. Having the advantage of her in altitude, the driver had stood his ground and even ventured to attempt to speak; and the result had been a furious altercation, which, continuing all the way down Ashland Avenue, had added a new swarm of urchins to the cortege at each side street for half a mile. This was unfortunate, for already there was a throng before the door. The music had started up, and half a block away you could hear the dull “broom, broom” of a cello, with the squeaking of two fiddles which vied with each other in intricate and altitudinous gymnastics. Seeing the throng, Marija abandoned precipitately the debate concerning the ancestors of her coachman, and, springing from the moving carriage, plunged in and proceeded to clear a way to the hall. Once within, she turned and began to push the other way, roaring, meantime, “Eik! Eik! Uzdaryk-duris!” in tones which made the orchestral uproar sound like fairy music.

“Z. Graiczunas, Pasilinksminimams darzas. Vynas. Sznapsas. Wines and Liquors. Union Headquarters”—that was the way the signs ran. The reader, who perhaps has never held much converse in the language of far-off Lithuania, will be glad of the explanation that the place was the rear room of a saloon in that part of Chicago known as “back of the yards.” This information is definite and suited to the matter of fact; but how pitifully inadequate it would have seemed to one who understood that it was also the supreme hour of ecstasy in the life of one of God’s gentlest creatures, the scene of the wedding feast and the joy-transfiguration of little Ona Lukoszaite! She stood in the doorway, shepherded by Cousin Marija, breathless from pushing through the crowd, and in her happiness painful to look upon. There was a light of wonder in her eyes and her lids trembled, and her otherwise wan little face was flushed. She wore a muslin dress, conspicuously white, and a stiff little veil coming to her shoulders. There were five pink paper roses twisted in the veil, and eleven bright green rose leaves. There were new white cotton gloves upon her hands, and as she stood staring about her she twisted them together feverishly. It was almost too much for her—you could see the pain of too great emotion in her face, and all the tremor of her form. She was so young—not quite sixteen—and small for her age, a mere child; and she had just been married—and married to Jurgis, of all men, to Jurgis Rudkus, he with the white flower in the buttonhole of his new black suit, he with the mighty shoulders and the giant hands. Pronounced Yoorghis Ona was blue-eyed and fair, while Jurgis had great black eyes with beetling brows, and thick black hair that curled in waves about his ears—in short, they were one of those incongruous and impossible married couples with which Mother Nature so often wills to confound all prophets, before and after. Jurgis could take up a two-hundred-and-fifty-pound quarter of beef and carry it into a car without a stagger, or even a thought; and now he stood in a far corner, frightened as a hunted animal, and obliged to moisten his lips with his tongue each time before he could answer the congratulations of his friends. Gradually there was effected a separation between the spectators and the guests—a separation at least sufficiently complete for working purposes. There was no time during the festivities which ensued when there were not groups of onlookers in the doorways and the corners; and if any one of these onlookers came sufficiently close, or looked sufficiently hungry, a chair was offered him, and he was invited to the feast. It was one of the laws of the veselija that no one goes hungry; and, while a rule made in the forests of Lithuania is hard to apply in the stockyards district of Chicago, with its quarter of a million inhabitants, still they did their best, and the children who ran in from the street, and even the dogs, went out again happier. A charming informality was one of the characteristics of this celebration. The men wore their hats, or, if they wished, they took them off, and their coats with them; they ate when and where they pleased, and moved as often as they pleased. There were to be speeches and singing, but no one had to listen who did not care to; if he wished, meantime, to speak or sing himself, he was perfectly free. The resulting medley of sound distracted no one, save possibly alone the babies, of which there were present a number equal to the total possessed by all the guests invited. There was no other place for the babies to be, and so part of the preparations for the evening consisted of a collection of cribs and carriages in one corner. In these the babies slept, three or four together, or wakened together, as the case might be. Those who were still older, and could reach the tables, marched about munching contentedly at meat bones and bologna sausages. The room is about thirty feet square, with whitewashed walls, bare save for a calendar, a picture of a race horse, and a family tree in a gilded frame. To the right there is a door from the saloon, with a few loafers in the doorway, and in the corner beyond it a bar, with a presiding genius clad in soiled white, with waxed black mustaches and a carefully oiled curl plastered against one side of his forehead. In the opposite corner are two tables, filling a third of the room and laden with dishes and cold viands, which a few of the hungrier guests are already munching. At the head, where sits the bride, is a snow-white cake, with an Eiffel tower of constructed decoration, with sugar roses and two angels upon it, and a generous sprinkling of pink and green and yellow candies. Beyond opens a door into the kitchen, where there is a glimpse to be had of a range with much steam ascending from it, and many women, old and young, rushing hither and thither. In the corner to the left are the three musicians, upon a little platform, toiling heroically to make some impression upon the hubbub; also the babies, similarly occupied, and an open window whence the populace imbibes the sights and sounds and odors. Suddenly some of the steam begins to advance, and, peering through it, you discern Aunt Elizabeth, Ona’s stepmother—Teta Elzbieta, as they call her—bearing aloft a great platter of stewed duck. Behind her is Kotrina, making her way cautiously, staggering beneath a similar burden; and half a minute later there appears old Grandmother Majauszkiene, with a big yellow bowl of smoking potatoes, nearly as big as herself. So, bit by bit, the feast takes form—there is a ham and a dish of sauerkraut, boiled rice, macaroni, bologna sausages, great piles of penny buns, bowls of milk, and foaming pitchers of beer. There is also, not six feet from your back, the bar, where you may order all you please and do not have to pay for it. “Eiksz! Graicziau!” screams Marija Berczynskas, and falls to work herself—for there is more upon the stove inside that will be spoiled if it be not eaten. So, with laughter and shouts and endless badinage and merriment, the guests take their places. The young men, who for the most part have been huddled near the door, summon their resolution and advance; and the shrinking Jurgis is poked and scolded by the old folks until he consents to seat himself at the right hand of the bride. The two bridesmaids, whose insignia of office are paper wreaths, come next, and after them the rest of the guests, old and young, boys and girls. The spirit of the occasion takes hold of the stately bartender, who condescends to a plate of stewed duck; even the fat policeman—whose duty it will be, later in the evening, to break up the fights—draws up a chair to the foot of the table. And the children shout and the babies yell, and every one laughs and sings and chatters—while above all the deafening clamor Cousin Marija shouts orders to the musicians. The musicians—how shall one begin to describe them? All this time they have been there, playing in a mad frenzy—all of this scene must be read, or said, or sung, to music. It is the music which makes it what it is; it is the music which changes the place from the rear room of a saloon in back of the yards to a fairy place, a wonderland, a little corner of the high mansions of the sky. The little person who leads this trio is an inspired man. His fiddle is out of tune, and there is no rosin on his bow, but still he is an inspired man—the hands of the muses have been laid upon him. He plays like one possessed by a demon, by a whole horde of demons. You can feel them in the air round about him, capering frenetically; with their invisible feet they set the pace, and the hair of the leader of the orchestra rises on end, and his eyeballs start from their sockets, as he toils to keep up with them. Tamoszius Kuszleika is his name, and he has taught himself to play the violin by practicing all night, after working all day on the “killing beds.” He is in his shirt sleeves, with a vest figured with faded gold horseshoes, and a pink-striped shirt, suggestive of peppermint candy. A pair of military trousers, light blue with a yellow stripe, serve to give that suggestion of authority proper to the leader of a band. He is only about five feet high, but even so these trousers are about eight inches short of the ground. You wonder where he can have gotten them or rather you would wonder, if the excitement of being in his presence left you time to think of such things. For he is an inspired man. Every inch of him is inspired—you might almost say inspired separately. He stamps with his feet, he tosses his head, he sways and swings to and fro; he has a wizened-up little face, irresistibly comical; and, when he executes a turn or a flourish, his brows knit and his lips work and his eyelids wink—the very ends of his necktie bristle out. And every now and then he turns upon his companions, nodding, signaling, beckoning frantically—with every inch of him appealing, imploring, in behalf of the muses and their call. For they are hardly worthy of Tamoszius, the other two members of the orchestra. The second violin is a Slovak, a tall, gaunt man with black-rimmed spectacles and the mute and patient look of an overdriven mule; he responds to the whip but feebly, and then always falls back into his old rut. The third man is very fat, with a round, red, sentimental nose, and he plays with his eyes turned up to the sky and a look of infinite yearning. He is playing a bass part upon his cello, and so the excitement is nothing to him; no matter what happens in the treble, it is his task to saw out one long-drawn and lugubrious note after another, from four o’clock in the afternoon until nearly the same hour next morning, for his third of the total income of one dollar per hour. Before the feast has been five minutes under way, Tamoszius Kuszleika has risen in his excitement; a minute or two more and you see that he is beginning to edge over toward the tables. His nostrils are dilated and his breath comes fast—his demons are driving him. He nods and shakes his head at his companions, jerking at them with his violin, until at last the long form of the second violinist also rises up. In the end all three of them begin advancing, step by step, upon the banqueters, Valentinavyczia, the cellist, bumping along with his instrument between notes. Finally all three are gathered at the foot of the tables, and there Tamoszius mounts upon a stool. Now he is in his glory, dominating the scene. Some of the people are eating, some are laughing and talking—but you will make a great mistake if you think there is one of them who does not hear him. His notes are never true, and his fiddle buzzes on the low ones and squeaks and scratches on the high; but these things they heed no more than they heed the dirt and noise and squalor about them—it is out of this material that they have to build their lives, with it that they have to utter their souls. And this is their utterance; merry and boisterous, or mournful and wailing, or passionate and rebellious, this music is their music, music of home. It stretches out its arms to them, they have only to give themselves up. Chicago and its saloons and its slums fade away—there are green meadows and sunlit rivers, mighty forests and snow-clad hills. They behold home landscapes and childhood scenes returning; old loves and friendships begin to waken, old joys and griefs to laugh and weep. Some fall back and close their eyes, some beat upon the table. Now and then one leaps up with a cry and calls for this song or that; and then the fire leaps brighter in Tamoszius’ eyes, and he flings up his fiddle and shouts to his companions, and away they go in mad career. The company takes up the choruses, and men and women cry out like all possessed; some leap to their feet and stamp upon the floor, lifting their glasses and pledging each other. Before long it occurs to some one to demand an old wedding song, which celebrates the beauty of the bride and the joys of love. In the excitement of this masterpiece Tamoszius Kuszleika begins to edge in between the tables, making his way toward the head, where sits the bride. There is not a foot of space between the chairs of the guests, and Tamoszius is so short that he pokes them with his bow whenever he reaches over for the low notes; but still he presses in, and insists relentlessly that his companions must follow. During their progress, needless to say, the sounds of the cello are pretty well extinguished; but at last the three are at the head, and Tamoszius takes his station at the right hand of the bride and begins to pour out his soul in melting strains. Little Ona is too excited to eat. Once in a while she tastes a little something, when Cousin Marija pinches her elbow and reminds her; but, for the most part, she sits gazing with the same fearful eyes of wonder. Teta Elzbieta is all in a flutter, like a hummingbird; her sisters, too, keep running up behind her, whispering, breathless. But Ona seems scarcely to hear them—the music keeps calling, and the far-off look comes back, and she sits with her hands pressed together over her heart. Then the tears begin to come into her eyes; and as she is ashamed to wipe them away, and ashamed to let them run down her cheeks, she turns and shakes her head a little, and then flushes red when she sees that Jurgis is watching her. When in the end Tamoszius Kuszleika has reached her side, and is waving his magic wand above her, Ona’s cheeks are scarlet, and she looks as if she would have to get up and run away.

The mill whistle blew at a quarter past six, and in the long rows of company houses that climbed the hill above the river, a thousand women lifted their heads from their work and listened. It was a sound that ruled their lives as the bells of the church had ruled the lives of their grandmothers in the old country. It woke them in the black of the morning, it told them when the soup must be hot, and it told them when to begin to watch the street for the men. To Agnieszka Dombrowska, standing at her window with the baby upon her arm, it was a sound of terror that night. She had been waiting for it since three o'clock in the afternoon, and now that it had come she would have given anything she possessed to call it back.

The house of the Dombrowskis was the fourth from the end in a row of thirty, all exactly alike, built by the Carnell Steel Company of yellow pine boards that had been painted red once, a long time ago. Now they were the color of everything else in Carnellsburg, which was the color of the smoke. The smoke came from the forty stacks that stood along the river like a row of black candles. It came by day and it came by night, and it settled upon the roofs and the window sills and the washing upon the lines, and upon the faces of the children who played in the street. The women of the row had long since given up the fight against it. They swept their doorsteps in the morning, and by noon you could write your name upon them with your finger. If you had asked them, they would have told you that the smoke meant work, and that when the smoke stopped, the babies went hungry. This was quite true, and was the only bit of political economy that any of them knew.

There were four rooms in the house, and for these the Company took nine dollars a month out of Wojciech's pay envelope before he ever saw it. It also took out the price of the coal, which it sold to its tenants at five dollars and a half a ton, from a yard at the end of the street, where a man with a little book wrote down every bucketful. In the mill, Wojciech Dombrowski worked twelve hours a day at the open-hearth furnaces, and every second Sunday he worked twenty-four, when the shifts were changed. For this he received sixteen cents an hour, which, if he did not lose a day, came to something more than fifty dollars a month. Out of that he had to feed and clothe a wife and three children, and pay the Company for its house and its coal, and pay the Company's doctor a dollar a month whether anyone was sick or not. And he had to put something by, as the priest and the newspapers and the president of the Company were forever telling him, against the day when the furnaces should take him, as they had taken so many others.

Agnieszka had figured it all, over and over, in her head; she had no head for figures, but she had figured it so many times that she could not have forgotten it if she tried. That was why her heart stood still at the whistle that night. In the next room, in the corner by the cold stove, crouched little Jasio, who was seven years old, and who had that afternoon been brought home by a Company policeman, with his ear between the policeman's thumb and finger, and his face black as a chimney sweep's, and his eyes swollen with weeping.

It had happened in this way. There was a railroad siding that ran along the bottom of the hill, between the row and the river, where the long trains of coal cars stood waiting their turn to be drawn into the mill yard. When the cars were shunted and bumped together, as they were a dozen times a day, lumps of coal would jar loose and roll down upon the cinders between the ties. There they lay, black and shining, and to the children of the row, whose mothers counted every shovelful that went into the stove, they were treasure as truly as any gold that lay in the streets of America in the stories that had been told in the villages of Galicia. The older boys went down with sacks and buckets and gathered them; and the Company, which possessed some forty thousand acres of coal land in three states, and dug some millions of tons out of the earth every year, had decided that this was not to be permitted. So it had put up a sign, in English, which none of the children could read, and it had set a man to walk up and down the siding with a club and a brass star upon his coat.

That afternoon the man with the star had been somewhere else. And the big boys, Felek Wozniak and the two Hunkie brothers from the end of the row, had done a thing they had long talked of doing—they had climbed up the iron ladder of a car and stood upon the top of the coal and thrown it down by the armful, while the little ones below scrambled and fought for it. Jasio had not climbed the ladder; he was too small, and too frightened. But he had stood below with his mother's market basket, and had filled it—he had filled it to the very top, with lumps as big as his two fists, and he had been staggering away with it, his face shining with a joy like that of a man who has found a gold mine, when a hand came down upon his collar from behind. The big boys had scattered like sparrows; they knew the hill and its fences and its ditches, and they were gone. Only Jasio, with his basket, was left, and he would not drop the basket, because it was his mother's.

The policeman had been a large, red-faced Irishman, with a voice that came from deep down in his chest; and when he had walked Jasio up the hill and into the kitchen, he had stood in the doorway and delivered himself of a speech. He was not a cruel man, as such men go; he had children of his own, and he did not enjoy his work. But he had his orders, and he had a family to keep, and a man who has a family to keep will do a great many things. He told Agnieszka, in English which she did not understand, and in a few words of Polish which he had picked up for the purpose and which she understood only too well, that the boy was a thief, and that this was the last time. The next time it would be the magistrate, and the name of the father would go to the superintendent. He took the basket of coal away with him, and he wrote the number of the house in a little book. It was the writing in the little book that Agnieszka could not get out of her mind.

For she knew, as every woman in the row knew, what it meant to have your man's name go to the superintendent. There was a family named Kovacs, three doors down, whose boy had been caught at the same thing the winter before. The father had been called to the office; he had come back that night with his time, and in a week the Kovacses had been put out into the street, with their beds and their kettles and their holy pictures piled upon the cinders, and a new family had moved into their house. Nobody knew where the Kovacses had gone. Somebody said Pittsburgh, and somebody said they had gone back to the old country; but nobody knew, and after a while nobody asked. That was the way in Carnellsburg. A family that went out of a Company house went out of the world, and the smoke closed over the place where it had been.

All this Agnieszka had been thinking for three hours; and when she saw her husband coming up the street at last, among the long line of men with their dinner pails, she went and sat down at the table, because her knees would not hold her.

Wojciech Dombrowski was a big, slow-moving man, with a heavy blond mustache and pale blue eyes that had been burned half colorless by the glare of the furnaces. He had been in America nine years, and in that time he had grown from a young man into an old one; there were deep lines in his face, and the backs of his hands were covered with little white scars, where the sparks of the molten steel had found him. He came in heavily, as he always came in, and set down his dinner pail upon the shelf, and hung up his cap upon the nail; and then he stood still, because he saw his wife's face. He had been married to her eleven years, and he knew her face as he knew the face of the furnace—every flicker of it.

"Co się stało?" he said. "What has happened?"

She told him. She had meant to tell it gently, a little at a time, as one breaks bad news to a sick person; but when she began it all came out in a flood, the coal and the policeman and the basket and the little book, and the Kovacses, and the superintendent—until at the end she was weeping, and the baby upon her lap had begun to wail in sympathy. Wojciech listened without a word. He did not sit down. He stood with his great scarred hands hanging at his sides, and the blood came slowly up into his face, and slowly went out of it again, and left it gray.

You must understand what was in the soul of this man, if you are to judge what he did. He was not an educated man; he could write his name and no more, and the Company had seen to it that he should have no time to learn. But he had been brought up in a village where the priest was the voice of God and the landlord was the voice of the priest, and he had been taught, from the time he could walk, that there were two sins which a poor man must never commit: he must never steal, and he must never be insolent to his betters. All his life he had kept these two commandments as other men keep their money, and they were all the wealth he had. He had never in his life taken a thing that did not belong to him; he had stood at the furnaces through heat that would have killed a horse, and he had never so much as lifted his voice to a boss. And now his son, his first-born, the one for whom he had come across the ocean, so that there might be one Dombrowski who would not live like a beast—his son had been brought home by the police for a thief!

And beneath this there was the other thing, the thing he would not have spoken of to anyone, not even to the priest: the fear. It was a fear that never left him, that lived in him as the smoke lived in the town—a fear of the little book, of the office, of the long walk down the hill with his time in his pocket and his family behind him. He was forty-one years old. He knew what happened to men of forty-one who lost their places. The Company had a long list of young men waiting at the gate every morning, Slovaks and Croats and Italians fresh off the boats, with strong backs and hungry bellies, who would take his place at fifteen cents an hour, or at fourteen; and the Company knew it, and he knew that the Company knew it.

"Where is he?" he said.

Agnieszka pointed to the other room, and then she caught at his sleeve. "Wojtek," she whispered, "he is only a little one. He did not know. He did it for the baby—"

But he shook her off, not roughly, and went to the door.

The little boy was crouched in the corner beside the stove, where he had been since the policeman went away. He had not washed his face, because no one had told him to, and the coal dust was streaked across it where the tears had run; and his hands, which were small and thin, with the nails bitten down, were black to the wrists. He had heard his father come in, and he had heard every word that had been said in the kitchen, and now he looked up at the great figure in the doorway with eyes in which there was neither defiance nor cunning, but only a dumb and utter terror—the terror of a small animal that knows it has done wrong and does not know what wrong it has done.

"Get up," said Wojciech.

The boy got up. He stood with his back against the wall, his arms at his sides. He was small for his age, as all the children of the row were small; the doctors of the Company would have told you that it was because their parents were of an inferior stock, and that the Slavic races matured late. There was a hole in the knee of his trousers, and his feet were bare, because his shoes were being saved for the winter, and for Sunday.

"Do you know what you have done?" said the father. He spoke in a low voice, which was worse than shouting. "Do you know what a thief is? A thief is a man who takes what is not his. A thief is a man the police come for. They put him in the jail, with bars upon the windows, and he never sees his mother again. Is that what you want to be? A thief?"

The boy's lips moved, but no sound came out of them.

"Answer me!"

"No, tatusiu," the child whispered.

"Then why did you do it? Did I not tell you never to go to the tracks? Did I not tell you? Did your mother not tell you? And still you went, with the Wozniak boy, and those others, the good-for-nothings—and you stole the coal of the Company, which is not yours, and which is not mine—and you let the police bring you up the street by the ear, so that all the row could see, and all the row could say, 'There goes the son of Dombrowski, the thief!'" His voice was rising now, in spite of him. "Do you know what they will do? They will write my name! They will take my work away! They will put us in the street, all of us—your mother, and Hania, and the baby—in the street, in the winter, like the Kovacses! And it will be you that did it! You!"

The child began to cry. He did not cry loudly—the children of Carnellsburg learned early that it did no good to cry loudly—but the tears ran down through the black upon his cheeks, and his thin shoulders shook. And then, because he was only seven years old, and because the words came up out of him of themselves, he said the thing that was in his heart.

"But the baby was cold, tatusiu! The baby was coughing all night, and mama said there was no more coal till Saturday—I heard her say it—and the coal was lying on the ground, on the ground, and nobody wanted it—and I thought—I thought—"

He could not go on. He put his black hands up before his face and stood there sobbing.

Wojciech Dombrowski had taken down the strap from its nail behind the door. It was an old razor strop, worn smooth, and it had hung there for years, more as a symbol than a weapon, as the policeman's club and the brass star were symbols. He had used it twice in Jasio's life, and both times he had been sick afterward. Now he stood with it in his hand, and looked at his son; and something happened inside of him which he could not have explained, and which he did not try to explain.

For it came to him, suddenly and dimly, as a man sees a shape through the smoke, that the child was right. The baby had coughed all night; he had heard it too, lying awake in the dark, and counting the days until Saturday. The coal had lain upon the ground. Nobody had wanted it. It would have been crushed under the wheels, or swept into the river with the cinders, or left to lie in the rain until the spring. And the Company that owned it had forty thousand acres of coal, and dug it out of the earth with the labor of men like himself, at wages like his own—men who went down into the dark at fourteen and came up at forty with their lungs full of black dust, coughing as the baby was coughing. And this same Company sold him back his share of it at five dollars and a half a ton, and wrote down every bucketful in a little book! Who was the thief, then? Who had stolen what from whom?

He did not think these things in words; he had not the words for them, and if anyone had said them to him he would have crossed himself and called it the talk of the anarchists, of whom the priest had warned him. But he felt them, and the feeling went through him like the heat of the furnace when the door is opened, so that for a moment he could not see.

Yet he knew, too, that it did not matter; that was the worst of it. It did not matter who was right. The coal belonged to the Company, because the Company said so, and the Company had the police and the magistrate and the little book; and the house belonged to the Company, and the job belonged to the Company, and in the end the very child belonged to it, for in seven years more he would be standing at the gate in the morning, with his dinner pail, waiting to be taken on. If the boy was to live in this world, he must learn the law of it; and the law of it was that the poor man must not take, though he starve, and though his children cough in the night. It was a lesson that must be learned, and learned early, and learned hard; and it was his business, as a father, to teach it.

So Wojciech Dombrowski raised the strap. And the child, hearing the movement, took his hands down from his face, and looked up—and did not run, and did not cry out, but only stood there, with the tears and the coal dust upon his cheeks, and waited. There was a kind of trust in that look, more dreadful than any reproach could have been: the trust of a little creature which believed that whatever its father did must be right, because he was its father, and because there was nothing else in the world to believe in.

The strap came down—upon the floor. Wojciech had flung it from him into the corner, where it struck the cold stove with a sound like a pistol shot; and then he sat down heavily upon the edge of the bed, and put his great scarred hands over his face, and his shoulders began to shake, as the child's had shaken.

Agnieszka was in the doorway. She did not come in. She had lived long enough with this man to know when he must be let alone. The baby was quiet now upon her arm, staring with round eyes; and behind her, in the kitchen, little Hania had crept out from under the table and was peering round her mother's skirts.

After a while the father took his hands from his face, and reached out, and drew the boy to him, and stood him between his knees.

"Listen to me, Jasio," he said, and his voice was hoarse and very low. "Listen, and remember. You must never go to the tracks again. Never. Not if the baby coughs, not if we are all cold, not if the coal lies there in heaps as high as the church. You hear me? Never."

"Yes, tatusiu."

"It is not ours. Nothing is ours. Do you understand that? Not the house, not the coal, not the street—nothing. Only what they give us, for the work. That is how it is. That is how it is in America." He stopped, and swallowed, and went on. "And if they catch you again, they will take me away from the furnaces, and then there will be no bread, and no house, and no anything. So you must be good. You must be better than the others. Because we are poor, you must be better than anybody. Do you promise me?"

"I promise, tatusiu," said the child; and he put his thin black arms about his father's neck, and the father held him, and neither of them said any more.

That night the Dombrowskis ate their soup in silence, and went early to bed, because there was no fire to sit by. The baby coughed again in the dark, a little dry cough, and the mother walked the floor with it until past midnight. In the other room Jasio lay beside his sister under the one quilt, wide awake, and stared at the ceiling, and turned over and over in his mind the great new knowledge that had come to him—that nothing was theirs. He did not understand it, and he would not understand it for many years; but he would never forget it, and it would grow with him as he grew, and harden as his hands hardened, until one day it would turn into something which would have frightened his father very much, if he had lived to see it.

And Wojciech Dombrowski lay upon his back beside his wife, and listened to the baby, and figured once more, in the slow, painful way of a man who cannot write his figures down, how many days it was to Saturday, and how much coal could be bought with what would be left. At four o'clock the whistle blew, and he rose and went down the hill in the dark, with his dinner pail, among the long line of silent men.

On that same Sunday, as it happened, the president of the Carnell Steel Company delivered an address before the Sunday school of the fashionable church which he attended in the city, upon the subject of "Honesty, the Foundation of Success." He told the children—who were well dressed, and well fed, and had never seen a coal car in their lives—that he had begun life as a poor boy, and had never taken a penny that was not his own; and that in this free country any boy who was honest, and industrious, and obedient to his superiors, might rise to be what he was. The address was printed in full in the newspapers the next morning, and was very much admired.

At a quarter to ten on a Thursday evening in October, in the living-room of the residence at 1419 Elmhurst Avenue, Ossawa Falls, Minnesota, Mr. Howard T. Duckworth sat in his Morris chair and read the editorial page of the *Ossawa Falls Clarion-Herald* with the air of a man who has earned his repose and intends that the universe shall know it.

He was forty-four. He was the proprietor of the Duckworth Motor & Implement Company, distributors of the Overland, the Willys-Knight, and the Superior Line of Cream Separators. He was a past Exalted Ruler of the Elks, a Deacon of the Wesley Methodist Church, a member in excellent standing of the Kiwanis, the Commercial Club, the Ossawa Falls Golf and Country Club (associate), and the Republican Party. He had a round, pink, freshly barbered face, rimless eyeglasses that pinched a red seam across his nose, and a waistcoat which had of late become a source of mild apprehension, like a creditor who is courteous but persistent. He believed in Service, in the Protective Tariff, in the Future of Ossawa Falls, and in the proposition that any man who would not boost was a knocker, a crab, and very probably a Socialist.

The room in which he sat was, by the measure of Elmhurst Avenue, a highly satisfactory room. It contained a davenport upholstered in a mulberry plush which had been advertised as Genuine Mohair-Effect; a Victrola in a cabinet of fumed oak; a library table bearing a bronze lamp, a copy of *The Saturday Evening Post*, a copy of *The Ladies' Home Journal*, a cut-glass bowl of wax fruit, and a set of the Works of Robert Louis Stevenson in maroon limp leather which no one had ever opened, because they had been purchased to fill the bookcase and they filled it. Over the mantel hung a steel engraving of a stag at bay, and beside the stag, in a gilt frame, Howard's certificate of membership in the Ossawa Falls Boosters' Booster Club, signed by the Mayor. The radiator knocked twice, in the manner of an embarrassed caller, and was silent.

Across from him, in the rocker, sat his wife Myrtle, and Myrtle was not reading.

She had in her lap an envelope. It was a long envelope, of the heavy cream stock favored by the First National Bank of Ossawa Falls, and it had been slit open with a hairpin. She had been holding it for eleven minutes. Howard had not noticed this, because Howard had been reading an editorial entitled "WHY NOT A GREATER OSSAWA?" which agreed with everything he thought, and which he was therefore finding singularly intelligent.

"Says here," he observed, with the generous impulse of a man sharing his wealth, "says here that if we get that new bridge over the Minnetonka River, Ossawa'll be a town of twenty thousand inside five years. Twenty thousand! Why, that'd put us right up ahead of Fergus Falls, and I'll tell the world it's high time somebody did. Those Fergus Falls birds have been blowing about their waterworks till you'd think—"

"Howard."

"—you'd think nobody else ever had a pump. Hm? What is it, Myrt?"

"Howard, what is this?"

She held up the envelope. She did not hold it up as a woman displays a recipe, nor as she displays a son's report card; she held it as a District Attorney holds up a revolver before a jury that has already been told whose fingerprints are on it.

Howard lowered the paper four inches. He peered over it. He peered, specifically, over the rims of his eyeglasses, which was a gesture he had learned from Mr. J. Wilbur Sloane, President of the First National, and which he employed when he wished to convey that he was a man of affairs and that the person addressing him was, however dear, not.

"Why, that's—where'd you get that?"

"It came in the afternoon mail. It's addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Howard T. Duckworth. I believe I am Mrs. Howard T. Duckworth. I've been told so, at any rate, for nineteen years."

"Now, Myrt, there's no call to get sarcastic."

"I'm not being sarcastic. I'm asking a question. It says"—she drew the folded sheet from the envelope and smoothed it upon her knee, with that terrible deliberation which is the weapon of women who have been taught never to raise their voices—"it says, 'Dear Mr. and Mrs. Duckworth, We beg to acknowledge receipt of the executed instruments in connection with the second mortgage upon the property at 1419 Elmhurst Avenue, in the amount of Six Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($6,500.00), and to advise that the proceeds have been credited as directed to the account of the Hiawatha Heights Development Corporation.' And then it says, 'Assuring you of our continued interest in your welfare,' and it's signed by Mr. Sloane's secretary. Howard, I didn't execute any instruments. I don't even know what an instrument is, unless it's a piano."

Howard folded the *Clarion-Herald*. He folded it once lengthwise and once across, and laid it upon the arm of the Morris chair, and smoothed it, and in all these operations he consumed perhaps nine seconds, which is, as anyone who has been married can attest, an exceedingly long time.

"Well, now," he said. "Well, now, Myrt. I was going to tell you about that."

"When?"

"Why, just as soon as—soon as the thing was all set. I didn't want to worry you with a lot of business details. You know how you get about figures."

"I do not 'get' about figures. I kept the books for Papa's store for three years before I ever met you, and they balanced, which is more than you can say for the Kiwanis picnic fund."

This was a low blow, and Howard felt it to be a low blow. The deficit in the Kiwanis picnic fund, amounting to eleven dollars and forty cents, had been the result of a misunderstanding about the ice cream, and it had been explained, fully and manfully, at the August luncheon, and he had believed the matter closed. He took off his eyeglasses and polished them upon his handkerchief, which was a gesture he had learned from no one in particular, but which gave him time.

"Now listen, Myrtle. Just listen to me a minute, will you, before you go flying off the handle? You know Charley Gartside."

"I know Charley Gartside."

There was a quality in the way she said it. Mr. Charles M. Gartside was a realtor. He had come to Ossawa Falls two years before from somewhere in Iowa, a place which, in his accounts of it, sometimes appeared to be Des Moines and sometimes Sioux City and once, after the Elks' Christmas party, Omaha. He wore a pearl-gray fedora and spats, and he had a laugh like a slammed door, and he called every man "old-timer" and every woman "little lady," and he had in eighteen months sold more lots than any realtor in the history of the county, chiefly to persons who had never seen them.

"Well, Charley's got hold of the biggest proposition this town's ever seen. Biggest. Now I'm not exaggerating. You know that tract out past the fairgrounds, the old Lindquist farm, runs clear down to the river?"

"The swamp."

"It is *not* a swamp! That's just exactly the kind of knocking talk that's held this town back for forty years. It's low-lying, I'll grant you that, but Charley's got an engineer—fellow from St. Paul, mighty high-class man—and he says all it needs is some drainage and fill, and you've got the finest residential development between the Twin Cities and Fargo. Hiawatha Heights. Curving streets, see, none of this checkerboard stuff, everything modern, cement sidewalks, restrictions so you don't get any undesirable element. And when they put the new bridge through—and they *will* put it through, Myrt, Senator Hogaboom as good as told me so himself at the Commercial Club—when they put that bridge through, those lots'll go up three, four hundred percent. I've got in on the ground floor. Ground floor! There's men in this town'd give their eyeteeth to get the chance I got."

"Then why didn't they?"

"Why didn't who what?"

"Why didn't the men who'd give their eyeteeth put up their eyeteeth? Why did Charley Gartside come to you?"

Howard looked at her with an expression of patient injury, the expression of a man who has brought home a fine fat pheasant and been asked whether he remembered to wipe his feet.

"Because," he said, with dignity, "because Charley happens to know a live wire when he sees one. Because Charley happens to think that Howard Duckworth is a man of vision. That's why. And I may say that's a good deal more than some people around here seem to think."

He was, as he said it, genuinely moved. He believed it. At the moment when Charley Gartside, leaning across a table in the grill of the Hotel Thorwaldsen with a cigar in one hand and a blueprint in the other, had said, "Old-timer, I'll be frank with you, there's maybe three men in this burg I'd let in on this, and you're the first one I thought of," Howard had felt a warmth spread through his chest that was not entirely attributable to the Hotel Thorwaldsen's pot roast. He had felt chosen. He had felt as he imagined Mr. Henry Ford must feel every morning on rising.

Myrtle did not appear to share this emotion. She sat very straight in the rocker. She was forty-one, a slight woman with brown hair turning, in streaks she did not trouble to hide, the color of weathered pine; and she had a way of pressing her lips together, when she was thinking, that made her look like her own mother, a fact which Howard had observed but had never had the courage to mention.

"Howard," she said, "this is our house."

"Well, I know it's our house. What d'you think I—"

"No. Listen to me. This is our *house*. We paid it off in March. You came home the day you made the last payment and you brought me a box of Whitman's and you said, 'Well, Myrt, she's ours, free and clear, and nobody can ever take her away from us.' You said that. You stood right there by the Victrola and said it. And I thought—I thought, well, all right then. All right. Maybe it was worth it."

"Maybe *what* was worth it?"

She did not answer at once. Out on Elmhurst Avenue a motor car went by, its cutout open, the sound rising and dwindling like a long derisive cheer; that would be the Pedersen boy in his father's Buick, on his way to the Bijou or to somewhere less respectable. Across the street, in the bungalow of Dr. and Mrs. Otto Schwab, a light went out in the front room and another came on upstairs, as regular as the turning of a page. It occurred to Myrtle, not for the first time, that she could have told the hour on any night of the year by the lights in the Schwab house, and that the Schwabs, very probably, could tell it by theirs.

"Everything," she said at last. "All of it. Pinching. Not getting the new dining set. Not going to Minneapolis when Sister had her operation, because the payment was due. Wearing that brown serge three winters running, so that Mrs. J. Wilbur Sloane asked me at the Altar Guild whether it was the same dress or whether I just liked the color. *Liked* the color! I thought, well, at least when it's done, it's done. At least we'll own something. At least there's one thing in this world that isn't owed to somebody."

"Now, Myrt—"

"And you've gone and given it to Charley Gartside."

"I have not given it to anybody! It's an *investment*. Don't you understand the first thing about money? You don't let capital lie idle. That's the whole principle of modern business. Why, a house that's paid off is just—it's just dead money, that's all it is. Every economist in the country'll tell you that. I read an article just last month in *Prosperity Magazine*—fellow that wrote it's a professor out at Northwestern or one of those places—and he said the American who sits on his equity is a—is a—well, I forget just what he said he was, but it wasn't anything good. The modern man puts his dollars to *work*."

"Then let him put his own dollars to work. That was half my dollars."

Howard sat up. The Morris chair, which had a mechanism for reclining, chose that moment to recline, and he went backward with a lurch that destroyed whatever effect of injured majesty he had been preparing. He righted himself, red to the ears.

"*Your* dollars! Well, I like that! I'd like to know who earned 'em. I'd like to know who's been down at that salesroom six days a week since nineteen-eleven, rain or shine, taking guff off every hayseed farmer in Wabasso County that wants to trade in a spavined horse on a new Overland, so's you could sit home and—and—"

He stopped. He was aware, even in the generous heat of his indignation, that he had walked into a room from which there was no good exit. Myrtle had grown very quiet, and when Myrtle grew quiet it was in the manner of a prairie sky before a hailstorm, a stillness so complete that the meadowlarks give up singing.

"And what, Howard?" she said. "So I could sit home and what?"

"Well, I didn't mean—"

"So I could sit home and put up three hundred quarts of tomatoes every August, because you said store-bought were a waste of money? So I could sit home and entertain the Kiwanis wives every time you were trying to sell old Gruenwald a tractor? So I could sit home and listen to Charley Gartside call me 'little lady' at your Fourth of July party and pinch my arm when he thought you weren't looking?"

"He what?"

"Oh, never mind. It doesn't matter."

"It does too matter! If Charley Gartside ever laid a hand on—"

"Howard, he's your business partner now. You've given him the house. You can't very well knock him down too."

There was a silence. The radiator knocked again, as though it had been waiting its turn and had concluded that no one else was going to.

Howard rose and walked to the window. He stood there with his hands in his trouser pockets, jingling his keys, and looked out at Elmhurst Avenue: at the even row of elms, planted in 1902 by the Ladies' Civic Improvement League; at the cement sidewalk that he had personally petitioned the City Council to lay, at a cost of fourteen dollars and sixty cents per frontage foot; at the square houses with their square porches and their square lawns, each lawn with its own wooden sign in the corner reading *Keep Off*. It was a fine street. It was as fine a street as any in the State of Minnesota. He had told a great many people so. And yet, standing there, he was visited by an emotion he could not name and had no wish to: a little cold breath, as if somewhere, far off, a door had been left open in a house he had believed to be locked.

He did not like the feeling. He set about dispelling it in the manner of his kind, which was by making a speech.

"Myrtle," he said, turning, "I want you to look at this thing in a big way. A *big* way. Now you take a man like J. Wilbur Sloane. Where'd J. Wilbur be today if he'd sat on his equity? You take Henry Ford. You take Mr. Rockefeller. Every one of those men took a chance. Every one of 'em put it all on the line, one time or another, and the other fellows laughed at 'em, and who's laughing now? That's the spirit that built this country, Myrt. That's what made America the greatest nation on the face of God's green earth. Vision. Faith. Get-up-and-go. And I'll be doggoned if I'm going to be the kind of a man that sits back in his rocker and lets the parade go by. No sir. Not Howard T. Duckworth."

He was rather pleased with this. He had delivered substantially the same address, with the substitution of "Kiwanians" for "Myrt," at the June luncheon, and it had been well received; Doc Hapgood had pounded the table and called out "Atta boy, Howard!" and the minutes had recorded it as "a peppy talk." He waited now for something analogous.

Myrtle looked at him for a long moment. Then she looked down at the bank's letter in her lap.

"Do you know what I wanted to be?" she said. "Before?"

"Before what?"

"Before I married you. Do you know what I wanted to be?"

He did not know. It had not, in nineteen years, occurred to him that she had wanted to be anything; it would have seemed to him rather like asking what the furnace had wanted to be before it was installed. He said, cautiously, "Well, you were clerking for your dad."

"I wanted to teach elocution. At the Normal, in Mankato. Miss Ingersoll said I had a gift. She said I had the best speaking voice she'd heard in eleven years, and she'd heard Maude Adams in St. Paul. I had a scholarship. Did you know that? A real one. Fifty dollars a term."

"Well, why in thunder didn't you—"

"Because you came into Papa's store to sell him a cream separator, and you had on a straw hat and a striped blazer, and you said Ossawa Falls was going to be the Minneapolis of the Minnetonka Valley inside ten years and you were going to be the biggest man in it. And I believed you." She smiled; it was not, precisely, an unkind smile, which made it a great deal worse. "You were so *sure*, Howard. Nobody I'd ever known was sure of anything except the price of hogs. And I thought, well, I'd rather be married to that than recite 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' to a lot of farm girls in Mankato. I thought it'd be—bigger."

"Well, by golly, it *has* been big! Look at this house! Look at that Victrola! There isn't a woman on this street that's got a better—"

"I know. I know it has. I'm not complaining, Howard. Really I'm not." She folded the letter, and put it back in its envelope, and laid it on the library table beside the wax fruit. "I'm only saying that I gave up one thing to have this, and now you've gone and given *this* to Charley Gartside, and you didn't even ask me. You signed my name. That's what it is, isn't it? That's what 'executed instruments' means. You signed my name, or you got me to sign something I didn't read, one of those nights you brought papers home and said 'just a little insurance thing, Myrt, put your John Hancock right there.' And I did. Because I always do."

Howard opened his mouth. He found, to his considerable surprise, that he had nothing to put into it. The speeches were all there, ranked and ready—Vision and Faith and the Spirit of America and the Ground Floor—but they appeared, at that moment, to belong to someone else, someone in a striped blazer whom he had once known slightly and had lost track of.

"It'll come out all right," he said at last. His voice was smaller than he had intended. "Honest it will, Myrt. Charley says—"
