It was a Thursday in June, and the city of Prosper, Nebraska, which in the literature of its Chamber of Commerce was known as "The Prairie Pittsburgh" and also, somewhat inconsistently, as "The Garden Spot of the Platte," lay sweating under a sky of bleached denim. On the platform of the Union Depot, a structure of yellow brick and municipal ambition which had cost two hundred and eleven thousand dollars and was referred to by every citizen as "our two-hundred-thousand-dollar depot," stood Mr. Harlan T. Pettibone, waiting for his cousin.

Mr. Pettibone was forty-seven. He was pink, he was firm in the jowl and softer below it, and he was the exclusive dealer for the Monitor Six motor car in Prosper and the eleven counties adjacent. He wore a suit of gray worsted, a straw hat with a band in the colors of the Brotherly Order of Bison, a gold watch-chain from which depended a Bison's tooth set in gold, and an expression of hearty readiness, the expression of a man who expects at any moment to be called upon to say a few words. He was, at the moment, thinking about his cousin Everett Lunt, whom he had not seen in twenty-two years, and he was thinking about him with a mixture of affection, curiosity, and the faint apprehension which a man of business feels toward any relative who has gone East and done something artistic.

For Everett had been an artist. That is to say, Everett had, in the year nineteen-one, departed from the farm outside Wahoo with a carpet-bag, a box of water-colors, and the announced intention of becoming a great painter, and the family had heard of him since chiefly through Christmas cards, which grew smaller and more peculiar in design as the years went on, and through a magazine cover once — a girl in a canoe — which Aunt Lettie had cut out and framed and hung in the front parlor between the Rock of Ages and the enlarged crayon portrait of Grandpa Lunt in his G.A.R. uniform.

"Course, Ev was always kind of a dreamer," Harlan had explained that morning to his wife, Myrtle, over the waffles. "But he's done mighty well for himself, I guess. Illustrating and that. They pay big money for that stuff back East. Big money. Why, a fellow told me — fellow from Omaha, in the advertising game — told me some of those fellows that draw pictures for the magazines pull down fifteen, twenty thousand a year. Think of that! Just for drawing pictures!"

"Well, I hope he isn't one of those Bohemians," said Myrtle, who had read about Bohemians in a Sunday supplement and believed them to subsist on absinthe and divorces.

"Bohemian nothing! He's a Lunt, isn't he? He's my own cousin!"

But now, on the platform, watching the Overland Limited heave in from the east with its brass-and-soot dignity, Harlan felt the apprehension rise. He hoped Ev wouldn't have a beard. He hoped Ev wouldn't wear one of those floppy ties. He hoped, above all, that Ev wouldn't say anything to the boys at the Bison Club that would make them look at each other.

The train stopped. Porters descended with the little steps. A fat drummer in a checked suit got off, then a woman with three children and a canary, then two young men in the bell-bottomed trousers that were beginning to be seen even in Prosper, and then, last, an elderly-looking person in a suit of brown tweed, rather baggy at the knees, carrying a cracked leather valise and a walking stick, who stood for a moment blinking at the yellow brick as though he had never before beheld a depot.

Harlan's heart did a curious thing. It was Ev; it was unmistakably Ev, for there was the long Lunt nose and the jaw that Grandpa had in the crayon portrait; but Ev was gray. Ev was thin. Ev had a little gray mustache clipped close like an Englishman's, and the skin about his eyes was crinkled and brown, and he looked, Harlan thought with a shock that he concealed instantly beneath a roar, at least ten years older than a man of forty-five had any business looking.

"Well, well, WELL!" Harlan bellowed, plowing down the platform with his hand outstretched like a man boarding a streetcar. "If it isn't the old son-of-a-gun himself! Ev Lunt! Ev, you old horse-thief! Say, you're looking great! Great! How the dickens are you?"

"Hello, Harlan," said Everett, and he smiled, and there was something in the smile, something shy and boyish, which made the twenty-two years shrink briefly to nothing. Then his hand was seized and pumped, and his shoulder was slapped, and his valise was snatched away, and he was being propelled toward the street by a force as irresistible and well-meaning as a Rotary luncheon.

"Got the car right outside," Harlan was saying. "Brand-new Monitor Six, the Sport Phaeton model, just came in from the factory Tuesday. Hundred and sixteen-inch wheelbase. Balloon tires. Four-wheel brakes — say, there's a feature for you! The old Monitor people sure are on their toes. Well, sir, you'll see. You'll see a lot of changes in Prosper, Ev. A whale of a lot of changes. Why, the last time you were through here — when was that? Nineteen-three? — this town didn't have but nineteen thousand population. Know what we've got now? Eighty-one thousand, three hundred and forty, by the last census, and that was three years ago, and conservative estimates put us well over ninety thousand today. Conservative estimates! Think of that!"

"That's very — remarkable," said Everett.

"Remarkable? It's the fastest-growing city of its size between Chicago and Denver, that's what it is! And I'm not saying that because I live here. Those are facts. You can look 'em up."

The Monitor Six stood at the curb, scarlet and nickeled, its top folded back, gleaming in the sun like a fire engine in a Fourth of July parade. Harlan regarded it with the tender pride of a father at a christening. He put the valise in the tonneau, held open the door for his cousin, went around and climbed in, and pressed the self-starter with a little flourish, as though he were bestowing the motor upon the world.

They drove up Platte Avenue. Harlan pointed out, with the zeal of a guide in Rome, the new Farmers' and Mechanics' National Bank Building, eleven stories, "tallest in the state outside Omaha, and they're only ahead of us by two stories, and there's talk of us putting up a fourteen-story job on the corner of Fifth and Douglas"; the Orpheum Theatre, "seats sixteen hundred, and they get the very same acts as Kansas City"; the Hotel Cornhusker, "running water in every room, and a ballroom finished in genuine Circassian walnut"; the Bison Temple, "cost us better than three hundred thousand, and every cent raised by popular subscription"; and the plate-glass establishment of Pettibone Motor Sales Company, Inc., before which he slowed reverently to five miles an hour.

"There she is," he said. "Started with one little shed and a secondhand Ford in nineteen-ten. Now we got twenty-two employees and a service department second to none. I'm not bragging, Ev. I'm just giving you the facts. But I tell you, a fellow can't help feeling kind of proud."

Everett looked at the showroom, at the three scarlet Monitors poised on the polished floor like tigers in a zoo, at the sign which said in gold letters "PETTIBONE — WHERE YOUR DOLLAR DRIVES FARTHER," and something flickered across his face, which might have been amusement and might have been envy and might have been merely the glare.

"It's a fine place, Harlan," he said. "You've done well. I'm glad."

And Harlan, who had been prepared for condescension, who had braced himself against some Eastern smartness about Main Street and Babbittry and the Booboisie, which he had heard was the fashion among the high-brows, was so disarmed by the plain words that he could think of nothing to say for a whole block, which was for Harlan T. Pettibone a silence of almost geological duration.

The Pettibone residence stood in Maple Crest, Prosper's newest and most exclusive residential section, which had been a cornfield in nineteen-sixteen and was now laid out in curving streets named Fairview Drive and Bon Air Lane and Kenilworth Circle, after the manner of all newest and most exclusive residential sections from Bangor to San Diego. It was a Dutch Colonial house with green shutters and a sun-parlor, and it contained a living-room with a fireplace which had never had a fire in it, a mahogany Victrola, a radio cabinet with seven tubes on which Harlan had once received Havana, Cuba, at two in the morning, a set of the Book of Knowledge, a set of the World's Best Literature in half-morocco, uncut, a floor lamp with a parchment shade depicting a Spanish galleon, a davenport, two overstuffed chairs, and a framed motto above the telephone stand reading "Smile, Darn You, Smile!"

Myrtle Pettibone received the visitor in the hall. She was a plump, kindly, anxious woman with a permanent wave and a voice which went up at the ends of sentences, and she had spent the morning in preparing a dinner of fried chicken, mashed potatoes, creamed corn, hot biscuits, three kinds of jelly, a molded salad of lime gelatin containing walnuts, celery, and maraschino cherries, and an angel food cake, and in hiding the copy of True Romances from the living-room table.

"We're just so glad to have you, Mr. Lunt — Everett — I may call you Everett, mayn't I? — seeing as we're family?" she said. "Harlan's talked about nothing else all week? Have you had a nice trip? Isn't it dreadful, the heat?"

Everett said that he was very glad to be there, that the trip had been quite pleasant, that it was indeed dreadful, the heat, and that she must call him Ev, as everyone in the family always had. Myrtle went pink with pleasure and fled to the kitchen, from which there presently arose the sound of a percolator and of a hired girl named Hulda being exhorted.

And after dinner, when Ev had praised the chicken with a sincerity that made Myrtle glow for a week, and when the children — Harlan Junior, sixteen, who was mad about radio and spoke a dialect consisting chiefly of "kilocycles" and "the bunk," and Gladys, fourteen, who wanted to be a movie actress and regarded her Eastern cousin with frank disappointment because he did not resemble John Barrymore — had been excused, the two men went out to the screened porch with cigars.

The cigars were Harlan's. They were El Supremos, at fifteen cents straight, and he offered them with a gesture which implied that they were the very same cigars smoked by Calvin Coolidge, Henry Ford, and the Prince of Wales. They sat in wicker chairs, and the evening came down blue and tender over Maple Crest, and the sprinklers whispered on the lawns of Fairview Drive, and somewhere a phonograph was playing "Yes, Sir, That's My Baby," and Harlan, tilting back and putting his feet on the rail, felt the large and expansive contentment of a man who has eaten well in his own house.

"Well, Ev," he said, "tell me all about yourself. I want to hear the whole works. How's the art game?"

Everett looked at the end of his cigar. "Oh, it goes along," he said.

"Still doing those magazine covers? Aunt Lettie's still got that one with the girl in the canoe. Says it's the prettiest picture she ever saw. Hangs right next to Grandpa."

"Does she?" Everett laughed — a short laugh, without much breath behind it. "That was in nineteen-twelve, Harlan. I haven't done a cover in — oh, eight or nine years now."

"That so? Went into something bigger, I suppose? Portrait painting? I hear there's big money in portraits. Fellow in Omaha had his wife done in oil, cost him twelve hundred dollars."

"No. Not portraits." Everett was silent a moment. Then, as though he had decided something, he said, rather quickly, "I teach, Harlan. Drawing. At a sort of school — a commercial art school, in Brooklyn. Teaching young fellows how to draw corsets and tooth-paste for the advertisements. Tuesdays and Thursdays and Saturday mornings. And I paint, on the side. For myself."

"Oh," said Harlan. He was not quite sure what response was called for, and he fell back upon the universal formula of the Bison Club. "Well, say, that's fine! That's a fine profession, teaching. Molding the youth of the nation, and so on. Mighty fine."

"It pays forty-two dollars a week," said Everett.

There was a pause. In that pause Harlan T. Pettibone, who sold eleven hundred motor cars a year and who had once spoken for twelve minutes on "Service: the Keynote of Modern Business" before the state convention of the Brotherly Order of Bison, found that he had absolutely nothing to say. Forty-two dollars a week! Why, his own head mechanic, Gus Stoltenberg, a Swede who could hardly write his name, drew forty-five! And here was Ev, who had gone away with all that talent, with all the family's hopes, Ev who had been going to be a great painter and show 'em all —

"Why, Ev," he said at last, and his voice was oddly gentle, "why, gosh, old man, I didn't — Say, if you ever need — I mean, if things ever get kind of — you know you can always —"

"I know, Harlan. Thank you. It's quite all right. I manage. I have a room on Columbia Heights with a north light, and I can see the harbor from it, and the ships go out in the morning with the sun on them, and I paint them. I paint them very badly, mostly. But once in a long while I paint one that's not so bad, and then I'm happier than you'd believe." He smiled again, that shy smile. "I sold one last spring. To a dentist from Philadelphia. Sixty dollars."

Harlan stared at him in the dusk. He was trying to comprehend it. He was trying to comprehend a man who could be happy at forty-two dollars a week and a room with a north light, a man who did not own an automobile nor a radio nor a membership in anything, who was going gray in a boarding house in Brooklyn painting ships, and who said, apparently meaning it, that he was happier than you'd believe. It was as though Ev had confessed to being a Mohammedan. And yet, under the bewilderment, Harlan felt something else stir, something he could not have named, a faint ache like an old football knee before rain.

"Well," he said heartily, "everybody to his own taste, as the old lady said when she kissed the cow!" And he laughed very loudly, and Ev laughed politely, and the phonograph down the street began "Barney Google."

They talked then of the family, which was safe. Of Aunt Lettie, who was eighty-one and still put up forty quarts of piccalilli every fall. Of Cousin Fred, who had gone into the hardware business in Hastings and failed, and then into insurance and succeeded, and had become a Methodist and a Mason and a power in the Hastings Kiwanis. Of Uncle Wendell, who had been, it was whispered, a free-thinker and a Populist, and had died reading Ingersoll. Of the old farm outside Wahoo, which had been sold in nineteen-eighteen when wheat was two dollars and twenty cents, and which was now owned by a Bohemian family — "real Bohemians, Ev, I mean, from Bohemia, not your kind" — who had put up a silo.

"The willows," said Everett suddenly. "Are the willows still there? Down on Sand Creek, below the pasture?"

"Willows? Why, I don't know, Ev. I haven't been out there in — well, quite a spell. I guess so. Why?"

"Do you remember the swimming hole? Below the willows, where the creek bent around? You and I used to sneak off there in July, when we were supposed to be shocking oats. Do you remember the time you dared me to swing out on the grapevine and drop in, and the vine broke, and I came down in the mud on the far bank up to my waist, and you laughed so hard you fell in yourself?"

Harlan was silent. His cigar had gone out. And for a moment, sitting there on the screened porch of the Dutch Colonial house in Maple Crest, with the Monitor Six in the garage and the Bison tooth on his watch-chain, he was not Harlan T. Pettibone, Exclusive Dealer, at all. He was a skinny, freckled, barefoot boy of twelve named Harley, lying on his back in the warm grass under the willows, with the sun coming down through the leaves in coins of gold, and the creek talking to itself over the stones, and the cicadas going like little sawmills, and nobody in the whole world expecting him to say a few words or to make his quota or to put over the Community Chest drive; and beside him, chewing a grass stem, his cousin Ev, who was going to be a great painter some day, and who was saying, very seriously, "Harley, when I'm famous I'm going to come back and paint this. Just exactly this. So it'll never go away."

"Yes," said Harlan, rather hoarsely. "Yes, I remember, Ev."

"I never did paint it," said Everett. "I tried, a dozen times. It never came out right."

Neither of them spoke for a while. The sprinklers whispered. A Monitor Six — not Harlan's — went by on Fairview Drive with its cut-out open, and a girl in it shrieked with laughter. And Harlan felt the ache in him grow until it was nearly unbearable, and he wanted to say something, he did not know what — that he too had been going to do something once, though he could no longer remember what it was; that the eleven hundred cars a year and the Bison Temple and the ninety thousand by conservative estimate were all very fine, but that sometimes, lying awake at three in the morning beside Myrtle, he wondered what they were for; that he would have given a good deal, a very good deal, to lie under those willows again for one afternoon with nobody wanting anything.

He did not say it. He had not the words, and if he had had them he would have been ashamed. A man in his position. A man who had addressed the state convention.

Instead he relit his cigar, and cleared his throat, and swung his feet down off the rail.

"Say, Ev," he said, "tomorrow noon I want you to come down to the Bison Club with me. Luncheon. We got a speaker coming — fellow from the National Association of Credit Men, going to talk on 'Pep, Push, and Prosperity.' Darn good speaker, they say. And I want the boys to meet you. Want 'em to meet my cousin the artist, from New York. Why, they'll eat it up! And afterwards I'll run you out to the country club and show you the new eighteen holes. Cost us better than ninety thousand, but believe me, there's not a finer course in the Middle West."

"That would be very nice, Harlan," said Everett.

"And, say — you'll tell 'em you're an artist, of course. An illustrator. A New York illustrator." Harlan hesitated. "No need to go into the — the teaching business, and that. Not that there's anything wrong with it. But you know how folks are."

Everett looked at him in the dusk for a long moment. Then he smiled, and the smile was kind, and a little tired, and very old.

"I know how folks are, Harley," he said.

Harlan started at the name. Nobody had called him Harley in thirty years. Then he laughed, loudly, and slapped his cousin on the knee, and said, "Well, it's getting late, and I guess you're pretty well tuckered out after that trip. Myrtle's fixed up the guest room. Got a new Simmons mattress in there — genuine coil springs. You'll sleep like a top."

He stood, and held open the screen door, and the light from the living-room fell across the porch, across the wicker chairs and the floor lamp with its Spanish galleon and the motto that said "Smile, Darn You, Smile!"; and the two men went in, talking of the weather, and of the price of wheat, and of whether Coolidge would run again, and of the fine new course at the country club, which had cost better than ninety thousand dollars.

But that night, long after the house was dark, Harlan T. Pettibone lay awake on his own Simmons mattress beside his gently snoring wife, staring at the ceiling, and listening, through the open window, past the whisper of the sprinklers and the far hoot of a freight on the Burlington, for something that he could not hear — the sound, perhaps, of a creek talking to itself over the stones, a long way off, below the willows, where two boys lay in the grass and were going to be great men.

The house of Homer Q. Gaddis stood on Ridgemere Drive, in the section of Elkhorn Falls which the Elkhorn Falls Realty & Development Corporation had for six years been advertising as "Restful, Restricted, and Refined." It was a Dutch Colonial house, which is to say that it was neither Dutch nor Colonial but was painted a sober cream and had a gambrel roof, two green shutters for every window, and a brass knocker in the shape of a lion's head which no one ever used, since there was also an electric bell. It had a sun-parlor with wicker furniture and a canary, a breakfast nook with a built-in bench upon which no one could sit comfortably for more than eleven minutes, a cedar closet, a laundry chute, and a basement furnished with a Torrid Twin-Draft Furnace which Homer Gaddis regarded with something of the pride with which a medieval baron regarded his keep.

It was, in all its particulars, precisely like the houses on either side of it, and Homer Gaddis knew this, and was content, for he believed that a man who wished his house to be different from his neighbors' was probably a Socialist, or at the very least a fellow who wrote poetry and did not pay his bills.

At a quarter past six on a Saturday evening in October, Homer Gaddis drove his sedan into the two-car garage, shut off the motor with the finality of a judge pronouncing sentence, and sat for a moment with his hands upon the wheel. He was forty-four. He was the proprietor of the Gaddis Office Appliance Company, sole agents in four counties for the Ever-Ready Rotary Duplicator and the Phalanx Steel Filing Cabinet ("A Phalanx Never Falls Down on the Job!"). He was a Kiwanian, an Elk, a deacon of the Wesley Avenue Methodist Church, and a member of the Tamarack Country Club, where he had that afternoon shot a ninety-seven and had been informed, between the fourteenth and fifteenth holes, of the most mortifying thing that had happened to him since 1911.

He sat in the garage and breathed heavily through his nose.

The informant had been Chet Applegate, of Applegate's Quality Footwear, a man of large and cheerful malice, who had approached him with the expression of a dog that has found something dead and wishes to share it.

"Say, Homer, old socks," Chet had said, "I hear your kid's turning into a regular little orator. Regular William Jennings Bryan. Yes sir, they tell me he gave Mrs. T. Lucius Beane a speech at the Ladies' Aid bazaar yesterday she won't forget in a hurry."

Homer had laughed, the large, comfortable, manly laugh of a father who supposes that his son has said something cute about Santa Claus. He had not continued laughing. For it developed, as Chet Applegate unwound the tale with the loving deliberation of a man reeling in a pike, that Homer's son Clifford, aged seven years and four months, had approached Mrs. T. Lucius Beane at the fancy-work booth, had studied her for some time with the grave candor of the very young, and had then informed her, in a clear and carrying voice, that his papa said Mr. Beane was a tight-fisted old pickerel who would foreclose on his own grandmother and who only came to church to count the house.

Mr. T. Lucius Beane was president of the Second National Bank of Elkhorn Falls.

Mr. T. Lucius Beane was the man to whom Homer Gaddis had, nine days ago, applied for a loan of eighteen thousand dollars with which to open a branch office in the thriving city of Pawnee Center.

It is true that Homer had said it. He had said it at dinner, on the evening when the loan committee had asked him for a second statement of assets, and he had said it with relish, between bites of pot roast, while his wife Ione murmured, "Now Homer, not in front of the children." He had not supposed that the children were listening. In twelve years of fatherhood he had never quite grasped that children were always listening, and that they listened most carefully precisely when they appeared to be building a fort out of mashed potatoes.

He got out of the car. He slammed the door, which was not necessary, and went in through the kitchen, which was.

Ione was at the stove. She was a plump, pleasant woman with a permanent wave of terrible regularity, and she had learned in fifteen years of marriage to read her husband's moods by the manner in which he hung up his hat. He hung it up now as though he were hanging a horse thief.

"Well," she said brightly, "how was the golf?"

"Golf," said Homer, "was rotten. Where is that boy?"

"I'll tell you what on earth. I'll tell you what on earth, and then you can tell me how a youngster brought up in a decent Christian home, with every advantage, with a father that's worked his fingers to the bone to give him everything a kid could want, with an Indian suit and a velocipede and a set of the Boy's Own Encyclopedia in eight volumes, bound in genuine imitation leather—how a kid like that comes to go around town shooting off his mouth like a—like a common I.W.W."

He told her. She listened with her mixing spoon held aloft, and when he had finished she said, "Oh, dear," and then, after reflection, "Well, you did say it, Homer."

This was not the support he required. He looked at her with the injured dignity of a senator who has been asked, in public, what he did with the money.

"That," he said, "has nothing whatsoever to do with it. What a man says in the privacy of his own home, to his own wife, in confidence, is one thing. It's his privilege. It's practically in the Constitution. It's a question of—of loyalty. Of discretion. Of knowing what's what. And that boy has got to learn it, and he's got to learn it now, before he grows up and goes around telling the whole world his old man's business. I'm going up there."

He climbed them slowly, and as he climbed, his indignation began to arrange itself, as his indignations always did, into a speech. Homer Gaddis was a celebrated speaker. He had addressed the Kiwanis Club on "The Office of Tomorrow," the Chamber of Commerce on "Pep, Punch, and Profits," and the Wesley Avenue Men's Bible Class on "Was Jesus a Go-Getter?" (He had concluded, after an analysis of the parable of the talents, that He was.) He had never been at a loss for words in his life, and he did not intend to be at a loss now before an audience of one, three feet nine inches high.

The door of Clifford's room bore a sign, lettered in red crayon on a piece of shirt cardboard, which read, KEEP OUT THIS MEANS YOU PRIVIT. Homer regarded the misspelling with a fresh pang, as further evidence of a general collapse of standards, and opened the door without knocking.

Clifford was sitting on the floor in the midst of a construction of Meccano strips and brass bolts which was either a crane or a suspension bridge or a very nervous giraffe. He was a thin child, with his mother's round face and his father's large ears, and he had a smear of machine oil across his forehead like the mark of some obscure religious order. He looked up. He saw his father's face. He put down his screwdriver with the slow care of a man who senses that the next few minutes may be the last in which he will be permitted to hold a screwdriver.

"Hello, Papa."

"Don't you 'hello Papa' me, young man."

Clifford considered this. It seemed to leave him no further conversational avenue, so he said nothing at all.

Homer shut the door. He looked about the room for a place of judgment. He examined the match, as though it might have been defective, and laid it in the terrier's mouth.

"Sit down, Harvey."

"Why, I'm all right standing. Been sitting all evening. You get so you need to stretch your legs, at those suppers. They had those darn little folding chairs, the kind the undertakers rent out." He laughed, heartily and alone.

She was still a handsome woman, in the solid, upholstered fashion approved by the Ladies' Home Companion; her hair was done in the marcel wave which Madame Yvonne (born Ida Schutz) renewed for her every second Thursday; she was treasurer of the Wednesday Afternoon Literary Circle, which had that winter covered Browning, Ibsen, and the Holy Land in fourteen sessions; and she had never, in nineteen years of marriage, raised her voice to her husband except in the matter of muddy rubbers on the hall runner. "I had a caller this afternoon," she said. "Mr. Voorhees, from the Farmers and Mechanics Savings Bank."

"That so? Old Bert Voorhees? Say, he's a great old scout, Bert is. Sits right across from me at the Brotherhood, too. Funny he didn't say anything to-night. What'd he want? "Oh, that," he said.

"Yes, Harvey. That."

She did not seem inspired with confidence. She waited.

"You know Clyde Ostrander."

"Well, now, there's no call to say it like that. Clyde's one of the most go-ahead young fellows in this town. He's on the Publicity Committee of the Chamber. Clyde's got the plans drawn up by an architect from Chicago. From *Chicago*, Lorry! The lots are going for eight hundred now. The day that spur's announced, they'll go for two thousand. Twenty-five hundred. You know what this town's going to be, ten years from now? Fifty thousand population. Easy. The Chamber's got the figures. And the men who get in on the ground floor—"

He made a small, deprecating gesture with the dead cigar. "Well—I took twelve lots."

"Twelve."

"Corner lots, a lot of 'em. Clyde gave me first pick. Because I'm in on the organization. I'm what you call a—well, he calls it a 'founding associate.' There's only five of us. Me and Clyde and Doc Herrold and Walt Bissell from the Bissell Hardware and a fella from over at Jefferson City that's got a lot of capital. It's practically a closed corporation."

"I didn't *pay* with the house. Good Lord, Lorry, you talk like I'd gone and sold it out from under you! I just put it up as security. That's all. It's done every day. It was the first sentence in nineteen years in which Lorena Kittredge had expressed indifference to the views of a Circuit Judge, and Harvey looked at her as though she had removed her marcel wave and revealed beneath it the head of a stranger.

"Well," he said, injured, "I'm only telling you."

Her hands, he noticed, were not quite steady, and the noticing made him angry, because he did not know what to do about it. "Harvey, when did you sign this?"

"October, I guess. Along in there."

"October. And it's April." "Now, the wrist-watch hasn't got a thing to do with it—"

He rose. He felt that a man explained himself better standing up; that the vertical posture was itself a kind of argument. He walked to the radio cabinet, which was walnut veneer and had a loud-speaker concealed behind a fretwork panel representing a Spanish galleon in full sail, and he put his hand upon it as though for support.

"Because," he said, "I didn't want to worry you."

"Harvey."

"That's the truth, Lorry, so help me. A man's got a right to protect his wife from worry, hasn't he? Business is a man's affair. I never asked you to bother your head about it. That's what a man's for. You run the house, and you run it fine, nobody better, and I run the business. That's the way it's always been, and that's the way it ought to be. You women go to your Literary Circle and talk about—about Ibsen and so on—and that's fine, I'm all for culture, I'm a hundred percent for it, but you don't want to go filling up your head with notes and interest rates and so on. "Well, he had no business—"

"I'm upset because I stood in my own front hall, with my apron on, and Bert Voorhees told me something about my own house that my own husband hadn't told me, and he looked at me—Harvey, he looked at me as if he were *sorry* for me." For the first time her voice wavered. "Bert Voorhees. Whose wife wears that awful fox scarf to church in July."

There was in this a logic which Harvey could not refute, because he could not, in fact, follow it; and like most men confronted with an argument they cannot follow, he concluded that it was not an argument at all but an emotion, and that emotions, like head colds, were best treated with patience and a few kind words.

"Now, honey," he said. He came toward her. He meant to put his hand on her shoulder. He had seen it done in a photoplay at the Bijou only the week before, by Mr. Lewis Stone, with great success. "Now, honey, you're just tired. You've been working too hard on that rummage sale. You're taking this all wrong. Ten years from now we'll laugh about this. Ten years from now you'll have a fur coat—a real sealskin, not any of your Hudson seal—and we'll have a place up on the lake, and you'll say, 'Harvey, I'll never doubt you again,' and—"

She moved her shoulder. It was a small movement, but his hand found nothing.

"Is the spur line going through?"

"Huh?"

"The Interurban. The spur line. Clyde's cousin. Is it going through?"

"Well—it's practically certain. It's all but signed."

"Bert Voorhees said the Interurban board voted in February not to build any more spurs this year. He said it was in the Courier."

"That," said Harvey with dignity, "is just the *Courier*. You know what the *Courier* is. Bunch of knockers. Always running down the town. If a fella wants to build anything in this town, the *Courier*'s against it. They were against the new viaduct, too. Clyde says—"

"What does Clyde say?"

He hesitated. In that hesitation, which lasted perhaps three ticks of the Tower-Tone clock, he saw, as clearly as though it were printed in the Courier in the twelve-point type reserved for local disasters, the twelve lots lying out past the fairgrounds, with the March mud on them and the Schiller cows standing in it, regarding with ruminative contempt the four surveyor's stakes which were all that existed of Ostrander Heights. He saw Clyde Ostrander at the last meeting of the founding associates, a month ago, talking very fast and laughing very much and saying that this was only a temporary setback, boys, only a temporary setback; and he saw the fellow from Jefferson City, the fellow with the capital, who had not been at that meeting, and who had not been at the meeting before that either.

"Clyde says," said Harvey, "it's only a temporary setback."

Lorena said nothing at all.

The silence of a wife is a thing for which the American husband has never been adequately equipped. He has been trained by the luncheon clubs to meet heckling with a joke, by the lodges to meet tragedy with a resolution of sympathy suitably engrossed, by the newspapers to meet doubt with a statistic. But for silence he has no slogan. Harvey Kittredge stood in the middle of his own living-room, with its Mulberry Mist davenport and its Spanish-galleon radio and its framed reproduction of "The Song of the Lark" over the mantel, and felt himself a stranger there, like a salesman who has rung the wrong bell.

"Darn it, Lorry," he burst out, "say something!"

"What do you want me to say?"

"Well—I don't know. Bawl me out. Go on. I'd feel better if you'd bawl me out."

"I know you would," said Lorena.

He had not expected that, and he did not like it. He took a turn to the window and back. "I suppose you think I'm a fool."

"No."

"Yes, you do. You think I'm a fool. You think I'm just a—a sucker. Well, let me tell you something. Let me just tell you something. Every man that ever amounted to anything in this country, people called him a fool. They called Edison a fool. They laughed at Columbus. If I'd listened to everybody that—what are you smiling at?"

"I wasn't smiling."

"You were too smiling."

"I was thinking," she said slowly, "that you'd say Columbus. I knew you'd say Columbus. You always say Columbus. You said it when you bought the radio stock, and you said it when you were going to sell those cement burial vaults with Elmer Platt, and you said it when you put that awful gold-fish pond in the back yard that froze and cracked." She looked down at the envelope. "Nineteen years, Harvey. I could say all your speeches for you. I could stand up at the Brotherhood and make every speech you'll ever make, and nobody would know the difference."

He stared at her, and his face, which was a large, pink, trustworthy face, a face which had sold a great many tires to a great many farmers on the strength of its trustworthiness, went slowly red from the collar up.

"That," he said, "is a heck of a thing to say to a man."

"Yes," said Lorena. "I suppose it is."

For a moment it seemed that something would happen—that she would weep, or that he would shout, or that one of them would say a thing that could not afterward be pretended away. The Tower-Tone clock drew in its breath and chimed the half-hour, sweetly, like a Methodist bell. Down the block the Havestick Ford came exploding home again.

Lorena stood up. She laid the envelope, very neatly, on the walnut veneer of the radio cabinet, squared with its edge, as she laid out his clean collars in the morning.

"What are you going to do?" he said. His voice was small. He was surprised at how small it was.

"I'm going to bed. I've got the Circle to-morrow. We're doing Bernard Shaw." She went to the foot of the stairs, and turned there, one hand on the newel post, which was of golden oak and had been a source of great pride when they built the house in 1916. "You'll go see Bert Voorhees in the morning. And you'll find out exactly how much we owe and when it's due, and you'll come home at noon and tell me. All of it. With figures. And then we'll decide what to do."

"*We'll* decide—"

"We'll decide," said Lorena.

He opened his mouth to explain that business was a man's affair, that a wife's place was—but the words, which had always come so readily, so roundly, like coins from a slot machine, did not come. He shut his mouth again.

She went up the stairs. He heard her steps cross the hall, heard the bathroom door, heard the water run in the basin, as it had run every night for nineteen years at precisely this hour.

Harvey Kittredge stood alone. He looked at the envelope. He did not touch it. He relit his cigar, and it tasted of ashes and of October, and he put it out in the mouth of the bronze Scotch terrier. Then, because he did not know what else to do, he went to the front door and set out the milk-bottles, two quarts and a half-pint of cream, which, he reflected, they would perhaps have to cut down to one quart and no cream; and he stood a while on the porch in the damp April dark, looking at the street-lamp, and he said aloud, to no one, in a voice that had lost its conviction:

"Looks like rain to-morrow."

From upstairs Lorena called, as she had called every night for nineteen years, "Harvey? Did you put the milk-bottles out?"

"Yes, dear," he said. And then, for the first time he could remember, he added nothing at all.

They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? “Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

Lyman Hoag drove home that evening in a state of placid triumph. He had sold, between three and four o'clock, a Hoag Thermo-Glo Furnace (Pipeless Model, with the Patented Humidifying Pan) to a retired harness-maker named Schwengel. He had sold it chiefly by assuring Mr. Schwengel that it would reduce his coal bills by one-third, possibly by one-half. He did not know whether it would reduce Mr. Schwengel's coal bills at all. No one knew. The manufacturer's circular said "up to forty per cent," and Lyman had found that a man is more readily moved by a half than by a forty per cent, half being a rounder and more Christian figure.

He drove his Wainwright Eight up Sheridan Boulevard through the thin February dusk and felt kindly toward the city of Ostrander, which had last year passed one hundred and eighty thousand in population and was going, according to the Chamber of Commerce, to pass a quarter of a million by 1930 if everybody would just get behind it and boost. He felt kindly toward the new bungalows of Glenwood Terrace, each with its sun-porch, its pergola, its garage built of the same stucco as the house and its concrete bird-bath frozen solid. He felt kindly toward his own house, a Dutch Colonial with green shutters and a brass knocker shaped like a lion that had cost eleven dollars at Brodsky's. He said aloud, "Well, sir, not a bad day's work, not a bad day's work at all," and he hummed "Smiles," and he backed the car into the garage on the second try.

His wife met him at the side door. Edna Hoag was a pleasant, anxious woman of thirty-eight who had once been the prettiest girl at the Methodist Sunday School picnic and who still, in her best moments, resembled that girl as a photograph resembles a face. She was not, this evening, in one of her best moments. She held a dish-towel as a magistrate holds a gavel.

"Lyman, I want you to go right in and talk to Delbert."

"Why, what's the trouble? What's the kid been up to now?"

"Mrs. Gurney was over here. She was over here not twenty minutes ago, and I never was so mortified in all my life."

Lyman took off his overcoat with the elaborate deliberation of a man who senses that he is about to be made responsible for something. "Well, what'd she want?"

"She wanted to know where she could buy some more of that genuine imported Scotch marmalade from the Highlands of Scotland."

"Huh?"

"That's what I said. *Huh.* And then she showed me the jar. It was my rhubarb jam, Lyman. My rhubarb jam that I put up last August, with a piece of paper pasted over the label and 'Imported' printed on it in crayon. And she paid thirty-five cents for it. And that isn't all. He sold one to Mrs. Sloat and told her it was good for rheumatism, and one to that new woman on the corner, the one with the Pekingese, and told her the King of England ate it for breakfast every single morning. A dollar and five cents he took in, Lyman. A dollar and five cents! And Mrs. Gurney laughed about it, she thought it was cute, but I could see what she was thinking. She was thinking she'd tell the whole Bridge Club. She was thinking that's what comes of the Hoags' raising."

Lyman said "Well, I'll be darned," and was immediately conscious that he had said it in the wrong tone. A certain unbidden admiration had crept into it. He corrected himself sternly: "Well, I'll be *darned*!"

"You've got to punish him. You've got to make him understand. I've talked and talked to that child till I'm blue in the face, and he just looks at me. He'll mind you."

It is one of the comfortable fictions of the American household that children mind their fathers. Lyman Hoag believed it as he believed in the protective tariff, the Republican party, and the superiority of the Wainwright Eight over all cars selling for less than two thousand dollars: without having examined it. He drew himself up. He was a man of thirty-nine, of the middle height, a little thick through the waistcoat, with a round pink face and rimless spectacles and thinning hair that he brushed carefully across a widening area of scalp. He was a past Exalted Wampum of the Ancient Arcanum of Hiawatha, Lodge No. 211. He had been on the committee that brought the Sunshine Bakery to Ostrander. He was not going to be defeated by a boy of seven.

"Where is he?"

"Up in his room. I sent him up there the minute she left."

"You send him down to the den. No, wait. I'll go wash up first. Let him stew a while. Do him good."

He went up to the bathroom, which was the pride of the house, with its tiled floor and its nickel towel-racks and its medicine cabinet full of bottles that no one ever threw away. He washed his hands with the green soap that was supposed to be made from olive oil and probably was not. He looked at himself in the mirror and arranged his face into the expression of a stern but just parent. He practiced it. He found that it resembled the expression he used when a bank refused to extend a note, and he was satisfied.

He was not, however, entirely easy in his mind. There was the matter of Mr. Schwengel's coal bills. It was not that he considered himself to have lied to Mr. Schwengel. He had merely put his best foot forward, as any live wire was bound to do in a competitive age. Still, the word "imported," painted in crayon upon a jar of Edna's rhubarb jam, gave him a curious small discomfort, like a pebble in a good shoe.

("Rats! Altogether different proposition. Kid's got to learn. Can't go around fooling people.")

He went downstairs to the den.

The den had been, in the plans of the Glenwood Terrace Development Company, a "Reading Nook." Lyman had converted it into a den by installing a Morris chair upholstered in imitation Spanish leather, a smoking stand with a bronze Indian on it, a radio set with three dials and a horn like a morning-glory, a framed photograph of the Hiawatha Lodge's 1922 pilgrimage to Atlantic City, a tarpon he had not caught but had bought, mounted, from a man in Tampa, and a bookcase holding a set of Kipling in maroon leatherette, a set of the *Little Leather Library*, eight years of the *National Geographic*, and a book called *Personality Plus: Your Road to Power*. Here he did his thinking. That is, here he sat after dinner and listened to the radio and read the sporting page and occasionally, when the static was bad, worried about money.

He sat down in the Morris chair. He lit a cigar, then decided that a cigar was undignified for the occasion and put it out, then decided that it was the most dignified thing about him and lit it again. He called, in what he believed to be a voice of thunder, "Del-*bert*!"

There was a long pause. Then there was a sound of feet, very slow feet, on the stairs.

Delbert Hoag was seven years old and small for his age. He had his mother's light hair and his father's round face, and he had, besides, a quality that belonged to neither of them, a kind of grave, considering stillness, as though he were always adding up figures behind his eyes. He wore knickerbockers, one stocking up and one stocking down, and a sweater with a reindeer on it that his aunt in Davenport had knitted. He came into the den and stood upon the hooked rug and looked at his father without fear and without particular interest, as a customer looks at a salesman who has not yet named his price.

"Well, young man," said Lyman Hoag.

Delbert said nothing.

"Well, young man, I guess you know why I called you down here."

"Yes, sir."

"Well, sir, why did I?"

"'Cause of the jam."

"Because of the jam. That's right. Because of the jam. Now I want you to tell me all about it. And I want the truth, mind you. I want the whole truth and nothing but the truth. You understand me?"

"Yes, sir."

"All right. Shoot."

Delbert considered. "I took four jars out of the fruit-cellar. Mama's got lots. She's got forty-one. I counted. And I made labels on the dining-room table. And I sold them."

"You sold them. And what did you tell the ladies?"

"I told them it was imported."

"Imported! And was it imported?"

"No, sir."

"No, sir! It most certainly was not imported. It was made right here in this house, by your own mother, with rhubarb out of our own back yard. And you told Mrs. Gurney it was from Scotland. Did you or didn't you?"

"Yes, sir. From the Highlands."

Lyman struck the arm of the Morris chair. A small cloud of ash rose from the cigar and settled upon his trousers. He brushed at it irritably and lost, for a moment, the thread of his indignation.

"Well, now, see here. You know what that is, don't you? That's telling a lie. That's telling a deliberate lie. That's just about the worst thing a boy can do. Why, I'd rather you'd—I'd rather you'd break a window. I'd rather you'd get in a fight. Anybody'll get in a fight. But a liar! You know what George Washington said when his father asked him about that cherry tree?"

"He said he couldn't tell a lie."

"That's right. He said, 'Father, I cannot tell a lie; I did it with my little hatchet.' And that's why he got to be President of the United States. Not because he was a fine soldier, though he was, and not because he was smart, though he was mighty smart, but because folks knew they could trust him. Folks knew George Washington was a square shooter. And the Hoags have always been square shooters. Your granddad Hoag never told a lie in his life. Ran a feed store in Mason Falls for thirty-two years, and there wasn't a man in Pottawatomie County that wouldn't take his word for anything." (This was not precisely true; Lyman's father had been sued twice over the weighing of oats, but it was a family convention that both suits had been instigated by Democrats.) "And here's you, seven years old, going around telling the neighbors that rhubarb jam comes from Scotland. And telling Mrs. Sloat it'd cure her rheumatism! Now how did you know it'd cure her rheumatism?"

"I didn't."

"Then what'd you say it for?"

Delbert's eyes moved, very slightly, upward and sideways, as if he were consulting an invisible ledger. Then he said, in the tone of one stating a law of nature:

"'Cause you said a fella's got to put pep in his product."

Lyman Hoag opened his mouth and found nothing in it.

"You said it Tuesday," Delbert went on helpfully. "At supper. You said nobody'd buy anything if you just said it was a furnace. You said you got to tell 'em what it'll *do* for 'em. You said you got to make 'em see it. You said if you sold furnaces like old man Pfeiffer sells 'em you'd be in the poorhouse."

"Now, see here—"

"And you said Mr. Pfeiffer just says it's a furnace and it burns coal and that's all, and that's why he's a back number. And you said a live wire tells 'em it's the finest furnace on the market and it'll save 'em half their coal. You said half. And Mama said, 'Lyman, does it really?' and you said, 'Well, it might, and anyway it don't hurt to say so.'"

There was a silence in the den. On the smoking stand, the bronze Indian gazed out over an ash tray toward some vanished prairie. Lyman could hear, from the kitchen, the clatter of a pot lid and his wife humming "Onward, Christian Soldiers" with the particular ferocity she reserved for occasions of domestic crisis.

"That's—that's entirely different," said Lyman.

"Why?"

It is a question that has undone philosophers. Lyman Hoag, who had read *Personality Plus* twice and had attended a three-evening course in Dynamic Salesmanship at the Y.M.C.A., had no more defense against it than had Socrates. He cleared his throat. He took off his spectacles and polished them on his handkerchief and put them on again.

"Why, because—well, because it is, that's why. Because in business a fella's—well, a fella's expected to—now look here, Delbert. When I tell a man my furnace is the best on the market, why, that's my honest opinion. See? I *believe* it's the best on the market. I've studied the proposition. That isn't lying. That's just—that's enthusiasm. That's what we call selling talk. Everybody understands that. The customer understands it. He knows I'm going to talk up my goods. That's just good business. That's the American way. But when you tell Mrs. Gurney that jam comes from Scotland, why, you know darn well—you know very well it don't come from Scotland. You see the difference?"

Delbert studied the hooked rug. "Does the furnace save half?"

"Well, now, that depends. That depends on a lot of things. That depends on the house, and the insulation, and the kind of coal, and how a man fires it. Some houses, why, I wouldn't be surprised if it saved more than half."

"Mrs. Sloat's rheumatism might've got better," said Delbert. "It depends."

Lyman Hoag rose from the Morris chair. He felt, obscurely, that he was losing the argument, and like all men who feel they are losing an argument, he determined to win it by changing the subject to authority.

"That's enough! That'll be about enough out of you, young man! I'm not going to stand here and be talked back to by any seven-year-old kid. When I tell you a thing's wrong, it's wrong, and that's all there is to it. You hear me?"

"Yes, sir."

"When I was your age, if I'd talked back to my dad like that, you know what he'd have done? He'd have taken me out to the woodshed, that's what he'd have done, and he'd have taken the strap to me, and I wouldn't have sat down for a week."

He remembered the woodshed in Mason Falls, the smell of kindling and harness oil, the hard brown hand of his father, the strap that hung on a nail beside the door and was called, with frontier humor, "Doctor Birch." He remembered how he had hated his father, for an hour, with a pure and murderous hatred, and how afterward he had gone and sat by the creek and planned to run away and join the circus. He looked at his son, small in the reindeer sweater, one stocking down, waiting with that grave and terrible patience; and he found that he did not in the least want to take Delbert to a woodshed, even if Glenwood Terrace had possessed such an institution, which it did not, the Development Company having specified that all outbuildings conform to the Dutch Colonial style.

("Darn it, kid's not a bad kid. Just smart. Too smart for his own good. Gets it from me, I guess.")

The thought warmed him, and he was instantly ashamed of its warmth.

"Now, I'm not going to lick you," he announced, with the air of a judge commuting a sentence. "Not this time. But you're going to be punished, and you're going to be punished good. First off, you're going to take that dollar and five cents and you're going to march right straight over to Mrs. Gurney's and Mrs. Sloat's and that lady with the Peke, and you're going to give every cent of it back, and you're going to tell 'em you're sorry, and you're going to tell 'em the truth. Understand?"

Delbert's face, for the first time, altered. "All of it?"

"Every red cent."

"But I spent fifteen cents for the crayons. At Kessler's."

"Then you'll pay it out of your bank. And second, there's no picture show for you Saturday. You can just sit home."

This, at last, struck through. For it was known throughout Glenwood Terrace that the Bijou was showing, that Saturday afternoon, a Western of unparalleled merit, in which a cowboy named Thunder Jack leaped from a cliff onto a moving train; and every boy between six and twelve had been discussing it for a week with the reverence of theologians. Delbert's lower lip began to tremble. His grave, considering eyes filled. He did not cry aloud. He stood upon the hooked rug and wept in silence, the tears running down past his round nose, which was so precisely the shape of his father's nose, and dropping onto the reindeer.

Lyman Hoag was a man who could refuse a loan to a widow, could foreclose on a mortgage when foreclosure was sound business, could speak at the Hiawatha Lodge against the closed shop with a vehemence that brought the brothers to their feet. He could not watch his son cry. He shifted from foot to foot. He coughed. He looked at the tarpon.

"Well, now," he said. "Well, now, that's all right. Now, don't take on. You'll see Thunder Jack some other time. They'll bring it back. They always bring 'em back. Here—here, take my handkerchief. Blow. That's the boy." He knelt, with some difficulty and a slight cracking of the knees, and put his arm around the small heaving shoulders. "You just remember. Honesty is the best policy. You remember that, and you'll never go wrong. That's what built this country. Honesty and—and hustle. Both of 'em. But honesty first."

"Yes, sir," said Delbert, into the handkerchief.

"All right. Now you go wash your face, and after supper I'll walk over with you to Mrs. Gurney's, so's you won't have to go alone."

Delbert went. Lyman sat down again in the Morris chair. His cigar had gone out, and he did not light it.

At supper, which was pot roast with browned potatoes and a lettuce salad with Thousand Island dressing out of a bottle, Delbert was subdued and Edna was gracious, in the manner of a woman whose husband has for once done what she asked. Lyman discoursed upon the Coolidge administration, upon a fellow at the Lodge who claimed to have gotten twenty-two miles to the gallon out of a Hupmobile, and upon the outrageous price of good cigars. Only when Delbert had been excused, and could be heard upstairs breaking open his tin savings bank with a screwdriver, did Edna lean across the table.

"What did he say, Lyman? How did you get him to see it?"

"Oh, I just talked to him. Man to man. Explained it to him." He helped himself to a second piece of lemon pie. "You know, Edna, that kid's got a real head for business. Four jars and a dollar five. Overhead fifteen cents. That's ninety cents clear, not counting the jam. Darn good margin."

"Lyman Hoag!"

"Well, I'm not saying it was right. I told him it wasn't right. I gave it to him good. I'm just saying—you got to admit he's got the instinct. You got to admit that."

"I don't have to admit anything of the kind," said Edna, and she rose and began to clear the plates, humming "Onward, Christian Soldiers" again, though now with somewhat less ferocity.

That night, when the house was dark and the radiators had ceased their clanking, Lyman Hoag lay awake beside his sleeping wife and listened to the wind in the bare elms of Glenwood Terrace. He thought about Thunder Jack and the moving train. He thought about the woodshed in Mason Falls. And he thought, with a persistence that annoyed him extremely, about Mr. Schwengel, the retired harness-maker, who would be firing his new Thermo-Glo Pipeless Furnace all the rest of the winter and adding up his coal bills at the end of every month, a careful, slow old man with a stub of pencil, waiting to see whether they came out to half.

The attendant said, “Naw, you can’t see any of the prisoners till three-thirty—visiting-hour.” It was three. For half an hour Babbitt sat looking at a calendar and a clock on a whitewashed wall. The chair was hard and mean and creaky. People went through the office and, he thought, stared at him. He felt a belligerent defiance which broke into a wincing fear of this machine which was grinding Paul—Paul— Exactly at half-past three he sent in his name. The attendant returned with “Riesling says he don’t want to see you.”

“You’re crazy! You didn’t give him my name! Tell him it’s George wants to see him, George Babbitt.”

“Yuh, I told him, all right, all right! He said he didn’t want to see you.”

“Then take me in anyway.”

“Nothing doing. If you ain’t his lawyer, if he don’t want to see you, that’s all there is to it.”

“But, my God— Say, let me see the warden.”

“He’s busy. Come on, now, you—” Babbitt reared over him. The attendant hastily changed to a coaxing “You can come back and try to-morrow. Mr. Lucas Prout, the mayor. He bribed the mayor’s doorman with a dollar; he was instantly inside, demanding, “You remember me, Mr. Prout? Babbitt—vice-president of the Boosters—campaigned for you? Say, have you heard about poor Riesling? Well, I want an order on the warden or whatever you call um of the City Prison to take me back and see him. Good. Thanks.” In fifteen minutes he was pounding down the prison corridor to a cage where Paul Riesling sat on a cot, twisted like an old beggar, legs crossed, arms in a knot, biting at his clenched fist. Paul looked up blankly as the keeper unlocked the cell, admitted Babbitt, and left them together. He spoke slowly: “Go on! I hope it won’t leave her skin all scarred.
