The rain had begun at four o'clock, and by six it had settled into that steady, monotonous, interminable downpour that comes up out of the Pacific in the late months of the year and hangs over the city for days together, drenching the hills, filling the gutters, beating upon the tin awnings of Folsom Street with a sound like the rattle of shot in a pan. From the bay, very far off, came at intervals the hoarse, lowing note of the fog-horn at Lime Point, a long, melancholy cry, the voice of some great beast lost in the gray.

In the rooms over Brannigan's harness shop, at the corner where the street-car turned, the lamp was lit. It stood upon the table in the middle of the sitting-room, a big lamp with a globe of ground glass painted with roses, and the light of it fell upon the red cloth, upon the plates that had not yet been cleared away, upon the half loaf, the dish of cold potatoes, the pitcher of beer with the foam gone flat in it. It fell, too, upon the hands of Anton Kranich, who sat with his elbows upon the table, his chin sunk into the hollow of his palms, staring at nothing.

They were enormous hands, red and thick-fingered, the knuckles split and seamed from the reins and from the cold. Kranich drove a dray for the Eureka Brewery, and for eleven years he had handled the great kegs, rolling them, lifting them, swinging them down from the tail-board to the sidewalk with a heave of his huge back, so that his whole body had grown into the shape of the work. He was a German of the second generation, born in Stockton, a great, blond, slow-moving fellow, heavy in the shoulders, heavy in the jaw, with a mane of coarse yellow hair that grew low upon his forehead, and small, pale blue eyes that blinked when he was perplexed. He was perplexed now. He was more than that. For the first time in his life he was possessed by an idea, and the idea was too large for him. It filled him; it pressed against the walls of his dull, honest brain like a thing alive; it would not let him rest.

His wife, Lida, was at the sink in the corner, washing the cups. She was a little woman, very neat, very trim, with a quantity of smooth black hair done up close to her head, and a small, pale, pretty face in which the mouth was pressed always a little too tightly together. She had been a shop-girl at the Emporium before her marriage, and she had kept something of the shop-girl's alertness, her quickness of hand, her sharp eye for a bargain. She moved briskly, making no unnecessary motion, wiping each cup and setting it upon its hook in a row, the handles all turned the same way.

Neither spoke. The clock upon the mantel, a cheap nickel clock that Lida had bought at a sale, ticked loudly, with a hurried, nervous beat. Outside, the rain drove against the window in gusts. Below, in the shop, Brannigan was moving about, and the smell of new leather, of oil and wax and harness-blacking, came up through the cracks of the floor.

At length Kranich stirred. He drew a long breath that lifted his great chest, and let it go again.

"Lida," he said.

"Well?"

"I seen Hansen again to-day. Down to the wharf."

She did not answer. She hung up the last cup and began to wipe the plates, holding each one up to the light to see that it was clean.

"He's going," continued Kranich. "Him and Pete Ekdahl and the two Morrisons. They got their tickets already. On the *Excelsior*. She sails the eighteenth. That's two weeks."

"Is that so?" said Lida.

"They want I should go with 'em."

The plate in Lida's hands paused for an instant, then went on again, round and round, under the dish-towel.

"Yes," she said, "I know they do. You told me that last night, and the night before that, and Thursday. I guess I know it by now."

Kranich passed one hand over his face, slowly, from the forehead down to the chin.

"But, Lida, you ain't ever said—you ain't ever said yes or no."

"Haven't I?" She set the plate down upon the shelf with a little click. "Well, I'll say it now, then. No."

He looked at her, blinking, his heavy jaw hanging a little open. It was as though he had expected the answer and yet had not believed in it.

"Ah, now, Lida, listen here—"

"I've listened. I've done nothing but listen for a week. Klondike, Klondike, Klondike. I'm sick to death of hearing about it."

She came over to the table and began to gather up the remaining dishes, reaching across him with quick, short movements, not looking at him. He watched her stupidly, his great hands lying open upon the cloth.

"There's gold up there," he said. "There's gold all over the ground up there. Hansen's cousin, he wrote him. He wrote him a letter. He says they're taking it out of the creeks in pans—in pans, Lida—a hundred dollars in a pan sometimes. He says a man that's strong, a man that can work—" He clenched one of his fists and looked at it, as though it were some tool whose use he had just discovered. "I can work. I guess there ain't a man on the wharf can lift what I can. Up there, it's the strong ones that get it. It ain't like down here, where it's all clerks and bosses and the fellow with the pull. Up there it's just the ground and a man and his two hands."

"And the cold," said Lida. "And the scurvy. And the snow fifty feet deep, and nothing to eat but beans, and men dying like flies, and the rest of 'em coming back without a cent. I read the papers, too, Anton Kranich."

"The papers!" he exclaimed. "What do they know, the papers? They write anything."

"They wrote about the gold, too, didn't they? That's where you got it from, and Hansen got it from. You believe that part of it, I notice."

He was silent, groping for an answer, and finding none. He was no match for her in words; he never had been. Her tongue was quick and sharp, and his was slow, and when they disputed she darted all about him, like a terrier about a great dray-horse, and he could only stand and turn his head this way and that, bewildered, unable to strike back.

Lida carried the dishes to the sink. Then she came back, took the lamp from the table, and set it on the mantel beside the clock, and took off the red cloth and folded it, and shook the crumbs into her hand. The light, removed from the table, threw the shadow of Kranich's huge head and shoulders enormous upon the opposite wall, where it hung motionless above the sofa, a vast, distorted silhouette.

"How much would it cost?" she said suddenly, standing before him with the folded cloth in her hands.

He looked up quickly, a gleam of hope in his little eyes.

"Well, there's the ticket. That's a hundred and twenty, steerage. And then the outfit. Hansen says you got to have an outfit—a year's grub, and blankets, and a stove, and picks and that, and a sled. He figures it'll run to three hundred, maybe three-fifty, with everything."

"Four hundred and seventy dollars," said Lida. "That's what it comes to, at the least. Four hundred and seventy."

"Well, about that."

"And where's it coming from?"

Kranich did not answer. He looked down at the table. The clock ticked. Down below, Brannigan had begun to hammer at something, a sharp, regular tapping, like a woodpecker in a tree.

"Where's it coming from?" repeated Lida. Her voice had risen a little. "Go on, say it. I know what you're thinking. I've known it all along. Say it out."

"There's the money in the bank," said Kranich, without raising his eyes.

There it was. It had been spoken. It lay there between them, upon the bare table, like a thing that could be seen.

The money in the bank. It was five hundred and sixty-two dollars, in the Hibernia, on Market Street, and Lida kept the little book that showed it, the gray paper book with the dates and the figures written in by the clerk in violet ink. She kept it in the top drawer of the bureau in the bedroom, under her handkerchiefs, wrapped in a piece of oiled silk against the damp. Every Saturday afternoon, when Kranich brought home his wages, she took out of them what was needed for the rent and the butcher and the grocer, and the rest—sometimes it was two dollars, sometimes it was four, once, when Kranich had done extra work at the Fourth of July, it had been nine—the rest she took down to the Hibernia herself on Monday morning, and stood in line at the window, and watched the clerk write it into the book. Then she would come home and sit down at the bureau and add it all up again with a pencil on the back of an envelope, to be sure that the clerk had made no mistake. He never had. Still she added it.

It was six years' saving, that money. It was every pair of shoes she had mended instead of buying new; it was every Sunday they had not gone to the Chutes; it was the theatre they had not seen, the dress she had not bought, the carpet she still meant to have for the sitting-room some day. It was the little house out in the Mission, with a bit of yard in front, that she meant to buy when the sum should reach a thousand. It was the future. It was safety. It was the one solid, tangible, certain thing in all that great, shifting, uncertain world of the city, where men lost their places overnight, and fell sick, and were hurt at their work and carried home on a shutter, and their widows took in washing. Lida had seen it. She had grown up among it. She knew.

And now he wanted it. He wanted to take it all, every cent of it, and carry it off with him to that frozen, howling, God-forsaken country at the top of the world, and throw it away there, into the snow.

"No," she said. Her lips were white. "No. No. You don't touch that money. Not one cent of it. Not one."

"Lida—"

"It's mine!" she cried. "I saved it. Who saved it? Did you? You'd have spent it on beer and pinochle and treating the boys at Schuetzen Park. I saved it. I went without for it. Look at this dress. I've had it three years. Three years! And you want to take it—you want to take it and—" Her voice broke; she caught her breath. "No. I tell you, no!"

Kranich got slowly to his feet. He was so tall that his head came close to the gas-fixture in the middle of the ceiling, the one they never lit because the gas cost more than oil, and he had to stoop a little beneath it. He stood there, swaying slightly, his great arms hanging. His face was red. Something was stirring in him, something heavy and dull and slow that had lain asleep for a long while, and was now turning over, beginning to awake.

"It ain't yours," he said thickly. "It's mine, too. I earned it. I earned every cent of it. Who rolls the kegs, eleven hours a day, in the rain, in the fog? Who gets up at four o'clock? Is it you? I earned it. It's mine as much as yours."

"You'd never have had it, only for me."

"I'd have had it. I'd have—" He stopped, and his fist came down upon the table, not hard, but the lamp on the mantel trembled and the clock jumped. "I want to go," he said. "I want to go up there. I ain't going to drive a dray all my life. Eleven years I been driving that dray. Eleven years. Every day the same. Up Folsom, down Third, out to the Potrero, back again. The same horses, the same kegs, the same saloons. I'm thirty-four years old, Lida. Pretty soon I'll be forty, and then fifty, and I'll still be driving that dray, and then I'll get too old and they'll put some young fellow in my place, and that'll be all. That's all there'll ever be. I want—I want—"

He could not say what he wanted. He stood there, his great chest heaving, his little eyes fixed upon her, struggling with it, and the words would not come. It was something vast and vague, something that had come to him upon the wharf, among the crowds that swarmed about the steamers loading for the North, among the shouting and the hurry and the piles of outfits stacked high on the planking, and the men—young men, old men, clerks and teamsters and bankrupt merchants and boys run away from school—all with that same look in their faces, that same light in their eyes, the look of men who see something a long way off. It was the call of the gold, the old, savage, primitive lust of the race for the yellow metal, the lust that had drawn his grandfathers' grandfathers out of the forests of the North to sack the cities of the South, the lust that had brought men round the Horn in '49 to die on the American River; it was this that had laid hold of him now, of him, Anton Kranich, the brewery driver, sober, steady, dull-witted, who had never in his life before so much as bet a dollar on a horse. It was stronger than he. It was a thing that did not reason. It only wanted.

"Up there," he muttered, "up there—"

Lida faced him. She was not afraid of him. She had never been afraid of him. She was so small beside him that her head came hardly above his breast; she could have been crushed by one sweep of that huge arm. But she stood her ground, her small hands clenched upon the folded tablecloth, her face very white, her eyes very bright and hard.

"And what about me?" she said. "Did you think of that? What's to become of me, while you're up there digging gold out of the snow? Am I to sit here and starve? Who's to pay the rent? Am I to go back behind the counter at the Emporium, at six dollars a week, and wait for you? Wait for a letter that'll never come? And then one day Hansen's cousin writes and says you died of the scurvy, or froze, or fell through the ice, and they buried you up there in a hole in the ground? Is that what you want? Is that it?"

"I'd send for you," he said. "When I'd struck it, I'd send for you, or come back. We'd be rich, Lida. We'd have a house—a big house, out on the Western Addition, with a bay-window. You'd have a hired girl. You'd have silk dresses. You wouldn't have to—"

"I don't want a big house! I don't want a hired girl!" Her voice was shrill now; it rang out in the little room. "I want what we've got. I want what's in the bank, that's safe, that nobody can take away. I want to know where the next month's rent is coming from. That's what I want. Oh, you fool! You big, stupid fool! Can't you see? Can't you see they'll take it all, the steamship people and the outfitters and the saloon-keepers up there, and you'll come back with nothing, nothing, nothing, and we'll have to start all over again, and we're not young any more—"

She stopped. She was trembling all over. The tears had come into her eyes in spite of her, and she turned her head sharply away so that he should not see them.

Kranich stared at her. The red was going slowly out of his face. Something in her voice, in that sharp, high note of fear under all the anger, had reached him; it had gone down through the thickness and the dullness of him and touched him somewhere.

The fog-horn sounded from the bay, long and low and mournful. The rain drummed upon the window. Below, Brannigan's hammer had stopped.

"I wouldn't take it all," said Kranich at last, slowly. "I'd leave you some. I'd leave you—a hundred."

Lida turned upon him in a fury.

"A hundred! A hundred dollars! Out of five hundred and sixty-two! And you'd take the rest, and you'd go off, and you'd leave me a hundred! Oh, you're generous. You're so generous, Anton Kranich. A hundred!"

She flung the tablecloth down upon the sofa and went past him into the bedroom, and he heard her pull open the top drawer of the bureau. For an instant a dreadful thought came into his slow mind—that she would get the bank-book, and tear it up, or burn it in the stove, as if that would destroy the money. But she only stood there before the open drawer, her two hands resting upon the edge of it, her head bent, and did not move. Through the doorway he could see her back, the narrow shoulders under the old brown dress, shaking a little.

He went and stood in the doorway, filling it, his head bent beneath the lintel.

"Lida," he said.

She did not turn round.

"Lida, listen here. I ain't going to take it if you don't want."

There was a long silence. The nickel clock ticked in the other room, loud and fast and nervous, like a little heart.

"You will," she said, without looking at him. Her voice was low and flat now, all the shrillness gone out of it. "You say that now. But you'll go down to the wharf to-morrow and see Hansen and the rest of them, and you'll come back, and it'll all start over again. To-morrow, and the next day, and the next. Until the eighteenth. And then you'll take it. I know you. I know you better than you know yourself."

"No, I won't."

"Yes, you will. You can't help it. It's got hold of you."

He did not answer. He stood in the doorway, his great hands hanging, and looked at her bent head, at the smooth black hair, at the little hands gripping the edge of the drawer; and he knew that she was right. He knew it in that dim, groping fashion in which he knew most things, without words, without reasons, the way an animal knows the weather. It had got hold of him. He had put it away from him a moment ago, out of pity for her, out of the old, slow, dumb affection he had for her, which was a real thing in him, as real as the strength of his arms. But it was there still. He could feel it, even now, crouching down underneath, waiting, patient, enormous. To-morrow he would go down to the wharf. He would see the *Excelsior* lying at her moorings, with the smoke coming from her funnel and the outfits piled upon her decks, and he would hear the men shouting, and see the light in their faces; and Hansen would clap him upon the shoulder and say, "Well, Tony, you coming?"—and then—

He turned away from the doorway and went back into the sitting-room, and sat down again at the bare table, and put his chin into his hands.

Up there, up there in the North, the snow was falling over the creeks. He could see it. He had never seen snow in his life, save once, far off, on the summits of the Sierra from the Stockton levee when he was a boy; but he could see it now, white and endless, over the gulches and the frozen rivers and the black spruce forests, and under the snow, under the frozen gravel, deep down, the gold. The gold, lying there in the dark, in the cold, heavy and yellow, waiting for the man who should be strong enough to dig it out. Waiting for him.

In the bedroom, Lida closed the drawer softly. Then she opened it again, and he heard the faint crackle of the oiled silk as she unfolded it. She was looking at the little gray book. She was adding up the figures once more, on the back of an envelope, with a pencil, by the light that came in through the doorway—five hundred and sixty-two dollars—as if, by adding them often enough, she could make them safe.

The clock ticked. The rain fell. Far out upon the bay, the fog-horn lowed again, long and hoarse and desolate, like a great beast calling in the dark.

It was a Saturday, toward six o'clock in the evening, when Ludwig Oberholtz, driver of the third wagon of the Mission Brewery, came off his route and turned his horses into the yard behind Folsom Street. He was a huge fellow, slow of thought and slow of movement, with enormous red hands and a neck that sat squarely upon his shoulders like the trunk of a tree upon its roots. His hair was the color of tow, cropped close to a round skull. His jaw was heavy, salient, the jaw of the men of his family, who had for generations back been carters and draymen and brewers in the little towns along the Main. He had the strength of a draught animal and something of its patience. He unhitched his team, a pair of gray Percherons as ponderous as himself, rubbed them down with a twist of straw, and stood for a long time in the warm, ammoniac dusk of the stable, listening to them crunch their oats. It was a sound he loved. It filled him with a vast and stupid contentment.

All that day he had thought of nothing but the letter. It had come on Thursday, addressed in a sprawling, uncertain hand to "Ludwig Oberholtz, Esq., care Mission Brewery, San Francisco, Cal.," and it had been brought to him by the timekeeper, who held it out between two fingers as though it were a curiosity. Ludwig had turned it over and over in his thick fingers before opening it, and had read it three times, his lips moving, at the end of the loading platform. It was from his cousin Carl, the son of his father's brother, whom he had not seen in eleven years. Carl was coming down from Seattle on the steamer Umatilla. He would be in the city Saturday. He would come round to the brewery. "We will have a glass together like old times," the letter said.

Like old times. Ludwig had repeated the phrase to himself all day long, as his wagon jolted over the cobbles of Mission Street and down along the water front, where he left his kegs at the saloons that catered to the stevedores and the deep-water men. Like old times. He saw again the two of them, boys of eighteen and nineteen, newly come over in the steerage of a Hamburg liner, their bundles on their backs, standing in the roar and confusion of Castle Garden; he saw the long, dirty train westward, the two of them sleeping upright on the wooden seats, sharing a sausage and a loaf of black bread; he saw the first lodging house on Pacific Street, the first jobs, the Sunday afternoons at the Schuetzen Park across the bay, the beer, the band, the girls in white dresses. Then Carl had gone north, to the logging camps, to the fisheries, to God knew where. There had been a postal card from Portland, another from a place called Juneau. After that nothing. Eleven years. Ludwig had married. He had a flat on Natoma Street and a wife and a canary. He had grown heavier. He had been made driver of the third wagon.

When he came out of the stable into the yard, a man was standing by the gate, his hands in his pockets, looking at the brewery chimney.

Ludwig stopped. He did not at once recognize him. The man was tall, but not so tall as Ludwig, and lean, almost gaunt, with a face burned to the color of saddle leather. He wore a suit of ready-made clothes, new and too large for him, and a soft hat pushed back from his forehead. A heavy watch chain of nugget gold looped across his vest. Then the man turned, and Ludwig saw the jaw, the Oberholtz jaw, square and protruding, and the pale, wide-set eyes, and he knew him.

"Carl," he said. He said it slowly, as though uncertain of the word.

"Hello, Lute," said the other.

They shook hands. They stood there in the yard, among the empty kegs and the smell of malt, shaking hands for a long time, not knowing what to say, grinning at each other with a kind of foolish embarrassment. Their two hands, locked together, were the same hands, huge, square, with blunt fingers and swollen knuckles, the hands of their grandfather, old Johann Oberholtz, who had been known in the village of Kitzingen for his ability to lift a full hogshead upon his knee.

"Well, well," said Ludwig at length. "Well, well, well."

"You got fat, Lute," said Carl.

"Sure," said Ludwig, delighted. "Sure, I got fat. You got thin. Ach, you got thin like a rail. What they feed you up there, hey? Fish, I bet."

"Fish and beans," said Carl. "Beans and fish."

They both laughed immoderately, as though this were a tremendous joke.

They went to Schroeder's, on the corner of Folsom and Sixth, where Ludwig was accustomed to take his glass of an evening before going home to supper. It was a long, low room, full of the smell of beer and sawdust and frying sausage. Along one wall ran the bar, of polished redwood, with a brass rail at the foot; behind it, a great mirror, flyspecked, reflected the rows of glasses and the colored bottles and the chromo lithograph of a stag at bay that hung opposite. At the back were tables, round, with marble tops, and a nickel-in-the-slot music box that played "Die Wacht am Rhein" and "Sweet Rosie O'Grady." Old Schroeder himself, fat and bald, with a white apron tied under his armpits, drew the beer. He drew it slowly, lovingly, scraping the foam from the top of the glass with an ivory spatula.

Ludwig ordered two steins. They sat at one of the round tables at the back. Carl drank his beer at a single draught, tilting back his head, his throat working, and set the empty stein down upon the marble with a little crash.

"Gott!" he said. "That's beer. Up there you don't get beer like that. You get whiskey. Rotten whiskey, made out of God knows what. Coal oil and red pepper."

Ludwig ordered two more. He was enormously pleased. It seemed to him that his cousin's praise of the beer was a compliment to himself, to the Mission Brewery, to the third wagon. He watched Carl drink the second stein with the same deep satisfaction with which he had watched his horses eat their oats.

"Where you been, Carl? Eleven years. You don't write. Nothing."

Carl wiped the foam from his mustache with the back of his hand.

"Everywhere," he said. "All over. Up the coast. Alaska. The Yukon country. I was on the Stewart River two winters. Forty below. You spit and it froze before it hit the ground. I seen men freeze. I seen a man freeze in his blankets, a big Swede, strong like you, Lute. In the morning he was like a log."

He told of it at length, in a flat, unemotional voice, his pale eyes fixed upon the empty stein. He told of the cold, of the long dark, of the scurvy, of the dogs that died in the traces and were eaten by the other dogs; he told of the creeks with their names, Bonanza and Eldorado and Hunker, and of the gravel thawed with fires and washed in the spring when the water came. He had made a stake, a good stake, and lost it at faro in Dawson in a single night. He had made another, smaller, and had kept it. He did not say how much. He touched the nugget chain on his vest, and Ludwig's eyes followed his hand.

Ludwig listened with his mouth a little open. The words passed over him like a wind. The cold, the gold, the faro bank—he could not imagine them. They were outside his world, which was bounded by the brewery and the water front and the flat on Natoma Street. But he was impressed. He was immensely impressed. Carl had become a great man. He had been to the edge of the world.

"Ach," he said, wagging his head. "Ach, ach. Forty below. And me, I drive the wagon."

"You got a good job," said Carl.

"Sure. Sure, I got a good job. Driver third wagon. Eighteen dollars. Next year maybe second wagon."

"That's good, Lute."

"Sure, that's good."

There was a silence. The music box, set going by a stevedore at the bar, began to play "Die Wacht am Rhein." Both men listened, their heads a little on one side, their great hands spread upon the marble. The tune stirred in them something old and obscure, something that lay beneath memory, a dim, racial recollection of beer gardens and linden trees and the slow, broad river. Ludwig hummed with it, deep in his throat, like the buzzing of a bee.

"You remember," he said suddenly, "you remember the time we fight the Irishman on Pacific Street? The big Irishman with the red whiskers?"

Carl's face broke into a slow grin.

"Sure I remember."

"He say something about the Dutch. And you hit him. And then he hit you. And then I come and I pick him up—so—and I throw him through the window of the Chinaman's laundry."

"And the cop came."

"And the cop came. And we run. Ach, how we run! All the way to the water front. You remember that?"

"I remember."

They laughed again, the same immoderate laughter, rocking in their chairs, slapping the marble with their palms. The stevedores at the bar turned to look at them. Old Schroeder, polishing a glass, smiled indulgently. Here were two of his own people, Dutchmen, square-heads, enjoying themselves.

"You remember the Schuetzen Park?" said Ludwig. "Every Sunday we go. You remember?"

"Sure."

"You remember the dancing? You remember the girls?"

Carl's grin faded a little.

"I remember," he said.

Ludwig did not notice. He was swept along upon the tide of his recollection. He remembered the boat across the bay, crowded with families, the fathers in their Sunday broadcloth, the mothers with their baskets of lunch, the children in starched pinafores; he remembered the band in the pavilion, the brass horns flashing in the sun; he remembered the shooting gallery and the bowling alley and the long tables under the trees, loaded with sausages and potato salad and rye bread and pickled herring. And he remembered a girl in a white dress with a blue sash, a plump girl, with yellow braids wound about her head and a face as round and pink as a peony.

"You come to supper," he said abruptly. "You come home with me. Minna, she cook. You remember Minna? Minna Hartwig?"

Carl was silent for a moment. He turned the empty stein round and round upon the marble.

"Sure," he said. "Sure, I remember Minna."

---

The flat on Natoma Street was on the second floor of a narrow wooden house, painted drab, with a bay window that overlooked the street. Below was a delicatessen, and the hallway was always full of the smell of sauerkraut and smoked fish. Ludwig mounted the stairs heavily, his cousin behind him, the steps creaking and groaning beneath their combined weight.

Minna met them at the door. She was a big woman now, deep-bosomed, broad of hip, her yellow braids still wound about her head, but thinner, and with a gray thread in them here and there. Her face was still round and pink. She wore a calico wrapper and an apron, and her sleeves were rolled to the elbow, showing her thick, white forearms, floured to the wrist. She had been told of the visit; she had been cooking since noon.

"So," she said. "So this is Carl."

She held out her hand, wiping the flour from it upon her apron. Carl took it. For an instant the two looked at each other, and something passed between them, something very brief and very obscure, a flicker, a recollection, gone as soon as it had come. Ludwig, hanging his hat upon the peg in the hall, saw nothing.

"You look good, Minna," said Carl.

"Ach, I get old," she said, and laughed, and turned back into the kitchen.

The supper was spread upon the table in the little dining room, under the hanging lamp with its shade of painted glass. There was a pot roast, enormous, swimming in brown gravy, with potato dumplings the size of a man's fist; there was red cabbage cooked with vinegar and apples; there was a dish of pickled beets, another of cucumbers in sour cream, a loaf of rye bread, a plate of sliced liverwurst, a great yellow wedge of cheese. There was beer in a pitcher, brought up in a tin pail from the saloon at the corner. On the sideboard waited a coffee cake, glazed with sugar and studded with raisins.

They fell to eating. They ate as the men of their race had always eaten, with a solemn, absorbed voracity, their heads bent low over their plates, their elbows wide, their jaws working with a slow and rhythmic power. They did not talk. Eating was not an occasion for talk. The only sounds were the clink of knives and forks, the sucking in of gravy, the gurgle of beer poured from the pitcher. Ludwig ate enormously; he had three helpings of the pot roast, five of the dumplings. He mopped his plate with bread. His face grew red and shone with perspiration. Carl ate almost as much. After eleven years of beans and fish, of bacon and flapjacks, of the frozen, monotonous rations of the camps, the food was like a revelation to him. He ate with a kind of ferocity, as though fearing it would be taken from him.

Minna did not sit. She moved back and forth between the kitchen and the table, bringing more gravy, more bread, refilling the pitcher. She watched the two men eat with an expression of placid satisfaction, the pride of a woman whose cooking is appreciated. Once, as she leaned over Carl to set down the dish of cabbage, her arm brushed his shoulder. He did not look up.

In the window, in a little gilt cage, the canary hopped from perch to perch and trilled.

At last it was over. Ludwig pushed back his chair and loosened his belt and sighed, a long, deep sigh of repletion. Minna brought the coffee cake and the coffee, in big cups with gilt rims that had been a wedding present. Ludwig lit his pipe, a porcelain pipe with a long cherry stem and a bowl painted with a picture of a hunter and his dog. Carl rolled a cigarette. The room filled with smoke. The lamp hissed softly.

"Carl, he been in Alaska," said Ludwig to his wife. "Forty below. He see a man freeze stiff like a log."

"So?" said Minna.

"He make a stake. Gold." Ludwig pointed with his pipestem at the nugget chain. "You see that, Minna? That's gold from Alaska."

Minna looked at the chain. Then she looked at Carl's face, burned and lean and hollow under the cheekbones, the face of a man who has been hungry and cold and alone for a very long time.

"It's a long time you been gone, Carl," she said.

"Eleven years."

"Eleven years," she repeated. "Ja. It's a long time."

There was a silence. Ludwig sucked at his pipe. He looked from his wife to his cousin and back again, and a slow, vague uneasiness began to stir somewhere at the bottom of his mind. He could not have said what it was. It was not a thought; it was something lower than thought, something instinctive and animal, the uneasiness of the bull that scents another bull upon the wind. He remembered, all at once and for no reason, the Schuetzen Park, the band, the girl in the white dress with the blue sash. He remembered that it had been Carl who had danced with her first. He remembered that it had been Carl who had walked with her along the paths under the trees, while he, Ludwig, had bowled ninepins with the men. He remembered that it was only after Carl had gone north that he had begun to call upon her on Sunday evenings, sitting stiff and silent in her mother's parlor, his hat upon his knees.

He had not thought of these things in eleven years. Now they rose up in him, dim and confused, and he did not know what to do with them. His great jaw set. His thick fingers closed upon the bowl of the porcelain pipe until the knuckles whitened. The blood came into his face.

Carl was looking at him across the table. The two men regarded each other in silence. It was a strange moment. They were alike, these two, alike in the square skulls and the pale eyes, alike in the protruding jaws and the enormous hands, and in each of them, at that instant, something old and savage lifted its head and looked out—the instinct of the male, the instinct of possession, the blind, primeval jealousy that had come down to them through generations of carters and brewers and peasants, from forgotten ancestors who had fought with clubs in the forests of Germany for their women and their meat.

Then Carl laughed. He leaned back in his chair and laughed, and reached across the table and struck his cousin upon the shoulder with his open palm, a blow that would have staggered a smaller man.

"You got a good wife, Lute," he said. "You got a good home. Good beer. Good supper. Gott! I never eat a supper like that. You're a lucky man."

Ludwig stared at him. Slowly the blood went down out of his face. Slowly his fingers relaxed upon the pipe. The thing that had lifted its head sank back again into the depths. He did not understand what had happened, but he felt that he had been praised, and the praise warmed him. He began to grin.

"Sure," he said. "Sure, I'm lucky. Minna, she's a good cook. Hey, Minna?"

Minna, who had been standing very still by the sideboard, turned away and began to clear the table.

"Ach, go on," she said.

---

It was past eleven when Carl rose to go. He had a room at a hotel on Kearny Street. He was going east in a week, he said, to look at some property in the Coeur d'Alene. He did not know when he would be back. Maybe never.

Ludwig went down with him to the street. A fog had come in from the ocean, thick and gray and wet, blotting out the street lamps, so that they hung in the air like blurred moons. From far off came the hoarse, intermittent bellowing of the foghorn at the Golden Gate, and nearer, the clang of a cable car on Mission Street. The delicatessen was dark. The street was empty.

The two men stood upon the sidewalk. Again they shook hands, the two huge hands locking, the hands of old Johann Oberholtz who had lifted the hogshead upon his knee.

"You write sometimes, Carl," said Ludwig. "Hey? You write."

"Sure, Lute. I'll write."

"You come back. We go to the Schuetzen Park. Like old times."

"Like old times," said Carl.

He turned and walked away into the fog. Ludwig watched him go. For a moment he could see the lean figure, the soft hat pushed back, the shoulders a little stooped; then the fog closed over it, and there was nothing but the gray wall of mist and the bellowing of the foghorn and the far-off clang of the cable car.

Ludwig stood there a long time. He was thinking, slowly and with difficulty, as he always thought. Something had happened that evening, something he did not understand. It troubled him, vaguely, the way a half-remembered dream troubles a man in the morning. He tried to lay hold of it, but it eluded him, slipping away from his slow mind as the fog slipped between his fingers.

Then he yawned, a huge yawn that opened his jaw to its fullest extent. He had eaten a great supper. He was full and warm and sleepy. Tomorrow was Sunday. He would sleep late, and Minna would make pancakes, and in the afternoon, perhaps, they would take the boat across the bay.

He turned and went heavily up the creaking stairs. In the dining room Minna had put out the lamp and covered the canary's cage with a square of green baize. She was in the kitchen, washing the dishes. He could hear the clink of the plates and the splash of the water. She did not turn round when he came in. She stood at the sink, her thick white arms in the water to the elbow, her head bent, and she did not speak.

Ludwig did not notice. He went into the bedroom and sat down upon the edge of the bed and pulled off his boots, grunting. In ten minutes he was asleep, flat upon his back, his great chest rising and falling, his breath whistling through his nose, sleeping the deep, dreamless, untroubled sleep of the brute.

In the kitchen the water had grown cold. Minna stood for a long time with her hands in it, looking at nothing, while outside, through the fog, the foghorn bellowed and bellowed, monotonous and inarticulate, like the cry of some huge animal lost in the dark.

It was Sunday, and Hans Oberlin was at home.

All the week long he drove one of the great drays of the Fredericksburg Brewery, sitting high upon the box behind his four Percherons, enormous, dappled brutes, whose hoofs, as large as dinner plates, struck sparks from the cobbles of Second Street and whose harness jingled with brass. From six in the morning till dark he drove, hauling the kegs and the half-barrels to the saloons of the Mission and South of Market, swinging them down from the tail of the dray with a rope and a hook, rolling them across the sidewalks and down the cellar stairs. At noon he ate his lunch from a tin pail upon the box, and drank the two glasses of steam beer the company allowed him, and at night he came home, slow, heavy, smelling of horses and of malt, and ate his supper and went to bed. But on Sunday he was at home, and that was his day.

He lived in three rooms over a harness shop on Natoma Street, a narrow street, given over to small trades and the families of workingmen. There was a bakery on the corner, kept by a Swiss, and opposite that a coal and wood yard, and farther down a Chinese laundry, where all the week the irons thudded and the steam curled out upon the sidewalk. On Sundays the street was quiet. The shops were closed. The children of the neighborhood played upon the doorsteps, and the women leaned from the bay windows, gossiping across the way, their arms upon the sills. From the flat below came always the smell of new leather, and from the bakery, faint and warm, the smell of bread.

Hans was a German, born in a village near Bremen. He was huge, a giant of a man, six feet two in his socks, with a great square head covered with hair that was almost white, so pale a yellow it was. His neck was thick and red as a bull's. His jaw was enormous, salient, and when he chewed his food the muscles stood out upon it like knots in a rope. His hands were the hands of a man who had handled barrels since he was fourteen, immense, red, the knuckles swollen, the palms cased in callous as thick as harness leather. Yet he was not a cruel man. He was slow, he was stupid; he did not read, he did not think. All that lay deep in him slept, and he was content that it should sleep. He loved his beer, his horses, his pipe, and his Sunday afternoons. He loved, too, in his dull, inarticulate way, his wife Minna and his little boy, Otto, who was six.

Of all his possessions the one he valued most was his pipe. It was a meerschaum, a great, curved, dangling affair that hung down nearly to his chest, the bowl carved into the head of a stag, with branching antlers and a little silver lid upon a chain. It had been his father's. It had come with him across the ocean in the bottom of his chest, wrapped in a woolen stocking. For twenty years he had smoked it, and the bowl had colored under his care to a deep, rich brown, like the brown of a chestnut, shading off to cream at the tips of the antlers. He never carried it to work. It lived upon the mantelpiece in the front room, between a china dog and a photograph of Minna's mother, upon a little rack that Hans had made for it himself out of a cigar box. On Sunday afternoons he took it down, and filled it slowly, pressing the tobacco in with his huge thumb, and sat in his chair in the bay window in his shirt-sleeves and his stocking feet, smoking, his eyes half closed, watching the street. This was his pleasure. It was the one hour in the week that was his own.

Upon this particular Sunday he had slept late, and had eaten an enormous dinner, pork and red cabbage and dumplings, and a pudding made of bread, and had drunk a pitcher of beer that Minna had sent Otto to fetch from the corner. Then he had gone into the bedroom and lain down upon the bed, for it was his habit to sleep a little after dinner. He had slept an hour, heavily, his mouth open, breathing loud. When he woke it was three o'clock. The sun was shining in the front windows. He sat up on the edge of the bed, yawning, rubbing his great hands over his face, and thought of his pipe.

He went into the front room. Minna was in the kitchen, washing the dishes; he could hear the rattle of the crockery in the pan. The front room was empty. The sun lay in a broad, yellow square upon the carpet, a carpet of red roses upon a green ground. He went to the mantelpiece.

The pipe was not there.

For a moment Hans stood looking at the rack, not understanding, his mouth a little open. He looked behind the china dog, behind the photograph. He looked upon the floor. Then he saw it. It lay upon the hearth, in the corner, half hidden by the coal scuttle. He stooped and picked it up. The stem was snapped clean across, close to the bowl, and one of the antlers of the stag was broken off.

He stood up slowly, holding the two pieces in his palm, looking at them stupidly. He turned them over. He fitted the broken ends together, and they parted again. He searched upon the hearth for the antler and found it, a little crooked tip of brown, no larger than a grain of wheat. He held it between his thumb and finger, and his huge hand trembled.

Then a slow, dull red began to mount into his face, beginning at his thick neck and creeping upward over his cheeks to the roots of his pale hair. He breathed heavily through his nose. His enormous jaw set itself and protruded.

"Otto," he called.

There was no answer.

"Otto!" His voice filled the little flat. In the kitchen the rattle of the dishes stopped.

"Ach, what is it, Hans?" called Minna.

He did not answer her. He went to the door of the little room off the kitchen where the boy slept, and pushed it open. The room was empty. He went to the back porch. There, in the corner, squeezed between the washtub and the wall, behind the hanging clothes, crouched the little boy, his knees drawn up to his chin, his eyes very wide.

"Come here," said Hans.

The child did not move.

"Come here, I tell you."

Otto got up slowly. He was a small boy for his age, thin, white-faced, with his mother's dark hair and dark eyes, and nothing of his father but the broad forehead and the square, heavy chin. He wore a little jacket of blue flannel that Minna had made for him out of an old skirt, and his stockings were wrinkled about his ankles. He came across the porch, dragging his feet, and stood before his father, his hands behind his back, looking up at him.

Hans held out his open palm, with the pieces of the pipe upon it.

"Who did this?" he said.

The boy looked at the pipe, and then at his father's face, and then down at the floor. He said nothing.

"Who did this? You hear me? Who broke my pipe?"

"I dunno," said Otto.

"You dunno?"

"Maybe the cat," said the boy. His voice was very small. "Maybe the cat knocked it off. I seen the cat up on the mantel this morning."

Hans looked at him. It was a long look. His small, pale-blue eyes, set deep under his shaggy brows, rested upon the child's face, and the child could not meet them. His glance wavered, slid away, came back, slid away again. His lower lip began to tremble. And upon his cheek, across the white skin, there was a little smudge of brown, the brown of meerschaum dust, where he had rubbed his face with his fingers.

Then Hans understood that the boy was lying.

It was this that roused the brute in him. Not the pipe. The pipe was broken, and that was bad, that was very bad; but a pipe was a thing, after all, and things broke. But the lie! The little white face looking up at him and lying, lying to him, Hans Oberlin, who had never told a lie in his life, who could not have told one had he tried, so slow, so plain, so honest was his dull brain. It seemed to him, in some obscure, inarticulate way, that something had been done to him that was worse than the breaking of a hundred pipes. A blind, unreasoning anger rose in him, rose from the very depths of him, from the hidden places where all that was animal in him lay asleep. It surged upward. He felt it mount in his throat like a sickness, felt it tingle in his enormous fists. His face grew darker; the veins stood out upon his forehead. He could have crushed the child as easily as he crushed the empty beer cans in the brewery yard, with one blow of his heel.

He reached out and caught the boy by the shoulder. His fingers closed upon the little blue jacket and upon the thin bone beneath it, and he shook him, once, so that the child's head snapped back and forth and his teeth clicked together.

"The cat!" he cried. "The cat, is it! You lie to me! You stand there and lie to me!"

"Hans!" Minna had come to the kitchen door. She held a dish-cloth in her hand, and her sleeves were rolled to the elbow, and her arms were red and wet. "Hans, what is it? What has he done?"

"Look at that," said Hans, thrusting out his palm toward her. "Look at that. My pipe. My father's pipe. Broke. And he tells me the cat done it."

"Ach, Gott," said Minna, under her breath. She looked at the pipe and then at the boy, and her face grew pale. She knew her husband. She had seen him angry perhaps three times in the eight years of their marriage, and each time it had frightened her. Once in a saloon on Howard Street a teamster had struck one of the Percherons over the head with the butt of a whip, and Hans had gone at him. Minna had not seen it, but she had heard of it afterward from the neighbors. They had taken the teamster to the Receiving Hospital.

"Hans," she said, "he is only a little boy. Hans, don't hurt him."

But Hans did not hear her. He was looking at the child. He still held him by the shoulder, and the boy hung in his grip, limp, his face gone gray with fright, too frightened even to cry. And as Hans looked at him, the anger in him swelled and swelled. His free hand rose slowly. It was open, the great red palm turned outward, hard as a board.

And then, all at once, a strange thing happened.

Hans saw himself. He did not know how it was; he could not have told it. But suddenly he was not in the flat on Natoma Street at all. He was a little boy, in the low, dark kitchen of a farmhouse near Bremen, with the smell of the cows coming in at the door, and the rain dripping from the thatch. He had broken something; he could not remember what—a bowl, a jug. And his father stood over him, his father, as huge as he himself was now, with the same white-yellow hair, the same enormous jaw, the same red, swollen fists. And his father's hand came down. Hans remembered it. He remembered the roar in his ears and the taste of blood in his mouth, and how he had lain upon the stone floor of the kitchen and could not get up. He remembered his mother crying in the corner, with her apron over her head. He had not thought of it in thirty years. And now he saw it all as plainly as though it were happening before his eyes, and the blood in his mouth was as salt as it had been then.

He had hated his father. He knew that now, all at once, with a dull, astonished certainty. He had hated him. And his father had smoked this same pipe, sitting by the fire of an evening, the stag's head bobbing upon his chest; and it was in his father's hand, that day upon the stone floor, that the pipe had been held while the other hand came down.

His own hand stopped in the air.

It hung there a moment, enormous, quivering. The child stared at it, his eyes like the eyes of a rabbit in a trap. Minna stood in the door, her dish-cloth pressed against her mouth. The flat was very still. Outside in the street a boy was crying papers, and his voice came faint and thin through the window: "Chronicle! Ex-amin-er!"

Slowly Hans lowered his hand. He let go of the boy's shoulder. He stood a moment breathing hard, his great chest heaving under his shirt, and the red began little by little to die out of his face, leaving it mottled, blotched with white. He did not understand what had happened to him. He felt only that something had risen up within him, some dark, terrible thing that had come down to him from far away, from his father and from his father's father, from the dark kitchens and the low thatched roofs and the stone floors, and that it had been very near, very near indeed, and that it had gone back again, sullenly, unwillingly, into the depths where it lived. He felt weak, as though he had been lifting barrels all day. His knees shook.

He went back into the front room and sat down heavily in his chair by the window. He still held the pieces of the pipe in his hand. After a moment the boy followed him, slowly, and stood in the doorway. Minna stood behind him, her hand upon his hair.

"Come here, Otto," said Hans.

The boy came, and stood before him.

For a long time Hans did not speak. He was not a man of words. He sat looking down at the broken pipe in his hand, turning it over and over with his thick fingers, and his brows were drawn together, and his lips moved, as though he were trying to find something to say and could not find it. At last he spoke, slowly, heavily, his voice thick.

"Look here," he said. "You see this pipe. This was my father's pipe. He brung it from Ulm when he was a young man. Then he give it to me. Then I brung it here, in my chest, on the ship. Twenty years I have had it. Now look at it. Broke."

The boy looked at it and said nothing. His chin quivered.

"Now look," said Hans. "A pipe, that's nothing. I can't help it. You broke it; all right. You was playing with it, hey? You climbed on the chair and took it down to play with?"

The boy nodded. The tears had begun to come now, sliding down his cheeks one after another, and he did not wipe them away.

"All right. That's bad. You don't touch what ain't yours. You know that. Your mother told you that, a hundred times. But that ain't the worst. You know what's the worst?"

Otto shook his head.

"You lie to me." Hans leaned forward, his huge hands hanging between his knees, the broken pipe dangling from his fingers. "You stand there and look at me in the face and you lie. You say the cat done it. The cat! And all the time you got the dust of it on your face. You think I'm a fool? Hey? You think your father is a fool, you can tell him any kind of lie?"

"No," whispered the boy.

"Listen here. I'm going to tell you something. You listen good. When a man breaks something, that's bad, but it's done. You can't help it. But when a man lies, then he's no good. Then nobody believes him. Then he's like—like a horse that kicks. You can't trust him. You got to watch him all the time. You don't never know what he's going to do. You want to be like that? Like a horse that kicks?"

"No."

"No. All right. Then don't you never lie to me. Never. You hear? You break something, you come tell me. You say, 'Papa, I broke it.' Then maybe I'm mad, maybe I holler. But I don't—" He stopped. His face worked. He looked down at his own enormous fist, the knuckles swollen and red, and opened it slowly, and looked at the palm. "I don't hurt you," he said at last, very low. "I don't never hurt you. You come tell me, and I don't never hurt you. You understand?"

The boy nodded. He was crying hard now, his whole thin body shaking, the sobs catching in his throat.

"Now you go to your room," said Hans. "You stay there till supper. You think about it. Go on."

The boy went, stumbling, his hands over his face. They heard the door of the little room shut behind him, and then, faint through the wall, the sound of his crying.

Minna came and stood beside her husband's chair. She put her hand upon his shoulder, upon the great, hard muscle under the shirt, and he could feel that her hand was trembling.

"Hans," she said. "Ach, Hans, for a minute I thought—"

"I know," he said. "I know."

She did not ask him what had stopped him, and he could not have told her. He did not know himself. He only knew, dimly, that he had come very near to something, and that he had drawn back from it, and that he was tired.

Minna went back to her dishes. Hans sat on alone in his chair by the window. The sun had moved across the carpet, and the broad yellow square of it had climbed halfway up the wall. The street was quiet. Across the way the women still leaned from the windows, gossiping. A Chinaman went by, carrying a great basket of washing upon a pole across his shoulders. From the bakery on the corner came the warm smell of bread. Hans sat still, his huge hands lying upon his knees, the broken pipe upon his palm. He fitted the stem to the bowl, and held it there a long time, and when he let go it parted again.

After a while the door of the little room opened softly, and the boy came out. He came across the carpet in his stocking feet, very slowly, and stood beside his father's chair, his face swollen and red with crying. He held out his hand. In it was a little tube of glue, the kind that Minna kept in the kitchen drawer for mending crockery.

"Papa," he said, "I broke it. I broke your pipe. I'm sorry. Maybe we could fix it?"

Hans looked at him. Then, without a word, he reached down his enormous arm and lifted the boy up and set him upon his knee. And together, in the yellow sunlight, the giant and the little boy bent their heads over the broken pipe, the stag's head with its one shattered antler, and Hans held the pieces steady in his great red fingers while the child, his tongue between his teeth, spread the glue.

Down in the street the newsboy was still crying his papers, his voice thin and far away, and the smell of the new leather came up from the harness shop below.

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. While allied by every tie of blood to the ranching interests, he had never been identified with them. He was city-bred. The Railroad would not be over-suspicious of him. He was a good lawyer, a good business man, keen, clear-headed, far-sighted, had already some practical knowledge of politics, having served a term as assistant district attorney, and even at the present moment occupying the position of sheriff's attorney. More than all, he was the son of Magnus Derrick; he could be relied upon, could be trusted implicitly to remain loyal to the ranchers' cause. The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. The campaign fund raised by contributions from Magnus, Annixter, Broderson, and Osterman was drawn upon to the extent of five thousand dollars. Only the committee knew of this corruption. The League, ignoring ways and means, supposed as a matter of course that the campaign was honorably conducted. For a whole week after the consummation of this part of the deal, Magnus had kept to his house, refusing to be seen, alleging that he was ill, which was not far from the truth. More than once, he had resolved to break with the whole affair, resigning his position, allowing the others to proceed without him. But now it was too late. He was pledged. He had joined the League. The other members of the League, present at the time, shook hands all around and spoke of opening a few bottles on the strength of the occasion. Annixter alone was recalcitrant.

“It's too easy,” he declared. “No, I'm not satisfied. Where's Shelgrim in all this? Why don't he show his hand, damn his soul? The thing is yellow, I tell you. There's a big fish in these waters somewheres. I don't know his name, and I don't know his game, but he's moving round off and on, just out of sight. The lamp upon the table, a squat affair of green glass with a cracked chimney mended with a strip of brown paper, threw a yellow, uncertain light over the room. It was a kitchen like a thousand others in the Sonoma country, low-ceiled, hot, smelling of fried pork and coal-oil and the sour yeast of the bread-sponge rising in its crock behind the stove. A calendar from a Santa Rosa feed store, showing a girl in a red bonnet holding a sheaf of wheat, hung by a nail near the door. There was a clock on the shelf, a nickel alarm clock, that ticked with a loud and insolent regularity. There was a rocking-chair with a calico cushion, a bench, a rag carpet worn through to the boards before the stove, a box of kindling, a pair of rubber boots, caked to the ankles with adobe, standing in a corner. Through the window, propped open with a stick of stove-wood, came the smell of the hop-yards, heavy, pungent, and somnolent, and the far-off creaking of a windmill turning in the night breeze.

At the table, in his shirt-sleeves, sat her husband, Ezra Lundy. He had pushed back his plate and had spread out before him a long envelope of stiff paper, much handled, and a single sheet of foolscap covered with figures. He was a huge man, enormously built, his shoulders bowed and rounded with years of labour, his neck thick and red, his hands, as they lay upon the oilcloth, square and heavy, the knuckles swollen, the nails broken and blackened. His hair was coarse and yellow, going grey above the ears; his face was broad, slow, and patient, the face of an ox that has worn the yoke so long it has forgotten the field. He breathed audibly through his nose as he read, his lips moving, following the figures with a forefinger thick as a wagon-bolt.

For a long time neither of them spoke. The clock ticked. The sand grated against the iron. Outside, a dog barked once, twice, and was silent.

"Well?" said Minna, without turning her head.

Ezra did not answer at once. He wet the end of his finger and turned the sheet of foolscap over, looked at the back of it, which was blank, and turned it again.

"Well," he said at length, "it don't come out no different, Min. I been over it four times."

"I didn't suppose it would."

She set down the spider upon the drain-board, wiped her hands upon her apron, and came and stood at the other side of the table, looking down at him. She was a small woman, very neat, very trim, her figure still slender in spite of her thirty-six years, her brown hair drawn tightly back from her forehead and twisted into a hard knot at the nape of her neck. Her face was thin, the cheek-bones high, the lips compressed into a line that was almost colourless; but her eyes, of a pale and very clear grey, were alert, watchful, quick to see, quick to reckon. She held herself very straight. Even in the heat of the kitchen there was no disorder about her, not a hair astray, not a fold of her calico misplaced. She was one of those women for whom thrift is less a virtue than an instinct, a thing of the blood, as ineradicable as the colour of her eyes.

"How much?" she demanded.

"Eleven hundred and forty, with the interest. Due the first of the month."

"And what's in the bank?"

Ezra rubbed his chin, the stubble rasping under his palm.

"Three hundred and twelve dollars," repeated Minna, slowly, distinctly, as though she were setting each word down upon the table between them, a little pile of coins. He did not look at her. He folded the sheet of foolscap in two, creasing it carefully with his thumb-nail, and then folded it again. It was a habit of his, this slow, deliberate folding, when he was troubled; she had seen him fold a single bill of sale into a pellet no larger than a pea, his great fingers working, working, while his mind laboured heavily behind his eyes.

"I'll see Rutledge at the bank," he said. "He'll carry it over. He's carried it before."

"Mr. Cutts was here again to-day."

Upon the instant Ezra's head came up. His hands stopped in their folding. For a moment the two looked at each other across the lamp, and in that moment something passed between them, something hostile, wary, alert, like the first touching of blades.

"I told that fellow not to come round here."

"You told him. I didn't. He came to the door at two o'clock while you were down at the lower field, and I gave him a glass of buttermilk and he sat in that chair and talked to me for the better part of an hour."

"I don't want him in my house."

"It ain't your house," said Minna. "Not hardly. It's Rutledge's house, and the bank's house, and the Sonoma County Savings and Loan's house. It'll be theirs for certain on the first of the month, every stick of it, unless something's done."

We could go to Oakland. You could get on at the planing mill, Mr. Cutts says they're always wanting men at the mills, big men, strong men. We could have a house on a street, a real street with sidewalks, and gas, and a water-closet, and a front room with a carpet. We could put the money in the savings bank and have the interest coming in regular every quarter, coming in all the time, whether it rained or not, whether there was frost or not, whether hops was nine cents or ninety. She stopped, breathless, her pale eyes shining, a spot of colour come into each thin cheek. Ezra sat looking at her heavily, his great jaw set, his lower lip thrust out.

He grubbed out them oaks along the creek. He built that barn. I helped him put the ridge-pole on when I wasn't but twelve. He's buried up on the knoll. My mother's buried there. Our boy is buried there."

Minna's face changed. Something shut down over it, swift and hard, like a door closing.

"You don't need to tell me where our boy is buried."

"Well, then."

"Well, then, what? What's that got to do with it? Do you think he'd want us to starve on account of a piece of dirt? Do you think your father'd want it? He'd have sold out in a minute if anybody'd offered him twenty-two dollars. He was a close man, your father. He knew the worth of a dollar. Ezra's face darkened slowly, a dull red creeping up from the thick neck to the roots of the yellow hair. His hands, lying upon the oilcloth, closed and opened, closed and opened. Minna saw the movement and was afraid, but her fear only drove her on. It was as though she had set her foot upon a down grade and must go on, faster and faster, unable to stop.

"Thirty-five hundred dollars in gold," she repeated. "I had it figured out to-day, after Mr. Cutts went. I sat right here and figured it on the back of the egg book. At four per cent. that's a hundred and forty dollars a year, and the principal never touched. Never touched, Ezra. Just lying there and making more. And with what you'd get at the mill . . ."

"I ain't going to no mill."

"Why not? Why not? Are you too good for it?"

"I ain't going to work for no man by the day. I been my own boss twenty years."

"Your own boss!" she cried, with a short, harsh laugh. "Your own boss! Rutledge is your boss. The weather's your boss. The hop-buyers in San Francisco is your boss. You ain't been your own boss one day in twenty years, and you know it. You work like a horse from dark to dark, and what have you got? A mortgage, and a kiln with the roof falling in, and three hundred and twelve dollars. And me. What have I got? Look at my hands." She thrust them out across the table under the lamplight, small hands, hard, red, the skin cracked across the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick. "Look at 'em. I was the best-looking girl in Healdsburg when you married me. Everybody said so. And look at me now. I'm old. I'm thirty-six and I'm old. I've cooked for hop-pickers, forty of 'em at a time, Chinamen and Portuguese and Indians, in that kitchen, in August, with the stove going and the flies. I've made my own soap. Her voice broke upon the last word. She drew back her hands and pressed them together in her lap, and sat rigid, staring at the lamp, her chin trembling, refusing to cry.

Ezra was silent. The clock ticked loudly in the hush. Outside, the windmill creaked and creaked, and somewhere down by the creek a frog began its monotonous croaking, interminable, persistent, indifferent. A moth had found its way through the open window and blundered about the lamp chimney, striking against it with little soft taps, falling, rising, striking again.

At last Ezra spoke, and his voice was low, almost gentle.

"Min, you don't know them land companies. You don't know that Cutts. He's slick. They're all slick, them fellows from the city. They come up here with their papers and their printed names, and they talk soft to the women, and they . . ."

"He didn't talk soft to me. He talked business."

"He talked business," repeated Ezra. "That's it. That's just it. Business. What's business? It's them that's got the money taking it away from them that ain't got it. That's what business is. You think they'd pay twenty-two dollars if the land wasn't worth fifty? You think they'd come clear up here from San Francisco to do us a favour? They know something. There's a railroad spur coming through, or something. They know, and we don't, and they want to get the land before we find out."

"And if they do? If it's worth fifty, what good does it do us, when we can't pay the note? Rutledge'll get it for eleven hundred, and sell it to Cutts for fifty, and we'll get nothing. Nothing! Can't you see that? Can't you get it through your head? Either way they get it. Either way. The only thing we can say is whether we get thirty-five hundred dollars or nothing at all."

He stared at her, his slow mind turning the thing over and over, heavily, laboriously, like a plough turning the adobe in a dry year, and she saw the truth of it sink into him by degrees, saw it settle upon him, saw his great shoulders bow a little lower beneath it. It was the thing he had known all along and had refused to look at, as a man refuses to look at a sore that he knows is mortal. And now she had made him look.

He got up suddenly, pushing back his chair so that it scraped harshly upon the boards, and went to the window and stood there, his huge bulk filling it, his hands thrust into the pockets of his overalls, staring out into the dark. Beyond him Minna could see nothing but blackness, and the faint grey shapes of the hop-poles marching away in their endless rows, line upon line, and above them a sprinkling of stars, very small, very far off, very cold.

"I been thinking," said Ezra, without turning round. "I been thinking about it all summer. Nights. When you was asleep."

"I wasn't asleep."

He was silent a moment.

"No," he said. "I guess you wasn't."

"I heard you get up and go out. I heard you walking round the kiln. Three, four o'clock in the morning. I'd lie there and hear you."

"I'd go up on the knoll," said Ezra. "I'd go up there and sit."

Minna said nothing. She sat very still upon the bench, her hands in her lap, and looked at the broad, bowed back of her husband outlined against the darkness. And for an instant, a single instant, something stirred in her, something that was not thrift, not calculation, not the hunger for the house on the paved street and the interest coming in every quarter; something older, softer, half-forgotten.
