She remembered the day they had buried the child on the knoll, in the rain, and how Ezra had dug the grave himself and would not let the neighbours help, and how she had found him afterwards in the barn, his face pressed against the flank of the old grey mare, his shoulders shaking. She remembered . . .

But the clock ticked upon the shelf, and the envelope from the bank lay upon the oilcloth, stiff, official, inexorable, and the moment passed. The softness went out of her as it had come. Her lips closed again into their thin line.

"Mr. Cutts is coming back Thursday," she said. "Thursday at ten. With the papers."

Ezra did not move.

"He'll want both our names," she went on. "Mine and yours. He says it has to be both, on account of it being community property."

Still he did not move. The moth fell from the lamp chimney upon the table, its wings scorched, and lay there feebly fluttering. Minna watched it a moment and then, with a quick, precise movement of her thumb, crushed it against the oilcloth and wiped her thumb upon her apron.

"Ezra."

"I hear you."

"Are you going to sign?"

He turned round then, slowly, and faced her. His face in the lamplight was grey and heavy, the lines in it cut deep as furrows, the eyes dull, bewildered, the eyes of a great beast that has been fighting a long time against something it cannot see and cannot understand, and has begun, at last, to tire.

"I don't know," he said. "God help me, Min, I don't know."

"You've got till Thursday."

"I know it."

She rose from the bench, smoothed down her apron with both hands, and went back to the sink. She took up the iron spider and turned it over, examined its bottom critically, and set it upon the back of the stove to dry. She emptied the dish-pan out of the back door into the darkness; the water fell with a splash upon the hard earth. She came back, hung the pan upon its nail, wrung out the dish-rag, folded it, and laid it over the edge of the sink. Then she wound the clock, turning the key with little sharp, decisive twists, and set the alarm for half-past four.

All the while Ezra stood by the window, watching her, saying nothing.

When she had done, she took up the lamp.

"Are you coming to bed?"

"After a while."

"You'll be going up to the knoll, I suppose."

He made no answer. She stood a moment with the lamp in her hand, the light striking upward upon her thin face, making hollows of her eyes; then she turned and went out of the kitchen and down the narrow passage toward the bedroom, and the light went with her, dwindling, fading, and the kitchen was left in darkness.

Ezra stood alone. Through the open window the smell of the hops came to him, heavy, rank, insistent, the smell of the land itself, of the soil he had turned and turned again since he was a boy, of the vines he had trained, of the kilns he had fired through so many September nights. The windmill creaked. The frog croaked on and on beside the creek. Far off, toward Santa Rosa, a train whistled, a long, wavering, melancholy note, and he heard, faint and diminishing, the rumble of its wheels upon the rails, going south, going toward the city, toward the bay, toward the world of business and printed papers and men who knew what he did not know. It passed, and the silence closed again over the valley, vast, indifferent, eternal.

After a long time Ezra Lundy took his hat from its nail beside the door and went out, and his heavy footsteps sounded upon the path, going up toward the knoll, slowly, slowly, until they too were lost in the night.

It was on a certain afternoon toward the end of October, at the hour when the lamps of Kearny Street were beginning to burn yellow against a sky still pale with the last of the daylight, that Ellis Kittredge, bookkeeper in the wholesale hardware house of Coombs & Haverly, closed his ledger, wiped his pen carefully upon the square of chamois kept for that purpose in the upper left-hand drawer of his desk, and went down to the Pacific Mail dock to meet his cousin.

He had not seen Gus Hockett in nine years. He had had, in all that time, perhaps four letters from him: one from Tacoma, one from Juneau, one, much blotted, written in pencil upon the back of a bill of lading, from some place on the Yukon whose name Ellis had never been able to make out, and the last, a week ago, from Seattle. This was brief. Gus was "coming down on the *Umatilla*, Thursday, and would Ellis meet him, and how was everybody, and he had a lot to tell." That was all. There was no signature but a great sprawling G, and under it, scored twice, the word "Sure."

The wharf, when Ellis arrived, was in a turmoil. The steamer was already warped in, her black sides towering above the stringpiece, her funnel still breathing out a thin, tired smoke, and down her gangway poured a stream of humanity that broke and eddied about the freight sheds like water about the piles of a pier. There were drummers in derby hats, carrying sample cases; there were women in long ulsters, looking about them bewildered, clutching children by the wrist; there were Chinamen in blue blouses, padding softly in felt-soled shoes; there were sailors, longshoremen, hack drivers, runners from the cheap hotels on Pacific Street shouting the names of their houses; and everywhere, conspicuous, unmistakable, the men from the North: big men, bearded men, men in mackinaws and duck trousers and high boots laced to the knee, men with faces burnt brick-red by wind and snow-glare, carrying their goods in canvas sacks upon their shoulders, rolling a little in their walk, staring about them at the city with a kind of truculent, half-suspicious joy.

Ellis stood a little apart, close to the wall of the shed, out of the way. He was a slight man, narrow-chested, a little stooped, of about thirty-four years, his hair, of an indeterminate brown, already thinning upon the crown. He wore steel-rimmed eyeglasses, which he had the habit of settling upon the bridge of his nose with the tip of his forefinger, pressing them back, delicately, three or four times in succession, whenever he was perplexed or ill at ease. He was dressed neatly, inexpensively, in a suit of grey mixed goods, a little shiny at the elbows, a black string tie, and a derby hat that he had brushed that morning before leaving his lodgings. Under his arm he carried, from long habit, a folded copy of the evening *Bulletin*. He watched the gangway anxiously, peering, his eyeglasses winking in the light of the arc lamps that had just sputtered into life overhead.

Suddenly there was a roar.

"Ellis! Hey—ELLIS! Ellis Kittredge, by the Lord!"

A huge man was shouldering through the crowd toward him, scattering a group of Chinamen, upsetting a drummer's valise, waving above his head an enormous hat of grey felt. Ellis had a confused impression of a great red beard, of a pair of shoulders that seemed to fill the whole width of the passage, of a voice that boomed and reverberated under the roof of the shed. Then his hand was seized in a grip that ground the knuckles together, and he was being pounded upon the back, so that his eyeglasses jumped upon his nose and the *Bulletin* fell to the planking.

"Well, well, well!" cried Gus Hockett. "Well, I'll be damned! It's old Ellis, all right. Same old specs. Same old Ellis. Say, you ain't changed a hair. Not a hair. Let's look at you."

He held his cousin off at arm's length and stared at him, grinning enormously, his small blue eyes twinkling out of the tangle of beard and eyebrow. Ellis, flushed, embarrassed, aware that people were looking at them, recovered his paper and settled his glasses.

"How are you, Gus?" he said. "You—you've grown a beard."

At this Gus threw back his head and roared again, a huge, full-throated laugh that brought tears into his eyes.

"Grown a beard! He says I've grown a beard. Well, I should say I had. You try shaving with forty below and the water froze in the kettle. Grown a beard! Oh, Lord, Ellis, you're the same. You're the same old feller. Come on. I'm hungry as a wolf. I've been eating that steamer grub for nine days, and if I see another plate of slumgullion I'll go crazy. Where can a man get a REAL feed in this town? You know. You live here."

He swung a canvas sack to his shoulder as though it had been a pillow, and the two went out together into the street.

It was the hour when San Francisco, its day's work done, gave itself over to the business of amusement with that easy, careless good humour that was its distinguishing trait. The sidewalks were thronged. The cable-cars went clanging past, crowded to the very steps, young men hanging from the rails, laughing, calling to one another. The windows of the saloons and cigar stores glowed warm and yellow; from the doors of the restaurants came the smell of broiling meat, of coffee, of hot bread. Newsboys shrilled the evening editions at every corner. Somewhere a German band was playing, the brasses blaring out a waltz, a little off the key. Over all hung the faint, pervasive odour of the sea, salt, keen, coming up from the wharves with the evening fog that was already beginning to roll in, grey and thick, from beyond the Golden Gate, blurring the electric lights, making halos about the street lamps.

Gus strode through it all with enormous delight, staring into the shop windows, turning his head after the women, sniffing the air, exclaiming at everything.

"Look at that, will you? Electric lights. Look at them cars. Say, it's alive, ain't it? It's ALIVE. You don't know what it's like, Ellis, coming down from up there. Nine months you don't see nothing but snow and spruce and the same eleven faces. Nine months. And then this. Lord, I'd like to grab the whole town in my arms and hug it."

It was a long, low room, with a sanded floor and a ceiling of dark wood, much smoked, the walls hung with steel engravings of Bismarck and the old Kaiser, with antlers, with beer steins of painted earthenware ranged upon a shelf, with a great clock in a carved case that ticked heavily in a corner. The tables were covered with cloths of red and white check. There was a long bar at one end, behind which a fat man in a white apron drew beer from a row of polished taps. The air was thick with the smell of sauerkraut and frying sausage and the smoke of cheap cigars.

They took a table near the stove. Gus flung his sack under it, his hat upon it, and dropped into his chair, which creaked under him. He ordered without looking at the bill of fare: a porterhouse steak, very thick, very rare, fried potatoes, fried onions, a plate of sliced tomatoes, bread and butter, coffee, a pot of beer, apple pie.

"And bring it QUICK," he added. "I'm starving."

Ellis, after some hesitation, his forefinger at his glasses, ordered the sixty-cent dinner.

"Not on your life," declared Gus. "Not tonight. This is my treat. Waiter, bring him the same as me. Bring him the same. And another pot of beer." He thrust his hand into the breast of his flannel shirt and drew out a little bag of buckskin, greasy, much worn, tied at the neck with a thong, and set it down upon the tablecloth with a dull, heavy thump. "There," he said. "There's where the money comes from. Real stuff. Out of the ground. I dug it."

Ellis looked at the bag. He could not keep his eyes from it. There was something fascinating in it, something that held the attention; the little sack, squat, shapeless, ugly, lying there among the cruets and the salt cellars, so small, and yet, as it were, so heavy, so dense, so charged with meaning. He touched it with a finger, timidly.

Ellis lifted it. It was astonishingly heavy. It sagged in his palm, cold, inert. He put it down quickly, as though it had burned him.

Ellis ate slowly, with little careful motions, cutting his meat into small squares, laying his knife across the edge of his plate between mouthfuls. He watched his cousin with a sort of wonder. He remembered Gus as he had been nine years before, a big, loose-jointed fellow of twenty-four, who drove a delivery wagon for a feed store in Stockton and was forever in trouble with the proprietor. He had been big then. Gus stared at him, his mouth a little open.

"Aunt Lena? Dead?" He put down his fork. "I never got it. Honest to God, Ellis, I never got it. I'd moved on by then. Aunt Lena." He was silent a moment, his great face suddenly sober, troubled, the little eyes blinking. "She was always good to me," he muttered. "She was good to me when nobody else was. "Her heart," said Ellis. "It was very quick. She didn't suffer."

"That's something," said Gus. "That's something." And again, after a moment: "Well, well."

"And the old place?" he said. "Grandpa's place, up at Sonora? Who's got that?"

"It was sold," answered Ellis. "After Uncle Rudolph died. There was a mortgage on it. Nobody could keep up the payments. A man named Teague bought it. A cattle man. He ran stock on it for a while. I heard he pulled down the house."

Gus leaned back in his chair, which creaked again. He stared at the ceiling.

"Pulled down the house," he repeated. "Well, I'll be—Say, Ellis, you remember that house? You remember the big front room with the melodeon in it, and Grandma's chair, and the Bible on the table that nobody was let touch? And the creek down below, where we used to go after crawdads? And the old Spanish oak, and the swing Grandpa put up in it? And the smell of the place in summer, all tarweed and dust and hot pine, and the grasshoppers snapping up out of the grass like popcorn? You remember?"

"I remember," said Ellis. He did remember. For an instant, sitting there in the smoke and the noise of the German restaurant, he saw it all again, sharp, vivid, distinct: the white house among the foothills, the long veranda, the oak, the creek shining over its stones, the brown hills shimmering in the heat, two small boys, barefooted, sunburned, wading with their trousers rolled to the knee. It came and went in a flash, and left him strangely shaken. He took off his glasses and polished them carefully upon his napkin.

"And Minnie?" he asked. "Have you heard from Minnie?"

Gus brightened.

"Sure. Got a letter in Seattle. She's all right. She married that feller Schutz, that runs the saloon on El Dorado Street in Stockton. Got three kids. Three! Little Minnie with three kids. He's a good enough feller, Schutz. Drinks some. But he's good to her." He laughed. "Lord, it makes a man feel old. Three kids."

He leaned forward, his elbows on the table, his huge hands clasped.

"Well, now, that's the folks. Now tell me about YOU. What you been doing all this while? Still at the hardware place?"

"Still at Coombs & Haverly's," said Ellis.

"Well—yes. That is, I'm head bookkeeper now. Since Mr. Sutro left. There's two under me."

"Good for you!" cried Gus. "Head bookkeeper. Say, that's fine. What do they pay you?"

Ellis hesitated, touching his glasses.

"Eighty-five dollars," he said. "A month."

Gus did not answer at once. "Eighty-five dollars," said Gus slowly.

"It's a good position," said Ellis, a little hurriedly. "It's steady. It's—there's men would be glad of it. And Mr. Haverly says there may be something better next year, when the new warehouse is built. It's a good house. It's one of the oldest houses on the street."

"Sure," said Gus. "Sure it is."

There was a pause. Then Ellis said, with an effort:

"And you, Gus? Did you—did you do well? Up there?"

Gus laughed, a short laugh, without much mirth in it. He picked up the buckskin bag and weighed it in his hand.

"Well," he said, "I'll tell you. That's about all of it. Right there."

It gets into your blood. You can't think of nothing else. You dream about it nights. He was leaning forward now, his voice lowered, his little eyes shining. Ellis listened, fascinated, his fork suspended.

"Then what?" he said.

"Two years' work. Three days."

"Oh, GUS," said Ellis.

"Oh, I know, I know," said Gus. "Don't say it. I've said it to myself enough. I'm a damn fool. I always was a damn fool. Pa used to say so." He laughed again, his good humour returning with a rush. He leaned across the table suddenly and laid one of his huge hands upon his cousin's wrist.

Ellis started.

They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. If you see Mr. Darrell, tell him that Mr. Derrick—you get the name—Mr. Derrick may not be able to get around this afternoon, but to go ahead with any business just the same.” The young man departed with the package and Lyman, spreading out the map upon the table, remained for some time studying it thoughtfully. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. While allied by every tie of blood to the ranching interests, he had never been identified with them. He was city-bred. The Railroad would not be over-suspicious of him. He was a good lawyer, a good business man, keen, clear-headed, far-sighted, had already some practical knowledge of politics, having served a term as assistant district attorney, and even at the present moment occupying the position of sheriff's attorney. More than all, he was the son of Magnus Derrick; he could be relied upon, could be trusted implicitly to remain loyal to the ranchers' cause. The campaign for Railroad Commissioner had been very interesting. At the very outset Magnus's committee found itself involved in corrupt politics. The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. The campaign fund raised by contributions from Magnus, Annixter, Broderson, and Osterman was drawn upon to the extent of five thousand dollars. Only the committee knew of this corruption. The League, ignoring ways and means, supposed as a matter of course that the campaign was honorably conducted. For a whole week after the consummation of this part of the deal, Magnus had kept to his house, refusing to be seen, alleging that he was ill, which was not far from the truth. The shame of the business, the loathing of what he had done, were to him things unspeakable. He could no longer look Harran in the face. He began a course of deception with his wife. More than once, he had resolved to break with the whole affair, resigning his position, allowing the others to proceed without him. But now it was too late. He was pledged. He had joined the League. He was its chief, and his defection might mean its disintegration at the very time when it needed all its strength to fight the land cases. More than a mere deal in bad politics was involved. There was the land grab. His withdrawal from an unholy cause would mean the weakening, perhaps the collapse, of another cause that he believed to be righteous as truth itself. He was hopelessly caught in the mesh. Wrong seemed indissolubly knitted into the texture of Right. He was blinded, dizzied, overwhelmed, caught in the current of events, and hurried along he knew not where. He resigned himself. In the end, and after much ostentatious opposition on the part of the railroad heelers, Lyman was nominated and subsequently elected. When this consummation was reached Magnus, Osterman, Broderson, and Annixter stared at each other. Their wildest hopes had not dared to fix themselves upon so easy a victory as this. It was not believable that the corporation would allow itself to be fooled so easily, would rush open-eyed into the trap. How had it happened? Osterman, however, threw his hat into the air with wild whoops of delight. Old Broderson permitted himself a feeble cheer. Even Magnus beamed satisfaction. The other members of the League, present at the time, shook hands all around and spoke of opening a few bottles on the strength of the occasion. Annixter alone was recalcitrant.

“It's too easy,” he declared. “No, I'm not satisfied. Where's Shelgrim in all this? Why don't he show his hand, damn his soul? The thing is yellow, I tell you. There's a big fish in these waters somewheres. I don't know his name, and I don't know his game, but he's moving round off and on, just out of sight. If you think you've netted him, I DON'T, that's all I've got to say.” But he was jeered down as a croaker. There was the Commission. He couldn't get around that, could he? There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. Some one rapped vigorously upon the door, which was immediately after opened, and Magnus and Harran came in, followed by Presley.

“Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down. Have a glass of sizz-water, Governor.” The others explained that they had come up from Bonneville the night before, as the Executive Committee of the League had received a despatch from the lawyers it had retained to fight the Railroad, that the judge of the court in San Francisco, where the test cases were being tried, might be expected to hand down his decision the next day. Very soon after the announcement of the new grading of the ranchers' lands, the corporation had offered, through S. Behrman, to lease the disputed lands to the ranchers at a nominal figure. The offer had been angrily rejected, and the Railroad had put up the lands for sale at Ruggles's office in Bonneville. At the exorbitant price named, buyers promptly appeared—dummy buyers, beyond shadow of doubt, acting either for the Railroad or for S. Behrman—men hitherto unknown in the county, men without property, without money, adventurers, heelers. Prominent among them, and bidding for the railroad's holdings included on Annixter's ranch, was Delaney. The farce of deeding the corporation's sections to these fictitious purchasers was solemnly gone through with at Ruggles's office, the Railroad guaranteeing them possession. The League refused to allow the supposed buyers to come upon the land, and the Railroad, faithful to its pledge in the matter of guaranteeing its dummies possession, at once began suits in ejectment in the district court in Visalia, the county seat. It was the preliminary skirmish, the reconnaisance in force, the combatants feeling each other's strength, willing to proceed with caution, postponing the actual death-grip for a while till each had strengthened its position and organised its forces.

Upon the ground floor of a narrow, two-storied frame house in Folsom Street, between Fourth and Fifth, Otto Kretschmar kept a locksmith's shop, and above the shop he lived with his wife and his son. The house was painted a dingy yellow, and the sign that hung over the door, a huge wooden key gilded long ago and now flaked and blistered by the sun and the fog of many summers, swung creaking upon its iron bracket whenever the trade-wind came in from the ocean in the afternoon. Within, the shop was a low, dusky room, smelling of machine oil, of brass filings, of tobacco smoke, and of the sauerkraut that, three times a week, simmered upon Mrs. Kretschmar's stove at the back. Along one wall ran the bench, scarred, black with grease, littered with files, punches, gravers, pincers, a little bench-vise screwed fast at one end and at the other a gas-jet with a blow-pipe attached, which roared like a small furnace when it was lit. Above the bench, on a long board studded with brads, hung the blanks, hundreds of them, brass and iron and steel, keys for doors, keys for trunks, keys for clocks, keys for safes, ranged in rows according to their sizes, glinting dully in the half-light. There were padlocks in a glass case, and a great iron safe, a "Hall's Patent," bought second-hand at a sheriff's sale, its door painted with a landscape of a lake and a castle and a swan, which Kretschmar would open for nobody. There was a stand of umbrellas left to be mended and never called for. There was a nickelled cash drawer under the counter, and, beside it, an empty cigar box of cedar-wood, labelled "La Flor de Habana," in which the locksmith kept his small change, the nickels and dimes and quarters of the day's petty trade, to save himself the trouble of unlocking the drawer.

Kretschmar himself was a heavy, slow, powerful man of forty, born in the Black Forest, and come to California by way of Hamburg and New York and the Isthmus. He was large-boned, thick through the shoulders, his neck short and red, his hands enormous, the fingers blunt and square at the tips, the nails broken, the palms ingrained with a blackness that no scrubbing would remove. His hair, a pale tow-colour, was cropped close to his round skull, and he wore a long, drooping mustache, yellowed at the fringe by the smoke of the porcelain pipe that hung from his teeth from morning to night. He was a good workman, patient, exact, plodding; there was no lock in the city that he could not pick, given time. He was not quick of thought; he could not be hurried; he arrived at his ideas by degrees, turning them over and over in his mind, as he turned a key-blank in his fingers, filing it a little here, a little there, trying it, filing again. Ordinarily he was a placid man, good-natured, slow to anger. But once roused, the anger in him rose, as it were, from a great depth, from some obscure, primitive source, and it was terrible. In the old country his father, a charcoal-burner, had been such a one, a giant of a man who drank schnapps and beat his children with the flat of a shovel; and the son, who had not forgotten, was sometimes afraid of what lay coiled in him, dormant, waiting.

It was a Saturday, late in the afternoon, in the month of September, the season when the fog comes in from the Heads with the evening, rolling over the hills by Twin Peaks, filling the hollows of the Mission, blotting out the sun. In the street the life of the quarter went on, noisy, unlovely, incessant. Drays from the foundries and the box factories rumbled by, the drivers cracking their whips and swearing at the horses; a car on the Folsom Street line passed every few minutes with a clangour of bells and a long, grinding shriek of the cable in the slot; children shrieked and quarrelled upon the sidewalks; a German band, four men in shabby green coats, blew a waltz at the corner before the saloon; and from the open doors of the dwellings came the smell of frying onions, of boiling coffee, of beer, of wet washing hung out upon the lines in the back yards. The day's work was over, or nearly over; the whole quarter was relaxing, loosening its belt, preparing for the Saturday night.

Kretschmar had just finished fitting a new lock to the door of a coal-dealer on Harrison Street and had come in, carrying his kit, his shoulders bent, tired, thinking of his supper. He set down the kit upon the bench, lit his pipe, and going behind the counter, pulled out the cigar box to drop into it the half-dollar the coal-dealer had paid him.

The box was empty.

He stood looking into it for a long moment, his pipe between his teeth, his little pale eyes blinking slowly. That morning there had been money in it; he knew there had been. He could have told almost to a nickel how much: a dollar and sixty-five cents. He had counted it before he went out, as he always counted it, methodically, laying the coins in little piles upon the counter. Now there was nothing, not a cent; only the smell of the cedar-wood and, at the bottom, a dried tobacco leaf that had come with the box from the cigar-maker's.

He did not at once understand. He felt about in the corners of the box with his thick fingers, as if the money might somehow be hiding there. He looked upon the floor behind the counter, stooping heavily, grunting. He pulled out the nickelled drawer; it was locked, as he had left it. He turned the box upside down and shook it. Nothing.

Then, by degrees, slowly, his brain moving like a wheel that turns stiffly upon a rusted axle, he began to think. Nobody had been in the shop. Gussie, his wife, had gone to the market on Sixth Street in the morning and had not touched the box; she never touched it; she had her own purse, a great leather purse with a steel clasp, and she would no more have taken money from his box than she would have taken it from the church plate. There remained only Emil.

Emil was six years old, the only child. He had been born in that very house, in the room above the shop, on a night of rain, after Gussie had lain in labour for thirty hours; and the doctor, a German from Sutter Street, had said there would be no more. He was a stout, round little boy, tow-headed like his father, with fat red cheeks and small blue eyes, and he had his father's hands, already broad and square. He went to the primary school on Silver Street, and on Saturdays he played in the street with the other children of the quarter, the children of draymen and foundry hands and saloon-keepers, coming in at nightfall dirty, torn, bruised, ravenous, smelling of the gutter.

Kretschmar went to the door of the shop and looked out. The band at the corner had finished its waltz and was beginning upon a march. A crowd of small boys was gathered upon the curbstone by the saloon, and among them, unmistakable, his round head shining white in the declining light, was Emil. He was blowing upon a tin trumpet, a gaudy thing painted red and gold, with a tassel of yellow worsted dangling from it, and, in the intervals of his blowing, he thrust into his mouth a long black stick of licorice, which he shared with no one, holding it out of reach of the others with a lordly, proprietary air. His cheeks were smeared with it. Around his feet lay the wrappings of other purchases, papers that had held candy, the shell of a pomegranate, a broken whistle.

"Emil!" called the locksmith.

His voice was not loud, but the boy heard it at once above the noise of the band, and he turned. The trumpet came away from his lips. For an instant he stood quite still upon the curbstone, looking toward the shop; then, his head lowered, the licorice clutched behind his back, he came slowly along the sidewalk, dragging his feet, scuffing the toes of his shoes, putting off the moment as long as possible. The other boys watched him go, nudging one another, grinning, interested, knowing well what it meant when a father called in that voice.

"Come in," said Kretschmar.

The boy came in. The locksmith closed the door behind him. The noise of the street was suddenly shut off, muffled, distant; the band, the cable-cars, the shrieks of the children became a vague, confused murmur, like the noise of surf heard from a long way off. In the shop it was very still. The clock upon the wall, a great round clock with a brass pendulum that Kretschmar himself had repaired, ticked loudly and slowly. The gas had not yet been lit, and the place was full of shadows. The keys upon the board glimmered faintly; the swan upon the door of the safe was a white blur.

Kretschmar went behind the counter and stood there, his two great hands resting upon the edge of it, his pipe still between his teeth. The boy remained near the door, his back against it, his eyes upon the floor.

"Come here," said the father.

Emil came forward, a step at a time, until he stood before the counter. His head reached barely to the top of it. He kept his hands behind his back.

"What you got there?"

The boy did not answer.

"Show me what you got."

Slowly, very slowly, the hands came round. In one was the tin trumpet, in the other the remnant of the stick of licorice, wet, sticky, bitten off short. The locksmith looked at them a long time without speaking. Then he set the empty cigar box upon the counter between them, turning it carefully so that the boy could see inside.

"Where is the money?" he said.

Emil looked at the box and then looked away. His lower lip began to tremble. "I don't know," he said.

"You don't know?"

"No."

"You don't know where is the money out of the box?"

"No, I don't know. I ain't seen it. Maybe somebody come in and took it. Maybe a robber come in."

The lie, so obvious, so childish, so clumsy, struck upon Kretschmar like a blow. He had been prepared for the theft. He had not been prepared for this. Something stirred in him at that moment, something heavy and dark, rising slowly upward from the depths of him. He felt the blood come thick and hot into his neck and his face; he felt it beating behind his ears. His hands closed upon the edge of the counter until the knuckles whitened. He took the pipe from his mouth and laid it down very carefully beside the box.

"Where you get the trumpet?"

"A boy gave it to me."

"What boy?"

"A boy. I don't know his name. A big boy. He lives on Tehama Street. He gave it me."

"And the licorice? The candy? He gave you those too, this boy on Tehama Street?"

"Yes."

"You lie," said Kretschmar.

He did not raise his voice; but the words came from him low and harsh, almost a growl, and the boy shrank back from the counter as though he had been struck. For the first time he raised his eyes to his father's face, and what he saw there frightened him. His mouth opened wide, square, and he began to cry, at first without sound, then in long, gasping wails, the tears making white channels through the grime and the licorice upon his cheeks.

"You lie," repeated Kretschmar. "You take the money out of the box, and you go to Schwartz's store, and you buy the trumpet and the candy, and then you come and tell me a robber took it. A robber! Ach, Gott! A robber!"

He came out from behind the counter. He was enormous in the dusk of the shop, his head almost touching the low ceiling, his shoulders blotting out the light from the window. The boy backed away from him until he stood against the bench, and there he cowered, his arms raised before his face, the trumpet still clutched in one fist, howling.

And then, all at once, Kretschmar knew what he was about to do. His right hand had risen of itself. It was open, the broad, black, horny palm turned outward, the fingers spread; it hung in the air above the boy's head, heavy, ponderous, like a weight suspended upon a chain. One blow of it would have felled a man. He could feel the strength gathering in his arm, in his shoulder, in his back; he could feel the old savage pleasure of it, the joy of the brute that strikes and crushes and destroys. It was not he who stood there; it was the charcoal-burner of the Black Forest, the giant with the shovel, roaring, drunken, merciless; it was a long line of such, stretching back and back into the dark of the forest, men of the woods and the charcoal-pits, men who struck first and thought afterward, or never thought at all. The blood of them was in him; he had brought it with him across the ocean and across the Isthmus to this little shop in Folsom Street; and now, in this moment, it surged up in him, a black flood, foul and hot, clamouring for its outlet.

He remembered—as by a flash of lightning upon a black night—a cottage of logs, smoke-blackened, a fire upon the hearth, and himself, small, smaller than Emil, crouching in a corner while the great shape advanced upon him. He remembered the smell of schnapps. He remembered the blow, the sound it made, the floor rising up to meet his face, and afterward his mother bathing his head in a basin, crying, saying nothing, afraid to speak.

His hand remained in the air. It trembled. Slowly, by an effort that set the veins starting upon his forehead, that made the sweat break out upon his upper lip, he brought it down, and closed it, and thrust it into the pocket of his apron. He stood there, breathing hard, his chest rising and falling, his little eyes fixed upon the boy.

At that moment the door at the back of the shop opened, and Gussie Kretschmar appeared, a fork in her hand, her sleeves rolled to her elbows, her face red from the heat of the stove. She was a small, plump, anxious woman, with sparse light hair drawn tight over her head and twisted into a hard knot at the back, and she wore a calico wrapper with a pattern of purple flowers. Behind her, through the door, came a sudden gust of the smell of the kitchen, frying potatoes, sausages, coffee.

"What is it?" she cried. "Otto, what is it? Emil, why do you cry so? What has happened?"

"Go back," said the locksmith without turning his head.

"But, Otto——"

"Go back to the kitchen, I tell you. This is mine. Go back."

She hesitated, the fork uplifted, looking from the man to the child and back again. She knew her husband. She had seen him angry perhaps five times in the eight years of their marriage, and she had never forgotten any one of those times. But something in his face now, a certain ghastly rigidity, reassured her even while it frightened her; she understood obscurely that the worst had passed. She went back, slowly, leaving the door ajar, and they could hear her moving about in the kitchen, the clatter of the frying pan, the scrape of a chair, all very subdued, discreet, listening.

Kretschmar drew a long breath. He took his hand from his apron pocket, looked at it a moment as though it were a thing apart from himself, then reached out and lit the gas over the bench. The jet flared up yellow and hissing, and the shop leaped into light—the keys upon their board, the files, the vise, the umbrellas in their stand, the safe with its castle and its swan, the boy cowering against the bench, his face upturned, smeared, swollen, wet, the tin trumpet still clenched in his fist.

The locksmith drew a stool from beneath the bench and sat down upon it, so that his face was on a level with the child's. He was very tired. The anger had gone out of him, leaving him empty, heavy, inert, as a man is after a long fever.

"Emil," he said, "stop crying. Listen to me."

The boy's howls sank to a series of hiccoughing sobs. He kept his arms half raised, still watching the great hands.

"I don't hit you," said Kretschmar. "Put down your arms. I don't hit you. Listen. You know what you did?"

The boy nodded, gulping.

"Tell me what you did."

"I took—I took the money."

"Out of the box?"

"Out of the box."

"How much?"

"I don't know. All of it. All there was."

"And you buy the trumpet and the candy?"

"And a whistle. And a pomegranate. And—and some peanuts."

"And then you tell me a robber took it."

The boy began to cry again, but more quietly.

"Listen," said Kretschmar. He spoke slowly, painfully, searching for the words, putting them together one by one, as he would have put together the wards of a difficult lock. "That money—you know what that money is? That is not my money only. That is your mother's shoes. That is the bread. That is the rent to Mr. Galloway for the house. That is the coal for the stove. Every nickel in that box, I work for it. I go to Harrison Street, I go to Mission Street, I go all over, I fix the locks, I make the keys, I lie on my back under the safes in the banks, I get my hands cut, I get dirty—so. For every nickel. You understand?"

"Yes."

"Then you take it, and in one hour it is all gone—licorice, peanuts, a trumpet that is broke tomorrow. That is bad. That is a bad thing to do. But the lie—" He paused, and his heavy face worked. "The lie is worse. Ten times worse. A man that steals, he can be sorry, he can give it back, he can work and pay it back. But a man that lies, nobody believes him any more. Nobody trusts him. He is like—like a key that don't fit. You put him in the lock, he turns and turns, and nothing opens, and you throw him in the box with the old iron. You understand that?"

The boy did not understand, but he nodded, impressed by the solemnity of his father's face, by the strangeness of being spoken to in that low, slow, laboured voice, by the very fact that he had not been beaten.

"Now," said Kretschmar, getting up from the stool, "give me the trumpet."

The boy held it out. The locksmith took it, turned it over in his hands, examined it with the critical eye of the craftsman, noting the flimsy solder of its seams, the cheap lacquer already beginning to scale from its bell. Then he put it upon the highest shelf above the bench, among the old lamps and the broken clocks, where the boy could see it and could not reach it.

"That stays there," he said. "One dollar sixty-five cents. Every Saturday, all winter, you don't play in the street. You come in here and you sort the blanks for me, the brass ones from the iron ones, and you sweep the shop, and you clean the files. And every Saturday I give you ten cents for it, and you put it back in the box—you, yourself, with your own hand. And when it is all back, the dollar and sixty-five cents, then I give you the trumpet. Not before."

The boy looked up at the trumpet upon its shelf, gleaming red and gold in the gaslight, the yellow tassel hanging down. Seventeen Saturdays—it might as well have been seventeen years. His lip quivered, but he did not cry again.

"And now," said Kretschmar, "you go up to bed. No supper. Go wash your face, and go up to bed."

The boy went toward the kitchen door, slowly, his head hanging. At the door he paused and looked back. His father was standing by the bench, his back turned, filling his pipe with his great clumsy fingers, pressing down the tobacco with the ball of his thumb.

"Pa," said the boy.

Kretschmar did not turn round. "Well?"

"Pa—I won't lie no more."

The locksmith struck a match upon the vise and held it to the bowl of his pipe, drawing at it with long, slow puffs, the flame rising and falling. "Go to bed," he said.

The door closed. He heard the boy's feet upon the back stairs, and then Gussie's voice, low, soothing, and the creak of the floor overhead as she followed him up. In a little while she came down again and stood in the doorway of the kitchen, wiping her hands upon her apron, saying nothing, looking at him.

"I put a piece of bread on the chair by his bed," she said at length. "Only bread. With a little butter."

He nodded, without looking at her. She went back to her stove.

For a long time Kretschmar remained there alone in the shop, smoking, his elbows upon the bench, staring at nothing. Outside the fog had come in. It had crept down over the hills and through the streets, silent, grey, impalpable, drowning the street lamps, blurring the lighted windows of the saloon at the corner into vague smudges of orange. The German band had gone. The drays had ceased to pass. Only the cable-cars still clanged by at intervals, their headlights looming suddenly out of the greyness and vanishing again, and from the foghorn at the Heads, miles away, came the long, hoarse, monotonous bellow, like the lowing of some vast beast lost in the dark. The life of the city went on, indifferent, unconcerned; men drank in the saloons, women quarrelled in the tenements, children slept, and in the little shop in Folsom Street the locksmith sat by his bench and looked at his hands.

They lay before him upon the scarred black wood in the yellow light of the gas, enormous, square, hard, ingrained with the dirt of twenty years of labour; good hands, patient hands, that could coax the most stubborn lock to yield, that could shape a key to the thousandth part of an inch. And yet within them, deep within them, lay the other thing, the inheritance, the blind, brute force of the charcoal-burner and of all his forefathers; and he knew now that it would never leave him, that it would lie there waiting all his life, coiled, dormant, ready, and that some day, perhaps, it would be in the boy as well.

He knocked the ashes from his pipe, turned out the gas, and went in to his supper.
