It was a raw evening in the latter part of November, with a wind off the lake that went whistling down Ogden Avenue and drove before it the soot and the shreds of paper and the dry leaves which had not yet been gathered into the gutters. The lamps had been lit for an hour, and in the small flat which Walter Ganz and his wife occupied on the third floor of a yellow brick building near Western Avenue the gas burned with that thin, bluish, uncertain flame which, in buildings of the cheaper sort, speaks so plainly of economy on the part of the owner. There was a front room, called by courtesy the parlor, in which stood a plush settee of a faded wine color, two rocking-chairs, a center-table with a crocheted cover and a lamp upon it of imitation onyx, and on the wall a large crayon enlargement of Mrs. Ganz's mother in a gilt frame. Beyond this was a dining-room, and beyond that again a kitchen no larger than a closet, with a gas-plate and a sink of zinc and one window which gave upon an air-shaft. It was the kind of home which thousands of couples in Chicago at that time were maintaining upon from fifteen to twenty-five dollars a week, and which represented to them not so much a place of rest as a way-station on the road to something better, or, as the case might be, something worse.

Walter Ganz came up the stairs at a little after six, as was his habit, and let himself in with his key. He was a man of thirty-four or -five, of medium height, inclined to be heavy about the shoulders and neck, with a round, good-natured, rather florid face, a small brown mustache which he kept carefully trimmed, and eyes of a pale, indeterminate blue which had in them, when he was at ease, a certain mild cheerfulness, and when he was troubled, as now, a look of furtive and hunted calculation. He wore a gray overcoat of the ready-made variety which had been good two winters before, a derby hat, and a pair of tan gloves which he took off finger by finger as he stood in the narrow hall. For nearly seven years he had been employed as a city salesman by the firm of Pettibone & Hersch, wholesale dealers in hardware and builders' supplies on Lake Street, and had earned in that capacity, with commissions, something like twenty-two dollars a week. But it is a fact, and one which must be stated at once, that for the space of sixteen days he had not been employed by Pettibone & Hersch or by anyone else, and that the leaving of the flat each morning at half-past seven and the returning of it each evening at six was a pantomime which he had been performing for the benefit of his wife.

How this came about need not detain us long. A new manager, a sharp young man from St. Louis, had come into the business in the early fall, and, looking over the accounts of the city men, had found that Ganz's sales had fallen off steadily for two years. There had been no quarrel, no great scene. He had simply been called in one Saturday afternoon and told, in that dry, impersonal fashion which the commercial world reserves for its dismissals, that the firm was "making some changes" and would not require his services after the first of the month. He had come out upon Lake Street with his last envelope in his pocket and had stood for a long time looking at the drays and the trucks and the hurrying clerks, feeling as a man feels who has been struck a blow from behind and does not yet know how badly he is hurt. And then, because he could not bring himself to go home and say it, because he could already see the look that would come into his wife's face, he had said nothing at all.

It is one of the curious weaknesses of temperaments such as his—and they are more numerous than the moralist is willing to admit—that they will choose almost any present evasion rather than a single moment of open pain. They are not liars by intention. They are rather like children who hide a broken dish behind the cupboard, hoping in some vague way that time or chance or a kind Providence will mend it before it is discovered. Ganz had told himself that he would find something within the week, that he would then go home and tell the whole thing as a joke—how old Hersch's new man had let him go and how he had landed something better within five days. But the week had passed, and another, and he had found nothing. He had walked the length of Lake Street and Wabash Avenue and Market Street; he had sat in the outer offices of jobbers and manufacturers' agents; he had answered advertisements in the *Daily News* and stood in line with thirty other men for a place that paid twelve dollars. And each night he had come home and eaten his supper and talked of the weather and of the price of coal, and had gone to bed and lain awake listening to the elevated trains and his own heart.

His wife was in the dining-room when he came in. She was setting the table, and she did not look up at once. Ella Ganz was a woman of thirty, slender, with a quantity of light-brown hair done high on her head in the fashion of the day, a rather thin but pretty face, and gray eyes which, though they could be soft, were more often keen and observing. She had been, before her marriage, a cashier in a restaurant on Madison Street, and she had brought with her from that position a certain sharpness in money matters, a certain alertness to the main chance, which had not always made her husband comfortable. She was not a hard woman, be it said—not by any means. She had loved him, and in her fashion loved him still. But she was one of those natures in whom the craving for the better things of life—for a flat on the North Side, for a silk waist and a sealskin jacket, for a Sunday dinner at a good hotel now and then, for the sense of being looked at and envied and thought well of—burns with a steady and consuming flame. And she had come, in the course of seven years, to measure her husband more and more by his capacity to feed that flame, and to find him, by that measure, wanting.

"Well," he said, coming to the door of the dining-room and trying to make his voice sound as usual, "it's blowing up cold, all right. I wouldn't be surprised if we had snow by morning."

She set down a plate with a little more emphasis than was necessary and looked at him. There was something in that look which he had never seen before, or had seen only in the very worst of their quarrels—a kind of fixed, white, waiting stillness, as of one who has made up her mind to a thing and is only biding the moment.

"Did you have a good day at the store?" she asked.

He felt a sudden coldness at the back of his neck, but he answered, as men will in such cases, with the habit of the lie rather than with any thought.

"Oh, so-so. About the usual. Things are kind of slow just now, with building letting up for the winter."

"Is that so?" she said. "Is that so, Walter?"

She came around the end of the table and stood with one hand resting upon the back of a chair. He saw that her fingers were trembling.

"Mrs. Ruddock was down at the Fair this afternoon," she went on, in a low, controlled voice. "She met Mr. Spearman—you know, that bookkeeper from your place, that comes from her town. And he asked her how you were getting along, and whether you'd found anything yet. He said it was too bad, the way they let you go. He said he thought it was a shame." She paused, and the color came up into her face in two hard red spots. "She came right up here to tell me. She thought I knew. She thought I'd *know*, Walter—my own husband!"

He stood perfectly still. It is a strange thing, the sensation of a long-dreaded blow when it actually falls. There is in it, mingled with the pain, an odd element of relief, as though some tension which has been unbearable has at last been snapped. But this lasted only a moment with Ganz. What followed was a sense of utter nakedness, of being seen through and through, and with it a wild desire to explain, to justify, to put the matter in a better light than it would bear.

"Now, Ella," he began, "now, listen here—"

"How long?" she demanded.

"Well—it was the first of the month. But I didn't want you to worry, see? I thought I'd have something else right away, and then I'd tell you, and it wouldn't amount to anything. That's all there was to it. I didn't want to have you upset."

"The first of the month!" She said it as though she could not credit it. "Over two weeks! And you've been going out of here every morning and coming in every night and sitting down at that table and letting me talk about—" She stopped, and her lips worked. "Where have you been? What have you been doing all day?"

"Looking for work," he said doggedly. "Where do you suppose? I've been all over this town. I've been to every hardware house on Lake Street and half the jobbers on Market. There isn't anything. It's a bad time of year. Everybody says so."

"And you couldn't tell me that? You couldn't come home and say, 'Ella, I've lost my place'? You had to make a fool of me before the whole building? Mrs. Ruddock'll have it all over the place by tomorrow. She was just *dying* to tell me—I could see it in her face."

"Well, I can't help what Mrs. Ruddock does," he said, with a touch of sullenness. "I didn't tell her anything."

"No, you didn't tell anybody anything. That's just it."

She turned away from him and went to the window, where she stood looking out at the flickering lamps of the street and the dim procession of figures bending against the wind. He remained in the doorway, his overcoat still on, his hat in his hand, feeling, as he afterward recalled, very much like a boy who has been called up before the teacher. The gas-jet hissed faintly. From somewhere below came the rattle of dishes and the voice of a child crying. It was the common stuff of the life about them, and yet to these two, at this moment, it seemed to belong to some other world entirely.

What was it that she felt, standing there at the window? Not merely anger, though anger was uppermost. There was in her, too, a sense of fright—the sudden opening of a pit at her feet, the realization that the little structure of their life, which had seemed so solid if so meager, rested upon nothing but the will of a man in an office on Lake Street whom she had never seen. And beyond that, and deeper, was something which she would not have known how to name, but which was in truth a kind of grief—the grief of a woman who has long half-suspected that the man she has married is not equal to the struggle in which they are both engaged, and who now sees that suspicion confirmed beyond any power of denial. She had made excuses for him. She had told herself that he was steady, that he was kind, that he would come along in time. And now this. Not only had he failed, but he had hidden his failure like a child, and she had been the last to know.

"How much money have we got?" she asked, without turning.

He hesitated. "Well, there was the last envelope—and I had a little put by. About forty dollars, I guess. Forty-one."

"And the rent due on the first."

"I know that."

"And the coal man not paid for October. And I owe Schlesinger's eight dollars on that skirt." She turned around. "Forty-one dollars! And you've been riding the street-cars all over town and eating your dinners downtown, I suppose, so I wouldn't notice."

"I've been eating a sandwich," he said. "I haven't been spending anything. I'm not a fool."

The word seemed to strike her strangely, and she laughed—a short, hard, unpleasant laugh which he had never heard from her before.

"Oh, no," she said. "You're not a fool. Not you."

He flushed a deep red and came a step into the room. The weakness that was in him, which had held him silent for sixteen days, now turned, as such weakness so often will, into a kind of blustering resentment.

"See here, Ella," he said, "I don't have to stand here and be talked to like that. I've done the best I could. I've worked for that firm seven years and never missed a day, and they let me out to make room for some young buck the new man brought up from St. Louis. That's not my fault. It's the way things go. A man gets along a little in years and they throw him over. You don't know what it's like down there. You sit home here all day—"

"I sit home!" she cried. "I sit home! And what do I do? I wash and iron and cook and sew and make one dollar go as far as two, and turn my old dresses, and walk six blocks to save a cent on potatoes, and go without everything I ever wanted, so you can have your cigars and your lodge dues—and you tell me I sit home!" Her voice rose and broke, and she put her hand to her throat. "I could have kept my place at Hartley's. Mr. Hartley wanted me to stay. He said I was the best girl he ever had on the desk. I could be making twelve dollars a week right now. And instead I married you because you said—you said—"

She did not finish what he had said. Perhaps she did not remember precisely. But it hung in the air between them nevertheless—all the large, warm, vague promises of a young man in love, of a flat on the North Side and a girl to do the work and a buggy on Sundays and a summer at the lakes, which he had believed as fully as she when he made them, and which the iron facts of the city had long since ground to dust.

Ganz sat down heavily in one of the dining-room chairs. The bluster had gone out of him as quickly as it had come. He was not, at bottom, a fighting man. He looked at the white tablecloth and the two plates and the cheap glass sugar-bowl, and he felt old and tired and beaten.

"I know it," he said finally, in a lower voice. "I know I haven't done what I said. I meant to. God knows I meant to."

There is a curious quality in the spectacle of a man's humiliation which, to some women, is softening, and to others is merely an added provocation. It depends upon the woman, and upon the man, and upon the history that lies between them, and upon a thousand obscure currents of temperament and mood which no one, least of all the participants, can fully trace. For a moment Ella felt the old tenderness stir in her—the memory of him as he had been, eager and laughing and confident, on the excursion boat to Milwaukee that first summer. But it was crowded out almost at once by a colder and more powerful feeling: the feeling of a creature that sees the means of its survival threatened and turns instinctively to save itself. We like to think that love is stronger than this, but in the lower and harder walks of life, where the margin between comfort and want is so narrow, the instinct of self-preservation is very old and very strong, and love, unless it be of the rarest sort, is often obliged to give way before it.

"Meaning to doesn't pay the rent," she said.

"I'll find something. I will, Ella. I heard today that Kimball & Ross might want a man after the first of the year. I'm going over there tomorrow."

"After the first of the year! And what do we do till then?"

"We've got the forty-one dollars."

"Forty-one dollars," she repeated. "And the rent's eighteen."

He made no answer. There was none to make. She came and stood across the table from him, looking down at him, and there was in her face now a set and thoughtful expression which troubled him more than her anger had.

"I'll tell you what I'm going to do," she said. "I'm going down to see Mr. Hartley in the morning. If he hasn't got a place, somebody else will. I'm not going to sit here and wait for the coal man to come and take the stove."

"You don't need to do that," he said quickly. "I won't have my wife going out to work. What would people say?"

"People!" she said. "What do I care what people say? They're going to say it anyhow, now. Mrs. Ruddock's seen to that." She paused, and then added, more quietly but with a significance that was not lost upon him: "Anyhow, I'd rather have my own money in my hand than wait for somebody else's that maybe never comes."

He looked up at her, and in that look there passed between them more than either could have put into words. He saw, dimly but certainly, that something had changed—that she was stepping away from him, not in body, perhaps, not yet, but in that inner region where dependence and loyalty are rooted. She would go back to the cashier's desk; she would handle money again and talk with men who came in from the street, men in good coats with heavy watch-chains, who would admire her quick fingers and her bright hair; she would discover that she could stand alone. And he, sitting here in his half-worn overcoat with his hat on his knee, was powerless to prevent it. He felt this as an animal feels the coming of a storm, without reasoning about it.

"Ella," he said, "you're not—you wouldn't—"

"Wouldn't what?"

But he could not say it. He did not know, in truth, what he had been about to say.

"Nothing," he said. "Only don't be too hard on me. I know I did wrong not to tell you. I was ashamed, I guess. That's all. I was ashamed."

She stood looking at him a moment longer. Then she turned and went into the kitchen, and he heard her lift the lid of the pot upon the stove and set it down again. When she came back she had the dish of potatoes and a plate of chops, and she put them down upon the table without a word.

"You'd better take off your coat," she said at last. "Supper's getting cold."

He rose and took off his coat and hung it in the hall, with his hat above it, and came back and sat down. She sat down opposite him. They ate in silence for some time. The wind shook the window-sash, and from the street came the clang of a cable-car bell, faint and far away. Once he looked up and found her eyes upon him, but she dropped them at once to her plate, and he could not tell what was in them.

"Is it good?" she asked presently, in a flat voice. It was the question she had asked every night for seven years.

"Yes," he said. "It's fine."

And that was all. They did not speak of it again that evening. When the dishes were done she sat in the front room under the onyx lamp, mending a stocking, and he sat across from her with the evening paper, turning to the columns of want advertisements and running his finger slowly down them, one after another. Neither of them was thinking of what was before their eyes. Each was thinking of the other, and of the morning, and of the long, gray, uncertain days which stretched beyond it. And over them, as over the whole vast, roaring, indifferent city, the forces which neither understood—of trade and chance and appetite and the unending struggle for a place in the sun—moved on their blind and ponderous way, shaping these two small lives as a river shapes the pebbles in its bed, without malice and without pity, and without the least awareness that they were there.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Theodore Dreiser, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
It was in the late fall of the year 1903, on one of those gray, smoky afternoons which Chicago, in its raw and as yet unfinished state, seemed especially to produce, that Mrs. Nora Lindquist, of Warsaw, Indiana, descended from a North Clark Street car and stood for a moment on the curb, looking about her with that mingled air of curiosity and apprehension which is so characteristic of the provincial in the presence of the great city. She was a woman of thirty-two or three, of medium height, inclined already to that heaviness of figure which bearing children and much housework had brought upon her, with a round, pleasant, rather freckled face, brown hair worn in a plain knot under a hat of black straw which had been retrimmed twice, and eyes of a soft, uncertain gray. Her coat, a brown cloth affair purchased three winters before at Kessler's Dry Goods in Warsaw, was decent enough, but she had become aware within the hour, and with a sinking sensation which she could not quite explain, that it was not what was being worn here. The women who passed her, some of them, wore coats with great puffed sleeves and fur at the collar, and hats with wings and plumes that nodded as they walked, and they moved with a briskness and an assurance which seemed to say that they knew exactly where they were going and why.

She had in her gloved hand a letter, and upon this letter, in a sprawling, careless, rather showy script, was an address: The Ashbury, Number 14, Belden Avenue. It was from her cousin, Harriet Berkey, or Hattie, as she had always been called at home, whom she had not seen in eleven years.

Now the history of these two, in so far as it bears upon what follows, may be quickly told. They had been raised within three miles of each other, outside of Warsaw, their fathers being brothers, both of them small farmers of a thrifty, Lutheran, God-fearing sort, who believed in work and in very little else. As girls they had been inseparable. They had gone to the same district school, sat upon the same bench at the same revival meetings, picked blackberries along the same fences in July, and confided to each other those vague, half-formed longings which come to all young creatures in whom life is beginning to stir. But there had been a difference between them, even then, which neither had understood. Nora had been the docile one, the one who took what was given and was content, or seemed so. Hattie, on the other hand, had been restless, quick, vain of her figure and her hair, which was a rich, coppery red, and given to strange moods of discontent in which she would stand at the end of the lane and look down the road toward the town as though she expected something to come up it for her. When she was seventeen nothing came, and so she went, taking the train for Chicago one March morning with eleven dollars and a carpetbag, and leaving behind her a note which had caused her mother to take to her bed for a week.

For a long time thereafter there had been only rumors. She was working in a department store. She was working in a candy factory. She had been seen, by a Warsaw man who had business in the city, riding in a carriage on Michigan Avenue with a gentleman. She had married. She had not married. Then, about five years since, letters had begun to come, at long intervals, to her mother, and with them, occasionally, money, ten and twenty dollars at a time, which the old woman accepted silently and spent on the mortgage, and about which nothing was said. And it was to this cousin, now Mrs. Harriet Thorne, as she signed herself, that Nora had written when she learned that she was to accompany her husband, Carl, to Chicago, where he had been called to see a lawyer about a small inheritance from an uncle—a matter of some four hundred dollars, which to the Lindquists represented a considerable sum.

The Ashbury, when she found it, proved to be a tall, new building of yellow pressed brick with bay windows rising one above the other and a vestibule of white marble in which there were brass letter-boxes and a row of little bells with names beside them in neat black type. Nora, who had expected she knew not what—a boarding house perhaps, or a flat over a store—was a little overawed. She pressed the bell marked "Thorne" with a hesitating finger, and after a moment there was a curious buzzing click at the inner door, which she did not at first understand, and then a voice, high and laughing, came down the stair well.

"Push it, Nora! Push the door! Oh, you goose, come on up!"

She pushed, and the door gave, and she climbed, and on the third landing there was Hattie.

It is one of the curious facts of our existence, and one which the moralists have never sufficiently explained, that the face and form of a human being are so largely the product of the conditions under which that being lives. Poverty pinches and coarsens; ease and luxury smooth and soften. Hard labor in the open air bronzes the skin and thickens the hands, while the shaded, cushioned life of the well-to-do produces a pallor and a delicacy which we have come, rightly or wrongly, to associate with refinement. And so it was here. For the creature who stood at the top of the stairs, with her arms out, was not the thin, freckled, hungry-eyed farm girl whom Nora remembered, but a woman of fashion, or what passed for such in the eyes of Warsaw—tall, full-bosomed, beautifully corseted, in a house gown of some pale green silky stuff with a great deal of lace at the throat and wrists, her red hair done high in a pompadour and glinting with a tortoise-shell comb, her skin white and fine, her lips perhaps a little redder than nature intended. A faint, sweet odor of violet came from her. On one hand, as she embraced her cousin, Nora caught the glitter of a ring with a stone in it so large that it seemed to her it could not possibly be real.

"Oh, Nora! Nora! Well, if this isn't the grandest thing! Let me look at you. Why, you haven't changed a bit—not one single bit. Come in. Come in this minute. I've got the kettle on. You'll have tea, won't you? Or would you rather have coffee? I don't care what you have. Oh, my, but I'm glad!"

And she drew her in, chattering, and closed the door.

The room into which Nora was ushered was, to her eyes, a marvel. It was not large—the flats of that day were not—but it was crowded with such things as she had seen only in the windows of the better stores, or in the illustrated pages of the magazines which sometimes found their way to Warsaw. There was a carpet of deep red, very soft underfoot, and over it, before the little grate where a coal fire glowed, a white bearskin rug with the head still on and glass eyes that stared. There were heavy portieres of green plush at the doorway into what was evidently a dining room, and lace curtains at the bay window, and a piano—an upright, of polished rosewood—with a fringed silk scarf thrown over it and a vase of yellow chrysanthemums atop. There were pictures in gilt frames, a great many of them: a girl with a dove, a shepherd and some sheep, a large engraving of some ladies in a garden. There was a lamp with a shade of red glass beads that tinkled when Hattie brushed against it. There was a Morris chair and a divan heaped with pillows of satin and velvet, upon which Nora was presently seated, sinking into it farther than she had expected, so that she clutched at her purse.

"Now take off that coat," said Hattie, "and that hat, and let me get the tea. No, don't you move. You just sit."

Nora took off the coat and the hat, conscious as she did so of her shirtwaist, which was clean but had been washed many times, and of her skirt, which had been let out at the waist after the birth of her youngest. She folded the coat with the lining outward and laid it beside her, and then sat with her hands in her lap and looked about her while from the kitchen came the clatter of cups and Hattie's voice, raised so as to carry.

"How's Aunt Minnie? And Uncle John? Is he still as cranky as ever? And how's that husband of yours? Carl, isn't it? I never saw him, did I? He came after my time."

"Pa's poorly," said Nora. "His back. He don't get around much. Ma's all right. Carl's well. He's down at the lawyer's now, on Dearborn Street. He'll be along for me at six, if that's all right."

"Why, of course it's all right. I want to see him. I want to see what kind of a man got you." And Hattie came in, bearing a tray on which were a china teapot with pink roses painted on it, and cups to match, and a plate of little cakes from a bakery, iced in white and pink. She set it on a small inlaid table and sat down in the Morris chair opposite, crossing her knees in a way that Nora had never seen any woman do, and showing a slipper of bronze kid and an ankle in a black silk stocking.

"Now," she said, pouring. "Tell me everything."

But it is not so easy, after eleven years, to tell everything. The mind does not know where to begin; the heart is shy. And between these two there had come up, in the instant of their meeting, a thing which neither could have named, but which each felt—a sense of distance, of the paths that had divided, of a world on the one side and a world on the other, with a gulf between which affection might reach across but could not close. Nora talked, at first haltingly, then more freely as the tea warmed her. She told of the children—there were three, Elsie, who was nine, and Walter, who was six, and the baby, Minnie, named for her grandmother, who was not yet two. She told of the house in Warsaw, a frame cottage on Lake Street which they were buying on time from the building and loan, and of the garden, and the chickens, and of Carl's work, which was carpentry, and which was steady enough in the summers but slack in the winters, so that they had to watch. She told of the church, and the new minister, and of who had married and who had died, of the Hostetter girl who had gone wrong and been sent away to an aunt in Ohio, and of old Mrs. Riegel who had been found dead in her chair with her Bible in her lap. And Hattie listened, nodding, laughing, exclaiming, but with a look in her eyes, at times, which Nora could not read—a look that was at once amused and pitying and a little sad, as though she were hearing an account of some far-off country which she had once visited and was glad to have left.

"And are you happy, Nora?" she asked suddenly, setting down her cup. "Really and truly?"

The question took Nora unawares. It was not one which people asked in Warsaw. One was married; one had children; one did one's work and went to church and paid what one owed. Happiness was a word that belonged to hymns and to the hereafter.

"Why, yes," she said slowly. "I guess I am. Carl's good to me. He don't drink. The children are healthy." She paused. "It's hard sometimes. Winters, mostly. But I guess everybody has it hard sometimes."

"Not everybody," said Hattie, and laughed, and looked at the fire.

There was a little silence then, and in it Nora gathered her courage. For there was a thing she wished to know, and dreaded to ask, and the asking of it had been on her mind all the way up in the train from Indiana, through the flat, brown, stubbled fields, and the little towns with their water tanks and grain elevators, and on into the smoke and noise and endless streets of this great, roaring, heartless place.

"Hattie," she said, "is—is Mr. Thorne here? Will I meet him?"

Her cousin did not answer at once. She took up one of the little cakes, looked at it, and put it down again. Then she turned and looked at Nora with an expression that was half defiance and half appeal.

"He doesn't live here, exactly," she said. "He comes. He's in the Board of Trade. Grain. He's got a house—over on the West Side. With a family." She paused, and her chin went up a little. "He's been mighty good to me, Nora. Mighty good. Five years now. There's not many would be so good."

Nora said nothing. She could not have spoken if she had wished. The blood had come into her face, and she looked down at her hands, which were red and roughened from the washtub, lying in her lap against the worn serge of her skirt. In Warsaw there was a word for what Hattie was, a hard and ugly word which was spoken in whispers, and Nora had heard it applied to the Hostetter girl and to others, and had herself, God forgive her, nodded in agreement. And yet here was Hattie—Hattie, with whom she had slept in the same bed under the eaves of her grandmother's house when they were children, listening to the rain on the shingles; Hattie, who had held her hand at the funeral of her little brother Paul; Hattie, who had given her the half of every apple and the larger half of every stick of candy—sitting before her in green silk and lace with a fire burning and a piano in the corner and a diamond on her finger. And Nora could not, try as she might, summon up the horror which she felt she ought to feel. What she felt instead, and what shamed her far more, was something very like envy.

For what is morality, after all, but the code which a given society has found it convenient to impose upon its members, and which these members, for the most part, accept because they know no other, or because they lack the strength or the opportunity to break it? Nora Lindquist had been good, as the world measures goodness, all her life. She had married the man her parents approved; she had borne his children and cooked his meals and scrubbed his floors; she had gone without a new coat for three winters so that the payments on the house might be met. And what had it brought her? A tired back, roughened hands, a waistline gone, and the prospect of thirty or forty more years of the same, until she too should be found dead in her chair some evening, with her Bible in her lap. And Hattie, who had been bad, sat here amid luxury and warmth and ease, with soft white hands and a face as smooth as a girl's. If there was a God who rewarded virtue and punished sin—and Nora had always believed that there was—He did not seem, at least in this world, to be attending very closely to His business.

"You think I'm awful," said Hattie softly.

"No," said Nora. "No, I don't, Hattie. I don't know what I think." And then, to her own astonishment, she began to cry—not loudly, but quietly, with the tears running down her freckled cheeks, and she fumbled in her purse for a handkerchief and could not find one.

Hattie was beside her in an instant, on the divan, her arm about her shoulders, pressing upon her a little square of fine linen edged with lace and smelling of violets.

"There, now," she said. "There, now, Nora. Don't. I didn't mean to make you cry. Oh, I'm a beast. I oughtn't to have told you. Only I couldn't lie to you. I never could lie to you, not even when we were kids. Remember when I broke Grandma's blue pitcher and you said you did it, and got switched for it? You never told. I've thought of that a hundred times."

"I remember," said Nora, and laughed through her tears.

And then, somehow, the gulf narrowed, if it did not close, and they were girls again, or nearly so, talking of the old days—of the creek behind Grandmother Berkey's farm where they had waded in summer and slid on the ice in winter; of the sorghum mill in the fall, and the smell of the boiling syrup; of the threshing dinners, when the long tables were set up in the yard under the maples and the men came in from the fields, sweating and laughing, and ate prodigiously; of the young schoolmaster, Mr. Eckhart, with whom both of them had been in love at thirteen, and who had married a girl from Goshen and moved to Iowa; of the night the barn burned, and the horses screaming; of the red-haired peddler who had come every spring with his wagonload of tinware and ribbons and had once given Hattie a little mirror in a brass frame which she had kept for years.

"I've got it yet," said Hattie suddenly, and rose and went into the other room, and came back with it—a cheap thing, tarnished, the glass cracked across one corner. "I brought it with me when I came. It was in the carpetbag. I don't know why I kept it."

She stood holding it, looking into it, and Nora, looking at her, saw something in her face which she had not seen before—a weariness, a shadow under the eyes which the powder did not altogether conceal, and the beginning of fine lines at the corners of the mouth. Hattie was thirty-one. In a few years more she would be thirty-five, and then forty, and the man from the Board of Trade, who had been so good, would perhaps be good no longer, or would die, or would find another. And then what? There was no house on Lake Street for Hattie, no children, no building and loan, no church to go to on Sunday where she would be received. There was only this—these rooms, these things, this warmth—and they were not hers, not really. They were lent, as her beauty was lent, and the lender would one day call them in.

It came to Nora then, dimly, as such truths come to simple minds, that neither of them had won, and neither lost; that they were two creatures caught up and carried by forces which they had not made and could not control—the force of hunger for things, and of beauty, and of youth, and of the fear of want; the force of custom and of family and of the little town with its watching eyes—and that the one had been carried this way and the other that, and that was all. Hattie had been born with that within her which cried out for color and ease and the bright lights of the city, and the city had answered, as it answers so many, with a gift that was also a snare. And she, Nora, had been born with that within her which asked for safety and the good opinion of her neighbors, and Warsaw had answered, giving her just that and nothing more. Who was to say which was the better bargain?

At six o'clock the bell rang, and it was Carl—a tall, rawboned, sandy-haired man of thirty-five, in his Sunday suit of blue serge, which was too short in the sleeves, holding his derby in his big hands and looking about him with an awkwardness that was almost painful. Hattie was charming to him. She gave him a chair and a cup of tea, which he held as though he feared it might break, and asked him about the inheritance, and laughed at his slow jokes, and told him that Nora had been the prettiest girl in Kosciusko County and that he was a lucky man, at which he reddened to the roots of his hair and said he guessed he knew it. And Nora, watching her, thought that she had never seen anyone so beautiful, nor so sad.

When they left, Hattie kissed her at the door, and pressed something into her hand, folded small. "For the children," she whispered. "Christmas. Don't you dare say no. And don't tell Carl if you don't want."

On the street car going back down Clark Street to the little hotel near the Polk Street depot, with the lamps coming on and the windows of the stores ablaze and the crowds surging along the sidewalks in the cold, Nora unfolded it in her lap, under cover of her purse. It was a fifty-dollar bill. She looked at it a long time. Then she folded it again and put it away, and sat with her hands clasped upon her purse, looking out at the lighted city going by—the saloons and theaters and restaurants, the hurrying figures, the carriages, the great buildings rising into the smoky dark—and thinking of the creek, and the ice, and two little girls in red mittens holding hands as they slid, shrieking, from one bank to the other.

"Your cousin seems like a real nice lady," said Carl beside her, after a while.

"Yes," said Nora. "She is."

And that was all she ever said.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Theodore Dreiser, depicting the following scene: A parent reprimanding a young child.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
It was in the late spring of a year when wages in the yards and shops of the West Side of Chicago were none too good, and when men who had been earning eleven and twelve dollars a week were glad enough to be earning nine, that the incident here set down took place in the small frame cottage of Thomas Wenzel, car-repairer, in Throop Street. It was not a large incident, as the world reckons such things. No newspaper would have troubled itself with it, and no neighbor, unless it were Mrs. Schaub, who kept the little candy and notion store at the corner, and who had a sharp ear for the doings of her customers, would have known anything about it at all. Yet in its way it was as illustrative of the forces which play upon all human beings, the great and the small, the wise and the unwise, as any battle or bankruptcy or scandal of which the papers make so much, and for that reason, if for no other, it may be worth the telling.

Thomas Wenzel was at this time a man of thirty-eight, stocky, rather heavy of shoulder, with a short sandy beard and a pair of pale blue eyes that had in them something of the patient, wondering look of an ox that has been long in harness. He had come over from Hesse as a boy of fifteen, had worked first on a farm near Belleville, then in a brickyard at Joliet, and finally, by dint of a slow and dogged industry which was the only gift life had seen fit to bestow upon him, had arrived at his present position in the shops of the railway, where he earned, when there was work, a dollar and seventy-five cents a day. Out of this he paid nine dollars a month for the cottage, which consisted of four small rooms and a lean-to kitchen, all of them heated in winter by a single soft-coal stove; he fed and clothed a wife and three children; he contributed a quarter each Sunday to the little Lutheran church in Racine Avenue; and he laid by, when he could, which was not often, a dollar or two toward that dim and ever-receding day when he should own a house of his own and be beholden to no landlord. It was a narrow life, a grinding life, and he knew it, though he would have been at a loss to say so in words. What he felt rather than thought was that the world was a hard place, full of temptations and pitfalls, of men who drank and gambled and came to nothing, of women who painted their faces and went to the bad, and that the only safety for a poor man lay in honesty, in thrift, and in the fear of God. These three things he held to as a drowning man might hold to a spar, and with something of the same desperation.

His wife, Hannah, was of a softer mould. She was a thin, pale, fair-haired woman, a little bent already from the washtub and the cookstove, who had been born in Milwaukee of German parents and who had in her, for all her drudgery, a certain wistful fondness for pretty things which she had long since given up any hope of possessing. She liked a bit of ribbon, a picture in a magazine, the sight of the fine carriages that went by on Ashland Avenue of a Sunday afternoon. She did not argue with her husband, for she had learned long ago that argument with him was useless, but she softened, where she could, the hard edges of his rule, and the children, quite naturally, turned to her rather than to him when they were in trouble.

Of the three children, it is the second, Albert, a boy of seven, with whom we are concerned. He was a slight, dark-eyed, eager little fellow, more like his mother than his father, and possessed of a temperament which was, in that household, a decided misfortune. For he was sensitive, imaginative, easily excited by color and sound and the movement of things, and drawn, as a moth is drawn to a lamp, by whatever glittered or shone. A brass band going by on the street would hold him rooted to the curb until it had passed out of hearing. The gilded sign of a saloon, the red and green bottles in the window of the drug store at the corner of Twelfth Street, the bright tin toys that hung in festoons in the doorway of the Jew's shop on Halsted, were to him so many visions of a world more wonderful than any he knew. And above all, and most dangerous of all, there were the glass jars in the window of Mrs. Schaub's store, filled with licorice whips and horehound drops and striped peppermint sticks and those round, hard, many-colored balls which the children called jawbreakers, and which could be had, two for a penny, by anyone who possessed a penny.

Albert did not possess a penny. He had never, in so far as he could remember, possessed one for longer than it took to walk from the place where it had been given him to Mrs. Schaub's counter. His father did not believe in giving money to children. It made them wasteful, he said; it taught them to want things; and wanting things was the beginning of all evil. And so the boy would stand before that window, his nose pressed flat against the glass, his eyes going from jar to jar, and dream. What he dreamed it would be difficult to say. Not of the candy merely, though that was a part of it. Rather of a kind of richness, a fullness and brightness of living, which the candy somehow stood for, and which was so entirely absent from the bare little rooms in Throop Street.

Now it so happened that on a certain Thursday in May, Hannah Wenzel, having been paid a dollar by a neighbor for a day's washing, had put the money, in the form of four silver dimes and a number of nickels and pennies, into a small black purse which she kept in the top drawer of the bureau in the front room. And it further happened that Albert, coming in from the street that afternoon while his mother was out in the yard hanging up clothes and his older sister was minding the baby in the kitchen, saw the drawer standing a little open, and the purse within it. What passed through his mind at that moment no one, least of all himself, could have told. It was not a reasoned thing. There was no weighing of right and wrong, no deliberate choice of evil. There was only the purse, and the memory of the jars, and a sudden, overwhelming impulse, as chemic and as blind as the impulse which turns a plant toward the sun. He opened the purse, took out a nickel, closed it again, and was gone from the house before he had fairly realized what he had done.

At Mrs. Schaub's he bought ten jawbreakers, a licorice whip, and a stick of peppermint, and he ate the greater part of them sitting on the curb behind the coal yard, where no one could see him. They were very good. And yet, even as he ate them, something had begun to stir in him which spoiled their sweetness, a vague, uneasy heaviness, a sense of having stepped outside some invisible line, which grew rather than lessened as the afternoon wore on. By the time he came home to supper he had two jawbreakers left, hidden in the pocket of his knee-pants, and a face so guilty that his mother, had she not been tired and preoccupied, must have noticed it at once.

It was not his mother, however, but his father who discovered the theft. Thomas Wenzel had a habit, which his wife found irksome but did not oppose, of going over the household money each evening after supper, counting it, and entering the sum in a small, greasy account book in which he kept a record of every cent that came into or went out of the house. On this particular evening, sitting at the kitchen table under the smoky lamp, with his spectacles on his nose and his stubby fingers moving slowly among the coins, he found that there were ninety-five cents in the purse instead of a dollar.

"Hannah," he said, looking up, "how much did Mrs. Kranz pay you?"

"A dollar," said his wife from the sink. "Why?"

"Did you spend some?"

"No. I put it right in the drawer."

He counted it again, slowly, his lips moving. It was still ninety-five cents. And then, as he sat there frowning, his eye fell upon Albert, who was sitting on the low stool by the stove, very still, with his hands between his knees, and something in the boy's attitude, in the stiffness of his small back and the way he would not look up, told the man everything.

"Albert," he said. "Come here."

The boy came. He came slowly, dragging his feet a little, and stood before his father with his eyes on the floor.

"Did you take a nickel out of your mother's purse?"

There was a silence. In that silence many things might have happened. Had the boy been of a bolder or a more calculating disposition, he might have lied, and very possibly been believed, for the evidence against him was nothing more than a look. But he was neither bold nor calculating. He was only frightened, and ashamed, and possessed by that terrible inability to dissemble which is the mark of so many sensitive natures. His lip began to tremble.

"Yes," he whispered.

Thomas Wenzel put down his spectacles. It is necessary, if one is to judge him fairly, to understand what that admission meant to him. To the outsider, the affluent, comfortable observer who has never had to count his pennies, it may seem a small thing indeed, a nickel, a little candy, a childish lapse such as all children are guilty of at one time or another. But to Thomas Wenzel it was not small. It was the very thing he had feared and fought against all his life, appearing suddenly in his own house, in his own child. He had seen men go down. He had seen, in the brickyard at Joliet, a young fellow of his own age who had begun by pilfering small sums from the paymaster's box and had ended, five years later, in the penitentiary across the road. He had seen families in this very street broken up and scattered because the father drank, or stole, or could not keep a job. The world, as he saw it, was a vast and pitiless machine which would grind to powder anyone who stepped out of the narrow path of rectitude, and his son had just stepped out of it. That the step was a small one made no difference. All great falls began with small steps. Was it not so written? And who was he, a poor ignorant workingman, to know where this one might lead?

So it was that something more than anger rose in him at that moment, something compounded of fear, and of shame, and of a dim, half-conscious bitterness against the life which had made him what he was, and which now seemed bent upon taking even his children from him. "Thomas," said his wife from the sink, in a low voice. "He's only little."

"Little!" He turned on her. "So he is little. And when he is big? When he is big, what then? He takes from the till where he works. He takes from his boss. And then they put him in jail, and then what do you say? He was only little?" He turned back to the child. "Look at me."

The boy looked up. His face was wet, his dark eyes swimming, his mouth drawn down into that square, quivering shape which a child's mouth takes when grief has passed beyond all control. It was a pitiful sight, and perhaps somewhere in the father's heart it was felt as such. But the man was caught now in the current of his own emotion, and it carried him on.

"Do you know what God does to thieves? Do you know what the Bible says? 'Thou shalt not steal.' It is one of the commandments. You know the commandments. Pastor Mueller teaches you. And you break it. In your own house you break it, from your own mother." He shook his head slowly, heavily, as if the weight of the thing were almost more than he could bear. "I work all my life. All my life I am honest. Never once do I take a penny that is not mine. Never once. And now my own boy."

He stopped. There was a silence in the little kitchen, broken only by the boy's sobbing and the ticking of the cheap nickel clock on the shelf above the stove. The older girl, Lena, had come to the doorway with the baby in her arms and stood there staring, round-eyed. Hannah Wenzel had turned from the sink and was wiping her hands slowly on her apron, her thin face drawn and anxious.

"Have you any left?" said the father at length.

The boy put his hand into his pocket and drew out the two jawbreakers, one red and one green, a little sticky now from the warmth of his body. He held them out on his palm. "Tomorrow," he said, "you go to Mrs. Schaub and you tell her what you did. You tell her you stole the money she has in her drawer. And on Saturday you carry coal for Mr. Brandt, and what he pays you, you give to your mother. Every cent. And tonight you go to bed with no supper tomorrow either, only bread. He did not quite know why he put it aside. Perhaps it was the look on his wife's face. Perhaps it was something in the child himself, some quality of fragility and helplessness which made the thought of striking him seem, even to this rigid and unimaginative man, a thing not to be done. At any rate he did not do it, and the boy, still sobbing, was sent off to the little back bedroom which he shared with his sister, and the door was closed upon him.

What the child felt, lying there in the dark on the hard straw mattress, with the sounds of the household coming faintly to him through the thin board wall, it would take a wiser pen than this to set down fully. There was shame in it, certainly, a deep and burning shame, and fear of God, whom he pictured, after the manner of Pastor Mueller's sermons, as a vast and bearded and very angry old man seated somewhere above the clouds, keeping a book not unlike his father's account book in which every sin was entered. There was misery at his father's anger, and a dread of the morrow and of Mrs. Schaub's sharp eyes. But there was something else too, something which he could not have named and which his father would not have understood, a kind of dull, bewildered resentment, not against his father exactly, nor against God, but against the whole order of things which set the bright jars in the window and then forbade him to have what was in them. Why should there be such things, if one could not have them? Why should Mrs. Schaub's window be so beautiful, and his own house so bare? He did not know. No one had ever told him. And lying there, with his face in the thin pillow and the taste of peppermint still faintly in his mouth, he felt for the first time, dimly and without words, that vast and insoluble disproportion between desire and possession which is perhaps the oldest and most universal of all human griefs.

In the kitchen, meanwhile, Thomas Wenzel sat for a long time at the table without moving. He had put away the account book and the purse, and his wife had finished the dishes and gone in to put the baby down, and still he sat there, his heavy hands lying loosely before him, his eyes on the lamp. The anger had gone out of him now, and what was left was a kind of weary heaviness, an aching sense of something wrong which he could neither define nor mend. He had done his duty. He was sure of that. A father must punish wrongdoing; otherwise the child grows up wicked. And yet he could not rid himself of the memory of the boy's face, and of the two jawbreakers lying on that small, sticky palm, and of the way the child had looked at him, not defiantly, but with a kind of terrible, uncomprehending appeal, as if asking for something which his father did not know how to give.

After a while he got up and went to the door of the back bedroom and stood listening. The sobbing had stopped. He opened the door softly and looked in. In the faint light from the kitchen he could see the boy lying on his side, asleep, one arm flung up over his head, his cheeks still streaked with dried tears. He looked very small. Thomas Wenzel stood there for some minutes, his hand on the latch, his heavy face working in a way that no one had ever seen it work. Then he closed the door again and went back to the table and sat down.

"Hannah," he said, when his wife came out again, "maybe Saturday, if he carries the coal, I give him a penny for himself."

His wife looked at him, and something softened in her tired face. But she said nothing, for she knew him, and knew that he would very likely not do it, or that if he did, he would give it in such a manner as to rob it of half its sweetness. And in this she was right. For Thomas Wenzel was what life had made him, as Albert was what life was making him, and neither of them could have been otherwise. The forces which had shaped the one, the poverty, the fear, the narrow creed, the long years of grinding toil, were even now at work upon the other, and would go on working, silently and inexorably, long after this small evening in Throop Street had been forgotten by everyone save, perhaps, the boy himself. Such is the way of things. We punish in our children the very hungers which the world has planted in them, and which it has refused, in ourselves, to satisfy; and we call it righteousness, and lie awake, not knowing why we are sad.

It was a little after eight o'clock of a raw November evening when Harvey Lusk, a clerk of some twelve years' standing in the shipping department of the Ohio Wholesale Hardware Company, let himself into the three-room flat on Bancroft Street, Toledo, which for the past six years he and his wife, Ida, had occupied together. And at once, even before he had hung his derby and his worn brown overcoat on the hook behind the door, he sensed that something was wrong. For the lamp in the little front room, ordinarily turned low and left burning for him upon the center table, was turned high, too high, so that the chimney was smudged with a faint ring of soot. And beside it, under the yellow glare, lay an envelope, long and buff-colored, of the kind that the Mutual Savings & Loan sent out once in each quarter, and which he, by a ruse that had served him well enough for a time, had arranged to have directed to him at the office rather than here. How, then, had it come? And opened? He stood quite still, his hand still upon the knob of the door, and felt the blood go out of his face and then come back with an uncomfortable rush to his ears.

For it must be explained that Harvey Lusk, a man of forty-one, of medium height, rather heavy-shouldered and soft of build, with thinning sandy hair and pale, uncertain blue eyes that gave him at times an air of mild apology, had been, for upwards of a year now, engaged in a secret enterprise of which his wife knew nothing. Some fourteen months before, through the agency of one Ed Hollister, a traveling man for a varnish concern whom he had come to know at the office, he had been drawn into the purchase of certain lots in a proposed suburb to be called Maumee Heights, lying several miles to the south and west of the city along a projected car line. The car line, as Hollister had represented it, was a certainty. The lots, so Hollister said, would treble in value inside of two years. And Harvey, who had been watching for twelve years the slow, almost imperceptible accretion of their savings at the rate of four and a half per cent (eleven hundred and forty dollars, the whole fruit of his and Ida's skimping and self-denial, intended, as both of them had long said, for a little house of their own), had been seized with a fever which he could not now very well account for even to himself. To be something more than a clerk! To walk into the office some day with a check for three or four thousand dollars in his pocket, and say to old Tuttle, the manager, that he was through! To buy Ida a sealskin coat such as Mrs. Rennick, the doctor's wife across the way, wore to church! These were the visions, cheap and gaudy as a chromo, and yet compelling as all such visions are to the starved, which had led him by degrees to draw out first two hundred, then three hundred and fifty, and at last nearly the whole of the account. And the car line had not come. And Hollister had gone to Indianapolis. And the lots—well, the lots were there still, a stretch of wet, stubbled pasture with a few weathered stakes in it, and a sign, now half blown down, which read MAUMEE HEIGHTS—THE COMING SUBURB.

He hung up his coat now very slowly, as though by delaying he might somehow alter what was before him. Then he turned. And there in the doorway of the little kitchen, drying her hands upon a gingham apron, stood Ida.

She was a woman of thirty-eight, small, rather thin, with a sallow, careful face which in her girlhood in Defiance had been called pretty, and which even now, when she was pleased, had a kind of pinched sweetness about it. But she was not pleased now. Her lips were drawn together into a thin line, and her eyes, which were brown and small and very steady, were fixed upon him with an expression which he had seen in them only once or twice before in all their married life—a look not so much of anger as of a cold, settled, appraising contempt, as though she were seeing him for the first time and did not like what she saw.

"Well," she said, "you're late."

"Yes, I—we had a car of stoves come in at five. Tuttle wanted it checked tonight." This was true, as it happened, and yet as he said it he was conscious that it sounded like a lie, and that she would take it for one.

"Supper's on the back of the stove. It's been there since six." She did not move from the doorway.

"I'm not very hungry." He went toward the table, not to the envelope, but around it, as one might skirt a hole in the floor, and sat down heavily in the Morris chair by the window. Outside, the arc light at the corner swung a little in the wind, sending a pale, shifting radiance across the wet pavement and the bare, dripping branches of the one maple that stood before the house. A street car went by, clanging, its windows full of tired faces. He looked at it rather than at her.

"Aren't you going to ask me what that is?" she said at last.

"What what is?"

"Harvey Lusk, don't you dare." Her voice did not rise, and that was the worst of it. Had she screamed, had she wept, he would have known better what to do. "Don't you dare sit there and act as though you didn't see it. Mr. Fenwick brought it. He came here himself, this afternoon, about three. He said they'd been sending things to you at the office and you hadn't answered, and he thought—he thought maybe there was some mistake, because he knew it was a joint account and I'd always been the one to come in and sign. He was very nice about it. Very nice." She laughed, a short, dry sound. "He sat right there in that chair and told me there's sixty-two dollars left. Sixty-two dollars. Out of eleven hundred and forty."

Harvey said nothing. What was there to say? He could feel his heart beating, slow and thick, and a kind of nausea rising in him, compounded of shame and fear and also—oddly, and this he could not have explained—of a dull resentment, as though it were she, and not he, who had done something wrong. For had he not done it for her? Partly? Or at least for the two of them? And was it his fault if Hollister had lied, or if the street railway people had changed their plans? Could anybody have foreseen that? And yet! And yet! He knew as well as she did, in that inner chamber of the mind where we do not lie to ourselves, or at least not very successfully, that it was not for her. It had been for himself—for that cheap, flaring dream of being somebody.

"Where is it?" she went on. "That's all I want to know. Where is it? Did you—" and here for the first time her voice faltered a little, and something came into her face that was not contempt but fear—"is it a woman?"

"A woman!" He sat up, really astonished, and for a moment almost relieved, because here at least was an accusation he could deny with a whole heart. "Good Lord, Ida, no! What do you take me for?"

"Well, and what if I did?" he flared, stung at last into a feeble defiance. "What if I did look? Is a man to go on all his life checking stoves in a freight shed at seventy dollars a month and never even look? Is that what you want? Is that all you want? Well, I don't. I didn't. "Something better," she repeated slowly, as though tasting the words. "Something better. I could stand the money. We've been poor before. They always do.

But would they? He looked at her and was not sure.

"Ida," he said again, and got up, and went over to her, and stood beside her chair, awkwardly, his hand hovering above her shoulder. "Ida, listen. I'll make it up. I swear I will. I promise you."

She did not answer for a long time. Then she sat up, and wiped her eyes with the corner of the apron, quite deliberately, and looked up at him. And what he saw in her face then he was to remember for many a year afterward—not forgiveness, exactly, nor yet its opposite, but a kind of final, weary knowledge, as though she had just added up a long column of figures and found the sum to be what she had always, in some secret place, feared it would be.

"Two years," she said. "Three years. I'll be forty-one, Harvey. And you'll be forty-four. And Baines's place will go to young Kessler, because Tuttle likes him, and you know it. I've heard enough. I'm tired."

"But you'll—you're not going to—" He did not know how to say it. Leave? Go back to Defiance, to her mother and her married sister and their pitying, knowing glances? "I don't know what I'm going to do," she said. "I'm going to wash up the supper things. That's what I'm going to do. And then I'm going to bed." She rose, and smoothed the apron, and picked up the buff-colored envelope from the table, and looked at it a moment, and then, very carefully, as one might put away a thing of value, slipped it into the pocket of her apron. And she went back into the kitchen. And presently he heard the clatter of the pump at the sink, and the scrape of the pans, and the small, ordinary, domestic sounds that he had heard every night for twelve years and had never once listened to before.

He stood where she had left him, in the middle of the little front room, under the too-bright lamp with its smudged chimney, his hands hanging at his sides. Outside, the wind had risen, and the arc light swung wider, and a few flakes of wet snow, the first of the year, drifted slantwise past the window and melted on the glass. A car went by. Then another. And Harvey Lusk, clerk, aged forty-one, owner of four lots in the coming suburb of Maumee Heights, stood and listened to his wife washing the dishes, and wondered, in his dim, groping, helpless way, what it was that a man was supposed to do with his life, and why it was that everything he had ever reached for had turned, at the very touch of his hand, to mud and ashes. Was it his fault? Was it anybody's? He could not tell. He only knew that something had happened tonight which could not be undone—that a door somewhere had closed, softly, without any slamming, and that he was on the wrong side of it.

After a while he went and turned the lamp down to where it ought to be.

It was raining, a thin, cold, insistent rain of late October, when Elmer Strader, having walked the six blocks from the elevated station in his one good overcoat (a brown herringbone, purchased two winters before at a sale at Rothschild's and now just slightly gone at the cuffs), made his way along Michigan Avenue toward the Hotel Grantham, where his cousin Walter, of whom he had not had so much as a line in eleven years, was stopping. The lamps along the boulevard, blurred and haloed by the wet, cast long wavering streaks of yellow upon the pavement, and the taxicabs and private cars, their tops glistening, drew up and departed before the great bronze-and-glass entrance with a kind of steady, purring importance which impressed him even before he had come near enough to see the doorman, a large man in a maroon coat and gold braid who seemed to Elmer to look upon everyone approaching on foot with a faint and practiced doubt. And Elmer, conscious of his wet shoes and of the fact that he had come on foot, felt this doubt, or imagined that he did, and was not a little troubled by it.

For what, after all, was he? A clerk, a sort of under-head in the order department of Bassett, Lowe & Company, wholesale hardware, at thirty-two dollars a week, with a wife, Lottie, and a little girl of four, and a flat of five rooms on the second floor of a frame building on Wrightwood Avenue, where the gas jets hissed and the radiators knocked in winter and the street cars clanged past the front windows at all hours. Not much, as he himself was well aware. And Walter? Well, that was just it. He did not know exactly what Walter was, except that the letter, a short, brisk note on heavy cream-colored paper with the name of a Minneapolis land and investment company engraved across the top, had said that he would be in Chicago for three days on business and would like nothing better than to "look up old Elmer and talk over the old times," and that he could be found at the Grantham. And the Grantham, as Elmer knew, was not a place where men of thirty-two dollars a week were likely to be found, either stopping or dining.

Inside, the warmth and the light and the soft murmur of voices struck him all at once. There was a great lobby with marble columns veined in green and gold, and deep leather chairs, and palms in brass tubs, and a long desk behind which young men in black coats moved with a quiet, efficient air. "Well, Elm," he said, "it's been a long time. A long, long time. Eleven years, isn't it? Twelve, almost. I was thinking about it on the train coming down. I said to myself, I wonder if old Elm remembers the time we swiped the watermelons out of old man Pfeiffer's patch and he set the dog on us?"

"I remember," said Elmer, and laughed, for he did remember, and the memory, coming upon him there in that glittering room, brought with it a sudden and curiously poignant vision—the hot, dusty road between the cornfields, the dull green of the melon vines in the August twilight, the barking of the dog, and the two of them, barefoot and breathless, running and stumbling down the ditch toward the creek, and lying afterward on the bank in the dark, eating the warm, sweet melon with their hands and laughing until they were sick. Walter's father had had the eighty acres next to Elmer's father's sixty, and both of them were poor and both mortgaged, and both families went to the same little white Lutheran church on the Carlisle road, and wore the same kind of clothes, and ate the same kind of food. "No," said Elmer quietly. "She died three years ago this past spring. Pa went the year before."

Whereas to him it had been—well, it had been the money which had bought the furniture for the flat on Wrightwood Avenue, and paid the doctor when little Edna was born, and there had been nothing left of it after that. It was a great country up there, a wonderful country, and growing all the time. And Elmer, listening, eating his oysters slowly and carefully (for he was not quite sure that he was eating them correctly, and kept glancing at Walter to see how it was done), felt within himself a strange commingling of emotions—admiration, certainly, and a kind of wonder, and pride, too, in a way, that a cousin of his, a Strader, out of the same dusty Indiana fields, should have come to this; and yet underneath all this, gnawing and insistent, a dull, heavy sense of his own failure, of his own smallness, of the meagerness and narrowness of the life that he himself had made. For what had he done? What had he to show? Eleven years—and here he was, at thirty-four, a clerk at thirty-two dollars a week, with no prospects, or none worth speaking of, beyond a possible raise of three dollars at the first of the year, if old Mr. Lowe remembered and was in a good humor. And he had worked—God knew he had worked! Ten hours a day, and Saturdays until three, and never late, and never sick, and always careful and exact and conscientious. And yet—and yet! In school, at the little brick schoolhouse at the crossroads, he had always been ahead of Walter, always. Was it luck, then? Or nerve? He did not know. He could not have said. He only knew that it was so, and that it hurt.

And here Elmer hesitated—for the fraction of a second only, but long enough to feel the temptation sharply. Walter would go back to Minneapolis on Thursday and very likely never come to Chicago again, or, if he did, never look him up. And yet something in him, some stubborn, plodding honesty which had been bred into him, perhaps, by his mother and the little Lutheran church on the Carlisle road, would not let him.

"I see," said Walter. And that was all. But there was a little silence after it, and in that silence Elmer felt, as plainly as though it had been spoken, the measuring and the weighing and the final placing of himself in his cousin's mind—not unkindly, perhaps, but definitely, finally, as one places a thing on a shelf where it belongs. And he looked out of the window at the rain, which was coming down harder now, and at the lights of the cars sliding past in the wet, and felt, for a moment, very tired.

The whitefish came, brown and steaming on its oaken plank, with a border of piped potato and little heaps of peas and carrots around it; and the orchestra behind the ferns began to play a waltz, slow and sentimental and somehow sad, and at a table across the room a woman in a gown of pale green silk laughed, a high, clear, careless laugh that rose above the murmur of voices and the clink of silver; and Walter, having helped himself liberally, began to talk again—of Minneapolis, of the Athletic Club to which he belonged, of a trip that he and Florence were planning to California in the spring, of a man named Hollister, a banker, who had taken a great liking to him and was going to put him in the way of something really big next year. And Elmer listened and nodded and said "Is that so?" and "Well, that's fine, Walt," at the proper intervals, and ate his whitefish, which was very good, better than anything he had eaten in a long time, though somehow he could not quite taste it.

It was only when the coffee had come, and Walter had lighted a long, dark cigar from a leather case and offered another to Elmer (who took it, though he seldom smoked cigars, and then only five-cent ones), that his cousin leaned forward across the table, his elbows on the white cloth, and looked at him with an expression which was different from any that he had worn thus far—more serious, and more searching, and with something in it, too, of that old Walter of the cornfields and the creek.

"Look here, Elm," he said. "I don't want you to take this wrong, now. But thirty-two a week—you can't get anywhere on that. Not with a wife and a kid. You know that as well as I do."

"I get along," said Elmer, a little stiffly.

"Sure you get along. But getting along isn't living. Not the way a man ought to live." He drew on his cigar and blew the smoke out slowly toward the chandelier. "Now, I'll tell you what. I could use a man up there. A man I could trust—somebody who's careful and honest and knows how to keep books and isn't going to try to put anything over on me. I've had two fellows in the office the last year and neither one of 'em was worth the powder to blow him up. I could start you at—well, say forty-five a week, and more later if things go the way I think they will. It isn't the city, of course. Not like Chicago. But it's a good town, and growing, and there's room for a man to get ahead. What do you say?"

And Elmer, sitting there with the unlighted cigar in his fingers and the warm, rich air of the dining room about him and the waltz still playing behind the ferns, felt something rise in him—something warm and swelling and almost painful, a kind of hope, which he had not felt in years. Forty-five a week! And more later! And a chance—a real chance, at last—to get out of the rut, out of the order books and the shipping slips and the dingy office on Lake Street with its one window looking out upon a brick wall. To give Lottie the things she ought to have, and Edna. A house, maybe, some day, with a lawn. And yet—at the same time, and quite as strongly, there rose in him something else, something he could not have put into words: a reluctance, a sort of shrinking, a dim and troubled sense that to go up there, to Minneapolis, to work for Walter, to be Walter's man, his clerk, his poor relation, beholden to him, nodding to him, watching his moods, would be in some way to acknowledge once and for all that Walter was the better man and he the lesser—that the thing which had been decided in that little silence a while ago was decided forever. Was that pride? Was it foolishness? Lottie would say it was foolishness. Lottie would say, "Why, Elmer, what on earth is there to think over?" And perhaps she would be right. Perhaps she would.

"Why, I—that's mighty good of you, Walt," he said at last, slowly. "Mighty good. I'd have to talk it over with Lottie, of course."

"Sure, sure. Talk it over. Take your time. I'm here till Thursday." Walter leaned back again, expansive, pleased with himself, the old ruddy glow upon his face once more. "Only don't take too long. Opportunities don't wait around for a fellow, Elm. That's one thing I've learned."

And afterward, when they had said good night under the great bronze marquee, and Walter had pressed upon him a dollar for a cab ("No, no, I insist—you're not going to walk in this, not after a dinner like that"), which Elmer had taken, flushing, and then had not used, but had put away in his vest pocket and walked to the elevated after all—afterward, riding north in the swaying, half-empty car, with the rain beating against the windows and the lights of the West Side flats flickering past, he sat and stared at his own pale reflection in the dark glass and thought and thought. Forty-five a week. Lowry Hill. A Pierce-Arrow. Yale. And old man Pfeiffer's dog, barking in the August dusk, and the two of them running, running, side by side, equal and free, down the long ditch toward the creek. Where had it gone, all that? And where, in the great, indifferent, glittering scheme of things—the hotels and the motorcars and the women in green silk laughing—where did he, Elmer Strader, belong? He did not know. He could not tell. And the car swayed on through the rain toward Wrightwood Avenue, where Lottie, he knew, would be waiting up for him, eager to hear everything.
