It was in that portion of the city which lay below the railroad yards and along the flats of the river, where the streets were unpaved for the most part and the houses, small, frame and of one pattern, stood shoulder to shoulder like so many weary workmen waiting for a car, that Henry Ostrander lived with his wife Minna and their two children, Della, eleven, and Willard, who was not yet eight. The house was a poor thing at best, four rooms and a lean-to kitchen, with a stove that smoked when the wind came from the east and a front step that had been patched more than once with boards of a different color. Yet inside, owing to the industry of Minna, who was a stout, practical and not unkindly German woman, and who had been raised in a home far poorer than this, there was an air of order and even of comfort, as these things went. There was a rag carpet, a sewing machine with a fern upon it, a horsehair sofa that had come from her mother's house in Fort Wayne, and on the wall a colored lithograph of a stag at bay among snowy pines, which Henry had won years before at a church raffle and which he still regarded, without quite knowing why, as a thing of some distinction.

On this particular evening in November, a raw, gray day with a fine sleet driving in from the river and the gas lamps along Kessler Street burning yellow and indistinct in the murk, Henry came home later than usual and in no very agreeable frame of mind. He was a checker in the shipping room of Haverly and Sons, wholesale grocers, a position he had held for nine years now at a wage which had advanced in that time from twelve to sixteen dollars a week, and which, so far as he could see, was not likely to advance further. And on this very afternoon young Mr. Pruett, a nephew of old Mr. Haverly, who had come into the business only the spring before from some college in the East and who knew no more about the shipping of goods than a cat (or so Henry thought), had stood over him in the presence of the other men and called him to account for a case of canned peaches that had gone to the wrong customer. It was not Henry's error. It was the error of a boy named Mulcahy, who had chalked the wrong number upon the crate. But Henry had not said so. Somehow, before this smooth, well-dressed youth, with his gray spats and his gold watch chain and his air of one who had never had to stand for anything in his life, Henry had found himself saying, "Yes, sir," and "I'll see to it, sir," and "It won't happen again, Mr. Pruett," the while a hot, choking sense of injustice rose in his throat and would not go down. And the other men had looked at him, or so he imagined, with a kind of pitying contempt, as much as to say, "There's Ostrander. Nine years, and he takes it from a kid like that." What else could he have done, though? There were Minna and the children, and the rent of eleven dollars a month, and the coal, and the doctor's bill from Della's sickness in the spring which was not yet paid. A man in his position could not talk back. He could not afford to have opinions, or a temper, or pride. That was a thing for people like Pruett, who had money behind them.

So, plodding home through the sleet with his collar turned up and his dinner pail swinging at his side, he had nursed this grievance, turning it over and over, until by the time he reached his own door it had grown into a kind of general resentment against life itself, against the city and the company and the weather and his own luck. He was not a bad man. Quite the contrary. He was, in the main, a sober, plodding, conscientious soul, not overly bright, not imaginative, who had been raised by a stern and religious father on a farm near Kendallville and who believed, without ever having examined the matter very closely, that the world was governed by certain fixed rules of right and wrong, and that those who kept them would in time be rewarded and those who broke them would be punished. Only of late, and in moments such as this one, a troubling doubt had begun to creep in upon him. Was it so? Was it really so? For here was he, who had kept the rules, and there was Pruett, who had kept none that Henry knew of and had needed none, and which of them was the better off? Yet he put the thought away from him. It was not a thing to think about.

Inside, the kitchen was warm and smelled of fried potatoes and boiled cabbage, and Minna, her sleeves rolled to the elbow and her face red from the stove, looked up and said, "You're late, Henry. Sit down. It's all ready." Della was setting the table, a thin, pale, serious child with her hair in two tight braids, and Willard was on the floor by the woodbox playing with something which, as his father entered, he thrust quickly into the pocket of his knee-pants.

Henry noticed the movement but said nothing at the time. He was tired. He washed his hands and face at the basin by the door, dried them on the roller towel, and sat down heavily at the head of the table. Minna said a short grace in German, as was her custom, and they ate for a while in silence, broken only by the clink of forks and the hiss of the sleet against the window. But presently, as if by some impulse of curiosity or perhaps because his father's mood oppressed him and he wished to escape from it into something pleasanter, Willard drew the object from his pocket under the edge of the table and began to turn it over in his fingers. It was a whistle—a small, bright, celluloid whistle in the shape of a bird, painted red and yellow and blue, with a little brass ring at the tail by which it might be hung on a string. And in the lamplight it shone with a gay, cheap, enticing brilliance which, to the child at least, was more beautiful than anything in the house.

"What's that you've got there?" asked Henry, laying down his fork.

Willard started and closed his hand over it. "Nothin'," he said.

"Don't tell me nothing. I saw it. Let's see it."

Slowly, and with a look first at his mother and then at his sister, as though one or the other might save him, the boy opened his hand. Henry took the whistle and examined it. It was new. There was not a mark upon it. He knew—for he had seen such things in the window of Bauer's notion store on Michigan Street, among the tops and marbles and candy hearts and cheap tin horns—that it had cost a dime. Perhaps fifteen cents.

"Where'd you get this?"

"I—I found it."

"Found it? Where?"

"Down by—down by the school. In the gutter."

Henry looked at it again. It was perfectly clean. And there had been sleet and mud in every gutter in the city since noon. He looked at Minna, and she, divining at the same instant what he was thinking, rose without a word and went to the shelf above the stove, where, behind the coffee mill, she kept a small tin box with a hinged lid, once a container for Huyler's cocoa, in which she put away the coins she saved from her market money against the coal man's monthly call. She opened it, counted, and turned around with a troubled face.

"There was a dollar and forty cents," she said in a low voice. "Now there's a dollar thirty."

There was a silence in the kitchen then, a heavy, dreadful silence, in which the ticking of the clock on the shelf and the hiss of the sleet and the faint bubbling of the kettle seemed suddenly very loud. Della had stopped eating and sat staring at her plate. Willard's face had gone first red and then white, and his lower lip had begun to tremble, though he did not cry—not yet. And Henry, looking at him, felt rising within him a feeling so complex, so commingled of anger and shame and fear and something else which he could not name, that for a moment he could not speak at all.

A thief! His son! And a liar besides! It was the thing of all things which his own father had most despised and most severely punished. He could remember yet—how vividly!—a day when he himself was perhaps nine and had taken two apples from a neighbor's tree, and his father had taken him out to the woodshed and whipped him with a harness strap until he could not sit down, saying all the while in his slow, heavy, Biblical way, "Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not steal." And he had never stolen again—never so much as a pin. That was how a boy was made honest. That was how a boy learned. And yet—and yet—even as he thought this, there came to him, unbidden, the memory of Pruett's smooth face that afternoon, and of the case of peaches, and of his own humiliation, and the thought, confused and only half-formed, that he was angrier now than he had any right to be, and that it was not altogether the dime, nor altogether the lie, which made him so.

"Come here," he said.

The boy did not move.

"Come here, I said!"

Willard slid down from his chair and came around the end of the table and stood before his father, his hands at his sides, his eyes fixed on the floor. He was a small, thin child, with light hair that fell over his forehead and large, gray, rather dreamy eyes—his mother's eyes—and a sensitive mouth that was always, as Minna said, "wanting something." For he was not like Della, who was serious and obedient and never asked for anything. He was forever stopping before shop windows on his way home from school, gazing at the bright things within—the painted soldiers, the toy engines, the bags of colored candy, the gilt-framed pictures, the sleds with their red runners—and coming home late, and being scolded for it, and doing it again. Something in these things drew him, as a moth is drawn to a flame, with a force he did not understand and could not resist. And it was so with the whistle. For a week he had passed Bauer's window and seen it there, hanging on a card among others like it, red and yellow and blue, and he had thought of it in school and at night in bed, and had wanted it as he had wanted nothing else in his short life. And this morning, alone in the kitchen while his mother was in the yard hanging out a wash, he had seen the cocoa box upon the shelf, and climbed upon a chair, and—well, he had not thought very much about it at all. It had seemed so easy. There were so many dimes in the box, and only one whistle in the world.

"Did you take that money out of your mother's box?" demanded Henry.

The boy said nothing.

"Answer me! Did you?"

"Yes, sir," whispered Willard, so low that he could scarcely be heard.

"And you went and bought this—this thing—with it?"

"Yes, sir."

"And then you sat there and lied to me about it! Found it in the gutter! Do you know what you are? Do you know what they call people who do things like that? A thief, that's what! And a liar! Do you know where thieves and liars end up? In jail, that's where! In the penitentiary over at Michigan City, with stripes on their backs and chains on their legs! Is that what you want? Is it?"

His voice had risen until it filled the little kitchen, and Willard, terrified now beyond all endurance, began at last to cry—not loudly, but in a low, choking, hopeless way, with his shoulders shaking and the tears running down his face. And Minna, who could bear a great deal but not this, came forward a step and put her hand on her husband's arm.

"Henry," she said. "Henry. He's only a little boy. He didn't know—"

"Didn't know! Didn't know it was wrong to steal? Didn't know it was wrong to lie? He knows, all right. He knew enough to hide it when I come in. You leave this to me, Minna. If I let it go now, where'll it stop? It'll be a quarter next time, and then a dollar, and then—" He did not finish. He did not quite know what came after that. But he had a vague, terrible picture of a long road leading downward, of saloons and poolrooms and police stations and newspapers, and of himself as an old man reading of his son's disgrace. "My father would've took the strap to me," he said. "And I'd have deserved it, too."

"Henry, please."

He looked at her, and then at the boy, and for a moment the two forces within him—the old, hard, inherited conviction that punishment was the only teacher, and some newer, softer, more uncertain feeling which he could not have put a name to—struggled together. It was not only Minna's pleading face. It was the boy himself, so small, so thin, so utterly helpless before him, as he, Henry, had been helpless that afternoon before Pruett. Was this what it came to, then? The big ones over the little ones, all down the line? Pruett over him, and he over this child? He did not think it in just these words. He was not a man who thought in words at all, very much. But something of the sort passed through him, like a cold draft through a warm room, and left him uneasy and confused.

And yet the thing had been done. It could not be let go. A boy who stole must be shown, must be made to feel. That much, at least, he was sure of. Or was he? Was he sure of anything any more?

"Hold out your hand," he said.

Willard, sobbing, held out his right hand, palm up, and Henry, with his own broad, calloused palm, struck it twice—sharply, so that the sound cracked in the little room like a breaking stick. The boy cried out and drew his hand back and held it against his chest, and Della, at the table, put her face in her hands. And Henry, the instant the blows had fallen, felt not satisfaction, as he had expected, nor righteousness, nor even the dull relief of a duty done, but a sudden, sickening shame which went through him from head to foot and left him almost weak.

"Now go to bed," he said roughly, to cover it. "No more supper. And tomorrow after school you take this thing back to Bauer's and tell him what you done and ask him for the dime back. And if he won't give it, you'll work it out somehow. You hear me?"

"Y-yes, sir."

"And don't you ever—ever—let me catch you at a thing like this again. Now go on."

The boy went, stumbling, through the door into the little bedroom off the kitchen which he shared with his sister, and they heard the creak of the bed as he threw himself upon it, and then his muffled crying, which went on for a long time and then slowly died away into silence.

For a while after that no one in the kitchen said anything. Minna cleared the table, her face set and averted, and Della helped her, and Henry sat by the stove with his elbows on his knees and the bright little whistle in his hand, turning it over and over. A cheap, foolish, gaudy thing. Ten cents' worth of painted celluloid. And yet, looking at it, he seemed to see, as in a kind of half-vision, the whole of his son's longing—the shop windows, the bright displays, the endless parade of things which other people had and which the Ostranders could not have and never would. Wasn't that what the world was, after all? One great window, full of bright things behind glass, and most people standing outside in the sleet, looking in? And was it so strange, then, that a child, not yet eight, not yet hardened to the way things were, should once put out his hand and take? He himself had wanted things, too, as a boy—a pair of skates, a jackknife, a red sweater such as the doctor's son wore. He had not taken them. His father would have killed him. But he had wanted them none the less, and that wanting had never quite died, had only gone underground, as it were, and become something else—a dull ache, a resentment, a sense of being cheated by he knew not whom.

"You was too hard on him, Henry," said Minna at last, quietly, wiping her hands on her apron.

"Maybe," he said. And then, after a pause, "I don't know. I don't know what's right any more, Minna. I swear I don't. You try to raise them decent. You try to teach them. And then—" He made a vague gesture with the hand that held the whistle, a gesture which took in the kitchen, the smoking stove, the sleet at the window, the whole poor, narrow, struggling circumstance of their lives. "What's the use of it? What's he going to have? What've I got?"

Minna did not answer. She had no answer. She came and stood beside him for a moment and put her hand upon his shoulder, and they remained so, the two of them, in the warm, dim kitchen, while the clock ticked and the kettle bubbled and the sleet drove on and on against the glass.

And in the little bedroom, Willard lay with his face to the wall, his hand still smarting, his eyes swollen and hot. He had stopped crying now. He was thinking—in so far as a child of seven can be said to think—of many things at once, confusedly. Of his father's face, red and terrible, which he had never seen so before. Of the penitentiary at Michigan City, with its stripes and chains, which he pictured as a vast, dark building like the roundhouse by the yards. Of Mr. Bauer, a fat, bald man with spectacles, to whom tomorrow he must go and say what he had done—a prospect so dreadful that he could scarcely bear to think of it. He was sorry. Yes, he was sorry. He would never do it again—never. And yet, beneath all this, beneath the fear and the shame and the smarting of his hand, there persisted in him, stubbornly and quite against his will, the image of the whistle itself—red and yellow and blue, shining in the lamplight—and the memory of the moment, earlier in the day, when he had first blown it in the alley behind Bauer's and heard its thin, sweet, piercing note go up among the wet roofs and chimneys like the cry of some strange, bright bird from another world than this. And he could not, try as he might, make himself feel that this had been wicked. It had been so beautiful.

So he lay, and the gas lamp in the street outside cast a pale, wavering square of light upon the ceiling, and the sleet ticked at the window, and presently, worn out, he slept. But the thing remained in him, as such things do—a small, bright splinter of desire, lodged deep and never wholly to be drawn out—and his father's blows, and his father's shame, and his mother's silence, and the gray, wet street, and the shop window with its painted toys, all became a part of him, mingling and combining in that obscure, chemic way in which the substance of a nature is formed, and in which, for good or ill, the man that is to be is shaped out of the child that is.

The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

In the night he was long getting to sleep because of too much thinking, and in the morning he was early awake, seizing with alacrity upon the same dear subject and pursuing it with vigour. He was out of sorts physically, as well as disordered mentally, for did he not delight in a new manner in his Carrie, and was not Drouet in the way? Never was man more harassed than he by the thoughts of his love being held by the elated, flush-mannered drummer. He would have given anything, it seemed to him, to have the complication ended—to have Carrie acquiesce to an arrangement which would dispose of Drouet effectually and forever. What to do. He dressed thinking. He moved about in the same chamber with his wife, unmindful of her presence. At breakfast he found himself without an appetite. The meat to which he helped himself remained on his plate untouched. His coffee grew cold, while he scanned the paper indifferently. Here and there he read a little thing, but remembered nothing. Jessica had not yet come down. His wife sat at one end of the table revolving thoughts of her own in silence. A new servant had been recently installed and had forgot the napkins. On this account the silence was irritably broken by a reproof.

“I’ve told you about this before, Maggie,” said Mrs. Hurstwood. “I’m not going to tell you again.” Hurstwood took a glance at his wife. She was frowning. Just now her manner irritated him excessively. Her next remark was addressed to him.

“Have you made up your mind, George, when you will take your vacation?” It was customary for them to discuss the regular summer outing at this season of the year.

“Not yet,” he said, “I’m very busy just now.”

“Well, you’ll want to make up your mind pretty soon, won’t you, if we’re going?” she returned.

“I guess we have a few days yet,” he said.

“Hmff,” she returned. “Don’t wait until the season’s over.” She stirred in aggravation as she said this.

“There you go again,” he observed. “One would think I never did anything, the way you begin.”

“Well, I want to know about it,” she reiterated.

“You’ve got a few days yet,” he insisted. “You’ll not want to start before the races are over.” He was irritated to think that this should come up when he wished to have his thoughts for other purposes.

“Well, we may. Jessica doesn’t want to stay until the end of the races.”

“What did you want with a season ticket, then?”

“Uh!” she said, using the sound as an exclamation of disgust, “I’ll not argue with you,” and therewith arose to leave the table.

“Say,” he said, rising, putting a note of determination in his voice which caused her to delay her departure, “what’s the matter with you of late? Can’t I talk with you any more?”

“Certainly, you can talk with me,” she replied, laying emphasis on the word.

“Well, you wouldn’t think so by the way you act. Now, you want to know when I’ll be ready—not for a month yet. Maybe not then.”

“We’ll go without you.”

“You will, eh?” he sneered.

“Yes, we will.” He was astonished at the woman’s determination, but it only irritated him the more.

“Well, we’ll see about that. It seems to me you’re trying to run things with a pretty high hand of late. You talk as though you settled my affairs for me. Well, you don’t. You don’t regulate anything that’s connected with me. If you want to go, go, but you won’t hurry me by any such talk as that.” He was thoroughly aroused now. His dark eyes snapped, and he crunched his paper as he laid it down. Mrs. Hurstwood said nothing more. He was just finishing when she turned on her heel and went out into the hall and upstairs. He paused for a moment, as if hesitating, then sat down and drank a little coffee, and thereafter arose and went for his hat and gloves upon the main floor. His wife had really not anticipated a row of this character. She had come down to the breakfast table feeling a little out of sorts with herself and revolving a scheme which she had in her mind. Jessica had called her attention to the fact that the races were not what they were supposed to be. The social opportunities were not what they had thought they would be this year. The beautiful girl found going every day a dull thing. There was an earlier exodus this year of people who were anybody to the watering places and Europe. In her own circle of acquaintances several young men in whom she was interested had gone to Waukesha. She began to feel that she would like to go too, and her mother agreed with her. Accordingly, Mrs. Hurstwood decided to broach the subject. She was thinking this over when she came down to the table, but for some reason the atmosphere was wrong. She was not sure, after it was all over, just how the trouble had begun. She was determined now, however, that her husband was a brute, and that, under no circumstances, would she let this go by unsettled. She would have more lady-like treatment or she would know why. Then the other complications of love, desire, and opposition possessed him. His thoughts fled on before him upon eagles’ wings. He could hardly wait until he should meet Carrie face to face. What was the night, after all, without her—what the day? She must and should be his. For her part, Carrie had experienced a world of fancy and feeling since she had left him, the night before. She had listened to Drouet’s enthusiastic maunderings with much regard for that part which concerned herself, with very little for that which affected his own gain. She kept him at such lengths as she could, because her thoughts were with her own triumph. She felt Hurstwood’s passion as a delightful background to her own achievement, and she wondered what he would have to say. She was sorry for him, too, with that peculiar sorrow which finds something complimentary to itself in the misery of another. She was now experiencing the first shades of feeling of that subtle change which removes one out of the ranks of the suppliants into the lines of the dispensers of charity. She was, all in all, exceedingly happy. On the morrow, however, there was nothing in the papers concerning the event, and, in view of the flow of common, everyday things about, it now lost a shade of the glow of the previous evening. Drouet himself was not talking so much of as for her. He felt instinctively that, for some reason or other, he needed reconstruction in her regard.

“I think,” he said, as he spruced around their chambers the next morning, preparatory to going down town, “that I’ll straighten out that little deal of mine this month and then we’ll get married. I was talking with Mosher about that yesterday.”

“No, you won’t,” said Carrie, who was coming to feel a certain faint power to jest with the drummer.

“Yes, I will,” he exclaimed, more feelingly than usual, adding, with the tone of one who pleads, “Don’t you believe what I’ve told you?” Carrie laughed a little.

“Of course I do,” she answered. Drouet’s assurance now misgave him. Shallow as was his mental observation, there was that in the things which had happened which made his little power of analysis useless. Carrie was still with him, but not helpless and pleading. There was a lilt in her voice which was new. She did not study him with eyes expressive of dependence. The drummer was feeling the shadow of something which was coming. It coloured his feelings and made him develop those little attentions and say those little words which were mere forefendations against danger. Shortly afterward he departed, and Carrie prepared for her meeting with Hurstwood. She hurried at her toilet, which was soon made, and hastened down the stairs. At the corner she passed Drouet, but they did not see each other. The drummer had forgotten some bills which he wished to turn into his house. He hastened up the stairs and burst into the room, but found only the chambermaid, who was cleaning up.

“Hello,” he exclaimed, half to himself, “has Carrie gone?”

“Your wife? Yes, she went out just a few minutes ago.”

“That’s strange,” thought Drouet. “She didn’t say a word to me. I wonder where she went?” He hastened about, rummaging in his valise for what he wanted, and finally pocketing it. Then he turned his attention to his fair neighbour, who was good-looking and kindly disposed towards him.

“What are you up to?” he said, smiling.

“Just cleaning,” she replied, stopping and winding a dusting towel about her hand.

“Tired of it?”

“Not so very.”

“Let me show you something,” he said, affably, coming over and taking out of his pocket a little lithographed card which had been issued by a wholesale tobacco company. “Isn’t that clever?” he said, handing it to her and showing her how it worked. “You never saw anything like that before.”

“Isn’t it nice?” she answered.

“You can have it if you want it,” he remarked.

“That’s a pretty ring you have,” he said, touching a commonplace setting which adorned the hand holding the card he had given her.

“Do you think so?”

“That’s right,” he answered, making use of a pretence at examination to secure her finger. “That’s fine.” The ice being thus broken, he launched into further observation pretending to forget that her fingers were still retained by his. She soon withdrew them, however, and retreated a few feet to rest against the window-sill.

“I didn’t see you for a long time,” she said, coquettishly, repulsing one of his exuberant approaches. “You must have been away.”

“I was,” said Drouet.

“Do you travel far?”

“Pretty far—yes.”

“Do you like it?”

“Oh, not very well. You get tired of it after a while.”

“I wish I could travel,” said the girl, gazing idly out of the window.

“What has become of your friend, Mr. Hurstwood?” she suddenly asked, bethinking herself of the manager, who, from her own observation, seemed to contain promising material.

“He’s here in town. What makes you ask about him?”

“Oh, nothing, only he hasn’t been here since you got back.”

“How did you come to know him?”

“Didn’t I take up his name a dozen times in the last month?”

“Get out,” said the drummer, lightly. “He hasn’t called more than half a dozen times since we’ve been here.”

“He hasn’t, eh?” said the girl, smiling. “That’s all you know about it.” Drouet took on a slightly more serious tone. He was uncertain as to whether she was joking or not.

“Tease,” he said, “what makes you smile that way?”

“Oh, nothing.”

“Have you seen him recently?”

“Not since you came back,” she laughed.

“Before?”

“Certainly.”

“How often?”

“Why, nearly every day.” She was a mischievous newsmonger, and was keenly wondering what the effect of her words would be.

“Who did he come to see?” asked the drummer, incredulously.

“Mrs. Drouet.” He looked rather foolish at this answer, and then attempted to correct himself so as not to appear a dupe.

“Well,” he said, “what of it?”

“Nothing,” replied the girl, her head cocked coquettishly on one side.

“He’s an old friend,” he went on, getting deeper into the mire. He would have gone on further with his little flirtation, but the taste for it was temporarily removed. He was quite relieved when the girl’s named was called from below.

“I’ve got to go,” she said, moving away from him airily.

“I’ll see you later,” he said, with a pretence of disturbance at being interrupted. When she was gone, he gave freer play to his feelings. His face, never easily controlled by him, expressed all the perplexity and disturbance which he felt. Could it be that Carrie had received so many visits and yet said nothing about them? Was Hurstwood lying? What did the chambermaid mean by it, anyway? He had thought there was something odd about Carrie’s manner at the time. Why did she look so disturbed when he had asked her how many times Hurstwood had called? By George! He remembered now. There was something strange about the whole thing. He sat down in a rocking-chair to think the better, drawing up one leg on his knee and frowning mightily. His mind ran on at a great rate. And yet Carrie hadn’t acted out of the ordinary. It couldn’t be, by George, that she was deceiving him. She hadn’t acted that way. Why, even last night she had been as friendly toward him as could be, and Hurstwood too. Look how they acted! He could hardly believe they would try to deceive him. His thoughts burst into words.

“She did act sort of funny at times. Here she had dressed, and gone out this morning and never said a word.” He scratched his head and prepared to go down town. He was still frowning. As he came into the hall he encountered the girl, who was now looking after another chamber. She had on a white dusting cap, beneath which her chubby face shone good-naturedly. Drouet almost forgot his worry in the fact that she was smiling on him. He put his hand familiarly on her shoulder, as if only to greet her in passing.

“Got over being mad?” she said, still mischievously inclined.

“I’m not mad,” he answered.

“I thought you were,” she said, smiling.

“Quit your fooling about that,” he said, in an offhand way. “Were you serious?”

“Certainly,” she answered. Then, with an air of one who did not intentionally mean to create trouble, “He came lots of times. I thought you knew.” The game of deception was up with Drouet. He did not try to simulate indifference further.

“Did he spend the evenings here?” he asked.

“Sometimes. Sometimes they went out.”

“In the evening?”

“Yes. You mustn’t look so mad, though.”

“I’m not,” he said. “Did any one else see him?”

“Of course,” said the girl, as if, after all, it were nothing in particular.

“How long ago was this?”

“Just before you came back.” The drummer pinched his lip nervously.

“Don’t say anything, will you?” he asked, giving the girl’s arm a gentle squeeze.

“Certainly not,” she returned. “I wouldn’t worry over it.”

“All right,” he said, passing on, seriously brooding for once, and yet not wholly unconscious of the fact that he was making a most excellent impression upon the chambermaid.

“I’ll see her about that,” he said to himself, passionately, feeling that he had been unduly wronged. “I’ll find out, b’George, whether she’ll act that way or not.” When Carrie came Hurstwood had been waiting many minutes. His blood was warm; his nerves wrought up. He was anxious to see the woman who had stirred him so profoundly the night before.

“Here you are,” he said, repressedly, feeling a spring in his limbs and an elation which was tragic in itself.

“Yes,” said Carrie. They walked on as if bound for some objective point, while Hurstwood drank in the radiance of her presence. The rustle of her pretty skirt was like music to him.

“Are you satisfied?” he asked, thinking of how well she did the night before.

“Are you?” He tightened his fingers as he saw the smile she gave him.

“It was wonderful.” Carrie laughed ecstatically.

“That was one of the best things I’ve seen in a long time,” he added. He was dwelling on her attractiveness as he had felt it the evening before, and mingling it with the feeling her presence inspired now. Carrie was dwelling in the atmosphere which this man created for her. Already she was enlivened and suffused with a glow. She felt his drawing toward her in every sound of his voice.

“Those were such nice flowers you sent me,” she said, after a moment or two. “They were beautiful.”

“Glad you liked them,” he answered, simply.

Excerpt 3: Carrie pondered over this situation as consistently as Hurstwood, once she got the facts adjusted in her mind. It took several days for her to fully realise that the approach of the dissolution of her husband’s business meant commonplace struggle and privation. Her mind went back to her early venture in Chicago, the Hansons and their flat, and her heart revolted. That was terrible! Everything about poverty was terrible. She wished she knew a way out. Her recent experiences with the Vances had wholly unfitted her to view her own state with complacence. The glamour of the high life of the city had, in the few experiences afforded her by the former, seized her completely. She had been taught how to dress and where to go without having ample means to do either. Now, these things—ever-present realities as they were—filled her eyes and mind. The more circumscribed became her state, the more entrancing seemed this other. And now poverty threatened to seize her entirely and to remove this other world far upward like a heaven to which any Lazarus might extend, appealingly, his hands. So, too, the ideal brought into her life by Ames remained. He had gone, but here was his word that riches were not everything; that there was a great deal more in the world than she knew; that the stage was good, and the literature she read poor. He was a strong man and clean—how much stronger and better than Hurstwood and Drouet she only half formulated to herself, but the difference was painful. It was something to which she voluntarily closed her eyes. During the last three months of the Warren Street connection, Hurstwood took parts of days off and hunted, tracking the business advertisements. It was a more or less depressing business, wholly because of the thought that he must soon get something or he would begin to live on the few hundred dollars he was saving, and then he would have nothing to invest—he would have to hire out as a clerk. Everything he discovered in his line advertised as an opportunity, was either too expensive or too wretched for him. Besides, winter was coming, the papers were announcing hardships, and there was a general feeling of hard times in the air, or, at least, he thought so. In his worry, other people’s worries became apparent. No item about a firm failing, a family starving, or a man dying upon the streets, supposedly of starvation, but arrested his eye as he scanned the morning papers. Once the “World” came out with a flaring announcement about “80,000 people out of employment in New York this winter,” which struck as a knife at his heart.

“Eighty thousand!” he thought. “What an awful thing that is.” This was new reasoning for Hurstwood. In the old days the world had seemed to be getting along well enough. He had been wont to see similar things in the “Daily News,” in Chicago, but they did not hold his attention. Now, these things were like grey clouds hovering along the horizon of a clear day. They threatened to cover and obscure his life with chilly greyness. He tried to shake them off, to forget and brace up. Sometimes he said to himself, mentally: “What’s the use worrying? I’m not out yet. I’ve got six weeks more. Even if worst comes to worst, I’ve got enough to live on for six months.” Curiously, as he troubled over his future, his thoughts occasionally reverted to his wife and family. He had avoided such thoughts for the first three years as much as possible. He hated her, and he could get along without her. Let her go. He would do well enough. Now, however, when he was not doing well enough, he began to wonder what she was doing, how his children were getting along. He could see them living as nicely as ever, occupying the comfortable house and using his property.

“By George! it’s a shame they should have it all,” he vaguely thought to himself on several occasions. “I didn’t do anything.” As he looked back now and analysed the situation which led up to his taking the money, he began mildly to justify himself. What had he done—what in the world—that should bar him out this way and heap such difficulties upon him? It seemed only yesterday to him since he was comfortable and well-to-do. But now it was all wrested from him.

“She didn’t deserve what she got out of me, that is sure. I didn’t do so much, if everybody could just know.” There was no thought that the facts ought to be advertised. It was only a mental justification he was seeking from himself—something that would enable him to bear his state as a righteous man. One afternoon, five weeks before the Warren Street place closed up, he left the saloon to visit three or four places he saw advertised in the “Herald.” One was down in Gold Street, and he visited that, but did not enter. It was such a cheap looking place he felt that he could not abide it. Another was on the Bowery, which he knew contained many showy resorts. It was near Grand Street, and turned out to be very handsomely fitted up. He talked around about investments for fully three-quarters of an hour with the proprietor, who maintained that his health was poor, and that was the reason he wished a partner.

“Well, now, just how much money would it take to buy a half interest here?” said Hurstwood, who saw seven hundred dollars as his limit.

“Three thousand,” said the man. Hurstwood’s jaw fell.

“Cash?” he said.

“Cash.” He tried to put on an air of deliberation, as one who might really buy; but his eyes showed gloom. He wound up by saying he would think it over, and came away. The man he had been talking to sensed his condition in a vague way.

“I don’t think he wants to buy,” he said to himself. “He doesn’t talk right.” The afternoon was as grey as lead and cold. It was blowing up a disagreeable winter wind. “How about this ad of yours?” asked Hurstwood, who rather objected to the looks of the place.

“Oh, dat iss all over,” said the German. “I vill not sell now.”

“Oh, is that so?”

“Yes; dere is nothing to dat. It iss all over.”

“Very well,” said Hurstwood, turning around. The German paid no more attention to him, and it made him angry.

“The crazy ass!” he said to himself. “What does he want to advertise for?” Wholly depressed, he started for Thirteenth Street. The flat had only a light in the kitchen, where Carrie was working. He struck a match and, lighting the gas, sat down in the dining-room without even greeting her. She came to the door and looked in.

“It’s you, is it?” she said, and went back.

“Yes,” he said, without even looking up from the evening paper he had bought. Carrie saw things were wrong with him. He was not so handsome when gloomy. The lines at the sides of the eyes were deepened. Naturally dark of skin, gloom made him look slightly sinister. He was quite a disagreeable figure. Carrie set the table and brought in the meal.

“Dinner’s ready,” she said, passing him for something. He did not answer, reading on. She came in and sat down at her place, feeling exceedingly wretched.

“Won’t you eat now?” she asked. He folded his paper and drew near, silence holding for a time, except for the “Pass me’s.”

“It’s been gloomy to-day, hasn’t it?” ventured Carrie, after a time.

“Yes,” he said. He only picked at his food.

“Are you still sure to close up?” said Carrie, venturing to take up the subject which they had discussed often enough.

“Of course we are,” he said, with the slightest modification of sharpness. This retort angered Carrie. She had had a dreary day of it herself.

“You needn’t talk like that,” she said.

“Oh!” he exclaimed, pushing back from the table, as if to say more, but letting it go at that. Then he picked up his paper. Carrie left her seat, containing herself with difficulty. He saw she was hurt.

“Don’t go ’way,” he said, as she started back into the kitchen. “Eat your dinner.” She passed, not answering. He looked at the paper a few moments, and then rose up and put on his coat.

“I’m going downtown, Carrie,” he said, coming out. “I’m out of sorts to-night.” She did not answer.

“Don’t be angry,” he said. “It will be all right to-morrow.” He looked at her, but she paid no attention to him, working at her dishes.

“Good-bye!” he said finally, and went out. Hurstwood could not conceal his feelings about the matter. Carrie could not help wondering where she was drifting. It got so that they talked even less than usual, and yet it was not Hurstwood who felt any objection to Carrie. It was Carrie who shied away from him. This he noticed. It aroused an objection to her becoming indifferent to him. He made the possibility of friendly intercourse almost a giant task, and then noticed with discontent that Carrie added to it by her manner and made it more impossible. At last the final day came. When it actually arrived, Hurstwood, who had got his mind into such a state where a thunderclap and raging storm would have seemed highly appropriate, was rather relieved to find that it was a plain, ordinary day. The sun shone, the temperature was pleasant. He felt, as he came to the breakfast table, that it wasn’t so terrible, after all.

“Well,” he said to Carrie, “to-day’s my last day on earth.” Carrie smiled in answer to his humour. Hurstwood glanced over his paper rather gayly. He seemed to have lost a load.

“I’ll go down for a little while,” he said after breakfast, “and then I’ll look around. To-morrow I’ll spend the whole day looking about. I think I can get something, now this thing’s off my hands.” He went out smiling and visited the place. Shaughnessy was there. They had made all arrangements to share according to their interests. When, however, he had been there several hours, gone out three more, and returned, his elation had departed. As much as he had objected to the place, now that it was no longer to exist, he felt sorry. He wished that things were different. Shaughnessy was coolly businesslike.

“Well,” he said at five o’clock, “we might as well count the change and divide.” They did so. The fixtures had already been sold and the sum divided.

“So long,” said Shaughnessy, scarcely deigning a notice. Thus the Warren Street arrangement was permanently concluded. Carrie had prepared a good dinner at the flat, but after his ride up, Hurstwood was in a solemn and reflective mood.

“Well?” said Carrie, inquisitively.

“I’m out of that,” he answered, taking off his coat. As she looked at him, she wondered what his financial state was now. They ate and talked a little.

“Will you have enough to buy in anywhere else?” asked Carrie.

“No,” he said. “I’ll have to get something else and save up.”

“It would be nice if you could get some place,” said Carrie, prompted by anxiety and hope.

“I guess I will,” he said reflectively. For some days thereafter he put on his overcoat regularly in the morning and sallied forth. On these ventures he first consoled himself with the thought that with the seven hundred dollars he had he could still make some advantageous arrangement. He thought about going to some brewery, which, as he knew, frequently controlled saloons which they leased, and get them to help him. Then he remembered that he would have to pay out several hundred any way for fixtures and that he would have nothing left for his monthly expenses. It was costing him nearly eighty dollars a month to live.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Where should he get such a position? The papers contained no requests for managers. Such positions, he knew well enough, were either secured by long years of service or were bought with a half or third interest. Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. His clothes were very good and his appearance still excellent, but it involved the trouble of deluding. People, looking at him, imagined instantly that a man of his age, stout and well dressed, must be well off. He appeared a comfortable owner of something, a man from whom the common run of mortals could well expect gratuities. Being now forty-three years of age, and comfortably built, walking was not easy. “The man was here for the rent to-day.”

The flat which the Lindquists occupied in Kenwood Street was of that order of dwelling which the city produces by the thousand for those who have risen a little above the level of the shop and the factory, and who mean, by every means at their command, never to sink back into it again. It was four rooms and a bath, upon the second floor of a yellow brick building of six apartments, with a small front parlour overlooking the street, a dining-room which received its light from a narrow shaft, and a kitchen in the rear whose single window commanded a view of back porches, clothes-lines, and the uneven roofs of sheds. The rent was twenty-two dollars a month. It had seemed, when they took it two years before, a very considerable thing.

Walter Lindquist was a clerk in the claims department of the Western Fidelity Insurance Company, a concern which occupied three floors of a large building in La Salle Street, and he had been in its employ for six years. He was thirty-four years of age, of medium height, somewhat spare of frame, with light hair which was already beginning to thin at the temples, and a manner which was at once careful and a little apologetic, as of one who has learned that the world rewards caution more often than it rewards boldness. He drew eighteen dollars a week. It was not much, as salaries go, but it was regular, and he had been given to understand by Mr. Pettibone, the head of his department, that a vacancy which was expected to occur in the spring would, in all probability, fall to him. This position paid twenty-eight dollars. Upon this expectation, which he had communicated to his wife in a moment of enthusiasm the previous autumn, a whole structure of hope had been erected.

It must not be thought that Alma Lindquist was a grasping or unreasonable woman. She was not. She was simply one of those natures, very common in the cities, upon which the spectacle of comfort and display operates as a constant and gentle pressure, like the pull of the moon upon the waters. She had come from a small town in Wisconsin, where her father kept a feed store, and she had married Walter partly because he was steady and kind, and partly because he represented to her a way into that larger world of which the newspapers and the shop windows spoke so eloquently. She was twenty-nine, pretty in a soft, rounded way, with brown hair which she wore in the fashionable manner, and a pair of grey eyes which could be very warm or very cool, according as her feelings were engaged. She kept the flat neatly, managed the household money with some skill, and read, of an afternoon, the society columns of the “Tribune” with an interest which she would have been ashamed to confess.

Now, the vacancy had fallen. It had fallen that very day, and it had not fallen to Walter Lindquist. It had gone instead to a young man named Corcoran, who had been with the company scarcely three years, but who was a nephew of one of the vice-presidents, and who possessed, besides, that easy, jovial, back-slapping address which carries a man farther in commercial life than any amount of diligent attention to ledgers. Walter had learned of it at eleven in the morning, when the announcement was made, and he had spent the remainder of the day in a condition of mind which it would be difficult to describe. He had worked on, outwardly composed, but inwardly there was a sinking, a hollowness, as though some prop upon which he had been leaning without knowing it had been quietly withdrawn. He had smiled at Corcoran and shaken his hand. He had said, “Well, I guess you deserve it.” And all the while a voice within him had been saying, “What will I tell Alma? What in the world will I tell her?”

The difficulty was this. Upon the strength of his expectation, Alma had, two weeks before, gone to look at a flat in Drexel Boulevard. It was a beautiful flat, of six rooms, with a bay window in the parlour, hardwood floors throughout, and a porch at the back upon which one might sit of a summer evening. The rent was thirty-five dollars. She had talked of it constantly since. She had planned where the furniture should go, what new pieces must be bought, how the bay window might be hung with lace curtains of a certain pattern which she had seen at Mandel’s. Only the Sunday before, she had walked him past it twice, pointing out the stone steps and the brass fittings upon the door, and he had agreed with her, in the warmth of the moment, that it would be a fine thing. More than that, she had told the agent, a smooth young man with a waxed moustache, that they would very likely take it by the first of April, and he had promised to hold it for her until the end of the month.

All this was in Walter’s mind as he rode home upon the Cottage Grove car that evening, wedged between a fat woman with a market basket and a labourer whose clothes smelled of lime. The car was crowded, as it always was at this hour, and the windows were steamed over, so that the lights of the stores and saloons along the way came through to him only as blurred yellow patches. He thought of a dozen ways of breaking the news, each of which seemed, upon examination, worse than the last. He would tell her at once, as soon as he came in. No, he would wait until after dinner, when she was in a better humour. Or perhaps he would say nothing at all for a day or two, until he could think of something to soften the blow. But this last he knew to be impossible. The agent must be answered, and Alma was not a woman to let a thing of that kind rest.

When he reached the flat it was half-past six, and the smell of frying potatoes met him upon the stairs. Alma was in the kitchen. She called out cheerfully as she heard the door.

“Is that you, Walt?”

“Yes,” he answered, hanging up his hat and coat upon the rack in the narrow hall.

“Supper’ll be ready in a minute. I’ve got some chops. Wash up, will you?”

He went into the bathroom and washed his hands slowly, looking at himself in the small mirror above the basin. His face seemed to him grey and tired, the face of a man who had been beaten. He dried his hands and came out into the dining-room, where the table was already laid with the white cloth and the blue-figured dishes which had been a wedding present from her aunt. A lamp with a green shade stood upon the sideboard. Everything had that air of modest neatness which he had always found pleasant, but which this evening seemed to him only to emphasise how small and narrow their life was.

Alma came in with the platter of chops and set it down. She was flushed from the stove and smiling.

“Well,” she said, seating herself, “I went by the Boulevard again to-day. Mrs. Hartigan was with me. She thinks it’s the nicest flat she’s seen this year. She says the woman who had it before us—I mean, before the people who are leaving—had a piano right there in the bay. Wouldn’t that be lovely?”

“Yes,” said Walter. He helped himself to a chop and a spoonful of potatoes, and began to eat without looking up.

“I think we ought to have a piano some time,” she went on. “Not right away, of course. But you can get them on payments now, you know. Lyon and Healy have a plan.”

“I know they have,” he said.

Something in his tone caused her to look at him more attentively. She was a woman who was quick to read the moods of those about her, though she did not always interpret them correctly, and she now perceived that her husband was not himself.

“What’s the matter, Walt?” she asked. “Don’t you feel well?”

“I feel all right.”

“You don’t look it. You look as if you’d been run over.”

He laid down his fork. There was no help for it. He had better have it out now and be done with it.

“Alma,” he said, “I didn’t get that place.”

She looked at him for a moment without understanding, the smile still lingering upon her lips, as a light lingers in a room after the lamp has been turned down.

“What place?” she said.

“Mr. Hasbrouck’s place. The one I was to get in the spring. They gave it to Corcoran.”

The smile went out. She sat very still, her hands resting upon the edge of the table, and he saw the colour leave her cheeks and then return more strongly than before.

“Corcoran!” she exclaimed. “Why, he’s only been there a little while. You told me so yourself.”

“I know it.”

“Then why did they give it to him?”

“Because his uncle is Mr. Brainard,” said Walter wearily. “That’s why. I might have known it. Everybody knew it but me, I guess.”

“But Mr. Pettibone told you——”

“Mr. Pettibone told me it would probably be me,” he interrupted. “He didn’t promise anything. He said ‘probably.’ I suppose he thought so himself. It wasn’t up to him.”

Alma said nothing for a time. She took up her knife and fork as if to go on eating, then laid them down again. Her mind was moving rapidly over a great many things at once—the flat upon the Boulevard, the lace curtains, the piano, Mrs. Hartigan, to whom she had spoken so confidently of moving, the agent with the waxed moustache. It was not the loss of ten dollars a week which pained her so much as the sudden collapse of an entire picture, carefully composed and lovingly dwelt upon, which had become, in the course of a few months, almost more real to her than the rooms in which she sat.

“Well,” she said at last, in a voice which she tried to keep steady, “I think it’s a shame. I think it’s a downright shame. After all the years you’ve put in there.”

“It is a shame,” he agreed.

“Didn’t you say anything to them?”

“What could I say?”

“Why, you could have gone to Mr. Pettibone and told him what you thought of it. You could have told him you’d been there six years and that you’d been promised——”

“I wasn’t promised,” he said, with a touch of irritation. “I told you that.”

“Well, you as good as were,” she returned sharply. “You came home and told me you were. You told me in October. I remember the very night. You said, ‘Alma, it’s as good as settled.’ Those were your words.”

He remembered them too, and the recollection was not pleasant. It is one of the peculiar cruelties of hope that it causes us to say things in moments of elation which rise up afterward to accuse us. He had said them. He had believed them. He had even, in the fulness of his feeling, bought her a little gold pin that night on the way home, which she still wore at her throat. He looked at it now and turned his eyes away.

“I thought it was,” he said. “I was wrong.”

“And now what are we going to do about the flat?”

This was the point which he had dreaded most of all, and he answered it as directly as he could.

“We can’t take it,” he said. “That’s all there is about it. We can’t pay thirty-five dollars on what I get.”

“I’ve told the man we would.”

“You told him we’d probably take it.”

“I told him we would,” she insisted. “I didn’t say probably. I said we’d take it the first of April. He’s holding it for us. He turned away a couple who wanted it last week. He told me so.”

“Then you oughtn’t to have done that,” said Walter, his voice rising slightly in spite of himself. “You oughtn’t to have told him anything until it was settled. I never said to tell him that.”

“You walked by there with me Sunday and said it was fine,” she retorted. “You said, ‘We’ll be sitting out on that porch this summer.’ What was I to think?”

He did not answer. He took up his fork again and moved a piece of potato about upon his plate, but he did not eat it. The clock upon the parlour mantel, a small black marble affair which they had bought at a sale, ticked loudly through the open doorway. Outside, in the street, a wagon rumbled by, and somewhere below a child was crying.

“I can’t help it, Alma,” he said at length, more gently. “I did the best I could. I worked as hard as any man in that office. Harder. I never took a day off, except when I had the grippe. It wasn’t my fault.”

“I didn’t say it was your fault.”

“You act like it.”

“I don’t act like anything,” she said, and her voice trembled. “I just can’t see why things like that have to happen to us. Other people get along. Look at the Hartigans. He was only a clerk at Siegel-Cooper’s two years ago, and now he’s a buyer, and they’ve got a girl to do the work. Look at Fanny Rausch’s husband. Everybody seems to get along but us.”

This comparison, which she had not meant to make in quite this way, struck him like a blow. It touched upon a sore which had long been festering in secret, for he had more than once suspected that she measured him against other men and found him wanting. A man may bear his own sense of inadequacy with a certain resignation, but to have it confirmed by the one person whose good opinion he most desires is another thing altogether. He pushed back his chair.

“Well,” he said bitterly, “maybe you ought to have married Hartigan.”

“Walter!”

“Well, maybe you ought. Or somebody like him. Somebody that can slap people on the back and get in with the bosses. I can’t do it. I never could. I do my work and I do it right, and that’s all I know how to do. If that isn’t good enough——” He stopped, for he felt his voice beginning to break, and he did not wish her to see it.

Alma looked at him with a mixture of anger and dismay. She had not anticipated this. She had been prepared to be disappointed, and even to show her disappointment, but she had not thought that he would turn upon her in this way. In her own mind she had said nothing unjust. She had only spoken what any woman might feel. That he should take it as an accusation seemed to her both unreasonable and unkind.

“I never said anything like that,” she said. “You needn’t put words in my mouth. I only said it seems hard.”

“You said everybody gets along but us. That means me.”

“It doesn’t mean anything of the kind.”

“What does it mean, then?”

She did not answer at once, and in the pause the truth of the matter hung between them, unspoken but perfectly understood. It did mean him. It could mean nothing else. And she, being honest in her way, could not bring herself to deny it outright.

“It means I’m tired,” she said finally. “It means I’m tired of living in four rooms and looking out at a lot of back porches. It means I want something nicer before I’m old. Is that so terrible?”

“No,” he said, “it isn’t terrible. I want it too. Do you think I don’t?”

“Then why can’t we have it?”

“Because we haven’t got the money!” he exclaimed. “That’s why. Because I make eighteen dollars a week, and I’m going to go on making eighteen dollars a week until somebody dies or quits, and then maybe they’ll give it to somebody’s nephew again. That’s why.”

He rose from the table and went into the parlour, where he stood by the window, looking down into the street. The arc lamp at the corner threw a cold white glare upon the pavement, and the shadows of the bare trees lay across it like cracks in a plate. A man and a woman passed beneath, arm in arm, laughing at something. He watched them out of sight with a feeling of strange and helpless envy, as though they possessed some secret of contentment which had been withheld from him.

There is in the relations of men and women who are bound together by marriage a curious law of reaction, by which the pain of the one, instead of drawing forth the sympathy of the other, frequently calls up only a corresponding resentment. Each feels himself the injured party. Each waits for the other to make the first advance. And so, between two people who are in reality fond of each other, and who have no wish to give pain, there grows up a wall of silence which neither can quite bring himself to break. It was so now. Alma sat at the table, staring at the cooling chops, feeling that she had been cruelly misunderstood. Walter stood at the window, feeling that he had been cruelly judged. Neither moved.

At last Alma rose and began, with a great deal of unnecessary noise, to clear away the dishes. She carried them into the kitchen and set them in the sink, and he heard the water running, and the clatter of plates. It was a sound which, on other evenings, had been pleasant to him, as signifying the ordered routine of their home. To-night it seemed to him only an expression of her displeasure.

After a time he went back to the kitchen door and stood looking in at her. She was bent over the sink, her sleeves rolled up, her back toward him. He could see that her shoulders were stiff.

“Alma,” he said.

She did not turn.

“Alma, I didn’t mean that—about Hartigan.”

“You said it,” she answered, without looking around.

“I know I said it. I was mad. I’ve been mad all day. I didn’t mean it at you.”

She went on washing a cup, turning it round and round in the water long after it was clean. He saw that she was struggling with herself, and he waited.

“I’ll have to go and tell that man to-morrow,” she said finally, in a low voice. “I don’t know what I’ll say to him.”

“I’ll go,” said Walter. “I’ll stop on my way in the morning.”

“No, I told him. I’d better go.”

“Then tell him we changed our minds. Tell him anything. It’s none of his business.”

“And Mrs. Hartigan,” she went on, as though she had not heard him. “I told her too. I told her we were going to move. She’ll ask me all about it.”

“Let her ask.”

“It’s easy for you to say that,” said Alma, turning at last, her eyes wet. “You don’t have to see her every day. You don’t have to sit there and listen to her talk about her new carpet and her girl and her this and that. I do. I have to sit there and smile and say how nice it is. And now I’ll have to tell her we’re not going anywhere at all.”

He came forward a step, awkwardly, as one who approaches an animal that may shy.

“We’ll get there some day,” he said. “I’ll find something. There are other companies. I could look around. A man with six years’ experience in claims—they ought to want somebody like that.”

“You’ve said that before.”

“I mean it this time.”

She looked at him searchingly, and for a moment he saw in her eyes the old warmth, the trust of the girl who had come with him from Wisconsin, believing that he would make a way for her in the great city. Then it was clouded over again by doubt, and she turned back to the sink.

“Well,” she said, “I hope so.”

It was not much, but it was something, and he accepted it as such. He stood a while longer in the doorway, watching her, and then went back into the parlour and sat down in the rocking-chair with the evening paper. He opened it to the want advertisements and ran his eye down the columns. “Wanted—Experienced bookkeeper, wholesale grocery, state salary.” “Wanted—Young man for office work, must write good hand.” “Wanted—Clerk, insurance office, references required.” He read this last several times, and then laid the paper down upon his knee and stared at the wall. Young man. He was not a young man any longer. He was thirty-four. In another year or two he would be thirty-six, and then forty, and the advertisements would go on asking for young men, and he would go on drawing eighteen dollars a week in the claims department of the Western Fidelity until he was grey.

In the kitchen the water had stopped running. He heard Alma moving about, putting the dishes away, and then the light went out, and she came through the dining-room and into the parlour. She did not sit down beside him, as she was wont to do of an evening, but went to the window and stood there, much as he had done, looking down into the street. The light from the arc lamp fell upon her face and made it pale.

“It was such a pretty flat,” she said softly, as if to herself.

He did not answer. There seemed nothing to say. He sat in the rocking-chair, and she stood by the window, and between them lay the evening, long and quiet and unconsoling, while out in the darkness the great city went on about its business, indifferent alike to their hopes and to their defeat, building its fine flats upon the boulevards for those who could pay, and leaving the rest to look on.

The dainty slippers and stockings, the delicately frilled skirts and petticoats, the laces, ribbons, hair-combs, purses, all touched her with individual desire, and she felt keenly the fact that not any of these things were in the range of her purchase. She was a work-seeker, an outcast without employment, one whom the average employee could tell at a glance was poor and in need of a situation. It must not be thought that any one could have mistaken her for a nervous, sensitive, high-strung nature, cast unduly upon a cold, calculating, and unpoetic world. Such certainly she was not. But women are peculiarly sensitive to their adornment. Not only did Carrie feel the drag of desire for all which was new and pleasing in apparel for women, but she noticed too, with a touch at the heart, the fine ladies who elbowed and ignored her, brushing past in utter disregard of her presence, themselves eagerly enlisted in the materials which the store contained. Carrie was not familiar with the appearance of her more fortunate sisters of the city. Neither had she before known the nature and appearance of the shop girls with whom she now compared poorly. They were pretty in the main, some even handsome, with an air of independence and indifference which added, in the case of the more favoured, a certain piquancy. Their clothes were neat, in many instances fine, and wherever she encountered the eye of one it was only to recognise in it a keen analysis of her own position—her individual shortcomings of dress and that shadow of manner which she thought must hang about her and make clear to all who and what she was. A flame of envy lighted in her heart. She realised in a dim way how much the city held—wealth, fashion, ease—every adornment for women, and she longed for dress and beauty with a whole heart. On the second floor were the managerial offices, to which, after some inquiry, she was now directed. There she found other girls ahead of her, applicants like herself, but with more of that self-satisfied and independent air which experience of the city lends; girls who scrutinised her in a painful manner. After a wait of perhaps three-quarters of an hour, she was called in turn.

“Now,” said a sharp, quick-mannered Jew, who was sitting at a roll-top desk near the window, “have you ever worked in any other store?”

“No, sir,” said Carrie.

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Well, we prefer young women just now with some experience. I guess we can’t use you.” Carrie stood waiting a moment, hardly certain whether the interview had terminated.

“Don’t wait!” he exclaimed. “Remember we are very busy here.” Carrie began to move quickly to the door.

“Hold on,” he said, calling her back. “Give me your name and address. We want girls occasionally.” When she had gotten safely into the street, she could scarcely restrain the tears. It was not so much the particular rebuff which she had just experienced, but the whole abashing trend of the day. She was tired and nervous. She abandoned the thought of appealing to the other department stores and now wandered on, feeling a certain safety and relief in mingling with the crowd. In her indifferent wandering she turned into Jackson Street, not far from the river, and was keeping her way along the south side of that imposing thoroughfare, when a piece of wrapping paper, written on with marking ink and tacked up on the door, attracted her attention. It read, “Girls wanted—wrappers & stitchers.” She hesitated a moment, then entered. The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”
