Joseph Wendt came up the narrow stairs of the tenement in Halsted Street at a quarter past six, heavy of foot and heavier of mind. He was a man of thirty-eight, broad in the shoulders and thick through the chest, with a short brown beard which he trimmed himself on Sunday mornings before the small glass by the kitchen window. For eleven years he had worked as a packer in the shipping room of a wholesale hardware concern on Lake Street, and in that time his wage had advanced from seven dollars to ten and a half a week, which, considering the times and the number of men who stood ready to take his place, he regarded as something of an achievement. He was not an imaginative man. He had no great notions of what the world owed him, nor any very clear idea of what it was that he wanted from it. He wanted, in a general way, to be let alone, to be paid on Saturday, to have his supper hot and his pipe after it, and to see his children grow up decent and God-fearing, as he himself had been made to grow up, under the hand of a stern father in a small town in Ohio. Beyond this his reflections did not ordinarily go.

On this particular evening, however, he was disturbed. A new foreman had been put over the shipping room that week, a young man of twenty-six, sharp of feature and quick of tongue, a nephew, it was said, of one of the partners, and this young man had seen fit, before the whole floor, to find fault with the manner in which Wendt had crated a consignment of stoves for Peoria. The criticism had been unjust. Wendt knew it, and the other men knew it, but none had said anything, and Wendt himself had stood with his hands hanging at his sides and his face reddening, saying only, "All right, Mr. Crane," because there was nothing else to say. A man with a wife and three children and eleven dollars in the bank does not answer back. He had carried the thing about with him all afternoon, turning it over and over, saying to himself the things he might have said, and growing hotter with each repetition. Now, as he climbed the stairs, it lay upon him like a weight, and he was in that condition, common enough to men of his station, in which the least additional irritation will set loose a wholly disproportionate force.

It should be understood that in such a household the matter of discipline is not, as with the more fortunate, a thing of theory and consideration. There are no books upon the subject at hand, no counsel of physicians or reformers, no leisure in which to weigh the effect of this word or that upon the tender nature of a child. There is only the tradition, handed down unexamined from father to son, that a child must be made to mind; and there is, in addition, the mood of the parent at the moment of offence, which, being compounded of fatigue, worry, the slights of the workshop, and the endless pressure of small wants, frequently determines the issue far more than the offence itself. The child, in these cases, stands as a kind of lightning rod, receiving into himself the accumulated charge of forces with which he has had nothing whatever to do.

The flat consisted of four rooms, two of which gave upon the street and two upon a narrow airshaft through which came, at all hours, the smells and voices of other families. Mrs. Wendt was in the kitchen, standing over the stove, where a pot of cabbage and a few pieces of pork were simmering. She was a thin woman, faded before her time, with pale hair drawn back tight from her forehead and a habit of glancing up quickly whenever a door opened, as though expecting some fresh demand. The two little girls, Lena and Margaret, aged five and three, were playing upon the floor with a rag doll and a spool. Of the boy, Ernest, there was no sign.

"Where's Ernie?" asked Wendt, hanging his hat upon the nail behind the door.

"He's in the front room," said his wife. She hesitated, stirring the pot with more attention than it required. "Joe," she said, "I wish you'd talk to him. I don't know what to do with him."

"What's he done?"

"Well, now, don't get excited," she said, for she saw at once, by the set of his face, how matters stood with him. "It ain't so much. Only you ought to know about it."

"What's he done?" he repeated.

Mrs. Wendt laid down her spoon. "He took fifteen cents out of the cup," she said. "Out of the blue cup on the shelf. I had it put by for the milk man. And he went down to Schuyler's and bought candy with it, and one of them tin horns, and he give some of the candy to the Mulcahy boys. Mrs. Mulcahy told me. I wouldn't have known only for her."

Wendt stood quite still. The blood came up into his face slowly, as it had come up that afternoon before the young foreman, but now there was nothing to restrain it.

"Fifteen cents," he said.

"I know," said his wife. "I talked to him. I give him a good talking to. But he only cried. You ought to say something to him, Joe. He's got to learn."

It was not the sum in itself, though fifteen cents, to a family whose whole weekly substance was ten and a half dollars, was a matter of real moment. It represented, at that time, a quart of milk for three days, or a loaf and a half of bread, or a car fare to and from the North Side, which Wendt, rather than spend, would walk. It represented a fraction of an hour of his life, bent over crates in the cold shipping room, under the eye of a young man who had never crated anything. It was all of this, and more, that rose in him now. He had been robbed, as he saw it, by his own flesh, and the robbery came upon a day when he had already been made to feel, more keenly than in a long time, how little stood between himself and want.

"Ernest!" he called.

There was no answer from the front room. The two little girls had stopped their play and were looking up at their father with that grave, attentive stillness which children assume in the presence of coming trouble. The younger put her thumb into her mouth.

"Ernest! You come out here."

The door of the front room opened slowly, and the boy came out. He was a slight child of seven, small for his age, with his mother's pale hair and a thin, peaked face in which the eyes seemed overlarge. He wore a pair of knee trousers which had been cut down from an old pair of his father's, and a blouse of faded blue calico, patched at the elbow. His face bore the marks of earlier weeping, and his lower lip was already beginning to tremble. In his hand, as if he had forgotten that he held it, was the tin horn—a cheap, bright thing, painted red and gold, with a little wooden mouthpiece.

It may be well to consider, for a moment, what had passed in the mind of this child. He was not, by any standard, a bad boy. He was quiet in the main, inclined to stand on the edges of things, and given to long spells of watching rather than doing. For weeks he had been passing, on his way to and from the public school on Maxwell Street, the window of Schuyler's little shop, where, among the slates and pencils and the jars of licorice and gum drops, there had been displayed a row of these tin horns, glittering in the sun. Other boys had them. The Mulcahy boys, who lived on the floor below, had each been given one by an uncle who worked on the railroad, and they had marched up and down the hallway blowing them, to the great annoyance of the tenants and the infinite envy of Ernest. He had asked his mother for one, and she had told him, as she told him of nearly everything, that there was no money for such things. He had accepted this, as he had accepted many such refusals, without understanding it. Money was to him a vague and mysterious substance, which came into the house on Saturday night and was put away in various places, and which was always, for some reason, insufficient. He did not connect it in any clear way with his father's labour, nor with the milk that appeared upon the table, nor with the rent which the agent came to collect on the first of every month. He knew only that there were coins in the blue cup, that the horn cost ten cents, and that the desire for it had become, in the course of these weeks, a thing larger than himself.

He had taken the coins in the morning, while his mother was in the yard hanging out the wash. He had felt, in doing it, a strange, sick sensation in his stomach, and had been half minded to put them back. But the thought of the horn, and of himself marching in the hallway with it, blowing it before the Mulcahy boys as an equal, had overcome him. At noon he had gone to Schuyler's. He had bought the horn, and with the remaining five cents a bag of gum drops, which he had divided, out of a kind of generous elation, with the Mulcahys. For an hour he had been entirely happy. Then the Mulcahy boys' mother had asked them where they got the candy, and the whole structure of his joy had come down about him.

"Come here," said his father.

The boy came forward a few steps and stopped. He did not look up.

"Come here, I said."

He came the rest of the way and stood before his father, his head bowed, the horn hanging forgotten at his side.

"Look at me."

The boy raised his eyes. They were swimming.

"Did you take money out of that cup?"

The child did not answer. His mouth worked, but nothing came of it.

"Answer me! Did you take that money?"

"Yes, sir," said the boy, in a voice scarcely to be heard.

"How much did you take?"

"Fif—fifteen cents."

"And what did you do with it?"

The boy looked down at the horn in his hand, as though it had betrayed him, and said nothing. Wendt reached out and took it from him. He turned it over in his thick fingers, looking at the cheap gilt and the red paint, already chipped at the bell. It seemed to him, in his present mood, a perfect symbol of all the foolishness and waste in the world.

"So that's what you bought," he said. "That's what you took your mother's milk money for. A piece of tin." He held it up. "Do you know how long I got to work for fifteen cents? Do you? Do you know what I got to stand for, down there, to bring home fifteen cents?"

The boy did not know. He could not have known. But he understood, from the tone of his father's voice, that it was something terrible, and he began to cry openly now, his narrow shoulders shaking.

"Stop that crying," said Wendt. "Crying won't do you no good. You should have thought about crying before you went and stole."

At the word "stole" Mrs. Wendt glanced up from the stove. "Joe," she said, "he's only little."

"Little!" exclaimed Wendt, turning upon her. "He's old enough to know better. He's old enough to go to school, ain't he? He's old enough to know it ain't his money. You want him to grow up a thief? You want him to end up in the Bridewell, like that Kearney boy over on Jefferson Street?" He turned back to the child. "That's where thieves go. Do you hear me? They lock 'em up. They lock 'em up and they don't let 'em out. Is that what you want?"

"No, sir," sobbed the boy.

"Then what did you do it for?"

The boy tried to answer. He wanted to say something about the Mulcahys, and the window at Schuyler's, and how long he had wanted the horn, and how he had asked and been told no. But these things, so large and real within him, would not shape themselves into words. They were too complex, too much bound up with feelings which he had no names for. He only stood and wept, his small fists pressed against his eyes.

"Answer me!"

"I—I wanted it," said the boy at last.

It was the simplest and truest thing he could have said, and it was precisely the thing which his father, at that moment, was least able to hear. For Joseph Wendt also wanted things. He wanted a better place than this, with a yard and a bit of garden, such as he had known as a boy. He wanted a decent suit of clothes, his own having gone shiny at the knees and elbows. He wanted to stand up before young men like Crane and tell them what he thought of them. He wanted, in some dim, unformulated way, to be more than he was. And he had learned, through long years, to choke these wants down, to put them away where they could not trouble him, because there was nothing else to be done with them. To hear his son speak so plainly of wanting, as though wanting were a reason, as though it justified anything, struck him as an insolence almost beyond bearing.

"You wanted it," he repeated. "You wanted it. Well, I want a lot of things. Your mother wants a lot of things. You think we go around taking what don't belong to us because we want it? You think that's how the world goes?" He shook the horn in the child's face. "Nobody gets what he wants in this world. You might as well learn that now. You get what you work for, and you're lucky if you get that."

He looked about him for some means of punishment that should be adequate to the offence and to his own feeling. His father, in Ohio, would have taken down the strap. Wendt had used it himself, upon occasion, though less often than he had been made to feel it. But something in the boy's thin, shaking figure, in the patched elbow of the blouse and the cut-down trousers, restrained him. Instead he took the horn in both hands and bent it. The tin was soft and gave easily. He bent it again, until the bell was crushed flat and the gilt cracked and flaked away, and then he opened the door of the stove and thrust it in among the coals.

"There," he said. "That's what comes of stealing."

The boy watched, his crying suddenly stilled by the shock of it. For a moment he stood quite motionless, his wet face upturned, his eyes fixed upon the stove door, behind which the bright thing he had wanted so long was blackening. Then a long, quavering wail broke out of him, not loud, but so desolate in its quality that even the little girls, who had sat silent throughout, began to whimper in sympathy.

"Now you go in there," said Wendt, pointing to the front room, "and you stay in there. You don't get no supper to-night. And to-morrow you're going down to Schuyler's with me before I go to work, and you're going to tell him what you done. And every Saturday till it's paid back you don't get your penny. You hear?"

"Yes, sir."

"Go on, then."

The boy went. He went slowly, his feet dragging, his shoulders still heaving, and the door of the front room closed behind him. They could hear him through it, sobbing in long, broken breaths, and then, after a while, more quietly.

Wendt sat down at the table. His wife set his plate before him without a word. He took up his fork and began to eat, but the cabbage had no taste to him and the pork seemed tough and stringy. The two little girls were put at their places and ate in silence, glancing now and then at their father and at the closed door. Mrs. Wendt did not sit down. She stood at the stove, her back to the room, doing nothing in particular.

"Well," said Wendt presently, without looking up, "he had to be learned."

"I know it," said his wife.

"You can't let a thing like that go."

"I know it, Joe."

He ate a little more, then pushed his plate away. The anger which had possessed him had spent itself and gone, and in its place had come a heavy, uneasy emptiness, in which the image of the boy's face, upturned toward the stove, kept rising unbidden. He was not a man given to self-examination. He could not have said, if anyone had asked him, that he had been unjust, or that a portion of the force he had loosed upon the child had belonged rightly to the young foreman on Lake Street. Such distinctions were beyond him. He only felt, obscurely, that something had gone wrong, that the thing he had done had been in some fashion larger than it ought to have been, and that he could not now take it back.

It is one of the curious features of our social state that the very forces which press most heavily upon the poor are thus passed on, almost intact, from one generation to the next. The man who is humbled at his labour comes home and humbles those beneath him; the child, so humbled, learns in his turn that the world is a place of narrow means and sudden blows, where desire is a thing to be ashamed of and where the strong may do as they will. Neither Wendt nor his son was in any sense to blame. They were moved, as all of us are moved, by currents whose source lay far beyond their sight—in the counting rooms of Lake Street, in the price of labour, in the thousand impersonal arrangements by which a city of a million souls is fed and housed and made to work. But the effect, upon the soft and impressionable nature of the child, was none the less real for being impersonal in its origin.

After a time Wendt rose and filled his pipe and went to the window, looking down into the street, where the lamps were being lit and the cars went clanging by toward the river. He smoked for some minutes. Then he went to the door of the front room and stood before it, his hand upon the knob. Through the panel he could hear nothing now. He hesitated, uncertain what it was he meant to do or say. He thought, perhaps, of going in—of sitting down upon the edge of the bed where the boy lay and saying something, he knew not what. But the habit of a lifetime, and the tradition of his own father, who had never once in Wendt's memory gone in to him after a punishment, held him back. It would look, he thought, like weakness. It would undo what had been done.

He took his hand from the knob and went back to the window.

In the front room the boy lay upon the bed in the dark, his face turned to the wall. He had stopped crying. He was thinking, in the dim, wordless way of children, of the horn, and of how bright it had been in the window at Schuyler's, and of the sound it had made when he blew it in the hallway, and of how it had looked going into the fire. He was thinking, too, of his father's face, red and strange above him, and of the words about the Bridewell and the locking up. These things went round and round in him, and out of them, slowly, there was forming something which he would carry with him for many years, though he would never be able to say what it was—a sense that the things one wants most are precisely the things that are taken away, and that wanting itself is a kind of crime, to be hidden and denied. Outside, in the hallway below, one of the Mulcahy boys was blowing his horn, a thin, bright, foolish sound, over and over, until a door opened somewhere and a woman's voice told him sharply to stop.

It was not until the last of their guests had been, as Mrs. Ferrand would herself have expressed it, satisfactorily disposed of (old Lady Ambrose to her brougham, and the two young men from the Foreign Office to whatever further diversion the hour might still be supposed to hold for persons of their buoyancy) that she permitted herself to recognise how long, and with what a strange stiffness of patience, she had been waiting. She had waited through the soup and through the fish; she had waited, more wonderfully still, through Lady Ambrose's account of her nephew's engagement, which had required of her a responsive brightness she would hardly have believed herself, an hour before, in a condition to supply; and she had waited, last of all, through the quarter of an hour in the drawing-room during which her husband, standing with his back to the fire and his hands behind him in the attitude she had for eleven years associated with his very finest ease, had talked to the younger of the two young men about the Danube. She had watched him do it. She had watched him, as it were, from the other side of a pane of glass, and it had come to her, with a kind of cold amusement that was not the least of her discoveries, that he had never talked better.

Now, with the door closed upon the hall and the servants' steps receding below, the room took on for her the aspect of a stage from which the supernumeraries have been cleared, leaving only the principals, and leaving them, she felt, with nothing in the world to do but begin. He had not moved from the fire. He had merely, in the absence of an audience, let his hands fall to his sides; and the small relaxation, which at another time she would scarcely have noticed, struck her now as the most eloquent thing he had yet done. It was the gesture of a man who has been holding something up and who, the necessity removed, has simply let it drop.

"Well," he said, "that went off."

"Oh, beautifully. Everything goes off with you."

He looked at her then, not quickly, but with the deliberation of one taking the measure of a remark rather than of a person. "You say that as if it were a charge."

"Do I?" She had sat down on the small sofa near the lamp, and she arranged, with an absorption she was aware he would see through, a fold of her skirt. "I didn't mean it as anything so grand. I meant it only as a fact. You make things go off. It's your genius. I've always admired it."

"Always?"

"Well, so very nearly always that the exceptions don't count."

He came a step away from the fire, and then, as if thinking better of the advance, stopped, so that he stood in the middle of the carpet with nothing to support him; and it was this, oddly, that she found she could least bear, his looking for an instant so unprovided. She had expected, she had even in a manner counted upon, his being defended. It would have been so much simpler to strike at a surface that gave back a sound.

"Maud," he said, "you've had something on your mind the whole evening."

"Is that what you saw?"

"It's what I felt. I don't know that I saw anything. You were perfect with Lady Ambrose."

"Ah, I was perfect with Lady Ambrose!" She gave a short laugh, which she immediately regretted, so little did it sound like any laugh of hers. "It would have been too odious not to be. She has nothing in the world but her nephews, and it costs one so little."

"It costs you something tonight. That's exactly what I mean."

She looked up at him, and for a moment neither of them said anything. The clock on the mantel, a small gilt affair they had brought back from Paris the first year, delivered itself of the half-hour with a tiny, fastidious chime; and she was conscious of thinking, absurdly, that it was the sort of sound one would remember afterwards, the sort of sound that attaches itself, by no right of its own, to the occasions one would give anything to forget.

"I had a visit this afternoon," she said at last.

"Yes?"

"From Mrs. Lisle."

She had wondered, often enough in the course of those long hours, how he would take the name. She had imagined him paling; she had imagined him, which was worse, not paling at all, but simply saying "Ah?" with the polite vacancy he reserved for the mention of people one has not seen for years. What she had not imagined was what actually occurred, which was that he turned, quite slowly, and looked at the fire, as if it were there, among the coals, that the name had fallen and that he must see where it lay.

"She came here?"

"She came here. At four. She sent up her card, and I very nearly didn't see her. I didn't, you understand, know her. I had to think who she was."

"And did you think?"

"Oh, I thought." She paused. "It came back to me. You spoke of her once, a long time ago. You said she had been kind to you in Rome, the year before we met. You said it in just that way, that she had been kind. I remember being touched by it. One so seldom hears a man say a woman has been kind to him. They generally say something else."

He was silent, and she allowed the silence to last, partly because she could not, for the moment, have trusted her voice with anything more, and partly because there had risen in her a curiosity, almost impersonal in its sharpness, to see what he would make of it. She had known him for eleven years; she had believed herself, in the main, to know him through and through; and she found now that she was watching him as one watches a stranger at a play, wondering in which direction the next movement will carry him.

"What did she want?" he asked.

"Ah, there you are. That's precisely the question."

"Isn't it the natural one?"

"Perfectly natural. Only it's the one I've been asking myself since four o'clock, and I haven't yet arrived at the answer. She didn't, you see, want anything. That was what was so extraordinary. She sat where you're standing, or nearly, and she talked to me for half an hour, and she asked for nothing at all."

"Then what did she talk about?"

Maud considered him. "About her son."

He did not move; but she had the impression, which she was never afterwards able to dislodge, that something in the room had moved for him, that the very air had shifted its weight from one foot to the other.

"I didn't know," he said carefully, "that she had a son."

"Didn't you?" She said it gently, and was herself surprised at the gentleness. "He's at Cambridge, it seems. At Trinity. He's nineteen, and very clever, and rather delicate, and they had, she told me, some fear last winter about his chest. But he's better now. A great deal better. He's to go abroad in the summer, to the Engadine, and she thinks it will set him up altogether."

"I'm glad to hear it."

"Yes. I thought you would be."

He turned then and faced her fully, and she saw that he had decided, as she had seen him decide on other occasions, in other rooms, about matters of infinitely less consequence, that the moment had come to stop retreating. It was one of the things she had most admired in him, this capacity for coming at last into the open; she had seen him do it with tradesmen and with ministers and once, memorably, with her own father; and she felt a pang, almost of pride, at seeing him do it now with her, even while she understood that the pride was the last thing in the world she could afford.

"Maud," he said, "what is it you want me to tell you?"

"Oh, my dear, I don't want you to tell me anything."

"That's not true."

"It's truer than you think. It's the truest thing I've said tonight." She rose, because she found she could no longer sit, and went to the window, where the curtains had been drawn against the street, and stood with her back to him, looking at the dull red folds as if they had been a view. "I've been thinking all evening what I wanted. I thought at first I wanted you to explain. Then I thought I wanted you to deny. Then I thought, which was worse than either, that I wanted you to confess, so that I might have the luxury of forgiving you. And then, at about the time Lady Ambrose was telling us about the bishop, it came to me that I didn't want any of those things, because every one of them would require me to know, and I'm not sure, Julian, that I can afford to know."

"Afford?"

"It's a question of expense, isn't it? Everything is, in the end. I'm thinking of what it would cost."

"To whom?"

She turned round. "Ah, that's just it. I can't make out to whom. To you, I suppose, a little. To me, a great deal. And to that poor woman, who sat on my sofa this afternoon and told me about her boy's chest, and never once, never once, Julian, said a word that I could have repeated to anyone as evidence of anything whatever. That's what I can't get over. She was so careful. She was so beautifully careful. She came here, and she risked, I should think, everything she has, and she did it in such a way that if I'd wished to turn her out of the house I shouldn't have had a single phrase to turn her out for."

He was looking at her now with an expression she could not read, an expression that seemed to her compounded in equal parts of dread and of something that, had the circumstances been other, she would have called admiration. "Then why," he said slowly, "do you suppose she came?"

"I've thought of that too. I think she came to see me."

"To see you?"

"To look at me. To find out what sort of woman I was. Whether I was the sort of woman to whom one might—" She stopped.

"To whom one might what?"

"To whom one might, someday, if it were needed, if there were no one else, come again." She held his eyes. "I think she's been ill, Julian. I think she's been more ill than her son. She has that look. And I think she wanted to know, before anything happened to her, whether there would be anyone in the world to whom the boy could be—what shall I say?—mentioned. Not given. Not handed over. Only mentioned. I think she wanted to be sure there was a door that wouldn't be shut."

He sat down, rather suddenly, in the chair nearest him, a stiff little chair of no comfort whatever, which nobody ever used; and she was struck, inconsequently, by the incongruity of his sitting there, he who in all their years together had never once failed to choose the best chair in any room. He put his elbows on his knees and looked at the carpet, and she saw that his hands, loosely joined, were not quite steady.

"And what did you tell her?" he asked, without raising his head.

"I told her nothing. What was there to tell? She asked me nothing. I gave her tea. She admired the Bonington. She said she had known a man in Rome who cared for Bonington, and she wondered if I'd ever heard of him, and I said I believed I had." Maud paused. "That was the nearest she came. She said it quite simply, looking at the picture. And then she got up and said she mustn't keep me, and she gave me her hand, and she held mine for perhaps a moment longer than was usual, and she went."

There was a long silence. Somewhere below, a door closed; a cab went by in the street, its wheels sounding, in the damp, curiously muffled and far.

"You haven't asked me," he said at length, "whether it's true."

"No."

"Why not?"

She came back from the window and stood before him, so that he was obliged, if he would see her face, to look up; and he did look up, and she saw in his own face a thing she had never seen there before, a kind of nakedness, a kind of waiting, that made her think, with a sudden contraction of the heart, of the photographs of him as a small boy that his mother kept in a velvet frame at Bournemouth.

"Because," she said, "if I ask you, you'll tell me. That's the dreadful thing about you, Julian. You will always, in the last resort, tell the truth. You've spent your whole life arranging things so that you need never be asked; but if you're asked, you answer. And if you answer, then we shall both know, and we shall have to do something with what we know. We shall have to put it somewhere. And I've been looking round this house all evening, through the soup and the fish and the bishop, and I can't think where in it we should put a thing of that size."

He stared at her. "You mean you'd rather not know."

"I mean that I know already. I knew at four o'clock. I knew, I think, the moment she looked at the Bonington. What I'd rather not have is your telling me. That's a different thing. Surely you, of all men, can see the difference."

"I can see it," he said, after a moment, "but I'm not sure I can bear it."

"Ah, my dear, but you'll have to. We both shall. That's the bargain."

"What bargain?"

She hesitated, and it seemed to her afterwards that in that hesitation the whole of the rest of their life was, in some manner she could never have explained, decided. "The bargain," she said, "that I'll make with you now, if you'll let me. That you'll never tell me, and I'll never ask. And that when the time comes, if it comes, and if that poor woman sends to this house, or someone sends for her, the door won't be shut. I'll see to that. You needn't. You needn't even know I've seen to it. It shall simply be open."

He rose, slowly, and stood looking at her with an expression so curiously mingled that she could not have said whether it was gratitude or despair that predominated in it. "Maud," he said, "you can't do that. You can't take that on."

"Can't I? I seem to have done it."

"But what will you have?"

The question struck her as so exactly the right one, and at the same time as so impossible to answer, that she very nearly laughed again, and only kept from it by an effort she felt in her throat. What would she have? She would have the house; she would have the dinners, and Lady Ambrose, and the young men from the Foreign Office; she would have him, standing before the fire with his hands behind him, talking about the Danube. She would have all of it exactly as it had been, and she would have, besides, the knowledge, which nobody would share with her, not even he, that it was not at all as it had been, and never again would be.

"I shall have," she said, "the satisfaction of having been, for once in my life, quite as clever as you."

He took it, she saw, as she had meant it, as a thing that was half a reproach and half a gift; and he did not try to answer it. He only came and took her hand, as that other woman had taken it, and held it, as that other woman had held it, for a moment longer than was usual. Then he let it go.

"It's late," he said.

"It's very late."

"Shall I ring for them to put out the lamps?"

"No," she said. "Let them burn a little. I think I'll sit here for a while."

He looked at her, and for an instant she thought he was going to say something more, something that would break the bargain before it had so much as been sealed; and she held her breath. But he only bent his head, as if in acknowledgment of a thing too large for words, and went out, closing the door very quietly behind him. She heard his step on the stair, going up, not quickly, but with a kind of measured care, as of a man carrying something that might spill.

When the sound had ceased she sat down again on the little sofa by the lamp. The clock on the mantel, after an interval that seemed to her immense, struck the hour; and she found that she was looking, without having intended it, at the Bonington on the opposite wall, a small grey view of a French coast with a boat drawn up on the sand and a single figure, no bigger than a fingernail, standing beside it, looking out to sea. She had looked at it a thousand times. She had never, until tonight, noticed the figure at all.

Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Henry James, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.

It was not till he had been shown up the narrow, rather oppressively carpeted stair, and had stood for some moments alone in the small drawing-room, with its two windows upon the square and its fire of a reticence almost moral, that Ralph Everard became aware of how much, during the whole of the long drive from his hotel, he had been bracing himself. He had been bracing himself, he now perceived, against something he could not have named, and which he would have been at a loss to describe even to so patient a confidant as his own conscience. It was not his cousin herself he feared, for there had never been anything in Julia to fear, unless one counted a certain way she had once had of looking at one as if one had already said the thing one was only about to say. Nor was it, precisely, the passage of time, though twelve years were a quantity he had not, until this afternoon, troubled to sum. It was rather, he decided, standing with his hat still in his hand and his eyes on a little water-colour of the old house at Brantham which he recognised with a pang, the *relation* he dreaded: the fact, that is, that there should have been one at all, and that it should now, in the next five minutes, either resume itself or show itself, quite simply and dreadfully, to have died.

The water-colour gave him something to do with his attention, and he was glad of it. It represented the south front, with the cedar and the low wall and the absurd little stone urns that their grandmother had imported, at ruinous expense, from somewhere vaguely Italian, and it had been done, he was all but sure, by Julia herself, in that summer before everything, when she had sat for whole mornings on a camp-stool on the lawn and he had lain on the grass beside her reading aloud from books she pretended to attend to. He had forgotten she could paint. He had forgotten, he now began to suspect, a great many things, and the suspicion was not wholly agreeable, since it suggested that his memory had been less a faithful steward than an indulgent one, keeping for him only those items of the inventory that would not reproach him.

The door opened behind him before he had got further, and he turned to find her already halfway across the room, her hands out, her face lighted with an expression he could only call, for want of a better word, *amused*, as if she had caught him at something.

"Ah, you've found it," she said. "I knew you would. I hung it there on purpose, you know, the very morning I had your letter. I said to myself, 'He'll go straight to it, and then he'll have to decide what to say.'"

He took her hands, and they were, he noted, cool and firm, the hands of a woman who had lately been doing something sensible, writing letters or ordering dinner. "And what *am* I to say?"

"Why, nothing at all, if you don't want to. That's the beauty of it. You can simply look, and I can simply watch you look, and we needn't either of us commit ourselves."

He laughed, and with the laugh he felt the first of his bracings give way, for it was so exactly the sort of thing she used to say, and in so exactly the old tone, that the twelve years seemed for an instant to have been folded up and put away like a screen. "You talk," he said, "as if committing oneself were the danger."

"Isn't it always?" She had released him and was drawing forward a chair for him, nearer the fire, with a little practical air that struck him as new. "But sit down, Ralph, and let me have a proper look at you. You've no idea how I've been wondering."

"Wondering whether I'd grown old?"

"Wondering whether you'd grown *different*. Old is nothing; we all manage that. But different is another affair altogether, and I wasn't sure I was prepared for it."

He sat, and she sat opposite him, and there followed one of those pauses which, between people who have once known each other very well, are less silences than consultations. He was able, in the course of it, to take her in, and he did so with a care that he hoped was not too visibly deliberate. She was thirty-eight, he knew, for she was a year younger than himself, and she looked it, but she looked it, he thought, in the way that certain fine old silver looks its age, by a deepening rather than a dimming of the surface. Her hair, which had been of that indeterminate brown that people called "nice" when they could think of nothing more to say for it, had taken on a few threads of grey at the temples, and she wore it more plainly than of old, drawn back in a manner that made the most of her forehead. Her dress was dark, with something at the throat, and he remembered, with a slight start, that it was only two years since Arthur Considine had died. She did not look, however, like a woman in whom grief had been allowed to establish itself as a tenant; she looked rather like one who had received it as a guest, entertained it with every civility, and seen it, in due course, to the door.

"Well," she said at last, "and have you?"

"Grown different? I hardly know. One isn't the best judge."

"One's the only judge, surely. Nobody else has had the materials."

"You had them once," he said, and was immediately aware that he had gone a step further than he had intended.

She took it, however, with perfect composure, only lifting her eyebrows a very little. "Once. But materials don't keep, you know. They go off, like everything else, if they're left lying about in a damp climate. And I've lived, you'll remember, in a very damp one."

He smiled. "You mean England?"

"I mean marriage," she said simply, and then, as if to forestall any response he might be fumbling for, she rang for tea.

It came, in its silver and its porcelain, with the solemnity proper to such rites in such houses, and for some minutes they were occupied with it, she pouring and he accepting, with those small exchanges of "sugar?" and "no, nothing, thank you" which serve, in English drawing-rooms, the function of the overture at the opera, allowing everyone to settle and nobody to be surprised. He was grateful for the interval; it gave him time to arrange, in some sort of order, the things he had meant to ask her, and to discover that he could not, after all, ask any of them. He could not ask whether she had been happy, because the question would have implied that he had a right to the answer. He could not ask whether she had thought of him, because the answer, either way, would have been insupportable. He could not even ask about Arthur, except in the most general and condoling terms, because he had never liked Arthur, and she knew it, and she would know that he knew she knew it, and the whole thing would collapse into one of those little avalanches of mutual consciousness from which there was no digging oneself out.

So he asked, instead, about the family, and she told him, with an admirable economy, what had become of them all. Aunt Harriet was dead, of course, he would have heard; she had died at Bournemouth, very slowly and very gallantly, quarrelling to the last with a succession of nurses whom she had suspected, each in turn, of designs upon her jewellery. Cousin Frederick had gone into the Church and come out again, no one quite knew why, and was now growing roses in Hampshire with a wife who had once been a governess and was, Julia said, "much the best of the lot of us, which is perhaps why the lot of us don't see her." And Brantham itself had been sold, three years since, to a man from Manchester who had put in electric light and a billiard-room and cut down the cedar.

"The cedar!" Ralph exclaimed, and was surprised by the genuineness of his distress.

"Ah, you see," she said, watching him. "That's the first thing you've really minded. I thought it would be."

"But it was the whole place. One can't imagine the south front without it."

"One needn't imagine it. One needn't go. That's what I tell myself, at least, and it's a great comfort, though I can't pretend it's a very noble one." She set down her cup. "I keep the picture instead. It's the cedar, you know, that makes the picture. I painted it, if you remember, the summer you were reading me Browning."

"I was reading you Browning?"

"You were reading me *something*. I believe it was Browning. You thought it improving, and I thought it very long, and neither of us, I fancy, attended to a word of it. We were thinking of other things."

He looked at her, and she looked back at him, with that old expression of hers, the one he had braced himself against, as if he had already said the thing he had not yet decided whether to say. "What things?" he asked, very quietly.

"Oh," she said, and her voice was perfectly light, "I was thinking about the cedar, of course, and the way the shadows fell under it, and whether I should ever get them right. And you, I suppose, were thinking about going abroad."

There it was, then, laid upon the table between them as neatly as the teaspoons, and he had the sensation, which he was afterwards to recall with a curious mixture of mortification and relief, of having been, for twelve years, the one person in the world who did not know a thing that everybody else had known perfectly well. He *had* been thinking about going abroad, that summer; he had been thinking of very little else. He had been thinking of Rome, and of the work he was going to do there, the great book on the Renaissance tombs that was to establish him, and of the freedom and the light and the largeness of a life unencumbered by Brantham and Aunt Harriet and the whole close, kind, smothering apparatus of family. And he had been thinking, too, though he had hardly admitted it even to himself, of Julia, and of how impossible it would be to take her with him, and of how impossible it would be to stay. He had resolved the dilemma, in the end, by the simple expedient of not resolving it, of going away in September with nothing said, and of letting the letters, which had been frequent at first, grow gradually rarer, until, at the news of her engagement to Considine, they had stopped altogether, with a little note of congratulation on his side which he had rewritten four times and still been ashamed of.

"You knew, then," he said.

"Knew what, my dear?"

"That I was going. Before I told you."

"Before you told *yourself*, I think. You had that look, you know. You'd had it since Easter. I used to watch it come over you at dinner, when Aunt Harriet was talking about the drains, and I used to think, 'He's in Rome now; he's walking about among his tombs.' I didn't grudge it you." She paused. "At least, I don't think I did. It's difficult, at this distance, to be quite sure what one grudged."

"You might have said something."

"I might. But what? 'Please don't go to Rome'? You'd have gone all the same, only you'd have felt worse about it. And I should have felt worse about having said it. No, it was much better as it was. We both behaved beautifully, Ralph. We were models of discretion. I've often thought so."

He could not tell, from her tone, whether she was mocking him, or herself, or the pair of them together, and he suspected that this indeterminacy was precisely her intention. It left him, at any rate, with nothing to defend and nothing to confess, which was perhaps the kindest thing she could have done; and yet he felt, in the very kindness of it, a kind of judgment, all the more searching for being so entirely without severity.

"And the book?" she asked, after a moment, in a different voice. "The tombs? I've been waiting for it. I've looked in every bookseller's list for ten years."

He hesitated. "There isn't any book."

"No book?"

"There are notes. There are a great many notes. There are trunks of them, at my lodgings in the Via Gregoriana, and drawings, and photographs, and a whole correspondence with a man in Siena about a doorway. But there isn't a book. I came to see, after a time, that there wouldn't be one. The subject kept getting larger, you know, the more I looked at it, and I kept looking, and it kept getting larger, and at last I understood that looking was what I did, and that writing it down was another thing altogether, a thing for another sort of man."

She was silent, considering this, and he was aware of waiting for her verdict with an anxiety out of all proportion to the occasion. He had told the same story, in Rome, to a dozen people, with a dozen different degrees of irony, and had grown used to their responses, the polite regret, the cheerful encouragement, the barely concealed satisfaction of those who had never expected anything of him and were pleased to have their judgment confirmed. But he had never told it to anyone who had known him before, who had seen him on the lawn at Brantham with his Browning and his ambitions, and he found that it mattered to him, it mattered to him enormously, what she would say.

"Then you were right to go," she said at last.

He stared at her. "Right? When nothing came of it?"

"But something did come of it. You found out what you were. You'd never have found it out at Brantham, or here in London, or married to me." She said it without the smallest emphasis, as though it were the most natural thing in the world to mention. "You'd have written the book, very likely, because I'd have made you, and it would have been a perfectly respectable book, and you'd have hated it, and hated me a little for it, and never known why. Whereas now you know. It seems to me a great deal to have got."

"It seems to me," he said slowly, "that you're being extraordinarily generous."

"Not in the least. I'm only being accurate, which is quite a different thing, and much rarer. I learnt it from Arthur, as it happens." She smiled at his expression. "Oh yes, I know you never liked him. Nobody did, much, except me, and I'm not sure I did, at first. But he had that one great quality: he always knew exactly what he was, and he never pretended to be anything else. He was a dull, upright, rather obstinate man, who was very good at managing other people's money and not very good at anything else at all, and he knew it, and he made the best of it, and he was, in his way, entirely content. I used to find it maddening. And then, after a few years, I began to find it restful. And then, after a few more, I began to find it something like wisdom." She looked down at her hands. "I didn't grieve for him as I should have grieved for a great love. But I grieved for him as one grieves for a good house, a house one has lived in long enough to know where all the draughts are and to have stopped minding them. It's not nothing, Ralph. It's not the cedar. But it's not nothing."

He did not answer at once, for there seemed to be nothing he could say that would not either diminish what she had told him or presume upon it. The room had grown dusky while they talked; the fire, for all its reticence, threw a stronger light now than the windows, and in that light her face had an expression he had not seen on it before, a kind of settled clearness, as of a landscape after rain. He understood, looking at it, that she had travelled further in her twelve years in Kensington than he in his twelve years in Rome, and that she had arrived somewhere, at some point of vantage, to which he could not follow her and from which she could see him, with all his trunks of notes and his correspondence about the doorway, very plainly indeed.

"And so," he said at last, "we've each had our life."

"We've each had *a* life," she corrected gently. "Whether it was our own is another question, and not, I think, one that it's very profitable to ask at tea-time."

"When is it profitable to ask it?"

"Never, perhaps. Or only very late, when the answer can't make any difference." She rose, and went to the window, and stood looking out at the square, where the lamps were being lighted one by one along the railings. "Are you going back?" she asked, without turning.

"To Rome? I suppose so. My things are there. My doorway is there." He tried to make it sound light, and was not sure he succeeded. "And you? You'll stay here?"

"I'll stay here. I have my friends, and my committees, and my nephew at Harrow who writes to me for money, and my picture of the cedar. I'm not unhappy, Ralph. I want you to know that. It's the one thing I particularly wanted you to know, when I had your letter. I thought you might be imagining all sorts of things, and I didn't want you to go away imagining them."

"I hadn't imagined anything," he said, and then, because that was not true, and because she would know it was not true, he added, "or nothing that I'll admit to."

She turned, then, and came back towards him, and he rose to meet her, and for a moment they stood facing each other on the hearthrug, very near, in the firelight, as they had perhaps stood once, long ago, on another hearthrug, in another house, with a cedar outside the window.

"You were always the one who looked," she said softly. "Even then. Especially then. I used to feel you looking at me, on the lawn, as if I were one of your tombs, as if I were something beautiful and finished that you wanted to understand. And I used to wish, sometimes, that you'd stop looking, and simply *do* something. And then I'd think, no, that's what he is, that's what he's for, and if he stopped looking he wouldn't be Ralph." She put out her hand, and touched, very lightly, the lapel of his coat, as if to set it straight. "Well, you've looked at me again this afternoon, and I hope you've seen what you came to see. I've seen what I wanted to see, at any rate."

"And what was that?"

"That you're exactly the same," she said, and smiled, and the smile had in it, he thought, everything: the summer and the cedar, the Browning and the camp-stool, the twelve years and the silence of them, the regret that had been outlived and the tenderness that had not. "Exactly the same, my dear. It's a great relief. I don't think I could have borne it if you'd changed."

He went down the narrow stair a little later, and out into the square, where the lamps were all lighted now and a fine rain had begun to fall, and he walked a long way, past his hotel and beyond it, before he became aware that he had left his hat behind in her drawing-room, beside the water-colour, where he had set it down when he first came in. He did not go back for it. It seemed to him, on the whole, the right place for it to remain.

It was not until the sound of Mrs. Wetherall's carriage had quite died away, had been absorbed, as it were, into the general muffled roar of the square, which seemed to Mrs. Considine at that hour to receive and dissolve all the small particular noises of her life as the sea receives the indiscretions of rivers, that she permitted herself to recognise what she had, for the full three-quarters of an hour of her visitor's presence, so admirably not recognised. Even then she recognised it at first only by the oblique method of going to the window and standing there with her back to the room, as if the room itself, with its cushions still dented and its cups still faintly warm, might have something to say to her that she was not yet prepared to hear. She stood, in short, and looked out at the plane-trees, which were doing nothing in particular in the thin October light; and she was aware, with a lucidity that had in it something almost of luxury, so long had she been obliged to postpone it, that she must now, in the phrase she had used to herself at the very moment of the catastrophe, "have it out" with Archie.

The catastrophe, if one could give so large a name to so small an occasion, and she had already, at the window, begun to suspect that the smallness was precisely what made it large, had befallen at the instant of the child's being brought down. He had been brought down, as he was always brought down for Mrs. Wetherall, in his blue velvet and his best manner, the latter having been a matter of some weeks' quiet cultivation on the part of Miss Pask. He had made his little bow, which was perfect; he had submitted to the passage of Mrs. Wetherall's gloved hand over his hair, which was more than perfect; and then, being asked, with that lady's large, indiscriminate benevolence, whether he was "glad to see his old friend," he had looked up at her with the gravest, the most candid, the most dreadfully considering of his gazes and had replied, in his clear small voice, that Mamma said she was the kind of person one had to be nice to.

It had been, Mrs. Considine now told herself, a thing of no duration whatever. Mrs. Wetherall had laughed, and the laugh, which she would hear, she believed, at odd hours for the remainder of her days, had been neither long nor loud. It had been merely the laugh of a woman who has been told the price of something she had supposed to be a present. And then, which was so much worse, the visitor had stayed. She had stayed on with a kind of terrible amiability, a bright, voluble, unwavering sweetness, as though to show that she, at any rate, knew how to be nice; and she had talked of Homburg and of the Bannisters' girl and of the new man at St. Jude's, while the child, removed by Miss Pask with a celerity that had itself been a confession, left behind him a void that the two women had filled, for forty minutes, with everything in the world but the one thing.

"Well," said Mrs. Considine aloud to the plane-trees, and then, with a movement that she was conscious of making rather handsomely, as one might put on a cloak for a cold drive, she turned from the window and rang the bell.

She had not, she was aware, the least idea of what she would say to him. She had a great many ideas, and that was the difficulty, for they did not, so to speak, compose; they stood about in her mind like guests who had arrived for different parties. There was the idea that he had been naughty, which was simple and which she clutched at. There was the idea that he had been merely truthful, which was not simple at all and which she put away. And there was, beyond and behind these, a third idea, so dim as scarcely to be an idea and yet so penetrating as to colour all the others: the idea that the person who had really been found out that afternoon, the person whose little bow had been seen through and whose best manner had been exposed, was not, by any means, the person in blue velvet.

He came in, when he came, alone. Miss Pask had evidently judged, with the tact for which Mrs. Considine paid her forty pounds a year and which she had never before so much appreciated, that the interview was one at which a third party would be de trop. He came in and closed the door behind him, reaching up to the handle with the slight, scrupulous effort that always touched his mother, and then stood just within the room, very straight, his hands at his sides, looking at her. He had been divested of the velvet and restored to his holland, and the change, which ought to have diminished him, had somehow the contrary effect. He looked, she thought, less like a child who had been sent for than like a small envoy who had come to treat.

"Come here, Archie," she said.

He came, not quickly and not slowly, and stopped at the precise distance from her chair at which, she could not but feel, he had calculated that she would be able neither to take his hand nor to complain that he held off.

"You know, I think," she began, "why I have sent for you."

He considered this, as he considered everything, with his head a very little on one side. "Is it because of Mrs. Wetherall?"

"It is because of what you said to Mrs. Wetherall."

"Oh," said Archie. And then, after a moment, with a kind of polite interest, as if he were helping her: "That she was the kind of person?"

"There is no occasion," said his mother, "to say it again."

"No, Mamma." He looked at her steadily. "But you did say it."

It was, of course, the very point she had foreseen; she had seen it, from the window, coming up the square like a cab one knows to be bound for one's own door. And yet now that it had arrived she found that she had made no preparation whatever to receive it. She found, indeed, that what she chiefly felt was a sort of wonder at the child's having so unerringly gone to it, as if he had been, all along, in possession of a map of her mind on which this particular place was marked with a cross.

"Whether I said it or not," she produced at last, "is not in the least the question."

"Isn't it?" He seemed genuinely to wish to know. "Then what is the question?"

"The question is," said Mrs. Considine, and stopped. She had meant to say that the question was one of manners, and she had meant to say it with a fine, bright finality that should close the matter as a door is closed upon a draught. But the word, as she approached it, seemed to recede; it seemed, in the presence of those grave eyes, to be the one word of all words that she could least afford to pronounce, inasmuch as it was precisely her manners, her beautiful, practised, unfailing manners, that had that afternoon been held up to the light and found to have a hole in them through which one could see the street. "The question," she said instead, "is that there are things one doesn't repeat."

"Even when they're true?"

"Especially," said Mrs. Considine, with a vivacity that surprised herself, "when they're true."

He took this in. She watched him take it in; she watched it go down, so to speak, into the depths of his small, serious intelligence, and she had the sensation, by no means agreeable, of having dropped a coin into a well and of waiting, and waiting, for the sound. When the sound came it was not at all the one she had expected.

"Then it was true?"

"Archie!"

"I only mean," he explained, with the patience of one who perceives that he has been misunderstood by a person whom he nevertheless wishes to spare, "that if it was true, then Mrs. Wetherall knows something true. And I thought people liked to know true things. Miss Pask says so. She says it is the whole object of lessons."

Mrs. Considine was conscious at this of an impulse, which she did not obey, to put her hand to her forehead. She was conscious, too, of a second impulse, which she obeyed even less, to laugh; and she was conscious most of all, beneath both, of something that was neither an impulse nor a sensation but rather a kind of slow illumination, as when, in a darkened room, one's eyes grow by degrees accustomed to the absence of the lamp and one makes out, one by one, the shapes of objects that have been there all the while. The object she made out now was the simple, the really rather dreadful fact that she had spent seven years, the whole of the little boy's life, in teaching him, through Miss Pask and the curate and the illustrated Scripture histories, that the truth was a beautiful thing; and that she had never, it now appeared, so much as mentioned to him the far more practical circumstance that it was also a thing one kept, like the good silver, in a locked cupboard and brought out only for particular guests.

"There is a difference," she said, and heard her own voice come out rather faint, "between a lesson and a visit."

"Is there?" said Archie. "What is it?"

She looked at him. She looked at him for what seemed to her a long time, and he bore it, she was obliged to own, a good deal better than she did. He was a beautiful child; she had always, with a certain pleasant complacency, known it; but she had not, until this moment, known that he was also a formidable one. It came over her that she had been in the habit of regarding him, very much as she regarded the pictures on her walls and the bindings in her bookcase, as a part of the charming appearance of things, a component, as it were, of the general effect she had so long and so successfully laboured to produce; and that it had never once occurred to her that the component might have a point of view. Yet here was the point of view, standing before her in holland, with its hands at its sides, and waiting with the most unmistakable politeness for her to explain herself.

"The difference," she said, and now she spoke slowly, as if she were picking her way across stepping-stones in a stream that was rather deeper than she liked, "is that at a visit one thinks of the other person. One thinks of what they will feel. Mrs. Wetherall is an old friend of mine. She has been kind to me. She was kind to me when your father was ill, before you were born, when it was not at all easy, I may tell you, to be kind. And when you said that to her, Archie, you hurt her. You hurt her very much. Did you not see that you did?"

For the first time the child's composure seemed to her to falter; not to break, for she had the impression that it was not of the breaking kind, but to waver, as the surface of water wavers when a cloud passes over it. He looked down at the carpet, at the place where the pattern made a sort of medallion of roses, and he seemed to be studying it.

"She laughed," he said at last.

"People laugh," said his mother, "when they are hurt and do not wish one to see it."

"Do they?" He raised his eyes again, and there was something in them now, a sort of dawning, an apprehension not yet arrived at, that she found almost harder to meet than his candour had been. "Do you, Mamma?"

Mrs. Considine did not answer. She could not, for the moment, have answered to save her life; and she was aware, with a precision that had in it something of the pain of a physical blow, that her silence was itself the most eloquent of replies, and that the child, who missed nothing, would read it as easily as he read the large-print primer that lay upstairs on the schoolroom table. She was aware, too, that he would be kind about it, and it was this, more than anything, that she felt she could not bear: that he would see, and understand, and be kind, and that his kindness would have in it, like his rudeness to Mrs. Wetherall, the terrible quality of being perfectly sincere.

She drew herself together. There was, after all, a part to be played, and if she had played it badly hitherto it was no reason for abandoning the stage. She was his mother; he was seven; he had been, by every rule that she had been taught and had faithfully taught in her turn, extremely naughty; and the circumstance that his naughtiness had consisted in an excess of the very virtue she had most laboured to instil was a complication that the rules, as she remembered them, did not provide for and that she must consequently, for the present, ignore.

"You will write to Mrs. Wetherall," she said, "and tell her that you are sorry."

"Yes, Mamma," said Archie at once, with a readiness that she had not looked for and that she found, on the whole, more disconcerting than any resistance. He seemed, indeed, to welcome the prospect; it seemed to present itself to him as a kind of opportunity. "And what shall I say I'm sorry for?"

"For having been rude."

"Was it rude?" He appeared to consider the point dispassionately, as though it were a sum. "I didn't say she was. I only said you said she was."

"That," said Mrs. Considine, "is precisely what was rude."

"Then shall I say that you didn't say it?"

There it was again, the cab at the door, and this time she had not even seen it coming. She sat quite still and looked at her son, and her son looked back at her with an expression in which she could detect no malice whatever, no triumph, no consciousness of advantage, nothing in the world but an earnest, a really touching, desire to be told what to do. And it was exactly this, she afterwards thought, that was the worst of it: that he had not cornered her, that he had not the least notion of cornering her, that he had merely, in his innocence, walked straight through all the beautiful doors and partitions of her life as if they had been made of air, and had come out on the other side to ask her, in perfect good faith, which of the two rooms he was meant to be in.

"You will say," she brought out at last, "that you are sorry to have caused her pain. That is all. You need say nothing about what I said or did not say. Do you understand?"

"Yes," said Archie slowly. "I'm sorry to have caused her pain." He seemed to be committing the formula to memory, testing it as one tests a plank before stepping upon it. "That is true," he added, with an air of relief. "I am sorry for that."

"I am glad to hear it."

"I didn't know it would. Cause her pain, I mean." He hesitated, and then, with a little rush, as if it were something he had been holding for some time and must now set down: "I thought, you see, that if she knew she was the kind of person one had to be nice to, she would be pleased. Because then she would know that everyone was being nice to her. On purpose."

Mrs. Considine closed her eyes for a moment. When she opened them the child was still there, still waiting, and the plane-trees were still doing nothing in the square, and the light had gone a shade thinner, and she felt, without at all being able to say why, that she had lived through something.

"You will have your tea in the schoolroom," she said, "and you will not come down this evening when your father comes in. And tomorrow you will write your letter, and Miss Pask will see that it is properly written, and I will read it before it goes. That is all, Archie. You may go now."

He bowed, the little bow, the perfect one, which seemed to her now to have acquired, since the afternoon, some quality that it had not possessed before and that she could only call, absurdly, an irony. He turned and went to the door and reached up for the handle with the same scrupulous effort as before. And then, with his hand upon it, he paused and looked back at her across the long, still room, across the dented cushions and the cooling cups and the whole charming, careful, elaborate composition of her life.

"Mamma," he said.

"Well?"

"I'm sorry you minded."

It was said so simply, with so complete an absence of anything but the plain wish to give comfort, that for a moment she could not take it in. Then she took it in, and it was as if he had laid something in her lap: something small and warm and alive that she had no idea what to do with. Before she could find an answer, before she could so much as decide whether an answer was required of her, the door had closed upon him and she heard, receding along the passage and up the stair, the light, regular, unhurried sound of his steps.

She sat on, after he had gone, for a long while. She did not ring for the cups to be taken away, nor for the lamps to be brought. She sat in the failing light and let it fail, and she thought, not about Mrs. Wetherall, whom she perceived she would be able to manage, Mrs. Wetherall being, after all, a woman of the world and therefore, in the last resort, a woman who could be dealt with, but about the small person upstairs who was not, and who would not be for a great many years, and who perhaps, she now dimly and rather fearfully felt, would never be. She thought of him writing his letter in his round, laborious hand, and of the formula he would set down, I am sorry to have caused you pain, and of how it would be, of all the letters Mrs. Wetherall was likely to receive that season, the only one that would contain no lie. And she thought, though this came last and she would have been glad not to think it at all, of the words he had left with her at the door; and she knew, with the strange, cold clearness that sometimes visits us at the end of a day on which nothing has happened, that she had sent for him to be reprimanded and that he had gone away forgiving her, and that between these two facts there lay a distance which all her cleverness, all her tact, all the admirable resources of her admirable manner, would never, so long as she lived, entirely contrive to cover.
