Here is an excerpt of Henry James's writing, to show you their style:

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. You don’t want to give me up, at all; you like me—you like me. I know you do; you have shown it, and I have felt it. After that, you may be as cold as you please! They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

The villa which Bernard Ashcombe had taken for the spring stood on the last of the olive-terraces below Bellosguardo, and it had the merit, as he had more than once pointed out to his wife, of looking at Florence without being looked at by it. The city lay beneath in the afternoon haze, its domes and towers softened into something that was less a place than a promise, and the long wall of the garden, crusted with lichen and fringed at the top with a ragged growth of iris, kept off whatever was not picturesque. Ashcombe was fond of the view; he was fond, in a general way, of things that could be held at a convenient distance and admired. He had come to Italy, at forty, with a fortune that had been made for him by a father who never set foot out of Philadelphia, and he had brought with him a capacity for enjoyment which he took, perhaps, a little too much for granted. Of his wife it is less easy to speak, for she was a person about whom her friends had never quite agreed. Some thought her cold and some thought her merely careful; one lady at the hotel in Rome, who had watched her across the table d'hôte for a month, had declared that she was the most unhappy woman in Europe, but that lady was given to large conclusions.

On the afternoon of which I speak, Ashcombe came in from the town by the steep road, with the dust of it on his boots and a parcel of old engravings under his arm, and found his wife in the long room on the ground floor, where the shutters were half drawn against the sun. She was seated at the writing-table near the window, but she was not writing; she had a letter open before her, and she sat with her hands folded upon it, as if it were something that might escape. She did not turn when he entered, and he had crossed half the room, talking of a print-seller in the Via de' Servi who had tried to cheat him with charming manners, before he perceived that she was not listening.

"My dear Helen," he said, laying down his parcel, "you look as if you had seen a ghost."

"I have had a letter from Arthur," she answered, and then she turned her face to him. It was a face which, in repose, had a sort of clear, grave fineness, like that of a portrait by some master who had cared more for character than for colour; but it was not in repose now. There was a faint flush on it, high up on the cheek-bones, and her eyes, which were grey and usually very still, had a light in them that he did not remember to have seen before.

"From Arthur? Well, I hope the young man is prospering. He generally writes when he is not."

"He is prospering," said Mrs. Ashcombe. "He tells me so. He tells me a great deal." She paused, and then she added, very quietly, "He tells me that you paid my father's debts."

Ashcombe stood still for a moment. He was a large, fair, comfortable-looking man, with a beard that was beginning to be touched with grey and a habit of standing with his feet planted wide apart, as if the world were a deck that might lurch beneath him; and now he planted them a little wider. "Did he, indeed?" he said. "That was very indiscreet of Arthur."

"Then it is true?"

"My dear, I don't see why it should trouble you, at this time of day."

"That is not an answer," said his wife.

He looked at her, and then he looked about the room, at the old brown cabinets and the faded damask of the walls, as if they might furnish him with something better; and then he gave a short laugh, which was meant to be easy and did not altogether succeed. "Well, it's true," he said. "I did pay them. I don't know what else Arthur has told you; I suppose he has made a romance of it. He was always a romantic boy. But there's no romance in it at all. Your father was in difficulties, and I happened to be in a position to relieve them. That was all."

"When did you relieve them?"

"Oh, some time ago."

"Before you asked me to marry you, or after?"

He did not answer at once, and in the little silence she rose from her chair and stood with one hand resting on the back of it. She was tall, nearly as tall as he, and she had a way of holding herself very straight, which he had used to admire as a kind of distinction, and which at this moment struck him, for the first time, as a kind of defence.

"Before," he said at last. "A month or two before. I don't remember exactly."

"You remember very well," said Mrs. Ashcombe. "You remember everything that concerns money; you have told me so yourself. You said it was the one talent your father left you." She spoke without bitterness, or with a bitterness so finely drawn that it might have passed for mere precision. "It was in March," she went on. "It was the March before we were married. Arthur says that you went to see papa at Bath, and that you were with him for two hours, and that when you came away the house was saved, and the lawyers were paid, and papa could hold up his head again. He says that papa told him the whole story the night before he died. He thought I knew it. He thought, I suppose, that it was a thing a wife would naturally know."

"It was a thing I wished you not to know," said Ashcombe.

"Why?"

He made a gesture with his large, well-kept hands, as of a man who should be asked to explain why he preferred the shady side of the street. "Because it had nothing to do with you. Because it was a matter between your father and me. Because—well, because I didn't want it to stand between us."

"And you thought," said his wife, "that by not telling me you would keep it from standing between us?"

"I thought it was the delicate thing to do."

She looked at him for a long moment, and an observer, had there been one, might have said that she was trying to determine whether he believed what he said. Then she turned away and walked to the window, where the hot light came through the slats of the shutter in thin golden bars and lay across her dress. "The delicate thing," she repeated. "Yes; I daresay it seemed so. You have always been very delicate with me, Bernard. I have often thought so. I have thought that no woman was ever treated with more consideration. You have never asked me for anything; you have never reproached me; you have never once, in two years, said a word that I could not have repeated to my grandmother." She paused. "I used to wonder at it. I wonder at it no longer."

"Helen," he said, "what on earth do you mean?"

"I mean that one is very considerate of what one has paid for."

He took a step towards her, and then stopped, as if the floor between them had become uncertain. "That's an ugly thing to say," he said, in a lower voice.

"It is an ugly thing to feel," she answered, without turning round. "I didn't choose to feel it. I have been sitting here for an hour, trying not to feel it. I read Arthur's letter at luncheon, and I have read it six times since, and every time I have said to myself, 'It doesn't matter; it was kindly meant; he is a generous man and he did a generous thing.' And every time I have come back to the same place. I can't get past it. I can't get round it. It is there."

"What is there?"

"The fact that I didn't know." She turned now and faced him, and he saw that her eyes were bright with something that was not quite tears. "Don't you see, Bernard? If you had told me—if you had come to me and said, 'Your father is ruined, and I have the means to save him, and I mean to do it whether you will have me or not'—I think I should have loved you for it. I think I should have married you with my whole heart. But you didn't tell me. You went to papa first. You settled it with papa. And then you came to me, and you asked me, very kindly and very modestly, as if you had nothing in your hands at all, and I said yes, and I thought—" She stopped, and her voice, which had been quite steady, gave way a little. "I thought it was my own yes."

"It was your own," he said. "Good heavens, Helen, it was your own! Do you suppose I would have had it any other way?"

"I don't know what you would have had," she said. "That is just it. I don't know. I don't know what papa said to me, in those weeks, because of what you had done for him; I don't know what he left unsaid. I remember that he was very gentle with me that spring; I remember that he spoke of you often, and always well, and that once, when I said you were rather dull, he looked at me in a way that I didn't understand. I understand it now. I remember that my aunt Caroline came down from London and talked to me for a whole evening about the duty a woman owes to her family, and that I thought she was very tiresome. I suppose she knew too. I suppose everybody knew except me." She gave a little laugh that was worse than the tears. "It is a curious sensation, to find that one has been the only person in one's own story who didn't know the plot."

Ashcombe sat down heavily in a great carved chair near the cold hearth, and for some moments he said nothing at all. He was not a man of quick speech; his mind, when it was moved, moved slowly, like a large vessel coming about, and he had learned to wait for it. When at last he spoke, it was with a kind of laboured honesty that was not without its dignity.

"I'll tell you exactly how it was," he said, "and you may make what you like of it. I had seen you three times. I had seen you at the Merivales', and at the concert in the Assembly Rooms, and once walking on the hill with your sister; and I had made up my mind, after the second time, that if I couldn't have you I would go back to America and never look at another woman. That's the plain truth, and you may laugh at it if you please. Then I heard—it was Merivale who told me—that your father was in a bad way, that he'd been speculating in some infernal mining concern, and that the house was to go, and the furniture, and that you and your sister would be turned out with next to nothing. I thought of you being turned out, and I couldn't stand it. I went to your father. I didn't go to bargain with him; I give you my word I didn't. I went because I couldn't stand it."

"And you didn't speak of me?"

"I did speak of you," he said, after a moment. "I told him what I felt. I told him I meant to ask you, and that he needn't think the money had anything to do with it, one way or the other. I told him he was free and you were free."

"And did he believe you?"

Ashcombe was silent.

"You see," said his wife gently, "you can't answer that. Nor can I. Papa was a proud man, and he was a frightened man, and he was very fond of me; and I think he believed you as much as a man can believe what it would ruin him to doubt. But I don't know what he said to me. I don't know what he made me feel. I only know that I was told I was free, by everybody, in a hundred ways; and that I am finding out, two years afterwards, that I was never free at all."

"You talk," said Ashcombe, with a sudden heat that surprised them both, "as if I had bought you at a fair!"

"I talk as if you had made it impossible for me to know whether you had," she said. "That is all. That is quite enough."

He got up again; it seemed impossible for either of them to remain long in one place. He walked the length of the room and back, and his heavy step sounded on the bare tiles with a kind of hollow insistence, like the ticking of some large clock. "And what do you want me to do?" he asked at last, stopping before her. "Do you want me to say I'm sorry? I am sorry—sorry Arthur couldn't hold his tongue. Do you want me to say I was wrong? I don't think I was wrong. I did what any man would have done who cared for a woman as I cared for you."

"Any man," said Mrs. Ashcombe, "would perhaps have told her."

"And had her refuse me out of pride!"

She looked at him with a sudden, strange attention. "Ah," she said slowly, "then you did think of that."

He coloured deeply, up to the roots of his fair hair, and for an instant he looked like a great schoolboy caught in a fault. "I thought of it," he admitted. "Of course I thought of it. I knew you. I knew you'd rather starve than be beholden to anybody. I knew that if I came to you with the money in one hand and myself in the other, you'd have sent me packing with both. And I wanted you. I wanted you more than I wanted to be—to be delicate, if you like. I won't pretend I didn't."

"No," she said; "don't pretend. It's the first thing you've said that I quite believe."

There was a pause, during which the faint sounds of the garden came in to them through the shutters—the dry whir of a cicada in the olives, the distant creak of a well-chain, the voice of the old contadino calling to his donkey on the terrace below. Mrs. Ashcombe had sat down again, not at the writing-table, but on a low sofa against the wall, and she sat with her hands in her lap, looking at them as if they belonged to someone else.

"I wonder," she said presently, in a different tone, almost musingly, "whether you have any idea what you have done. Not to papa; you did him nothing but good, and I shall always be grateful to you for that. I mean to me. You have taken away the one thing I was sure of. I was never very sure of anything, Bernard; I was brought up among people who said one thing and meant another, and I learned very early to distrust what was told me. But I was sure of that. I was sure that when I married you, I did it of my own will, with my eyes open. I didn't marry you for love—I won't pretend that either; we have agreed not to pretend. But I married you because I thought you were good, and honest, and kind, and because I thought I could make you a decent wife; and I was proud of having chosen so sensibly. It was the one sensible thing I had ever done. And now I find that it wasn't my doing at all. It was arranged. I was arranged, like the flowers on a dinner-table."

"Helen, you are cruel."

"Am I? I don't mean to be. I am only trying to tell you the truth, since we have come to that. It seems to me we have never told each other the truth before. We have been very polite."

He stood looking down at her, and there was in his large, simple face an expression of trouble so genuine, so unguarded, that if she had raised her eyes she might have been moved by it. But she did not raise them. "And now that we have told it," he said, "what are we to do?"

"I don't know," she said. "I have been asking myself that all the afternoon. I don't know."

"You're not thinking of leaving me?"

The question fell into the silence with a kind of crudeness, as if he had dropped something heavy on the floor; and she winced at it, very slightly. "I am not thinking of anything so dramatic," she said. "Where should I go? To Arthur, who would be horrified? To my sister, who would tell me I was a fool to quarrel with my bread and butter? No, Bernard; I shall stay. I shall go on being your wife. I shall order the dinners and receive your friends and go with you to look at pictures, and I shall do it all, I hope, quite as well as before. But you must not ask me to feel as I felt before. That is gone. You took it away in March, two years ago, and I only found out this morning that it wasn't there."

He was silent for a long time. Then he did a thing which she had not expected, and which, as she afterwards admitted to herself, was perhaps the most intelligent thing he could have done: he said nothing more in his own defence, but went quietly to the window and pushed open the shutter, so that the full light of the declining afternoon poured into the room, and the whole wide valley lay before them—the river shining like a blade, the city dreaming in its rosy dust, the far hills turning violet against a sky of pale, transparent gold.

"I'm a slow man, Helen," he said, with his back to her. "I've always known it. Things take a long time to get into my head, and a longer time to get out of it. I've been thinking, while you talked, that you're right in a way—more right than I like. I did take something from you. I didn't mean to, but I did. And I don't know how to give it back. I don't suppose it can be given back, any more than one can give back a man the years he's lost." He paused. "But I'll tell you one thing, and you may believe it or not, as you please. I've never once, in these two years, thought of you as a thing I'd paid for. I've thought of you every day as a thing I didn't deserve. That's been my trouble, if you want to know; that's why I've been so—so polite, as you call it. I was afraid of you. I'm afraid of you now."

She raised her eyes at last and looked at his broad back, framed in the golden square of the window, and something passed across her face which it would be too much to call tenderness, but which was at least the beginning of a doubt. "Afraid of me?" she said.

"Afraid you'd find out exactly what you've found out to-day. I've been waiting for it. I think I knew it would come." He turned round, and his face, against the light, was in shadow. "Well, it has come; and I'm still here, and so are you. Perhaps that's something."

"Perhaps," said Mrs. Ashcombe. She rose, slowly, and stood for a moment irresolute, as though she might go to him; and then, with a slight movement of the head which might have meant anything, she took up Arthur's letter from the table, folded it very carefully along its creases, and put it into her pocket. "I shall answer Arthur to-morrow," she said. "I shall tell him that I knew it all along. It will be better for him to think so."

"And will it be better for you?"

She considered this with the gravity she gave to everything. "I don't know yet," she said. "I shall have to find out. You must give me time, Bernard. You have given me everything else."

He winced, as she had winced before; and she saw it, and for a moment she seemed sorry. But she did not unsay it. She went past him to the door, very straight and quiet, with the long bars of light sliding over her dress; and on the threshold she paused and looked back, not at him, but at the view, which was at its loveliest just then, and which she had never cared for.

"It is very beautiful," she said. "You were quite right to take this house. One sees everything from here, and nothing sees one."

And she went out, leaving him alone with the parcel of engravings, which he did not open that evening, nor for many evenings after.

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. “Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. “I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Edmund Fane had been told, at the little station on the lake, that the Villa Morosini was not above a mile from the landing, and he had elected to walk the distance, partly because the afternoon was of that soft, gilded Italian kind which seems to have been arranged expressly for the indulgence of strangers, and partly because he wished to give himself a little time. Fane was not a man who habitually composed his face. He had passed the greater part of his life in Boston, in the transaction of a business which required him rather to read the faces of others; and he had been told, more than once, by people who wished him well, that his own expression was of so open and candid a character that it would have been a positive indiscretion in a less honest man. He had laughed at this, but he had not forgotten it, and he remembered it now, as he went along the dusty road between the walls over which the roses tumbled, and the lake, on his left hand, lay as blue and as still as a painted floor.

His cousin had written to him in the winter. It was the first letter he had had from her in six years, and he had read it three times before he had quite made out that it was an invitation. It was a very charming letter; Harriet had always written charming letters, even as a girl, when her spelling had been the despair of her governess and her sentiments the despair of her mother. It spoke of her husband's death, which had occurred two years before and of which Fane had heard at the time through the ordinary channels of family report; it spoke of the climate, and of the villa, which she had taken for the spring, and of the extraordinary quantity of nightingales; and it ended with a phrase which he had turned over in his mind a good many times during the voyage. "I am so tired of the people here," she had written, "who know everything about me except the one thing that matters, which is that I was once a little girl in a pinafore. You are the only person left in the world who knows that. Come and remind me of it."

He had come, at any rate; and as he passed at last through a gate set in the wall, and up an avenue of cypresses that rose on either hand like a double row of solemn, dark-robed sentinels, he asked himself, with a sort of humorous apprehension, what it was precisely that he had come to remind her of.

The house was large, yellow, and somewhat dilapidated, with green shutters and a loggia from which a flight of steps descended to a terrace above the water. A servant in a striped waistcoat received him with that air of benevolent indifference which Fane was to learn is peculiar to Italian domestics, and conducted him through a succession of lofty, half-furnished rooms, smelling faintly of damp plaster and orange-blossom, to the loggia itself. Here, for a moment, he was alone. He stood looking out at the lake and the mountains beyond it, which were of a delicate violet colour and had the air of having been placed there by somebody with excellent taste; and he was still looking when he heard a step on the marble behind him and turned round.

It would be too much to say that he did not know her; but it may be confessed that, during the first instant, he knew her rather as one knows a portrait of a person than the person herself. She had been a slim, quick, brown-haired girl, with a great deal of colour and a great deal of impatience; she was now a tall, quiet woman, still slender, still brown-haired, but with a pallor which the black of her dress made almost luminous, and with a manner in which the impatience appeared to have been not so much extinguished as very carefully put away, like a jewel that is no longer worn but is too valuable to be sold. She stood still for a moment, as he had done, and they looked at each other across the width of the loggia; and then she came forward with both her hands held out.

"You are exactly the same," she said. "It's perfectly monstrous."

"I'm a great deal heavier," said Fane, taking her hands. "And I'm rather bald on the top, though you are too well-mannered to look."

"I looked at once. It's the first thing a woman looks at. But you are the same, all the same. You have the same way of standing as if you were waiting for somebody to tell you that you might sit down." And she laughed, and released her hands, and pointed him to a chair. "Sit down, then, Edmund. I give you leave. I have been giving myself leave to do all sorts of things lately, and it's a great comfort to have somebody else to give it to."

He sat down, and she placed herself opposite him, on a low cane seat, with her hands folded in her lap. A tray with tea-things had been set out on a little table between them, and she busied herself with it for some moments in silence; and Fane, watching her, had time to observe that her hands, which he remembered as rather rough and brown and perpetually scratched from the briars of their grandmother's garden, were now very white and very still, and that she wore on one of them a single ring which was not, so far as he could judge, a wedding-ring.

"I can't tell you how strange it is," she said presently, giving him his cup. "I have thought so often of what it would be like to see you again that now it has happened I feel as if I had rehearsed it badly. I had all sorts of clever things prepared, and I can't remember one of them."

She looked at him over the rim of her own cup. "Do you remember the summer at Newport when I wrote the play, and made you act the wicked uncle, and you refused to learn your part?"

"I remember that you told me I was too stupid to learn it."

"The play was silly," said Fane, with that mild directness which had always been, in the family, a source alternately of amusement and of exasperation.

Harriet threw back her head and laughed, and for an instant the woman in black was gone and the girl in the pinafore had come back. "There!" she cried. "You see? You are exactly the same. "And you held the ladder," she said, more softly.

"And I held the ladder," Fane assented.

There was a short silence, during which the nightingales, of whose numbers she had not exaggerated, made themselves heard from the dark mass of laurels below the terrace. Fane drank his tea, and Harriet looked out at the lake; and it occurred to him that there was something in her face, as it was turned thus away from him, which he had not seen in it before, and which he was at a loss to name. It was not exactly sadness, nor was it exactly fatigue; it was rather the expression of a person who has made, at some period, a very considerable calculation, and has been engaged ever since in verifying the sum.

"You have been very good to come so far," she said at last. "I didn't really expect it. I wrote that letter in a mood, and posted it before the mood was over, and then I was ashamed. I thought you would send me a polite note, and a box of Boston candy at Christmas."

"I very nearly did," said Fane honestly. "But I had nothing in particular to keep me. And then there was that phrase about the pinafore."

"Ah, the pinafore!" She turned back to him with a little smile. "I thought that would fetch you. You were always sentimental, Edmund, under all your Boston crust. You used to keep the shells I gave you in a cigar-box with a label on it."

"I have the cigar-box still," said Fane.

He had not meant to say this, and he was conscious, the moment it was out, that it had the effect of a stone dropped into a well. She did not answer it directly. She looked at him for a moment with those clear grey eyes, which had grown, he thought, a little larger in her thinner face, and then she began to speak of other things—of his mother, whom she had loved; of his business, which she declared she did not understand and did not wish to; of the various cousins and aunts and connections by marriage who had multiplied in her absence to a degree which she professed to find positively alarming. She asked a great many questions, and she listened to the answers with an attention which Fane found extremely flattering, until it dawned upon him that she was listening, perhaps, not so much to what he said as to the sound of his voice saying it, as one listens to an old tune that one has not heard for many years, not for the sake of the tune, but for the sake of the place and time at which one heard it first.

"And you?" he said, when she had at last exhausted her catalogue. "You have told me nothing about yourself."

"There is nothing to tell. I have lived in Europe for fourteen years. You know what that means. It means that one has seen a great many pictures and a great many people, and that one can no longer distinguish between them."

"That's very neat," said Fane. "But it's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have." She made a little gesture with her white hands. "I married Mr. Lomax. You know that, at least. You sent me a silver inkstand, which was very appropriate, because I never wrote to anybody afterwards."

"You wrote to me once," said Fane.

"Did I? What did I say?"

"You said you were very happy."

She was silent for a moment. "Then I suppose I was," she said. "One generally is, when one says so in a letter. It's afterwards that one finds out."

Fane put down his cup. He was not a man who was fond of approaching a subject indirectly, and he had always found, in his business, that the shortest way to the bottom of a matter was to walk straight at it. But he was aware, at this moment, of an impulse which was new to him—the impulse to stand still and let the matter come to him; and he obeyed it, with a curious sense that he was learning something.

"He was a very distinguished man," Harriet went on presently, in a lower voice. "Everybody said so. He was very clever, and very well-connected, and he knew all the right people, and he was never unkind to me—never once. I want you to understand that, Edmund, because people have said things—I daresay they have said them in Boston—and they were not true. He was never unkind. He simply—" she hesitated, and seemed to search for the word, "—he simply never noticed that I was there. I was like a very handsome piece of furniture that he had bought because it went well with the room. And when one is a piece of furniture for twelve years, one gets into the way of standing still."

"I see," said Fane gravely.

"No, you don't," she said, with a flash of the old impatience. "You can't. You have never stood still in your life. You have always been going somewhere, and doing something, and being of use. That's what I envied you for, even when we were children. You were always of use. You held the ladder."

"I'm afraid that's all I'm good for," said Fane, with a smile.

"It's a great deal," said Harriet. "It's a great deal more than most people are good for. Most people only want to climb."

She got up, as she said this, and went to the edge of the loggia, and stood there looking down at the terrace and the water. The sun had begun to sink behind the mountains on the farther shore, and the lake had turned from blue to a sort of molten gold, across which a little boat with a striped awning was moving very slowly, like an insect on a sheet of glass. Fane rose too, after a moment, and went and stood beside her; and they remained there together for some time without speaking, while the shadows of the cypresses grew longer on the gravel below them, and the nightingales redoubled their efforts in the laurels.

"Edmund," she said at last, without turning her head, "I want to ask you something. I want to ask you a great favour; and I want you to tell me honestly whether it is too great."

"Ask it," said Fane.

"I am going to be married again."

He had been expecting something; he could not have said what; but he had not been expecting this, and he was conscious of receiving it as a man receives a blow upon a bruise which he had forgotten was there. He did not move, and his face, so far as he could tell, did not change. But he was aware that she was watching him out of the corner of her eye, and that she had seen whatever there was to see.

"I congratulate you," he said.

"Don't," said Harriet quickly. "Not yet. Wait until I have told you. He is an Italian; his name is Count Alvisi; he has a house in Florence and another in Venice, and not a penny to keep up either of them. He is not clever, and he is not distinguished, and he knows none of the right people, because the right people have all quarrelled with his family for three hundred years. He is very kind, and he laughs a great deal, and he notices that I am there. That's all. I told myself I would never marry again, and I find that I am going to do it, and I am frightened to death."

"Frightened of what?"

"Of everybody. Of my husband's relations, who will say that I have thrown myself away. Of the people here, who will say that he is marrying me for my money—which is quite true, in a way, though it isn't the whole truth. Of our own people at home, who will say that I have become a foreigner and forgotten who I am. Of myself, most of all, because I have made one mistake already, and I don't know whether I have the right to make another."

"And what is it that you want me to do?"

She turned round then and faced him, and he saw that her eyes were full of tears, though her voice was perfectly steady.

"I want you to tell me that I am not doing wrong. I want somebody who knew me before—before I became a piece of furniture—to look at me and say that it is still I, and that I am still allowed to be happy. You are the only person who can say it, because you are the only person who remembers. I wrote to you because of that. I didn't know it at the time, but I know it now. I wanted you to hold the ladder."

Fane looked at her for a long moment. He thought of the cigar-box, with its absurd label, which was at that moment reposing in a drawer of his writing-table in Mount Vernon Street; he thought of the summer at Newport, and the princess in the tower, and the play which he had refused to learn; he thought—it may be confessed—of a certain evening, fifteen years before, on the steps of their grandmother's house, when he had been on the very point of saying something to her, and had not said it, because she had been talking with such animation of Europe, and of all the things she meant to see there, that it had seemed to him a kind of cruelty to interrupt her. He had always told himself, since, that he had been right; and he told himself so again now, standing on the loggia above the golden lake, with a conviction which was very nearly perfect, and which only fell short of being quite so by an interval so small that no one but himself would ever have been able to measure it.

"My dear Harriet," he said, and he said it with that oddly humorous gentleness which his friends had always found so difficult to resist, "you are not doing wrong. You were never meant to be a piece of furniture; I could have told you that at Newport, if you had asked me. You were meant to climb ladders and read the books on the top shelf. Marry your Count, and let him laugh, and let him notice you. And if the relations say anything, you may refer them to me."

She gave a little cry, half a laugh and half a sob, and put out her hand, and he took it and held it.

"You are very good," she said. "You were always very good. I don't deserve it."

"Nobody deserves anything," said Fane. "That's what makes it pleasant to get it."

She laughed outright at this, and wiped her eyes, and the girl in the pinafore came back once more, and stayed, he fancied, a little longer than before. "You will stay?" she said. "You will stay and meet him? He is coming tomorrow. I told him about you; I told him you were the most sensible man in America, and he was dreadfully afraid. He thinks Americans are all very sensible and very rich, and he can't understand how anybody can be both at once."

"I'll stay," said Fane. "I'll be as sensible as I can manage, and I'll try not to look too rich."

"You couldn't look rich if you tried," said Harriet. "You look like a man who has come to see about the drains." And she took his arm, and led him down the steps to the terrace, where the nightingales were singing, and the cypresses stood up black against a sky of the clearest amber, and the little boat with the striped awning had reached the farther shore.

They walked up and down there until it was dark, talking of a hundred things—of Newport, and their grandmother, and the cousin who had married the missionary, and the aunt who had kept parrots—and Fane laughed a great deal, and Harriet laughed more, and if, at certain moments, there was a little pause in their talk, during which each of them seemed to be listening to something which the other did not hear, it was nothing that either of them chose to notice. It was only much later, when he had gone up to the great, bare, lofty room which had been assigned to him, and had opened the shutters upon the starlit lake, that Edmund Fane permitted himself to reflect that he had come four thousand miles to hold a ladder, and that he had held it very well; and that if there was nothing, after all, at the top of it for him, that was perhaps no more than he had always known, and no less than, in his quiet, sensible, Boston way, he had always been prepared to accept.

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. “I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”
