The Hallam house in West Eleventh Street had been built in the decade when New York still believed that a front door should be approached by a flight of brownstone steps steep enough to discourage the casual, and Mrs. Lucius Hallam, who had lived in it for twenty-eight years, had never questioned the principle. She had, indeed, come to regard the steps as a kind of moral qualification, and was faintly surprised, on the March afternoon when her cousin was announced, to hear the visitor's voice already in the hall before the parlour-maid had finished pronouncing her name.

"Madame de Saulnier," said the maid, and stood aside. In the doorway stood a small woman in grey, who seemed to have come in on a gust of some lighter air than ever blew down West Eleventh Street.

Mrs. Hallam rose, conscious, as she did so, of the exact weight of her own figure and of the long folds of her black poplin, which she had put on that morning with a sense of its appropriateness and now perceived to be merely heavy. She had been widowed eighteen months, and the poplin was a concession to the second year of mourning; but she saw at once that her cousin, whose own husband had been dead for three, wore no mourning at all, unless the faint lavender of a bow at her throat could be construed as an allusion to it.

"Augusta!" said Madame de Saulnier, and came forward with both hands out.

It was twenty-two years since the cousins had met, and in that interval each had kept, in the inner cabinet where we store the images we have no further use for and cannot bring ourselves to destroy, a portrait of the other at twenty-four. Mrs. Hallam's portrait was of a slender, rather sallow girl with a quick laugh and an incorrigible habit of saying the thing that was felt by everyone and expressed by no one; and she had braced herself to find this girl effaced by the years, or else, which would have been more painful, preserved in a kind of embarrassing caricature. She was not prepared to find her simply transposed into another key, smaller and more finished, as if life had worked over the original with a fine tool and removed only what was superfluous.

"You look exactly—" Mrs. Hallam began, and stopped, because it was not true, and because the old habit of veracity that had been bred in the Danes for three generations rose up in her before the conventional phrase could escape.

"Oh, don't," said Madame de Saulnier, laughing. "I look exactly my age, and so do you, and we may as well be thankful we have kept our teeth. Is that the same sofa? It can't be the same sofa."

"It was re-covered," said Mrs. Hallam, with dignity, "in eighty-four."

They sat down upon it together, and Mrs. Hallam rang for tea, and for a few moments the conversation was carried on by the furniture, as it so often is in rooms that have been long inhabited by people of settled habit. Madame de Saulnier's glance travelled over the Landseer engraving above the mantel, the pair of Sèvres vases that had come from old Mrs. Dane's house in Bond Street, the case of Lucius Hallam's mineralogical specimens that his widow had not yet found the courage to remove; and Mrs. Hallam, watching her, had the odd sensation of seeing these objects with a stranger's eye, not as the inevitable accompaniments of existence but as things that had been chosen, and might have been chosen otherwise.

"You've kept the Sèvres," said Madame de Saulnier.

"Of course I have kept them. Grandmamma left them to me."

"Of course," her cousin agreed; and Mrs. Hallam could not have said why the assent should have sounded to her like a mild impertinence.

The tea came, and with it a plate of the thin bread-and-butter that the Hallam cook had been cutting in exactly the same manner since the Centennial; and while Mrs. Hallam poured out, she reviewed in her mind the facts that a quarter of a century of correspondence had furnished her with regarding her cousin's existence.

They were not few, for Julia Dane had been a faithful correspondent. Her letters, arriving at first fortnightly and then monthly, and at last, in the later years, at the seasons of Christmas and Easter, had been for a long time the principal intellectual event of the Dane connection. They had been written on thick cream-coloured paper stamped with a small coronet, which old Mrs. Dane, in the beginning, had affected not to notice and had afterwards come to examine with a magnifying glass; and they had described, with a lightness that the family at first deplored and later came to depend upon, a life of such variety and animation that West Eleventh Street had grown accustomed to living a little vicariously upon it. There had been the apartment in the Rue de Varenne, with its painted panels; the summers at the Saulnier château in Touraine, where the chimneys smoked and the dowager Marquise received in a bonnet of the Second Empire; there had been an ambassador who quoted Horace at dinner, and a Russian princess who kept a tame marmoset, and a novelist, very much talked of, who had once read aloud from a manuscript in Julia's own drawing-room. There had been no children; but this deficiency, which in any other member of the family would have been the subject of a decent and prolonged commiseration, had seemed in Julia's case merely to leave more room for the marmosets and the novelists.

Mrs. Hallam had read these letters aloud—to her mother while her mother lived, to her aunts, to Lucius, who listened behind the *Evening Post* and occasionally said "H'm" at the mention of a title. She had read them, in short, as a public trust; and it was only now, with her cousin actually beside her, stirring her tea with a little gold spoon that she had evidently brought with her in her reticule, that it occurred to Mrs. Hallam that she had never once considered whether Julia herself had been happy.

"You must tell me everything," she said, handing the cup. It was the formula of a hundred reunions, and she uttered it with the faint guilt of one who knows that the request is not meant to be literally fulfilled.

Madame de Saulnier looked at her over the rim of the cup.

"Everything? My dear, you know everything. I put it all in the letters."

"Yes—the letters were wonderful. We all said so. Aunt Harriet used to say you ought to have been an authoress."

"Did she? Poor Aunt Harriet. I suppose that was meant as a reproach."

"I don't think so," said Mrs. Hallam, after a moment's honest reflection. "I think she meant it kindly. She was proud of you, Julia—we all were, after a time. At first, of course—"

"At first, of course, you were all quite sure I should come home within the year, with nothing but a trunk of Worth gowns and a broken heart." Madame de Saulnier set down her cup. "I know. Mamma wrote to me at the time that she prayed nightly I might be preserved from the consequences of my own impetuosity. She underlined *impetuosity* twice. I have the letter still."

Mrs. Hallam coloured slightly. She remembered that winter—the winter of the engagement—with a distinctness that years of subsequent events had done nothing to blur. The young Comte de Saulnier had come to New York with a letter to the Danes from a Paris banker, and had been asked to dine in Bond Street because it would have been discourteous not to ask him, and had been asked a second time because Julia had laughed more at the first dinner than anyone could remember her laughing; and within two months he had proposed, and within four Julia had sailed, leaving behind her a family divided between scandal and a kind of awed admiration that none of its members would have acknowledged. Augusta herself, already engaged to Lucius Hallam, had stood on the pier and waved her handkerchief and wept, and had gone home afterwards to her mother's house and wondered, for perhaps the only time in her life, whether it might not have been more interesting to do something wrong.

"Mamma was very fond of you," she said now, inadequately.

"Yes. That was what made it so tiresome." Madame de Saulnier leaned back against the re-covered sofa and folded her small gloved hands. "But tell me about yourself, Augusta. You never told me anything—or rather you told me everything, which comes to the same thing. Lucius's promotion at the bank, and the new furnace, and the children's measles, and the year you went to Saratoga instead of Newport because of the drains. I knew the very colour of your parlour curtains. I could have found my way blindfold to the linen-closet."

"I'm afraid my letters were very dull."

"They were the only letters I ever kept," said her cousin.

Mrs. Hallam looked up quickly, suspecting irony; but Madame de Saulnier's face, in the grey afternoon light from the street, was perfectly grave. It had, Mrs. Hallam now observed, a fine network of lines about the eyes that she had taken at first for the marks of laughter, and that she now perceived might equally have been made by something else.

"You kept them? But why?"

"Because they were true," said Madame de Saulnier simply.

There was a pause, during which the clock on the mantel—it was a French clock, and had been a wedding present from Julia herself—ticked with a deliberation that seemed to Mrs. Hallam unusually loud.

"Mine were true too, you know," Julia went on, in the same light tone. "Every word of them. There really was an ambassador who quoted Horace. He quoted him at every dinner for eleven years, and always the same ode. And the Russian princess really had a marmoset; it bit me, and I was ill for a fortnight. And the novelist did read his manuscript in my drawing-room—it was a very long manuscript, and Raoul went to sleep, and snored, and the novelist put us both into his next book, which was much admired. Oh, it was all true. I never told you a single lie."

"But then—"

"I simply chose what to tell. One does, you know, when one is writing for an audience; and I always knew I was writing for an audience. I could see you reading the letters out to Aunt Harriet, and Aunt Harriet sniffing at the coronet, and Lucius saying 'H'm' behind his newspaper." She smiled. "Did he say 'H'm'?"

"Very often," Mrs. Hallam admitted.

"I was sure of it. And so I wrote for Aunt Harriet's sniff and for Lucius's 'H'm,' and I left out the rest. I left out the days in Touraine when it rained for three weeks and the dowager Marquise talked of nothing but her digestion and my failure to give the family an heir. I left out the year Raoul spent at Monte Carlo, and the reason he spent it there, and the lady who was the reason. I left out the apartment in the Rue de Varenne being let, in eighty-one, to pay his debts, and our living for two winters in a hotel in the Rue de Rivoli, which I described to you as a 'charming little pied-à-terre.'" She paused. "It had a view of the Tuileries. That part was true."

Mrs. Hallam sat very still. She was aware of a confused sense of having been, all these years, a party to something—of having lent her voice, in her mother's parlour and her own, to a performance whose nature she had not understood; and she was aware, beneath this, of a feeling she could not at once identify, and which, when she did identify it, she was ashamed of. It was not pity, though she supposed pity was what she ought to feel. It was something much more like relief.

"Julia," she said slowly, "why are you telling me this?"

Madame de Saulnier did not answer at once. She took up the little gold spoon and turned it over, examining the hallmark as if she had never seen it before.

"Because Raoul is dead," she said at last, "and the Marquise is dead, and Aunt Harriet is dead, and there is no longer anyone to perform for. And because I came up those dreadful steps of yours this afternoon thinking that I should sit on this sofa and tell you about the Duchesse d'Uzès's ball, and when I saw you standing there in your black poplin, looking so exactly like everything I had run away from, I found I couldn't do it. I found I wanted to tell you the truth, for once, to someone who would know what it was worth." She laid down the spoon. "You needn't look so stricken, Augusta. I wasn't unhappy—not, at any rate, all the time. It was a life. It had its compensations; I had friends, and I learned to see things, and I was never once bored in the particular way one is bored in West Eleventh Street. But it was not the life in the letters. I wanted you to know that before I go back."

"You are going back?"

"In April. I have a little flat now, near the Luxembourg, and I find I can't imagine dying anywhere else. One gets used to the light."

Mrs. Hallam rose, rather abruptly, and went to the window. Below her, in the gathering dusk, a lamplighter was making his way down the street, and the brownstone fronts opposite, which she had looked at every day for twenty-eight years, were receding one by one into a uniform obscurity. She stood there for some moments with her back to the room, and when she spoke it was without turning round.

"Since we are being truthful," she said, "there is something I ought to tell you also."

"My dear Augusta, you have never in your life done anything that required confession."

"No," said Mrs. Hallam. "I suppose that is what I ought to tell you."

She came back to the sofa and sat down, and for the first time that afternoon she looked her cousin full in the face.

"I stopped reading your letters aloud," she said, "about the year eighty-two. Not because of anything in them—I hadn't the least idea there was anything to read between the lines. But because nobody wanted to hear them any longer. Aunt Harriet had begun to find them frivolous; Mamma said they unsettled the girls; and Lucius—" She hesitated. "Lucius said once, quite kindly, that he thought you must find it very tiring to be so amused all the time. After that I used to read them by myself, in my room, after the house had gone to bed. I read every one of them, Julia, two and three times. I used to keep them in the drawer of my dressing-table, under my handkerchiefs."

Madame de Saulnier said nothing; but her gloved hands, which had lain folded in her lap, slowly tightened.

"I didn't envy you," Mrs. Hallam went on, with a sudden effort, as though she were lifting something heavy. "At least, I told myself I didn't. I had Lucius, and the children, and this house, and everything one is supposed to want; and I was not unhappy either—not, as you say, all the time. But there were evenings—there was one evening particularly, the winter Lucius was ill and I had sat up with him three nights running—when I took out your letter about the ball at the Austrian Embassy, the one where you wore the yellow tulle and danced the cotillion with the Duc de something—"

"De Morcerf. He was sixty-eight and had a glass eye."

"—and I sat on the edge of my bed and read it, and I thought, *She did it. She actually did it. She got out.* And it seemed to me, just for that one evening, that it didn't matter what happened to me afterwards, because one of us, at least, had got out." Mrs. Hallam's voice, which had been perfectly steady, faltered for the first time. "I suppose I have been living on your yellow tulle for twenty years, Julia. And now you tell me the Duke had a glass eye."

For a long moment neither woman spoke. The clock ticked; a carriage went by in the street, its wheels grinding on the frozen ruts; somewhere in the depths of the house a door closed, and the parlour-maid's step could be heard descending to the kitchen. Then Madame de Saulnier began, very softly, to laugh, and Mrs. Hallam, after a startled instant, found to her astonishment that she was laughing too—laughing as she had not laughed since they were girls together at their grandmother's cottage at Newport, and had hidden in the boathouse to escape a sermon on deportment.

"Oh, Augusta," said her cousin at last, wiping her eyes with a handkerchief of absurdly fine lawn. "What a pair of fools we have been. You living on my tulle, and I living on your furnace."

"My furnace?"

"Your new furnace, in seventy-nine. You wrote me four pages about it—the man from Hartford, and the trouble with the flue, and Lucius going down to the cellar in his dressing-gown at two in the morning. I read that letter in the hotel in the Rue de Rivoli, in a room so cold the water froze in the jug, and Raoul had been gone for a week and I didn't know where; and I thought, *There is somebody in the world whose husband goes down to the cellar in the middle of the night to make sure she is warm.*" She folded the handkerchief carefully. "I kept that letter longest of all."

Mrs. Hallam looked down at her own hands, which were broad and capable and wore, beside her wedding ring, the heavy garnet that Lucius had given her on their tenth anniversary.

"He went down," she said, "because he was afraid the pipes would burst, and he would have to pay the plumber."

"I know," said Madame de Saulnier gently. "I guessed that, even then. It didn't matter in the least."

The lamps had been lit in the street now, and their light came in through the lace curtains and lay in a pattern on the carpet between the two women. Mrs. Hallam rose again, more slowly this time, and rang for the maid to light the gas; and when the girl had come and gone, and the familiar room had sprung back into its familiar shapes—the Landseer and the Sèvres and the case of minerals, the French clock and the re-covered sofa—the cousins looked at each other across the little tea-table with the kind of shyness that sometimes follows upon a confidence, when each party is uncertain how much the other will wish to remember.

It was Madame de Saulnier who spoke first. She had drawn on her gloves again, and was buttoning them with great precision.

"You will come and see me in Paris," she said. It was not a question.

Mrs. Hallam opened her lips to say that it was impossible—that there was the house, and her daughter's confinement in June, and the question of Lucius's estate, which the lawyers had still not settled; and she heard herself saying instead, in a voice she scarcely recognised:

"I should like to see the view of the Tuileries."

"You shall see it. And I shall take you to the Austrian Embassy, if they will still have me, and you shall wear yellow tulle."

"At my age! And in mourning!"

"Grey, then," said Madame de Saulnier. "Grey with a touch of lavender. It is what one wears in Paris for a husband one was fond of." She stood up, and shook out her small skirts, and for an instant the two cousins stood face to face beneath the gas-light, the one so slight and finished, the other so solid and so unaccustomed to her own emotion. Then Madame de Saulnier put up her hand and touched Mrs. Hallam's cheek, very lightly, as she might have touched a piece of old porcelain whose value she alone in the room was in a position to appreciate.

"We shall write to each other," she said, "until then. And this time, Augusta, we shall leave nothing out."

When she had gone—when the front door had closed behind her, and her light step had gone down the brownstone flight, and the sound of her carriage had been absorbed into the general murmur of the evening—Mrs. Hallam stood for a long time in the middle of her drawing-room. She looked about her at the furniture she had lived among for twenty-eight years, and it seemed to her that she was seeing it for the first time; and then, with a sudden movement that she would have been unable to explain to anyone, least of all to herself, she crossed to the mantelpiece, took down one of her grandmother's Sèvres vases, and turned it over in her hands to look at the mark on its base.

It was, she discovered, a very good mark. She had never before taken the trouble to examine it.

She set the vase back in its place, a quarter of an inch to the left of where it had always stood; and then she went upstairs to her room, and opened the drawer of her dressing-table, and took out from beneath her handkerchiefs a bundle of letters on thick cream-coloured paper, and sat down on the edge of her bed to read them, for the first time, as they had actually been written.

The interview took place, as such interviews in the Amory household invariably did, in the small upstairs sitting-room which Mrs. Henry Amory called her "morning-room," though it faced the north and received the sun only by reflection from the brick fronts across Waverly Place. It was a room of a deliberate and almost penitential plainness, furnished with the rosewood and horsehair that had come to her from her grandmother Schermerhorn Drake, and it had been chosen for the purpose precisely because it offered nothing to distract the eye. Mrs. Amory held that a child under correction should be conscious of nothing but the correction, and she had observed that her drawing-room, with its Sèvres and its crystal pendants and its little gilt chairs, had a way of drawing the attention of the culprit away from the matter in hand. In the morning-room there was only the clock, the engraving of Lady Jane Grey at her devotions, and the fire, which on this particular December afternoon had been allowed to sink rather low, as if it too had been instructed in the gravity of the occasion.

Mrs. Amory had been sitting there for nearly a quarter of an hour before the child was brought in, and she had employed the interval in rehearsing what she meant to say. She was not a woman to whom speech came easily in moments of feeling, and she distrusted, as her mother had distrusted before her, any utterance that had not been weighed beforehand. Her conversation in company was admired for its propriety rather than its warmth; she said the right thing to the right person, and she said it at the right length, and it was generally agreed that no one had ever regretted anything Louisa Amory had told them. But a child was not a dinner-guest, and she had found, in the seven years of her daughter's existence, that the most carefully prepared phrases had a way of curling at the edges, like paper held too near a candle, under the steady gaze of a creature who had not yet learned to pretend that she understood.

On the table at her elbow lay two pieces of evidence. The first was a note, written on the heavy cream-laid paper with the narrow black border which old Mrs. Tracy Dunstan had continued to use for eleven years after her husband's death, on the principle, as she said, that one did not stop grieving merely because one's friends had stopped noticing. It was brief, and it was couched in terms of the most perfect consideration, and Mrs. Amory had read it three times with a sensation of having been struck across the face by a glove. The second piece of evidence was not on paper. It was the report of Mary Ellen, the nursemaid, delivered in the back hall in a whisper that had nevertheless managed to be shrill, and supplemented, during the past hour, by such inferences as Mrs. Amory's own imagination had been unable to refuse.

The facts, stripped of Mary Ellen's embroidery and Mrs. Dunstan's tact, were these. At about three o'clock that afternoon, while walking in Washington Square under the nursemaid's supervision, Clementine Amory had caught sight of a lady in a sealskin jacket and a small bonnet trimmed with violets, who was standing near the fountain and looking, as Mary Ellen put it, "as if she was waiting for someone and knew they wouldn't come." The child had uttered a cry, slipped her hand from the nursemaid's, and run across the frozen gravel straight into the lady's arms; and there, in full view of the north side of the Square and of Mrs. Dunstan's barouche, which happened at that moment to be drawn up before the Rhinelander house, she had kissed the lady on both cheeks and announced, in the high clear voice which her governess had been at some pains to moderate, that she had missed her dreadfully, and that Mamma said she was never to be visited any more, but that she, Clementine, would visit her whenever she liked.

The lady in the sealskin jacket was Mrs. Archibald Marrable.

Mrs. Amory had not needed Mrs. Dunstan's note to tell her what this meant. Lydia Marrable had come back from Europe in October, after an absence of two years, without her husband and without any explanation that New York was disposed to accept. It was known that Archibald Marrable remained in Paris; it was known that his wife had taken a small house in East Eleventh Street, a street which no one of her kind had ever lived in; and it was known, or at least universally believed, that there had been someone at Baden, a Hungarian or a Pole, whose name was never mentioned and therefore never forgotten. Lydia Marrable had not been divorced; New York in those days did not quite admit the possibility of divorce among people one knew. But she had been, by a process as silent and as irresistible as the freezing of a pond, dropped. Her cards were returned unacknowledged; her carriage, when it passed, was not seen; and the ladies who had danced at her wedding had arrived, without ever discussing it, at the conclusion that it would be kinder to her, as well as safer for themselves, to behave as if she had died abroad.

Mrs. Amory had arrived at this conclusion with the others. She had arrived at it, indeed, rather sooner than some, and with less apparent effort, and if it had cost her anything she had taken care that the cost should not show. She and Lydia had been girls together; they had shared a dancing-master and a confirmation class, and had once, at the age of fourteen, sworn eternal fidelity over a pressed heliotrope in the summer-house at Rhinebeck. But Mrs. Amory had long since learned that the vows of fourteen were not the vows by which a woman of thirty-four was expected to govern her conduct, and she had put the heliotrope, figuratively speaking, where she had put a good many other things: in a drawer which she did not open.

It had not occurred to her that the child would remember. Lydia had been gone two years, and two years, at Clementine's age, was more than a quarter of a lifetime. Mrs. Amory had supposed, in so far as she had considered the matter at all, that the memory of Mrs. Marrable's sugared almonds and Mrs. Marrable's music-box and Mrs. Marrable's habit of letting a little girl try on her rings had been quietly overlaid, like the faded pattern of an old carpet, by the newer impressions of the intervening years. She saw now that she had been mistaken, and the discovery affected her with something more disagreeable than surprise; it was as if a piece of furniture she had thought securely fastened had suddenly been found to move.

The door opened, and Miss Pettigrew, the governess, ushered the child in, and withdrew with the air of a sexton who has seen the body safely to the chancel and does not propose to stay for the service.

Clementine stood just inside the door. She was a small, square, dark child, with her father's heavy brows and her grandmother Drake's determined chin, and nothing whatever of her mother's fairness; and Mrs. Amory, looking at her, was conscious, as she often was, of a faint perplexity, as though the child had been delivered to the wrong address and she had been too well-bred to return her. She had on her dark-blue merino with the white collar, and her hair had been freshly brushed, and her hands were folded in front of her in the attitude which Miss Pettigrew had taught her to assume in the presence of her elders. Only her eyes, which were fixed on her mother with an expression of anxious inquiry, betrayed that she understood herself to be in disgrace without understanding why.

"Come here, Clementine," said Mrs. Amory.

The child came, and stood by the table, and her eye fell on the black-bordered note, and lingered there with the uneasy fascination which children feel for any object associated with death.

"You know, I think, why I have sent for you."

Clementine considered this. She was a truthful child, and her truthfulness had already caused a certain amount of inconvenience in a household where truth was valued chiefly as a commodity to be dispensed in measured quantities and on suitable occasions.

"Is it because I let go of Mary Ellen's hand?" she asked.

"It is partly that. You know that you are never to let go of Mary Ellen's hand in the street. But it is chiefly something else. You spoke to a lady in the Square this afternoon."

"It was Aunt Lydia," said Clementine; and her face, which had been clouded, cleared suddenly, as if the mention of the name had let in a light. "She had violets in her bonnet, Mamma, real ones, not silk, and she said they came from a man in a cart who brings them all the way from New Jersey. And she remembered about the music-box. She said it was still in her parlour and it still played the tune about the shepherdess, and I might come and hear it—"

"Clementine."

The child stopped. The light in her face did not go out at once; it wavered, like a gas-jet when a door is opened somewhere in the house.

"Mrs. Marrable," said Mrs. Amory, laying a slight but unmistakable emphasis on the name, "is not your aunt. She was never your aunt. It was a foolish habit of yours to call her so, and I ought to have checked it long ago."

"But she said I might—"

"It does not signify what she said. You are not to speak to her again. If you should see her in the street, or in a shop, or anywhere at all, you are to look the other way, and if Mary Ellen or Miss Pettigrew is with you, you are to keep hold of their hand and walk on. Do you understand me?"

Clementine looked at her mother for a long moment. Mrs. Amory had expected tears, and had braced herself to meet them with the firm, cool kindness which she considered appropriate; but the child did not cry. She only frowned, with a contraction of the heavy brows that made her look absurdly like her father when he was adding up the household accounts.

"Why?" she said.

It was the question Mrs. Amory had dreaded, and for which, in all her rehearsing, she had found no satisfactory reply. She had considered several. She might say that Mrs. Marrable had been ill, and that her illness was of a kind that might be caught; but this was a lie, and Mrs. Amory did not tell lies to children, not from any particular scruple, but because they were so apt to be found out. She might say that Mrs. Marrable had done something wrong; but this would invite the further question of what she had done, and that was a question to which there was no answer that could be given to a child of seven, or indeed, in Mrs. Amory's opinion, to anyone at all. She might say, as her own mother would have said, that little girls did not ask why; but she had a disagreeable suspicion that this particular little girl would continue to ask it, silently, for the rest of her life.

"Because I say so," she said at last; and then, feeling the inadequacy of this, she added, "Because it is not done."

"What isn't done?"

"Speaking to Mrs. Marrable."

"But I did it," said Clementine reasonably. "So it is done."

Mrs. Amory felt the colour rise in her cheeks. She was not accustomed to being argued with, and she was even less accustomed to finding the argument unanswerable. She took up Mrs. Dunstan's note, not because she meant to read it aloud, but because the feel of the stiff paper between her fingers seemed to restore to her a sense of the world as it was properly constituted.

"There are things," she said, "which people of our sort do not do. You are too young to understand the reasons for them, and it is not necessary that you should understand. It is only necessary that you should obey. When you are older you will see that these rules are not made unkindly; they are made to protect us, and to protect the people we love. What you did this afternoon was seen by Mrs. Dunstan, and by others, and it has caused your father and me a great deal of distress."

She paused, aware that the last sentence was not quite accurate. Henry Amory did not yet know what had happened; he would be told at dinner, and he would say "Dear me," and look at his wife over his spectacles with an expression of mild alarm, and then he would ask whether anything need be done about it, and on being assured that everything had already been done, he would return with visible relief to his consommé. It was Mrs. Amory alone who was distressed, and she was not perfectly certain that it was the child's conduct which distressed her.

"Did Mrs. Dunstan write you a letter about me?" asked Clementine, looking at the black border.

"Mrs. Dunstan was kind enough to let me know what she had seen."

"Is she angry?"

"Mrs. Dunstan is never angry. She was sorry."

Clementine digested this. "Aunt Lydia was sorry too," she said. "When I kissed her she cried. Not loudly. She just had tears, like when you have a cold. And she said I mustn't tell you, because it would make trouble for me, and she would rather go away again than make trouble for me. And I said I didn't care about trouble." She looked up at her mother with a sudden earnestness. "Mamma, was it because of me that she cried? Did I hurt her?"

Mrs. Amory did not answer at once. The fire had sunk to a dull red glow, and the room had grown so dark that the engraving of Lady Jane Grey was no more than a pale smudge above the mantelpiece. Somewhere below, a door closed, and she heard the measured tread of Bostwick, the butler, crossing the hall to light the lamps in the drawing-room. It was nearly five; in an hour she must dress for dinner; and she was seized by a strange, unreasonable reluctance to light the lamp on the table beside her, as though what she had to say could be said more easily in the dark.

She was remembering, against her will, the summer-house at Rhinebeck, and the smell of the heliotrope, and Lydia's voice, a little breathless, saying, "Whatever happens, Lou, whatever anyone says, we shall always be on each other's side." She remembered, too, a scene which had taken place not in this room but in one very like it, in her mother's house on Second Avenue, when she was about Clementine's age and had been discovered in the kitchen garden sharing a slice of bread and butter with the coachman's little boy. Her mother had not raised her voice; Mrs. Drake had never raised her voice in her life. She had merely explained, with a terrible gentleness, that there were people with whom one did not share bread and butter, and that a little girl who did not understand this would grow up to be the kind of woman whom nobody visited. Louisa had wept for an hour afterwards, not because she was sorry, but because she had not known until that moment that there was such a kind of woman, and the knowledge had frightened her more than any punishment. She had never spoken to the coachman's boy again. She could not now recall his name.

"No," she said at length, and her voice sounded strange to her in the darkened room. "You did not hurt her. But you might have hurt yourself, and that is what I must prevent. Mrs. Marrable understands that. That is why she told you not to tell me."

"Then she knows it isn't done?"

"Yes. She knows."

"Then why did she let me kiss her?"

Mrs. Amory rose abruptly and went to the bell-rope. She did not ring it; she stood with her hand upon the tasselled end, looking down at the dying fire, and it seemed to her that the question hung in the air of the little room like the smoke of a candle that has just been snuffed.

"I think," she said slowly, "that she could not help it."

There was a silence. Then Clementine said, in a small voice, "I couldn't help it either."

Mrs. Amory turned. The child had not moved from her place by the table; she was standing very straight, with her hands still folded in front of her, and her face in the dimness was a pale oval in which the dark eyes were the only living thing. And Mrs. Amory, looking at her, felt for an instant something she had not expected to feel, something that was neither anger nor pity but a kind of fearful recognition, as if she had caught sight of her own reflection in a glass she had not known was there.

The moment passed. She was a woman of thirty-four, the mistress of a well-ordered house, the wife of a man whose name stood for probity on two continents and in three clubs; and she had a duty to the child which was not lessened, but rather increased, by the child's resemblance to someone she had once been. She rang the bell.

"You will go to bed without your supper tonight," she said, "and tomorrow you will not walk in the Square. Miss Pettigrew will take you to the Bible-reading at Mrs. Dunstan's on Thursday, as usual, and you will behave there as if nothing had happened. If Mrs. Dunstan should speak to you of this afternoon, you will tell her that you are very sorry, and that it will not occur again." She paused. "And it will not occur again, Clementine. You understand me?"

"Yes, Mamma."

"You will not speak to Mrs. Marrable, nor of her, to anyone."

"Yes, Mamma."

There was a knock at the door, and Miss Pettigrew appeared on the threshold, having evidently been waiting in the passage with the patience of a woman whose wages depended on her being within call. Clementine went towards her obediently; but at the door she stopped, and turned, and looked back at her mother with an expression which Mrs. Amory was to remember, at odd moments, for a great many years afterwards.

"Mamma," she said, "I won't love anybody again without asking you first."

She said it quite simply, as a child repeats a lesson, and with an evident desire to please; and then Miss Pettigrew's hand closed upon her shoulder, and the door shut behind them both, and Mrs. Amory was alone in the darkened room.

She stood for some time without moving. Then she lit the lamp, carefully, as her mother had taught her, turning the wick up by degrees so that the chimney should not crack; and in the soft circle of light that sprang up around the table she saw Mrs. Dunstan's note lying where she had dropped it, its black border as narrow and as uncompromising as a line drawn under a sum. She took it up and read it a fourth time, and then she folded it and put it into the pocket of her gown, meaning to answer it after dinner. She would write that Clementine was a thoughtless child, but an affectionate one, and that the incident had been dealt with; and Mrs. Dunstan would reply, in her beautiful pointed hand, that she had never doubted it, and that dear Louisa must not distress herself; and on Thursday at the Bible-reading the two ladies would greet each other with a warmth that would set the seal of forgetfulness upon the whole affair.

It was all quite simple, and quite settled, and she could not think why she should feel, as she went down the dark staircase towards the lighted hall, as though she had left something of value behind her in the little room upstairs, something she could not name, and would not, if she went back to look for it, be able to find.

At dinner her husband said "Dear me," and looked at her over his spectacles, and asked whether anything need be done.

"Nothing," said Mrs. Amory. "It has all been done."

And Henry Amory, with visible relief, returned to his consommé.

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

The letter had come by the afternoon post, and Mrs. Thorold had carried it about with her for three hours before she resolved to speak of it. She had read it first in the morning-room, standing by the window that looked down the long slope of lawn to the river; then she had put it in the pocket of her grey cloth skirt and gone out to cut the last of the asters, as though the act of filling a basket with something might fill also the curious hollow it had opened in her. She was aware, as she did these things, of a faint irony in them, like the irony of a person who tidies a room before announcing that she means to leave it. But she was not leaving it; she was only going to ask permission to be absent from it for a day, and the preparations she made were less a defiance than a kind of propitiation, offered to a deity whose temper she had never quite been able to forecast.

Dinner passed as their dinners always passed when they were alone. Stephen Thorold talked of the new drainage at the lodge, of a letter from his agent in Albany, and of the regrettable tendency of their neighbour, old Mr. Pell, to fell trees that obstructed nobody's view but his own. He talked well, as he did everything well; there was in his conversation the same finish, the same avoidance of the superfluous, that showed in the cut of his coat and in the arrangement of the books in his library. It was not until they had gone into the library, and the man had brought the coffee and withdrawn, that she spoke.

"I had a letter today from Mrs. Gaillard."

Her husband, who was cutting the end of a cigar, did not look up. "Mrs. Gaillard? I didn't know you kept up with her."

"I don't. She wrote to tell me that Hugh Dalby is ill."

There was a pause, of the length required to bring a match to the cigar and to draw upon it until it was evenly alight. Then Thorold dropped the match into the brass tray at his elbow and said, in the tone of one acknowledging a piece of general news: "I'm sorry to hear it. Is it serious?"

"She thinks he is dying."

"Ah." He leaned back in his chair. "That's very sad. He can't be much over fifty."

"He is fifty-one."

The lamplight fell on the smooth grey of his temples and on the long, well-kept hand that held the cigar, and she reflected, not for the first time, that her husband's face had the quality of certain old portraits, which seem to give back to the observer only what the observer has brought to them.

"He is at the Albemarle," she went on. "In town. Mrs. Gaillard has been to see him. She says he has asked for me."

Thorold examined the ash of his cigar. "Asked for you?"

"He would like to see me. Once. Before—" She stopped, and the unfinished sentence hung between them like a garment neither cared to pick up.

"I see," said her husband.

She waited for him to say more, but he did not, and the silence became one of those silences, familiar to her through twelve years of marriage, in which it was understood that the next move was hers, and that whatever move she made would be quietly weighed and found to have been, if not precisely wrong, at least less felicitous than another she might have chosen. She had learned to dread these pauses more than any outburst; for an outburst she might have met with an outburst of her own, whereas against this patient vacancy there was nothing to be done but to fill it, and to hear her own voice going on alone, as a traveller hears his footsteps in an empty street.

"I should like to go," she said.

"To the Albemarle?"

"Yes. Tomorrow, if you have no objection. I could take the ten o'clock train and be back for dinner."

It was his habitual attitude when he had a decision to make, and she had once found it rather touching, as though he needed the warmth of the coals to thaw some resolution frozen within him. She found it touching no longer; she merely noted it, as one notes the familiar signal of an approaching train.

"My dear Anne," he said at length, "you know I have never interfered with your friendships."

"I know it."

"And I should not dream of interfering now, if this were a question of friendship."

"What else should it be a question of?"

He turned and looked at her, and she perceived that he was considering how much it would be decent to say.

"You must see," he observed mildly, "that the situation is a little unusual. A man who was once—how shall I put it?—a candidate for your hand, and who has not, so far as I know, communicated with you in a dozen years, sends word through a third person that he wishes you to visit him at an hotel. Mrs. Gaillard is not the most discreet of women. I don't doubt she has already told half a dozen people of her errand."

"He is dying, Stephen."

"So you say. So Mrs. Gaillard says. I don't question it. But you will allow that the fact of his dying does not alter the way in which the thing will be talked about. It may even give it a certain—piquancy."

The word, so delicately chosen, struck her like a small cold blade. She had known that he would speak of what people would say; it was the first refuge of everyone she had ever known, and she would have been surprised if he had not taken it. But she had not foreseen the elegance with which he would make use of it, nor the faint distaste in his voice, as though it were she, and not the world, who had introduced the vulgar element into their discussion.

"I don't care how it is talked about," she said.

"No," he agreed, "you never have. It is one of your charms. But I am obliged to care a little, for both of us."

The curtains had not been drawn, and beyond the reflection of the lamp and of her own dim figure in the black lace she could make out the pale band of the river and the dark mass of the hills on the farther shore. There had been an evening, thirteen years ago, when she had stood at another window and looked at another river, and Hugh Dalby had come up behind her and said, without preamble, that he had nothing to offer her but himself, and that he knew it was not enough. She had believed him; she had been twenty-three, and the belief had seemed to her the beginning of wisdom. Within the year she had married Stephen Thorold, who had a great deal to offer besides himself, and whose offering had been made with such tact that she had scarcely felt herself to be choosing at all.

"You speak," she said, without turning, "as if I were proposing to elope with him."

"I speak as if you were proposing to do something that could be misunderstood. I don't for an instant suppose you would misunderstand it yourself."

"Then why should you mind?"

"I have not said that I mind."

She turned at that, and faced him across the length of the room, and for a moment the old impulse rose in her to break through the smooth surface he presented and discover whether anything lay beneath it. But she had made the attempt too often, and had learned that the surface did not break; it merely received the blow and closed over it, as still water closes over a stone.

"You have not said it," she answered, "but you have made it very plain."

"Have I?" He smiled slightly. "Then I have been clumsy, and I apologise. Let me try to be clearer. If you wish to go to New York tomorrow, you will go. I shall order the carriage for the ten o'clock train. It was characteristic of him that he should put it so, and characteristic, too, that she should find no immediate answer. For there was a part of her that acknowledged the justice of the question. What, after all, did she expect to find in the room at the Albemarle? A sick man, propped against pillows, with the greyness of approaching death on his face; a nurse hovering at the door; a few constrained sentences, a pressure of the hand, and then the long journey home in the darkening train. She could not tell Hugh Dalby anything he did not already know, nor could he tell her anything that would alter by a hair's breadth the fixed design of her life. And yet the thought of not going was intolerable to her, with an intolerableness she could not have explained, as though some door that had stood ajar in her for thirteen years were about to be shut upon her fingers.

"I don't know whether it will comfort him," she said slowly. "I only know that he has asked, and that I should be ashamed to refuse."

"Before myself."

He was silent a moment. Then he said, with a gentleness more disconcerting than any harshness: "My dear, you have nothing to be ashamed of. You behaved, thirteen years ago, with perfect propriety. He had no claim on you then, and he has none now."

"I am not speaking of claims."

"Of what, then?"

She did not answer at once; and as she hesitated she became aware, with a strange sinking of the heart, that she did not herself know. She had spoken of shame because it was the nearest word, as one snatches at the nearest object in the dark; but now that he held it up to the light she saw that it did not fit the thing she had meant. It was not shame that drew her toward the Albemarle; it was something at once humbler and more imperious, a need to look once more upon the face of the only person who had ever seen her as she might have been, before that possible self was buried with him and nobody remained who remembered it.

"Of what I owe him," she said at last.

"And what do you owe him?"

"The truth, perhaps."

Thorold's cigar had gone out. He looked at it for a moment, as if surprised to find it in his hand, then laid it carefully in the tray and came across the room toward her. He stopped a few feet away, and she noticed that he did not touch her; he had never been a man who touched people in moments of difficulty, and she had sometimes wondered whether it was from delicacy or from a dread of committing himself.

"Anne," he said, "I am going to tell you something that I had not meant to tell you."

She waited, her hand on the cold edge of the window-frame.

"I have known for a long time," he went on, in the same even voice, "that you married me without being in love with me. I knew it on the day you accepted me. I was not deceived, and I don't think you tried very hard to deceive me. You liked me, you respected me, and you were tired of your aunt's house and of being poor. Those are not ignoble reasons, and I have never held them against you. I thought—I still think—that they were as good a foundation as most marriages are built on."

She had grown very pale, and she was conscious of the colour leaving her face as one is conscious of water draining from a basin. She had imagined many things he might say, but never this; and the shock of it was not so much in the words themselves as in the revelation that he had carried them about with him for twelve years, folded and put away, as she had carried the letter in her pocket all the afternoon.

"Stephen—"

"Let me finish. I knew, too, that there had been someone else, and I had no difficulty in guessing who it was. I made it my business never to inquire. I thought, if I left the thing alone, it would wither of itself, as such things usually do. I have no idea whether it has withered or not. I have never asked, and I am not asking now." He paused, and for the first time a faint roughness came into his voice, like a flaw in a polished surface. "But I should be glad if you would not do me the injustice of supposing that I am jealous of a dying man. I am not. I am only—tired, perhaps, of being the person you are always making allowances for."

The words fell into the quiet room with a weight out of all proportion to their sound. Anne stood motionless, looking at him, and it seemed to her that she was seeing him for the first time without the smooth frame of his manner about him: a man of fifty, a little stooped, with lines about the mouth that she had attributed to the fatigues of business, and that she now perceived to have been graven by something else. She had always believed herself the injured party in their marriage, the one who had given up most; and the belief had been, she now understood, a kind of luxury, a soft cushion on which she had rested her pride through all the years of mild discontent. He had taken the cushion from under her with a single sentence, and she felt the hard boards beneath.

"I didn't know," she said, and her voice sounded thin and far away in her own ears. "I never thought you—"

"No," he said. "I took some pains that you shouldn't."

There was a long silence. The fire had sunk to a dull glow, and somewhere in the house a clock struck ten with a deliberate, old-fashioned resonance. Anne thought of the train that left at that hour in the morning, of the carriage drawn up at the door, of the long run down the river with the autumn woods flaming on either hand; and the picture, which an hour before had glowed in her mind like a lamp seen through a window, seemed suddenly to have grown small and remote, like something viewed through the wrong end of a telescope.

"You may go, of course," her husband said at length. He had recovered his usual tone, and the momentary roughness had vanished as if it had never been. "I meant what I said. I will order the carriage. I shall tell the Pells, if they ask, that you have gone up to see your dressmaker. No one need know anything else, unless Mrs. Gaillard chooses to enlighten them; and I fancy I can manage Mrs. Gaillard."

He said it kindly, almost tenderly, and she understood that he was making her a gift; and she understood, too, with a slow and dreadful clarity, that it was a gift she could not accept. For if she went now she would go with his permission, under cover of his lie, sheltered by his forbearance; she would carry his generosity with her into the room at the Albemarle, and it would stand between her and the bed like a third presence. Whatever she had meant to say to Hugh Dalby—and she was no longer sure that she had meant to say anything—could not be said in the shadow of that magnanimity. He had not forbidden her to go; he had done something far more effectual. He had made her going an act of ingratitude.

She moved away from the window and went slowly back to her chair, and sat down in it, and folded her hands in her lap. The black lace lay about her in soft shadowy folds, and the diamond star at her throat caught the lamplight and gave it back in small cold sparks.

"I don't think I shall go," she said.

He looked at her a moment, and she could not tell whether what she saw in his face was relief or disappointment, or some subtler emotion for which she had no name. Then he inclined his head, as he might have done at the close of a business conversation in which both parties had behaved with credit.

"As you think best," he said. "Perhaps you would like to write to him. I could have the letter sent round by hand tomorrow; Brewster is going to town in any case."

"Thank you," she said. "Perhaps I will."

He picked up the extinguished cigar, examined it, and seemed to decide against relighting it. Then he crossed to the table and took up the evening paper, which had come by the same post as Mrs. Gaillard's letter, and settled himself in his chair under the lamp. After a few minutes she heard the familiar rustle of the turning pages, and the small dry sound he made in his throat when he came upon something in the financial columns that displeased him.

She sat on in the circle of the firelight, looking at the dying coals. She knew she would not write; there was nothing that could be put into a letter that would not seem, beside the thing she had failed to do, a poor and furtive substitute. In a day or two, perhaps in a week, there would be a paragraph in the newspaper her husband was now reading, and he would fold the page so that she might see it, and say nothing; and she would say nothing either; and the silence would close over that too, as it had closed over everything else. She thought of the years ahead of them, the long succession of quiet dinners and decorous evenings, the drainage at the lodge and Mr. Pell's trees and the letters from the agent in Albany; and it seemed to her that she had tonight been shown the true dimensions of the room in which she was to spend her life, and that it was smaller than she had supposed, and that the person who shared it with her was larger.

Toward eleven her husband folded his paper and rose.

"You look tired," he said. "You had better go up."

"Yes," she said. "I think I will."

He held the door for her, and as she passed him she paused, for an instant, as though some word were on her lips. But she did not know what the word was, and he did not help her to find it; and she went out and up the wide shallow stairs, her hand on the cold mahogany of the rail, while below her she heard him moving about the library, putting out the lamps one by one.
