There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

The carriage which Mrs. Venable had sent to meet the afternoon train was late, as everything at Hollins Bridge had always been late; and Kate Ormsby, standing on the wooden platform with her dressing-bag at her feet and her travelling-cloak gathered against the September wind, had leisure to observe that nothing in the place had changed except herself. The station was the same yellow box, with the same tin advertisement of a stove-blacking nailed beside the door; the same elms leaned their tired heads above the road; and the hills beyond, which in her girlhood had seemed to shut in the whole visible world, still lay folded one behind another in the same tranquil blue, as if twenty-two years were no more to them than the passing of a cloud. It was she who had grown older, and she felt the fact with a kind of humiliation, as though the landscape had caught her out in some small dishonesty.

When at last the carriage appeared, swaying between the ruts with an air of having been roused from sleep, she recognized in the driver the son of the old coachman who had driven her grandmother to church; and the young man, touching his hat with an embarrassed deference, seemed to recognize her too, though he could have been no more than a child when she went away. She guessed that she had been talked of in the kitchen, and the guess was not displeasing. To be talked of was, after all, to be remembered; and she had lived long enough in places where she was merely seen to have learned the difference.

The drive to Silverbrook was a short one, and she spent it in a state of suspended feeling which she was too experienced to mistake for calm. She had told herself, in the train and on the steamer, and before that in the shuttered rooms of her apartment on the Lungarno, that she was coming back only because Laura had asked her, and because a woman of forty-four cannot decently refuse the first invitation of a widowed cousin; but she knew that the reasons one gives oneself are seldom the reasons one acts upon, and she was curious, with a curiosity that had something of dread in it, to discover what the real ones would turn out to be.

The house came into view at the turn of the avenue, its white columns paler than she remembered, its long windows reflecting the yellowing maples with the blank composure of eyes that have done with weeping. Someone had added a glazed porch at the south end, and the effect was that of a new bonnet on an old face: a concession to the times which only emphasized the distance the times had travelled. Then the door opened, and Laura was on the steps.

She had prepared herself for a stranger, and she found instead a woman whom she would have known anywhere, and yet in whom she could not at first discover a single feature of the girl she had left. Laura had grown stout, not with the comfortable amplitude of contentment, but with a kind of settled heaviness, as if life had pressed down upon her from above and she had spread a little under the weight. Her hair, which had been the colour of a chestnut fresh from its burr, was dulled to a soft brown streaked with grey, and arranged in a fashion that had been admired in New York some ten years earlier. But her eyes were the same: wide, grey, a little short-sighted, with that look of anxious kindness which had always made people confide in her and then forget to ask how she did.

"Kate! Oh, Kate, my dear!"

They kissed, and in the kiss each felt the other's cheek with a faint surprise, as one touches a familiar piece of furniture in the dark and finds it smaller than one had supposed.

"You haven't changed," Laura said, holding her off at arm's length, and Kate, who knew that she had changed very much, accepted the statement as the first of those graceful untruths which were to be the currency of the visit.

"Nor you, dearest," she returned; and they went in together, each a little ashamed of the other's falsehood and a little grateful for it.

---

Tea was laid in the library, the room in which, as children, they had been permitted to sit on Sunday afternoons while their grandmother read aloud from the *Christian Year*. The portraits were in their places: old Judge Ormsby in his black stock, his wife in a turban, and between them the Copley of an earlier Ormsby whose authenticity had been doubted by every visitor of taste and defended by every member of the family. The horsehair sofa had been re-covered in a flowered chintz, and there were photographs everywhere, in silver frames, on the tables and the mantelpiece: Laura's children at various ages, Laura's husband in the uniform of some regiment of the National Guard, Laura herself in the white satin and orange-blossoms of a wedding which Kate had not attended.

"You'll find everything very old-fashioned," Laura said, pouring the tea with a little nervous clatter of the spoons. "Gerald always meant to do the house over, but somehow there was never the time. And since he went—" she paused, and set the pot down carefully, as if it were a thing that might break—"since he went I haven't had the heart."

"I should hate to have it done over," said Kate. "I like to find it as it was."

"Ah, you say that because you live among such beautiful things. When one has Italy, one can afford to be sentimental about a horsehair sofa."

Kate smiled, and did not answer. She had learned long ago that people who had never left home pictured her life abroad as a perpetual progress through galleries and palaces, and she had never had the courage, or perhaps the cruelty, to tell them that it consisted chiefly of a third-floor apartment with a smoking stove, a cook who stole the candle-ends, and a small circle of compatriots who had come to Florence for their lungs or their reputations and stayed because they could not afford to go anywhere else.

"Tell me about the children," she said instead; and Laura, with the instant illumination of a lamp that has been turned up, began to tell her.

There were three of them. Gerald, the eldest, was at the Law School, and was thought very clever by his professors, though he worried his mother by his opinions, which were, she feared, a little advanced. Margaret was engaged to a young man in the Navy, a nice young man, with a nice family in Baltimore; but the Navy took people so far away, and Laura could not reconcile herself to the thought of China. And then there was little Dorothy, who was only fifteen, and at school in Farmington, and who wrote such amusing letters that her mother read them aloud to the rector.

Kate listened, and made the appropriate rejoinders, and looked from time to time at the photographs; and it seemed to her that the voice in which Laura spoke of her children was the voice in which she herself had once, long ago, spoken of her own hopes, a voice carrying the whole weight of a life upon a few small and fragile names. She was conscious of a pang which she did not choose to examine, and she set down her cup with a deliberate steadiness.

"And you, Kate?" Laura said at last, with the air of one who has postponed a difficult subject as long as civility allows. "You've told me nothing about yourself. Are you happy over there? Do you never think of coming home for good?"

"Home?" Kate repeated, and the word seemed to hang in the air between them like a question neither could answer. "I hardly know where that is any longer. One becomes a kind of permanent visitor, you know: one has one's lodgings, and one's habits, and a few friends who are visitors too; and after a while one forgets that one ever expected anything else."

"But you were always so—" Laura hesitated, searching for a word that should be kind—"so independent. Grandmamma used to say you would never be content to sit at home and darn stockings. I remember she said it the very winter before you went."

"Did she? I don't remember."

But she remembered perfectly. She remembered the winter, and the stockings, and the tone in which her grandmother had spoken, a tone of dry approval tempered by apprehension; and she remembered, too, a certain evening in February when the snow lay blue under the moon, and a young man had stood with her in this very room, before this very fire, and said things which she had answered in a manner that had seemed to her at the time the only one possible to a girl of spirit.

---

After tea they walked down through the garden to the brook, as they had walked a thousand times when they were young. The paths were overgrown, and the box-borders, which had been their grandmother's pride, were ragged and brown in places; but the old stone bench still stood at the end of the walk, under the copper beech, and they sat down on it by a common impulse, as if their bodies remembered what their minds had chosen to forget.

The light was going. Over the hills the sky had turned to that pale clear green which in New England is the colour of autumn evenings, and the brook ran with a cold shallow sound over its stones. Laura drew her shawl about her shoulders and looked at the water.

"Do you remember," she said, "how we used to come here and tell each other what we should do when we were grown up? You were going to write a great novel, and live in Paris, and have a salon like Madame Récamier."

"And you," said Kate, "were going to marry a clergyman and have eleven children and keep bees."

They laughed, and the laughter, rising together in the still air, made them for an instant the girls they had been; then it died away, and they were two middle-aged women on a damp bench, each wondering how much the other had guessed.

"Well, I didn't marry a clergyman," Laura said at length. "And I only had three. And the bees never would stay." She was silent a moment. "But I've been happy, Kate. I want you to know that. People used to say—I daresay you heard it—that Gerald and I were not suited; that he was too restless for Hollins Bridge, and that I held him back. Perhaps it was true. But we were happy, in our way."

"I never doubted it," said Kate; and she wondered, as she said it, whether it was the truth or another of the courteous fictions with which they had been furnishing the afternoon.

Laura turned and looked at her with those wide, short-sighted eyes.

"I've sometimes thought," she said slowly, "that you didn't come to the wedding because you disapproved. You were always so clever, and Gerald was not clever, not in your way. I thought perhaps you felt I was throwing myself away."

The words fell upon Kate with a shock that was almost physical. For twenty-two years she had supposed that Laura knew; that Laura must have known; that Gerald, in the long intimacy of marriage, could not have failed to tell her; and she had built upon that supposition a whole edifice of delicate avoidances: the letters that were always a little too affectionate, the presents that were always a little too costly, the visits that were always postponed. And now, in an instant, the edifice dissolved, and she saw that it had rested upon nothing; that Laura had lived all those years in a perfect innocence which her own scruples had done nothing to protect, because it had never been in danger.

She was conscious of an immense relief, and, underneath the relief, of something less creditable: a faint, unreasonable resentment that the great renunciation of her youth, the act upon which she had secretly modelled her whole conception of herself, should have passed so entirely unobserved. She had refused Gerald Venable because she would not be shut up in Hollins Bridge; because she believed, with the ardent arrogance of twenty-two, that life held something larger for her than a white house and a garden and a husband who would never read a book; and she had gone abroad to find that larger thing, and had found instead a third-floor apartment and a smoking stove. But she had always consoled herself with the knowledge that her refusal had been a choice, and that the choice had cost somebody something. It was humiliating to discover that it had cost nobody anything at all; that Gerald, within the year, had turned with perfect contentment to her cousin; and that her cousin had never so much as suspected that she was being offered what another woman had declined.

"Disapproved?" she said, and was surprised to hear how steady her voice was. "My dear, how absurd. I was in Rome that spring with Mamma; she was ill, you know, and the doctors wouldn't hear of her travelling. I wrote you, I think."

"Yes, you wrote." Laura smoothed the fringe of her shawl. "It was a beautiful letter. I kept it. I've kept all your letters, Kate. When the children were small and Gerald was away so much, I used to read them over in the evenings. They made me feel—I don't know—as if there were a window open somewhere."

Kate turned her head away. The brook went on with its small cold talk among the stones, and a leaf from the copper beech drifted down and lay on the water, turning slowly before it was carried off.

"I used to envy you," Laura went on, in the low, even voice of one who has rehearsed a confession so often that it has lost its power to frighten her. "Not your clever friends, or Italy, or any of that, though I liked to hear about it. But your freedom. You could get up in the morning and go wherever you liked, and nobody needed you to be anywhere. I used to think that must be the most wonderful thing in the world."

Kate was silent for so long that Laura glanced at her uneasily, as if afraid she had said too much. Then Kate laughed, a little unsteadily, and laid her gloved hand on her cousin's.

"And I," she said, "have envied you."

"Me?"

"Yes. Isn't it ridiculous? I used to think of you here, with Gerald and the children and the garden, and the rector coming to dine on Thursdays, and the same people at church every Sunday, the same people who had known you all your life; and it seemed to me that you had the one thing I'd never managed to get. You belonged somewhere. You were part of something. Nobody needs me to be anywhere, as you say; and you can't think, Laura, how tired one grows of being free."

Laura looked at her in wonder, and Kate saw that she did not believe it; that she would never wholly believe it, because the image of her cousin's brilliant liberty was too precious to be surrendered, having served her too long as the window of which she had spoken. And Kate understood, too, that she herself would never wholly believe in Laura's envy, because her own image of Laura's contentment had served her in the same fashion, as a fixed point by which she had measured the extent of her own wandering. They had each, she perceived, been living upon the other's imagined happiness; and it would have been a kind of theft for either to take it away.

"Well," said Laura at last, with a little sigh that seemed to settle the matter, "I suppose nobody ever has exactly what they want."

"No," said Kate. "I suppose not."

The green had faded from the sky, and the first star had come out above the hill. From the house a bell rang faintly, the old dinner-bell that had summoned them in from this same garden on so many summer evenings, its cracked note unchanged by time.

"That will be Martha," Laura said, rising and shaking out her skirts. "She's been with me nineteen years, and she still rings that bell as if I were a child who'd run off to the brook. I've never had the courage to tell her it isn't necessary."

"Don't tell her," said Kate. "Let her ring it."

They went up the path together in the dusk, their arms linked as they had been linked when they were girls; and if each was thinking of the thing she had not said, and the thing she had discovered, and the thing she would never know, they walked none the less closely for it. At the turn of the box-walk Laura stumbled a little on a loose stone, and Kate steadied her; and in that small, involuntary movement there passed between them something that was neither envy nor pity, nor the counterfeit affection of the afternoon, but the plain, unlovely, indestructible bond of two people who have shared a childhood and must go on sharing the knowledge of what it promised.

The lamps were lit in the library when they came in, and the portraits looked down on them with their customary indifference: the Judge in his black stock, his wife in her turban, and the doubtful Copley between them, whose claims, Kate reflected, had been maintained for a hundred years by nothing but the family's determination to believe in them. She caught her own reflection in the dim glass above the mantel: a thin woman in a dark travelling-dress, with a face that had been called distinguished in Florence and would be called worn in Hollins Bridge. Beside it, in its silver frame, the young Gerald Venable smiled out from under his military cap with the easy assurance of a man who had never in his life been refused anything that mattered.

She looked at him a moment longer than she had intended; then, hearing Laura's step behind her, she turned away and held out her hands to the fire.

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

The November dusk came early into Mrs. Fenwick's drawing-room, which looked north upon West Twenty-third Street and had never, even at midsummer, received more than an oblique and grudging share of the sun. At four o'clock the lamps were already lit, and their light, filtered through shades of fluted rose silk, fell on the crimson brocade of the sofas, on the ebonized cabinet with its row of Sèvres cups, and on the tea-table, where the silver kettle still murmured over its spirit-flame as if unaware that the occasion it had been summoned to grace was at an end. The horses were fat and slow, like everything belonging to Mrs. Cope; the coachman sat as stiffly as a figure on a clock; and the whole equipage, as it rolled toward Fifth Avenue under the first gas-lamps, had the air of carrying away something that would not soon be brought back.

Mrs. Fenwick let the curtain fall. She was a slender woman of thirty-four, with a narrow, well-cut face and the kind of fair hair that fades early into a uniform pallor; and she had the habit, common to women who have been taught to regard composure as the first of the virtues, of keeping her features perfectly still when she was most disturbed. She kept them still now, while she crossed the room and extinguished the flame under the kettle; and it was only when she had done this, and had set the lid back on the sugar-bowl with a small decisive click, that she turned toward the corner by the piano, where her daughter sat on a footstool with a doll in her lap.

"Nora," she said, "come here."

The child got up at once. She was seven years old, a small, square, dark creature who resembled neither of her parents, and who had been a perpetual source of mild perplexity to both. Mrs. Fenwick, in moments of discouragement, was apt to ascribe this difference to a Dutch great-grandmother on her husband's side, of whom nothing was known but a portrait in a cap and a reputation for plain speaking; and it was of this ancestress that she thought now, with a sharpened sense of grievance, as Nora advanced across the carpet, still holding the doll by one limp arm.

"Put Arabella down."

Nora laid the doll on the sofa, arranging its skirts with a deliberation that seemed to her mother to border on insolence, though it was in fact only the child's instinctive effort to postpone whatever was coming. Then she stood with her hands behind her back, and her round dark eyes fixed on a point just below her mother's chin.

Mrs. Fenwick seated herself in the high-backed chair by the fire. She had been brought up in a world where nothing was ever said in a hurry, and where the gravity of a reproof was measured less by its vehemence than by the length of the silence that preceded it; and she allowed this silence to extend itself until the clock on the mantel-piece had struck the quarter and the little silver bell inside it had ceased to vibrate.

"Do you know what you said to Cousin Lavinia just now?"

Nora considered. "I said thank you for the peppermints."

"You know very well that is not what I mean."

The child's eyes travelled slowly upward to her mother's face, and down again. She did know; she had known from the moment the words were out of her mouth, when she had seen Cousin Lavinia's long upper lip draw itself down over her teeth, and the black jet beads on her bosom cease, for an instant, to rise and fall. But she had not known why she knew; and it was this uncertainty, rather than any sense of guilt, that made her stand so still.

"I said you told Papa we must all be very nice to her because of the money," she said at length, in the flat, careful voice of a child repeating a lesson.

Mrs. Fenwick's hand closed on the arm of her chair. She had heard the words once already, across the tea-table, in the hush that followed Mrs. Cope's innocent inquiry as to whether Nora was fond of her old cousin; and she had believed that nothing could make them more dreadful than they had sounded then. But they were more dreadful now, spoken in the empty room, without even the poor screen of Mrs. Cope's presence to absorb a part of their shock; and she was aware that a slow colour was rising under her skin.

"And do you think," she said, "that was a proper thing to say to a lady who had come to pay us a visit?"

Nora did not answer. She was looking at the tea-table, where a plate of the small iced cakes from Purssell's stood almost untouched, and she was wondering, with the detached part of her mind that went on working whatever happened, whether they would be sent down to the kitchen or kept for tomorrow.

"Nora, I am speaking to you."

"Yes, Mamma."

"Do you think it was a proper thing to say?"

"I don't know," said Nora.

It was the truth, and Mrs. Fenwick recognized it as such; but the recognition did not soften her. On the contrary, it filled her with a kind of helpless exasperation, as if she had been called upon to explain to a foreigner some custom of her country so deeply rooted that she had never thought of it as requiring explanation. The trouble with Nora, she reflected, was that she always took things literally. Other children—the little Lydigs, for instance, or the Sedgwick girls, whom she sometimes had to tea—seemed to come into the world with an intuitive knowledge of what might and might not be said; they absorbed it, as they absorbed their manners at table, without being able to remember the moment when it was learned. But Nora had to have everything spelled out for her, like a backward pupil in a spelling-class; and Mrs. Fenwick, who had never in her life spelled out anything of the kind, found herself at a loss for the letters.

"It was not proper," she said. "It was extremely improper. It was rude, and unkind, and it has made Cousin Lavinia very unhappy."

Nora's eyes came back to her mother's face, and this time they stayed there.

"But you did say it, Mamma. You said it at breakfast on Sunday. You said it when Papa was reading about the bank."

There was another silence, of a different quality from the first. Mrs. Fenwick remembered the breakfast perfectly: the grey light on the tablecloth, the smell of the kidneys under their silver cover, her husband's face behind the newspaper, so mild and so worried, and her own voice, lowered but not lowered enough, saying the thing she had said. She had not noticed Nora at all. Nora, at breakfast, was a part of the furniture of the dining-room, like the sideboard or the engraving of Washington crossing the Delaware; one did not lower one's voice before the sideboard. And it struck her now, with a disagreeable sense of having been spied upon, that this small, square, silent person had been sitting there all the while with her mug of milk, gathering up the words as a squirrel gathers nuts, and storing them away against the winter.

"What I say to Papa," she said, "is a very different thing from what you say to Cousin Lavinia."

"Why?"

The question was not impertinent; Mrs. Fenwick could see that it was not. It came out of the child with a kind of painful earnestness, as if a great deal depended on the answer. And for a moment, sitting there with the firelight on her hands, Mrs. Fenwick had the sensation of standing on the edge of something—some open place in her own mind, which she had always been careful to fence off, and into which she had no wish to look.

"Because," she said, "there are things one says, and things one repeats. You are old enough to understand the difference."

"Miss Pell says we must always tell the truth."

She examined them now, with a sudden distaste.

"Miss Pell is perfectly right. You must always tell the truth. But telling the truth does not mean saying everything that comes into your head. A little girl who says everything that comes into her head is not truthful—she is merely ill-bred."

She was pleased with this; it had the ring of one of those sayings with which her own mother used to close a discussion, sayings that seemed to descend from some region of absolute authority where there was no appeal. But Nora was not her own mother's daughter, and the saying fell on her as a stone falls into water, sinking without a trace and leaving only a series of slowly widening circles.

"Then was it true," she asked, "what you said to Papa?"

Mrs. Fenwick rose from her chair. She had not meant to rise; it was as if her body had acted of its own accord, in obedience to an instinct older and more reliable than reason. She went to the mantel-piece and stood looking down into the fire, with one hand resting on the cold marble beside the clock; and from this position, with her back half turned to the child, she found it easier to go on.

"Cousin Lavinia," she said, "is a very old lady, and a very lonely one. She has no children of her own, and she has been kind to Papa ever since he was a little boy. We are all very fond of her. When I said—what I said—at breakfast, I meant only that we must be especially careful to show her how fond of her we are, because she might otherwise think we were not. Old people are very easily hurt. You have hurt her very much today, and I don't know—" she paused, and her voice for the first time lost a little of its evenness—"I don't know whether she will ever be able to forget it."

This was nearer the truth than anything she had yet said, and she felt the nearness as one feels the draught from an opened door. For it was not Cousin Lavinia's feelings that concerned her: Cousin Lavinia had survived two husbands, a lawsuit, and the marriage of her favourite nephew to a Roman Catholic, and was not likely to be permanently wounded by the indiscretion of a child. What concerned her was the will—the long, carefully drafted document lying in the safe of Mr. Bancroft Ledyard's office in Wall Street, which had been altered three times in the last ten years, always after some trifling offence, and which was understood in the family to resemble a barometer more closely than a legal instrument. And what concerned her even more than the will, though she would have denied it with indignation, was the thought of Mrs. Cope's carriage stopping, on its slow progress up Fifth Avenue, before the door of Mrs. Henry Lydig, who was Mrs. Cope's other cousin, and who had three sons at Columbia and a husband who had never had anything to do with a bank.

She turned back from the fire. Nora had not moved; but her face had changed. The look of earnest inquiry had gone out of it, and in its place was something Mrs. Fenwick had never seen there before—a kind of shut, considering stillness, as if the child had drawn a blind across a window and was standing behind it, looking out.

"I didn't want to hurt her," Nora said. "She asked me if I loved her. I didn't know what else to say."

"You might have said yes."

"But I don't, Mamma. Not very much. She smells of camphor, like Miss Pell, and she pinches."

Mrs. Fenwick sat down again. She was conscious of an extraordinary fatigue, as if the half-hour since Mrs. Cope's departure had been a day's journey over rough roads. The fire had sunk to a dull red glow, and the room, with its rose-coloured lamps and its crimson brocades, seemed to her suddenly oppressive, like the interior of a jewel-case in which she and the child had been shut up together.

"Listen to me, Nora," she said. "When a lady asks you if you love her, you are to say, 'Yes, Cousin Lavinia, very much.' You are not to stop and think about it. You are not to tell her about the camphor, or the pinching, or anything that you may have heard Papa and me say at breakfast. You are simply to say, 'Yes, very much,' and then you are to offer her the cakes. Do you understand?"

"Yes, Mamma."

"And now you are going upstairs to the schoolroom, and you are going to write Cousin Lavinia a little letter. You will tell her that you are very sorry you said a foolish thing, and that you did not mean it, and that you hope she will come to see us again soon. I will look at it before it is sent."

Nora's eyes widened slightly. "But I did mean it, Mamma. I only said what you—"

"You did not mean it," said Mrs. Fenwick. She spoke very quietly, and with great distinctness, as if she were dictating to a clerk. "You did not understand what you were saying, and therefore you cannot have meant it. That is what you will write. And you will not have any supper until it is done."

For a long moment the child stood looking at her. Mrs. Fenwick, meeting the look, had the curious impression that it was not her daughter who was being judged, but herself; and she held her face perfectly still under it, as she had held it still under Mrs. Cope's cold, appraising glance across the tea-cups. Then Nora picked up the doll from the sofa and went slowly out of the room, and Mrs. Fenwick heard her steps going up the stairs, one at a time, with a pause on each landing.

She sat for a while without moving. Below, in the basement, she could hear the cook rattling the range, and from the street came the clatter of a passing omnibus and the long cry of a boy selling evening papers. Presently the door opened and the parlour-maid came in to take away the tea-things; and Mrs. Fenwick, with an effort, told her to leave the cakes on the sideboard in the dining-room. Then she went to the writing-table between the windows, and took out a sheet of her thick cream-laid paper, and began, in her small, sloping, Brearley hand, to compose a note of her own to Mrs. Cope. It was a difficult note to write, since it had to convey regret without admitting the occasion for it, and affection without appearing to solicit anything in return; and she tore up two drafts before she arrived at a form that satisfied her. When it was done she sealed it and laid it on the hall table, and as she did so she heard the schoolroom door open overhead.

Nora came down the stairs with a sheet of ruled paper in her hand. She had evidently taken great pains with it: the letters, though large and uneven, were carefully formed, and there was only one blot, near the bottom, which she had tried to remove with the corner of her handkerchief. She held it out without a word, and Mrs. Fenwick took it and carried it to the gas-jet by the drawing-room door.

*Dear Cousin Lavinia,* it ran. *I am very sorry I said a foolish thing. I did not understand it so I did not mean it. I love you very much. I hope you will come again soon and we will have the cakes. Your affectionate cousin, Nora Fenwick.*

Mrs. Fenwick read it twice. It was exactly what she had asked for—more, indeed, since she had said nothing about the cakes, and the touch seemed to her a happy one, of the kind that Mrs. Cope, who was greedy, would be sure to appreciate. She folded the paper and looked down at her daughter, meaning to say something kind; and the words died on her lips.

Nora was standing quite still at the foot of the stairs, with her hands clasped behind her and her face turned up toward the light. It was a perfectly composed face, smooth and blank and attentive, with nothing in it that anyone could object to; and Mrs. Fenwick, looking at it, had the odd sensation of having caught sight of her own reflection in a strange mirror, at the end of some long corridor she had not known was there.

"That will do very nicely," she said.

"May I have my supper now, Mamma?"

"Yes. Tell Ellen you may have one of the cakes."

Nora thanked her and went down the basement stairs; and Mrs. Fenwick, after a moment, laid the child's letter beside her own on the hall table, where the two lay side by side under the gas-light, the cream-laid envelope and the folded sheet of ruled paper, like a lesson and its exercise. She stood looking at them for some time. It occurred to her that she ought to feel relieved, and she supposed that she did; the thing had been managed, as things in her world were always managed, quietly and without unpleasantness, and tomorrow Mrs. Cope would read the two letters at her breakfast-table and decide, in all probability, that the child had been properly brought up after all. But as she turned away and went back into the drawing-room, where the fire had gone out and the rose-coloured lamps burned on in the emptiness, she found herself remembering, with a persistence she could not account for, the expression with which Nora had asked her whether it was true; and it seemed to her, for no reason that she could have given, that she would never be asked that question again.

She too needed friends—she had tasted the pang of loneliness; and her resentment of Bertha Dorset’s cruelty softened her heart to the poor wretch who was after all the chief of Bertha’s victims.

“I still wish to be kind; I feel no ill-will toward you,” she said. “But you must understand that after what has happened we can’t be friends again—we can’t see each other.”

“Ah, you ARE kind—you’re merciful—you always were!” He fixed his miserable gaze on her. “But why can’t we be friends—why not, when I’ve repented in dust and ashes? Isn’t it hard that you should condemn me to suffer for the falseness, the treachery of others? I was punished enough at the time—is there to be no respite for me?”

“I should have thought you had found complete respite in the reconciliation which was effected at my expense,” Lily began, with renewed impatience; but he broke in imploringly: “Don’t put it in that way—when that’s been the worst of my punishment. My God! what could I do—wasn’t I powerless? You were singled out as a sacrifice: any word I might have said would have been turned against you——” “I have told you I don’t blame you; all I ask you to understand is that, after the use Bertha chose to make of me—after all that her behaviour has since implied—it’s impossible that you and I should meet.” He continued to stand before her, in his dogged weakness. “Is it—need it be? Mightn’t there be circumstances——?” he checked himself, slashing at the wayside weeds in a wider radius. Then he began again: “Miss Bart, listen—give me a minute.
