Ed Prather came home from the grain elevator at the end of a hot day in August, and when he had washed his hands and face at the pump in the yard he did not go at once into the house. He stood by the pump with the water running off his chin and looked at the kitchen window, where a lamp had been lighted although it was not yet dark. His wife Kate was moving about in the kitchen. He could see her shadow pass across the window and then come back again. It went back and forth like that, and Ed stood and watched it.

He was a man of forty-two, tall and somewhat stooped, with long arms and large hands that were always cracked across the knuckles from handling the sacks of grain. In the town everyone said he was a good man. He did not drink, and on Sundays he went with his wife to the Methodist church and sat with his hands on his knees and looked at the back of the head of the man in front of him. When the hymns were sung he did not sing, but he held the book open before him and his lips moved a little. He had been born on a farm three miles out of town on the Medina road, and when his father died and the farm was sold he had come into town and gone to work at the elevator. That had been eighteen years before. He had married Kate Larrabee, the daughter of the druggist, in his second year in town.

On this evening Ed had something in his mind that he wanted to say to his wife, and he had been carrying it about with him all day. He had carried it up and down the ladders of the elevator and into the office where old Mr. Fenner sat with his feet on the desk, and he had carried it home along the street under the maple trees. It was a thing that Will Holcomb, the section boss on the railroad, had told him at noon. Will Holcomb had come into the elevator to get out of the sun and had sat down on a pile of empty sacks, and after a time, when he had talked of the heat and the price of wheat and of a man who had been killed by a freight train down at Wellington, he had said a thing about Kate.

"Your wife walks out pretty late," Will Holcomb had said. He had not looked at Ed when he said it. He had looked at the floor and spat between his feet. "I seen her out by the trestle over Black Creek three, four times now. Along about ten, eleven o'clock. I been going down there nights to see about a rail that's been working loose. I thought I'd tell you. A woman alone out there. It ain't safe, I thought."

That was all Will Holcomb had said. He had got up then and gone out of the elevator and into the hot sunlight, and Ed had stood holding a sack of oats against his chest, and it was as though the sack had grown very heavy and he could not put it down.

Now he stood by the pump in his own yard and looked at the window of his own house, and his wife's shadow went back and forth.

---

It should be said here that there was nothing in Ed Prather that would have made him a jealous man. He was not one to think much about such things. When he was a young man on his father's farm he had sometimes, on summer nights, lain awake in the hot little room under the roof and thought of women, but the thoughts had been vague and had not stayed with him. When he married Kate it had seemed to him a thing that happened, as the coming of spring happens, and he had been glad of it in a quiet way and had not questioned it. She had been a slender, dark girl with a quick way of moving her head, and when he had walked out with her in the evenings she had talked a great deal, about books she had been reading and about a city called Philadelphia where she had an aunt and where she had once spent a summer. Ed had listened. He did not know what to say about books or about Philadelphia. He had walked beside her with his big hands hanging and had felt very large and awkward, and sometimes when she had stopped talking and looked at him in the darkness he had felt that she was waiting for something. He had not known what it was. He had only taken her hand and they had walked on.

They had no children. In the first years Kate had wanted children very much, and then after a time she had stopped speaking of it. Ed had not wanted children particularly, but he had wanted what she wanted, and when she stopped speaking of it he stopped thinking of it. He thought that she was content. She kept the house very clean, and she had planted hollyhocks along the fence and morning glories over the woodshed, and in the evenings she sat on the front porch and rocked while he read the Cleveland paper, and when the darkness came they went in to bed.

But there had been, Ed now remembered, standing by the pump, a thing that had happened in the spring. He had waked in the night and Kate had not been in the bed beside him. He had lain still and listened, and after a while he had heard the screen door at the back of the house, very softly, and her feet on the stairs. She had come in and undressed in the darkness and got into the bed, and she had lain very stiff and still, and her body had been cold as though she had been out in the night air for a long time. He had not said anything. In the morning she had been just as always, and he had thought perhaps he dreamed it. He had put it away out of his mind. Now it came back.

---

Ed went into the kitchen. Kate was standing by the stove with her back to him. She was forty years old now and still slender, but her shoulders had grown sharp and thin and there was gray in her hair. She did not turn around when he came in.

"It's been hot," she said.

"Yes," Ed said. "It's been hot all right."

He sat down at the table, and she brought him his supper, fried potatoes and cold ham and a dish of sliced tomatoes, and she sat down across from him. She did not eat. She sat with her hands in her lap and looked at the lamp. Ed ate slowly. He did not taste the food. He kept thinking of the words he would say. "Will Holcomb told me a thing today," he would say, and then she would say something, and then it would be all right. He thought that perhaps she would laugh. Perhaps there was nothing in it. Perhaps she went out to the trestle to look at the water. People did things like that. There was no harm in it.

But he did not say anything. He finished the potatoes and pushed the plate away. Outside the window it had grown dark, and the insects had begun their singing in the grass along the fence. A buggy went by in the street, and someone in the buggy laughed, a woman's laugh, high and quick, and then the sound of the wheels went away.

"I thought I'd sit out on the porch a while," Kate said, getting up. "It's cooler out there."

"I'll come too," Ed said.

She stopped by the door and looked at him. It was a queer look. It was as though she were surprised, as though she had not expected him to say that, and Ed felt it and was ashamed without knowing why he should be. In all the years they had been married he had sat on the porch with her in the evenings. But lately, he now remembered, he had not. Lately he had been tired when he came home, and he had gone up to bed early and left her sitting there alone. He had not thought of it until now.

---

They went out onto the front porch and Kate sat in the rocking chair and Ed sat on the top step with his back against the post. The street was dark under the maples. Down at the corner there was a street lamp, and moths were flying about it, and beyond it Ed could see the lighted windows of Mrs. Wyant's house, where Mrs. Wyant lived alone since her husband had gone off to the Dakotas and not come back. Across the street old Judge Turner was sitting on his porch, and the red end of his cigar glowed and faded and glowed again.

Kate rocked. The chair made a little creaking sound on the boards, back and forth, back and forth, and Ed sat and listened to it. He thought of the shadow going back and forth across the kitchen window. He thought of Will Holcomb sitting on the sacks and spitting between his feet.

"Kate," he said.

The rocking stopped.

"What is it, Ed?"

He did not answer at once. He looked at his hands. In the darkness they were only pale shapes on his knees, and he turned them over and looked at the palms. It seemed to him that he had never in his life said anything that mattered. All his life he had talked about the weather and about the price of grain and about whether it would rain, and now he wanted to say something that mattered and he did not know how it was done. The words were in him somewhere but they would not come up.

"Will Holcomb was in at the elevator today," he said finally.

Kate did not say anything. Ed heard her breathing. Across the street the end of the Judge's cigar glowed and faded.

"He said he'd seen you out by the trestle. Nights. Out by Black Creek." He stopped. Then he said, "He said it wasn't safe. A woman alone."

For a long time Kate did not answer. Ed waited. He did not turn around to look at her. He was afraid to look at her. He sat with his back against the post and his hands on his knees and waited, and the insects sang in the grass, and from somewhere far off, down by the railroad, there came the sound of a freight train whistling for the crossing.

"Yes," Kate said. "I go out there."

That was all. She said it quietly, and there was nothing in her voice, not anger nor fear nor shame, and Ed did not know what to do with it. He had thought she would laugh or that she would deny it. He had thought she would say something that would let him off. But she only said, "Yes. I go out there," and then she was quiet again, and he understood that she was waiting for him.

"What do you go out there for?" he said. His voice sounded loud and strange to him. "Is there somebody? Do you meet somebody out there, Kate?"

He heard the rocking chair creak as she leaned forward. And then she did laugh, but it was not the laugh he had hoped for. It was a short, hard little laugh that seemed to hurt her.

"Oh, Ed," she said. "Oh, Ed. No. There isn't anybody. There isn't anybody at all."

---

There is a thing that happens sometimes between two people who have lived a long time together. They come to a place, and it is as though a door stood before them that they had never noticed. All the years they have been walking past it, and now suddenly there it is, and one of them must open it or they must both go away and never come back to that place again. Ed Prather felt this, sitting on the step in the darkness, although he could not have put it into words. He felt that his wife was very near to him and at the same time very far away, as though she were standing on the other side of a wide field and calling to him and he could not hear what she said.

"Then what do you go out there for?" he said again, and this time his voice was gentler.

Kate got up out of the rocking chair. She went to the edge of the porch and stood with her hand on the railing, and Ed could see her now against the light from the street lamp, her thin shoulders and her head bent a little forward.

"I don't know," she said. "I don't know how to tell you. I've tried to think how I'd tell you if you ever asked me. I thought you'd never ask me."

She was quiet a moment, and then she began to talk. She talked fast and in a low voice, and some of the things she said Ed did not understand, and some of them he understood only afterward, lying awake in the bed, or the next day at the elevator, or years later.

"It began in the spring," she said. "I don't know how it began. I was sitting here one night after you'd gone up, and I got to thinking about when I was a girl. About Father's store and the smell of it, and the books I used to read up in the room over the store, and that summer in Philadelphia. And I thought, that was twenty years ago. Twenty years. And I couldn't think of a thing that had happened since. Not a single thing, Ed. I sat here and tried, and I couldn't think of one. It was as though I had gone to sleep and woke up and I was old."

She stopped. Ed did not say anything. He sat very still.

"So I got up and walked," Kate said. "I didn't know where I was going. I went down past the depot and out along the tracks, and I came to the trestle, and I stood there and looked down at the creek. It was all black, and you could hear it running over the stones, and the frogs were going. And there was a freight came through. I stood off to the side and it went past me, right close, and the ground shook and the wind of it pulled at my dress, and the cars went by and went by, and I could see the doors open on some of them and it was dark inside. And I thought, they're all going somewhere. Every one of them is going somewhere. To Chicago and to places out west I never heard of. And I stood there and cried. I don't know why. I just stood there and cried like a child."

She turned around then and looked at him, though he could not see her face.

"That's all it is, Ed. I go out there and wait for the trains. I wait for the freights to come through, and I stand there and let them go by. It's a foolish thing. I know it's a foolish thing. I'm a grown woman and I know it. But I go."

---

Ed Prather sat on the step and looked at his wife, and something went through him that he had never felt before. It was not anger. He had been ready for anger, all day he had been ready for it, but it did not come. It was more like the feeling he had once had as a boy on his father's farm, when he had gone out early one morning in March and found that a ewe had died in the night giving birth and the lamb was lying beside her, still alive, trying to get up on its legs in the cold. He had stood looking at it and had not known what to do, and something had filled up his chest until it hurt.

He wanted to get up and go to her. He wanted to put his arms around her. But he did not. He sat there. His big hands lay on his knees and he could not make them move.

"I didn't know," he said. "Kate, I didn't know you felt like that."

"How would you know?" she said, and there was something sharp in her voice now, though it went away again almost at once. "How would you? I never told you. I never told anybody. I didn't know it myself." She came and sat down again in the rocking chair, heavily, as though she were very tired. "It isn't your fault, Ed. I don't want you to think it's your fault. You've been good to me. Everybody says what a good man you are. It's only that—" She stopped.

"Only what?"

"I don't know. Only that I wanted something. I always wanted something, ever since I was a girl. When you came walking out with me I thought maybe it was you. I thought maybe you'd be the one to—" She stopped again, and then she said, very low, "And then we got married and it was just the house and the hollyhocks and you going to the elevator. And I kept waiting. I kept thinking it would come. And it never came."

Ed did not answer. He could not. Across the street Judge Turner got up out of his chair and went into his house, and the screen door banged behind him, and a little later a light went on upstairs and then went off again. The street was very dark now. Only the lamp at the corner was burning, and the moths still went round and round it.

---

They sat there a long time without speaking. Ed thought of many things. He thought of the evenings when he had walked beside her as a young man, and how she had talked about books and about Philadelphia, and how she had stopped sometimes and looked at him in the darkness, waiting. He understood now what she had been waiting for. She had been waiting for him to say something. Anything. She had been waiting for him to tell her what was in him, and he had not told her because he had not known there was anything in him to tell. He had only taken her hand and walked on.

And then he thought that there was something in him, after all. He had felt it often, on certain mornings at the elevator when the sun came in through the dusty windows and lay in long yellow bars across the floor, and the grain dust floated in the light, and he stood and looked at it and could not have said why it made him want to stand there forever. He had felt it in the fall when the wagons came in from the country loaded with wheat and the farmers sat up high on the seats with the reins in their hands and their faces brown and tired. He had felt it once, years ago, walking home late along the Medina road under the stars. He had never spoken of these things to anyone. He had not thought they were things a man spoke of. He had thought every man had them and kept them to himself.

He wanted now to tell Kate about the sunlight on the elevator floor. It seemed to him suddenly the most important thing in the world that she should know about it. He opened his mouth to speak.

"Kate," he said. "Sometimes in the morning—"

But he could not go on. The words would not come. He sat there with his mouth open, and after a moment he closed it, and he felt his face grow hot in the darkness.

"What, Ed?" Kate said. "Sometimes in the morning what?"

"Nothing," he said. "It ain't anything."

He heard her sigh. It was a small sound, hardly a sound at all, but Ed heard it, and he knew that he had come to the door and had not opened it, and that she knew it too.

---

After a while Kate got up and went into the house. Ed heard her moving about in the kitchen, putting away the dishes, and then he heard her go up the stairs. He did not follow her. He sat on the step with his back against the post and looked out into the dark street.

It was very late when he finally rose. The lamp at the corner had been put out, and the moths were gone, and there was no light anywhere except the stars. Ed stood in the yard and looked up at them. Then, without quite knowing why, he went out through the gate and down the street toward the depot.

He walked past the depot, where the night operator sat asleep with his head on his arms beside the telegraph key, and out along the tracks. The ties were uneven under his feet and once he stumbled. He walked a long way. He came at last to the trestle over Black Creek and stood there in the darkness, and he could hear the water running over the stones below and the frogs going, just as she had said.

He stood there a long time. Then, far off to the east, he heard a whistle, and after a while he saw the light of the engine coming, small at first and then growing larger, and the rails beside him began to hum. He stepped off to the side and stood in the weeds. The freight came on. The ground shook under him and the wind of it pulled at his clothes, and the cars went by and went by, dark and heavy, and some of the doors stood open and it was black inside. Ed Prather stood and watched them go. He was a big, stooped man of forty-two standing alone in the weeds beside a railroad track at two o'clock in the morning, and he did not know why he was there.

When the last car had gone and the red lantern on the end of it had grown small and disappeared, he turned and walked back toward the town. He walked slowly. His hands hung at his sides.

When he came into the bedroom Kate was lying in the bed with her face turned toward the wall. He thought she was asleep. He undressed in the darkness and got in beside her and lay on his back looking at the ceiling. After a time he felt her move, and then her hand came across the sheet and found his hand and held it. Neither of them said anything. They lay like that, holding hands in the darkness, until the windows grew gray and the first wagons began to come in along the road from the country.

Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Sherwood Anderson, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
When Albert Kearns came back to the town of Pymatuning, Ohio, after an absence of eighteen years, he was a man of forty and had grown a little stout. He came on the noon train from Cleveland, and as he got down from the coach with his yellow bag in his hand he stood for a moment on the station platform and looked about. Nothing much had changed. The freight house was there with its sliding door half open, and the same kind of boxes were piled inside, and a boy was sitting on a truck swinging his legs. The boy looked at Albert and Albert looked at the boy. It seemed to Albert that he himself had once sat on that truck and swung his legs in just that way, looking at strangers who got off the train and wondering what cities they had come from and what had happened to them there.

He had come because his Aunt Sarah had died. That was the excuse. The letter had come to him in Chicago, where he worked in an office on the fourteenth floor of a building on Wabash Avenue writing advertisements for a company that made farm machinery. The letter was from his cousin Mary, Aunt Sarah's daughter, and it was short. "Mother passed away on Tuesday," she wrote. "The funeral will be Friday. I do not suppose you can come but I thought you would want to know." That was all. There was no "Dear Albert," and at the bottom she had written only her name, "Mary Kearns," as though he might have forgotten which Mary she was.

He did not get to the funeral. There was a delay about a contract at the office and he wired flowers. But a week later, on a Saturday, he found himself on the train, and when it had passed Painesville and began to run through the flat country with the woodlots standing back from the tracks and the fences going along beside the fields, he felt something inside himself grow tight and then loosen, the way a man's throat will tighten when he hears an old tune played on a street organ.

Mary Kearns lived alone now in the house on Maple Street where she had always lived. Albert walked there from the station carrying his bag. It was in the month of October and the leaves of the maple trees had turned and many of them had fallen, and they lay in the gutters and on the brick sidewalks. A man was burning leaves in a yard and the smoke drifted across the street. Albert breathed it in. In Chicago there was smoke too, but it was a different smoke. It came out of the stacks of factories and it got into a man's clothes and his hair and it was sour. This smoke was sweet. He thought of that and then he thought that it was a foolish thing to think, a thing a man thinks when he is getting older and has begun to grow soft.

Mary was in the yard when he came up. She was raking leaves into a pile by the fence, and she had on an old brown coat that had belonged to her mother. She did not hear him at first. He stood at the gate and watched her. She was thirty-eight years old, two years younger than himself, and she was tall and thin, and her shoulders had a kind of stoop in them. She was the teacher of the fourth grade in the Pymatuning school. She had taught there for sixteen years.

When she turned and saw him she did not cry out. She stood holding the rake and looked at him, and he saw her face go red and then white. "Well, Albert," she said. "Well, you came after all."

"I couldn't get away for the funeral," he said. "I'm sorry, Mary. There was a thing at the office."

"I know," she said. "The flowers were nice. Everyone said they were the nicest."

They went into the house. It was dark inside, and it smelled of furniture polish and of something else, a smell of old women and of medicine bottles and of rooms that have been shut up. Aunt Sarah had been sick for three years before she died, and Mary had taken care of her, coming home from the schoolhouse at noon to give her her dinner and going back again, and sitting up with her at night. Albert knew that from the letters, which had come at Christmas, one letter each year, always short. He had answered them, but not always.

Mary made coffee in the kitchen and they sat at the kitchen table and drank it. She had cut some slices of cake and put them on a plate, and the plate was one Albert remembered. It had blue birds painted around the edge. When he was a boy and came to this house on Sunday afternoons, his mother would say to him, "Now don't you break any of Aunt Sarah's dishes," and he would hold the plate with both hands.

They talked. That is to say, words passed between them. Mary asked about his work in Chicago and he told her about it, making it sound larger and more important than it was. He told about the men he worked with and about a trip he had made to New York. She listened and nodded her head. Then he asked about people in the town, and she told him who was dead and who had married and who had gone away. "Ed Hostetler has the hardware store now," she said. "His father died. You remember Ed. He was the one who fell through the ice on Hamer's pond."

"I remember," Albert said. He remembered very well. It was he who had pulled Ed out, lying flat on the ice and reaching with a fence rail. For a week afterward he had been a kind of hero in the town. He wanted to tell Mary that he remembered that, but he did not. It seemed a boastful thing to bring up.

All the time they were talking Albert was looking at Mary's hands. They lay on the oilcloth on the table beside her coffee cup and they were long hands, very thin, and the knuckles were large. They did not keep still. The fingers moved, they picked at the edge of the oilcloth, they turned the cup a little on its saucer, they went up and touched her hair and came down again. It was as though the hands were trying to say something that Mary herself could not say, as though they belonged to another woman who lived inside her and who was impatient and wanted to be let out.

Albert had a habit too. When he was uneasy he laughed. It was a short laugh, a kind of bark, and it came out of him at the wrong times, so that people in the office sometimes looked at him in a puzzled way. Now as Mary talked he laughed several times, and each time he did it he was ashamed. Once she was telling him about the last days of her mother, how the old woman had lain in the bed and talked about her girlhood on a farm near Ashtabula and had not known Mary at all but had called her by the name of a sister who had been dead for fifty years. And in the middle of this Albert laughed. He did not know why. He put his hand over his mouth and his face burned.

Mary looked at him. "It's all right," she said quietly. "It is a kind of funny thing, when you think about it. I used to laugh too, sometimes. Sitting by the bed. I would laugh and then I would go out into the kitchen and cry."

In the late afternoon they went for a walk. It was Mary who proposed it. "You'll want to see the town," she said, and she put on the old brown coat again and a hat with a feather that had gone limp. They walked down Maple Street to Main and along Main past the stores. Some of the men standing in front of the stores spoke to Albert and called him by name, and he was surprised that they knew him. They were men he had gone to school with and they had grown heavy and their faces had grown red and coarse. One of them, a man named Tom Fenner who had been a great baseball player when they were boys, took hold of Albert's arm and shook it and said, "Well, by God, Al, you've done all right, ain't you? You've done all right for yourself in the city." Albert laughed his short laugh and said yes, he guessed he had done all right.

When they had got past the stores Mary said, "Tom drinks. His wife left him. She went to live with her people in Erie." She said it without any feeling in her voice, as one might tell the price of potatoes.

They kept on walking. Without saying anything about it they both went out along the road that led past the cemetery and on to the fairgrounds. The fairgrounds were at the edge of town where the fields began. There was a race track there, with a fence around it, and a grandstand, and long sheds where the cattle were kept at fair time. Now in October everything was empty. The grass had grown up along the track and the paint was peeling from the grandstand. They climbed up into the grandstand and sat on one of the high seats and looked out over the fields. The sun was going down. It was a large red sun and it hung over a woodlot to the west, and the corn shocks standing in the fields threw long shadows.

It is a strange thing about people who have known each other as children. They carry the children about inside them all their lives, and when they meet again after a long time the grown people sit and talk politely of this and that, and all the while the children inside them are restless and want to come out and play, or want to say some word that was never said. Albert and Mary had been children together. They had been more than cousins. Albert's father had died when Albert was six, and his mother had moved into a little house on the same street as Aunt Sarah, and the two children had been always together. They had gone to school together and come home together, and in the summers they had gone barefoot along the creek that ran below the town, catching crawfish under the stones. Mary had been a thin, brown, quick girl then, quicker than Albert, and she could climb higher in a tree than he could and she was not afraid of snakes.

There was a thing that had happened once between them. It was not a large thing. Anyone else would have forgotten it. But Albert had not forgotten it, and sitting now in the empty grandstand with the sun going down, he knew that Mary had not forgotten it either.

It had happened when Albert was sixteen and was about to go away. He was going to Cleveland to work in a printing shop. It had all been arranged, and he was to go on a Monday, and on the Sunday before, he and Mary had walked out to the fairgrounds. It was in the late summer and the fair had been held the week before, and there was still straw scattered about and the smell of animals in the sheds. They had gone into one of the cattle sheds, for no reason, just walking about, and it was dim in there and quiet.

Mary was fourteen. She stood in the shed by one of the stalls and suddenly she began to talk. She talked very fast, in a low voice, and what she said was that she did not want him to go away. She said that she was afraid. She said that if he went away she would be left in the town, and that she would grow up and become like her mother and like all the other women, and that she would never get out. "You don't know," she said. "It's different for you. You can go. You're a boy. But me, I'll have to stay. I'll stay here and stay here and pretty soon I'll be old." And then she said something else. She said, "Take me with you, Albert. I could get work in Cleveland. I could do something. Take me along."

He had not known what to say. He was frightened by her. He stood in the shed with his hands in his pockets and looked at the straw on the floor. Then he laughed. It was the first time that laugh had come out of him, that short bark of a laugh, and it came out of him then in the cattle shed and it was as though he had struck her. She turned and ran out of the shed and across the race track, and he did not follow her. The next day he went away to Cleveland, and Mary did not come to the station to see him off.

That was all. It was twenty-four years ago. He had been in Cleveland three years and then in Chicago. He had married a woman in Chicago and she had died, and he had not married again. He had come back to Pymatuning only once before, for his mother's funeral, and on that visit he had stayed only one night and he and Mary had hardly spoken. She had been taking care of her mother even then.

Now they sat in the grandstand. The sun had touched the tops of the trees in the woodlot. A crow flew over, going toward the woods, and then another one. Mary had taken off her hat and was holding it in her lap, and her hands were picking at the limp feather.

Albert wanted to say something. He wanted to say, "I remember the shed. I remember what you said." He wanted to tell her that many times in Chicago, at night in his room, he had thought of her standing there in the dim light with the straw about her feet, and that he had thought that if he had been a different kind of boy, a braver kind, he might have taken her hand and said, "All right, Mary, come along." He did not know what would have happened then. Perhaps nothing good. Perhaps she would have been unhappy in the city. Perhaps they would both have been unhappy. But it seemed to him that the moment in the shed had been a door standing open, and that he had laughed and the door had closed, and that it had closed not only for her but for himself as well.

He opened his mouth to speak. What came out was, "They ought to paint this grandstand. It's going to pieces."

"There's no money," Mary said. "The fair doesn't pay any more. People go to Cleveland for their pleasure now. They have automobiles."

They sat a while longer. The light was going. Over at the edge of the fairgrounds the long cattle sheds stood up dark against the sky. Albert looked at them and Mary looked at them, and neither one said anything.

Then Mary spoke. She did not look at him. She looked straight ahead at the sheds. "I got out once," she said. "Did you know that? I went to Columbus to the normal school. I was there two years. I had a room on a street near the university, and in the evenings I used to walk by myself up and down the streets and look in the windows of the houses. I thought I would never come back here. And then Father died, and Mother was alone, and I came back. I said it would be for one year." She laughed then, and it was strange to hear her laugh, because it was something like his own laugh, short and hard. "One year," she said.

Albert sat very still. He felt that she was going to say more. He felt that she was going to say the word, the thing that lay between them, and he was afraid of it and wanted it at the same time. He looked at her hands. They had stopped moving. They lay quite still in her lap on the old hat.

But she did not say any more. After a time she put on her hat and stood up. "It's getting cold," she said. "We had better go back. I have some ham for supper."

They climbed down out of the grandstand and walked back toward the town. It was nearly dark now and the lamps were being lighted in the houses. As they passed the cemetery Mary said, "Mother is over there, by the big elm. I'll show you tomorrow if you like." Albert said yes, he would like to see it.

They ate supper in the kitchen. Afterward Mary washed the dishes and Albert dried them, and he was very careful with the plate that had the blue birds around the edge. Then they sat in the front room for a while. Mary had some papers to correct, the arithmetic papers of the fourth grade, and she sat at the table under the lamp with a red pencil and Albert sat across the room in Aunt Sarah's rocking chair and pretended to read a newspaper. Now and then he looked up at her. The lamplight fell on her face, and she frowned a little as she worked, and her lips moved as she added up the figures. It came to him that she was a good teacher, that the children of the fourth grade were probably a little afraid of her and also loved her, and that she would go on teaching them for many years, one fourth grade after another, until she was old.

He went to bed in the little room at the head of the stairs. It was a room he had slept in sometimes as a boy, when his mother was away, and the wallpaper was the same, a pattern of faded roses. He lay in the bed and could not sleep. He heard Mary moving about downstairs, and then he heard her come up the stairs and go into her room and close the door. After that the house was still. A wind had come up and the branches of a maple tree scraped against the side of the house.

Albert lay in the dark and thought. He thought that in the morning he might go to Mary and say to her, "Come to Chicago. Sell the house and come. There is nothing to hold you here now." He thought he might say it at breakfast. He imagined how she would look when he said it, and how her hands would stop moving, and what she would answer. He lay for a long time imagining it, and it seemed very real to him and very possible, and his heart beat fast.

But in the morning when he came down Mary had already been up for a long time. She had made biscuits and fried eggs and the coffee was hot. She had on a black dress, because it was Sunday, and she was going to church. "You'll want to come," she said. "People will want to see you." And he went to church with her, and sat in the pew where Aunt Sarah had sat, and many people came up afterward and shook his hand. In the afternoon they went to the cemetery and looked at the new grave by the big elm. The earth on it was still raw and yellow. Mary stood looking down at it and Albert stood beside her with his hat in his hands.

He left on the evening train. Mary walked with him to the station. They stood on the platform and waited, and when the train came in, the same boy, or another one like him, was sitting on the baggage truck swinging his legs. Albert took Mary's hand to say goodbye. Her hand was cold and thin and the knuckles were hard under his fingers.

"Well, Mary," he said.

"Well, Albert," she said.

He climbed into the coach and found a seat by the window. When the train began to move he looked out and saw her standing on the platform in the old brown coat. She did not wave. She stood there with her hands hanging at her sides and watched the train go, and then the train went around a curve and the station was gone and there were only the dark fields and the woodlots going past.

Albert sat in the coach and looked out the window at the dark. After a while he laughed, that short laugh of his, and a woman sitting across the aisle looked at him. He turned his face toward the window so that she could not see it, and he sat that way for a long time, until the lights of Cleveland began to show, scattered across the flat land like sparks blown out of a fire.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
Ezra Pruitt worked at the stave mill on the edge of the town of Pickering, Ohio, and on the evening of which this is told he came home late. There had been trouble with the big saw. A belt had broken and a man named Joe Kinsey had got his arm cut, not badly, but there had been blood on the sawdust and the men had stood about in a ring looking at it and saying nothing. Ezra had gone with Joe Kinsey to the doctor's office over Hern's grocery and had sat in a chair by the window while the doctor sewed the arm. All the time he had been sitting there he had looked out of the window at the street below where the farmers' wagons were going home and he had thought of nothing at all. He was a man who often did not think of anything. His mind was like a field in the late fall when the corn has been cut and the shocks stand about and the crows walk between them.

He was a tall man and his shoulders were stooped. His hands were very large. They were the kind of hands that seem to belong to another and larger man, and when he was not working he did not know what to do with them. He put them in his pockets and took them out again. At the supper table he laid them on the oilcloth on either side of his plate and looked at them as though they were two animals that had followed him home.

When he came into the kitchen that evening his wife Kate was standing by the stove. She was a small quick woman with a sharp chin and her hair was drawn back tight from her forehead. She did not turn around when he came in. "You had better go see about your son," she said. "He is out in the woodshed. I put him out there. I told him to wait for you."

Ezra stood by the door with his hat in his hand. He did not ask what had happened. He knew that Kate would tell him, and she did. She told it with her back to him, stirring something in a kettle on the stove, and her voice was high and thin and it shook a little.

What had happened was this. The boy, whose name was Harley and who was six years old, had got into the bureau in the front room where Ezra kept the watch that had been his father's. It was a large silver watch with a lid that snapped shut, and on the lid there was a picture cut into the silver of a deer standing beside a stream. Ezra never carried the watch. It lay in a little box lined with faded red cloth, and on Sundays sometimes he took it out and wound it and held it to his ear and then put it away again. The boy had taken the watch out into the back yard and had sat on the ground by the rain barrel and with a nail he had pried off the back of it. He had wanted to see what was inside. Kate had found him there with the little wheels and springs spread out on a flat stone before him, and he was poking at them with the nail, and he was not crying or afraid at all. He had looked up at her, she said, with his face all lit up.

"He looked up at me like it was Christmas," Kate said. "Like he had found something. And it is all in pieces. I picked up what I could find. Some of it went into the grass."

She took a saucer from the shelf above the stove and set it on the table and Ezra came and looked at it. In the saucer lay the silver case of the watch, and the back that had been pried off, bent at one edge, and a little heap of wheels and tiny screws and a spring that had come uncoiled and lay in a loose bright curl like a shaving of tin. Ezra put out one of his big fingers and touched the spring. Then he took his finger away.

"You will have to whip him," Kate said. "I would have done it but I wanted you to do it. It was your father's watch."

---

It is a strange thing about fathers and sons. There is something between them that is never said. A man may live in a house with his son for twenty years and they may eat at the same table and work in the same field, and still there will be a thing between them like a wall of glass. They can see each other through it but they cannot touch. Often the man thinks that some day he will break through. He thinks that some day he will sit down with his son and say a thing that has been lying in him for a long time, a thing about life, about what it is like to be a man and to go on day after day working and eating and sleeping and not knowing why. But the day does not come. The son grows up and goes away to the city or he stays and becomes a man like his father, with big hands and a stooped back, and the thing is never said.

Ezra Pruitt's father had been a farmer in the hill country south of Pickering, a hard silent man who had worked a poor farm with stones in it and had whipped his sons with a harness strap. Ezra remembered the strap. It hung on a nail inside the barn door and when you went into the barn you saw it hanging there. He remembered that his father did not get angry when he whipped. That was the worst of it. His father's face did not change. He took the strap off the nail and did what had to be done and hung the strap back on the nail, and then he went on with his work, forking hay down out of the mow or rubbing down the horses, and he did not speak of it again. Ezra had been afraid of his father all his life. When the old man died Ezra had stood beside the bed and his father had looked up at him and had tried to say something. His lips moved but no words came. Then he had reached out and taken the silver watch from the table beside the bed and put it into Ezra's hand and closed Ezra's fingers over it. That was all. He died that night.

Ezra had thought about it a great deal. He thought that his father had perhaps wanted to say something that went with the watch. He did not know what it was. Sometimes on Sunday when he held the watch to his ear and heard it ticking he had a queer notion that if he listened long enough the watch would tell him what his father had wanted to say.

---

He went out of the kitchen door and across the yard toward the woodshed. It was nearly dark. The sky over the Hern pasture beyond the alley was a pale yellow color and there was one star. Somewhere down the street a woman was calling a dog. "Shep," she called. "Shep. Shep." Her voice went up at the end each time like a question.

The woodshed was a low building with a slanting roof and the door stood open. Ezra stopped in the doorway. At first he could not see anything. Then he saw his son. The boy was sitting on the chopping block in the corner with his legs hanging down. His feet did not reach the floor. He had his hands folded in his lap the way he had been taught to fold them in Sunday school, and he was looking at the door, and when he saw his father standing there he did not move.

Ezra came in and stood in the middle of the shed. The smell of the cut wood was strong. It was a smell he knew from the mill and he did not like it. It made him think of the blood on the sawdust and of Joe Kinsey's face, which had gone white, and of how Joe Kinsey had said over and over, "I'll be all right, boys, I'll be all right," though no one had said that he would not be.

"Your mother told me," Ezra said.

The boy said nothing. He looked at his father. In the dim light his face was a small white spot and his eyes were two dark spots in it.

Ezra did not know how to go on. He had thought on the way across the yard that he would say certain things. He had thought he would say, "That was your grandfather's watch and you had no business touching it." He had thought he would say, "Don't you know a thing like that can't be fixed?" But now he stood there and the words would not come. He put his hands into his pockets and took them out again.

On the wall of the woodshed, on a nail beside the door, there hung an old leather strap. It was not a harness strap. It was a piece of belting that Ezra had brought home from the mill one time to use for something, he did not remember what. It had hung there for a year. Ezra looked at it and then he looked at the boy, and he saw that the boy was looking at it too.

He went and took it down off the nail.

When he had it in his hand he felt a queer thing happen inside him. It was as though his father had come into the woodshed and was standing behind him. He did not turn around but he felt it. He felt the old man standing there with his face that did not change, and he felt his own face becoming still and hard like his father's, and he was afraid. He stood with the strap in his hand and he was more afraid than the boy was.

"Get up," he said. His voice sounded strange to him.

The boy slid down off the chopping block and stood on the floor. He was a thin boy with a big head and his hair stuck up at the back. He was wearing a pair of overalls that Kate had cut down from a pair of Ezra's, and they were too big for him and the straps kept slipping off his shoulders. One strap had slipped off now. He did not push it back up.

"Why did you do it?" Ezra said.

He had not meant to ask that. It was not a thing his father would have asked. His father would not have wanted to know. But Ezra found that he wanted to know. He wanted to know more than he had wanted anything for a long time.

The boy looked at the floor. Then he looked up again. "I wanted to see," he said.

"See what?"

"What made it go."

Ezra stood still. The strap hung down from his hand and the end of it touched the floor. Outside the woman had stopped calling her dog and it was very quiet. A wagon went by in the street, the wheels grinding in the gravel, and then it was quiet again.

"I could hear it," the boy said. He was talking fast now, the way children talk when they have decided to tell everything. "When you hold it. On Sunday. I could hear it going in there, and I thought there was something in there, and I wanted to see it. I thought maybe it was alive. I thought maybe there was a little thing in there, a little bug or something, that made it go. And I opened it and there was all the wheels. There was all little wheels going around. And then I took them out to see what was under them, and it stopped." He stopped talking. Then he said in a low voice, "I couldn't make it go again."

---

Ezra Pruitt stood in the woodshed with the strap in his hand and he did not move for a long time. The boy began to cry, not loudly, but with his mouth shut, so that his chest went in and out and little sounds came through his nose. He stood with his hands at his sides and the strap of his overalls hanging down and he cried, and still his father did not move.

What was in Ezra's mind at that moment it would be hard to tell. He was not a man who could have told it himself. Perhaps he was thinking of his own father, of the hill farm with the stones in it, of the barn door and the strap that hung inside. Perhaps he was thinking of the deathbed and the old man's lips moving and no words coming out. Perhaps he was thinking that he also, when he was a boy, had wanted to know what made things go. He had wanted to know why the creek ran downhill and where it went, and why the crows gathered in the dead tree by the road in the evenings, and what his father thought about when he sat on the porch after supper and looked off at nothing. He had never asked. You did not ask such things in his father's house. And after a while he had stopped wanting to know, and now he worked at the stave mill and when a man's arm was cut he sat by a window and looked out at the street and thought of nothing.

It may be that he was thinking that the watch had stopped and could not be made to go again, and that this was a terrible thing, and that it was also not a terrible thing at all. It may be that all of these thoughts were in him at once, tangled together like the wheels and springs in the saucer on the kitchen table, and that he could not have sorted them out if he had tried.

At last he spoke. "You should not have done it," he said.

"I know," said the boy, crying.

"It was your grandpa's. He gave it to me when he died."

"I know."

"It can't be fixed. Maybe old Banning down at the jewelry store could fix it but I don't guess so. I don't guess it can be fixed."

The boy cried harder. Ezra lifted the strap. He lifted it a little way and held it there. Then he looked at it as though he did not know what it was or how it had come into his hand. He went over and hung it back up on the nail beside the door.

He came back and sat down on the chopping block where the boy had been sitting. His knees came up nearly to his chin. He put his big hands on his knees and looked at them, and then he reached out and took hold of the boy by the shoulders and drew him in close, between his knees. He did it awkwardly. He was not a man who touched people. The boy stood stiff for a moment and then he leaned against his father's chest and cried into the front of his shirt, and Ezra could feel the wet coming through.

"You should not have done it," Ezra said again. He said it very softly. It was as though he were saying something else. "You hear? You don't take things that ain't yours. You don't break things. You hear me?"

"Yes."

"All right then."

He pushed the strap of the boy's overalls back up onto his shoulder. His fingers were clumsy and it took him a long time. Then he sat with his hands on the boy's shoulders and looked over the boy's head at the dark doorway. He wanted to say something more. He felt it there in him, the thing he wanted to say. It was something about the wheels and how they went around and what made them go. It was something about his father and the watch and the old man's lips moving. The boy Harley grew up and went away from Pickering. He went to the city of Cleveland and became a machinist and later he had a shop of his own where he made parts for automobiles. It does not matter what it was.

Harley Pruitt looked at his son and he felt a queer thing happen inside him. It was as though someone had come into the room and was standing behind him. He did not turn around. He remembered the woodshed and the smell of the cut wood, and the strap on the nail, and his father sitting on the chopping block with his knees up nearly to his chin and his big hands on the boy's shoulders. He sat in his kitchen in Cleveland and looked at his own son and he wanted to say the thing too, and the words would not come.

"Come here," he said finally.

Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. “I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. In the town of Lattimer, Ohio, there lived a man named Hal Brodie who kept the feed and seed store on the corner of Main and Duane Streets, across from the hotel. He was a thick slow-moving man of thirty-eight with heavy shoulders and small grey eyes, and in the town he was thought to be a good fellow. In the evening men came into the store and sat on the sacks of bran and talked of the price of clover seed and of the doings of the county fair, and Hal sat behind the counter on a high stool and listened and laughed. He did not talk much himself. When he laughed his shoulders shook and he put his hand over his mouth like a boy laughing in church. "Hal's all right," the men said. "You can't get a rise out of Hal." They did not know that in the night when he lay beside his wife in the house on Elm Street he sometimes lay awake for hours staring at the ceiling and that thoughts went through his mind that would have made them stare at him and wonder.

Hal's wife was named Mary and she had been a school teacher before she married him. She was a small dark woman with a sharp chin and quick hands and she had come to Lattimer from a town in Indiana to teach in the grammar school. For three years she had taught there and had boarded at the house of the Methodist minister, and then one summer evening Hal Brodie had walked home with her from a strawberry festival on the church lawn and after that he walked home with her many times. He did not know how it had happened that they were married. It seemed to him that one day they were walking under the maple trees on Elm Street and that on the next day she was in his house and he was coming home to her at noon to eat his dinner. They had been married eleven years and there were no children.

On an evening in October Hal did not come home to supper. He had closed the store at six as was his custom and had stood for a moment on the sidewalk before the door. The sun had gone down and over the roofs of the stores across the street the sky was red. A farmer's wagon went past, the wheels rattling on the hard road, and a boy sat on the tail of the wagon swinging his legs. Hal did not know why he did not go home. He walked along Main Street past the hotel and past the bank and the hardware store and turned into the Trunion Pike that went out of town past the cemetery and the fair grounds. He walked a long time. When he came to the bridge over Wine Creek, two miles from town, he stopped and leaned on the railing and looked down at the water. It was dark by that time and he could not see the water but he heard it running over the stones. He stood there a long time and then turned and walked back to town.

When Hal came into the kitchen of his house it was after nine o'clock. Mary sat by the table under the lamp with her hands in her lap. The supper dishes were on the table, and his plate with the food on it. The food had grown cold and a skin had formed over the gravy. Mary did not get up when he came in. She looked at him and then she looked at the plate. Hal stood by the door with his hat in his hand. He felt like a boy who has been caught stealing apples and at the same time he felt something else, something hard and stubborn that rose up in him and made him want to laugh. He did not laugh. He hung his hat on the nail by the door and sat down at the table across from his wife.

"Well," Mary said, "you might as well eat it. It's there." Her voice was thin and quiet. Hal looked at the plate and took up his fork and then put it down again. "I'm not hungry," he said. "I went for a walk." Mary laughed. It was not a pleasant laugh. "A walk," she said. "Three hours you walked. I suppose you walked to Cleveland and back." She got up and began to take the dishes from the table and to put them into the pan on the stove. Her back was toward him and he looked at her back, at the narrow shoulders and the knot of dark hair at the back of her head. He thought of the first time he had walked home with her from the strawberry festival and how she had talked all the way of a book she was reading, a book about a man who went to live in the woods alone, and how he had not understood what she was saying and had been ashamed. "She knows a lot," he had thought then. "She's been to the normal school. She can talk." He had been proud that she would walk with him.

Now as he sat by the table he wanted to tell her about the walk. He wanted to tell her about the bridge and the sound of the water running over the stones in the darkness. He did not know why he wanted to tell her. It seemed to him that something had happened to him out there on the bridge, that something had come into his mind that had never been there before, and that if he could only say it to her everything would be different between them. He opened his mouth to speak and then closed it again. The words would not come. He sat looking at the lamp and the moths that flew about the chimney of the lamp, and Mary rattled the dishes in the pan.

"I'll tell you what it is," Mary said suddenly. She turned around from the stove and her face was white and her lips trembled. "I'll tell you what it is. You're tired of me. That's what it is. Eleven years and you're tired of me. Well, I'm tired too. I'm tired of sitting here in this kitchen every night and waiting for you to come home and then when you do come home you sit there like a post and don't say anything. You talk to the men down at the store. I've heard you. Mrs. Wilmot told me she heard you laughing clear across the street. You laugh with them. You never laugh here."

Hal looked at his wife. A strange thing happened in him. He had expected to be angry and he was not angry. He felt only a great tiredness and under the tiredness something that was almost tenderness. He wanted to get up and go to her and put his big hand on her shoulder. He did not do it. "I don't laugh with them," he said slowly. "I just sit there. They talk and I sit there. That's all it is."

Mary came and sat down again at the table. She put her elbows on the table and her chin in her hands and looked at him. Her eyes were bright and hard. "Then what is it?" she asked. "What did you go out walking on the pike for? Who did you see out there?" Hal shook his head. "I didn't see anybody," he said. "I went out to the Wine Creek bridge and stood there. I don't know why I went. I just went."

It is a strange thing about the people of small towns that they live side by side for years and do not know each other. In Lattimer there was a man named Joe Ransom who had been married for thirty years and who one day got up from the dinner table and walked out of his house and was never seen again. His wife sat for a week by the front window watching the street. Afterward she went to live with her sister in Sandusky. When the people of the town talked of Joe Ransom they shook their heads and said he must have gone crazy. Nobody thought that perhaps he had been crazy for thirty years and had only kept it hidden, or that perhaps he had been sane all that time and had at last grown tired of hiding his sanity. Hal Brodie had known Joe Ransom. He had sold him oats for his horse. As he sat in the kitchen with his wife looking at him across the table he thought of Joe Ransom and of how Joe had stood in the store one day with a sack of oats on his shoulder and had looked out of the window at the street and had said, "Hal, did you ever think a man could just walk off?" Hal had laughed. He remembered now that he had laughed and that Joe had looked at him with a queer look and had gone out of the store without saying anything more.

"You're thinking about something," Mary said. "I can see it in your face. You've been thinking about something for a long time. I'm not a fool. I know when a man's thinking." She leaned toward him across the table and her voice grew softer. "Hal," she said, "what is it? Tell me what it is. Is it some woman? Because if it is some woman I'd rather know it. I'd rather know than sit here and wonder."

Hal laughed then. He could not help it. The laugh came up out of him and he put his hand over his mouth as he did in the store. Mary's face grew red and she got up quickly from the table. "Oh, you can laugh," she cried. "You can laugh. That's what you can do." She went to the window and stood looking out into the darkness with her back to him. Her shoulders shook and Hal knew that she was crying. He took his hand away from his mouth and sat looking at her. He was ashamed. "There isn't any woman," he said. "There isn't anybody. I don't know any woman but you."

Mary did not turn around. "Then it's worse," she said in a low voice. "If there was a woman I'd understand. I'd know what to do. I'd hate her and I'd know what to do. But if there isn't anybody—" She stopped and Hal heard her breath catch in her throat. "If there isn't anybody then it's just me. It's just that you're sick of me."

Hal got up from his chair. He went across the kitchen and stood behind his wife. He was a big man and he stood over her like a tree. He wanted to touch her and his hands hung at his sides. "I'll tell you," he said and his voice was husky. "I'll try to tell you. I don't know as I can." He stopped and swallowed. "Out there on the bridge," he said, "I got to thinking. I got to thinking about when I was a boy. There was a time when I was a boy, maybe sixteen, when I thought I'd go somewhere. I don't know where. I used to lie in the hay mow at father's place out on the Medina road and think about it. I thought I'd go west maybe, or to the city. I thought I'd be something. I don't know what. Then father died and there was the store and I just stayed. I've stayed ever since. I didn't think about it. Tonight on the bridge I heard the water running and it came back to me like it was yesterday. I thought, 'Why, I'm thirty-eight years old. Why, I'm thirty-eight.'"

Mary turned around slowly and looked up at him. Her face was wet with tears and in the light of the lamp her face looked old. Hal had never noticed before that there were lines about her mouth. He looked at the lines and something hurt in his breast. "You wanted to go away," she said. "That's it. You wanted to go away and you married me instead." Hal shook his head. "No," he said, "it isn't that. You don't understand. It isn't anything to do with you."

"Everything you do has to do with me," she said fiercely. "Don't you know that? I'm your wife. You can't think anything that hasn't got to do with me." She pushed past him and went back to the table and sat down. She put her face in her hands. "Do you think I didn't want things?" she said through her fingers. "Do you think I came here from Indiana to teach in a school because I wanted to teach in a school? I wanted things too. I read books. I used to think—" She took her hands away from her face and laughed a short bitter laugh. "I used to think I would write books. Imagine that. Me. I used to sit up nights in Mrs. Ellsworth's front room at the minister's house and write things on paper. Then you came walking home with me from the festival and you were so big and quiet and I thought, 'There is a man who is strong. There is a man who doesn't talk foolishness like the others.' I thought you had things in you. I thought you were thinking things all the time. And you were thinking about clover seed."

Hal stood in the middle of the kitchen floor. He did not know what to say. A great confusion came over him. He had not known that his wife had written things on paper. He had never thought of her as wanting anything. It seemed to him that she had always been there in the house, getting the meals and sweeping the floors and sitting in the evening by the lamp reading the Cleveland paper, and that she had been satisfied. He looked at her now as though she were a stranger. "I didn't know that," he said stupidly. "I didn't know you wrote things."

"No," Mary said, "you didn't know. You never asked. In eleven years you never once asked me what I was thinking." She got up and went to the stove and lifted the lid and looked at the fire, and put the lid back. Her hands moved quickly and aimlessly. "I burned them," she said. "The papers. The first winter we were married I burned them in that stove. One night when you were down at the store. I sat here and put them in one at a time and watched them burn. I thought, 'I'm married now. I've got a husband. I don't need them.'"

The two people stood in the kitchen and looked at each other. Outside a dog barked and somewhere down the street a door slammed. The clock on the shelf over the sink ticked loudly. Hal thought that he had never heard the clock tick so loudly. It seemed to him that it was counting something, counting the years, eleven years, thirty-eight years. He wanted to go to his wife and take her in his arms and he wanted at the same time to go out of the house and walk again on the pike in the darkness. The two wants fought in him and he stood still, his big hands opening and closing at his sides.

"Well," Mary said at last, "what are we going to do?" Her voice was flat and tired. Hal looked at the floor. "I don't know," he said. "I don't know as there's anything to do." Mary nodded her head slowly. "No," she said, "I don't suppose there is. You'll go down to the store in the morning and I'll get the breakfast and that's all there is. That's all there's ever going to be." She began to wipe the table with a cloth, rubbing hard at a spot where the gravy had spilled. "You'd better go to bed," she said. "It's late."

Hal did not go to bed. He went to the door and took his hat from the nail. Mary looked up quickly. "Where are you going?" she asked, and her voice was sharp with fear. "I'm just going out to the barn," he said. "I want to see to the horse." There was no need to see to the horse. He had fed and watered the horse at noon and had told the boy who worked for him to bed it down at five. They both knew there was no need. Mary stood with the cloth in her hand and looked at him. "Hal," she said, and then she said nothing more. He stood in the doorway with the darkness behind him and waited for her to speak and she did not speak. After a while he went out and closed the door.

In the barn Hal stood in the darkness beside the horse. He could hear it moving in the stall and smell the warm smell of it and of the hay. He put out his hand and laid it on the horse's neck. The horse turned its head and pushed its nose against his shoulder. Hal stood there a long time.
